That guard is real and **points the wrong way**: it checks rows against the vocabulary, never the vocabulary's several definitions against each other. The direction that had actually drifted was the one nothing watched |
| **Status** | ✅ **DONE 2026-08-02** (no migration — the database was already right; the Java copies were wrong). `common.model.CommitteeTypes` is now the single statement; both DTOs validate against it and yield a 400 naming the field. **Two ratchets, deliberately split:** `CommitteeTypeVocabularyTest` ties every Java copy together in the ordinary suite, and `CommitteeGoldenPathIT` ties Java to `CK_com_type` **against a real database** — with a failure message naming which side is missing what and which failure it will cause. No unit test can make the second assertion, which is the clearest argument for W1-5 existing at all. **Mutation-proven in both directions** |
| **⚠ Not a defect, and worth stating** | The vocabulary has **no `CAB` or `ECAB`**, and that is ADR-017 D-2: *"the CAB is a role, not necessarily a standing committee."* The golden path's first draft tried to constitute a committee of type `CAB`; widening the vocabulary would have made the test pass **by reversing the decision that unblocked the whole change-governance epic**. `CommitteeTypeVocabularyTest#cabIsARoleNotACommitteeType` now pins the absence with the citation |
| **References** | `common.model.CommitteeTypes` · `CommitteeDtos.CommitteeCreateRequest` · `BoardPackDto#audience` · `V154` · `V331` · ADR-017 D-2, D-11 |
| **Lesson** | **A guard that checks data against a vocabulary is not a guard on the vocabulary.** D-11's claim was true and answered a different question — and the reflex fix for the 500 (add `CAB`) would have quietly overturned an owner-ratified decision, so *the first thing to check when a test fails on a vocabulary is whether the vocabulary is right* |


## F2-92 · The tenant write guard broke every insert in production, and nothing could log in

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-92 *(found by the 2026-08-02 prod deploy's own smoke test, not by a report)* |
| **Category** | Availability / a control that disabled the thing it protects |
| **Severity** | ~~**P0.** Production could not authenticate a single user, and no entity could be inserted~~ → ⚠ **P3, corrected 2026-08-06 from the deployed logs.** **One** login failed, **once**, at 14:25:37 on 2026-08-02 — two log lines, one event, `err.log` empty, and no occurrence on any of the other 23 days of WinSW logs. "Every insert" and "a single user" were inferred from one request |
| **Current State** | With `grc.security.tenant-write-guard.enabled=true` — **hardcoded true in `application-prod.yml`, unset and therefore false in dev** — every insert into a table carrying an identity/`ROWVERSION` fails with `SQLServerException: A result set was generated for update.` Measured: `POST /api/auth/login` → **500** `"Unable to record refresh token — please retry."` because `platform.refresh_token` could not be written. Flip the flag off and the same request returns **200**. |
| **Problem** | ~~It is the interceptor being **registered on the session factory** that breaks inserts~~ — ⚠ **refuted 2026-08-03, see Status: dev has run with it registered since 2026-07-26 and inserts fine.** What survives is the narrower half: the interceptor's own logic never ran, because `platform.audit_log` holds **zero `SECURITY_BLOCK` rows, ever** (re-confirmed in both databases). So a defence-in-depth backstop coincided with the platform going down without blocking anything — the *coincidence* is established, the *causation* was inferred and is now disproved |
| **How long it was live, and why nobody knew** | The most recent successful prod login before this was **2026-07-28** — five days. The interceptor is **inert in dev by flag**, and its own javadoc says so out loud: *"a dev-machine HTTP probe exercises the per-service stamp, **never this bean**."* `application-prod.yml`'s own comment adds the condition that was skipped: *"Activate only after the documented staging soak … watch the audit log for any `SECURITY_BLOCK` entries on legitimate flows before relying on it."* Nothing exercised it, so nothing caught it |
| **Ruled out, by measurement rather than reasoning** | Not caused by the 2026-08-02 deploy: `TenantWriteGuardInterceptor`, `TenantWriteGuardConfig`, `RefreshTokenStoreService`, `RefreshToken` and `AuthController` are **byte-identical** between the previous jar and this one (`md5` over the extracted `.class` files), and **none of V337–V344 touches `refresh_token`**. Not schema drift: prod and dev column types, nullability, defaults, identity and `ROWVERSION` are identical, on the **same SQL Server instance and build** (`15.0.2000.5`) with identical `compatibility_level` and every ANSI/isolation database option equal. Not a trigger: `sys.triggers` has exactly one trigger in the database and it is on `socops.forensics_custody_event` |
| **Root Cause** | Prime suspect is Hibernate 6's handling of the deprecated legacy `Interceptor#onSave(...)` hook: implementing it changes the insert strategy so the generated-value read-back is executed through `executeUpdate()`, and SQL Server answers a result set. **Not yet proven** — the proof needs the flag enabled in dev, which is precisely the reproduction nobody has ever run |
| **Business Impact** | The deployed platform was unusable — a 500 on the first screen — for anyone who tried between 07-28 and 08-02. Discovered by our own probe rather than by a customer, but only just |
| 🔑 **THE MITIGATION NEVER TOOK EFFECT (2026-08-06, ADR-017 D-16)** | `external.properties` reaches the app through `spring.config.import` in `application.yml`, and a **profile-specific** document outranks `application.yml` and everything it imports. `application-prod.yml` set `grc.security.tenant-write-guard.enabled: true` **literally**, so the operator's `=false` was outranked and discarded — no error, no warning. **Production booted 2026-08-03 11:02:18 logging `[TenantWriteGuard] interceptor WIRED`**, a line `TenantWriteGuardConfig` emits *only* in the `enabled == true` branch. The guard has been ON continuously since, four days, **zero** occurrences of the error — so the supervised soak this row was waiting for has already run. Root cause of the inert override filed as [[F2-149]] |
| ⚠ **And the diagnosis is refuted by the same logs** | Refresh-token rows were written at **11:32:13 and 11:34:17 on 08-02**, three hours before the failure, with the flag already true. The guard had been on for days *with working logins*. What changed at 14:23 was a **deploy that applied V337–V344 in-process**, not the flag. So *“the tenant write guard broke every insert”* cannot be right as stated |
| ⚠ **“Verified working afterwards” is not in the data** | This row records the mitigation as verified with *“login 200 … refresh-token rows written again”*. Production's `platform.refresh_token` has **no row after 2026-08-02 11:34:17** — before the mitigation was written at 14:33. **Nobody has logged into production since**, so the login path is unverified since the incident: not demonstrated broken, not demonstrated working. Smoke-test it at the next restart |
| **What the stack trace narrows it to** | Read from the log for the first time on 2026-08-06: `GetGeneratedKeysDelegate.performMutation` → `ResultSetReturnImpl.executeUpdate` → the driver throwing `A result set was generated for update.` with **SQL Error 0, SQLState null** — thrown by the **JDBC driver**, not by SQL Server. Both databases were re-diffed and are identical on every dimension that can produce a result set: 1 trigger each (same table, unrelated), `refresh_token` 18 columns identical, no computed columns, no change tracking, no temporal table, identical compat level / ANSI options / RCSI. **Still not root-caused, and this row no longer claims to be** |
| **Interim disposition** | ⚠ **Flag set to `false` in `D:\Deployment\tss-grc\app\external.properties`** — ⚠ **which did nothing; see the row above.** with a long operator note giving this finding's id and the re-enable condition. Prod verified working afterwards: login 200, five authenticated reads 200, refresh-token rows written again. Per-service `setOrganisationId(TenantContext.getCurrentTenant())` stamps remain the **primary** tenant control; this bean is only the backstop, and a backstop that prevents all writes protects nothing |
| **Recommendation** | (1) **Enable the flag in dev** and reproduce — that single missing step is the finding's real root cause and it is one line of config. (2) Migrate the hook to the non-deprecated Hibernate 6 API (`onPersist`/an event listener) and re-verify inserts with generated values. (3) Add an integration test with the guard **on**, in the `it` profile W1-5 just created — `CommitteeGoldenPathIT` writes committees, meetings, votes and changes, so it is already the right harness. (4) Only then re-enable in prod |
| **Effort** | **S** to reproduce and probably S to fix; the test is the durable part |
| **Status** | ⬜ **Still open — P0, mitigated. ⚠ ROOT CAUSE CORRECTED 2026-08-03 — the one recorded here is refuted.** The fix plan's own first step (*enable the flag in dev and reproduce*) was carried out and **the defect does not reproduce.** (1) The flag has been `enabled: true` in `application-dev.yml` since `695c907c` — **2026-07-26, seven days before this finding was filed** — contradicting the premise that it was unset in dev. (2) The dev backend logs `[TenantWriteGuard] interceptor WIRED` on every boot and `platform.refresh_token` holds **2,075 rows, the newest written that morning**. (3) `TenantWriteGuardInterceptor` and `TenantWriteGuardConfig` are **byte-identical between the deployed commit `473da706` and HEAD**. (4) Both databases sit on the same SQL Server instance and match on schema, compatibility level 150, collation, snapshot options, the single trigger in either database (on an unrelated table), and `refresh_token`'s exact `IDENTITY`+`ROWVERSION` shape. Now **pinned by `TenantWriteGuardOnIT`** (4 tests, `it` profile, 21 s): the real application boots with the flag ON, logs in, writes the refresh-token row, completes an identity insert, and still refuses a cross-tenant one. **The profile is now eliminated too (2026-08-03, second pass).** Booted locally on the **`prod` profile** with the guard explicitly ON, SSL and Flyway off, against the dev database: `[TenantWriteGuard] interceptor WIRED`, `POST /api/auth/login` → **200**, and `platform.refresh_token` went **2100 → 2101**. So the code, the schema, the database options *and the profile* all fail to reproduce it. **What is left is the deployed runtime itself** — Flyway-at-startup (the one variable deliberately excluded, since running it against dev would migrate a Python-bootstrapped schema), the named-instance JDBC URL (`localhost\SQLEXPRESS` vs `localhost:1433`), the WinSW service account, and the rest of `external.properties`. Narrowing further needs the flag switched back on in production under supervision, which is an operator decision and not a test's. ⚠ *Two incidental notes for whoever does it: the prod profile refuses to boot without an SSL keystore (`server.ssl.*`, supplied by `external.properties` on the server) and pins **both** `server.port` 8090 and the management port — a local prod-profile boot must override both or it collides with the live service.* Flag stays `false` in prod meanwhile, so **production still has no Hibernate-level cross-tenant backstop**; the per-service `setOrganisationId` stamps remain the only control |
| **References** | `TenantWriteGuardInterceptor#onSave`/`#decideInsert` · `TenantWriteGuardConfig` · `application-prod.yml` `grc.security.tenant-write-guard.enabled` · `RefreshTokenStoreService#recordIssuance` · `docs/security/MASS_ASSIGNMENT_DEFENSE.md` · [[F2-18]] |
| **Lesson (2026-08-03)** | **A root cause that was never reproduced is a hypothesis wearing a conclusion's clothes — and this one was load-bearing.** Believed, it says a P0 control is inherently unsafe and must stay off forever. The finding even *named* the missing step — "enable the flag in DEV and reproduce — that missing step **is** the root cause" — and then wrote a causal sentence as though the step had been taken. Worse, the environment claim it rested on ("unset in dev") was **already false in the repository**, one `git log` away, when it was written. **If a fix plan says "reproduce it first", the causal sentence waits.** |
| **Lesson** | **A control that is off in dev and on in prod is not tested — it is deployed and hoped for.** This is the same shape as F2-62's dead flag and A17-D2's fail-open WARN, with the polarity reversed: instead of a control that did nothing, a control that did far too much. Both were invisible for the same reason — *the only environment that runs it is the one nobody probes.* Its javadoc named the gap ("never this bean") and its config named the missing precondition ("only after the documented staging soak"); **two accurate warnings, written by us, consumed by nobody** |


## F2-156 · The attachment registry mirrors each record's read guard, and two entries kept naming roles after their parents stopped

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-156 *(measured 2026-08-07 by the scan [[F2-52]] built to close its own documented blind spot)* |
| **Category** | Authorisation / **a mirror that drifted from what it mirrors** — and the drift direction refuses legitimate holders rather than admitting strangers, so nothing about it looks like a security bug from outside |
| **Severity** | **P2 High.** Not disclosure: the failure is a **403 on your own record's files**. `attachment/AttachmentAccessPolicy` (SCR-004) makes an attachment exactly as confidential as its parent by copying the parent's read guard, so where the parent authorises by role it holds a Java role list. When a parent is converted to `hasPermission`, every permission holder who is not also on the stale list loses the files while keeping the record |
| **Provenance** | Not sought. [[F2-52]]'s ratchet javadoc had already written the shape down — `TPRM_LEAD` "in a Java role `Set` that no `@PreAuthorize` scan sees", and "the ghost count falling is **not** evidence the name is gone from the authorisation surface" — and nobody built the scan for two slices. The prediction came true verbatim |
| **Current State** | ✔ **FIXED 2026-08-07** in the same commit as V373, both entries moved to the parent's permission. Measured before: `IA_ENGAGEMENT` listed **11** role names while `IaController` had been `hasPermission('AUDIT','READ')` since F2-05 — **4** of the 11 (`CHIEF_AUDIT_EXECUTIVE`, `AUDIT_DIRECTOR`, `INTERNAL_AUDITOR_LEAD`, `AUDIT_COMMITTEE_MEMBER`) matched no row in `iam.roles` at all, and **5** roles holding `AUDIT:READ` were unnamed, so `compliance` and `viewer` were refused. `VENDOR_BCP_CAMPAIGN` named `TPRM_LEAD` while `VendorBcpCampaignController` had become `hasPermission('TPRM','READ')` — **17** roles hold that permission and **13** were unnamed, affecting `auditor`, `compliance`, `so_officer` and `viewer`. Live-proven 200 for the previously-refused holders and **403 for `ranalyst`**, which holds neither permission |
| **Why it survived two conversions** | ⚠ **The instruction existed and was not enforced.** The class's own `FRAUD_CASE` comment says an entry "has to move WITH the parent, not later", and spells out the exact consequence. Two converting slices (F2-05 on `audit_lc`, F2-145(e) on `tprm`) read past it. `RoleNameSurfaceRatchetTest.anEntryDoesNotNameRolesWhenItsParentIsPermissionGuarded` now pins the four converted entity types by name and fails the build; mutation-proven by reverting each entry |
| **Recommendation** | The remaining role-list entries mirror parents that are *still* role-guarded, which is correct. When F2-05 converts one of those modules, the registry entry moves in the same commit — the test names the types it knows about, so extend it there rather than trusting the note |

## F2-157 · The user-admin role picker offered seven roles, four of which do not exist, out of sixty-nine that do

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-157 *(measured 2026-08-07 while sweeping [[F2-52]]'s ghost names across every surface that names one)* |
| **Category** | Provisioning / **a hardcoded option list standing in for the role catalogue** — the ghost-role defect on the one surface an administrator actually operates |
| **Severity** | **P3 Medium.** Wrong in both directions at once. Picking `PRIVACY_OFFICER`, `COMPLIANCE_LEAD`, `BCM_COORDINATOR` or `CYBER_ANALYST` provisions a user with a role no guard anywhere names — the assignment appears to succeed and grants nothing; and with 7 options against **69** active roles, `CISO`, `DPO`, `SUPPLIER_MANAGER` and the newly seated `CRO` could not be granted from the admin screen at all |
| **Provenance** | Not sought. Grepping the eight ghost names across the frontend as well as the backend, on the principle that a name absent from `iam.roles` is worth finding wherever it is written |
| **Current State** | ✔ **FIXED 2026-08-07.** `AdminPage.tsx` builds the options from `adminApi.roles()` — already loaded on that page for the Roles tab — filtered to active roles and labelled with `displayNameEn`. The fallback is deliberately **empty**: a picker that invents options is worse than one that is briefly empty, because the invented choice fails silently at the far end. ⚠ The same edit removed `roles.length \|\| ROLE_OPTIONS.length` from the Roles KPI, a count that could not read zero and reported the fictional seven when the server returned nothing — F2-42's fabricated-aggregate shape, one tile over |
| **Recommendation** | Not every hardcoded vocabulary in the SPA is wrong, but one shadowing a server-side catalogue is. No ratchet is proposed here: `tss-grc-ui-v2` has no live role catalogue to check against at build time, and inventing a pinned copy in the frontend would create the third copy of `iam.roles` in this repository |

## F2-158 · The only endpoint in Role Management answered 500 for every caller, and a mock fallback made that look like success

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-158 *(measured 2026-08-07, three edits into [[F2-157]] — the fix made the page depend on this call for the first time)* |
| **Category** | Correctness / **a handler returning a JPA entity with a lazy association**, plus the frontend fallback that concealed it |
| **Severity** | **P2 High.** `GET /api/v1/admin/roles` is the whole of the Role Management API and it had **never worked**, in dev or in production: it returned `List<Role>`, whose `permissions` is a `@ManyToMany`, so Jackson serialised after the transaction closed and every call ended `LazyInitializationException` → `HttpMessageNotWritableException` → **500**. Landmine 9 in `CLAUDE.md` verbatim — *"lazy-collection entities 500 outside the session — return DTOs"* — sitting in the codebase the landmine list describes |
| **Provenance** | Not sought, and it could not have been found by reading either artefact alone. [[F2-157]] repointed `AdminPage.tsx`'s role dropdown from a hardcoded seven to `adminApi.roles()`; the very next live check returned 500 |
| **Current State** | ✔ **FIXED 2026-08-07.** `RoleController.list` returns a `RoleSummary` record — exactly the six fields `AdminRoleDto` declares, permissions deliberately excluded (that is the Access Governance console's job, and including them would restore the collection that caused the failure). Live-verified through the Vite proxy: **HTTP 200, 69 roles**, and browser-verified — the picker now renders **69 options** where it rendered 7, containing `CIO`, `CRO`, `PRIVACY_MANAGER` and **none** of the four fictional names |
| **🔑 Why it survived, which is the transferable part** | ⚠ **The client-side fallback was load-bearing.** `AdminPage.tsx` wired mock `ADMIN_ROLES` into *all three* failure paths — unauthenticated, empty response, and `.catch` — so the Roles tab always rendered plausible rows and the dropdown always had options. **A workaround indistinguishable from success is why nobody filed the 500**, and the hardcoded dropdown that [[F2-157]] treats as the defect was in fact a *symptom*: someone hit the broken endpoint once and routed around it. Same shape as [[F2-42]]'s fabricated board-pack aggregate and [[F2-38]]'s client-side directory — this is the third time in this programme that a frontend fallback was found to be hiding a server-side failure rather than tolerating one. ⚠ Note also what the fix had to be careful about: reading the picker off `roles` closed nothing while the mock fallback populated it, so the corrected page tracks **provenance** (`rolesAreReal`) and offers an **empty** picker rather than a fictional one |
| **Instrument** | `LazyEntitySerialisationInvariantTest` — reflection over all **255** `@RestController` classes and **2,210** handlers: no handler may return a JPA entity that owns a `@OneToMany`/`@ManyToMany` or a `LAZY` to-one. ⚠ **Deliberately an invariant, not a ratchet**, and the measurement is why: **883** handlers return *some* entity, but only **8 of 407** entities own such an association (`Role`, `User`, `IntakeRecord`, `IntakeEvent`, `TreatmentPlan`, `TreatmentAction`, `BiaQuantitative`, `BiaQuantitativeLossLine`), and **0** of the 883 return one of the 8 now. A ceiling at 883 would have tolerated the next `Role` while generating 883 units of noise about handlers that work. The test also asserts its own **detector** still recognises ≥ 5 lazy entities, because a detector that stopped working would pass this test on a platform full of 500s |
| **Recommendation** | The remaining 883 entity-returning handlers are not swept: returning an entity with no collections is unfashionable, not broken, and a sweep of that size is its own programme. If one of the 8 lazy entities gains a handler, the invariant refuses it. ⚠ Do **not** resolve such a refusal by making the association `EAGER` — that trades a 500 for an unbounded join on every read; in this case it would have fetched the whole permission catalogue per role row |

## F2-159 · The entity-ownership check four findings were blocked on already existed — as a stub that silently ignored the record id

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-159 *(measured 2026-08-07 while looking for the mechanism [[F2-52]] and [[F2-145]] both recorded as missing)* |
| **Category** | Authorisation / **a decoy extension point** — the standard Spring hook for per-record permission checks, implemented to answer a different question and tested as if that were correct |
| **Severity** | **P2 High, latent.** `ModulePermissionEvaluator`'s four-argument `PermissionEvaluator` overload — the one that exists precisely to ask *"may this caller act on THIS record?"* — was `return hasPermission(authentication, targetType, permission)`, i.e. it **discarded `targetId`**. A developer writing the idiomatic `hasPermission(#id, 'RISK', 'READ')` would have got "may I read risks?" answered in place of "may I read THIS risk?" — a cross-record hole that compiles, reads correctly and passes review. ⚠ Measured: **no guard in the platform used the four-argument form**, so nothing was exposed. The trap was unsprung, not absent |
| **Provenance** | Not sought. Four items (**[[F2-52]]**'s `MODEL_OWNER` 14 sites and `FACILITATOR` 18, **F2-145(c)**, **F2-145(d)**) each recorded their remedy as *blocked on an ownership/SpEL mechanism that does not exist*. It existed. **Every one of those four entries was written without opening the evaluator** — including three of mine |
| **🔑 Why it survived: a test asserted it** | The replaced test was named `the_targetId_overload_delegates_to_the_module_level_check` and asserted `hasPermission(auth, 42L, "EVIDENCE", "WRITE")` is **true** for a holder of `EVIDENCE_WRITE` — pinning, as intended behaviour, that the id is discarded. So this was not an undocumented oversight: **a green test with a reassuring name made it look like a design decision**, and anyone who questioned the overload would have found the suite agreeing with it. 🔑 **A test can lock in a defect, and it is hardest to see when it describes what the code does accurately** — that test was not wrong about the behaviour, it was wrong about the behaviour being correct, and no suite can tell those apart |
| **Current State** | ✔ **FIXED 2026-08-07** and consumed by its first caller in the same commit. `EntityOwnershipResolver` (SPI) + `EntityOwnershipRegistry` + `MlModelOwnershipResolver`; the overload now resolves ownership and **refuses** an unregistered target type or a relation other than `OWNER` rather than falling through to the module check. `MODEL_OWNER` left [[F2-52]]'s ghost list by the third route — not seated (looser than the column), not dropped (loses the intent), not module-converted (would admit every `AI:READ` holder to every model) — but **bound to `ml_model.model_owner_user_id`**. Ghost names **5 → 4**, second surface **4 → 3**, pure role sites **430 → 425** |
| **What it measurably fixed** | Dev's 25 models are owned by `admin` (19, irrelevant — `PLATFORM_ADMIN` bypasses) and **`ranalyst` (6)**. `ranalyst` holds `AI:READ` **and** `AI:WRITE` and could open **none** of the models it owns, because the guard asks who you are and not what you may do — F2-05's thesis in one persona. Live-proven: **200 on its six, 403 on four of the nineteen it does not own**, same user, same token. That per-record property is exactly what seating a `MODEL_OWNER` role could never have given, which is ADR-017 D-14's whole argument |
| **⚠ Five endpoints deliberately NOT bound, and this is the part most likely to be "simplified"** | All ten `/{externalId}` routes *could* take the ownership leg. Five must not: `transition` and `decommission` move the lifecycle stage, `MlModelAuditController#record` files the fairness/bias/AIA result, and the drift `record`/`acknowledge` are the drift verdict. Each is a **judgement about the model, and the owner is its subject** — admitting them is V367's self-review defect (the Sharia auditor approving what it audits) transplanted into AI governance. *"It has an id, so bind it"* is a one-word change no other test would notice, so `MlModelOwnershipGuardTest` asserts the boundary **in both directions, by name** — per [[F2-156]], an instruction with no enforcement gets read past |
| **⚠ My own coverage gap, found by mutation not by review** | The first mutation run left **two survivors**: dropping the resolver's `organisationId` filter (a cross-tenant ownership check) and replacing the owner comparison with a null check (ownership becomes *existence*) both kept the suite **green**. Cause: the mechanism was tested against a **fake** resolver and the guard shape was tested by reflection, so the one real implementation was unasserted — only the live probe would have caught it. 🔑 **Testing the abstraction is not testing the implementation, and a well-behaved fake makes that gap invisible.** `MlModelOwnershipResolverTest` closes it, including a `verify` that the tenant reaches the *query* rather than a post-filter |
| **Filed, not fixed** | `AttachmentAccessPolicy` cannot express ownership — `ParentGuard` speaks modules, roles and exact authorities, so a model owner opens their model and is still refused its attachments. Recorded at the site rather than papered over; inventing an entity-bound `ParentGuard` kind for one entry is how [[F2-156]]'s drift began. Whether the owner may acknowledge drift or transition their own model is a **policy** decision for the owner |
| **Recommendation** | `FACILITATOR` (18 sites) is the same shape and now needs only a second resolver: `bcm.exercise_run.facilitator_user_id` is populated 4/4. The three `AUDIT_*` committee-seat names need a **different** question — seat membership, not record ownership — so they stay out. ⚠ When adding a resolver, add its `MlModelOwnershipResolverTest` equivalent: the registry test will not catch a broken implementation |

## F2-160 · The unit suite failed on Saturdays, and nothing in the repository said the clock was an input

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-160 *(hit 2026-08-08 when the date rolled over mid-session and a green suite went red with no code change)* |
| **Category** | Test integrity / **an untracked input** — the wall clock, in a platform whose SLAs are counted in Saudi business days |
| **Severity** | **P3 Medium**, and the severity is about trust rather than function: the product code is correct. A suite that passes six days a week and fails on the seventh **spends the failure budget of a real defect** and trains the next reader to re-run rather than investigate. It also lands on the deployed CI every Friday and Saturday |
| **Provenance** | Not sought, and not findable by reading. `mvn -o clean package` was green at 23:5x on 2026-08-07 and red at 00:00 on 2026-08-08 with an unchanged tree. ⚠ I could have attributed it to my own in-flight slice; instead the two classes were run in a **clean `git worktree` at HEAD**, where they failed identically. **"Unrelated to my change" is a claim that needs the same proof as any other** |
| **Current State** | ✔ **FIXED 2026-08-08.** Two tests, two different defects, both weekday-sensitive: <ul><li>`EmergencyRatificationSlaSchedulerTest` built every fixture from `LocalDateTime.now()` and asserted *"9 calendar days past the deadline is at least 6 Saudi business days"*. From a Saturday, a 9-day window contains **two** Fridays and **two** Saturdays, so only **5** business days have elapsed. Now anchored to a fixed Sunday (`2026-03-15`), keeping the assertion at ≥ 6.</li><li>`EmergencyRatificationTest.implementationStartsTheClockAtFiveSaudiBusinessDays` asserted `dueAt >= implementationStarted.plusDays(6)` under the comment *"5 business days spans at least 7 calendar days once the weekend is skipped"*. True only from a **working-day** start: the service stamps `implementationStarted = now()`, and from Saturday 8 Aug five business days lands Thursday 13 Aug — **+5**, not +7. Now asserts the **business-day distance is exactly 5**, plus the original ≥ +7 claim guarded by the condition that makes it true.</li></ul> |
| **⚠ Why loosening the assertion was rejected** | `>= 6` → `>= 5` and `plusDays(6)` → `plusDays(4)` would both have gone green in one character. That **weakens a real control check to accommodate a test-design flaw** — the ≥ 6 figure is what distinguishes a business-day SLA from a calendar-day one, which is the entire point of the Saudi workday calendar. The clock had to become deterministic instead. 🔑 **When a date-dependent test fails, the fix is to remove the dependence, not to widen the band until today fits.** |
| **⚠ And the business-day assertion is not circular** | The service computes `dueAt` with the same `SaudiWorkdayUtil`, so asserting the business-day distance looks tautological. It is not: a calendar-day implementation (`start.plusDays(5)`) lands on the Friday from a Sunday start, and `businessDaysBetween` would then read **4**. The sibling assertion that the deadline never falls on a Friday or Saturday catches it too |
| **Recommendation** | No ratchet is proposed, because the honest instrument is a build that runs on every weekday and this repository's CI does not (see [[F2-36]]: `on:` is still push-to-master only). ⚠ `CLAUDE.md` calls the unit suite *"hermetic: needs no database and no secrets"* — accurate about both, and silent about the clock. That sentence now says so. Any new test doing date arithmetic should take a fixed reference instant; `LocalDateTime.now()` in a fixture is the smell |

## F2-163 · Five detail screens with no way in — and a headline of "eighteen" that was my own scan's blind spot

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-163 *(filed 2026-08-08 delivering [[F2-07a]]'s route matrix; **corrected and closed the same day**)* |
| **Module** | frontend — `App.tsx` route table vs every navigation surface |
| **Severity** | **P2** — built, API-wired, reachable by nobody. Two of the five are the *governed* path for an ERM control, and three are screens [[F2-161]] hardened two days earlier |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-08.** All 5 linked; `routeDetailReachability.test.ts` inverted from a ceiling to an **invariant** (`UNREACHABLE_BY_DESIGN` is empty and no detail route may be unreachable); `ExerciseRuntimeReachability.test.tsx` added — **9 tests, the first this runtime has ever had** |
| **⚠⚠ THE FILED FIGURE WAS 18 AND 13 OF THOSE WERE FALSE POSITIVES OF THE INSTRUMENT THAT PRODUCED IT** | The gate matched `to:`/`href:`/`route:`/`path:`/`to=`/`href=`/`navigate(` and was blind to **`rowHref`** — `DataTable`'s per-row navigation prop, whose value is a *function returning a path* (`rowHref={r => \`/ai/models/${r.externalId}\`}`), rendered as `onClick → navigate(href)` plus an Enter handler. **34 sites, and it is THE canonical way this codebase links a list to its detail screen.** Thirteen of the eighteen were linked all along, from exactly the list the finding said should link them. Four register pages also destructure `useNavigate()` as `nav`, which no `navigate\(` pattern sees. Corrected population: **5** |
| **🔑🔑 The correction is the same error as the finding it corrects, one slice later** | F2-07 was filed P1 on a figure ~7× too large because navigation here has several surfaces and it counted **one**. F2-07a said so, then counted **three** and missed the fourth — the dominant one for detail screens. ⚙ **A plausible answer that confirms the story you are already telling is where measurement stops.** All 18 were `:param` routes and the narrative was tidy, so the 13 counter-examples were never opened one at a time. **Eighteen is a small enough population to adjudicate by hand, and it was not.** The correction came from opening the first list page the finding accused, before writing a link into it |
| **⚙ What could NOT have caught it — this bounds two techniques** | The gate's non-vacuity check passed (it saw 300+ link targets, so "matches nothing" was excluded). Mutation testing the gate passed **7/7**. **Mutation proves a gate notices changes to itself; it cannot prove the gate's definition matches the world.** Nor could the second-implementation rule as then applied: both implementations shared the same *definition*, so agreement was worthless. Defences now: a **witness assertion** per fragile pattern (a route reachable only via `rowHref`, one only via a `nav()` alias — losing either pattern fails the run instead of inflating the count) and two implementations with *deliberately different* definitions, cross-checked at **5 = 5** |
| **🔑 A THIRD instrument already held the evidence, in an allow-list** | `apiClientReachability.test.ts` ([[F2-68]](c)) listed `lib/exerciseRuntime.ts#listRunsForExercise` and `#startRun` under `KNOWN_UNREACHED`. Read out loud that is *"no screen lists or starts an exercise run"* — the same defect, from the API side, sitting as a **tolerated entry**. It fired on this slice as progress. ⚙ **A tolerated entry in one instrument's allow-list can be the proof another instrument needs**; when an export sits on such a list, ask what the USER cannot do, not merely which function is unused |
| **🔴 The three BCM runtime screens — the real half, and the cross-instrument blind spot** | `/bcm/exercises/run/:runId/{facilitate,observe,participate}` — **1,862 lines** — had **no textual reference anywhere in `src/`**, not merely no link. [[F2-161]] converted their guard on 2026-08-06 so a facilitator could drive their own run instead of only a platform administrator. **The authorisation was corrected on three screens that had no entry point.** ⚠ And a real run had existed in dev since **2026-06-27** (`RUN-2026-0004`, facilitator user 2, SCHEDULED): live-probed 200 on both `getRun` and `observer-dashboard`, so the screens worked — nobody could open them. Fixed by `ExerciseRunsPage` (`/bcm/exercises/:exerciseId/runs`), linked from the exercise row in `/bcm?tab=exercises` |
| **🔴 The two ERM wizards were worse than unreachable — they were the *governed* path** | `/workflows/erm/risk-{treatment,acceptance}/:riskId` are the **only** UI routes that write a canonical `risk_lc.treatment_plans` row (which `RiskService.close` requires before a HIGH or over-appetite risk may close) and a formal, time-boxed, CRO-approved acceptance. **Unbound, both wizards save a generic inbox draft and toast *"open from a risk to record it"* — which nothing in the UI let the user do.** Both are now launched from `RiskDetailPage`. ⚠ Making them reachable is what exposed **[[F2-164]]**: the *reachable* `Accept` button on that same page bypasses the control the newly-reachable wizard satisfies |
| **Business Impact** | Before: an exercise could be scheduled but never run from the UI; a HIGH risk could not be given the treatment plan its own close error demanded. After: both paths are one click from the record that owns them |
| **Fix** | `ExerciseRunsPage` (new, 190 lines — run list, three per-run console links, start-a-run, **no mock fallback**, 403 surfaced verbatim) · route + exercise-row link · two governed-path buttons on `RiskDetailPage` with titles saying what each writes · gate corrected and inverted to an invariant · generator corrected with witness assertions · `UX/ROUTE_RECONCILIATION.md` regenerated (§1 records six passes and that pass 4 shipped wrong; §2a the five; §2b the thirteen) |
| **Verification** | FE **388/388** in 41 files (+9), `tsc` clean, `vite build` clean, census drift **0** (`fe_pages` 352→**353**, `fe_routes` 329→**330** — the first route added since CE-13, and pages/routes move together, which is what a real new screen looks like). Live: `/bcm/exercises` 200 · `by-exercise/3` 200 with 1 run · same read as `ranalyst` **403** (the branch the page renders) · `/risk-lc/treatment-plans?riskId=1` 200 with `TP-2026-001` · **51 risks, 8 open HIGH+, `risk 21` HIGH with 0 plans** |
| **Effort** | S — as filed, and the correction cost more than the fix |
| **Lesson** | 🔑 **A filter that makes an instrument's answer clean is where the next defect hides** — *"legitimately off-nav"* was sound for a **sidebar** audit and unsound for a **reachability** audit. 🔑🔑 And the harder one: **an instrument's own blind spot is indistinguishable from a finding.** The wrong number reached a register row, a plan row, a CI gate and a memory file before a human-scale check — open the first file you are about to accuse — caught it. Adjudicate a population you can count on your fingers; never let a tidy narrative stand in for that |

## F2-164 · The mandatory-treatment gate had a one-click bypass at WRITE level, and the bypass was permanent

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-164 *(filed 2026-08-08 while fixing [[F2-163]] — making the governed path reachable is what exposed that the reachable path was ungoverned; fixed the same day)* |
| **Module** | `risk` — `RiskController#accept` / `RiskService.close` / `RiskAcceptanceService` |
| **Category** | Authorisation + control integrity. **Not** a navigation defect: F2-163 was the navigation defect, and this is what it uncovered |
| **Severity** | **P2 High.** ERM's headline control — *a HIGH/VERY_HIGH/CRITICAL or over-appetite risk may only close once it carries a live treatment plan* — was bypassable by any holder of `RISK:WRITE` in one click, and the bypass could not expire. ⚠ Deliberately **not** filed P1: the bypass left a state change and an audit-ledger entry, so this was under-governance rather than an invisible hole |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-08.** Endpoint retired, exemption rebuilt on the record, approval surface built, three guards + 17 tests, live-probed end to end |
| **The three facts, each read from the code** | 1. `RiskService.close` refused a HIGH/over-appetite risk unless `treatmentPlanRepository.existsBy…(org, id, status ≠ 'REJECTED')` — a row in **`risk_lc.treatment_plans`** — **or the risk was already `ACCEPTED`**, which was exempt.<br>2. `POST /api/v1/risk/risks/{id}/accept` was `@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('RISK','WRITE')")` calling `doTransition(id,"ACCEPTED",{"OPEN","UNDER_REVIEW"})` — **a bare status flip with no justification, no compensating controls, no expiry and no sign-off**.<br>3. The *designed* path is `POST /risks/{riskId}/acceptances` (`RISK:WRITE`) then `POST /acceptances/{id}/approve` (**`RISK:APPROVE`**), and it is the approval that flips the risk, *"the acceptance record is the authority"* |
| **🔑 So `RISK:WRITE` reached an outcome the design reserves for `RISK:APPROVE`** | Both paths landed on the same `status='ACCEPTED'`, and only one of them asked an approver. The close gate then treated that status as proof of *"the documented, approval-gated decision to retain the risk"* — its own comment's words — when the reachable route documented and gated nothing |
| **⚠ And the bypass was PERMANENT, which is the part a reviewer would miss** | `RiskAcceptanceService.expireSweep()` reopens risks via `findByStatusAndExpiresAtLessThan("APPROVED", today)` — it iterates **acceptance records**. A risk flipped by the bare endpoint had **no acceptance record at all**, so the sweep could never see it. The class comment states *"an acceptance can never silently outlive its expiry"*; that was true of acceptances, and the bare endpoint produced an ACCEPTED risk with **no acceptance**, which outlived everything |
| **🔴🔴 What the fix slice found that the finding had no way to know** | **The governed path could not be completed.** `riskAcceptanceApi` has five methods; exactly **one** had a caller anywhere in `src/` — `create`, from the wizard F2-163 had just made reachable. `approve`, `reject`, `revoke` and even `listForRisk` had **none**. So an acceptance could be raised and then never approved — and *approval is what flips the risk to ACCEPTED*. **The reason the ungoverned one-click flip was load-bearing is that it was the only path that worked**, and this finding's own recommendation ("retire it in favour of the E-A flow whose approve step already flips the status") would, taken literally, have removed the platform's only way to accept a risk. ⚠ Third occurrence in this programme of a recommendation that assumed a reachable path |
| **⚠ F2-68(c) could not see it, and the reason generalises** | The unused-export scan resolves at the granularity of the exported **object**. `riskAcceptanceApi` had a caller, so it counted as reached, and **four dead methods hid inside a live export**. 🔑 **An instrument's granularity is its blind spot** — the identical shape as [[F2-163]], where a per-`<Link>` route scan could not see a `rowHref` navigation surface. A per-method check is now pinned for this client specifically; generalising the scan is filed as [[F2-165]] |
| **⚠⚠ And retiring the bypass would have SILENCED a detective control** | V132 seeds an F8 automation rule on `RISK_TRANSITIONED` with `{"status":"ACCEPTED","previousStatus":"OPEN"}` — the SAMA §10.4 flag for *accepting a risk without formal review*. The governed `approve()` set the status with a bare `setRiskStatus()`: **no `RISK_TRANSITIONED` event and no `TRANSITION` audit row**. So that rule's only possible trigger was the **bypass it exists to flag**, and the risk's own activity timeline showed nothing for a governed acceptance. 🔑 **The governance rule that watches for the ungoverned action was fed exclusively by the ungoverned action** — deleting the endpoint alone would have read as a pure security improvement while turning the alarm off. `approve()` now routes through `doTransition`, so either door emits |
| **The fix, in five parts** | **(a)** `close`'s exemption reads a **live formal acceptance** — `existsByOrganisationIdAndRiskIdAndStatusAndExpiresAtGreaterThanEqual(org, id, "APPROVED", today)`. The time-box is in the query, not left to the sweep's punctuality: the gate fails closed.<br>**(b)** `POST /risks/{id}/accept` and `RiskService.accept` are **gone**; `acceptOnApprovedAcceptance` replaces them, reachable only from `RiskAcceptanceService.approve`, and it goes through `doTransition` so the flip is audited and emitted.<br>**(c)** The refusal message names the store the gate **reads**: *"draft an approved treatment PLAN (Draft treatment plan; the simple entries on the Treatments tab are not the same record)"*.<br>**(d)** `RiskAcceptancesPanel` — the approval surface. Lists acceptances, approves (prompting for Board sign-off when the server will require it), rejects, revokes; flags the live time-box, because that is what the gate keys on. No mock fallback; a 403 is surfaced verbatim.<br>**(e)** Both bare-accept buttons (`RiskDetailPage`, `RiskRegisterPage`) now open the acceptance wizard |
| **⚠ The regression the LIVE PROBE caught and no unit test would have** | Routing the flip through `doTransition` imposed the state machine on it — and the retired `accept()` allowed only `{OPEN, UNDER_REVIEW}`, while the old governed flip was a bare `save()` with **no state guard at all**. So approving an acceptance for a `MITIGATING` risk had worked, and after the change answered **400 *"Risk must be in [OPEN, UNDER_REVIEW]"*** — for a request `request()` had happily created, since it refuses only CLOSED. **A governed path you can enter and cannot finish: the exact defect class this finding exists to remove, re-created by its own fix.** Now one constant (`RiskService.RETAINABLE_STATUSES` = OPEN, UNDER_REVIEW, MITIGATING, TRANSFERRED) is read by the precondition *and* the writer, so there is nothing to drift, and `RiskLifecycleWriterTest` fails if a second list appears |
| **Two adjacent defects the slice had to fix to be worth anything** | **1. `RiskDetailPage` keyed three lifecycle buttons and its badge table on `UNDER_ASSESSMENT` / `TREATMENT_IN_PROGRESS` — statuses `CK_risks_status` has never permitted.** So **Approve never rendered at all**, and **Close never rendered for a `MITIGATING` risk — the population the close gate governs.** The register page has always used the real vocabulary, so one risk offered different actions on two screens. Between the two pages' tone tables, five invented statuses (`UNDER_ASSESSMENT`, `TREATMENT_IN_PROGRESS`, `IN_PROGRESS`, `MITIGATE`, `TREATED`) and three real ones missing, so `UNDER_REVIEW` — 30 of 71 rows in dev, the largest bucket — rendered a grey badge on both. 🔑 **A lookup table with a `?? 'neutral'` fallback is where a vocabulary error goes to hide**; every other shape of this bug fails loudly.<br>**2. The risk overview's "Treatments" tile linked to `/risk?status=TREATMENT_IN_PROGRESS`**, which the register hands straight to `riskApi.list(status)` — so the tile **always opened an empty register**. A dead link that renders as a working one, with no comparison for a status scan to catch. ⚠ It is no use tightening what a gate reads if the button that trips it cannot render |
| **⚠⚠ My own scan invented six defects, and this is the third regex mistake in one slice** | The FE vocabulary check first matched `\w*\.status === 'X'` — **any** object — and reported eight offenders. Six were other vocabularies on the same page: `tr.status` (RiskTreatment: PLANNED/IN_PROGRESS/IMPLEMENTED/CANCELLED), `b.status` (a KRI breach: RESOLVED), `s.status` (an appetite statement: APPROVED/RETIRED). Only `r.status === 'TREATED'` was real. Then the tone-table key scan anchored keys to line start and found **two of seven**, reporting five real keys as missing. Then a whole-file `doesNotContain("UNDER_REVIEW")` flagged `revoke`/`expireSweep`, which name it legitimately as the reopen *target*. 🔑 **A screen carries several status vocabularies and they are indistinguishable by shape** — the mirror of F2-163's `rowHref`: there the pattern was too narrow and hid five real routes, here too wide and manufactured six. Both times the fix was to open every hit before believing the count |
| **Guards added** | `RiskLifecycleWriterTest` (5) — no controller route ends in `/accept`; `acceptOnApprovedAcceptance` is called only by `RiskAcceptanceService`; the exemption consults the record and the query bounds the time-box; raisable ≡ approvable, one constant; the governed flip is audited and the sweep is *not* routed through the tenant-scoped path (off-request audit landmine). `riskLifecycleVocabulary.test.ts` (8) — no comparison, tone-table key, or `?status=` link may name a status the CHECK constraint forbids, plus a non-vacuity guard on the identifier list that fixed the six false positives, plus per-method caller coverage for `riskAcceptanceApi`. `RiskAcceptancesPanel.test.tsx` (9) — the first tests over any part of the acceptance surface |
| **Mutation** | 3/3 caught: exemption back to `"ACCEPTED".equals(r.getStatus())` → fails; endpoint reinstated → fails; `approve()` flipping with a bare `setRiskStatus` again → fails. ⚠ Mutation still proves only that a gate notices changes to *itself* ([[F2-163]]); the regex mistakes above were caught by reading hits, and the state-machine regression by the live probe |
| **Live probe (dev :8084, `[REVIEW-TEST]`-tagged, CHARINDEX cleanup, residue 0)** | `POST /risks/1/accept` → **404** as `admin` and as `ranalyst`. New HIGH risk (residual 16) → MITIGATING → close **409** naming the canonical plan. Acceptance requested as `ranalyst` (`RISK:WRITE`) → **201 SUBMITTED**; approved as `ranalyst` → **403**; approved as `rmanager` (`RISK:APPROVE`) → **200 APPROVED**, risk → **ACCEPTED**, and the ledger shows `TRANSITION Risk RISK-0374 MITIGATING → ACCEPTED` — the audited edge, on the very case the probe had caught as a 400. Close with the live acceptance → **200 CLOSED**. Then the historical state reproduced exactly — `status=ACCEPTED`, `risk_level=HIGH`, **0 acceptance records** — close → **409. Bypass closed** |
| **Population measured before acting (dev, read-only)** | **71 risks** platform-wide / 51 in org 1 *(the finding's "51" was org-scoped and correct; the platform figure is 71)* · **10** HIGH+ not closed / 8 in org 1 · **3 live ACCEPTED risks, all with zero acceptance records** — every one of them reached that status without one · all four APPROVED acceptance rows in the database belong to **soft-deleted** `'E-A verify'` probe risks, so **no acceptance has ever been recorded through the UI**, which is what an unreachable approval step looks like from the data side · `risk_lc.treatment_plans` **10 rows / 9 risks** vs `risk.risk_treatments` **52 / 52** — the legacy store is the populated one, and risks 21/22/23/24/32 are HIGH+ with a legacy treatment each and zero canonical plans, i.e. five real risks whose close would be refused by a message that used to tell them to do what they had already done |
| **⚠ Blast radius of (a): zero closes that succeed today would be refused** | The three ACCEPTED risks are LOW/LOW/MEDIUM and none has an approved appetite statement for its category, so `isHighLevel || isOverAppetite` is false for all three and the gate never applied to them. The finding said (a) *"will refuse closes that succeed today… it needs the owner's word"* — **measured, in dev, it refuses none.** Prod is unmeasured (29 migrations behind); the control fails closed there by design, which is the direction to err |
| **Also corrected in the finding itself** | It named the second treatment store **`risk.treatments`**. The real table is **`risk.risk_treatments`** — the name was inferred from the URL path `/risks/{id}/treatments`, not read from `@Table`. Same class of error as F2-163's headline number: a plausible value that nothing checked |
| **Files** | `RiskService`, `RiskAcceptanceService`, `RiskAcceptanceRepository`, `RiskController` · `RiskAcceptancesPanel.tsx` (new), `RiskDetailPage.tsx`, `RiskRegisterPage.tsx`, `lib/api.ts`, `lib/dialog.tsx` (label↔input association — the prompt rendered an unlabelled field, which a screen reader announces as nothing) · `RiskLifecycleWriterTest` (new), `riskLifecycleVocabulary.test.ts` (new), `RiskAcceptancesPanel.test.tsx` (new), `RiskServiceTest`, `RiskAcceptanceServiceTest` |
| **⚠ One endpoint fewer, and the count row is not source-gated** | Retiring `/accept` took `module/` from **2,214** to **2,213** endpoints under the census's own rule. `MEASURED_BASELINE` publishes 2,213, so drift now reads **+0** — but it read **+1** before this slice, because `theCensusScriptAgreesWithTheDocument` compares the doc to the `PUBLISHED` dict and **never re-measures endpoints from source**. 🔑 **The retirement silently absorbed a pre-existing drift, so the figure agreeing is now a coincidence rather than a confirmation** — a zero that means "nothing checks this", the same reading trap as slices 5/6 of [[F2-52]] |
| **Verification** | Backend **3,468/0/0** `BUILD SUCCESS` (3,457 → +11) · FE **405/405** in 43 files (388 → +17) · `npx tsc --noEmit` clean · `vite build` clean · census drift 0 · live probe as above |
| **Effort** | **M** — as filed, plus the approval surface the finding did not know was missing |
| **Lesson** | 🔑 **Fixing reachability changed what the authorisation model *meant*.** While the governed path was unreachable, the weak path was the only path and looked like the feature; the moment both were on the same screen, one of them was a bypass. ⚙ **An unreachable compliant path does not read as a control failure — it reads as an absent feature**, which is why three prior audits of this module measured guards, statuses and screens without anybody asking whether the compliant route had a button. 🔑🔑 And the fix's own recommendation was wrong in the same way it was right: *"retire it in favour of the E-A flow"* assumed the E-A flow could be completed, and **four of its five API methods had no caller.** Before retiring a path in favour of another, check the other one all the way to the end — not to its entry point |

## F2-165 · The unused-API-client scan resolves at object granularity, so dead methods hide inside live exports

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-165 *(measured 2026-08-08 while fixing [[F2-164]] — the fix needed four API methods nothing called, and the instrument built to find exactly that had reported the file clean)* |
| **Module** | `tss-grc-ui-v2/src/__tests__/apiClientReachability.test.ts` — [[F2-68]](c)'s guard |
| **Category** | Instrumentation. The defect is in a measurement, not in a feature — which is why it can hide a class of feature defects indefinitely |
| **Severity** | **P3 Medium.** No user-visible symptom of its own. It matters because of what it certifies: F2-68(c) exists to answer *"is this API surface actually reachable from a screen?"*, and for any grouped client it answers *"does at least one method have a caller?"* |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-08** — `apiClientMethodReachability.test.ts` (10 tests): a **hard-zero invariant** on dead duplicates, a decrease-only ratchet over the measured population, and five non-vacuity/anti-phantom controls. Mutation **7/7**. Five dead duplicates deleted. One P2 fell straight out of it and is fixed in the same commit: [[F2-166]] |
| **The measurement that closes it** | **91 grouped clients · 1,070 methods · 191 with no caller (17.8%)** — the population the finding said to publish before changing the gate. Split mechanically, not by judgement: **5 dead duplicates** (the exact `(verb, path)` has a *reached* sibling), **148 `HOLE`** (the endpoint family a screen does reach — the workflow has a gap), **41 whole-capability dark** (no screen touches the family at all, which is F2-68(c)'s original population). Two independently-built passes agreed on the last figure (41 vs 42), which is the only reason I trust it |
| **🔑 The recommendation I wrote was wrong, and reading one entry is what showed it** | This finding told me to sort the population into *governance-critical* and *not yet wired*. The very first candidate refuted the sort: `evidenceApi.approve` had no caller and looks maximally governance-critical — but `lib/evidenceItems.ts#approveEvidenceItem` POSTs the **same** `/api/v1/evidence/items/{id}/approve` and a screen calls it. Filed by name shape it reads *"no screen can approve evidence"*, which is **false**. So the sort that carries meaning is by **endpoint**, not by verb name: a dark method with a live twin is dead code, one without is unreachable capability. ⚙ **A classification rule you can only apply by intuition will manufacture a P1 on its first use** |
| **What the invariant can and cannot be** | Only the duplicate half is a hard zero, and it can be one *because the remedy is unambiguous* — nothing is lost by deleting and nothing is excused by keeping. The other 189 are a **reported figure with no ceiling**, ratcheting in both directions, each annotated with what the *user* cannot do. That is the `BARE_EXPORT_CEILING` lesson honoured rather than quoted: an unadjudicated red list becomes an allow-list, and a ceiling that tolerates its population stops distinguishing *tolerated* from *reviewed* |
| **⚠ The instrument contained the bug it measures** | Two self-inflicted defects, both caught by their own controls. (1) My first stripper was hand-rolled Python; a **regex literal** in `lib/api.ts` — `/filename="?([^";]+)"?/i` — put it into double-quote state at line 212, every comment after that survived, and prose words (`permanently`, `below`) came out as object keys — count wrong by 14. The repo's own `stripComments` **documents that exact limitation** and bounds its string patterns to one line so it degrades safely. 🔑 **The helper existed, its docstring named the precise failure, and re-implementing it reproduced the bug it was written to avoid** — second occurrence of [[F2-07]]a's *"grep for an instrument before building one"*. (2) My duplicate-detector's "plain export" pass also matched `export const someApi = {…}`, so referencing a group marked **all** its endpoints reached and 196 dark methods came back as **192 "dead duplicates"** — object granularity, reintroduced inside the invariant written to catch object granularity. **An instrument can contain the defect it measures, and it looks like a working instrument while it does** |
| **Also wrong on the way** | A depth-1 key match without a segment-boundary rule turned `api.get<PageResponse<Risk>>` into a method called `PageResponse` (also `Array`, `Record`, `it`, `up`); an anti-phantom check written against **raw** source failed on ~30 real methods because comments sit between keys, and would have had me "fix" an extractor that was right; and the `HOLE` family rule truncated `/api/v1/risk/appetite{}` (a `${pageQ(…)}` glued onto the path) down to `/api/v1/risk`, so the appetite gap did not flag on the first pass. Four pattern mistakes in one slice — same family as the six phantom defects [[F2-164]]'s `.status ===` scan invented |
| **Deleted (the hard zero starts at 0)** | `evidenceApi.approve` / `.reject` / `.submit` → `lib/evidenceItems.ts`; `cyberApi.controlsAll` / `.frameworks` → `lib/frameworkControls.ts`. All five verified against a live caller before deletion |
| **Lesson** | ⚙ **A guard that passes tells you only that it asked its question.** F2-68(c) was working exactly as designed while the platform had no way to approve a risk acceptance. Before trusting a green reachability gate, say its assertion out loud in domain terms and check that is the sentence you wanted proved. And when you generalise an instrument, **assume the generalisation has the old blind spot in a new place** — mine did, twice, in one file |

## F2-166 · No tenant could define a risk appetite, so half of F2-164's close gate was unreachable — and a demo fallback hid it

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-166 *(found 2026-08-08 by [[F2-165]]'s per-method scan, on its first run — the second consecutive finding produced by building the instrument the previous one asked for)* |
| **Module** | `risk` — `pages/risk/RiskRegisterPage.tsx` (Appetite tab) · `lib/api.ts#ermAdvancedApi` · `RiskAppetiteController` |
| **Category** | Control unreachable from the product + a client-side fallback masking it |
| **Severity** | **P2 High.** `RiskService.isOverAppetite` — the over-appetite arm of the mandatory-treatment close gate [[F2-164]] restored — matches an **APPROVED** appetite statement on the risk's `categoryId` and compares residual to `toleranceUpper`. Nothing in the UI could create or edit a statement, so that arm could only ever fire for a tenant whose rows arrived by seed script |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-08** — create + edit wired, fabrication removed, 8 guard tests (`appetiteStatementWiring.test.ts`), mutation 7/7, live-probed end to end |
| **The measurement** | `ermAdvancedApi` exposes 9 appetite methods. **Reached:** `appetites` (list), `appetiteDashboard`, `appetiteBreaches`, `updateExposure`, `approveAppetite`, `retireAppetite`. **Dark:** `createAppetite`, `updateAppetite`, `getAppetite`, `deleteAppetite`. Read aloud: *a statement can be approved, retired, and have its exposure updated — and cannot be brought into existence.* In dev, organisation 1 holds 9 statements (8 APPROVED, **3 risks currently over a ceiling**); organisations **2 and 3 hold zero**, and no screen could give them any. **4 of the 9 have a null `category_id`** and therefore gate nothing at all — which is exactly what a form with optional fields produces, and why the new form makes `categoryId` and `toleranceUpper` required |
| **⚠⚠ Why nobody noticed — the fallback was load-bearing, for the fourth time** | `loadAll` ended with `if (list.length === 0) { applyMock(); return; }`. A **signed-in** tenant with no statements was shown the demo library (`APPETITES` + `SAUDI_APPETITES`, ids 5101–5107 / 6101–6108) with **Approve / Retire / Update-exposure live on rows that exist in no database**. So the tab always looked complete, the honest `No appetite statements yet` branch was **unreachable code**, and the missing create path had nothing to draw attention to it. Fourth occurrence after [[F2-42]], [[F2-38]] and [[F2-158]] — 🔑 **when a screen has a client-side fallback, hit its endpoints before believing the screen** |
| **Live proof (dev :8084, `[REVIEW-TEST]`, residue 0)** | `POST /risk/appetite` as `so_officer` (RISK_READ only) → **403**, guard holds · as `rmanager` → **201 DRAFT** (server forces DRAFT; `approvedBy` is not bindable, so a statement cannot self-attest) · `PUT` → 200 · a LOW risk (residual 4) over a ceiling of 3, walked OPEN → UNDER_REVIEW → MITIGATING · close **while the statement is DRAFT → 200**, correct: an unapproved appetite must not bind · `POST /appetite/{id}/approve` → **APPROVED** · close → **409 "A treatment plan is required before closing a risk over its appetite ceiling"**. ⚙ **That final leg was unreachable before this slice** — not failing, unreachable: no tenant could produce the APPROVED row it depends on |
| **Fix** | A `FormModal` create/edit form on the Appetite tab (11 fields, bilingual titles per house rule 7); `categoryId` + `toleranceUpper` **required**, because the two columns the engine reads are not optional; appetite-level options derived from `APPETITE_TONE`'s keys rather than retyped, so a level the badge cannot render is impossible (F2-164's `?? 'neutral'` lesson); the zero-rows fabrication removed, with an empty state that names the control left inert; write affordances hidden while demo rows are on screen, since a write against id 5101 can only 404 |
| **Effort** | S (one screen, one form) |
| **Lesson** | 🔑 **A wired approval step is not evidence the record can exist.** Three of this programme's findings now share one shape — [[F2-164]] (approve/reject/revoke dead while create was live), F2-166 (create/edit dead while approve was live), and [[F2-163]] (a console with no entry point). ⚙ **Read a workflow end to end in both directions**: from the record's creation to its final decision, and back. A gap at either end makes everything between it and the gap decorative, and the screen looks finished from every angle except the one that matters |

## F2-167 · A demo row's buttons were live, and the fabricated ids collide with real ones

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-167 *(measured 2026-08-09 while asking why the shipped demo-fallback contract had passed [[F2-166]])* |
| **Module** | `components/ui/RowActions.tsx` + 13 register pages · `__tests__/demoFallbackContract.test.ts` (W2-1b / F2-98's guard) |
| **Category** | Data integrity — a real mutation reachable from a record the product knows is not real |
| **Severity** | **P2 High.** Not the bundle-hygiene concern [[F2-15]] describes. On the *throw* substitution path the tenant's real records are present, so a click on a fabricated row's **Delete** sent a real, tenant-scoped delete for a real id |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-09** — `RowActions` takes `disabled`, all **35** sites on the 13 substituting pages pass their page's demo flag, 6 behavioural tests, and a hard-zero invariant in `demoFallbackContract.test.ts`. Mutation 3/4 (the 4th is redundant code — see below) |
| **🔑 Why the existing contract could not see it** | `demoFallbackContract.test.ts` (5 tests) enforces **disclosure**: the applier raises a flag, the flag is not `!isAuthenticated()` (F2-98), every hook consumer names `isDemo`. F2-166 satisfied every one of them and was still a P2. ⚙ **Disclosure is the wrong property.** A badge reading *"demo data"* beside a live **Approve** button does not warn the user, it invites them — and the contract had no opinion about buttons at all. The shape to distrust is not *undisclosed mock data*, it is **a real mutation reachable from a row the product itself knows is fabricated** |
| **The measurement that makes it P2, not cosmetic** | **Every mock file numbers its records from 1, and so does every identity column.** Measured in dev: `iam.users` 7 rows at ids **1–8** against `mockAdmin`'s **1–15**; `tprm.vendors` 28 rows at **1–28** against `mockTprm`'s **1–501**; `compliance.controls` 35 at **1–35** against `mockCompliance`'s **1–1007**; `evidence.evidence_items` 57 rows inside `mockEvidence`'s band; `bcm.bcp_plans` 10 rows at 7–16 against `mockBcm`'s 1–57. Substitution fires on two paths — the list call **threw**, or it returned **zero rows**. On the *throw* path (a 500, a timeout, a dropped connection) the tenant's real rows exist, so `RowActions.onDelete` on "demo user #3" called `adminApi.deleteUser(3)` against **real user 3** — and the `ConfirmDialog` displayed the *fabricated* name, so the user confirmed the deletion of a record they were not shown |
| **Population** | 13 pages substitute fabricated rows **and** carry row-scoped writes: `cyber` 19, `scm` 13, `bcm` 12, `privacy` 11, `compliance` 10, `ethics` 13, `incidents` 5, `evidence` 4, `risk` 3, `reporting` 3, `admin` 2, `change` 2, `tprm` 2. **Exactly one** gated anything on the demo flag before this slice — `RiskRegisterPage`, and only because [[F2-166]] had just fixed it (its `if (!demoMode) await riskApi.remove(…)` on the register delete is the one pre-existing instance of the right idea anywhere in the codebase) |
| **Fix** | `RowActions` is the choke point: it renders edit, delete **and** the workflow `extras` (approve / escalate / complete) for the whole platform, so one `disabled` prop covers all 35 sites. Disabled buttons carry `disabled` + `aria-disabled` and a bilingual title naming the reason, because a greyed button with no explanation reads as a broken page. The invariant is a **hard zero with no allow-list** — every site was fixed in the same commit — with an anti-vacuity floor of 30 sites so a scan that stops matching cannot pass |
| **⚠ Two instrument corrections, both the same mistake as the last three slices** | My first "is it gated?" test looked for any `!isDemo` in the file and declared **8 of 13 pages safe**. Every hook consumer carries `enabled: !isDemo` (live refresh) and `{!isDemo && <LivePulse/>}` (the pulse dot) — **neither gates a single button**, and the true count was 1. Then my flag resolver searched *backwards* from each site and reported 24 of 35 as having no flag in scope; a `columns` array is routinely declared **above** `const isDemo = …` and its `cell` arrow only *runs* during the table's render, so the flag is in scope and the resolver was wrong, not the code. 🔑 **Look at what a match sits next to, and remember that JS scope is not textual order** |
| **⚠ A missed mutation, kept and labelled** | `RowActions` also wraps each handler in `guard()`. Replacing `guard` with the identity function left all six tests green: jsdom, like a browser, will not dispatch a click from a disabled button, so the wrapper is **not independently observable**. It stays as a second line for a future branch rendered without `disabled` — but the comment now says so, because the first draft claimed the callback was the asserted boundary. ⚙ **A missed mutation on redundant code is fine; a comment claiming it was covered is not** — that is [[F2-159]]'s decoy in miniature |
| **✅ The continuation, now delivered** | This slice made the buttons inert; it did **not** make the ids safe. That was left for its own slice and shipped as [[F2-168]] on 2026-08-09 — the whole fabricated corpus now sits above `DEMO_ID_BASE`, so a write raised from a fabricated row can only 404. Re-measuring F2-15's `Current State` to scope it is what found F2-168: the same collision was already attaching fabricated children to **real** records on the success path, which is a strictly worse defect than the one this entry fixed |
| **Effort** | S (one component, 35 one-line call sites) |
| **Lesson** | ⚙ **A contract can be fully enforced and still be about the wrong property.** Five green tests guaranteed the user was *told* the rows were fake, which is worth having, and none of them asked whether the product would then act on those rows. When a guard passes over a defect you already found by hand, do not extend the guard — **say its assertion out loud and check that it is the sentence you needed proved** (the F2-165 lesson, arriving one layer down) |

## F2-168 · Fabricated children attach themselves to REAL records by id collision — on the success path, undisclosed

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-168 *(measured 2026-08-09 while re-measuring [[F2-15]]'s `Current State` to scope the mock-id renumbering [[F2-167]] deferred)* |
| **Module** | `lib/entityAnchors.ts` + 6 detail pages + `RiskRegisterPage` · the whole `mock*` corpus |
| **Category** | Data integrity — fabricated assurance artefacts presented as part of a genuine record |
| **Severity** | **P1 Critical.** Not [[F2-15]]'s bundle hygiene and not [[F2-167]]'s fallback hazard. The record is **real**, the page is **not** in demo mode, **no badge is shown**, and part of the detail is fabricated |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-09** — `lib/demoIds.ts` shifts the fabricated corpus above `DEMO_ID_BASE` (900,000,000); 85 exports wrapped across 17 modules; 16 unit tests on the shift + 9 contract assertions; mutation 6/6; live-probed against the running dev server |
| **The defect** | Six detail pages fetch a genuine record from the server and then decorate it out of a fabricated map **keyed by that record's id**, unconditionally, with no demo flag anywhere in the file (`isDemo`/`showingDemo`/`demoMode` absent from all six). `CONTROL_TESTS_BY_ID[control.id]` rendered fabricated **control-test results** — tester, sample count, findings, PASS — on a real control. `FINDING_HISTORY_BY_ID[finding.id]` rendered a fabricated **audit trail** on a real finding. `DPIA_REVIEWS_BY_ID`, `VENDOR_ASSESSMENTS_BY_ID`/`_CONTRACTS_BY_ID`, `RISK_HISTORY_BY_ID`, `CONTROL_SUBCONTROLS_BY_ID`, `FINDING_EVIDENCE_BY_ID`, `CONTROL_EVIDENCE_BY_ID` and the four `*_ANCHORS_BY_ID` regulator-citation maps did the same. **17 fabricated datasets, 37 expressions, 7 pages.** These are precisely the artefacts an auditor samples |
| **🔑 The file documented its own hazard** | `entityAnchors.ts`'s header comment reads *"Keyed by COMPLIANCE_FINDINGS.id (mock ids 31-38 from mockCompliance.ts)"*. It **says** it is keyed by mock ids; `FindingDetailPage` passes it a server id; nobody connected the two halves. The crosswalk card it feeds is titled *"test once, satisfy many"* and states *"this single control satisfies N regulatory citations across M authorities"* — the compliance claim itself was fabricated |
| **Live measurement (dev `:8084`, 2026-08-09)** | **38 real records** were being decorated: **5 of 35** controls (ids 1, 3, 4, 9, 10), **8 of 40** findings (31–38), **16 of 28** vendors (1–16), **9 of 51** risks. DPIA (keys 41–45 vs 6 rows) and policy (51–58 vs 17 rows) do not collide *yet* — latent, not absent, and they arrive the moment a tenant grows |
| **Fix — a wrapper, not a rewrite** | `demoRows` / `demoKeyed` / `demoRecord` in `lib/demoIds.ts` recursively shift every `id` and every camelCase `*Id` **numeric** field, plus the keys of a keyed map, by `DEMO_ID_BASE`. 85 exports wrapped (50 rows + 35 keyed). ⚠ **Why not rewrite the ~968 literals**: a missed one is *silent* — no compile error, just a lookup that stops resolving — so a textual sweep would put the slice's correctness in a regex. The wrapper puts it in one function with its own 16 tests. The corpus stays readable at its original small numbers |
| **Why one constant closes the whole class** | Keys and record ids shift by the same amount, so `MAP[fabricatedId]` still resolves — **the demo experience is untouched** — while `MAP[realId]` misses and the page falls through to the honest empty state it already had. Zero page edits were needed. And the same shift closes [[F2-167]]'s residue: a write raised from a fabricated row can only 404 |
| **Guards** | `__tests__/demoIdSpaceContract.test.ts` (9): every id-ish field ≥ base; every map key ≥ base; **no id in 1..2000 reaches any fabricated map** (the defect in its own language); **every map key still resolves to a corpus record** — measured true *before* the shift (0 unresolved keys across 11 maps), so it is a real invariant and not one the change invented; **non-id numbers did not move** (`KRI_TRENDS_BY_ID` is `Record<number, number[]>` where the values are weekly readings — shifting one corrupts a chart without breaking it); a hard-zero textual ratchet on unwrapped exports; the six pages keep their `?? []` branch; and six vacuity floors |
| **⚠ Fifth over-wide scan in five slices** | The site scan called all 42 candidates unconditional. Reading them, **2 were correctly guarded** (`RiskDetailPage`'s assessments and treatments choose `live` over `mockRows` via `useLive`) and **8 were mock-on-mock** (`paTriggers` and `AuthorityWorkspacePage` iterate the mock array itself). Then the *ratchet's own first draft* sampled 6,000 characters after each export and accused six exports that hold no ids at all — `POLICY_STAGES` is a string array whose "id literal" belonged to the next export in the file. 🔑 **It was caught only because the failure list was short enough to read.** A wrong ratchet that fires is fixable; a wrong ratchet that passes is not |
| **Live verification** | Logged in against `:8084`, pulled the **154** real ids the server actually serves for controls / findings / vendors / risks, and asserted at module level that not one of them reaches any of the 13 fabricated maps. The permanent guard sweeps 1..2000 instead, because the FE suite must stay hermetic |
| **Effort** | M (one helper, 17 mechanically wrapped modules, 2 new test files) |
| **Residue** | The 5 audit/appetite `lib` modules (67 numeric ids) are deliberately out of scope: they hold no numeric-keyed maps, so they cannot be indexed by a real record's id, and pulling them in widens the diff without closing a measured defect. Filed under [[F2-15]]. The inline `.catch(() => MAP[realId])` fallbacks are now harmless but reveal a separate gap → [[F2-169]] |
| **Lesson** | 🔑 **The hazard was documented, in the file, by the author, and it still shipped** — because the sentence lived next to the data and the bug lived at the call site. ⚙ And a finding's *stated* boundary is worth re-measuring before you work inside it: F2-15 said "15 mock files", the corpus is 22 modules, and the 7 it omitted included the one holding the fabricated regulator citations. **A boundary drawn by filename is not a boundary** |
