| **Provenance** | [[F2-256]] filed *"nine event registers declare `actorName` beside an `actorUserId` their service DOES write"* as the largest sub-shape of its 27-member work list, deliberately left whole rather than adjudicated nine times ([[F2-188]]). |
| **Current State** | ✔ **FIXED 2026-08-20** (`3ba40611`). Each register's single timeline writer now stamps `setActorName(currentActorName())` beside its existing id write, from `CurrentActor.username()`; `actorUserId` is on the wire for the three responses that carried only the name; and `UnwritableActorColumnContractTest` gains a pair invariant (hard zero, no exemptions) plus a fix-shape leg. Probed live 14/14 across three registers as three personas. |
| **Problem** | Every one of the ten services wrote `setActorUserId(currentUserId())` inside a private `timeline(...)` helper and never the name half; `setActorName` appeared **nowhere in the platform** outside the register [[F2-248]] closed. |
| **Root Cause** | RC-D — a governance record whose attribution is only half written, the fourth variant after [[F2-223]] (the caller owns it), [[F2-236]] (it arrives as a parameter) and [[F2-256]] (nobody owns it). |
| **Evidence** | `sys.columns` in both databases, ASM over `target/classes`, live probe 14/14, pre-fix control 4 of 12 legs |


**Finding.** Ten event/timeline registers declare `actor_user_id` **and** `actor_name`. Every
service writes only the id — `e.setActorUserId(currentUserId())` inside a private `timeline(...)`
helper — and **nothing in the platform writes the name anywhere**. The response DTO carries it, so
every event the platform itself produced described its actor with a null.

Resolved from `sys.columns` (never guessed — [[F2-252]]), identical in dev and prod: ten tables
declare both halves, and the population divides into four data shapes, so the filed claim was true
of only part of it —

| register | rows | id | name | shape |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `reginspect.reginspect_inspection_update` | 20 | 20 | **0** | id only |
| `rrp.rrp_event` | 14 | 14 | **0** | id only |
| `regreporting.regreport_event` | 51 | 33 | **0** | id only |
| `dataclass.dataclass_event` | 0 | 0 | 0 | latent |
| `cpty.cpty_event` | 75 | 75 | 75 | both |
| `ai_governance.ai_lifecycle_event` | 13 | 13 | 9 | both |
| `outsourcing.outsourcing_event` | 10 | 10 | 6 | both |
| `fraud.fraud_case_update` | 16 | 16 | 12 | both |
| `sharia.sharia_event` | 33 / **30 prod** | 3 / **0 prod** | 30 | name only |
| `openbanking.ob_event` | 10 / **6 prod** | 4 / **0 prod** | 6 | name only |

⚠ **dev and prod disagree on two of them**, which is unusual for this programme and worth stating:
prod's `sharia_event` and `ob_event` carry **no ids at all**.

🔑🔑 **The stored names are almost never people, and that decides which fix is correct.**
`'Credit Officer / Risk Management Secretariat'` on all 75 cpty rows,
`'Procurement Officer / موظف المشتريات'`, `'Internal Audit / المراجعة الداخلية'`,
`'Sharia Audit Team'`, `'Finance Reconciliation Team'`; the AI ones are **committees**
(`'لجنة أخلاقيات الذكاء الاصطناعي — AI Ethics Committee (COM-AIETHICS)'`) and one is an **external
regulator** (`'هيئة الحكومة الرقمية — مراجعة مستقلة (DGA)'`, the Digital Government Authority); and
`ob_event` holds **machine actors** — `'System (cert-monitor)'`, `'System (SIEM detection)'`,
`'System (consent-cache audit)'`. So this is [[F2-251]]'s case, not [[F2-249]]'s: **the label is not a
copy of the id's identity, so deriving it from the resolved user would destroy information**, and
[[F2-245]]/[[F2-246]]/[[F2-250]]'s derive-from-the-parent fix is the wrong instrument here. **Ask
whether the label is a copy before reaching for the fix that worked last time.**

⚠⚠ **THE THREE SHARPEST ARE THE ONES WHOSE RESPONSE CARRIED ONLY THE NAME.**
`AiLifecycleDtos.EventResponse`, `DataclassDtos.EventResponse` and `OutsourcingDtos.EventResponse`
declare `actorName` and **no `actorUserId`** — while the column beside it is populated on 13 of 13,
0 of 0 and 10 of 10 rows. So for those three the response's *only* actor field was the half nothing
wrote, and the half that was written was never on the wire at all: [[F2-198]]'s `crossBorderTransfer`
shape, both halves in one record. The id is now on the wire for all three.

🔑 **The pre-fix witness was in the data and needed no probe.**
`ai_governance.ai_lifecycle_event` id=1 — `RECERTIFICATION_EXPIRED`, `actor_user_id = 1`,
`actor_name` NULL, `created_at` 2026-05-26 04:33:40 — is the [[F2-256]] transition, **the only row
in that register the platform itself has ever written**, and the only row of the thirteen with an id
and no name. The other nine were seeded in one bulk write at 2026-06-27 11:53:35 and all carry a
name. *One register, one API-written row, and it is the one with the blank.*

⚠⚠ **F2-256's filing was wrong in two ways and both corrections matter.**
(a) It said **nine** registers and its own javadoc **listed ten** — the tenth, `FraudCaseUpdate`, is
outside the census because its clock is a **field initialiser** ([[F2-215]]'s third filling
mechanism), which is an *instrument blind spot* and not a judgement on the merits.
🔑 **A member excluded by a blind spot reads exactly like a member that was checked and cleared**,
and the prose and the list disagreed by one in the reassuring direction.
(b) It claimed *"every timeline entry renders a blank actor"*. Measured across `tss-grc-ui-v2`:
**no screen renders any of these ten actors.** `EthicsPage` is the only surface in the platform that
reads an `actorName`, and that is the register [[F2-248]] closed. The blank reached **API consumers**,
not a page. 🔑 **A claim about a consequence is the least-verified part of a filing** ([[F2-192]]) —
and it is a fact about today rather than a property of the control ([[F2-182]]): the field is on the
wire, so the next client to declare it renders nothing.

**Fix.** At each register's single timeline writer, beside the existing id write:
`setActorName(currentActorName())`, where `currentActorName()` is a private one-line sibling of the
`currentUserId()` helper that every one of the ten already has. One writer per register ([[F2-245]] —
the claim that prevents drift is about *where* the writes live).

⚠ **Deliberately `CurrentActor.username()` and not `requireUsername(...)`.** The id half is nullable
and comes from the same primitive, so refusing on the name would make the two halves behave
differently in a writer whose only job is to record a side effect — a timeline write that throws
aborts the business operation it exists to describe ([[F2-191]]) — and `ob_event`'s six machine-actor
rows show that an actorless event is a real category in this family. **Both null together** is the
invariant, not *never null*.

⚠ **Deliberately not [[F2-249]]'s `TenantUserDirectory`.** Measured: **none of these ten modules
contains a single `com.tss.grc.module.iam` import**, so a directory would add ten edges to a
decrease-only module-graph ratchet that may never be raised (house rule 3). `CurrentActor` lives in
`common/`, which sits outside that population entirely, and it is the precedent [[F2-248]] set when it
closed this same shape on `ethics.case_actions`. **One primitive, not a second mechanism**
([[F2-190]]).

**Instrument.** `UnwritableActorColumnContractTest`'s `WORK_LIST` drops the nine (census 33 → 24) and
gains two legs:
- **the pair invariant** — every shipped `@Entity` declaring both halves must have both written; a
  hard zero with **no exemption map**, which is safe rather than strict ([[F2-214]]): a register that
  does not want a display name should not declare the column, and one that does has
  `CurrentActor.username()` available with no new edge, so there is no correct code for it to fail on;
- **the fix shape** — per register, the name must come from the principal and never from a request
  body ([[F2-223]]), and the helper must not refuse.

⚠⚠ **MY OWN PAIR INVARIANT WAS VACUOUS AS FIRST WRITTEN AND THE MUTATION HARNESS PROVED IT.** It read
`if (writtenOn(e,"actorUserId") && !writtenOn(e,"actorName")) collect;` and asserted the collection
empty. Forcing that condition false **SURVIVED**: on a fixed tree there is nothing left to collect,
and **an empty list is what both a correct gate and a dead one produce.** Rewritten as the **positive
equality of two measured sets** — `nameWritten` must contain exactly `idWritten`, with a floor of ten
under `idWritten` so the two cannot match by both being empty. 🔑 **Assert the positive**
([[F2-208]]), and note this is the same family as [[F2-256]]'s own M8 one slice earlier: *a condition
that cannot fail passes forever, and its output is indistinguishable from success.*

⚠ **One survivor is a recorded equivalent mutant, not a hole.** Pointing the `nameWritten` collector
at `actorUserId` is undetectable on a clean corpus, because on this tree every register writes both;
its only discriminator is the pre-fix control ([[F2-206]] — a surviving mutant is a hole only if the
mutated code is wrong, and here it is wrong in a way no clean corpus can show). A fifth mutation was
**withdrawn as invalid**: deleting the `requireUsername` ban is the delete-an-assertion family, and
M3 — a register that actually refuses — already demonstrates the ban discriminates, from the side
where the mutated code is genuinely wrong.

⚠ **The pre-fix control is the load-bearing verification, and my first run of it did not run at all.**
The `git checkout master --` paths were backend-relative against a repo-root `cwd`, so every checkout
failed, the gate stayed green, and the harness printed *"THE CONTROL DID NOT FIRE — the new legs are
vacuous."* 🔑 **A control that cannot restore the pre-fix tree reads exactly like a gate that is
vacuous**, and both readings end with the author editing the gate. Corrected, it fires **4 of 12
legs** naming `AiLifecycleEvent`, `CptyEvent`, `ShariaEvent` and `RegReportEvent` exactly.

⚠⚠ **MY PROBE MUTATED A REAL SEEDED GOVERNANCE ROW — [[F2-206]]'s rule broken by my own leg.** Leg 3
transitioned `REC-2026-FRD` (recertification id=2) from DUE to IN_REVIEW rather than planting its own
victim. Restored field-for-field from prod, which holds the identical seed and was never in scope,
**including `updated_by` and `updated_at`** — a status restored under a row stamp naming the probe is
a repair that still records the intrusion. All five touched tables reconciled against prod afterwards.

⚠ **And the cleanup missed a row for a reason worth knowing: the service composes the note, so the
`[REVIEW-TEST]` tag never reaches `note_en`.** A `CHARINDEX` cleanup keyed on a tag can only see rows
whose text the probe wrote; a child row the *service* authored carries nothing to match.
🔑 **Clean a child row by its parent id, not by a tag the child never carries.**

⚠ **Two guessed names again, both caught by running things** (the family recurring since [[F2-198]]):
`cpty.counterparties` — it is `cpty.counterparty` — and a `sharia/nc-events` payload missing the
`@NotBlank reference` and `@NotNull snciAmountSar` the request record declares. Resolve table names
from `sys.tables` and payload shapes from the request record, never from the plural of the entity.

**Verification.** Post-fix live probe **14/14** across three registers as three personas —
`compliance` (`SHARIA:WRITE`), `rmanager` (`CPTY:WRITE`) and `admin` for `ai-lifecycle`, whose route
is `hasAnyRole('PLATFORM_ADMIN','CRO','CIO','DPO')` with no live holder for any of the three domain
roles ([[F2-255]]'s open filing), so `admin` is the only caller and the leg is about data semantics
rather than authorization. The cpty leg is the sharp one: that register already held an **office
label on all 75 rows**, and the probe asserts the stored value is `rmanager` and *not* the seed's
label — proving the fix stamps the principal rather than echoing whatever was there. Gate pre-fix
control 4 of 12 · mutation harness **4 killed / 1 recorded equivalent / 1 withdrawn / 0 anchor-miss**
· gates 73 green across this gate and the four sibling attribution gates · suite green. No migration.

**Filed.**
- ⚠⚠ **`reginspect.reginspect_inspection_update` holds 6 of 20 rows whose `actor_user_id` names a user
  in ANOTHER TENANT**, identical in dev and prod — all six are `admin` (organisation 1) on rows
  belonging to organisations 2 and 3, all written at one timestamp (`2026-05-25 19:40:34`, 4 distinct
  seconds across 20 rows), so **seed-origin**: the writer takes the actor from `currentUserId()` and
  is correct. This is [[F2-242]]/[[F2-243]]'s unverified-reference shape in a SAMA/NCA regulatory
  inspection register. Repair rewrites live governance rows in two databases with no mapping from
  `admin` to the officer each tenant meant — **owner decision**.
- ⚠⚠ **Five of the ten registers have no `WRITE` or `APPROVE` row in `iam.permissions` at all** —
  `DATACLASS`, `OUTSOURCING`, `REGINSPECT`, `REGREPORTING`, `RRP`. That is [[F2-255]]'s catalogue-gap
  shape, so no tenant administrator can grant those permissions. ⚠⚠ **CORRECTED by [[F2-264]]: the
  consequence this cell drew — *"those five registers are reachable only through the PLATFORM_ADMIN
  code bypass and no tenant administrator can grant access to them"* — is FALSE for four of the five,
  and [[F2-258]], [[F2-259]] and [[F2-260]] each carried it forward as the next work.** Only `RRP` was
  a lockout, and it was the one with **no administrator remedy at all**. The other four are guarded by
  `hasAnyRole`, which never reaches `ModulePermissionEvaluator`, so the empty catalogue costs nothing at
  run time — probed live, a non-admin holder writes at **200/201** and an off-tier persona is **403**.
  🔑 **A statement about the CATALOGUE reads as a statement about REACHABILITY, and they coincide only
  for a permission guard.** `CPTY:APPROVE` exists with **0 holders**
  ([[F2-253]]'s attrition shape). Both are **owner decisions** with a per-tenant impact question.
- The **24** remaining `WORK_LIST` members, still with no verdicts ([[F2-188]]).
- The columns now hold **two vocabularies** — seeded office/committee labels and platform usernames —
  which is [[F2-236]]'s already-filed office-versus-person question, now in ten more columns. None of
  the ten has an `*_ar` sibling, so the label is English-only on an Arabic-primary UI (house rule 7).
- `data_officer.do_event` and `cpty.rating_action` declare `actor_user_id` and **no name column**, so
  their responses carry a raw user id and nothing else — [[F2-249]]'s *unjoinable* shape, a different
  question with a different answer, deliberately not folded into this one.

## F2-256 · A decision recorded WHEN and never WHO — and the gate built to find a forged actor cannot see an absent one

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-256 *(measured 2026-08-20. Provenance is [[F2-255]]'s own filing. Re-deriving it first ([[F2-221]]) confirmed the site and sharpened it: the filing said *"2 of 13 rows already carry a decision with no decider"* and one of those two was written **through the API**, not by the seed.)* |
| **Category** | Attribution — a people column with **no writer in any code path**, beside an act clock the server stamps · an instrument family every member of which is keyed on a write EXISTING |
| **Severity** | **P2.** Every ISO/IEC 42001 model recertification granted, renewed, revoked or allowed to lapse through the API recorded the moment of the decision and not the person who made it. No data loss and no forgery — an absence, which is why nobody found it: a blank decider on a governance row reads as missing data. |
| **Provenance** | [[F2-255]] filed *"`ai_governance.recertification.approver_user_id` has no writer in any code path while `decided_at` is stamped from the server's clock — 2 of 13 rows already carry a decision with no decider in both databases, and `currentUserId()` sits in the same service feeding the timeline event, so F2-223's split attribution here is *the server owns WHEN and nobody owns WHO*."* All of that holds; the row-origin half is corrected below. |
| **Current State** | ✔ **FIXED 2026-08-20** (`c0577f6d`). One private `recordDecision()` is the sole writer of the `(decided_at, approver_user_id)` pair and takes the actor from `CurrentActor.requireUserId`. New `UnwritableActorColumnContractTest` (10 legs) measures the population; new `RecertificationDecisionAttributionTest` (6 legs) covers a service that had no test of any kind. Suite **4,337/0/0** (up 16). No migration. |
| **Problem** | `AiLifecycleService#transitionRecertification` stamped `decidedAt` from `LocalDateTime.now()` in two switch branches and wrote `approverUserId` **nowhere in the platform**. Neither `CreateRecertificationRequest` nor `TransitionRecertificationRequest` declares the field, so the caller could not supply it either — the column was declared, returned on the wire by `RecertificationResponse`, and unwritable. |
| **Root Cause** | RC-D — a governance record whose attribution has no owner, the third variant after [[F2-223]] (the caller owns it) and [[F2-236]] (it arrives as a parameter). |

🔑🔑 **BOTH HALVES OF `SplitAttributionContractTest`'s PAIR ARE BUILT FROM SETTER CALL SITES, SO A
COLUMN NOBODY SETS CONTRIBUTES TO NEITHER.** Its derivation is literally:

```java
Matcher sm = SETTER.matcher(body);
while (sm.find()) { … clockKeys.add(…) … callerActors.put(…) … }
```

A field with no setter produces no `find()` hit, so it can never join `callerActors` and can never
pair with a `clockKey`. **"Nobody owns WHO" is invisible to the instrument built to find "the caller
owns WHO"** — and the same is true of the three gates beside it: `ParameterBorneActorTest` and
`PrincipalStampedFieldContractTest` narrow that same population further (a scalar parameter, resolved
at its call sites), and `ServerStampedFieldContractTest` intersects *fields a guarded route stamps*
with *fields a write path takes from the request*, sets a never-written field is in neither of.
**All four are keyed on a write existing.** The invariant is real; the narrowing is none of the ones
already on the record (a filename, a three-entry allow-list, a module name, an `extends` clause, a
field-name list inside a fix, a claim shape in a gate) — it is **the existence of a setter call**.

🔑 **THE CORRECT ARTEFACT HAS THE IDENTICAL HELPER, AND THIS SERVICE HAS IT TOO.**
`DataclassService#transitionException` declares the same `private static Long currentUserId()`
delegating to `CurrentActor.userId()`, and writes:

```java
case "APPROVED" -> {
    e.setApprovedAt(LocalDateTime.now());
    e.setApproverUserId(currentUserId());   // <- the half AiLifecycleService never wrote
}
```

`AiLifecycleService` has that helper **three lines below the switch**, where it feeds
`timeline(...)`'s `setActorUserId(currentUserId())`. So the mechanism was present, used for the
event, and not used for the row — [[F2-215]]'s two-of-N, with the two artefacts being sibling
services rather than sibling methods.

### It was not latent, and the row says so

| id | reference | status | created_at | decided_at | updated_at | updated_by | approver_user_id |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `REC-2026-CRD` | EXPIRED | 2026-05-26 **03:00:54** | 2026-05-26 **04:33:40.174675** | 04:33:40.**182667** | **1** | **NULL** |
| 3 | `REC-2025-AML` | RECERTIFIED_WITH_CONDITIONS | 2026-05-26 03:00:54 | 2025-06-10 (back-dated) | = created_at | NULL | NULL |

Byte-identical in dev and prod. Row 1 was seeded in the 03:00:54 batch with rows 2–4 and then
**decided through the API ninety-three minutes later**: `decided_at` 8 ms before `updated_at`,
`updated_by` = 1. 🔑 **The framework's row stamp captured the actor while the domain's own
attribution column stayed empty** — which is exactly why a row stamp can never substitute for an
attribution ([[F2-226]]'s rule, arriving from the other side). Row 3 is a back-dated seed row. So of
the two, **one is API-written and one is seed-written**, and F2-255's filing did not distinguish them.

### Evidence — probed live, pre 9/9 and post 9/9, against a planted `[REVIEW-TEST]` victim

| Leg | Pre-fix | Post-fix |
|---|---|---|
| victim planted `IN_REVIEW`, no clock, no decider | ✓ | ✓ |
| `rmanager` (RISK_MANAGER — holds the WRITE guard) on the APPROVE transition | **403** | **403** |
| `admin` decides `IN_REVIEW → RECERTIFIED` | **200** | **200** |
| the server stamped WHEN | `decided_at` set | `decided_at` set |
| the row's decider | **NULL** | **1** (the principal) |
| the wire's `approverUserId` | **null** | **1** |
| the timeline event's actor | `actor_user_id = 1` | `actor_user_id = 1` |
| `model_validation` has a completer column | **no** | **no** — filed |
| `retraining_event` has an approver column | **no** | **no** — filed |

The pre-fix run was taken against the running listener with the fix stashed and recompiled, because
the fixed tree alone can never show it ([[F2-244]]). ⚠ The transition guard is
`hasAnyRole('PLATFORM_ADMIN','CRO','CIO','DPO')` and the last three are held by nobody, so `admin` is
the only caller who can reach it — **`admin` proves nothing about authorization and does prove the
column is written**, and the guard itself remains F2-255's separately filed question.

### Both decision branches, including EXPIRED and REVOKED

Whatever the target state, `decidedAt` asserts *a decision was recorded at this moment* and the
register has exactly one column for who recorded it. Leaving `EXPIRED` and `REVOKED` blank would
reproduce the defect on a certification allowed to lapse and one withdrawn — the two an assurance
reader asks about hardest. The per-state nuance is not lost: `timeline(...)` writes an event carrying
both the event type and the actor, so the row-level column summarises a trail that already
distinguishes them.

⚠ **It refuses rather than storing null.** `CurrentActor.requireUserId` is [[F2-236]]'s primitive and
not a second mechanism ([[F2-190]]); a fallback would leave the hazard latent instead of absent
([[F2-213]]). ⚠ **A decision overwrites a prior ASSIGNMENT**: two live `DUE` rows carry an approver
with no `decided_at`, i.e. the seed used the column as *who is due to approve*. Once `decidedAt` is
stamped the column is an attribution ([[F2-236]]'s window rule) — a stale assignment left standing
beside a real clock would credit the decision to whoever was queued for it. Nothing in the platform
can make that assignment (no request field, no picker); adding one is a product decision, **filed**.

### The instrument, and four of my own drafts that were wrong — three of them under-reporting

`UnwritableActorColumnContractTest`: 432 entities by reflection, setter call sites by owner type from
the constant pool via ASM, a server-stamped act clock as the premise, entity-bound types subtracted
because Jackson writes those by reflection with no `INVOKEVIRTUAL` anywhere. **33 members** — 6
adjudicated, 27 on a work list with **no verdicts** ([[F2-188]]).

1. **Draft 1 asked whether the FIELD NAME was written anywhere in main sources** — so
   `Recertification#approverUserId` read as *written*, because `DataclassService` and
   `RegReportingService` each write a **different** entity's `approverUserId`.
   🔑 **A field-name fallback silently clears exactly the columns most likely to be spelled the
   same elsewhere, and it hid the site the gate was written for.** [[F2-187]] recorded that for
   methods (*"resolve per owner type"*); it recurs one noun across.
2. **Draft 2 resolved the owner from the SOURCE FILE NAME**, and `Entities.java` declares eleven
   nested `@Entity` classes — all eleven collapsed into one key called `Entities` whose field set was
   their union and whose owner name matched no bytecode at all. Eleven phantom rows, each looking
   exactly like a measured one. 🔑 **A source file is not a type.**
3. **Draft 3 claimed `getDeclaredFields()` excluded `BaseEntity`'s nine "by construction"** — it
   excludes *inherited* fields, not *redeclared* ones, and [[F2-215]] measured 259 entities declaring
   their own `createdBy` (111), `updatedBy` (104), `deletedBy` (56). The census went **62 → 209**,
   almost entirely row stamps. 🔑 **Moving to reflection fixed one bug and reintroduced the noise
   the source draft had excluded — a correction is not a monotone improvement, and "by construction"
   is a claim to check rather than a reason to stop checking.**
4. ⚠⚠ **The mutation harness then proved the CLOCK half VACUOUS.** It matched the clock setter by
   name across all sources, so across 432 entities the time-field names collide constantly and the
   answer was effectively always yes — **the mutation deleting the requirement altogether SURVIVED**.
   A surviving mutant is a hole only if the mutated code is wrong ([[F2-206]]); here it was, and the
   wrongness was that the condition could not fail. Resolved per owner from bytecode (a setter call
   on this entity, from a class that also calls a `java.time` `now()`), which makes it load-bearing.

⚠ **That tightening correctly excluded one member, and the exclusion is asserted rather than
hidden.** `FraudCaseUpdate#actorName` dropped out because `occurredAt` is a **field initialiser**
(`= LocalDateTime.now()`), [[F2-215]]'s third filling mechanism, which has no setter call for any
scan to find. [[F2-225]]/[[F2-226]] measured that population at 82 entities / 87 act-clock fields, so
it is large and it is **not** measured here — named with `FraudCaseUpdate` as its exemplar in both
directions, because a hard zero over a population an instrument cannot see is the most reassuring
possible artefact ([[F2-205]]).

⚠ **My own substantiality check refused my own verdicts on its first run.** Two `ADJUDICATED`
entries read *"DARK TWICE — see Policy#approverId."* at 35 characters, and the leg demanding a
consequence-naming reason fired — [[F2-188]]'s rule landing on the slice that wrote it.

### The largest sub-shape, left whole rather than adjudicated nine times

**Nine event registers declare `actorName` beside an `actorUserId` their service DOES write**:
`AiLifecycleEvent`, `CptyEvent`, `DataclassEvent`, `ObEvent`, `OutsourcingEvent`,
`RegInspectionUpdate`, `RegReportEvent`, `RrpEvent`, `ShariaEvent`. For the one that was read,
`AiLifecycleService#timeline` writes `setActorUserId(currentUserId())` and never the name, while
`toEvent` returns `e.getActorName()` — 🔑 **the id is stored and the NAME is the half the response
carries**, so every timeline entry renders a blank actor (confirmed live: `actor_user_id = 1`,
`actor_name = None`). Whether the other eight share that is a question for a reader.

### Verification

Pre-fix live probe **9/9** · post-fix **9/9** twice · gate pre-fix control **2 of 10 legs fire**,
naming `Recertification#approverUserId` exactly (the other 8 are tree-invariant by design: the noise
pinning, the positive control, the anti-vacuity floors, the reverse leg, the verdict substantiality,
the sibling-column assertions, the no-`@Builder` premise and the named blind spot) · mutation harness
**11 killed / 0 survived / 0 anchor-miss** · full suite **4,337/0/0**.

### Filed

- **`model_validation` has no completer column and `retraining_event` no approver column at all** —
  both stamp their clock from the server (`completed_at`, `approved_at`), and their only person
  columns are `validator_user_id` and `owner_user_id`, written from the request at creation, i.e.
  **assignments** ([[F2-226]]'s classification). `validation_type` admits `EXTERNAL_AUDIT`, so a
  validator need not be a platform principal at all ([[F2-224]]'s `auditorExternalParty` rule).
  Adding the columns is a migration and a **product decision**; asserted in the gate so the absence
  is countable rather than implied ([[F2-215]]'s two-of-N, pre-empted).
- The **27-member work list** with no verdicts, and the nine-register `actorName` sub-shape within it.
- **`ai_governance.recertification` cannot record an assigned approver through any route** — two live
  `DUE` rows hold one from the seed. A picker plus a request field is a product decision.
- **The `ai_governance` schema has zero CHECK constraints** on any of the three registers' `status`
  columns, so all three vocabularies are narrowed only by the Java machine ([[F2-221]]'s shape). Now
  cheaper for `recertification`, whose only writer this slice touched ([[F2-183]]'s rule).
- F2-255's guard question is unchanged: those three transitions remain
  `hasAnyRole('PLATFORM_ADMIN','CRO','CIO','DPO')` with all three domain roles held by nobody
  (`CIO`/`CRO` **ghosts in prod**), so only a platform administrator can reach them.

## F2-255 · A permission nobody can hold, and unlike a role nobody holds there is no administrator remedy

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-255 *(measured 2026-08-20. Provenance is [[F2-254]]'s filed §B2b work list — and re-deriving it first ([[F2-221]]) is what produced the finding: the filed conversion had **no target**, and asking why led one module over to a guard citing a permission that exists nowhere.)* |
| **Category** | Authorisation — a `@PreAuthorize` citing a `(MODULE, ACTION)` pair no migration creates · an instrument that emits a report and asserts nothing about it |
| **Severity** | **P2.** `POST /api/v1/audit-log/integrity/seal` — the F2-31 tamper-evidence seal — admitted `PLATFORM_ADMIN` and nobody else, in dev and prod alike, and **could not be granted to anyone**. Not data loss: a governance control built specifically to be demonstrable on request that none of the four roles able to observe it could exercise. |
| **Provenance** | F2-254 filed *"`module.ai` 3 (`AiLifecycleController#transition`/`#transitionRec`/`#transitionRetraining`) … readiest: one controller, one vocabulary, and `AI` has its own permission module."* Re-deriving that measured **`AI:APPROVE` does not exist** — the catalogue holds only `AI:READ`, `AI:WRITE`, `AI:EXPORT` — so *"`AI` has its own permission module"* was true and told me nothing about the action the guard needed. Asking *"how many guards cite a pair the catalogue does not define?"* found `AUDIT_LOG:WRITE`. |
| **Current State** | ✔ **FIXED 2026-08-20** (`f07f5b63`). **V380** catalogues `('AUDIT_LOG','WRITE')` and grants it to `ORG_ADMIN`, `GRC_ADMINISTRATOR`, `CISO` as literal role names. `PermissionCatalogueUsageTest` gains four legs that close the comparison inside the build. Suite **4,321/0/0** (up 4). **No main-source Java changed** — a migration, a test and two gated figures — so the running dev app matched the tree and the probes stand. |
| **Problem** | V272 catalogued `('AUDIT_LOG','READ')`; V320 added `('AUDIT_LOG','EXPORT')`. **`AUDIT_LOG:WRITE` appears in no migration in the packaged set and in neither database** (dev 140 pairs, prod 114). `ModulePermissionEvaluator` string-matches the granted authority `MODULE + '_' + ACTION`, so it could only ever answer false, and the route reduced to the code bypass. |
| **Root Cause** | RC-C — authorisation written as identity rather than capability, one dimension across from [[F2-253]]. |

🔑🔑 **A ROLE NOBODY HOLDS HAS AN ADMINISTRATOR REMEDY; A PERMISSION NOBODY CAN HOLD DOES NOT.**
F2-253 measured 24 guards *"left admitting PLATFORM_ADMIN alone, by attrition"* and recorded that a
tenant administrator can fix that without a jar — *"a remedy, not a defence, and says nothing about
the platform as shipped."* Here the remedy is gone: nothing can be granted, because there is nothing
in `iam.permissions` to grant. Closing it needs a migration, i.e. a jar.

🔑 **THE ROUTE'S OWN JAVADOC IS THE WITNESS.** *"Guarded on `AUDIT_LOG:WRITE` — it mutates the three
integrity columns. **It exists so the control can be EXERCISED rather than only observed**: a sealing
pass whose only trigger is a timer is a control nobody can demonstrate on request, and DF-1 showed
what an unobserved scheduled sweep costs (48 silent failures a day for eight days)."* Built for the
sole purpose of being demonstrable by whoever is asked — and demanding a permission nobody the
request would be put to could hold.

⚠⚠ **THE OBSERVE HALF, IN THE METHOD IMMEDIATELY ABOVE, IS CATALOGUED AND HAS FOUR LIVE HOLDERS.**
`GET /integrity` is `hasPermission('AUDIT_LOG','READ')`, held by `AUDITOR`, `CISO`,
`GRC_ADMINISTRATOR`, `INTERNAL_AUDITOR` (6 roles, 4 with a live holder, identical in dev and prod).
**Two adjacent methods, one permission each, and the one that was catalogued is the one that already
worked** — [[F2-215]]'s two-of-N at the finest range yet.

### Evidence — probed live, pre 10/10 and post 10/10 (twice, once against a freshly started app)

| Persona | Role | `GET /integrity` | `POST /integrity/seal` pre | post |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `admin` | PLATFORM_ADMIN (code bypass) | 200 | **200** `sealed:5` | 200 |
| `compliance` | GRC_ADMINISTRATOR | 200 | **403** | **200** |
| `so_officer` | CISO | 200 | **403** | **200** |
| `auditor` | AUDITOR | 200 | **403** | **403** — the narrowing holds |
| `ranalyst` | RISK_ANALYST (no `AUDIT_LOG` grant) | 403 | 403 | 403 |

⚠ **A 200 with `sealed:0` is indistinguishable from a 200 that wrote nothing**, and both non-admins
got exactly that because `admin` sorted first and had already sealed the five rows. A separate leg
proves the granted persona does the **work**: 0 unsealed → 3 reads → 1 unsealed → CISO seal
(`sealed:1`) → 0 unsealed.

### V380 narrows the READ tier rather than promoting it, and that is the V362 lesson as an assertion

V320 granted `EXPORT` to the whole six-role READ tier, which is coherent because exporting is
read-shaped. Sealing is not. Per role, with the reason recorded in the migration: `ORG_ADMIN`,
`GRC_ADMINISTRATOR`, `CISO` **granted** (they operate the platform's governance substrate);
`AUDITOR` **withheld** — an examiner watches the demonstration rather than performing the write;
`INTERNAL_AUDITOR` **withheld** — operating the seal would make internal audit the author of the
evidence it then examines; `IAM_LEAD` **withheld** — its `AUDIT_LOG:READ` is for identity events;
`PLATFORM_ADMIN` **withheld** per V272's own header (*"needs no grants (evaluator bypass)"*). Four
self-checks THROW: catalogued, granted to exactly three role names, **containment** (nobody may seal
a ledger they cannot read) and **strictness** (`|WRITE| < |READ|`, because containment alone is
satisfied by granting the whole tier — V362's defect). Applied twice to dev via pyodbc; prod
preconditions verified read-only first ([[F2-183]]).

⚠ **Widening it is an owner decision and is filed, not smuggled in under a catalogue fix.** What is
*not* a decision is that the route admitted nobody but the platform administrator and could not be
configured to admit anyone else.

### 🔑🔑 The instrument finding: the gate exists for exactly this, and asserts nothing about it

`PermissionCatalogueUsageTest`'s own javadoc names the class of defect and its two prior instances:
*"**Code guards on a permission nobody holds** — fail-closed dead code. This is **F2-23**
(`ADMIN:APPROVE` guarded 59 committee methods while not existing in `iam.permissions` at all) and
**F2-27**'s `AI:EXPORT`. Both were found by hand, months apart."* `grant_tightness.py`'s header calls
it failure mode **A**, *"GUARDED, UNGRANTABLE — the code demands a permission no role holds **(or
that the catalogue does not define)**."*

Its two build-time assertions were: the extraction found ≥ 85 pairs, and no guard names a
non-`UPPER_SNAKE` token. **Neither compares a cited pair against the catalogue.** That comparison was
deferred to a two-step manual script, on this stated premise: *"Measuring either direction needs the
guard set from the code joined to the grant counts from the database. **The suite has no database**,
so this half runs here… The tightness verdict itself is the script's job."*

🔑 **That premise is true of one of the two questions bundled under "tightness" and false of the
other.** *Who holds this permission* is a fact about `iam.role_permissions`. *Does this permission
exist at all* is a fact about the **migrations**, which sit in `src/main/resources` and are read
hermetically by a dozen tests in this suite already. The harder question's constraint was carried
over to the cheaper one — and the header's own parenthesis, *"(or that the catalogue does not
define)"*, is the half that never needed a database. Third instance of the defect, first one a build
can see.

⚠ **The gate is not a bare hard zero, and that is measured rather than conceded.** A fresh Flyway
install from V1 creates **93** catalogue pairs while the guards cite **128**: `V1` only `CREATE`s
`iam.permissions` and `V239`'s own header says BCM *"shipped with permission rows (BCM
READ/WRITE/DELETE)"*, so **36** core pairs are created by no migration at all and are present in both
live databases only because the bootstrap made them. Asserting `cited ⊆ migrations` would fail over
most of the platform ([[F2-214]]). They are declared as `CREATED_BEFORE_THE_MIGRATION_SET`, enforced
in **both** directions — a pair a migration starts creating must leave the list, and a pair no guard
cites any more must leave it too, or it would silently absorb a future ghost of the same name.

⚙ Controls: **pre-fix**, without V380, **2 of 6 legs fire** and both name `AUDIT_LOG:WRITE`, with
`createdByMigrations` 93 → 92 and `ungrantable` 0 → 1. **Mutation harness 4 killed / 0 survived /
0 anchor-miss** — dropping a BASE entry, adding an uncited one, making the parser file-scoped (so
`iam.role_permissions` triples like `('ORG_ADMIN','AUDIT_LOG','READ')` leak in as pairs) and dropping
the `VALUES` requirement. The parser carries positive controls for **both** insert idioms and negative
controls proving the two 3-argument guard forms are not read as module pairs — `hasPermission(#id,
'EXERCISE_RUN','OWNER')` ([[F2-159]]) and `hasPermission('AUDIT_COMMITTEE','COMMITTEE','SEAT')`
([[F2-177]]), whose first argument **is** quoted so only the closing paren distinguishes it. And the
Java gate agrees with the throwaway Python locator **exactly** (128 / 93 / 36), which is [[F2-213]]'s
rule earning its place rather than being quoted.

### Filed

- ⚠⚠ **A fresh Flyway install is 36 catalogue pairs short of what its own guards demand**, measured:
  `RISK:READ`, `RISK:WRITE`, `RISK:DELETE`, `BCM:READ/WRITE/DELETE`, `COMPLIANCE:READ/WRITE`,
  `CYBER:READ/WRITE/DELETE`, `PRIVACY:READ/WRITE`, `SCM:READ/WRITE/DELETE`, `ADMIN:READ/WRITE`,
  `REPORTING:READ/WRITE`, `CHANGE:APPROVE/DELETE`, `SUST:APPROVE`, `TPRM:APPROVE` and eight EXPORT
  pairs. Every guard citing them would be closed to all but the platform administrator, and **a
  missing catalogue row cannot be fixed from the role-admin screen the way a missing grant can**. Same
  family as the recorded *"225 grants short of dev"* gap, one table up. Back-filling is a migration
  with a per-tenant impact question — **owner decision**, and the declared list makes it countable.
- **`module.ai`'s three transition guards remain administrator-only**, and the filed conversion has no
  target. `APPROVE = hasAnyRole('PLATFORM_ADMIN','CRO','CIO','DPO')` on
  `/validations|retrainings|recertifications/{id}/transition`; `CRO`/`CIO`/`DPO` all hold **0 users**
  in dev and `CIO`/`CRO` are **absent from `iam.roles` in prod**. **15 live rows in each database sit
  on a state with an outgoing edge** (`recertification` DUE 8 + IN_REVIEW 1, `retraining_event`
  PROPOSED 3 + IN_PROGRESS 2, `model_validation` IN_PROGRESS 1). ⚠ The module has **two conventions**:
  `AiSuggestionController` uses `hasPermission('AI','WRITE')` throughout while the three ML-model
  controllers use role lists naming `RISK_MANAGER`/`CISO`, **which are held** — so only the lifecycle
  controller is locked out. ⚠ And the guards were never carrying a four-eyes bar: `WRITE` and
  `APPROVE` **overlap on `CIO` and `DPO`**, and no transition compares the actor against anything, so
  collapsing them onto one permission retires nothing — unlike [[F2-254]]'s BIA tiers, whose audiences
  are disjoint. `AI:WRITE` (41 roles, 8 live) is the module's own convention and the honest target;
  cataloguing `AI:APPROVE` instead is a grant decision. **Owner decision.**
- **`ai_governance.recertification.approver_user_id` has no writer in any code path.**
  `transitionRecertification` stamps `decided_at` from the server's clock and never touches the
  approver, which the response DTO declares. Measured identically in dev and prod: **2 of 13 rows hold
  `decided_at` with no approver** and the 5 that carry one were written by the seed — so every
  recertification decided through the API from now on lands in that bucket. [[F2-223]]'s split
  attribution in its purest form: the server owns WHEN and **nobody** owns WHO, on an ISO/IEC 42001
  model-recertification decision. `currentUserId()` already exists in the same service and is used for
  the timeline event's actor, so the attribution is available and simply not stored on the row.
- The remaining **§B2b** guards after F2-254: `module.audit_committee` **3** (`BOARD_SECRETARY`, 0
  holders), `module.bcm` **2** (the BIA tiers), `module.rrp` **1** (`RRP_OWNER`, a **ghost** in both
  databases). No verdicts ([[F2-188]]).
- **In prod, 27 cited pairs are absent from `iam.permissions`** across `AML`, `AUTOMATION`,
  `CONSUMER`, `CPTY`, `ETHICS`, `OPENBANKING`, `SHARIA`. ⚠ **This is the migration gap, not a defect**
  — prod is at applied head V344 and V345–V380 are pending, so Flyway closes it on the next deploy.
  Stating the distinction matters: reported as-is it would read as 27 live findings. The discriminator
  is the migration set, and it took reading the migrations to find. 🔑 **The authority for "does this
  permission exist in the platform" is the migrations — never either database, since one can be behind
  (prod) and the other ahead via bootstrap (dev).**

### ⚙ Two self-inflicted errors, both caught by running things

- **`iam.permissions.description_en` is `NVARCHAR(300)`** and my first draft was ~520 characters. SQL
  Server **2628** names the column and the truncated value but **not the limit**, so the fix is to
  resolve the length from `sys.columns` — the guessed-name family since [[F2-198]], now at a column
  *width* rather than a column *name*.
- **`BUILD FAILURE` with no `Tests run:` line meant nothing ran** ([[F2-252]]) — and the cause was
  neither a compile error nor a stale report: my working directory had drifted to the repo root, where
  there is no POM. 🔑 **The rule generalises past JDK version mismatches: the absence of that line is
  the tell, whatever the cause.**

## F2-254 · A role nobody holds made thirteen BCM writes administrator-only, and the COMPOSED bucket hid five of them

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-254 *(measured 2026-08-20. Provenance is [[F2-253]]'s own filing — the `module.bcm` block of §B2b, re-derived against BOTH databases before anything was touched, because a filed item inherits the population of the slice that filed it ([[F2-221]]).)* |
| **Category** | Authorisation — thirteen write guards decided by a role held by nobody · two pre-existing gates keyed on a spelling rather than on their own claim |
| **Severity** | **P2.** Thirteen write routes across seven controllers admitted `PLATFORM_ADMIN` and nobody else, identically in dev and prod: archiving a BCP binder or a quantitative BIA, starting an exercise run, instantiating a scenario, publishing an MTPD inheritance assessment, the entire process-vendor-dependency register (**12 live rows**), and five run-scoped writes on the exercise runtime and observer consoles (**4 live runs**). Not data loss; a block of BCM capability unavailable to every persona, with a 403 indistinguishable from a deliberate refusal. |
| **Provenance** | F2-253's filed work list. Executing it required re-deriving §B2b first — and the re-derivation found **five more members the census cannot see**, so the filing's "10" was an undercount of the module's real total by half. |
| **Current State** | ✔ **FIXED 2026-08-20.** Thirteen guards now ask `hasPermission('BCM','WRITE')` or `…'DELETE'`. `BASELINE_PURE_ROLE_SITES` **397 → 389**, role-leg sites **496 → 483**, both re-derived from the build's own stdout ([[F2-207]]) and the census regenerated in the same commit. §B2b **17 → 9**; `module.bcm` **10 → 2**. |
| **Problem** | `hasAnyRole('BCM_MANAGER','PLATFORM_ADMIN')` on eight routes, and the same role leg ORed with F2-161's ownership clause on five more. **`BCM_MANAGER` is held by no user** — 0 holders in dev, 0 in prod. A role guard never reaches `ModulePermissionEvaluator`, so it never reaches the `PLATFORM_ADMIN` bypass either: the expression passed review only because it happened to *name* the administrator. Probed live as `compliance`, who holds `BCM:WRITE`, `BCM:DELETE` **and** `BCM:APPROVE`: **13 of 13 answered 403** while `admin` reached the handler on every one. |
| **Root Cause** | RC-C — authorisation written as identity rather than capability. A role name is not grantable without a jar and carries no admin bypass, so a role that is never assigned turns a guard into a permanently-narrow one with no diagnostic. |
| **Business Impact** | ISO 22301 / SAMA BCM. A BCM lead could not start a scheduled exercise run, instantiate a scenario from the library, publish an MTPD inheritance assessment, or maintain the process-to-vendor dependency register that the whole MTPD inheritance calculation reads. Every one of those is the BCM function's own routine work, and the only account that could do it was the platform administrator — whose acting on those registers produces an attribution nobody intended. |
| **Technical Impact** | ⚠⚠ **The census sees eight of the thirteen and calls the other five "already tight".** It files a guard as COMPOSED when the expression MENTIONS `hasPermission`, not when the permission is **ANDed** — F2-253's own third finding, left filed because splitting that bucket changes a published artefact's schema. So `ExerciseRuntimeController#dispatch`/`#customInject`/`#transition` and `ExerciseObserverController#assignObserver`/`#removeObserver` never appeared in §B2b at all. **A filed count is only as complete as the bucket that produced it.** |
| **UX Impact** | None visible, which is the problem. A 403 from a role guard looks exactly like a 403 that was meant. |
| **Recommendation** | 1. As shipped. 2. The **two BIA approval tiers** are deliberately unconverted — see Trade-offs; F2-152 is the prerequisite. 3. **9 guards remain** in §B2b (`ai` 3, `audit_committee` 3, `bcm` 2, `rrp` 1) — still a work list with no verdicts ([[F2-188]]). 4. The COMPOSED-bucket split is now twice-filed and should be its own slice. |
| **Alternatives** | Granting `BCM_MANAGER` to a seeded user was rejected for F2-253's reason: it fixes one seed, leaves the class, and says nothing about a customer who never assigns the role. Converting the **read** guards was rejected on a measurement — `CISO` is named on them and holds only `BCM:EXPORT`, no `BCM:READ`, so converting one would DROP a live role (`so_officer` reads these registers today). |
| **Trade-offs** | ⚠⚠ **`cfoApprove` and `boardApprove` are NOT converted, and that is a decision rather than an omission.** They are the CFO tier and the board tier of one quantitative BIA; `BCM:APPROVE` is a single permission, so landing both on it lets one principal take both tiers — and `BCM:APPROVE` also includes `BCM_MANAGER`, which is stage **one** of the same chain. The four-eyes bar that would make one shared permission safe **cannot be built today**: `sys.columns` says `bcm.bia_quantitative` carries `cfo_approver_name` (a caller-supplied string) and **no `board_approved_by` column at all**, so neither tier has an identity to compare. Choosing who holds a financial versus a board approval is an owner decision plus a migration. ⚙ `ExerciseObserverController#removeObserver` → `BCM:DELETE` creates one asymmetry worth naming: `RISK_MANAGER` holds WRITE and not DELETE, so they can now assign an observer and not remove one. That is the permission catalogue's decision, not this slice's, and the facilitator — who actually manages a run's roster — is admitted by the ownership leg on both routes. |
| **Effort** | **S** for the thirteen guards; **XS** each for the two gate repairs. No migration; V379 remains head. |
| **Verification** | Live probe **25/25 pre-fix** and **27/27 post-fix** as `compliance` (`admin` proves nothing about authorization). Every destructive leg aims at a **nonexistent id**, so the discriminator is 403 (guard refused) vs 404 (guard admitted) and nothing real is written — the one live quantitative BIA is a seeded governance record parked at `CFO_APPROVED` and was never archived to prove a point. One leg writes for real, on `process_vendor_dependency`, planting its own row ([[F2-206]]) and hard-deleting it with `CHARINDEX` in a `finally`; residue 0 and both registers back to their seeded counts (12 and 4). Non-regression: `auditor` and `viewer` still 403 on every write, `rmanager` gains WRITE and stays 403 on DELETE. **F2-161's ownership leg isolated** by planting a run facilitated by `ranalyst`, who holds no BCM grant at all: admitted on the run they facilitate, **403 on `#start`**, 403 on `rmanager`'s run — the same in both modes, which is what makes it a non-regression rather than a claim. `BcmAdminOnlyGuardConversionTest` **6/6**; pre-fix control **2 of 6 legs fire on master**, and the four that do not are tree-invariant *by design* and say so: a synthetic self-test over literal fixtures, and three pins (the two BIA tiers, the read guards, the map disjointness) whose subject is unchanged by this slice. Both repaired gates **still pass on master's guards**, which is the control that matters for a detector repair — the repair preserved the original claim rather than weakening it. Three ratchets green; backend suite **4,317** with the one failure being the repaired gate. |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-20** — thirteen guards and two instruments. The two BIA tiers, the nine remaining §B2b guards and the COMPOSED-bucket split are filed. |
| **References** | `module/bcm/binder/controller/BcpBinderController#archive`, `module/bcm/controller/BiaQuantitativeController#archive` (+ the `BOARD_APPROVE_GUARD` and `#cfoApprove` pins), `module/bcm/cycle/runtime/controller/ExerciseRuntimeController#start`/`#dispatch`/`#customInject`/`#transition`, `module/bcm/cycle/runtime/observer/controller/ExerciseObserverController#assignObserver`/`#removeObserver`, `module/bcm/cycle/controller/ExerciseScenarioLibraryController#instantiate`, `module/bcm/mtpd_inheritance/controller/MtpdInheritanceController#publish`, `…/ProcessVendorDependencyController#create`/`#update`/`#delete`, `BcmAdminOnlyGuardConversionTest` (new), `ExerciseRunOwnershipGuardTest` (repaired), `BiaApprovalChainGuardTest` (repaired), `RoleGuardConversionRatchetTest.BASELINE_PURE_ROLE_SITES`, `Appendix/ROLE_GUARD_CENSUS.md` (§B2b) |
| **Lesson** | 🔑🔑 **THREE SEPARATE SLICES EACH CORRECTED A GHOST INSIDE ONE OF THESE EXPRESSIONS AND LEFT A ZERO-HOLDER ROLE STANDING BESIDE IT, BECAUSE "DOES THIS NAME EXIST?" WAS THE ONLY QUESTION ANY OF THEM ASKED.** [[F2-52]] on `SubprocessorController` (closed by [[F2-253]]); F2-52 again on `BOARD_APPROVE_GUARD`, which chose `EXECUTIVE_REVIEWER` because it *"already holds `BCM:APPROVE`, so it is a role the platform already trusts"* — **a fact about GRANTS, where whether a guard admits anybody is a fact about `iam.user_roles`**; and [[F2-161]] on `ExerciseRuntimeController#start`, whose own comment removed `FACILITATOR` for matching no row in `iam.roles` and *"admitting nobody"* while keeping `BCM_MANAGER`, **which admits nobody**. A role's grant list tells you what the platform trusts it with; only its holders tell you whether it is anybody. F2-253 had one instance of this and read as bad luck; three is a shape. 🔑 **And the ownership leg cannot rescue a create.** F2-161 added `or hasPermission(#id,'EXERCISE_RUN','OWNER')` so a facilitator could drive their own run, and `#start` has no such leg **because there is no run yet to own** — so of the five composed writes, four were carried by the facilitator and the one that creates the record was not. Probed: `ranalyst` transitions the run they facilitate and is 403 on `#start`. **A facilitator could drive an exercise run they were not allowed to create**, and the seeded runs exist because an administrator made them. ⚠⚠ **Both pre-existing gates failed on the CORRECT conversion, and both were keyed on a spelling rather than on their own claim** — the one failure a gate must never have ([[F2-214]]), and it trains the next reader to edit the assertion instead of the code. `ExerciseRunOwnershipGuardTest` asserted `!guard.contains("hasAnyRole(")` while its claim is that an oversight leg EXISTS: **it failed on the change that made its own claim more true**, since the "oversight" it was checking for admitted the administrator alone and `hasPermission('BCM','WRITE')` admits three live roles ([[F2-197]]: a gate keyed on an identifier breaks on your own refactor). `BiaApprovalChainGuardTest`'s ghost detector ran a quoted-token regex over the whole expression, so `hasPermission('BCM','DELETE')` read as two roles called `BCM` and `DELETE` — **a ghost-role gate that flags every role-to-permission conversion F2-05 exists to make**; and its body walked every method while its name says *"no STAGE"*, so it owned an opinion about routes it had never reviewed. ⚙ Smaller ones. **Five guessed names in one slice** — three tables (`bcp_binder_exports`, `exercise_scenario_library`, `business_processes`), one column (`run_id` for `exercise_run_id`) and one method (`listAssessments`) — and the column one threw **inside a `finally`**, which is the worst place for it: the cleanup died and left a planted row live until I noticed. Resolve from `sys.tables`/`sys.columns`; a near-miss resolver is what turned three of those into one line of output instead of three false "no data" claims. And **my own patch-script assertion failed on a correct edit** because an insertion-style edit legitimately keeps its anchor — F2-206's rule, applied to an assertion. |

### Filed

- **The two BIA approval tiers**, with the prerequisite now measured rather than asserted:
  `bcm.bia_quantitative` has **no `board_approved_by` column**, so the four-eyes bar that would let
  `cfo-approve` and `board-approve` share `BCM:APPROVE` has no identity to compare. **F2-152 is the
  prerequisite, and it is the same finding**: that row already records *"a board approval with no
  signer, and a CFO approval whose signer is whatever the request says"*. 🔑 **The guard lockout and
  the missing attribution are one problem and F2-52 filed them as two** — the recorded blocker
  ("nothing enforces that they are different people") is removable by building the thing it says is
  missing, which is [[F2-178]]'s rule about re-measuring a blocker before believing its estimate.
  Owner decision on who holds a financial versus a board approval, plus a migration.
- **9 guards remain in §B2b** — `module.ai` 3 (`AiLifecycleController#transition`/`#transitionRec`/
  `#transitionRetraining`, naming `CRO`/`CIO`/`DPO`, all unheld), `module.audit_committee` 3
  (`AuditCommitteeDashboardController#finalizeSnapshot`/`#generate`/`#recordResolution`, naming
  `BOARD_SECRETARY`), `module.bcm` 2 (the BIA tiers above), `module.rrp` 1 (`RrpController#submit`).
  No verdicts ([[F2-188]]). ⚠ `module.ai`'s three are the readiest: they are one controller, one
  vocabulary, and `AI` has its own permission module.
- **`COMPOSED` means "mentions `hasPermission`", not "ANDed onto one"** — filed by F2-253 and now
  demonstrated to hide real members, not just mislabel them. Five of this slice's thirteen sat in
  that bucket. Splitting the kind changes the census's published schema, so it is its own slice, and
  it should re-run §B2b afterwards because **the count will go up**.
- **`SubprocessorService.create` honours a client-supplied `subprocessorCode`** — carried from
  F2-253, still open, outside `ClientSuppliedReferenceRatchetTest`'s `setExternalId`/`setRefNumber`
  key ([[F2-248]]'s headline that a gate key is a spelling).
- **`bcm.exercise_run` has two CHECK constraints and `bcm.process_vendor_dependency` has none**,
  while the latter's `dependency_type` and `dependency_strength` are narrowed only by `@Pattern` on
  the request record. Cheap now that this slice closed the register's only write path to a
  permission-guarded one, but it is [[F2-183]]'s rule: the constraint and its writer land together.

## F2-253 · Every PDPL Article 30 write was administrator-only, and the census bucket for exactly that read 0

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-253 *(measured 2026-08-20. Provenance is a sentence in `CLAUDE.md`, not a filed item: "existing is not held — several surviving names resolve to roles with **0 active users**, which fails identically and **is not counted by anything**.")* |
| **Category** | Authorisation — a role-name guard naming a role nobody holds · an instrument whose bucket for that defect tests existence instead of holding |
| **Severity** | **P2.** All seven write routes of the PDPL Article 30 sub-processor register — create, update, transition, **approve**, **review**, material-change and the event ledger — admitted `PLATFORM_ADMIN` and nobody else, identically in dev and prod, over **8 live sub-processors** (Azure KSA, SIMAH, the SDAIA Tawakkalna platform). Not data loss; a governance capability the Data Protection Officer owns, unavailable to every persona including the DPO's own, with a 403 indistinguishable from a deliberate refusal. |
| **Provenance** | Not a filed finding — a **parenthetical warning in `CLAUDE.md`** that said this population existed and was uncounted. Executing it required re-deriving the population first ([[F2-221]]): `Appendix/scripts/role_guard_census.py` already computes a holder count, so the question was why its report showed none. |
| **Current State** | ✔ **FIXED 2026-08-20.** `SubprocessorController.WRITE_GUARD` is `hasPermission('PRIVACY','WRITE')`. `BASELINE_PURE_ROLE_SITES` **404 → 397**, re-derived from the build rather than subtracted ([[F2-207]]). The census script grew section **B2b** and now runs at all. |
| **Problem** | `WRITE_GUARD` was `hasAnyRole('DPO','PLATFORM_ADMIN')` and **`DPO` is held by no user** — 0 holders in dev and 0 in prod. A role guard gets no `PLATFORM_ADMIN` bypass (`ModulePermissionEvaluator` is never called), so that expression passed only because it happened to *name* the administrator. Probed live as `compliance`, who holds `PRIVACY:WRITE`: **7 of 7 write routes answered 403** while `admin` created at 201 and the read guard admitted the same caller at 200. |
| **Root Cause** | RC-C — authorisation written as identity rather than capability. A role name is not grantable without a jar and carries no admin bypass, so a role that is never assigned turns a guard into a permanently-narrow one with no diagnostic. |
| **Business Impact** | PDPL Article 30 requires a controller to authorise and keep records of sub-processors. The register holds 8 approved sub-processors, three of them Saudi national infrastructure. Recording a **12-month review**, a **material change** (which forces re-review) or a **DPO approval** was impossible for anyone but a platform administrator — who is not a data-protection officer, and whose acting on that register produces an attribution nobody intended. |
| **Technical Impact** | ⚠⚠ **The instrument built for this defect reported 0.** `ROLE_GUARD_CENSUS.md` has a bucket named *"left admitting PLATFORM_ADMIN alone, by attrition"* and it read **0**, because it tests whether the other named roles are **absent from `iam.roles`** rather than whether anybody **holds** them. The script computes `holders` at the top and uses it in exactly one bucket, `thin`, which requires *every* alive name to be unheld — and almost every guard in this platform names `PLATFORM_ADMIN`, which is held, so `thin` can never fire for them. **The question the report exists to answer was being asked of existence.** Measured: **24 pure guards** admit nobody but an administrator, identically in dev and prod. |
| **UX Impact** | None visible, which is the problem. A 403 from a role guard looks exactly like a 403 that was meant. |
| **Recommendation** | 1. As shipped. 2. **17 guards remain** in the same state — a work list, deliberately with no verdicts ([[F2-188]]). 3. The read half is an **owner decision** (see Trade-offs). 4. Two ghosts exist in the deployed database — see Alternatives. |
| **Alternatives** | Granting `DPO` to a seeded user was rejected: it fixes one seed and leaves the class, and says nothing about a customer who never assigns the role. ⚠ **Filed, and sharper than it looks:** `BASELINE_GHOST_ROLE_NAMES` is a **hard zero** asserted against `ROLE_CATALOGUE`, a constant whose own javadoc says it was *"read 2026-08-06 (58 rows), then 2026-08-07 (69)"* — i.e. from **dev**. Prod holds exactly **58** roles, and `CIO` and `CRO` are recited by guards and **absent from `iam.roles` there**. So that invariant is a statement about the *packaged* platform, and the deployed database has **2 real ghosts** until the 35 pending migrations land. |
| **Trade-offs** | ⚠⚠ **`READ_GUARD` was deliberately NOT converted, and the reason is a measurement rather than caution.** It names `CISO`, `COMPLIANCE_OFFICER` and `RISK_MANAGER`; all three are **HELD**, and **none holds `PRIVACY:READ`**. So converting drops three live roles — probed: `so_officer` (CISO, no privacy grant at all) reads the register at 200 today — and granting them `PRIVACY:READ` instead widens them from this register to the **whole privacy read surface**, the DSR queue and the breach register, which carry data subjects' identities. That is a decision about who may read personal data, not a side effect of a guard fix. Conversely `VIEWER` holds `PRIVACY:READ` and is refused this register today, so converting would also *add* it. **Owner decision.** |
| **Effort** | **S** for the guard; **XS** for the census script. No migration; V379 remains head. |
| **Priority** | Done. |
| **Verification** | Live probe **9/9 pre-fix** and **9/9 post-fix** as `compliance` (`admin` proves nothing about authorization), against a sub-processor the probe **planted itself** ([[F2-206]]) — never one of the 8 seeded PDPL records — hard-deleted with `CHARINDEX` in a `finally`, residue 0, register back to 8 rows both times. Plus a **6/6 non-regression** probe: `viewer` (holds `PRIVACY:READ`, not `WRITE`) still refused every write, `so_officer` still reads at 200, `ranalyst` refused both. `SubprocessorPermissionConversionTest` **5/5**; pre-fix control: the shipped gate fires **4 of its 5 legs on master**, and the one that does not is named in the test as a deliberate pin whose tripwire is in the future. ⚠ Its FIRST run fired only **3**, which is how the fifth leg was caught — it was scoped to routes whose guard *already equalled* the permission, so on the pre-fix tree it inspected an empty set and could only pass. Rescoped to the seven write routes by name. `RoleGuardConversionRatchetTest` 4/4 at the re-derived 397, `RoleNameSurfaceRatchetTest` 2/2, `ControllerAuthorizationRatchetTest` 3/3. Census independently reproduced by a throwaway script over both databases: **380 of 397** pure guards reachable by a non-administrator, matching the regenerated report exactly. |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-20** — the guard and the instrument. The read half, the 17 remaining guards and the two prod ghosts are filed. |
| **References** | `module/privacy/subprocessor/controller/SubprocessorController` (`WRITE_GUARD`, `READ_GUARD`), `SubprocessorPermissionConversionTest` (new), `RoleGuardConversionRatchetTest.BASELINE_PURE_ROLE_SITES`, `Appendix/scripts/role_guard_census.py` (§B2b), `Appendix/ROLE_GUARD_CENSUS.md`, `module/attachment/service/AttachmentAccessPolicy` (`SUBPROCESSOR`, unchanged **on purpose**) |
| **Lesson** | 🔑🔑 **A ROLE THAT EXISTS AND IS HELD BY NOBODY FAILS EXACTLY LIKE A GHOST, AND EVERY BUCKET IN THE INSTRUMENT WAS KEYED ON EXISTENCE.** `hasAnyRole('X')` tests for the granted authority `ROLE_X`; an unassigned role grants it to no one. The only difference from a ghost is that an administrator can fix it without a jar — **which is a remedy, not a defence, and says nothing about the platform as shipped.** The census's own header even explains why ghosts matter *"because a role guard has no administrator bypass"*, and then tests for absence, on a corpus where almost every guard names the administrator. 🔑 **And the guard's own javadoc is the finding's witness.** [[F2-52]] audited this exact pair, wrote eleven lines correcting a ghost on `READ_GUARD` — *"Correcting a ghost widens access and dropping one does not"* — and left `WRITE_GUARD` naming a zero-holder role **one line below**. That rule is about *existence* and has no vocabulary for the case one line down. [[F2-215]]'s two-of-N, in a comment whose entire subject is this question. ⚠⚠ **A third finding, measured and filed rather than fixed, and it nearly caught me:** `RoleGuardConversionRatchetTest` line 929 is `boolean composed = HAS_PERMISSION.matcher(expr).find()` — **presence, not conjunction** — while the census prints that bucket as *"role leg ANDed onto a permission — already tight"* and the ratchet's javadoc counts it out of F2-05's backlog on that basis. Measured: **96 of the 99 are ORs**, and an OR leg is *wider* than the permission alone. Most are correct designs (`permission or admin`; [[F2-159]]/[[F2-161]]'s `roles or record-OWNER`), but roughly ten still carry their **general** audience on a role list while being labelled tight. I was about to add `or hasPermission('PRIVACY','READ')` to the read guard to close a write-without-read hazard — which would have made a widened guard read as a tightening, and passed. ⚙ Two smaller ones. **The script could not run at all**: it prints an arrow and an em-dash, a Windows console is cp1252, so every invocation died in `emit` before writing a line — *"nothing runs it"* was literally true. And **a prose claim wraps**, so asserting one needs FLOWED javadoc with quoted spans stripped *after* isolating the comments — line-scoped stripping cannot cross the newline inside a wrapped quotation, and whole-file stripping pairs a citation's quote with an unrelated string literal's ([[F2-216]]). |

### Filed

- **17 pure guards still admit nobody but a platform administrator** — a work list with **no verdicts**
  ([[F2-188]]), printed as §B2b of `ROLE_GUARD_CENSUS.md` and identical in dev and prod:
  `module.bcm` **10** (`BcpBinderController#archive`, `BiaQuantitativeController#archive`, `#boardApprove`,
  `#cfoApprove`, `ExerciseRuntimeController#start`, `ExerciseScenarioLibraryController#instantiate`,
  `MtpdInheritanceController#publish`, `ProcessVendorDependencyController#create`/`#update`/`#delete`) ·
  `module.ai` **3** (`AiLifecycleController#transition`, `#transitionRec`, `#transitionRetraining`) ·
  `module.audit_committee` **3** (`AuditCommitteeDashboardController#finalizeSnapshot`, `#generate`,
  `#recordResolution`) · `module.rrp` **1** (`RrpController#submit`). The unheld roles are `BCM_MANAGER`
  ([[F2-161]] already found it unheld once), `EXECUTIVE_REVIEWER`, `CFO`, `CRO`, `CIO`, `DPO`
  ([[F2-209]] already found *that* one), `BOARD_SECRETARY`. 🔑 **Two of these roles have each been
  reported unheld before, one endpoint at a time — which is what a population looks like when nothing
  counts it.** Read each guard and measure its permission's grant diff before converting; two of them
  (`#cfoApprove`, `#boardApprove`) are **distinct approval tiers of one BIA** and collapsing them onto
  one permission would retire a four-eyes distinction, so they are not a mechanical sweep.
- **The read half of this controller** — an owner decision, stated in Trade-offs above and pinned by
  `SubprocessorPermissionConversionTest#theReadGuardStillNamesRolesAndTheAttachmentSurfaceStillMirrorsIt`
  so that converting it fails the build until `AttachmentAccessPolicy`'s entry moves in the same commit.
- **`COMPOSED` means "mentions `hasPermission`", not "ANDed onto one"** — 96 of 99, with roughly ten
  still authorising their general population by role name while sitting outside F2-05's backlog. Fixing
  it means splitting the kind in the extractor and in the script that parses its output, which changes a
  published artefact's schema, so it is its own slice.
- **`CIO` and `CRO` are ghosts in the deployed database** (58 roles at Flyway head V344 against a
  packaged head of V379). The hard-zero ghost invariant holds against the packaged catalogue only.
- **30 of the 38 recited role names are held by nobody in dev** (28 in prod). No pure guard is closed to
  everyone, because each also names a held role — so the harm is narrowness rather than closure, and
  that distinction is what §B2b now measures.
- **`SubprocessorService.create` honours a client-supplied `subprocessorCode`** — F2-172(d)'s family, on
  the reference an auditor cites. Outside `ClientSuppliedReferenceRatchetTest`'s key, which is
  `setExternalId`/`setRefNumber`: [[F2-248]]'s headline that a gate key is a spelling.
