  `cyber.cyber_incidents :: affected_asset_id` (12 of 24) are sharper by harm but need an
  owner decision first, because there are **multiple disjoint asset registers**
  (`cyber_lc.assets`, `socops.ot_asset`, `asm.assets`) and picking the target is F2-196's
  shape.
* **The 32 live unlinked rows.** Linking them means deciding, per row, which registered
  vendor an annotated free-text label meant (`'AWS (managed cloud services)'` →
  `'AWS'`?) — repair rewrites live rows in two real databases, so it is an **owner
  decision** (F2-183/F2-196).
* **`scm.vendors` exists for organisation 1 only** (31 rows, ids 17–80), so the vendor picker
  is empty for any other tenant and the `emptyHint` is the whole of what they see. Not a
  defect; worth knowing before reading the picker's behaviour on a fresh tenant.
* **The four tables still have no FOREIGN KEY on their vendor column.** Now cheap to add,
  since this slice closed every open writer (F2-183's rule) — but it needs the 32 unlinked
  rows settled first, because a NOT NULL FK cannot be added over them and a nullable one adds
  nothing this slice has not already enforced.
* **`prod` is missing `change_mgmt.change_requests.cab_decision_by_id`** — an ordinary
  consequence of prod being ~35 migrations behind (head V344 against a packaged V379), noted
  because the measurement script had to grow a state for it so that "the column is not there"
  could not read as "the measurement is broken".

## F2-245 · A soft FK that also carries the parent's identity is making two claims, and only the parent can answer the second

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-245 |
| **Title** | `risk.scenarios` stores `risk_id` (which row) beside `risk_code` and `risk_title_en` (what it is called), and `RiskScenarioService.create` took all three from the request. **11 of 11 live scenarios in dev and prod store a `risk_title_en` that is not the title of the risk their `risk_id` names**, and every `risk_code` is an `RSK-2026-NNN` value from a code space `risk.risks` does not have. The create form collected the two labels as free text and never collected `riskId` at all, so a scenario raised through the platform's own screen could never be found from its risk |
| **Severity** | 🟠 P2 (a quantitative FAIR / Monte-Carlo / stress-test register — the artefact a risk committee reads — where the risk named on screen is not the risk the row is joined to, on **every** live row in both databases; and the only surface that creates scenarios could not link them at all. Reproduced live at 201 against the exact seeded shape, then refused) |
| **Status** | 🟢 CLOSED 2026-08-19 |
| **Programme** | Platform Bible F2 · control integrity / reference integrity |
| **Modules** | `risk/scenario` (the resolver, the create DTO), `tss-grc-ui-v2` (`lib/riskScenarios.ts`, `RiskScenariosPage`, both dictionaries); 2 gates added (1 invariant + 1 census), 5 behaviour tests on a service that had **none**; F2-244's 22-site store-side filing re-derived |

### Re-deriving F2-244's filing first (F2-221), and what that corrected

F2-244 filed a 22-site store-side work list and named three sites as sharpest by harm. Re-deriving
before executing corrected the ordering and refuted two of the named seven:

* **`AuditEngagementService#create::annualPlanId` — the filing's own top pick — is the LEAST urgent
  kind.** There are **two** classes with that simple name (`module/audit_eng` and
  `module/compliance`), which is one of F2-222's filed 15 duplicate-simple-name hazards, and the
  filing keyed on the simple name. Only `audit_eng` declares the field; it is
  **`String(64)`, not a numeric FK**, and its only two readers are the setter and the DTO mapping it
  out — **nothing dereferences it**. Re-ranked by F2-239's *what the reference's target IS*, that is
  the least urgent shape.
* **`NdiGapService#updateGap::riskId` — REFUTED.** It validates on **both** write paths through
  `NdiCrossLinkService.validateRiskExists`, which does `findById` + an organisation filter + a throw.
* **`RiskControlFindingPivotService` — REFUTED at all three sites.** Each dereferences
  `link.getRiskId()` with a bare `findById`, and each is followed by
  `.filter(r -> orgId.equals(r.getOrganisationId()))`. A grep located them; reading adjudicated them.

🔑 **`NdiCrossLinkService`'s own javadoc is why seven peers looked covered.** It calls itself
*"the single place where those soft links are validated against their real targets"* — true **of
NDI**, and the sentence scopes the claim to one module while eight services write the same
`risk_id` column into the same target table. **Exactly 1 of the 8 body-bound writers validates it.**
F2-215's two-of-N, where the phrase that reassures is the phrase that narrows.

### The finding

`risk.scenarios` carries `risk_id`, `risk_code` and `risk_title_en`. The create wrote all three from
the request:

```java
s.setRiskId(req.riskId());
s.setRiskCode(req.riskCode());
s.setRiskTitleEn(req.riskTitleEn());
```

That is **two different claims** — an id saying *which row*, and two strings saying *what that row is
called* — and nothing compared them. Measured against `risk.risks`, identical in dev and prod:

| | measured |
|---|---|
| live scenarios | 11 |
| scenarios whose `risk_title_en` ≠ the parent's `title_en` | **11 of 11** |
| scenarios whose `risk_id` resolves to no risk at all | 1 (`risk_id = 25`, `MAX(id)` is 152) |
| `risk_code` values in `RSK-2026-NNN` form | 11 of 11 |
| columns in `risk.risks` that could hold such a code | **0** — `external_id` is its only reference, and it is a UUID |

Scenario 1 is *"Aramco contract delay — Monte Carlo (base case)"* and stores
`risk_title_en = 'Aramco contract renewal delay'` against `risk_id = 4`, which is
**"Non-Compliance with NCA ECC Controls"**. Scenario 3 stores *"Riyadh datacentre power outage"*
against risk 12, *"Non-Compliance with Saudi PDPL"*. Every stored label is coherent; none is the
title of the risk it names.

🔑 **The two halves were read by different surfaces, and nothing ever put them side by side.** The
stored copy is what the register renders; the id is what `GET /by-risk/{riskId}` joins on. So the
quantitative analysis a risk committee reads under one risk's name was, in the database, hanging off
another — and because the label was always plausible, nothing invited the question. This is
F2-205's *consistency among copies is not evidence* with only one copy having a vote, except here
the copy with no vote is the one on screen.

🔑 **`risk_code` was worse than stale — it named a code space that does not exist.**
`RSK-2026-NNN` appears nowhere in `risk.risks`; the register's only reference is a UUID. That is
F2-203's disjoint-code-space shape, and the create form **placeholdered the input `'RSK-2026-042'`**,
so the screen taught the operator to invent one. F2-236's rule about invented values in
placeholders, applied to a register reference rather than a person.

### The frontend collected the LABEL and never the LINK

`RiskScenariosPage`'s create form had two free-text fields, `riskCode` and `riskTitleEn`, and
**`onCreate` never sent `riskId` at all** — there was no risk picker. The consequence is structural
rather than cosmetic: `forRisk` is
`findByOrganisationIdAndRiskIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc(orgId, riskId)`, so **a scenario created through
the platform's own screen could never be found from its risk**, because the column the join uses was
never set. The `by-risk` client is also **dark** — no page calls it — which is consistent: the link
was neither written nor read from the client, and the seeded rows have it the other way round (an id
that is set and a label that disagrees with it).

### The fix

* One private `applyParentRisk(scenario, riskId, orgId)` — **the only writer of all three columns**.
  It resolves the risk with `findById(...).filter(org)` and **derives** `risk_code` from the risk's
  own `external_id` and `risk_title_en` from its own `title_en`.
* `riskCode` and `riskTitleEn` are **deleted from `CreateRequest`**. A field the bound type does not
  declare can never arrive — the strongest closure there is, stronger than an annotation (F2-233).
  They stay on `Response`, because the server derives them and the register renders them.
* **No parent ⇒ all three null.** A risk label on a scenario with no risk is the same false claim in a
  different shape (F2-209's three states).
* An unresolvable id is **refused**, with one message for *"no such risk"* and *"another tenant's
  risk"* alike — copied from `CoiService#requireOwnUser` (F2-244), which records why: distinguishing
  them lets a caller enumerate foreign ids from the error text. A soft-deleted risk is refused too,
  because `Risk` carries `@Where(is_deleted = 0)`: a new scenario may not be opened against a risk the
  register has retired.
* Frontend: the two free-text inputs become **one `select-searchable` over the tenant's own
  register** (`riskApi.list`), so a risk the tenant does not own cannot be named at all and the
  server's refusal should never be reached from this screen. The table renders the **derived title**
  with the reference as its `title` tooltip — printing the code would have made the fix render
  *worse*, since it is now a UUID.

⚠ **Refusing can break a request that succeeds today, and here that is correct** (F2-182's test):
nothing coerces upstream, `risk_id` carries **no foreign key**, and the caller is a present operator
who can act on a 400 that names the id — not the public-intake case where a lost record is worse than
a mis-graded one. And no module edge is created: `risk/scenario → risk` is **intra-module**, checked
against `ModuleGraphRatchetTest` rather than assumed. `NdiCrossLinkService` could not be reused —
ADR-012/018 forbid a peer importing another module's internals, which is precisely why every module
that needs this hand-rolls it (the `CyberInputValidation` situation CLAUDE.md already records).

### The instruments

**`ParentIdentityCopyContractTest`** (hermetic, 7 legs) is deliberately two things, because they fail
for different reasons:

* an **invariant** over this register — no writer may feed any of the three setters from the request;
  all three are written **only inside** the tenant-resolving helper; the bound type may not declare
  the copies and the response must still carry them; the FE create type and form must send the link
  and must not offer the labels. A hard zero with **no exemptions**, which is safe because a derived
  copy is always available, so there is no correct code for it to fail on (F2-214).
* an **exactly-asserted census** of the shape platform-wide, derived by reflection over every shipped
  `@Entity`: an entity carrying `X_id` **and** one of `X_code` / `X_title_*` / `X_name_*`. **49 pairs
  across 425 entities.** Two carry a verdict — `platform.audit_log` and `ndi.audit_event`, **BY
  DESIGN**, because an audit row must keep the code the entity carried *when the event happened*.
  The rest is a **work list with no verdicts** (F2-188): two of the seven candidates this slice read
  were refuted, and roughly half the raw population is `*_by_id + *_by_name`, which is F2-236's
  **actor-attribution** family — a different question with a different answer.

**`RiskScenarioParentBindingTest`** (5 legs) — the service had **no unit test of any kind** before
this slice, which is part of the finding.

### What ran

* `ParentIdentityCopyContractTest` 7/7 · `RiskScenarioParentBindingTest` 5/5
* full backend suite **4,196 / 0 / 0** (was 4,184) · `npx tsc --noEmit` clean · `npx vitest run`
  **797 / 797**
* **pre-fix control, 12 detectors against `git show master:`** — 9 fire on the defect and are silent
  on the fix, 3 inverted legs are absent before and present after. **12/12 correct.** Read through
  `git show`, never `git checkout`: F2-244 nearly lost its own fix to a `git checkout HEAD -- <files>`
  in a `finally`, which with uncommitted work restores the *committed* version.
* **pre-fix LIVE control** (the two backend files reverted to master, recompiled, DevTools restart
  confirmed by a second `Started GrcApplication in` line): the create stored
  **`(4, 'RSK-2026-042', 'Aramco contract renewal delay')`** — *byte-identical to the seeded
  divergence* — and a **cross-tenant risk (72) and an absent risk (999999) were both accepted at
  201**.
* **post-fix live probe 16/16** as `rmanager` (RISK_MANAGER, organisation 1 — resolved from
  `iam.role_permissions`, never `admin`), run **twice**, cleaning up in a `finally` with `CHARINDEX`
  hard deletes. The load-bearing leg is that a body still carrying `riskCode: 'RSK-2026-042'` and the
  invented title answers 201 and stores **neither** — both derived from the risk instead. Both
  databases verified back at 11 live scenarios, 0 tagged.

### Lessons

* 🔑🔑 **A soft FK that also carries the parent's identity is two claims, and only the parent can
  answer the second.** F2-243 established that a *presence* test on an id is not a check on the thing
  it names; F2-244 that an *authority* check on the caller is not a check on the referent. This is the
  next one along: a reference can be **stored, dereferenceable and still describe the wrong row**,
  because the description travelled beside the id instead of being read from it.
* 🔑 **The half that is on screen is not necessarily the half with a vote.** Here the register
  rendered the caller's copy and the join used the id, so the two were never compared by anything —
  and the copy was always coherent, which is what a fabrication needs to survive.
* 🔑 **A form that collects a label instead of a link produces a row nothing can join.** Ask what the
  create form *sends*, not what it *shows*: this one had inputs for the parent's code and title and
  none for the parent.
* ⚠ **My own gate failed on the correct fix on its first run**, and the gate was wrong rather than the
  code: it asserted *"exactly one call site"* per setter, and `applyParentRisk` legitimately writes
  each in both branches (null parent and resolved parent). F2-206's rule applied to an assertion — a
  red leg is a finding only if the code is actually wrong. The claim that was wanted is *"the only
  writer is the resolver"*, which is about **where** the writes live and is also the claim that
  actually prevents drift.
* ⚠ **A fixture that cannot reach a branch proves nothing about it.** `Risk` declares
  `private UUID externalId = UUID.randomUUID()` (F2-241's field-initialiser family), so my "risk with
  no reference" helper silently held a random UUID and the test of the null branch failed for a reason
  unrelated to the code.
* ⚠ **A probe leg that asserts more than its claim fails for reasons unrelated to the claim.** Leg 4b
  compared the whole `ProblemDetail` envelope rather than its `detail`, and failed on a correct server.
* ⚠ **The Python locator and the Java gate disagreed (52 vs 49) and the Java gate is the
  measurement** (F2-213's rule, fourth consecutive slice). Also: my first `sys.columns` probe passed
  three parameters for two markers, and two column names (`title_en` on `risk_lc.treatment_plans`,
  `risk_code` on `risk.risks`) had to be resolved rather than guessed — *"Invalid column name" reads
  exactly like "the data isn't there"*.
* ⚠⚠ **FOUND IN THE BROWSER AFTER EVERY GATE WAS GREEN, and it was a comment of mine claiming a
  behaviour that did not exist.** The register's risk cell rendered `title={r.riskCode}` under a
  comment reading *"The `title` states that"* about the English-only limitation — it stated the
  UUID and nothing else. **F2-184's shape, self-inflicted, in the same commit that filed the gap
  it claimed to disclose.** 🔑 **A comment describing a behaviour that does not exist is worse
  than no comment, because it answers the question a reader was about to ask** — and writing the
  filing and the comment in one sitting is exactly how the two come apart. Closed with
  `parentRiskTooltip(row, lang)` (the reference, plus the reason in Arabic), 4 vitest cases, and a
  gate leg asserting the **call shape** `parentRiskTooltip\s*\(` while banning the
  `title={r.riskCode` form that produced it. ⚙ The browser also settled the filing's shape:
  **`risk.risks` DOES store `title_ar`** — the new picker renders 51 risks in Arabic — so the gap
  is the snapshot column, not the data.

* ⚠ **F2-210's rule earned its place again: the pairing IS the measurement.** I compared
  `risk.scenarios.risk_code` against `risk.risks.external_id` *by assumption* and only then resolved
  `risk.risks`' column list to confirm there is no `risk_code` column for it to have meant instead.

### FILED

* ⚠ **Correction (F2-246): the census is 48 pairs, not 49, and the work list 45, not 47.** The gate prints 48 (45 unadjudicated + 2 BY DESIGN + `risk.scenarios` itself); the figures below were written from an earlier draft detector and nothing gated them — F2-195's rule that a baseline lifted from a measurement of something else is worse than none, because it looks measured. The gate asserts a FLOOR deliberately, since the population shrinks as slices adjudicate members, so publish the names and read the printed figure.
* **The work list** — every other entity carrying a parent id beside a copy of that
  parent's identity, printed by the gate as `NEEDS-READING` and asserted exactly, deliberately with
  **no verdicts** (F2-188). Read the writer before writing a reason. Classification a reader needs
  first: roughly half are `*_by_id + *_by_name`, i.e. F2-236's **actor attribution**, whose answer is
  the authenticated principal rather than a derived copy. The parent-register members are the ones
  this shape is about, and **F2-243's own filing already noticed one**: `scm.exit_plans`, where
  *"`vendor_name` is separately caller-supplied and NOT NULL, so the register can contradict
  itself"* — now measured as one of four `scm` members alongside `supplier_resilience_tests`,
  `alternate_suppliers` and `fourth_party_exposures`.
* **The 11 live divergent scenarios and the 1 dangling `risk_id = 25`**, identical in dev and prod.
  Every stored label is a coherent sentence about a risk the row does not name, so repair means
  choosing, per row, whether the id or the label was the operator's intent — that rewrites live
  governance rows in two databases and is an **owner decision** (F2-183 / F2-196 / F2-206).
* **`risk_lc.treatment_plans` holds a live cross-tenant row in both databases** — plan 1 is
  `organisation_id = 2` with `risk_id = 1`, and risk 1 belongs to organisation 1 — plus plan 4 naming
  the absent `risk_id = 3`. Plans 1 and 2 share `external_id = 'TP-2026-001'`, so this is seed-origin.
  `TreatmentPlanService.create` stores `riskId` unverified and `risk_lc` **dereferences the risk
  nowhere** (no repository, no event consumer), so it is a dangling reference rather than a leak —
  F2-239's least-urgent kind, but the row proves F2-242's *"waiting for the row that dereferences
  it"* is not hypothetical.
* **`risk.scenarios` has no `risk_title_ar` column**, so the register's risk label is English-only on
  an Arabic-primary UI (house rule 7). Adding it is a migration plus a decision about whether the
  snapshot should be bilingual; the tooltip states the gap rather than letting it read as an absent
  risk.
* **`risk_id` has no FOREIGN KEY on any of the 21 tables that declare a soft link to `risk.risks`**
  except `risk.risk_assessments` and `risk.risk_treatments` (1 each). So an *absent* id is storable
  platform-wide, and a foreign key would not help with tenancy anyway (F2-242).
* The **structural root**, unchanged from F2-242 / F2-243 / F2-244: a caller-supplied foreign key is
  representable on every create in the platform, so a `@TenantOwned`-style binding that resolves a
  reference through the tenant automatically — and, for this shape, derives any identity copy from
  what it resolved — rather than 200-odd services each remembering, is an **owner decision**.

## F2-244 · An authority check on the caller is not a check on the referent — the COI recusal register's subject was never resolved, and the register named the person nowhere

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-244 |
| **Title** | `CoiService#recordRecusal` stored `req.userId()` verbatim three lines below a comment announcing that it validates the *other* foreign key; `declarantFor` was rigorous about the authority to file on somebody else's behalf and never asked whether the person it named existed. `coi_recusal_event.user_id` is NOT NULL with no FK and **no name column of any kind**, so 11 of the 28 live COI rows in dev and prod identify their subject by an id that resolves to nobody — and the response DTO never carried the name its own frontend has always read |
| **Severity** | 🟠 P2 (a SAMA Article 30 / CMA CG Art.41–43 governance record attributable to a person who does not exist or belongs to another tenant, writable by any `ETHICS:WRITE` holder through the register's own route, needing no second tenant to reproduce; **live in the data** — 11 of 28 rows already affected, identical in both databases — and demonstrated live at 201 against a victim the probe planted) |
| **Status** | 🟢 CLOSED 2026-08-19 |
| **Programme** | Platform Bible F2 · control integrity / tenant isolation |
| **Modules** | `ethics/coi` (both writers, the response record, the shared predicate), `iam` (the directory read — an ordinary business edge, checked against the ratchet), `tss-grc-ui-v2` (the register's first person column); 1 gate added, 1 widened; 6 behaviour tests; F2-243's 26-site store-side filing re-derived |

### Re-deriving F2-243's filing first (F2-221), and what that alone corrected

F2-243 filed **26 store-side sites** with no verdicts, and named `module/scm/resilience` as the
sharpest because it sits one package from the module F2-242 swept. Re-derived, that recommendation
was **wrong in three ways at once**, and every correction came from measuring rather than reading the
filing:

| the filing said | measured |
|---|---|
| two services (`ExitPlanService`, `SupplierResilienceTestService`) | **three** — `AlternateSupplierService#create` stores `primaryVendorId` the same way |
| "no FOREIGN KEY on `vendor_id`" | **no foreign key on any of the three tables at all**, so the three `linked*Id` columns are unconstrained too |
| "13 + 11 live rows" | **40** (13 exit plans, 11 tests, **16** alternates) |
| — | `vendor_id` is **NULL on 25 of the 40**, because the create form has no vendor picker and sends only free-text `vendorName` |

🔑 **A filing inherits the population of the slice that filed it**, and this one also inherited its
*ordering*. F2-239's rule — harm-if-reached and reach are two orderings and they disagree — says to
carry both, so the population was re-ranked by **what the foreign key's target IS**: does the
target's state or identity discharge a control (F2-243's shape), does the storing service later
write to it (F2-242's shape), or is it a reference only ever read back inside the caller's own
tenant? On that ranking `scm/resilience` is the *third* kind: nothing dereferences the stored id to
write to a vendor, and no coverage question joins on it yet, so it is latent — **filed again, with
the corrected measurements**, and the slice went to the register whose reference identifies a
*person*.

⚠ **Two of my own detector's 24 candidates were refuted by reading, both over-reporting.**
`GhgEmissionRecordService:127` resolves `emissionFactorId` in `applyDerivation`, a helper — F2-231's
rule that a guard sits in at least four places a setter-site regex cannot see;
`ObligationAttestationService#recordAttestation` resolves the obligation on its **first line** with
`findByOrganisationIdAndIdAndIsDeletedFalse`, which my `findByIdAndOrganisationId` pattern could not
match because the **organisation comes first in the method name**. Roughly two in ten of a slice's
own candidates fall on first run (F2-188, F2-192, F2-204, F2-211, F2-243) — and both errors were in
the loud direction, which is the one to prefer.

### The defect

```java
// If a declaration id is provided, validate it belongs to this tenant.
if (req.declarationId() != null) {
    loadDeclaration(req.declarationId());
}
CoiRecusalEvent r = new CoiRecusalEvent();
r.setOrganisationId(orgId);
r.setDeclarationId(req.declarationId());
r.setUserId(req.userId());          // ← the subject of the recusal, unresolved
```

**The method verified one of its two foreign keys, with a comment saying so, and left the other** —
F2-215's two-of-N at its shortest range yet, and shorter than F2-243's, which was three lines apart
in a different method. **And the split ran the same way in the database:** `declaration_id` carries
`FK_coi_recusal_decl`, `user_id` carries no constraint at all. So the code check and the schema
constraint both landed on the same reference, and the other got neither.

The second writer is the sharper one. `declarantFor` decides *who may file on somebody else's
behalf*, and F2-145(e) put real care into it — converting three recited role names to
`ETHICS:WRITE` so a tenant granting that permission to a fourth role would not silently lose the
capability:

```java
Long caller = CurrentActor.userId();
boolean mayFileForOthers = CurrentActor.isPlatformAdmin() || hasAnyAuthority("ETHICS_WRITE");
if (mayFileForOthers && req.userId() != null) {
    return req.userId();            // ← rigorous about WHO MAY NAME, silent about WHO IS NAMED
}
```

🔑🔑 **THE REUSABLE RULE: an authority check on the caller is not a check on the referent.** F2-243
established that a *presence* test on an id is not a check on the thing it names; this is one notch
further — a method can be careful, documented and correct about the *right to name a party* while
never asking whether the party exists. The two questions look like one because both are about
"is this allowed", and only one of them was being asked.

⚠ **`CoiDeclarantBindingTest`'s own javadoc offered the hole as a virtue.** It read *"it touches
none of the service's six collaborators"*, presented as evidence of clean isolation. It was true,
and it was true **because** the resolver resolved nothing. 🔑 **A resolver that touches nothing
cannot resolve anything** — so the isolation the comment praised was the shape of the defect. Its
tests were all about *authority* and every one of them is kept; what it never had is a leg asking
whether the named declarant is real, which is now three legs.

### Why this is not merely a dangling reference

`CoiRecusalEvent` declares `user_id` **NOT NULL** and has **no name column of any kind**, so that id
is the only thing identifying who recused. The entity's own javadoc says who that is:

> The Board Secretariat records a recusal whenever a **director, committee member, or senior
> executive** abstains from voting on an agenda item because of a declared … conflict of interest …
> the Compliance Officer relies on this for **SAMA Article 30 reporting**.

Measured live, identical in dev and prod:

| register | live rows | `user_id` NULL | **resolves to NO USER** | cross-tenant |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ethics.coi_recusal_event` | 8 | 0 (NOT NULL) | **3** | 0 |
| `ethics.coi_declaration` | 20 | 12 | **8 of the 8 non-null** | 0 |

**11 of 28 live rows reference a user that does not exist** — ids 1001–1007 against
`MAX(iam.users.id) = 8`. The declaration table models a non-platform declarant *correctly*
(`user_id` NULLABLE plus NOT NULL `full_name_en` and an `employee_no`), which is what the 12 NULLs
are; the recusal table has neither, so its seed had no way to record a director except by inventing
an id. **The register's per-person query is `GET /recusals/user/{userId}`, so those three recusals
can never be reached from any real person.**

⚠ And the operator-facing half: the create form takes the subject as a **raw numeric id typed into a
text box** (`parseInt(rUser, 10)`), with the filter's empty state reading *"Enter a user ID to load
their recusals."* There is no picker. Inventing ids is what a human typing ids produces.

### Proven live, both directions

As `compliance` (holds `ETHICS:WRITE`; **not** `admin`, whose PLATFORM_ADMIN bypass proves nothing
about authorization), against a foreign user the probe **planted in organisation 2** — `iam.users`
holds 7 live users all in organisation 1, so there was no foreign row to borrow, and a probe
demonstrating a forgery must never use a real governance row (F2-206):

| leg | pre-fix | post-fix |
|---|---|---|
| recusal naming a user id that exists in no tenant | **201, stored** | **400**, naming the id |
| recusal naming **another tenant's** director | **201, stored** (org-1 row, org-2 subject) | **400**, same message |
| declaration naming a declarant that resolves to nobody | **201** | **400** |
| the response names the subject | no `userNameEn` key at all | `Sara Al-Ghamdi` + Arabic |
| a seeded row whose id resolves to nobody | rendered blank | `userResolved: false`, disclosed |

**5/5 pre-fix behaviours demonstrated · 12/12 post-fix.**

⚠ **One probe leg of mine was passing for the wrong reason on BOTH trees, and only the pre-fix run
exposed it.** The declaration leg sent `campaignId: null`, and `submitDeclaration` calls
`loadCampaign(req.campaignId())` **before** `declarantFor` — so it answered 400 on the campaign, on
master and on the fix alike. It read as proof in both directions. Repointed at a real OPEN campaign
(resolved from `ethics.coi_declaration_campaign`: ids 1–3), it then showed **201 pre-fix / 400
post-fix**, which is the claim. 🔑 **The Nth instance in this programme of a check satisfied by
something other than its claim — this time in my own probe, and the fixed tree alone could never
have revealed it.**

### The fix

**One resolver, called by both writers** — modelled on `CommitteeMemberRegistryService`'s
`requireUserInTenant` rather than hand-rolled, because a second mechanism is how this platform grew
four DSR registers and five CAPA vocabularies (F2-190):

```java
private User requireOwnUser(Long userId, String what) {
    Long org = org();
    return users.findById(userId)
            .filter(u -> org.equals(u.getOrganisationId()))
            .filter(u -> Boolean.TRUE.equals(u.getIsActive()))
            .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException(
                    "User " + userId + " is not an active user in this organisation, so "
                  + what + " cannot be recorded against them. …"));
}
```

⚠ **One message for "no such user" and "another tenant's user", copied deliberately** from that
exemplar, which records why: distinguishing them would let a caller enumerate other tenants' user
ids by reading the error text.

⚠ **This can refuse a request that succeeds today, and that is the point.** F2-182's mechanical test
does *not* clear it — there is no upstream coercion and no FK, so a caller typing 1007 gets 201 today
and 400 after. But that 201 stores a recusal attributed to nobody, and the Board Secretariat is a
present operator who can act on a 400 naming the id. This is not the public-intake case where a lost
record is worse than a mis-graded one (F2-179/F2-183): it is an internal governance register with a
human at the keyboard.

**The display half, because a fix nobody can see is F2-215 waiting to happen.** The response record
now carries `userNameEn` / `userNameAr` — *fields `lib/coi.ts` has declared all along*, which is why
`CoiRegisterPage`'s `selected.userNameEn && …` guard could never fire (F2-211: the client nominates,
the entity adjudicates) — plus an explicit **`userResolved`**, because a resolvable user with a blank
name and an id that resolves to nobody are different facts and 11 of 28 rows are the second kind.
The register gains its **first person column**; an unresolvable id is announced with `role="status"`
and a bilingual `title` rather than blanked, since blanking would let the register's broken rows read
as its tidiest (F2-197, F2-209's three states).

### The gate

`CoiUserReferenceResolutionContractTest` — 9 legs, hermetic, reading the two frontend files from
disk as `ConnectorBackingContractTest` does:

* the raw-reference ban is scoped to the **shape**, not the spelling deleted (F2-205/F2-209 each had
  a leg banning the literal they had just removed);
* **both** writers must call the resolver, asserted per method body, so a one-site fix fails;
* the refusal must not distinguish the two cases — `containsOnlyOnce("orElseThrow")` plus a ban on
  "another tenant"/"another organisation" wording;
* `resolveSubjects` must filter every `findAllById` row on the tenant;
* the response record's components asserted by **reflection**, and the frontend's interface in both
  directions, with the page asserted by **call shape** (`recusalSubjectLabel\s*\(`) rather than the
  bare token — F2-194's substring-satisfied-by-an-import, twice recorded;
* the **external-director gap pinned as a filing**: the test fails if somebody adds
  `subjectNameEn`/`employeeNo`/`noPlatformUser`, so the owner decision cannot rot into silence;
* two synthetic self-tests carrying the literal pre-fix *and* post-fix shapes, and a stripper test.

⚠ **My own `methodBody` helper matched a CALL, not the declaration**, because `recordRecusal` calls
`requireOwnUser` earlier in the file than the declaration appears — so the tenant-filter leg read a
different method's body and failed on a correct tree. 🔑 **A name-keyed lookup finds the first thing
with that name, and a call is not a declaration** (F2-234's "resolve per owner type", one level
down). It failed loudly here; had the wrong body happened to contain the token, it would have passed
for the wrong reason. ⚠ Its first fix then blew the stack: `(?:public|private|protected|static|
final|\s)+[\w<>,.\[\]?]+\s+` is an alternation of single tokens under `+`, which backtracks
catastrophically over ordinary whitespace — three legs died with `StackOverflowError`.

⚠⚠ **F2-243's own plural-load gate caught the site this slice added.** `resolveSubjects` calls
`findAllById` on a tenant-bearing entity, and the gate demanded a verdict for it. 🔑 **That is the
verdict-per-site rule earning its place immediately: a decrease-only count would have absorbed a new
site inside a tolerated total, where a per-site map made an addition fail loudly.**

### Verification

`CoiUserReferenceResolutionContractTest` 9/9 · `UnverifiedForeignKeyWriteContractTest` 10/10 ·
`CoiServiceTest` 18 → 20 · `CoiDeclarantBindingTest` 5 → 8 · full suite **4,184/0/0** (from 4,170) ·
frontend `npx tsc --noEmit` clean and `npx vitest run` **797/0** · pre-fix control **11/11 detectors
fire on master, 0 silent** · live probe **5/5 pre-fix, 12/12 post-fix** on a backend restarted after
the build (F2-217) · both registers restored to **dev 8/20/7 = prod**, 0 residual `[REVIEW-TEST]`,
0 non-organisation-1 users. **No migration** — V379 remains head; adding a CHECK or an FK to
`user_id` would be F2-183's defect while 11 live rows violate it, and repairing those rows is an
owner decision.

⚠ **My first probe run crashed printing an Arabic name (Windows console is cp1252) AFTER planting
rows, so its inline cleanup never ran and two `[REVIEW-TEST]` rows were left live in dev.** 🔑 **A
probe that plants rows must clean up in a `finally`** — a harness bug is not a reason to leave rows
in a real database. Rewritten with the legs in a function and cleanup in a `finally`, and a
standalone `f244_clean.py` that verifies both databases against the pre-slice baseline.

### Filed

* **The external-director gap — OWNER DECISION.** `coi_recusal_event.user_id` is NOT NULL with no
  name column, so a recusal by a non-executive director who has no platform login cannot be recorded
  truthfully; the seed's ids 1001–1007 are what that produces. F2-26's committee roster already
  models the population properly (`LINKED | EXTERNAL | UNLINKED` via `noPlatformUser`), so the shape
  to copy exists — but adopting it means a migration, a form field, and a decision about whether a
  recusal's subject should be a **committee seat** rather than a platform user. Pinned by a gate leg.
* **The 11 live unresolvable rows in both databases** — repair rewrites live governance rows
  (F2-183/F2-196's rule), and which of the 1001–1007 ids maps to which real person is not derivable
  from the platform.
* **`scm/resilience`, re-measured**: three creates (`ExitPlanService`, `SupplierResilienceTestService`,
  `AlternateSupplierService`) store a caller-supplied vendor reference unverified; **none of the
  three tables has any foreign key at all**, so a nonexistent *and* an absent id are storable, and
  the three `linked*Id` columns are unconstrained too. 40 live rows, `vendor_id` NULL on 25 of them,
  0 dangling and 0 cross-tenant today, dev = prod. The create form has **no vendor picker** and
  sends only free-text `vendorName`, so a SAMA outsourcing exit plan cannot be joined to its supplier
  — latent because nothing asks that coverage question yet.
* **The remaining store-side work list**, deliberately unverdicted (F2-188), now 22 sites after this
  slice's closures and two refutations. Readiest by harm: `AuditEngagementService#create::annualPlanId`
  (IIA Standard 2010 — the engagement hangs off the approved annual plan),
  `DpiaService#update::processingActivityId` (PDPL Art. 25/31), `MlModelAuditService#recordAudit::capaTaskId`.
* **Three `ExitPlan` registers for one concept** (`module/scm/resilience`, `module/outsourcing`,
  `module/tprm/outsourcing`) — F2-196's disjoint-register shape, and two of them share the simple
  name `ExitPlan`, which is one of the 15 duplicated entity names F2-222 filed.
* **The structural root, unchanged from F2-242/F2-243**: a caller-supplied foreign key is
  representable on every create in the platform. A `@TenantOwned`-style binding that resolves a
  reference through the tenant automatically, rather than 200-odd services each remembering, is an
  **owner decision**.

## F2-243 · A four-eyes gate that consumes a foreign key must RESOLVE it — the platform's own "GHG verify needs evidence" control was discharged by any non-null number

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-243 |
| **Title** | Rule 2 asked `cur.getEvidenceItemId() == null`, so a GHG emission record could be marked VERIFIED citing the register's one REJECTED evidence item, or any of the 31 EXPIRED ones — the gate built to consume the evidence module's four-eyes review and its nightly staleness sweep was discharged by their rejected output, on an ISAE 3410 assurance input |
| **Severity** | 🟠 P2 (a documented four-eyes control bypassable by any `SUST:WRITE` holder through the register's own routes, needing no second tenant; latent in the data — 0 of 18 live rows cite an evidence item — and demonstrated live against records the probe planted) |
| **Status** | 🟢 CLOSED 2026-08-19 |
| **Programme** | Platform Bible F2 · control integrity / tenant isolation |
| **Modules** | `sust/ghg` (Rule 2 + the store side), `evidence` (the vocabulary and the resolving predicate), `sust/evidence` (the bridge's route as a constant); 2 gates widened or added; 5 behaviour tests; F2-242's 7-site residue adjudicated to zero |

### The filing that started it, and what re-deriving it found

F2-242 filed a **7-site load-then-write-later residue**, printed and deliberately unverdicted.
Read, **all seven are REFUTED** — the reference is verified at every one. They were invisible to
that gate's residue leg because it looks for **one spelling** of the predicate,
`<var>.getOrganisationId()` on the loaded variable, and this tree verifies a reference in at least
four different ways:

| site | mechanism the detector could not see |
|---|---|
| `OutsourcingService:372/429` | a tenant-scoped **finder** (`findByOrganisationIdAndId`) on both the create and the load |
| `TprmService:172/211` | a helper resolving the **parent** (`getVendor`, which filters and throws) |
| `RiskTreatmentService:66` | a helper resolving the **parent risk** (`ensureRiskInTenant`, 404 not 400 so ids cannot be enumerated) |
| `AccessGovernanceService:94` | the id **is not caller data** — it comes from an org-scoped native query |
| `NotificationService:271` | scoped by **recipient identity**, which is narrower than the tenant |

🔑 **A detector reporting zero defects over its own population is a statement about the
detector, not about the code.** So the count is no longer the assertion (F2-234): the residue leg now
demands a **verdict per site**, and a reverse leg requires every verdict to still name a site the scan
finds — without which a detector that stopped matching would report success on every site at once.

### The defect the re-derivation found, one question further on

F2-242's discriminator is *was the reference verified when it was **stored**?* Measuring that on the
**store** side platform-wide — 37 caller-supplied FK stores whose target carries `organisation_id`,
31 in a method with no tenant predicate — led to `GhgEmissionRecordService`, where CLAUDE.md's own
list of server-enforced four-eyes gates includes *"GHG verify needs evidence"*:

```java
if ("VERIFIED".equals(to)
        && cur.getEvidenceItemId() == null
        && (cur.getEvidenceRef() == null || cur.getEvidenceRef().isBlank())) throw …
```

**A presence test on an id is not a check on the thing it names.** `FK_ghg_evidence_item` exists, so
a *nonexistent* id is refused by the database — the comment calling it *"a real evidence-item FK
(S-C)"* is **true**, verified rather than assumed (F2-227). Every **other** number the caller can send
is one the gate accepts.

Measured, identical in dev and prod: `evidence.evidence_items` holds **EXPIRED 31 · APPROVED 27 ·
PENDING_REVIEW 15 · DRAFT 4 · REJECTED 1** — **51 of 78 are not APPROVED**. Probed live as
`so_officer` (SUSTAINABILITY_OFFICER, holding SUST WRITE; `admin` proves nothing about
authorization) against GHG records the probe planted itself (F2-206 — the register's 18 live rows
were never touched):

* citing the one **REJECTED** item → **HTTP 200**, stored `status = VERIFIED, verified = true`
* citing an **EXPIRED** item → **HTTP 200**, same
* citing an **organisation-2** item → stored on an organisation-1 record
* **10/10 legs on master**, including the controls that the gate does refuse a null and that an
  APPROVED in-date item verifies

🔑 **No second tenant is needed**, which is what makes this live rather than latent: the
evidence module's four-eyes review (`EvidenceReviewService`) and its nightly APPROVED→EXPIRED sweep
both exist to decide whether an item *is* evidence, and the gate consuming their output never asked.

### ⚠⚠ The asymmetry sat inside one method, three lines apart

`update` wrote two caller-supplied foreign keys:

| line | field | what happens to it |
|---|---|---|
| 115 | `emissionFactorId` | `applyDerivation` resolves it with `findByIdAndOrganisationId` **and throws** — *"not found in this tenant's factor library"* |
| 121 | `evidenceItemId` | stored raw |

🔑 **The reference feeding a NUMBER was verified and the one discharging a CONTROL was not.**
F2-215's two-of-N at its shortest range yet.

### ⚠⚠ Two writers of one FK column, and only one of them is the bridge

`SustEvidenceLinkService.link()` is the declared S-C attachment path. It resolves the item **in the
caller's tenant**, records a generic `EvidenceLink` **so `buildPackage()` can bundle the file and its
SHA-256 for an assurer**, and writes a `LINK_EVIDENCE` audit row. `GhgEmissionRecordService.update`
wrote the same column straight from the request body and did **none of the three** — so a record
could be VERIFIED citing an item the **ISAE 3410 evidence package would not contain**. That is
F2-188/F2-189/F2-191's shape, in the evidence fabric rather than a state machine: *the duplicate
agrees with the original on the part that is easy to check (the column) and differs on the parts
nothing asserts.*

### 🔑 The reusable rule: two questions, two places

* the **TENANT** is verified where the reference is **STORED** (F2-242's discriminator)
* the **STATE** is verified where the reference is **CONSUMED** — because an item can be approved on
  the day it is attached and expired by the time somebody verifies against it

So the store side is closed **structurally**: the bridge is now the single writer, and the
entity-bound PUT accepts an **echo** of the stored id (a round-trip edit must keep working) and
refuses a **change**, naming the route that owns it (F2-231/F2-234's echo-versus-change rule). The
state check lives in Rule 2, at consumption.

The vocabulary stays in `module/evidence` (F2-196's rule: a caller that cannot name an evidence
status cannot invent its own idea of what counts as evidence) — `EvidenceItem.APPROVED` plus
`EvidenceItemRepository.findUsableAsEvidence`, an **inclusion of exactly one state** rather than an
exclusion list, because that column has no CHECK constraint and an exclusion list silently admits
every token nobody remembered. **No new module edge**: `sust → evidence` already exists through the
bridge, checked rather than assumed — `ModuleGraphRatchetTest` is unmoved.

### ⚠ What was already closed, and therefore left alone

`POST /api/sustainability/ghg` binds `GhgCreateRequest`, which declares `evidenceRef` and **not**
`evidenceItemId` — F2-233's fourth and strongest wire-closing mechanism, *a field the bound type
does not declare can never arrive*. Adding a refusal there would be an **inert construct** (F2-184),
so the closure is **asserted** instead, and the gate fires if the component is ever added. The legacy
free-text `evidence_ref` branch is likewise untouched: it is what the five APPROVED rows in both
databases were verified against (BV and KPMG assurance statements predating the bridge), and
tightening it would refuse requests that work today for no gain the caller can act on (F2-182).

### ⚠⚠ My own diagnostic cited a route that does not exist

The refusal named `/api/sustainability/evidence/link`. The bridge is mapped at
`/api/sustainability/evidence-links`. **The live probe found it by receiving 400 from the very path
the error message had told it to use** — and the gate could not tell, because it asserted the path as
a **literal**, and a literal-matching check cannot resolve a route. 🔑 **A diagnostic whose only
job is to send the caller somewhere is worthless if the somewhere is invented**: the guessed-path
error this programme has recorded since F2-198, arriving inside a fix's own error text. The path is
now one constant read by the `@RequestMapping` and by the citation, and the unit test asserts against
the constant rather than a typed-out copy.

### ⚠⚠ The plural form sat outside every leg of F2-242's gate by construction

`(\w+)\s+(\w+)\s*=\s*(\w+)\.findById\(` is **singular**, so a caller-supplied **id LIST** was
invisible to it. **9 receivers** call `findAllById` on a tenant-bearing entity; 8 refuted (the ids
come from rows already fetched tenant-scoped, or the row is filtered in the loop), **1 filed** —
`UserService#assignRolesByNameOrId`, whose `roleNames` branch resolves through
`findByOrganisationIdOrOrganisationIdIsNull(orgId)` and whose `roleIds` branch is a bare
`findAllById(roleIds)`. Latent: all 69 active roles in dev (58 in prod) are `organisation_id IS NULL`
global templates, and both write routes are `hasRole('PLATFORM_ADMIN')`, who is already trans-tenant
by design. ⚠ `createIn`'s javadoc explains why role resolution is tenant-correct and describes the
`roleNames` branch **only** — F2-215's two-of-N, in the comment a reader consults first.

⚠ **My Python locator found 6 of those 9.** The Java gate found nine, and the three it missed
(`CommitteeMemberRegistryService#users`, `EvidenceAdapter#items`,
`AttackSurfaceFindingService#assetRepo`) are all correctly scoped — `EvidenceAdapter`'s under a
comment citing **F2-106** for exactly this hazard. **Third consecutive slice where the throwaway
locator undercounts the shipped gate** (F2-213: 5 vs 9; F2-214: 3 vs 11). *Write the sweep as the
gate, over the same tree, in the same language.*

### ⚠⚠ An existing test asserted the defect as correct, in its name

`verify_acceptsWhenEvidenceItemIdPresent_evenIfRefBlank` — *"verify accepts when evidenceItemId is
**present**"* — which is precisely the defect. The Nth instance in this programme (F2-159, F2-175,
F2-227, F2-234, F2-236), and a test **name** that states the behaviour under review is the strongest
possible reason not to look further (F2-216). **Repurposed, not deleted**: the half that protects the
record (a real evidence item discharges Rule 2 with no free-text ref) is kept, and the half that was
missing is asserted beside it.

## F2-242 · An unverified foreign key is a cross-tenant write waiting for the row that dereferences it, and the platform-wide backstop guards the tenant COLUMN rather than the tenant ROW

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-242 |
| **Title** | `ScmService#startOnboarding` stored a caller-supplied `vendorId` without verifying the vendor belonged to the caller's tenant, then dereferenced it with an unpredicated `findById(...).ifPresent(...save...)` — so an organisation-1 caller holding only `SCM:WRITE` moved an organisation-2 supplier from BLACKLISTED to ACTIVE, with the platform-wide cross-tenant write backstop watching and saying nothing |
| **Severity** | 🔴 P1 (a cross-tenant WRITE on a third-party register, reachable by any `SCM:WRITE` holder through a documented route; latent in the data — 0 foreign references in dev or prod — and demonstrated live against a planted victim) |
| **Status** | 🟢 CLOSED 2026-08-19 |
| **Programme** | Platform Bible F2 · tenant isolation |
| **Modules** | `scm` (6 reference-storing sites, 3 transitions), `evidence` (the nightly sweep + its create), `risk` (a safe site closed anyway); 1 new gate; 6 behaviour tests; 1 F2-241 comment corrected |

### The filing that started it, and what re-deriving it found

F2-241 filed: *"`ScmService#createAssessment` never resolves the vendor, where
`TprmService#createAssessment` calls `getVendor()` to 'verify org ownership' — so an SCM assessment
can name a vendor id the caller's tenant does not own. A dangling reference, not a leak: the row is
still stamped with the caller's org."*

Both halves of that are true and it was **the mildest instance of the shape**. Re-derived per F2-221,
`module/scm` stores a caller-supplied vendor reference at **six** sites and verifies it at none — and
at four *other* sites it then **writes to the referenced vendor** through
`vendorRepo.findById(vendorId).ifPresent(v -> { …set…; save(v); })` with no tenant predicate. The
assessment was the one member of the family with nothing downstream to dereference it.

### 🔑 The discriminator is not the unscoped load — it is whether the reference was verified when it was STORED

`RiskAcceptanceService#setRiskStatus` carried the **identical** shape:

```java
risks.findById(riskId).ifPresent(r -> {
    if (!"CLOSED".equals(r.getStatus())) { r.setStatus(status); risks.save(r); }
});
```

and was **correct**, because `request()` had already resolved that `riskId` with
`.filter(r -> Objects.equals(r.getOrganisationId(), orgId))` before ever writing it to the column. So
an unscoped load by a stored id is safe **exactly when the id was verified as it was written** — which
makes the create the primary fix and a scoped load defence in depth. That is why this finding is about
foreign keys and not about `findById`.

⚠ It was closed anyway. **What made it harmless is a predicate in a different method, and nobody was
maintaining that relationship** (F2-177's rule). A row arriving by another route — a data fix, a
restore, a future second producer — walks straight through, and reachability is a fact about today,
not a property of a control (F2-182).

### ⚠⚠ `TenantWriteGuardInterceptor` cannot see this, and that is not a hole in it

`decide` returns `false` the moment `Objects.equals(oldOrg, newOrg)` — its own comment reads
*"Tenant unchanged — the normal case."* The guard is correct for the question it asks: it catches a row
being **moved** between tenants (F2-22b) and an insert **landing** in the wrong one (F2-216). **It
guards the tenant COLUMN.** Writing another tenant's row without touching its `organisation_id` is
outside its question *by construction*.

`application-prod.yml` describes the bean as the *"platform-wide Hibernate-level cross-tenant write
backstop … so a single missed per-service guard cannot silently write across tenants"* — true of the
two shapes it sees, false of this one. 🔑 **So the per-service predicate is the only control there is,
and until this slice nothing was counting the places it is missing.** F2-216 found the null-value hole
in `decideInsert`; this is the same class of question asked of `decide`, and the answer is that the
missing coverage is structural rather than a bug.

### The live demonstration — 12 of 13 legs, F2-206's planted victim

Probed as **`ranalyst`** (organisation 1; holds `SCM:READ/WRITE/EXPORT` and nothing else — `admin`
proves nothing about authorization). The victim is a `[REVIEW-TEST]` vendor planted in
**organisation 2** (*Aramco Trading Company*, which has **no users at all**, so the victim tenant has
nobody who could notice), `status = BLACKLISTED`, `onboarding_status = REJECTED` — because that is the
value whose loss matters.

| leg | call | result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `POST /api/v1/scm/onboarding {vendorId: <org-2 vendor>}` | **201** · victim `onboarding_status` REJECTED → **IN_PROGRESS** · row stored `(org 1, vendor 81)` |
| 2 | `POST /onboarding/{id}/approve` | **200** · victim `status` BLACKLISTED → **ACTIVE**, `onboarding_status` → COMPLETED |
| 3 | `POST /onboarding/{id}/reject` | **200** · third writer reaches it too |
| 4 | `POST /api/v1/scm/assessments {vendorId: <same>}` | **201** · a SAMA outsourcing assessment filed against a supplier the tenant does not own |
| 5 | visibility | the attacker **cannot read the vendor back** (`GET /vendors` is tenant-scoped, 31 rows, victim absent); their own onboarding row renders with **no vendor name**; **0 audit rows** name the mutated vendor |

🔑 **A supplier another tenant had struck off, reinstated by a stranger, invisible from both sides of
the boundary.** In a SAMA-outsourcing register `status` is what gates whether the organisation may
transact with a supplier, so the write is not cosmetic.

⚠ **The FK does not help, and it is worth being precise about why.** `FK_scm_ob_vendor` and
`FK_scm_assess_vendor` both exist — so a **nonexistent** vendor id is refused by the database. A
foreign key knows nothing about tenancy, so a **cross-tenant** id is a perfectly valid reference. *The
constraint that looks like it protects the reference is the one that cannot.*

### ⚠⚠ My own leg 0 was wrong TWICE, and the second failure is what exposed the first

The probe carried a sanity leg — *"F2-241's `require` is active on the running listener"* — asserting
that `status: "planned"` answers **400**. It answered **201**, and I recorded that as F2-217's stale
listener: *"the listener was serving pre-F2-241 bytecode while answering `/actuator/health` 200."*

**That inference was unfounded.** The post-fix run, against a backend restarted 40 seconds earlier on
the fixed tree, failed the identical leg. `ClosedVocabulary.require()` **normalises case before testing
membership** — which is precisely what F2-241's own
`applyAssessment_normalises_the_casing_the_collation_would_have_let_through` asserts — so `'planned'`
becomes `'PLANNED'`, which is legal, and **201 is the correct answer**. The assertion was wrong, not
the server.

🔑 **A wrong expectation and a stale listener produce the identical red line, and the stale-listener
reading is the more interesting story — which is exactly why it was the one I reached for.** F2-217 is
a real hazard and it was not this. The discriminator that actually tests the running tree is a token
legal in **no** casing: `"DRAFT"`, the literal pre-F2-241 initialiser. Corrected leg 0 now asserts both
halves — `DRAFT` → 400, `planned` → 201 — so it cannot pass for the wrong reason in either direction.

⚙ It changes nothing about legs 1–5: `ScmService`'s onboarding path is untouched by F2-241, and the
post-fix probe was run on a restarted backend regardless. What it changes is the claim: **there is no
evidence the pre-fix listener was stale.**

### The second confirmed instance: the on-request sibling filters and the sweep six methods away does not

`EvidenceItemService#expireStaleEvidence` is the nightly all-orgs sweep. It reopened the originating
evidence request through `requestRepository.findById(item.getRequestId())` with **no** predicate, while
`fulfilRequest` — the on-request path, in the same class — has **always** carried
`.filter(r -> r.getOrganisationId().equals(orgId))`. **F2-215's two-of-N shape**: a reader who finds the
predicate on one reader of a foreign key has no reason to check the other.

⚠ The correct anchor there is **the item's own tenant**, not `TenantContext` — the sweep sets the tenant
per row and has no request tenant of its own. And the root is the same as SCM's: `applyRequest` stored
`req.requestId()` unverified, so the create now refuses a request belonging to another tenant.

### Adjudication of the derived population

The decidable shape is the single-expression `findById(x).ifPresent(v -> { …set…; save(v); })` on an
entity carrying `organisation_id`. **7 sites; 6 fixed, 1 by design, 0 open.**

| site | verdict |
|---|---|
| `ScmService` ×4 (onboarding start/advance/approve/reject) | **CONFIRMED, live** — probed cross-tenant write |
| `EvidenceItemService#expireStaleEvidence` | **CONFIRMED** — sibling filters, sweep did not |
| `RiskAcceptanceService#setRiskStatus` | **SAFE — verified at store; closed anyway** (F2-177) |
| `LoginAttemptService#onSuccess`/`onFailure` | **BY DESIGN** — authentication, before any tenant exists; the id is the principal the authenticator just resolved, `TenantContext` is unset, and `orgId()` would throw. Scoping it would break login lockout bookkeeping |

### ⚠⚠ The detector bug that produced the gate, because it is the reusable part

The reconnaissance pass matched `\.ifPresent\(([^;]{0,600}?)\)` and reported **0 sites on a tree holding
7**. **A lambda body is a statement list**, so a character class excluding `;` can never match the very
shape being hunted. 🔑 **A detector that cannot match reads exactly like a clean tree, and it
UNDER-reports** — the quiet direction, and the ~12th instance of this shape on the register.

`UnverifiedForeignKeyWriteContractTest` extracts the argument with a **paren-balanced walk** (string
and char literals skipped so a `")"` in a message cannot end it), and carries a **synthetic self-test**
driving the detector across the literal pre-fix source *and* the literal fixed form, plus two shapes it
must never flag (a read; an entity with no tenant column) so the invariant cannot be satisfied by
over-matching.

Its population is **derived**, never listed: repository fields are read from each class's own
declarations and resolved **per owner type** (F2-187 — a name-only fallback is how that slice lost
`PolicyService#create`), each repository is resolved to its entity, and an entity is in scope only if it
carries `organisation_id`. Floors sit above the largest *wrong* answers (F2-215): ≥380 entities, ≥340
tenanted, ≥380 repositories resolved, ≥1500 files walked — because "the walk found nothing" and "no
repository resolved" both make the invariant vacuously green.

⚠ **The one exemption is a named map with a reason, enforced in both directions**, not an empty set —
a hard zero here would fail on correct code, the one thing a gate must never do (F2-214). And the
reverse leg is the direction nobody writes first (F2-199): an exemption for something no longer in the
population reads exactly like an exemption for something that is.

### The residue is measured, printed and FILED unread

The broader *load-then-write-later* shape (an assignment, a setter below, a save at the end) is a
**dataflow** question a regex cannot answer (F2-182), so the gate prints it and asserts only
decrease-only + non-empty. **7 sites, none read:**

```
module/iam/governance/service/AccessGovernanceService.java:94   roles.findById -> Role (as revived)
module/outsourcing/service/OutsourcingService.java:372/429      arrangementRepo.findById -> OutsourcingArrangement
module/platform/service/NotificationService.java:271            notificationRepository.findById -> Notification
module/risk/service/RiskTreatmentService.java:66                treatments.findById -> RiskTreatment
module/tprm/service/TprmService.java:172/211                    assessmentRepo.findById -> VendorAssessment
```

Deliberately **no verdicts** (F2-188 — five fluent claims, five false). Read the route and probe it.

⚙ **The Java gate reproduced the Python recon's residue exactly** — same 7 sites, same files — which is
the first exact locator/gate agreement in this lineage since F2-220 (F2-213 measured 5 vs 9, F2-214 3 vs
11, both because the locator's resolver was narrower than the gate's).

### Verification

* `UnverifiedForeignKeyWriteContractTest` **8/8**; `ScmServiceTest` **20 → 26**; `RiskAcceptanceServiceTest` 8/8; `EvidenceItemServiceTest` 20/20.
* **Pre-fix control**: master's three main sources restored under the new gate → **2 of 8 legs fail, naming exactly the six closed sites**. The other six are synthetic/floor legs that correctly pass on both trees.
* Full unit suite green; live probe **12/13 pre-fix** (leg 0 = my own wrong assertion, corrected below) and **16/16 post-fix** on a **restarted** backend.
* Both databases restored: `scm.vendors` **31**, `scm.vendor_onboarding` **17**, `scm.vendor_assessments` **15**, **0 residual `[REVIEW-TEST]`**, **0 rows naming a foreign or absent vendor** — dev = prod throughout.
* **No migration.** The FKs already existed and no live row violates the new rule; this is a service-layer refusal, not a schema change.

### 🔑 Reusable

1. **An unverified foreign key is a cross-tenant write waiting for the row that dereferences it.** Fix it where the reference is *stored*; scope the load as defence in depth.
2. **A guard's population is its question.** `TenantWriteGuardInterceptor` guards the tenant *column*; nothing guarded the tenant *row*. Before trusting a backstop, say out loud which noun it protects.
3. **A foreign-key constraint refuses a nonexistent reference and is blind to a cross-tenant one** — so the constraint that looks protective is the one that cannot help.
4. **A character class excluding `;` cannot match a lambda body.** Extract arguments with a balanced walk, and carry a self-test over the literal defect.
5. **A safe instance of a dangerous shape is safe because of something in another method.** Close it anyway.

### ⚙ Filed

- **The 7-site load-then-write-later residue above**, unread and unverdicted. `TprmService:172/211` is the readiest — it is the twin register of the one this slice closed.
- **`scm.vendors.status` and `onboarding_status` are written by `stampVendorOnboarding` as Java literals against CHECK-constrained, case-insensitively-collated columns** (`CK_scm_vendor_status`, `CK_scm_vendor_ob_status`). The literals are all legal today; the register has no other open writer for them, so closing them with `ClosedVocabulary` is cheap (F2-183) and was left out of scope only to keep this slice's diff to the tenant question.
- **`scm.slas` still has no server surface of any kind** (14 live rows, dev = prod) — F2-204's `NO_SERVER_SURFACE` population, whose derived registry is scoped to the four `*_lc` modules and so has never seen it. Carried from F2-241.
- **The structural root is unchanged**: a caller-supplied foreign key is representable on every create in the platform. A `@TenantOwned`-style binding that resolves a reference through the tenant automatically — rather than 200-odd services each remembering — is an owner decision, and it is the same shape as F2-213's *"a purpose-built request record per endpoint would make this class unrepresentable."*

## F2-241 · An entity's field initialiser is a one-token vocabulary, and no instrument had ever compared one against its column's own CHECK

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-241 |
| **Title** | Two `module/scm` entities initialised a `status` column to a token that column's own CHECK constraint refuses, so the register's create could not succeed without the caller naming the state — and F2-240's filing, which started this, named the wrong table because it was written from the duplicate-simple-name twin |
| **Severity** | 🟠 P3 (latent-by-caller on one register: `ScmPage` always sends a status, so the browser never met it; unreachable on the other, which has no create path at all. Both refusals are hard — the database rejects the INSERT — and one initialiser is the flattering value) |
| **Status** | 🟢 CLOSED 2026-08-19 |
| **Programme** | Platform Bible F2 · server-owned state |
| **Modules** | `scm` (2 entities, 1 service); `support/MigrationVocabularies` extended; 1 new gate; 1 existing fixture corrected |

### F2-240's filing was wrong in both halves, and the cause is a hazard already on the register

F2-240 filed: *"`tprm.vendor_assessments` has 3 CHECK constraints and `assessment_type` is
unconstrained — cheap now that this slice closed the register's open writers."* Re-derived per
F2-221, measured in dev **and** prod:

* `tprm.vendor_assessments` has **2** CHECK constraints and **no `assessment_type` column at all**.
* The 3-CHECK table whose `assessment_type` **is** constrained (`CK_scm_assess_type`) is
  **`scm.vendor_assessments`** — a *different table*, in a *different schema*, mapped by a *different
  entity that happens to have the same simple name*.

🔑 **F2-222 filed exactly this hazard — 15 of 433 entity simple names are declared in two packages —
and recorded that "nobody is maintaining that."** F2-240's own write-up even records the moment it
bit: *"my helper's `findFirst()` picked `module/scm`'s twin over `module/tprm`'s."* That was corrected
in the gate and **leaked into the prose**, where nothing checks it. A filing is the least-verified
artefact in a slice (F2-178, F2-188), and this is the first instance in this lineage of one being
wrong about *which table it was talking about*.

⚙ The correction is not the finding. Reading the twin to check the filing is what found the defect.

### The defect: an initialiser the column refuses

`module/scm/entity/VendorAssessment` declared `private String status = "DRAFT"`;
`CK_scm_assess_status` admits `PLANNED | IN_PROGRESS | COMPLETED | ESCALATED`. `ScmService`
`#createAssessment` does `new VendorAssessment()` then overwrites `status` only
`if (req.getStatus() != null)` — so **any caller that omitted the state sent `'DRAFT'` and the
database refused the INSERT.**

⚠ **The column's DB DEFAULT does not rescue it.** Both columns carry one (`'PLANNED'`,
`'NOT_MEASURED'`) and the entity maps both insertable, so Hibernate names the column in the INSERT
and sends the initialiser's value — F2-240 measured exactly that on the *tprm* twin's `status`.
🔑 **The DEFAULT is still the useful artefact: it is the schema author's own statement of which token
the initial state should be. Where the entity disagrees with it in the direction the CHECK refuses,
the entity is the half that is wrong** — and both fixes took the column's own default.

`module/scm/entity/Sla` declared `status = "ON_TRACK"` against `CK_scm_sla_status`'s
`NOT_MEASURED | AT_RISK | BREACHED | MET`. 🔑 **`ON_TRACK` is also the FLATTERING value** — it asserts
the supplier is meeting the target — so had anyone "fixed" this by widening the CHECK instead of
correcting the entity, a brand-new SLA would have claimed compliance it had never demonstrated.
F2-238 measured that inversion from the other side.

⚠ **Corrected rather than deleted, which is the opposite of F2-240's remedy for the adjacent shape,
and the discriminator is whether a create path exists to own the default.** `scm.slas` has none at
all — no controller, no route, no frontend client, and `SlaRepository` is injected into `ScmService`
and **never used** (F2-204's `NO_SERVER_SURFACE` shape; 14 live rows in dev and prod). Deleting the
initialiser would leave a NOT NULL column with no writer to fill it, the one hazard F2-238 flagged
for that fix shape.

### A third site on the same create: NOT NULL with no filling mechanism at all

`scm.vendor_assessments.risk_rating` is NOT NULL with DB default `'MEDIUM'`, the entity gave it **no
initialiser**, and `applyAssessment` writes it only under a null-guard — so an omitted key arrived as
an explicit null. Probed live, this fires **first** and **masks the other defect**: the handler
answers **400 "A required field was not supplied"** with `constraint: null`, naming no field, which is
F2-210/F2-214's recorded shape where the diagnostic sends the caller nowhere. 🔑 **Two defects on one
create, and the louder one hid the quieter one** — F2-238's *the throw was holding the write shut*,
in the other direction.

### Why every existing instrument was blind

The platform has four vocabulary/column instruments and this population sits outside all of them,
because **a field initialiser is never DECLARED as a vocabulary**:

| instrument | its population |
|---|---|
| `ClosedVocabularyPinTest` | narrows on the source string `ClosedVocabulary.of(` and that field type |
| `HandRolledVocabularyMirrorTest` | six mirrors named in a list |
| `StateMachineColumnMirrorTest` | a named machine constant — a one-token default is not a machine |
| `NeverFiringNullGuardContractTest` (F2-240) | **entity-bound** updates; this PUT binds a purpose-built DTO, so the register was outside it by construction |

Ninth appearance of F2-198's shape, and the narrowing is none of the previous ones (a filename, a
three-entry allow-list, a module name, an `extends` clause, a field-name list, a claim shape): it is
**the absence of a declaration**. 🔑 **A value nobody wrote down as a vocabulary is still a
vocabulary to the database.**

### The gate constructs the entity and asks the field

`EntityInitialiserAcceptedByColumnTest` — a **hard zero with no exemption map**, safe because there is
no correct code for it to fail on (F2-214): a value the column refuses is either a create that cannot
succeed or an initialiser stating something the register cannot hold, and every CHECK-constrained
column has at least one legal value.

⚠ **Reflection over the constructed object, never a source regex.** The reconnaissance needed three
hand-written cases — the `@Column` on the line above, the `@Column` column-aligned on the *same* line
(this codebase does that), and an initialiser that is a **constant reference** rather than a literal
(`ChangeModelStatus.DRAFT`) — and it silently skipped the four entities whose `@Table` carries no
`schema=`. Constructing the entity is fooled by none of them.

Measured, published to `target/entity-initialiser-checks.txt`: **432 shipped entities constructed and
walked** (the same 432 CLAUDE.md records, which is the corroboration), **170 comparisons against a
CHECK vocabulary across 22 schemas**, **13 against a numeric range**, 0 unprobeable, 0 with no
`@Table`, 0 on an `insertable = false` column — and **2 REFUSED**, both fixed.

⚠⚠ **The range half is included on purpose, and F2-230 is why.** That slice established that a range
is not a vocabulary and asserted the limit deliberately. But a value outside a range CHECK produces
the *identical* refused INSERT, so excluding ranges would have shipped an invariant whose population
was half its claim — this programme's most-repeated defect. `MigrationVocabularies` grew `ranges()`
as a **separate accessor** over **one shared declaration walk**, so the three traps its javadoc
records are not copied into a second parser.

⚠⚠ **The `(table, column)` lookup refuses an ambiguous bare table name rather than guessing, and this
slice is the reason.** `vendor_assessments` exists in `scm` **and** `tprm`, both carry a vocabulary
CHECK on `status`, and **the tokens differ** — `ESCALATED` is legal in one and not the other. A
bare-name lookup would have compared `scm`'s initialiser against `tprm`'s vocabulary and answered
confidently. Asserted in both directions.

### Two instrument errors of mine, both found by running things

⚠ **Publishing the NAMES instead of the count found that the scan reached the test tree.** The first
draft reported "1 `@Entity` with no `@Table`" and the count was unremarkable; the name was
`ServerOwnedFieldsInvariantTest$SyntheticUnprobeableEntity` — F2-215's own fixture.
`ClassPathScanningCandidateComponentProvider` walks the whole classpath, so a hard zero would have
failed on a fixture a later slice deliberately builds to be refused. 🔑 **A count cannot tell you its
members are the ones you meant** (F2-235). Excluded by **code source**, not by a name ending in
`Test` — F2-192 recorded that a name test lets any member escape by being renamed.

⚠ **The case-sensitivity leg asserted the vocabulary SET rather than the gate's comparison.**
`admissible.contains("planned")` is false whether the gate compares case-sensitively or not, so it
proved neither. Extracted as `accepts()` and asserted directly; mutation M9 (make it
`equalsIgnoreCase`) is killed only because of that change. **Near the claim rather than the claim** is
the failure this register has recorded most often.

### The writer, on the same lines

The slice that corrected this register's *defaults* found the *caller's* value unguarded on the same
lines — F2-215's two-of-N at its most literal, since a reader who sees the initialisers agree with the
CHECKs has no reason to ask whether the writer does. Three `ClosedVocabulary` declarations, each
naming its constraint so `ClosedVocabularyPinTest` mirrors it against the migration SQL.

⚠ `require`, not `coerce`, by F2-182's mechanical test — **is there already a coercion upstream?**
No: `AssessmentDtos.Request` carries no validation annotation of any kind and `applyAssessment`
checked nothing, so the CHECK was the only thing refusing anything. Every value that succeeds today
is therefore a case-variant of a legal token, and `require` cannot break a working request.

⚠⚠ **The casing half is live, not hypothetical.** Probed against the real database:
`status = 'planned'` is **ACCEPTED and stored verbatim** (the columns collate case-insensitively),
and `ASSESS_STATUS_OPTIONS` plus the register's tone map compare case-sensitively — F2-179's defect on
a SAMA outsourcing register. ⚙ All three frontend dropdowns were checked against their CHECKs before
enabling `require`, and all three match exactly; 🔑 **the frontend's own comments state the four-token
status vocabulary correctly, while the entity three files away initialised to a fifth token no
vocabulary anywhere contains** — F2-205's *which of them is the server?*, with the FE right and the
entity, which owns the default, wrong.

### An existing test's fixture used the illegal token

`escalateAssessment_sets_escalatedToRisk_and_status_ESCALATED` set `status("DRAFT")`, describing a row
that could not exist in either database. 🔑 **A mocked repository has no constraint, which is exactly
why the illegal initialiser it was copied from looked normal for as long as it did** — and why no unit
test in the suite could ever have caught this. Corrected to `PLANNED`.

### The probe refuted four of my own expectations, and the corrections are the finding

⚠ **I expected 500s and got a 400 and three 409s.** Pre-fix: omitting both fields is a **400
REQUIRED_FIELD naming no field** (the NOT NULL masking the CHECK), and a caller-supplied bad token is
a **409 `VALUE_NOT_ALLOWED` naming the column** — F2-180's improved 547 diagnostic doing its job,
better than I assumed. ⚠ And my first leg 1 **asserted both defects at once**; splitting it (F2-206's
one-field-per-question) is what isolated the initialiser defect: omitting *only* `status` reaches the
column with `'DRAFT'` and is refused, with nothing masking it.

⚠ A separate asymmetry the `UnnecessaryStubbing` failure exposed, filed not fixed:
**`ScmService#createAssessment` never resolves the vendor at all**, where `TprmService#createAssessment`
calls `getVendor()` to *"verify org ownership"* — so an SCM assessment can name a vendor id the
caller's tenant does not own. The row is still stamped with the caller's org, so it is a dangling
reference rather than a leak.

* `MigrationVocabulariesTest` **9/9** (4 new: the range interval including an exclusive lower bound,

* `ScmServiceTest` **20/20** (5 new behaviour tests + 1 fixture corrected)

* Full suite **4,142 / 0 / 0** (+15 on F2-240's 4,127, reconciling exactly)
* Mutation **11 killed / 0 survived / 0 anchor-miss**, plus 2 recorded EQUIVALENT and 1 INVALID
* Live probe **pre-fix 12/12** on a backend restarted onto master's entities and **post-fix 14/14**

* No migration: both CHECK constraints already existed and the live rows already agree with them.
  No frontend file touched.

* **`scm.slas` has no server surface of any kind** — 14 live rows in dev and prod, no controller, no

* **The adjacent bucket: NOT NULL columns with no entity-side filling mechanism.** Measured 45, but
