## F2-231 · A gate's hard zero is only as wide as its predicate

| | |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-231 |
| **Title** | `ServerStampedFieldContractTest` recognised 280 of 409 server-stamped field pairs, and its hard zero was green over the other 32% |
| **Severity** | P2 |
| **Status** | 🟢 CLOSED 2026-08-17 |
| **Programme** | Platform Bible F2 · security / integrity |
| **Modules** | `policy`, `sust/tcfd`, `sust/cma`, `privacy`, `security` (the gate) |

### What was measured

Executing the plan's open F2-22a mass-assignment item, the *instrument* was measured before its
population. `isGuardedRoute` decides which routes count as guarded transitions, and therefore which
fields count as server-stamped; `BASELINE_CONTRADICTED_SERVICES = 0` was a hard zero over whatever it
could see.

```
409  server-stamped Type#field pairs exist across 327 shipped services
280  the shipped predicate recognised            (68%)
129  it could not see                            (32%)
```

Two clauses were narrower than their intent, and **both fired on `PrivacyService`**, hiding all five
of its guarded routes at once:

1. `if (isWritePath(name)) return false;` — and `isWritePath` matches `record`, so
   `recordSdaiaSubmission` never reached line two of the method. It loads the breach, refuses with
   `IllegalStateException` on the terminal ACKNOWLEDGED state, and stamps `sdaiaSubmittedAt` — the
   discharge of the PDPL Article 31 clock.
2. `refuses` named exactly two exception families, inline. `containBreach`, `closeBreach`, `startDsr`,
   `fulfilDsr` and `rejectDsr` all refuse with `IllegalArgumentException`, and `DpiaService#approve`
   refuses through a shared `require(d, "IN_REVIEW")` helper whose body throws it — **both misses at
   once**. F2-182's rule ("a guard sits in at least four places a setter-site regex cannot see", one
   of them a shared `validate()`) applied to **refusal** detection rather than to setter detection.

🔑 **The name test was never load-bearing.** A `create` cannot refuse on a state it has not loaded,
because the row does not exist yet — so "loads a row AND refuses on that row's own state" is the whole
discriminator, and the name clause only ever removed *transitions*. Widened as a provable **UNION**
with the original predicate: replacing it outright LOST 96 pairs the original finds, so the union is
what makes the change additive (F2-225 — verify a widening by what it ADDS, in both directions).
280 + 129 = 409.

### The five contradictions it exposed, all adjudicated here

The gate's own output said **five sites in three services** where my working note had said three.
🔑 **The run is the authority, not the note** — and all three services were already in `CLOSED`, the
set asserted as a hard zero because they "have been read and fixed".

| Site | Verdict |
|---|---|
| `PolicyManagementService#createException` :: `reviewedAt`, `rejectedAt` | **CLOSED** — fixed, probed live |
| `NdiImprovementPlanService#addItem` :: `sequenceOrder` | **REFUTED** — detector false positive |
| `NdiImprovementPlanService#updateItem` :: `sequenceOrder` | **REFUTED** — same |
| `TcfdItemService#create` :: `lastReviewedAt` | **CLOSED** — fixed |
| `TcfdItemService#create` / `#update` :: `disclosureStatus` | **BY DESIGN**, with the residual defect inside it fixed |

#### The live one: a policy waiver granted by the route that files it

`createException` bound the entity and used **defaults, not guards** — `if (body.getStatus() == null)
body.setStatus("REQUESTED")` discards nothing the caller sent (F2-218's headline). Probed live as
`auditor`, who holds `COMPLIANCE:WRITE` — **the same permission `/transition` carries**, so this is
not a privilege escalation: the object-level state machine was the only control, and the create sat
beside it without one.

`POST /api/policy/exceptions` answered **200** and stored `status = APPROVED`,
`approver_name = "Nobody Who Approved This"`, `reviewer_name = "Nobody Who Reviewed This"`, a 2001
`reviewed_at` / `rejected_at` / `requested_at`, and an invented `rejection_reason` — on a **CRITICAL**
exception. A policy exception is a formal acceptance of residual risk with compensating controls and an
expiry; this class's own comment calls the approved ones *"the legally significant"* ones. The audit
ledger held **one CREATE row and no TRANSITION row**, so the trail an auditor reads had no record of
the approval at all, and `POLICY_EXCEPTION_APPROVED` never fired.

🔑 **`approvedAt` was already refused**, because `PolicyException` annotates that **one** field
`@JsonProperty(READ_ONLY)` and not its five siblings. Its refusal in the same probe is the
discriminator: the wire mechanism works, and the omission is F2-215's two-of-three shape — here **one
of six** — in a service F2-219 had put in `CLOSED` **for the attestation register**.
🔑 **A service declared closed for one register it owns is not closed for another.**

Fixed with one coherent rule: a create **files a request**, so `status` goes through
`ServerOwnedState.requireInitial` (read from the same constant the machine's root now uses),
`requestedAt` is the server's clock unconditionally, and every column the review / approval / rejection
states produce is cleared. `require`, not `coerce`, per F2-182: `ck_policy_exc_status` already refuses
anything outside the six tokens, and `PolicyManagementPage` sends `status: 'REQUESTED'` explicitly with
no input for any stamp — so nothing that works today starts failing.

#### The refuted pair: an identity read is not a state read

`reorder` was classified a guarded transition of `sequenceOrder` because it does
`byId.put(r.getId(), r)` and `if (r == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("not in plan")` — an
**identity** read and a **membership** refusal. It then renumbers every item from a counter **without
ever reading the previous value**, so F2-220's discriminator (the value accepted depends on the value
already there) is not satisfied. `sequence_order` is display order: no CHECK, 1–4 and 10–40 across 15
rows (dev = prod), and `addItem` openly defaults it when absent. Narrowed with `IDENTITY_ACCESSORS`,
asserted in **both** directions — add one real state read to the same shape and it counts again.

#### The by-design pair, and the defect that was hiding inside it

`disclosureStatus` on `create`/`update` is legitimate, and the reason is mechanical rather than a
matter of taste: `TcfdItem` declares `= "UNDER_REVIEW"` as a **field initialiser**, so an omitted key
deserialises to that value and `update()`'s null-guard cannot tell absence from a real UNDER_REVIEW.
Both ESG tabs therefore echo the current status back on every save, in a comment that says exactly
that. Refusing the field would silently downgrade every reviewer's classification.

But the residual **was** a defect: `update` performed the same classification change `transition`
performs while leaving `last_reviewed_at` stale and writing only a generic *"TCFD item updated"* audit
row. F2-188/F2-191's shape — **a duplicated transition agrees with the original on the row and differs
on the parts nothing asserts.** Both routes now go through `markReviewed()`, the one writer of the
`(disclosure_status, last_reviewed_at)` pair: `transition` calls it unconditionally (an explicit
re-mark *is* a review), `update` only when the incoming value differs. **An echo is not a review; a
change is.** Fixed identically in `CmaDisclosureService`, the service TCFD's own javadoc says it
mirrors — because closing one instance of a shape is not closing the shape.

`TcfdItem#lastReviewedAt` on create is the fourth: all three guarded routes stamp it from the server's
clock, so accepting it let a brand-new item carry the date an IFRS S2 / TCFD reader takes as *when this
recommendation was last looked at* (populated on 16 of 85 rows, dev = prod). 🔑 **The correct artefact
was in the sibling file the whole time** — `CmaDisclosureService#create` has carried exactly this scrub
under an SEC-ESG-003 comment since it was written.

### Also fixed, and honestly attributed

`PrivacyService#createBreach` / `#createDsr` were two-line methods binding the entity, so
`sdaiaSubmittedAt`, `sdaiaSubmissionRef`, `pdpcNotifiedAt` and `completedAt` were caller-writable —
the exact fields F2-209 and F2-213 wrote careful comments to protect on the *updates* two lines below.
All four hold 0 non-null values in dev and prod and none is client-declarable, so clearing them cannot
break a working request.

⚠ **This one is NOT a gate finding, and the pre-fix control is what established that**: stash the fix,
re-run, and `PrivacyService` does not appear either way. It stands on reading the two-line methods plus
`sys.columns` plus both databases. Recording it as something the widened gate caught would have been a
better story and a false one.

### The instrument findings

⚠⚠ **My own fix fell into the gate's other blind spot, and the closure it produced was fake.**
Extracting `markReviewed()` — the right design, one writer of the pair — took the `setDisclosureStatus`
call out of `update()`'s body, and `TcfdItemService#update` left the population **looking closed**.
🔑 **To a setter-site scan, a refactor that relocates a write is indistinguishable from a fix that
removed it, and the population shrinks either way — the quiet direction.** `writesFromRequest` now
follows a one-hop private helper, keyed by the helper's own declared parameter types and only when the
call passes something that reads the request.

⚠⚠ **The MIRROR of that widening was built, measured and REJECTED.** Following helper **stamps** is
the symmetric question, and enabling it moved the unexplained population from **11 services to 15**.
It needed two narrowings to get back to 13 (a route may not be its own stamping route; a helper the
write path itself calls is not a control it bypasses — `applyRules` and `maybeAutoCapa` are invariants
every route shares). At 13, one of the two net-new findings was **still a demonstrated false
positive**: `ChangeManagementService#addLink` reported as accepting `ChangeLink#changeRequestId`,
`entityId`, `entityType`, `linkType`, `notes` *"stamped by transition"* — the link's own data fields,
on the route whose entire purpose is to supply them. 🔑 **F2-214 settles it: a gate that fails on
correct code is worse than no gate**, and raising a decrease-only ceiling to accommodate noise is house
rule 3's own warning. So the write half ships and the stamp half is recorded as a **measured blind
spot** — asserted, with its numbers, a demonstrating corpus, and the one unread lead named
(`CommitteeResolutionService#create` :: `voteFor`/`voteAgainst`/`voteAbstain`, a resolution created
with its vote tallies already filled in). Its consequence is worth stating plainly: a service that
extracts its stamping into a helper drops out of the population **entirely**, not one field.

⚠⚠ **A per-service verdict could not express a per-field finding.** `TcfdItemService` is closed for
everything except one genuinely-by-design field, and the old `BY_DESIGN` map keyed on the service name
forced a false choice: drop the whole service out of the hard zero, or refuse a correct design. Re-keyed
to `Service::Type#field` — **F2-185b's headline one level up, the granularity of the verdict has to
match the granularity of the finding** — which also means a service already carrying an exemption no
longer hides a NEW contradiction on a different field of the same type.

⚠ **Three services were declared CLOSED against a predicate that saw 68% of the population**, so
"closed" meant *closed as far as the instrument could see*. F2-215's headline at the level of a closure
claim.

### What shipped

- `isGuardedRoute` widened as a union; `guardedTypes` returns the entity types a body **loaded and then
  refused on**, so the row a route refused on must be the row it stamps.
- `refusingHelperNames` — every refusal convention this codebase uses (F2-226 measured three).
- `readsAStateOf` + `IDENTITY_ACCESSORS` — the narrowing, asserted both ways.
- `writesFromRequest` follows a one-hop forwarding helper; `helperWrittenFields` / `helperStampedFields`
  classify **per setter**, never per helper, because `markReviewed` does both.
- `BY_DESIGN` re-keyed to `Service::Type#field`, 7 entries, each read in this slice, enforced in both
  directions plus a key-shape assertion.
- `stampedBy` takes `src` as a **required** parameter, so forgetting the refusing-helper resolution is a
  compile error rather than a silent under-report.
- The measured figure is printed into `target/server-stamped-fields.txt` so the next slice re-derives
  the ceiling instead of copying a number from elsewhere (F2-195).
- Ceiling **13 → 11**, re-derived from the gate's own printed figure (F2-207).

### Verification

- Full backend suite **4,047 / 0 / 0**; the gate 16/16.
- **Live probe 11/11 pre-fix and 17/17 post-fix** as `auditor`, on a `[REVIEW-TEST]` row the probe
  plants itself (F2-206), cleaned with `CHARINDEX`. Post-fix asserts both directions: the forged
  payload is refused **400** with a message naming `/transition`, the payload the frontend actually
  sends still returns **200**, all six attributions and stamps are cleared, `requested_at` is the
  server's clock, and the guarded route still reaches APPROVED stamping both clocks and recording
  `auditor` — without which a slice that closed the bypass by breaking the workflow would score
  identically.
- **Pre-fix control: 5 of 5** — the gate's hard zero and all four new behaviour tests fail on the
  un-fixed services, naming exactly `PolicyManagementService#createException` and
  `TcfdItemService#create`.
- **Mutation harness 14 killed / 3 survived / 0 anchor-miss.** All three survivors predicted: one
  **equivalent** (a compile-time-constant `case` label is the literal), one **invalid** (weakening an
  assertion always passes — F2-206), and one **real gap I named in advance** — reverting the CMA half
  survived because only the TCFD half had behaviour tests. 🔑 **Fixing two services and testing one
  leaves the untested one free to drift back, which is how the pair diverged in the first place.**
  Closed with two CMA tests.
- ⚠ Two harness bugs of mine, both loud: `shell=True` on Windows is cmd.exe, where a bash-style
  `VAR='x' mvn …` prefix is a syntax error and the run prints **nothing** — which the baseline check
  read as "red"; and `| grep` in the same place has no cmd.exe equivalent. Filter in Python.
- ⚠ **The heredoc landmine fired three times in one slice** — `<<'PYEOF'` collapsed `\\b` to `\b`,
  `\\s` to `\s` and `\\n` to a literal newline inside Python string literals, even with a quoted
  delimiter. Two were loud (a Java compile error, a `SyntaxError`); the dangerous mode is the silent
  one this file already records. **Use the Write/Edit tools for anything containing escapes.**

### ⚠⚠ Correction (F2-232, same day) — both net-new findings are false positives, 2 of 2

This spec said of the second one: *"the one unread lead named (`CommitteeResolutionService#create` ::
`voteFor`/`voteAgainst`/`voteAbstain`, a resolution created with its vote tallies already filled in)"*.
Read, it is **BY DESIGN with provenance, and F2-40 built the mechanism.** The secretariat form posts the
tally straight from the minutes for a committee that votes in the room — the normal path — and the row
records *which kind of tally it is*: `ASSERTED`, with the recorder taken from `Authentication` and never
from the body (the DF-3 rule; `tallyRecordedByUserId`/`Name` are explicitly nulled before being set),
versus `COMPUTED` for a resolution created empty and decided through `recordVote`.

Measured 2026-08-17: **22 live rows in dev, 20 in prod**, of which `ASSERTED_LEGACY` **20 / 20** —
F2-40's honest label for rows that predate the mechanism, carrying no recorder because none was ever
recorded through the API — and **0** carrying `ASSERTED` with a recorder, so the provenance path is
latent and correct rather than bypassed.

🔑 **That is the argument for the rejection rather than a footnote to it.** A population produced by a
detector already judged unsafe refuted at **2 of 2**, where this programme's usual rate against a
predecessor's claims is about 2 in 10 (F2-188, F2-192, F2-204, F2-211, F2-228). **Do not re-enable the
stamp half expecting a defect behind either name.** If it is ever revisited, the missing distinction is
between a helper implementing a GUARDED ROUTE's stamp and one implementing an invariant every path
shares — and neither refuted site turned on that distinction, which is exactly why two narrowings did
not rescue it.


### Filed

- The **11-service work list** in `target/server-stamped-fields.txt`, with the fields that put each
  there and which of the service's own routes stamps them. Deliberately **no verdicts** (F2-188).
- The **helper-stamp blind spot**, with its measurement (11 → 15, one demonstrated false positive at
  13) and its one unread lead.
- `privacy.data_subject_requests.due_date` — the PDPL Article 4 statutory deadline is
  **client-declarable** and nothing refuses it today. Only the server may issue a statutory deadline
  (F2-202), but `DsrRequestLifecycle` declares only a terminal set, so `requireInitial` has no initial
  state to enforce and the fix needs a product decision about back-dated imports first.
- `status` on `privacy.data_breaches` and `privacy.data_subject_requests` — **no CHECK, no declared
  machine**, so there is nothing for a create to be held to (F2-221's shape).
- `sust.cma_disclosure.clause` holds two disjoint notation schemes plus the literal `'None'` on 10
  rows; `consumer.complaint.complaint_no` never restarts its sequence per year.
- The remaining **45** `MassAssignmentRatchetTest` NEEDS-VERDICT rows (F2-217's 55, minus F2-218's 7
  and this slice's 3).

## F2-230 · Grading is only one way to be ordered, and a lexical sort ranks neither

| | |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-230 |
| **Title** | An ORDERED vocabulary ranked by an alphabetical sort — four registers, and the population was keyed on a NAME |
| **Severity** | P2 |
| **Status** | 🟢 CLOSED 2026-08-17 |
| **Programme** | Platform Bible F2 · reliability / correctness |
| **Modules** | `tprm/cyber`, `admin/committee`, `ndi/gap`, `change_mgmt`, `scm/fourthparty`, `common/validation` |

### What was measured

Executing F2-229's filed six-entry graded-String work list, the population was **re-derived first**
(F2-221) — and re-derived from the values the columns actually *store* rather than from the words in
their names, because a graded-name locator is the instrument class F2-217 proved measures its own
author's vocabulary.

```
483  columns are sorted by some repository query (853 ORDER BY terms across 429 repositories)
118  of those are String-typed
 57  hold a closed vocabulary (<= 12 distinct UPPER_SNAKE values in the live database)
  6  of the 57 are ORDERED — a ladder. The other 51 are CATEGORICAL.
```

Four other shapes were checked and are **absent**: `MAX()`/`MIN()` over a graded column (0),
`>`/`<`/`>=`/`BETWEEN` against a graded token (0), `Sort.by(<graded>)` at a call site (0), and Java
`compareTo`/`Comparator.comparing` on a graded getter (2, both on a numeric `riskScore`). The four
frontend `.sort` sites on graded fields already used explicit rank maps. **That is a result, not a
dead end** (F2-216): the family really does live in `ORDER BY`.

### The four defects, adjudicated

| Column | Verdict |
|---|---|
| `tprm.third_party_cyber_assessments.residual_risk_tier` | **CLOSED** — five-rung ladder, DESC ranked MODERATE > LOW > HIGH > ELEVATED > CRITICAL |
| `admin.committee_member_skills.skill_level` | **CLOSED** — DESC ranked INTERMEDIATE above EXPERT on the CMA Article 54 query |
| `ndi.gap.severity` | **CLOSED** — ASC is right on the top two rungs and transposes MEDIUM and LOW |
| `change_mgmt.change_authorisation_matrix.risk_level` | **CLOSED** — presentation: the grid could not be read as an escalation |
| `ai_governance.ml_model.risk_tier` | **REFUTED**, and the refutation is now *checked* rather than argued |
| `bcm.mtpd_inheritance_finding.severity` | **REFUTED** — an in-memory `severityRank` overrides the DB order |

**2 of 6 refuted, in opposite directions** — the same ~2-in-10 rate F2-188, F2-192, F2-204, F2-211
and F2-228 each measured in their predecessor's claims.

#### The sharpest: a paged register that put its most exposed vendor last

`ThirdPartyCyberAssessmentService.recompute` derives a **five**-rung ladder
(`LOW < MODERATE < ELEVATED < HIGH < CRITICAL`) that existed **only as an inline ternary chain**. The
register's default ordering was the derived method
`findByOrganisationIdOrderByResidualRiskTierDescIdDesc` — a lexical sort of an NVARCHAR column
presented as a severity ranking. Descending alphabetically those five read
**MODERATE > LOW > HIGH > ELEVATED > CRITICAL**, so **CRITICAL sorted last and LOW sorted second**.

Measured 2026-08-17, byte-identical in dev and prod: 16 rows holding LOW 7 / MODERATE 7 / ELEVATED 2,
and `ORDER BY residual_risk_tier DESC` returned six MODERATE rows before either ELEVATED one. The
endpoint is **paged**, so on a larger tenant the most exposed third parties are not merely
mis-ordered — they are on a page nobody opens. There is an index on
`(organisation_id, residual_risk_tier)` from V53, which is what made the wrong ordering fast: **a
lexical sort backed by a covering index reads like a considered decision.**

The vocabulary was declared nowhere server-side: no CHECK, an entity carrying only a `"MODERATE"`
default, and the service's own `INHERENT` set is a *different* four-token risk vocabulary on the same
entity overlapping this one only at LOW. 🔑 **The frontend had it right all along** —
`TpcResidual` declares all five rungs in order with a complete tone map. The half that was wrong is
the half that decides what an operator sees first (F2-205: when two copies disagree, ask which is the
server).

#### The governance one: an alphabetical sort answering a CMA Article 54 question

`CommitteeMemberSkillRepository#findByDimension` ended `ORDER BY s.skillLevel DESC` over
`BASIC | INTERMEDIATE | EXPERT`, whose alphabetical descent reads **INTERMEDIATE, EXPERT, BASIC**. Its
own javadoc says what it is for: *"Used to answer 'does this committee have a financial expert?' (CMA
Article 54, SAMA RGov 5.3.2)"*. Probed live in dev and prod: the query returned six INTERMEDIATE
members and the **single EXPERT last of seven**.

That javadoc also described a filter that does not exist — it claimed to return members "at a given
level or above" and the method takes no level parameter of any kind (F2-184's shape). The **ordering**
is fixed; the missing threshold is **not added**, because no caller asks for one and inventing a
capability to make a comment true is the wrong direction. The comment is corrected instead.

⚠ Blast radius stated honestly: no frontend client calls that endpoint, so today the wrong order
reaches API callers rather than the skills-matrix screen. **A fact about today, not a property of the
control** (F2-182).

### The reusable lesson

🔑 **The property that decides whether a lexical sort is a defect is whether the vocabulary is
ORDERED — and grading is only ONE way to be ordered.** Measuring from stored values rather than from
names surfaced two ordered vocabularies whose names sound like nothing of the kind:

- `consumer.complaint_aggregate_report.report_period` holds `Q4-2025`, and a lexical sort of
  `Q<n>-<year>` orders by **QUARTER before YEAR** — so `'Q4-2025' > 'Q1-2026'` and the most recent
  SAMA quarterly complaints return is not first. Latent (1 row each). The column is `@NotBlank` free
  text with **no format contract**, so a fix has to settle a format first — **FILED**.
- `tprm.questionnaire_templates.version` sorted lexically would put `'10.0'` before `'9.0'`. Latent
  (only `'1.0'` stored) — **FILED**.

**Time and version are ordered too.** F2-229's name-keyed locator could not see either by
construction.

### What shipped

- **`common/validation/OrderedVocabulary`** — a `ClosedVocabulary` plus an order: `rank`, `outranks`,
  `atLeast`, `bottom`, `top`, and `isAlphabetical()`, which exists so an accidentally-correct sort is
  *expressible* rather than argued about in a comment. `ConcentrationTier` (F2-229) now delegates to
  it rather than being a second mechanism (F2-190).
- Four declared ladders — `ResidualRiskTier`, `SkillLevel`, `NdiGapSeverity`, `ChangeRiskLevel` — plus
  `FourthPartyExposureService.DOWNSTREAM_CRITICALITY_LADDER` (see the instrument note below).
- Six repository queries re-ranked with an explicit `CASE` ladder. `recompute` now **indexes** the
  ladder via declared score bands instead of naming the five rungs in a ternary, with a static check
  that the bands divide the ladder exactly.
- **`OrderedVocabularySortContractTest`** — the invariant (no declared ladder is sorted lexically
  unless the sort is *provably* safe) plus the census (every CHECK-constrained column still sorted
  lexically, exactly asserted, **no verdicts**, because a hard zero over 57 would fail on correct
  code — F2-214).
- **V378** — the register's first three CHECK constraints, scoped to the writers this same commit
  closed (F2-183), measured clean in both databases first, applied twice to dev.
- The create no longer *defaults* its status but **forces** the initial state — F2-220's shape,
  tenth instance. `if (status == null) status = "DRAFT"` is a default, not a guard, so a caller could
  create an assessment already APPROVED and skip `submit()`/`approve()`, the only writers of
  `assessedAt`, `approvedAt` and `approverName`.
- Frontend: `TPC_RESIDUAL_LADDER` + `isResidualAtLeast`, replacing **six** separately-spelled readers.

### The instrument findings

⚠⚠ **Introducing a wrapper type around a value an instrument discovers by exact type silently removes
it from that instrument's population.** `ClosedVocabularyPinTest` narrows on the source string
`ClosedVocabulary.of(` and reflects on `ClosedVocabulary.class.equals(f.getType())` — so all four new
ladders would have been invisible **twice over**. Fixed in the same commit, and their constraint names
are in `MUST_BE_FOUND` precisely so the widening cannot quietly un-widen. Tenth instance of F2-198's
shape after a filename, a three-entry allow-list, a module name, a controller-bearing table, an
`extends` clause, a field-name list inside a fix, a name list in a census and a claim shape in a gate.

⚠⚠ **My own anti-vacuity floor found a real hole by being wrong.** I set the CASE-ladder floor to 8
and the parse found 7 — because F2-229 wrote a `CASE` ladder for
`scm.fourth_party_exposures.downstream_criticality` into the register's `@Query` and **declared no
ladder for it**, so the SQL held an order nothing in Java could contradict. 🔑 **A ranking written
only in SQL is still a second copy of a vocabulary's order; it just has nothing to disagree with.**

⚠ **One of my gate's own assertions was wrong and the gate was right.** I asserted that widening
`IN ('CRITICAL','HIGH')` to include MEDIUM would break the safety proof; it does not —
alphabetically CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM has ranks 3, 2, 1, which is monotone, so that subset is
genuinely safe. LOW is the token that breaks it. F2-206's rule (a surviving mutant is a hole only if
the mutated code is actually wrong) applied to an assertion rather than a mutation.

### Verification

- Backend suite (hermetic, `mvn -o clean package`) — see the plan row for the count.
- Frontend `npx tsc --noEmit` clean, `npx vitest run` **771/771**.
- **Pre-fix control: 13 of 13 detectors fire on `master` and are clean on the fixed tree.** Two
  harness bugs of my own on the way there, both loud: reading the "after" side as `git show HEAD:`
  compared master with itself while the fix was uncommitted (F2-229 recorded this exact misuse), and
  five detectors reported STILL THERE because **my own comments quote the shapes they retired** —
  F2-193's rule, so the harness strips comments, except for the one detector whose *claim is about a
  comment*, which uses `unquoted()` instead.
- **Live probe 33/33** against the running dev stack: the register leads with both ELEVATED rows where
  the lexical sort led with MODERATE; the CMA Article 54 query leads with the EXPERT; the NDI register
  no longer transposes MEDIUM and LOW; the matrix rises within each change type; a create naming
  APPROVED or RETIRED is refused **400** while one naming nothing returns **201 / DRAFT**; all three
  V378 constraints refuse an out-of-vocabulary value; and the 16 seeded rows are byte-identical
  afterwards.
- ⚠ Two probe bugs, both mine: the route was **guessed** (`/api/v1/tprm/...`; it is
  `/api/tprm/cyber-assessments`, no `v1` — recurring since F2-198), and the constraint checks targeted
  `WHERE id = (SELECT MIN(id) … tagged)` with no tagged row planted, so `WHERE id = NULL` matched zero
  rows and every UPDATE "succeeded". 🔑 **An operation that touches nothing looks exactly like an
  operation that was allowed** — the section now plants its own victim (F2-206) and asserts the row
  count with a legal value first.

### Filed

- **10 of 16 rows' stored `residual_risk_tier` is LOWER than the service's own derivation from the
  `risk_score` stored beside it; 0 are higher. Identical in dev and prod.** Found in the browser after
  every gate was green — **seventh consecutive slice**. The sharpest is `TPC-GOV-001`, score **90.00**
  of 100 (higher = worse) recorded as **LOW** residual risk, and `TPC-GOV-003` at 88 likewise; the
  register renders both figures on the same row, so it contradicts itself in one line (F2-203's
  shape). `recompute` runs only on create and `recordPosture`, so these seed-written rows have never
  been through the derivation — and the first operator to record posture on TPC-GOV-001 will watch it
  jump LOW → CRITICAL. Uniformly **flattering**, the direction F2-196 warned not to assume. Re-deriving
  rewrites 10 live rows in two real databases: **an owner decision** (F2-183/F2-196), not a side
  effect of an ordering fix.
- The two ordered-but-not-graded members above (`report_period`, `version`).
- The **51 categorical** lexically-sorted vocabularies: no defect unless a reader finds one of them
  ordered, which is a question this gate deliberately does not answer.
- F2-221's **201** state-ish columns with no CHECK, which no leg of this gate can see.

## F2-229 · A derived value narrower than its own column destroys what it cannot express

**Found** 2026-08-17, executing F2-228's filed concentration-recompute defect. **P2** — every write
anywhere in the SAMA fourth-party register flattened nine of its thirteen concentration tiers, the
register's default ordering put its most concentrated row last, and the top tier was invisible to
every surface that reads it. **Closed** the same day. V377; 3 backend classes, 4 frontend files, 3
gates, 2 behaviour test classes.

### The recompute ASSIGNED where the code's own two comments said ELEVATE

`FourthPartyExposureService.recomputeConcentration` runs across the whole tenant on every create and
every update. Three artefacts described it as an elevation:

* the service javadoc — *"when the same fourth party appears behind ≥3 primaries it's auto-elevated
  to HIGH"*;
* `FourthPartyExposureRepository#concentrationCounts`'s javadoc — *"the service uses this to elevate
  `concentration_risk` to HIGH"*;
* the auto-CAPA hook, written as a **rising edge** (`"HIGH".equals(tier) && !"HIGH".equals(previous)`)
  — a shape that only makes sense if the value is monotone.

The code did `ex.setConcentrationRisk(tier)`, unconditionally. Measured 2026-08-17 and **identical in
dev and prod**: all 13 live rows carry **13 distinct** fourth-party names, so `concentrationCounts`
returns an empty map and the computed tier is LOW for every row — and any write **lowered 9 of the
13**, including all three HIGH rows and the sole CRITICAL one (*"Underlying hyperscaler region
(sub-infrastructure)"*). Same family as F2-195's `|| N`: the correct rule was written down in prose
beside the place it was not applied.

🔑 **The range of the derivation is a strict subset of the range of the column, which is what made
the flattening irreversible.** Multiplicity can justify LOW, MEDIUM or HIGH; no row count produces
CRITICAL. So a CRITICAL assessment overwritten by the derivation could never be restored by it. That
is the reusable shape, and it generalises past this register: **a recompute whose output range is
narrower than its column's vocabulary destroys the values it cannot express.**

The fix is one declared ladder (`ConcentrationTier`) read by the recompute, the CAPA rising edge and
the ordering. `multiplicityFloor` says what the row count alone justifies; `outranks` decides whether
that floor is worth raising a stored assessment to; nothing lowers one. A **RETIRED** edge no longer
props up anybody's floor — which matters *more* under elevation than it did under assignment, because
an inflated floor is now permanent. Latent today (no fourth-party name appears twice in either
database), so it is asserted by test rather than observed in data.

### The ordering was an alphabetical sort presented as a severity ranking

`findByOrganisationIdOrderByConcentrationRiskDescDownstreamCriticalityDesc` is a derived Spring Data
method on two `NVARCHAR` columns. Descending **alphabetically**, LOW|MEDIUM|HIGH|CRITICAL reads
MEDIUM, LOW, HIGH, CRITICAL. Measured read-only against the live register: the row that came back
**last of 13 was the CRITICAL/CRITICAL one**, with the three HIGH/CRITICAL rows 10th, 11th and 12th.
The frontend requests `size=200` and renders the server's order, so the most concentrated fourth
party in the register was the last row on the page.

🔑 **A lexical sort is a ranking only where the vocabulary happens to be in alphabetical order, and
severity ladders never are.** Replaced with a `CASE` rank whose tokens are checked, in order, against
`ConcentrationTier.ladder()` by reflection over the `@Query` annotation — a `@Query` string is
necessarily a second copy of the order, and that is what stops it drifting from the first.

### CRITICAL had no declaration anywhere, and six reader questions each dropped it

The entity's field javadoc said `LOW | MEDIUM | HIGH`. The frontend's `FpConcentration` said the
same. The table had **no CHECK constraint of any kind**. And the column held CRITICAL on one row in
both databases. Consequences, all measured:

* `FP_CONC_TONE[r.concentrationRisk]` was `undefined` for that row;
* the concentration tab filtered `HIGH || MEDIUM`, so **the tab built to surface concentration risk
  excluded the most concentrated row in the register**;
* its chip under-counted (8 where 9 qualify), and it was computed by summing *two separately spelled*
  inclusion lists rather than by the predicate the tab filters with (F2-197);
* `TprmConsolidatedOverview`'s roll-up and per-vendor count, and the dashboard widget's `fpHigh`, all
  asked `=== 'HIGH'`.

F2-196's rule on a tier instead of a status: **"elevated" must be a threshold over a declared ladder,
never a second inclusion list.** Measured against master, **7 equality comparisons across 3 files**
implementing those 6 reader questions; all 7 now ask `isConcentrationAtLeast`. ⚠ The rule was already
in the tree one component over — `TprmConsolidatedOverview` ranks the *adjacent* `residualRiskTier`
with its own `tierRank()` helper, and the concentration column beside it never used it.

### V377 — the table's first CHECK constraints, scoped to the writers this slice closed

Four constraints on a table that had zero, per F2-183: `concentration_risk` and `status` are
server-owned (two literal write sites each), and `dependency_type`/`downstream_criticality` are
routed through `ClosedVocabulary.require()` in the same commit. Measured in **both** databases
first — 13 rows each, **0 violations and 0 non-canonical casings** in all four columns — so no
`WITH NOCHECK`, and **no casing UPDATE**, checked rather than assumed because every writer either
normalises or writes a Java literal. Applied twice to dev via pyodbc; the dev rows were byte-identical
afterwards.

⚠ `require` rather than `coerce` throughout, per F2-182's test: the hand-rolled `Set.contains` this
replaces already **refused** anything outside the vocabulary, so nothing that succeeds today starts
failing. What changes is that `'high'` is now normalised to `HIGH` instead of 400-ing.

### The platform-wide measurement, and the detector bug that hid most of it

`LexicalSeveritySortContractTest` is reflection over `target/classes` — repository interfaces and
their `@Query` annotations are runtime-retained, so no regex reads Java. Measured: **429 repository
interfaces, 644 derived `OrderBy` methods, 91 `@Query` with an `ORDER BY`, 857 lexical order terms**,
of which **15 columns** carry a CHECK vocabulary of three or more tokens.

⚠⚠ **A hard zero over those 15 would fail on correct code, which is the one thing a gate must never
do (F2-214).** Most are **categorical**: `sust.esg_metric.category` is
[ENVIRONMENTAL, SOCIAL, GOVERNANCE], `admin.committee_form_templates.form_type` is
[AGENDA, ATTENDANCE, MOTION, …], and sorting those alphabetically is a deterministic grouping that
claims nothing. Only an **ordered** vocabulary turns an alphabetical sort into an assertion about
which row matters most. So the leg is an exactly-asserted **census** with no verdicts (F2-188), and a
separate 6-entry graded-String work list covers the two columns that have no CHECK and are therefore
invisible to it.

⚠ **Two of the six were read while measuring, and they fall in opposite directions** — which is the
argument for the work list carrying no reasons. `MlModelRepository`'s two queries are **accidentally
correct**: `WHERE m.riskTier IN ('CRITICAL','HIGH')` narrows the vocabulary to two tokens whose
alphabetical order *is* their severity order. `CommitteeMemberSkillRepository#findByDimension` sorts
`skillLevel DESC` over [BASIC, INTERMEDIATE, EXPERT] to answer *"does this committee have a financial
expert?"* (CMA Article 54) — so it ranks INTERMEDIATE above EXPERT.

⚠⚠ **MY OWN DETECTOR UNDER-REPORTED, AND ONLY THE ANTI-VACUITY LEG KNEW.**
`MigrationVocabularies` keys its vocabularies `schema.table.column`; my first draft built the
entity-side key as `table.column` from `@Table(name)`, ignoring `@Table(schema)`. Every lookup
therefore missed, every column read as having **no CHECK**, and the hard zero I had written
**passed** — over a population of 15. The throwaway census using the same key printed *"total columns
affected: 0"* and I read that as a measurement. What caught it was
`theCheckDrivenLegIsNotVacuous` asserting that V377's own four constraints are findable. 🔑 **A
detector that cannot match reads exactly like a clean tree, and it under-reports — the quiet
direction.** Nothing about the shape of the wrong answer looked wrong: two of the fifteen are in
`admin`, four in `sust`. `theSchemaSegmentOfTheKeyIsLoadBearing` now asserts the failure mode
directly, and the mutation that restores the bug is killed.

### The narrowing that matters is the field TYPE, and it is pinned by measurement

A name-based locator over graded-sounding column names returns **10** lexically-sorted columns after
the fix (12 before it), and **4 of them are numeric** — `platform.automation_rules.priority`,
`sust.climate_risk_opportunity.risk_score`, `bcm.communication_contacts.escalation_level`,
`socops.ot_asset.purdue_level` — where a lexical sort *is* a correct numeric sort. Counting those
would inflate the population by 40%. `theNumericNarrowingIsLoadBearing` holds them exactly, so
deleting the String narrowing changes an answer rather than an opinion.

* **17/17 mutations killed**, plus **one recorded EQUIVALENT** (the CAPA rising edge asking `equals`

  can never be CRITICAL, so the two agree on every reachable input — F2-206's rule that a surviving
  mutant is a hole only if the mutated code is wrong).
* ⚠ **Two harness results were mine, not the gate's.** M10 (the first `CASE` ladder flipped to `ASC`)
  **survived** a bare `contains("END DESC")` because the *second*, untouched ladder still matched —
  F2-194's substring-satisfied-by-something-else, so the leg now asserts by **count**. And M13's first
  form mutated the gate's own assertion to a weaker one, which always survives (F2-206); replaced by

* ⚠ **The CRLF trap fired for the third time in this lineage** (F2-212, F2-219): the frontend files
  are CRLF and the harness's anchors are LF, so two multi-line anchors reported ANCHOR-MISS. The

* ⚠ **The pre-fix half was deliberately NOT re-run.** F2-228 already observed the flattening live —
  and damaged this exact register doing it — while the arithmetic (13 distinct names → every computed

* **Pre-fix control**: every text detector run against `git show master:` — 7 comparisons on master,

## F2-228 · The reading confirmed three sites the probe refuted, and the fatal one is the INSERT

**Found** 2026-08-17, executing F2-227's filed six-site work list. **P2** — the
conflict-of-interest register could record everything except a conflict, and the CCM
consecutive-failure escalation recorded neither the Issue nor the failing run. **Closed** the same
day. No migration; 2 backend services, 1 gate, 2 behaviour tests.

### Two detector errors in opposite directions, which is why a green build pinned the wrong set

The population was re-derived before the filing was executed (F2-221). F2-227's detector was wrong
**both ways**, and the errors cancelled:

* It **over-matched**. The query receiver was unconstrained, so `all.stream()`, `gates.count()` and
  `x.findFirst()` — Java Stream API calls on an in-memory `List` — read as database queries. That
  alone is why `WorkflowRequestService#advanceRouting` was on the work list: it touches no
  repository at all. ⚠ Keying the receiver on the field NAME is also wrong —
  `PolicyManagementService` calls its repository `docs`, so a `*repo*` rule cannot see it (F2-197).
  Resolve it from `private final …Repository`.
* It **under-matched**. `findById(` is **not** a flusher: `EntityManager#find` raises a LoadEvent,
  not an AutoFlushEvent, and returns the managed instance straight from the persistence context. A
  *derived* query method (`findByIdAndOrganisationId`) compiles to JPQL and does auto-flush. And the
  flush may be **transitive**, one level deeper than the callee.

🔑 **The loose `find\w*` matched `assetRepo.findById(` and so put `recomputeRiskScore` in the
population for a reason that is not true, while the real flush sat in `pickHighestOpenSeverity`.
Fixing either error alone would have been worse than fixing neither** — the over-match fix deletes a
site, the under-match fix keeps a phantom. F2-224's headline, one slice later, in the same gate.

### The reading confirmed three sites and the live probe refuted all three

| Site | Read as | Probed |
|---|---|---|
| `AttackSurfaceAssetService#recomputeRiskScore` | confirmed | **200, twice** |
| `ObService#recountTpp` | confirmed | **200** |
| `FourthPartyExposureService#recomputeConcentration` | confirmed | **201** |

🔑 **The load-bearing premise was never checked: `FourthPartyExposure` does not extend
`BaseEntity`, so it carries no `@Version` and no `row_version` column at all.** Two UPDATEs of it
are simply two UPDATEs. Only **172 of 432** entities inherit the version, so for 260 of them this
whole family is unrepresentable — F2-206's *"an invariant enforced by a superclass covers exactly
its subclasses"*, inverted: **the defect enabled by a superclass reaches exactly its subclasses.**

### The discriminator the probe forced

F2-227's site differed from these in exactly one way: **its first save was of a freshly-constructed
entity.** `@GeneratedValue(IDENTITY)` makes Hibernate execute that INSERT immediately to obtain the
id, and `row_version` is `insertable = false`, so the in-memory version is **null** afterwards and
the follow-up `UPDATE … WHERE row_version = null` matches zero rows. That is precisely what
Hibernate's own hint — *"or unsaved-value mapping was incorrect"* — had been saying all along. A row
that was **loaded** carries a real version and two UPDATEs of it both succeed.

🔑 **For an INSERT the first save IS the flush**, so no intervening query is needed and the
flush-between requirement F2-227's gate rests on does not apply to the shape that actually fires.

### The two live sites, both probed at 409 against planted rows

**`CoiService#submitDeclaration`** saved the declaration, inserted the disclosed items to get their
`declarationId`, then re-saved the declaration to carry the auto-flagged outcome. Probed as
`viewer`: a declaration disclosing **nothing** returns 201 (because `computeAutoOutcome` returns
`PENDING`, the value already set, so nothing is dirty), and a declaration disclosing **an actual
conflict of interest** answers **409** and rolls back. 🔑 **A conflict-of-interest register that
could record everything except a conflict.** The route is `isAuthenticated()`, so the affected
population is every employee.

**`CcmService#recordRunInternal`** saved the run, opened the Issue, then re-saved the run to carry
the Issue id. Probed: the **third consecutive failure of a CRITICAL control test** answers **409**
and rolls the whole transaction back, so **neither the Issue nor the failing run itself is
recorded** — on both `POST /ccm/tests/{id}/run-now` and the 60-second `CcmSchedulerService` tick.
F2-175's defect, in another module, on the escalation ladder.

Both fixed F2-175's way — **do the other work first, save once**. The COI items are built in memory
and the outcome decided before the single save; the CCM Issue is opened before the run is inserted,
and `openConsecutiveFailureIssue` only ever read the run's `failureReason`, never its id.

### The gate's question was wrong, so it was re-scoped rather than raised

Per F2-204: a cross-method re-save of a **loaded** row is not a defect, so a hard zero over that
population would be a gate failing on correct code — the one failure a gate must never have
(F2-214). It becomes an **exactly-asserted census** of 7 measured-harmless sites, each carrying a
verdict that names its evidence, enforced in both directions so a new member forces the next reader
to ask the only question that matters: *is the first save an INSERT?* The **hard zero moves to the
INSERT shape**, with the two literal pre-fix shapes, both fixed forms, F2-227's own site and one
must-not-count refutation as positive controls.

⚠ **My own verdict vocabulary rejected a correct, verified verdict.** The first draft enumerated
`REFUTED BY LIVE PROBE` and `REFUTED BY READING` — the two sources this slice happened to reach
first — and then refused `REFUTED BY THE ENTITY`, which is the strongest of the seven. That is
**F2-224's own lesson recurring inside a gate written after quoting it**: the rule is that a verdict
must NAME its evidence, not that it must be one of the sources already used.

⚠ **A probe of `recomputeConcentration` altered 9 real seeded rows.** That recompute is
authoritative over the whole tenant and disagrees with the seed, so it reset 9 of 13
`concentration_risk` values to `LOW`. Restored field-for-field from prod, which holds the identical
seed and was never in scope (F2-206's precedent). **Filed as its own defect** — any create or update
in the fourth-party register silently rewrites other rows' SAMA concentration tier.

| | |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-228 |
| **Severity** | **P2.** A conflict-of-interest declaration that disclosed a conflict could not be filed by any employee; the CCM CRITICAL escalation recorded neither its Issue nor its failing run. |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-17** (`PENDING`). Backend 3,995/0/0, gate 7/7, probe 8/8 post-fix; 2 live sites closed, 7 refuted (3 of them by live probe against the reading). |
| **Filed** | The fourth-party concentration recompute rewriting 9 of 13 seeded rows on any create or update; `openbanking.ob_tpp` having zero CHECK constraints; and the structural root carried from F2-227 — `@Generated(INSERT, UPDATE)` on `rowVersion` would make the family unrepresentable at the cost of a post-write select on all 172 `BaseEntity` subclasses. |

## F2-227 · The double save nobody could gate, and the handler that hid it

**Found** 2026-08-17, executing F2-226's filed 500. **P2** — the facilitator's ordinary
"throw an inject now" action on a live BCM exercise answered HTTP 500 for every tenant, and the
platform-wide defect family behind it had been undiagnosable from a response since the handler was
written. **Closed** the same day. No migration; 2 backend classes, 1 new gate.

### The diagnostic had to come first, because the defect could not be diagnosed without it

F2-226 identified the 500 **by inference** — the dedicated dispatch route answered 200 on the
identical row, the combined path 500 — and recorded it as a ROWVERSION double flush. That was a
good inference and it was not a measurement.

Measuring it meant fixing the diagnostic. `OptimisticLockingFailureException` is a
`DataAccessException`, so every one of them fell into `handleMissingDbObject` and came back as a
bare *"An unexpected database error occurred."* with **no exception class, even in dev with
`grc.errors.verbose=true` explicitly on** — because that handler built its own `ProblemDetail`
instead of delegating to `handleGeneral`, which is the only place the verbose diagnostics live. Its
comment said *"let the catch-all handle it with a 500."* It did not.

🔑 **The handler that intercepted this exception class was the one handler that discarded the
diagnostic verbose mode exists to provide** — and the exception class in question is the one
CLAUDE.md's second landmine produces, recorded at F2-175 and hit again at F2-226. **A
platform-wide defect family was undiagnosable by construction.** F2-180's rule inverted: a
wrong-but-specific diagnostic at least sends the reader somewhere; a *generic* diagnostic from a
*specific* handler sends them nowhere and looks deliberate. F2-184's shape, in an exception handler.

With the handler in place the response named it: **`ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException` on
`ExerciseRunInject 16`, "Row was updated or deleted by another transaction (or unsaved-value
mapping was incorrect)"**. A stale row is now a **409** that names the entity and its id, because
"retry?" is not a diagnosis.

### Why the shape is fatal, from the mapping

`BaseEntity.rowVersion` is
`@Version @Column(name = "row_version", insertable = false, updatable = false) byte[]` — a SQL
Server ROWVERSION the **database** generates and Hibernate never re-reads. So the instant a flush
reaches the database the in-memory version is stale, and the next `UPDATE … WHERE row_version = ?`
matches zero rows. Hibernate's own parenthetical, *"or unsaved-value mapping was incorrect"*, is
the hint that the version was never populated.

### ⚠⚠ The discriminator, corrected — and a scan gets this wrong in the flattering direction

A first derivation treated any intervening repository write as the flusher and reported **18 live
sites**. The tell was `PolicyManagementService#update`: it has the shape and F2-222 probed it
**13/13 working**. Reading `AuditLogService.log` settled it — it is `@Transactional` (joining the
caller's transaction) and saves an IDENTITY-generated row, so Hibernate executes that one insert
immediately to obtain the id **without flushing the caller's other pending changes**.

🔑 **`audit.log` and `emit` are not flushers. A QUERY is** — flush-before-query sends everything
pending. That single correction is the whole difference between 18 live sites and one, and it is
why this platform works while carrying the shape in **39** places (18 with a query between the
saves, 21 without).

### The population, and what is decidable

| | |
|---|---|
| **Cross-method** (save, then a sibling re-loads that repository's row and saves it) | **8 sites.** 1 FIXED (`ExerciseRuntimeService#dispatchInject` — the live 500). 1 REFUTED by reading: `ApprovalChainTemplateService#clearOtherDefaults` queries `…AndIdNot(`, so it provably saves *other* rows. **6 on a decrease-only work list.** |
| **Same-method** (`save(x)` … `save(x)`) | Measured and filed. The scan cannot tell "the same row twice" from "a different row", and a hard zero over unread code is a gate failing on code the slice never examined (F2-214). |

The six ship as a **work list and deliberately not as reasons** (F2-188 measured what happens when
a slice writes a reason for something it has not read: five claims, five false, and the fluency was
what made them look verified): `AttackSurfaceAssetService#recomputeRiskScore`,
`FourthPartyExposureService#recomputeConcentration`, `ObService#recountTpp`,
`PolicyManagementService#supersedePriorPublished`, `WorkflowRequestService#advanceRouting`,
`WorkflowRequestService#notifyStep`. Each needs one question answered by reading: **does the
sibling save the row the caller just saved, or a different one?**

### The fix, and why it is not "call dispatchInject later"

`addCustomInject` now stamps the dispatch **in memory** before its single save, and both entry
points share one `announceDispatched` rather than one calling the other. F2-188 measured what a
duplicated transition does: the duplicate agrees with the original on the row, which is easy to
check, and differs on the audit trail, which nothing asserts. `setActualDispatchedAt` has exactly
one writer, asserted.

⚠ **The existing test stubbed the re-load with the comment *"After save, the dispatchInject step
needs the inject to be findable"* — and that stub was the defect.** It became an
`UnnecessaryStubbingException` the moment the fix landed, which is the cleanest possible evidence.
Repurposed to assert `times(1)` on save and `never()` on the re-read, since — as CLAUDE.md says —
no mock can reproduce the failure itself.

### Lesson

🔑 **A landmine that cannot be diagnosed from a response will be rediscovered instead of fixed.**
This one was recorded three times over two years of slices and never once identified from an error
message, because the handler for its exception class threw the class name away. **Before measuring
a defect family, check that its failure is legible** — and: **the discriminator that separates live
from latent is worth more than the count, because getting it wrong inflates a population 18-fold in
the direction that manufactures findings.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-227 |
| **Severity** | **P2.** The default path of a facilitator control on a live BCM exercise answered 500 for every tenant; and a documented defect family produced anonymous 500s platform-wide. |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-17** (`20c7c634`). Backend 3,992/0/0, gate 6/6, probe 9/9 post-fix, three-stage evidence chain (500 → 409 naming the class → 201 DISPATCHED). |
| **Filed** | The 6 unadjudicated cross-method sites; the 21 latent same-method sites; and the structural root — annotating `rowVersion` `@Generated(INSERT, UPDATE)` would make the whole family unrepresentable at the cost of a post-write select on every one of 174 `BaseEntity` subclasses, which is an owner trade-off and not a side effect of a bug fix. |

## F2-226 · The clock the caller cannot reach at all — and a request that named its own approver

**Found** 2026-08-17, executing F2-225's filed field-initialiser work list. **P2** — the
cross-module approval register recorded a raiser the caller named and let that caller choose who
may approve it; a BCM exercise response recorded a participant the caller named while the server
measured their reaction time. **Closed** the same day. No migration; 2 backend services, 2 request
DTOs, 2 frontend surfaces.

### Re-deriving the filing found that it measured one of four mechanisms

F2-225 filed four sites, measured over entities carrying a clock-**initialised** act field. That is
**one of F2-215's four filling mechanisms**. Re-derived across all four — initialiser, lifecycle
callback (`@PrePersist`/`@PreUpdate`), Hibernate `@CreationTimestamp`, and `insertable = false`
where the database default fills the column — the denominator is **82 entities / 87 act-clock
fields**, not 68: **73 initialiser · 6 callback · 8 database default**.

🔑 **The two mechanisms it missed are the ones a caller can never reach at all.** A `@PrePersist`
fires at flush time *after* every setter and an `insertable = false` column is never sent, so both
are **stronger** evidence that the server owns WHEN than an initialiser — which F2-225 itself found
can be overridden (`CoiService#recordRecusal`). Permissively re-paired: **30 sites — 17 candidate,
11 assignment, 2 noise**. The widening surfaced no new confirmed attribution, which is a result
rather than a dead end (F2-216).

### ⚠⚠ Two of the four filed sites were mis-bucketed, and F2-225's own classifier said so

- `AuditEngagementService#create::leadAuditor` and `::auditCommitteeChair` — **assignments.** They
  sit beside `auditorFirm`: an IIA engagement is routinely led by an external firm's partner, who
  is not a platform principal at all (F2-224's `auditorExternalParty` lesson).
- `InvocationService#create::incidentCommander` and `::bcmCoordinator` — **crisis role
  assignments**, refuted decisively by the sibling column. `Invocation` declares `declaredBy`
  separately, and that is the attribution F2-224 closed.

🔑 **F2-225 built the three-bucket classifier AND hand-filed a work list its own classifier
contradicts, and nothing compared the two.** Its headline was *"the classification is as much the
finding as the count"*; the work list was then filed by hand. This is the shape this register keeps
recording — two artefacts, nobody maintaining the agreement (F2-177) — committed inside the
instrument built to answer it. `theWorkListAgreesWithTheClassifier` now applies the classifier to
the work list mechanically, so a member that classifies as an assignment cannot sit in a list of
unadjudicated attributions.

⚠ **`participantUserId` classifies as an ASSIGNMENT and was still fixed, which is not a
contradiction.** The classifier reads a NAME; that site was adjudicated by reading the CODE. It is
the reason a classifier triages a population and never decides a verdict, and it is recorded in the
gate rather than papered over by special-casing the word *participant*.

### The two confirmed sites, probed live against PLANTED rows (F2-206)

**Leg A — `ApprovalRequestService#create::requestedBy`.** `approvals.requests.requested_at` is a
field initialiser (`= LocalDateTime.now()`), so the server owns WHEN with no `setRequestedAt`
anywhere for the F2-223 detector to pair; `requested_by` is NOT NULL and was `@NotBlank` from the
body — the **fifth** instance of a server *requiring* an attribution it never verifies. Probed as
`viewer` (holds `WORKFLOW:WRITE`, **not** `WORKFLOW:APPROVE`): a request for a POLICY publication
stored `requested_by = "Nobody Who Raised This"` beside a server clock, and omitting the field was
a **400**.

🔑 **The rule was already written down in the client.** `lib/approvalsApi.ts` says of the transition
payload: *"There is no `decidedBy` here on purpose. The server takes the deciding identity from the
authenticated principal (SEC-IAM-002) — sending one would be a field the server ignores."* That
comment sits one screenful above the `requestedBy: string` the service trusted. F2-215's headline
again: generalising an invariant one field at a time leaves the remainder looking covered, because
the mechanism that covers them is visibly present.

**Leg B — four eyes, and it is the sharper half.** `assignedTo` is not decoration: it **is** the
authorisation input `transition()` checks (`callerUsername.equals(r.getAssignedTo())`, SEC-IAM-002).
So whoever creates the request decides who may approve it. Probed as `compliance`, who holds both
`WORKFLOW:WRITE` and `WORKFLOW:APPROVE`: raised a P1 risk-acceptance approval assigned to
`compliance`, then **approved it** — 200 then 200, with `decided_by` correctly recording them both
times. **The audit trail told the truth about who acted while nothing stopped them** (F2-222's leg
2). The gate compares case-**insensitively** because the column collates CI (F2-179).

**Leg C — `ExerciseRuntimeService#recordResponse::participantUserId`.** `responseAt` is initialiser-
stamped *and* re-stamped, the route is `isAuthenticated()` (correctly — filing a response is a duty,
the ADR-010 shape), and `participantUserId` was `@NotNull` from the body. Probed: `viewer` (id 6)
filed a response **as `compliance` (id 3)**, stored verbatim; omitting it was a **400**.

🔑 **The server does not merely record WHO here, it MEASURES them.** `responseTimeSeconds` is
computed from the inject's dispatch to now, so the row is the evidence an ISO 22301 / NCEMA reviewer
reads to accept that a named participant reacted within N seconds. The audit row **quoted the
caller's claim** (`" by participant " + req.participantUserId()`) — F2-223's exact defect, and what
makes a forged attribution invisible to whoever audits it. Every audit line and event payload now
reads off the saved row. The open route made this worse rather than better: the population who could
forge was every authenticated user.

### What the measurement passed on the way — filed, not fixed

| finding | measured |
|---|---|
| **9 of 11 PENDING approval requests can be decided by nobody** | `assigned_to` holds a free-text person name matching no username in `iam.users`, so `transition()`'s check can never pass and `myInbox` never returns them. Identical in dev and prod. Every one is self-assigned to the same invented officer named as its requester — F2-207's cast, in a server register. Repair is an owner decision (rewriting 21 live rows in two databases, F2-183/F2-196); a resolvability check at create needs a user-directory port `approvals` does not have. |
| `FindingService#transition::mgmtResponseAuthor` | The author of a **management** response is the auditee, who need not be the caller — the same judgement as F2-224's `standDownAuthoriser`. `mgmt_response_author` is null on all 20 rows in both databases, so it is latent. Owner decision. |
| `POST /exercise-runs/{id}/custom-inject` answers **500** on its default path | `dispatchNow` defaults to **true**, and the combined path is a ROWVERSION double-flush: `addCustomInject` saves the INSERT, `audit.log` + `emit` flush, then `dispatchInject` re-loads and saves the same row again in one transaction. The dedicated dispatch route answers 200 on the identical row, which is the discriminator. Exactly the landmine F2-175 widened — *any* flush between the two saves does it. Found while planting this slice's fixture. |
| `StartRunRequest.runCode` is an *"optional override; otherwise auto-generated"* | F2-172(d)'s family on a code cited in the NCEMA after-action record. `ClientSuppliedReferenceRatchetTest` keys on `setExternalId`/`setRefNumber`, so a `runCode` sits outside it. |

### ⚠ Master was red before this slice, on a docs gate

`FindingsRegisterCoverageTest#specsOwedOnlyEverDecreases` was failing 30 > 29: F2-225's docs commit
referenced F2-225 in the plan and wrote no register spec. F2-219 recorded the lesson —
*"a targeted re-run after a docs commit is not the suite, and the docs gate is precisely the gate a
docs commit can break"* — and it recurred in the **next** slice, on a **different** docs gate,
because the targeted re-run named four gate classes and this was not one of them. 🔑 **Naming the
trap does not exempt you from it, and the fix is a rule about the command rather than about the
list: after a docs commit, run the suite.** Both specs are written here, so owed goes 30 → 28.

### My own instrument errors

- **The re-derivation's first pairing under-reported: 3 sites where F2-225's permissive scan found
  19.** I had re-imposed the root pairing — which is the narrowing this blind spot is *about*, since
  a clock with no setter has no verb root to take. Under-reporting is the direction that reads
  exactly like a clean tree (F2-223's seven corrections, all seven shrinking).
- **The pre-fix control compared `master` with `HEAD` before anything was committed**, so it compared
  master with itself and reported **all 12 legs SILENT** — which reads exactly like every detector
  being broken. Loud rather than quiet, which is the only reason it cost one iteration.
- **`classify()` called `.start()` on a second matcher instance after `.find()` on a first**, which
  throws *"No match available"*. `lookingAt()` is the anchored-prefix primitive that was wanted.

### Lesson

🔑 **A work list and its classifier are two artefacts, and a slice that builds both must make them
agree — otherwise the next slice inherits confident false candidates from the instrument that was
supposed to prevent them.** And: **when a filing's population was measured by one mechanism, ask how
many mechanisms exist** — F2-215 had already enumerated four, and F2-225 measured one of them.

|---|---|

| **Severity** | **P2.** A cross-module approval register that records a raiser the caller invented, and lets that caller name the only principal permitted to approve it. A BCM exercise response whose measured reaction time is attributed to whoever the caller named. |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-17.** Both actors resolved from `CurrentActor`; four-eyes gate added at create; both request DTOs and both frontend surfaces cleaned. Backend 3,987/0/0, gate 16/16, probe 14/14 pre-fix and 14/14 post-fix, pre-fix control 12/12 FIRE. |
| **Filed by this slice** | The 9 undecidable PENDING approvals (owner); `mgmtResponseAuthor` (owner); the `custom-inject` 500; `runCode` as a client-supplied reference. |

## F2-225 · A nominalised clock, and a forged field that decided who may withdraw

**Found** 2026-08-17, executing F2-224's filed blind spot. **P2** — the NCA ECC regulator
self-assessment recorded a CISO approver the caller named, and an approval chain recorded an
originator the caller named on the one field its withdraw route reads. **Closed** the same day.
No migration; 2 backend services, 3 request records, 2 frontend surfaces.

*(Spec written 2026-08-17 alongside [[F2-226]], because the register is what an external auditor is
handed and a finding recorded only in the plan disappears when the plan is superseded. Master was
red on `FindingsRegisterCoverageTest` until this was written — see [[F2-226]] for why the targeted
re-run missed it.)*

### The population was re-derived first, and the classification was as much the finding as the count

A permissive (clock, actor) co-occurrence scan reports **79** unpaired candidates where the shipped
gate reports 4. The honest split: **18 NOISE-WORD** (ordinary English words the agent-noun suffix
matches — `lineNumber`, `stepOrder`, `isCrossBorder`, `regulatoryAnchor`), **34 ASSIGNMENT** (who
WILL act, or the act's target), **27 CANDIDATE**. 🔑 **A suffix rule measures spellings, and two
thirds of what it returns is not an attribution at all.**

### DETECTOR GAP 9 — a nominalised clock, on a regulator return

`NcaEccFilingService#transition` stamps `cisoApprovalAt` from the server's own clock and copied
`cisoApprover` out of the request body **in the same `switch` branch** — F2-223's shape exactly, on
the NCA ECC self-assessment this organisation files with the National Cybersecurity Authority. It
was invisible because `cisoApprover` reduces to `approv` while `cisoApprovalAt` reduces to
`approval`: 🔑 **the clock half is named after the NOUN and the actor half after the VERB, so one
attribution's two halves share no root.** Probed 13/13 pre-fix and 13/13 post-fix as `compliance`
against planted rows: *"Nobody Who Approved This"* stored as the CISO who approved the filing,
beside two server clocks 0.14 s apart. Structurally different from F2-224's role-named actor
(`standDownAuthoriser`), which is still blind and still asserted — **two distinct ways for the
halves to share no root; assume a third.**

### The same register carries a second split no setter-matching scan can ever see

`drafted_at` is a **field initialiser** (F2-215's third of four filling mechanisms), so the server
owns WHEN with no `setX(now())` anywhere, while `draftedBy` was `@NotBlank` from the body. Found by
reading the entity, not by any instrument. Measured before filing (F2-221): of 67 entities carrying
a clock-initialised act field, **19 sites** also take an actor from the request — 4 noise, 6
assignments, 9 attributions; 1 fixed, 4 refuted, 4 filed. One refutation is its own rule:
`CoiService#recordRecusal`'s clock is `req.recusalDate() != null ? … : now()`, so **a field
initialiser is only a server stamp while no writer overrides it.** ⚠ `createdAt`/`updatedAt` are
**row** stamps, never act clocks — every row has one, so they can never be the proof F2-223's rule
rests on; including them inflates 19 to 46.

### A forged attribution that is also an authorisation input has three outcomes

`ApprovalChainInstanceService#startChain` took `originatorUserId` from the body, and `withdraw()`
reads that column with **no other input**. Probed as `compliance`(3) naming `so_officer`(8): the
chain stored 8, **the real raiser was then refused 403 on their own chain, the named stranger was
GRANTED the withdraw, and naming a nonexistent id left the chain withdrawable by nobody.**

🔑 **`ApprovalChainController` had hardened AND documented the other two identity-bearing routes
(SEC-IAM-001, on `recordAction` and `withdraw`) and left this one — the route that ESTABLISHES the
identity the other two check against.** All three request records declared
`@NotNull @Positive Long <x>UserId`: **identical wire shapes, opposite fates** — two
required-and-ignored, one required-and-honoured, with nothing a caller or a reader could see
distinguishing them. All three deleted.

### F2-117 is half closed, and the half that moved is the one its blocker said could not

That row reasoned a four-eyes comparison would be inert because **0 of 4 people-labels resolve to a
platform user** — correct about **SEGREGATION** (approver ≠ reviewer, which does need identity
columns) and **applied to ATTRIBUTION** (who the approver IS, which needed nothing but
`CurrentActor`). 🔑 **The dependency ran the other way: comparing a reviewer against an approver is
meaningless while the approver is whatever the caller typed, so attribution was the PREREQUISITE
for the comparison the blocker was protecting.** Segregation stays OPEN, blocker unchanged.

### The codebase's own record of this defect was invisible

`NcaEccFilingLifecycleTest` pinned the mechanism honestly, with an explicit exit condition — and
surfaced nothing, because 🔑 **a pinned known-defect test passes on a defective tree BY DESIGN, so
a green pin and a green clean tree are indistinguishable from outside.** The finding had to be made
twice, independently. Its tripwire then fired exactly as designed the moment the service read a
principal, and `FindingsRegisterConsistencyTest` refused the commit until the register cell was
updated. ⚠ **A binary closure gate cannot express a half-closed finding, and the safe direction is
for the TEST to under-claim rather than the register to over-claim** — the register is what an
auditor is handed, so marking a P1 closed to satisfy a regex would have retired a control that is
still half unbuilt.

### Lesson

🔑 **Two distinct ways for one attribution's two halves to share no root have now been found — a
nominalised clock and a role-named actor — so assume a third.** And: **a required field the server
discards tells the caller their value matters; one it TRUSTS for an authorisation decision is worse
again, and nothing on the wire distinguishes the two.**

|---|---|

| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-17** (`b0d3906f`). Backend 3,976/0/0, FE 756/756, gate 14/14, probe 13/13 both ways, pre-fix control 4 narrow / 5 widened. |
| **Still open** | F2-117's **segregation** half — no `*_user_id` column on `nca_ecc.filings` for either assurance role; V357's shape is the remedy. The 4 field-initialiser work-list sites → executed by [[F2-226]]. `standDownAuthoriser` (F2-224, owner). |

## F2-224 · Two detector errors in opposite directions, and the green neither earned

**Found** 2026-08-16, executing F2-223's filed work list. **P2** — six governance registers,
including two statutory attestation-of-record surfaces, recorded a person the caller named. One
frontend screen filed **every** attestation on the tenant against user id 1. **Closed** the same
day. No migration; 6 backend services, 8 request-DTO fields, 2 frontend surfaces.

### The filing was executable, and re-deriving it first is what found the instrument bug

F2-223 shipped **10 unadjudicated sites** as a work list, deliberately without reasons (F2-188).
Per F2-221 — *a filed item inherits the population of the slice that filed it* — the denominator
was re-derived before the list was executed. A deliberately **permissive** pairing (a set of
candidate verb keys per field rather than one reduced root) found **15** sites where the shipped
detector's green build pins the population at exactly **13**.

The two extra were `EvidenceReviewService#create::reviewerId` and
`MlModelAuditService#recordAudit::auditorUserId` — and **both are refuted**, by the rule F2-223
itself recorded: the clock in each is `req.x() == null ? now() : req.x()`, a caller-supplied value
with a fallback, not a server stamp. An ISO/IEC 42001 model audit is routinely performed by an
external firm; `MlModelAudit` declares `auditorExternalParty` one line below `auditorUserId`.

🔑 **The finding about the instrument: the two sites were absent from the population for an
accidental reason, and absent reads identically to correctly excluded.** The root reduction could
not pair `auditDate` with `auditorUserId`; had it been able to, `isServerClock` would have
reported both as splits. **Two defects in opposite directions produced a green that neither
earned** — F2-219's rule, now inside the gate F2-223 built. The widening (`…Date`/`…On` are WHEN
fields; pair on a key SET) and the narrowing (a clock the caller may override is not a stamp) are
therefore one commit. Widening alone manufactures two confident false findings whose obvious
"fix" forges an attribution onto an external auditor's work.

### The ten, adjudicated

**8 CONFIRMED and closed · 2 BY DESIGN (verified, not guessed) · 0 left open.**

| site | verdict |
| `ObligationAttestationService#recordAttestation::attestedByUserId` | CLOSED — attestation of record |
| `ObligationAttestationService#reviewAttestation::reviewerUserId` | CLOSED |
| `VendorBcpAttestationService#transitionAttestation::reviewedByName` + `reviewedByUserId` | CLOSED — all three routes `TPRM:WRITE` |
| `ErmGapService#attestRisk::attestedByName` | CLOSED — a named person confirms a residual score |
| `InvocationService#transition::declaredBy` | CLOSED — `declaredAt` is *now*, so the act is this call |
| `RegulatoryChangeService#transition::assessedBy` | CLOSED |
| `MtpdInheritanceService#publishAssessment::publishedByUserId` | CLOSED |
| `VendorBcpAttestationService#doSubmit::submittedByContactEmail` + `…Name` | **BY DESIGN** |

🔑 **F2-223 guessed exactly one thing and marked it a guess — and it was right.** The vendor-portal
pair is by design: `doSubmit`'s second caller is `submitByToken`, whose route is
`@PreAuthorize("permitAll()")`, so there is no principal to resolve at all. **A correct guess and
a verified claim are indistinguishable in prose**, which is the entire argument for keeping
`WORK_LIST` and `BY_DESIGN` as two buckets rather than one map of reasons.

### The live half — probed 12/12 pre-fix and 12/12 post-fix on PLANTED rows

Every leg as `compliance` (user 3), forging user 4 / `"Nobody Who Approved This"`. F2-206: a probe
demonstrating a forgery plants its own victim.

| leg | pre-fix | post-fix |
| obligation attestation with `attestedByUserId: 4` | **stored 4** (actor is 3) | stored 3 |
| the same, **omitting** the attester | **400 — required** | 201, records the principal |
| obligation review with `reviewerUserId: 4` | **stored 4** | stored 3 |
| regulatory change → ASSESSED with a forged `assessedBy` | **stored the forgery** | `"compliance"` |

| risk attestation with a forged `attestedByName` | **stored the forgery** | `"compliance"` |

⚠⚠ **`AttestationRecordRequest` carried `@NotNull @Positive Long attestedByUserId`, so the server
REQUIRED an attribution it never verified** — third instance of that exact shape after F2-223's
annual plan, and the reason the fix refuses rather than storing null: the request contract already
made it mandatory, so no working caller is broken.

### The frontend half

`ObligationDetailPage` sent `attestedByUserId: 1, // current user — wired via JWT claim in v2` and
`reviewerUserId: 1`. **Every obligation attestation and every review recorded from that screen was
filed against user id 1 regardless of who was signed in** — a comment promising a fix, load-bearing
for two years. `VendorBcpCampaignDetailPage` asked the operator to TYPE the reviewer into a prompt
placeholdered `'e.g. Salman Al-Otaibi (TPRM Lead)'` — **seventh recorded instance of an invented
officer in a placeholder teaching an operator to type somebody else's name.**

### The shape no root-matching detector can see, named rather than papered over

`InvocationService#transition` writes `setStandDownAt(now)` and, three lines below the `declaredBy`
this slice closed, `standDownAuthoriser` from the request. Structurally the same split — and
**invisible to the shipped detector AND to the permissive re-derivation**, because the actor field
names the ROLE PERFORMED (`authoriser`) rather than the verb (`standDown`), so the two halves share
no root. It was found by reading. `anActorFieldNamingTheRoleRatherThanTheVerbIsNotPaired()` asserts
the blind spot so it cannot be mistaken for coverage; the site itself is **filed, not blessed** — a
crisis stand-down is authorised by the CMT chair and typically recorded by the coordinator.

### Two more instrument corrections, both in gates written by earlier slices of this lineage

⚠ **`noReasonIsABareLabel` demanded `REFUTED` or `FILED`** — the two verdicts F2-223 happened to
have reached — and rejected a correct, verified `BY DESIGN` reason. F2-217's headline (*a census
keyed on a list measures the list*) applied to a **gate's own verdict vocabulary**. The failure
mode is the benign-looking one: it hides no defect, it pushes the next author to reword a true
statement until the regex is happy.

⚠ **The gate keys sites on a SIMPLE class name**, and `RegulatoryChangeService` exists in both
`module/compliance` and `module/regchange` (F2-222 measured 15 entity names declared twice). Only
one has the pair, so nothing collapses today — *a fact about today, not a property of the key, and
nobody was maintaining it*. `aSiteKeyResolvesToExactlyOneFile()` now fails if two files ever
produce one key.
