| **⚠⚠ THE DEFECT: [[F2-206]]'s own headline, unclosed by [[F2-206]]** | `BaseEntity` declares **nine** server-owned fields, marks every one `READ_ONLY`, and its javadoc explains each: forged audit attribution, backdated records, *"an ordinary update could soft-delete or resurrect a record, bypassing whatever guard the DELETE endpoint carries"*, optimistic locking defeated. [[F2-206]] correctly widened that protection from *"`BaseEntity` subclasses"* to *"every mapped type"* — **for `id`**. Its own lesson, *"one field per question"*, was about the **probe**, and silently became the scope of the **fix**. |
| **🔑 Why two months of green** | **Generalising an invariant one field at a time leaves the remainder looking covered, because the mechanism that covers them is visibly present.** A reader who finds a platform-wide introspector named for server-owned identity does not then go and check which fields it names. Fifth depth of [[F2-198]]'s shape — *the invariant is real, its POPULATION is narrower than it looks* — and the narrowing here is neither a filename, an allow-list, a module name nor an `extends` clause, but **a field-name list inside the fix**. |
| **⚠⚠ And the gate said so, in a comment, one test method below the leg that had just widened the same population** | `ServerOwnedIdentityInvariantTest` skipped every non-`BaseEntity` type in its audit leg: *"createdBy/updatedBy/isDeleted are `BaseEntity`'s own columns; **a type that does not extend it has no such property for a caller to set.** Asserting over the whole 407 would pass vacuously on 252 of them and read as coverage."* **The premise is false.** 🔑 **The comment names exactly the right worry and reaches the wrong conclusion, because it assumed rather than measured — and it is the kind of assumption nothing can contradict, since a skipped entity and a clean entity produce the same green.** [[F2-184]] and [[F2-199]]'s shape: an artefact that answers the question a reader was about to ask is worse than silence when the answer is wrong. |
| **Measured by reflection over `target/classes`** | Of the **259** entities that do not extend `BaseEntity`: `createdAt` **222**, `isDeleted` **209**, `updatedAt` **146**, `createdBy` **111**, `updatedBy` **104**, `deletedBy` **56**, `rowVersion` **52**, `deletedAt` **50** — **960 declarations, and not one carried an annotation.** Intersected with the entity-bound write endpoints: **170 of 214**, across **102** entities. |
| **⚠⚠ A probe's SHAPE is part of its population, and [[F2-206]] recorded the observation without drawing this edge** | Its note says the `Short`-typed `isDeleted` made 34 entities *unprobeable* by a combined body — casualties `TreatmentPlan`, `Vulnerability`, `DsrCase`, `Finding`, `CrossBorderTransfer`, *"precisely the statutory registers"*. That typing never made them **safe**: `{"isDeleted": true}` binds on 177 and throws on 35, while **`{"isDeleted": 1}` binds on all 209**. A body built from one literal silently excludes every entity that types the field unusually, and an excluded entity scores exactly like a clean one. The new gate builds its hostile value from each field's **declared type**, and a self-test asserts the builder **throws** on a type it does not know rather than returning something harmless. |
| **Proven live** | As `compliance` (not `admin` — PLATFORM_ADMIN bypasses in code) on `POST /api/v1/controls`, which binds `platform.controls.Control`. Every row planted by the probe and removed with a `CHARINDEX` delete ([[F2-206]]'s rule). **(a)** `"createdBy": "ceo@tss.sa"` stored verbatim in `platform.controls.created_by` — the DF-3/DF-4 forged-attribution defect. **(b)** `"createdAt": "2001-01-01T00:00:00"` stored, overwriting the entity's own `= LocalDateTime.now()` initialiser. **(c)** `"isDeleted": true` on a **create** stored the row soft-deleted, and `Control` carries `@Where(clause = "is_deleted = 0")`. |
| **🔑 (c) is sharper than the claim I set out to prove** | The ghost row is invisible to every query **including the service's own duplicate check**, while the UNIQUE index still sees it. So the control code becomes permanently unusable and the caller is told only that *"a record with these values already exists — change it and try again"* for a code the register shows nothing for. **The status code is itself the evidence**: 409 from the raw index pre-fix, **400 from the service's own named check post-fix**, because the row is no longer hidden from the query that check runs. |
| **⚠⚠ REFUTED, and recorded rather than dropped: soft-delete through the UPDATE endpoint** | That was my headline claim — `PUT /controls/{id}` is guarded by `CONTROL_LIB:WRITE` while `DELETE /controls/{id}` needs `CONTROL_LIB:DELETE`, and **2 roles hold WRITE without DELETE**, so it would have been a privilege escalation. `updateControl` copies a **nine-field whitelist** onto the loaded row, so `isDeleted` never reaches it ([[F2-22]]b's `INERT` verdict). The probe disproved my own claim. ~2-in-10 again ([[F2-188]], [[F2-192]], [[F2-204]], [[F2-213]]). |
| **🔑 And the refutation is the argument for closing it at the WIRE rather than endpoint by endpoint** | Whether a bound field **reaches the row** depends on each service, and `MassAssignmentRatchetTest`'s own risk-profile header says exactly that. Auditing 170 endpoints to find the subset that lets `isDeleted` through produces a list that is wrong the next time somebody writes `repo.save(body)` — and `createControl` does precisely that, four lines after hand-scrubbing `setId(null)` and `setOrganisationId(org())`. **The author knew to scrub the two fields that had a recorded defect, and there was no mechanism for the other eight because a superclass was supposed to own them.** |
| **⚠⚠ Safety was MEASURED before the change, and the scan's answer was wrong in the dangerous direction** | Nulling a field the wire used to supply is only safe if the server supplies it. Three mechanisms are visible to reflection — a JPA auditing annotation, a lifecycle callback, a field initialiser — and by those, `isDeleted` and `rowVersion` have **zero** unfilled entities, while `createdBy`/`updatedBy`/`deletedAt`/`deletedBy` have zero unfilled **NOT NULL** ones. `createdAt` reported **10 entities with a NOT NULL column and nothing filling it**, which would have been a 500 on every create. **All ten declare `insertable = false`** — Hibernate never writes the column and the **database default** does. 🔑 **The scan located; reading measured. A fourth mechanism the instrument cannot see reads exactly like a missing value**, and acting on that 10 would have been the [[F2-40]] trap in reverse — refusing to fix a real defect because a scan mis-scored ten entities. |
| **Also checked before changing anything** | **No service copies one of these from a request body** — 378 setter sites, every argument a server value (`false`, `now()`, `CurrentActor.username()`, an authenticated-actor parameter). The **frontend** sends one in exactly two payloads, and both are browser-local corpora: `NewCommunicationModal` passes `createdBy: 'GRC Operator'` into `lib/communications.ts`, which is `localStorage`-backed and never reaches a server ([[F2-204]]'s and [[F2-207]]'s already-filed populations). |
| **The fix** | `ServerOwnedIdentityModule` → **`ServerOwnedFieldsModule`**, its `SERVER_OWNED_FIELDS` now **mirroring `BaseEntity`'s field list** rather than naming one of them. An introspector **has no population to get wrong**; the alternative was ~960 annotations across 259 files. `READ_ONLY` and never `@JsonIgnore` — serialise as before, refuse to deserialise — and the property is deliberately **not removed** from the deserialiser, because the frontend echoes whole records back and `FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES` would turn working requests into 400s. **0 endpoint changes, 0 migrations.** The rename is deliberate: a name that understates what a security control does is how the next reader concludes it does not cover their case. |
| **Gates** | `ServerOwnedIdentityInvariantTest` → **`ServerOwnedFieldsInvariantTest`**. The audit leg is now the same shape as the id leg — full population, positively counted, **2,352 (entity, field) pairs verified, 0 bind**. **`theModuleMirrorsBaseEntitysOwnFieldList` is the leg that would have caught the original gap**: the module's set must **equal** `BaseEntity`'s `READ_ONLY` set, asserted in **both** directions, because module ⊂ BaseEntity is this defect and BaseEntity ⊂ module is somebody deleting an annotation while only half the platform notices. The negative control's second subject is **derived** — whichever entity outside `BaseEntity` declares the most of the eight — because controlling on `ProcessingActivity` alone covers 3 of 8, and a control that covers *some* fields is exactly what let the id-only fix read as complete. |
| **⚠⚠ Two of my own instrument errors, both caught by running things** | **(a)** The first probe asked *"is the field set?"* and reported **161 false positives**, almost every `createdAt`, because those fields carry a `= LocalDateTime.now()` initialiser and are non-null whether the hostile value arrived or not. 🔑 **An initialised field cannot be probed by presence, only by identity — the test is "does it hold WHAT I SENT".** **(b)** The anti-vacuity floor was **1,000**. Re-narrowing the audit leg back to `BaseEntity` subclasses leaves 174 × 8 ≈ **1,392** pairs, so that floor would have **SURVIVED** the mutation that recreates the original blind spot. 🔑 **A floor set to "obviously not broken" cannot see a population narrowed to a real subset; it has to sit above the largest WRONG answer, which means knowing what the wrong answer would be.** Now 2,000, and the mutation is killed. |
| **⚠ A third, from the tooling rather than the code** | Three `git worktree` copies live under `.claude/worktrees/`, so a bare `find . -name X.java` resolves to whichever copy sorts first. It reported `Control extends BaseEntity` — from a worktree — for an entity that does not, and `npx vitest run` from the repo root picked up **182 failures** across those trees. Scope every filesystem sweep to the working tree; reflection over `target/classes` is immune and is why the measurements held. |
| **Verification** | Backend **3,861/0/0**. Mutation harness **7/7 killed, 0 anchor-miss** (which is a distinct outcome that exits non-zero — [[F2-212]]'s rule), including reverting the introspector to [[F2-206]]'s id-only shape, restoring the deleted `continue`, unregistering `@Component`, deleting a `READ_ONLY` from `BaseEntity`, and making the value builder return a wrong expectation. Live probe **12/12 post-fix**; **pre-fix control** — introspector reverted to id-only, recompiled, probe re-run in `pre` mode — **12/12**, so the probe distinguishes both states rather than passing either way. FE typecheck clean, **749/749**. |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED** for all nine fields over all 433 entities, gated in both directions against `BaseEntity`. **OPEN as a population:** `organisationId` still binds — it is `MassAssignmentRatchetTest`'s own TENANT tier, it produced [[F2-25]], and services assign it explicitly from `TenantContext`, so closing it at the wire needs its own measurement and is deliberately not done here. `externalId` likewise stays per-service ([[F2-172]](d)). |
| **Filed by this slice** | **(a)** `organisationId` binds from the body on every entity-bound endpoint; F2-25 was a real bypass through exactly this field. **(b)** `platform.controls`' duplicate check `findByOrganisationIdAndControlCodeAndVersion` is subject to `@Where(is_deleted = 0)`, so a soft-deleted control makes its code permanently unusable with a diagnostic that tells the operator to pick a different code — now unreachable through the wire, but the underlying asymmetry between the service's check and the UNIQUE index remains. **(c)** **2 roles hold `CONTROL_LIB:WRITE` without `:DELETE`** and **0 users hold that combination today**, so the separation the two guards express is not currently exercised by any persona — worth knowing before relying on it. **(d)** `MassAssignmentRatchetTest`'s risk profile ranks by four vocabularies (TENANT/AUTHORITY/OUTCOME/STATE) and **none of the nine server-owned fields appears in any of them**, so they were structurally unrankable by the scan built to rank this defect — the same sentence [[F2-206]] wrote about `id`, still true of the other eight until this slice. |

## F2-214 · The PDPL Article 20 breach wizard has never created a record, and the write type beside the corrected read type kept every retired name

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-214 *(measured 2026-08-15. Lineage: [[F2-198]] → [[F2-199]] → [[F2-203]] → [[F2-205]] → [[F2-208]] → [[F2-209]] → [[F2-210]] → [[F2-211]] → [[F2-212]] → [[F2-213]] → this. Chosen from [[F2-213]]'s own javadoc, which states the gap in its own words: "the coverage leg covers only the sites whose frontend client this test names" — **twelve of eighty-three**. A gate that says what it does not cover is the cheapest place to look next.)* |
| **Severity** | **P1 for the live half.** `POST /api/v1/privacy/breaches` answers **HTTP 400 on every submission** from the PDPL Article 20 breach notification wizard, with a diagnostic naming no field, on a form where nothing looks missing. The statutory breach register has never been creatable from the surface built to create it; all 17 rows in dev and prod are seeded. **P2 for the latent half** — five updates that erase columns the moment anyone wires the edit screen the reachability red list invites them to build. |
| **⚠⚠ THE DEFECT: a request type has no wire to be nominated from, so the whole write vocabulary sat outside [[F2-211]]'s instrument by construction** | [[F2-211]]'s rule is *the wire nominates, `sys.columns` adjudicates*. It only ever nominated from the **read** wire. Nothing ever returns a `*Request`, so no amount of running that gate could reach one. `PrivacyBreachRequest` sits **eight lines below** the `PrivacyBreachDto` that [[F2-211]] corrected, in the same file, and still declared `severity` and `affectedRecords` — two of the exact four [[F2-211]] retired — plus `description` for `descriptionEn`, `reportedToAuthority` for nothing, and `titleAr` for a column that does not exist. 🔑 **Third instance in this lineage of the correct artefact sitting beside the wrong one** ([[F2-209]]'s reader 200 lines below, [[F2-213]]'s `CyberEvidenceService`). |
| **Why a wrong name is a 400 and not a type error** | `POST\|PUT /api/v1/privacy/breaches` binds the `DataBreach` **entity**, and Spring Boot disables `FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES` — so the four unknown keys are discarded in silence, and the one thing the wizard never sent, NOT NULL `breach_type`, produces the 400. [[F2-210]]'s defect exactly, one endpoint over, on the register [[F2-209]] and [[F2-211]] had both just worked on without probing its create. |
| **Proven live** | Wizard payload verbatim → **HTTP 400, "A required field was not supplied"**. The entity's own names → **201**, with `description_en`, `breach_type`, `data_subjects_affected_count` and `pdpc_notification_required` all stored. `sys.columns` says only `breach_type` of those is NOT NULL, so the other three were the silent losses and it was the fourth that made the failure loud. |
| **Two more live instances of the same key, both discarding a governance record** | `DsrFulfilmentWizard` composed the identity-verification evidence, RoPA scope, data summary, delivery method and both approvals into a `description` string and sent it — `DataSubjectRequest` has **fourteen properties and not one is free text**. The comment above it claimed that "captures the wizard context without needing a dedicated subschema": [[F2-184]]'s shape, a comment describing a mechanism that does not exist, which is worse than none because it answers the question a reader was about to ask. And `PrivacyPage` offered a **Description textarea** on the DSR form that stored nothing and came back empty on the next open. Closes [[F2-213]]'s filed item (b). |
| **⚠⚠ THE LATENT HALF: a `Partial<T>` client against an unconditional server is a contradiction, and it DEFEATS [[F2-213]]'s coverage leg by construction** | That leg asks whether a written field is *declarable* by the client type. `Partial<T>` makes **every** field declarable and **none** mandatory — so the leg is green precisely where the client is positively typed to send subsets. `DpiaService#update` would erase a PDPL Article 25 assessment's title in both languages, its trigger, its residual-risk rating, its assessment date, its next review date and its conclusion (**5/5, 5/5, 5/5, 5/5, 4/5, 2/5** live rows, dev = prod); `CrisisCommsService` would erase a crisis template's body in both languages and an audience's entire contact list (**5/5** and **4/4**). |
| **🔑 A recorded gap is an invitation, and nobody had asked what accepting it would do** | All five clients are dark, and `apiClientMethodReachability` already records them — *"HOLE: a breach can be created, contained and closed — never corrected"*. That entry adjudicates the **client** and says nothing about the **endpoint**. It reads as *the fix is to add an edit screen*, and adding one is exactly what would have fired the erasure. **The inverse of [[F2-201]]**, where a complete server side with no client had been *hardened* first and was safe to wire. |
| **⚠⚠ MY PYTHON LOCATOR FOUND 3; THE GATE FOUND 11** | [[F2-213]]'s lesson recurring one slice later, for a different reason: my scan reported only sites where its own resolver found unguarded writes, so the eight already-guarded ones read as *absent* rather than *classified*. The gate computes the intersection structurally and asserts it exactly. **8 of the 11 were already correct** — and the one I checked by hand first, `PolicyManagementService#update`, is twenty setters every one of which is null-guarded. |
| **⚠ Which is [[F2-182]]'s rule arriving on my own instrument** | A setter-site regex cannot see an `if` wrapped around the setter, so `PolicyManagementService#update` read as twenty unconditional writes and is in fact a correct partial update. Had the gate been built on that scan it would have failed on correct code — **the one thing a gate must never do, because it trains the next reader to edit the assertion instead of the code** ([[F2-207]], [[F2-213]]). The guard detector is therefore the load-bearing part, and it carries a positive control for the two shapes that fooled the first draft: a **block-bodied** guard and an **`isX()`** boolean accessor. |
| **The fix** | `PrivacyBreachRequest` / `PrivacyRopaRequest` / `PrivacyDsrRequest` corrected against their entities. `BreachNotificationWizard`: the entity's real names, a required **breach-type** input whose twelve options are the values the column already holds (**no CHECK added** — other writers are open and collapsing the stored `UNAUTHORISED`/`UNAUTHORIZED` split rewrites live rows, [[F2-183]]'s rule), and `severity` kept **in the narrative** because it has no column ([[F2-209]]'s third state). DSR wizard: the narrative is **disclosed as not retained**, bilingually, on the step where the operator submits — not silently re-homed and not quietly dropped. `pdpcNotifiedAt` removed from `updateBreach` — `notifyDataOffice` stamps it ([[F2-213]]'s `completedAt` precedent). `DpiaService` + `CrisisCommsService`: absent means leave alone, with `recipientCount` moved **inside** the `contactsCsv` guard because recomputing it from an absent list is not a null but a **0**, and a zero recipient count reads as "this audience has nobody in it". **0 backend endpoint changes, 0 migrations.** |
| **⚠ The citation was wrong in two places** | The wizard cited **PDPL Article 23** for the 72-hour breach window in its header and its countdown badge. Article 23 is the data-subject-request article by every other usage in the tree, and `lib/moduleAnchors.ts` — the regulator-citation catalogue W2-1a-i deliberately keeps — records **Article 20**. Same shape as [[F2-207]]'s ROPA "Article 22" for "Article 31". |
| **Gates** | `WireContractTest`'s write-side leg was **ROPA-only** — the shape [[F2-210]] had just found, and scoping a gate to the shape that produced the finding returns a smaller population that reads like "the rest are fine". Generalised to a declared `WRITE_REGISTERS` list adjudicated against the bound entity by reflection; **it refuted the DSR field on its first run**. `FullReplaceUpdateContractTest` gains *a `Partial<>` client requires a guarded server write*, with its population computed as `Partial<>` ∩ entity-bound and asserted **exactly** in both directions — a decrease-only ceiling would let a new offender hide behind a removed one. |
| **⚠ [[F2-213]]'s reverse leg then caught this slice** | Removing `description` from `PrivacyDsrRequest` left a stale entry in `DECLARED_BUT_NOT_WRITTEN`, and the exact assertion failed until it was deleted. That is the leg working as designed: **a fixed field must lose its entry**, or a tolerated one becomes indistinguishable from a reviewed one. |
| **Verification** | Backend **3859/0/0**. **Pre-fix control: stashing the two services turns the new leg red on exactly the three sites, with the field lists matching the measurement.** Live probe **17/17** on rows the probe planted itself ([[F2-206]]'s rule), residue 0, re-runnable. FE typecheck clean, **749/749**. |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED** for the live create defect on three surfaces, the five erasing updates, and the shape gated in both codebases. **OPEN as a population:** the coverage question now has two instruments and neither covers all 83 entity-bound PUTs — `WRITE_REGISTERS` names three registers, `PARTIAL_PAYLOAD_ENTITY_PUTS` eleven endpoints. **A field is not proven safe by these passing.** |
| **Filed by this slice** | **(a)** `privacy.data_breaches.breach_type` is free text with **no CHECK**, holding 12 distinct values over 17 rows including both `UNAUTHORISED_ACCESS` and `UNAUTHORIZED_ACCESS` — [[F2-196]]'s disjoint-vocabulary shape inside one column; collapsing the spelling variants rewrites live rows in two databases and is an owner decision. **(b)** The breach `status` vocabulary is likewise open (7 values, no CHECK) — re-confirmed from [[F2-209]]'s filing. **(c)** `privacy.data_breaches` still has **no `title_ar` and no `description_ar`**, so a PDPL statutory record cannot be described in the platform's primary language (house rule 7). **(d)** A DSR has nowhere to record its identity-verification evidence; the wizard now says so, which is a disclosure, not a fix. **(e)** The Article 20 / 25 / 31 citations for the breach lifecycle are used inconsistently across `PrivacyPage` and `PdplBreachConsole`; only the wizard's plainly-wrong Article 23 was corrected here. |

## F2-213 · Editing a record erased every column the form could not carry — including the flag saying an authority had been notified

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-213 *(measured 2026-08-15. Lineage: [[F2-198]] → [[F2-199]] → [[F2-203]] → [[F2-205]] → [[F2-208]] → [[F2-209]] → [[F2-210]] → [[F2-211]] → [[F2-212]] → this. Chosen NOT from [[F2-212]]'s filed items but from [[F2-212]] ITSELF: it fixed **one** instance of "a full-replace PUT plus a payload that omits what the service writes" and never measured the population. [[F2-208]]'s rule — six survivors after seven fixes is what fixing instances of a shape produces; sweep the population and gate the shape.)* |
| **Severity** | **P1.** Editing a cyber security incident wrote NULL over its detection, report and resolution timestamps and its own reference number, and flipped `notification_sent` from TRUE to **false** — the flag recording that an authority had been told. Silent, irreversible, and reachable from the ordinary edit button on `/cyber`. |
| **⚠⚠ THE DEFECT: the service persisted the REQUEST OBJECT, so the field set was not a list anyone wrote down** | Nine services did `repo.save(req)` after copying back only id / organisationId / externalId / createdAt. Every other column therefore became whatever a freshly-deserialised entity holds. [[F2-212]] was the mitigated version of this — there the service at least named the fields it wrote, so the loss was four. Here the written set is **every property the entity has**, which is why no amount of checking the *declared* fields could have found it. |
| **🔑 A RESET IS WORSE THAN A NULL, and this family produces resets** | `CyberIncident.notificationSent = false`, `Vulnerability.overdue = false`, `reopenedCount = 0`, `ControlAssessment.evidenceCount = 0`, `CyberAsset`'s three link counters — all **field initialisers**. A null reads as missing data and invites a question; `notification_sent = false` reads as a fact, and the fact it asserts is that nobody told the regulator. |
| **Proven live, against a planted victim ([[F2-206]]'s rule)** | `POST` a `[REVIEW-TEST]` incident, give it the state a worked incident carries, then send **exactly** what `CyberPage#submitInc` builds when an operator edits the title. Result: `incident_number` `'RT-213'` → NULL · `affected_asset_name` → NULL · `detected_at` / `reported_at` / `resolved_at` → NULL · `notification_sent` TRUE → **false** · both link counts → 0. Residue 0. Nothing pre-existing was touched. |
| **Blast radius, measured, dev = prod** | `cyber.cyber_incidents` 24 live rows: `incident_number` populated on **24/24**, `detected_at` **25**, `reported_at` **24**, `resolved_at` **10**, `affected_asset_name` **17**, `notification_sent` TRUE on **19**. `cyber.cyber_action_plans` 13 rows: `source_ref` 17, `linked_control_id` 14, `reminder_count > 0` on 14, `escalated_at` 5. `cyber.vulnerabilities` 20: `asset_name` 20, `overdue` TRUE on 1. `cyber.control_assessments` 21: `evidence_count > 0` on 4. `tprm.vendors` 28: contact name / email / contract start on **8** each. `compliance.regulatory_changes` 35: status and `controls_updated_count` on **35/35**. `iam.users` 7: `job_title_en` on 2. |
| **⚠ The one that is real and LATENT is the PDPL register, and that is why it survived** | `PrivacyService.updateDsr` wrote `assignedTo` and `completedAt` from a `PrivacyDsrRequest` that declares neither — so an Article 23 request's owner and its **completion timestamp, the evidence the statutory response was made in time**, were written null on every edit. Both columns are null on all 20 live rows in both databases, so there has never been anything to destroy. 🔑 **A defect with nothing to damage yet is not a smaller defect; it is one nobody can notice until the feature is used.** |
| **🔑 The codebase already knew, at one site, for two fields** | `CyberEvidenceService` carried `staleSince` and `reRequestId` across by hand under a CY-J comment calling them *"sweep-managed, never client-editable"* — the correct rule. `assessmentId` sat beside them, unprotected. And the premise the comment gave was false: the frontend does **not** *"round-trip the whole entity"*, it sends `CyberEvidenceRequest`, eleven fields of nineteen. **Naming two fields to rescue is what a reader does when the editable list is implicit.** Same shape as [[F2-195]]'s `\|\| N`, where the correct rule sat in prose three lines from where it was not applied. |
| **⚠⚠ MY OWN SCAN FOUND 5 SITES; THE GATE FOUND 9** | The Python locator required `findById(` and the four it missed use `findByIdAndOrganisationId(` — so `CyberAssetService#updateAsset`, `#updateEvidence`, `#updateSubControl` and `#updateException` read as *absent* rather than *unresolved*. [[F2-206]]'s rule at full strength: **unresolved reads identically to missing**, and it hid 44% of the population from the instrument I was about to trust. The gate is written in Java over the same tree for exactly this reason. |
| **Refuted by reading — 3 of 12, and the loudest one first** | **`UserService`'s `passwordHash`** is written inside `if (req.password() != null && !req.password().isBlank())`; my guard detector missed it because the guard tests `password()` while the setter is `setPasswordHash`. **`/api/v1/scm/vendors`** was a guessed pairing — it goes to `ScmService.updateVendor(id, VendorDtos.Request)`, a real DTO, not `TprmService`. **`CyberControlRequest`** declares all thirteen editable columns, so `updateControl` was losing nothing. ~2-in-10 again ([[F2-188]], [[F2-192]], [[F2-204]]), and the most alarming-sounding candidate was one of the false ones. |
| **⚠ And 4 more the gate flagged that reading refuted, all the same way** | `DetectionRuleService#save`, `ThreatIntelService#save`, `AppsecFindingService#ingest`, `LicensingService#upsertInternal` are create-or-update methods: **both branches live in one body**, so "saves the request" and "has a loaded same-type local" are both true of perfectly correct code. The discriminator is what the method does to the id first — `setId(null)` is a create, `setId(existing.getId())` aims the payload at a row. |
| **⚠⚠ My first detector counted the save's OWN RESULT as evidence of a load** | `CyberIncident saved = incidentRepo.save(inc);` declares a same-type local, so the first version reported **41** sites, nearly all legitimate creates. It failed loudly only because those were creates; had it over-narrowed instead, the leg would have passed and said nothing. The Nth instance in this programme of a detector satisfied by something other than its claim. |
| **The fix — nine sites, each applying only what its client can send** | `applyEditable(existing, req)` per service, mutating the loaded row: incidents (the NIST 800-61r2 timeline + the notification flag), vulnerabilities (the SLA-breach flag and reopen counter), action plans (the source link and the whole escalation trail), assessments (`evidence_count`, `capa_id`), assets (three counters), evidence (`assessment_id`), sub-controls (**`description_ar`** — the Arabic half, on an Arabic-primary platform, house rule 7), exceptions (**`approved_at`**, the stamp evidencing the exception's own approval). `CyberControlService` was converted **although it was losing nothing**, so the hazard is absent rather than latent and the family reads as one shape. Plus four DTO-side sites that stopped writing a column their client cannot express. **0 migrations.** |
| **Gates** | New **`FullReplaceUpdateContractTest`** (hermetic, 6 legs, reads `api.ts` from disk as [[F2-193]]'s pair does): a **structural hard zero** — no method may load a `T` and then persist its own `T` parameter; a **coverage hard zero** — every field an update writes from its request must be declarable by the frontend type feeding it; the **reverse direction** as an exactly-asserted map with a reason each; two positive controls carrying the literal pre-fix and post-fix shapes; and the entity-bound PUT population (**83**, F2-22's) asserted decrease-only so a green run cannot come to mean a shrunken scan. |
| **⚠⚠ The mutation harness found a hole in my own gate, and it was directional** | The coverage leg is a SUBSET test, so deleting a write from an `applyEditable` shrinks the written set, stays a valid subset, and leaves the gate green while a form input silently becomes decorative. 🔑 **A one-directional check over a two-directional contract.** `everyIgnoredClientFieldIsAccountedFor` closes it. |
| **⚠ That new leg then refuted two of my own claims on its first run** | I predicted an entry for `regulatory-changes :: status`; there is none, because `RegulatoryChangeRequest` never declared `status` **at all** — which is exactly why the server writing it was the defect. And adding `UserService` to the covered sites made the leg report `passwordHash` as unsendable: the endpoint transforms `password` through the encoder and `roles` into join-table rows. 🔑 **A gate that fails on correct code is worse than no gate — it trains the next reader to edit the assertion instead of the code** ([[F2-207]]'s deleted third leg, same call). Scoped out with the reason recorded rather than papered over with an exemption. |
| **⚠ An anti-vacuity floor elsewhere failed, and was right to ask** | `ClientSuppliedReferenceRatchetTest` counts reference-setter sites with a floor of 40 and found **39**. The drop is exactly the nine `req.setExternalId(existing.getExternalId())` lines this slice deleted — lines whose only purpose was to carry the reference **across a full replace**. 🔑 **They were compensation for the defect, not reference writes; removing the defect removed the need for them.** Floor re-measured to 33 with that reason recorded, because a population that falls after a fix is not automatically rot — but it is always worth asking which. |
| **Verification** | Backend **3856/0/0**. Gate 6/6. **Pre-fix control against the parent commit: the structural leg fires on exactly the 9 sites, and the anti-vacuity leg fires too — 9 caught, 0 silent.** Mutation **10/10 killed, 0 survived, 0 anchor-miss**, restore SHA-256 CLEAN. Live probe **18/18** across six registers as `so_officer` (CISO, holds CYBER_READ+WRITE — not `admin`, which proves nothing about authorization), residue 0. FE typecheck clean. |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED for the thirteen sites measured and the shape gated. OPEN as a population:** 83 PUT handlers bind a JPA entity directly (F2-22's finding). The structural leg covers all 83; the coverage leg covers the twelve sites it names. **A field is not proven safe by this test passing** — what is proven is that no listed site writes something its client cannot send. |
| **Filed by this slice** | **(a)** TPRM vendor contact name / email / contract start, and a user's job title, are now preserved but still **not editable** — no form input exists for any of them. Offering them is a product change, not a fix. **(b)** `PrivacyDsrRequest` declares `description`, which matches no column on `privacy.data_subject_requests` — [[F2-211]]'s shape on a fifth register. **(c)** The 83-strong entity-bound PUT population is F2-22's and remains the structural root: a request DTO per endpoint would make this whole class unrepresentable, and is a larger piece of work than any one slice. |

## F2-212 · Editing an incident silently erased its post-incident record, and the lessons register showed invented lessons while hiding every real one

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-212 *(measured 2026-08-15. Lineage: [[F2-198]] → [[F2-199]] → [[F2-203]] → [[F2-205]] → [[F2-208]] → [[F2-209]] → [[F2-210]] → [[F2-211]] → this. Chosen by taking [[F2-211]]'s instrument past privacy, to [[F2-210]]'s own filed items (b) `CyberVulnDto` and (c) `IncidentDto` — both re-measured before being built on, which corrected one of them.)* |
| **Severity** | **P1.** Editing any incident wrote NULL over its lessons learned, resolution date and response timeline — silent, irreversible loss of a governance record (NIST 800-61r2 §3.4) that no surface was even able to display; and the register built to show those lessons admitted **0 of the 3** incidents that have one, presenting invented text in their place. |
| **⚠⚠ The adjudicator is the type the HANDLER RETURNS, not always the entity** | [[F2-211]] established that `sys.columns` adjudicates. Generalising it needed one refinement: `/api/v1/privacy/*` and `/api/v1/cyber/vulnerabilities` return **entities**, but `/api/v1/incidents` returns `Page<IncidentResponse>` — a response record. Adjudicating `IncidentDto` against `Incident` would have been measuring the wrong artefact. `WireContractTest` therefore declares the **resolved handler return type** per register rather than assuming the entity. |
| **⚠ `CyberVulnDto`: 3 of [[F2-210]]'s 4 filed fields are dead, and the 4th is refuted** | `cyber.vulnerabilities` (22 columns) has no `status`, no `discovery_date` and no `target_resolution_date`; `CyberPage` was defended by `r.workflowStatus ?? r.status`, a chain whose second operand is dead — the third instance of that shape after [[F2-211]]'s two. **`capaId` is REFUTED**: `capa_id` is a real column, null on all 20 live rows because no vulnerability has yet been linked to a CAPA. The same 1-in-4 correction rate as [[F2-211]]'s DPIA half, and for the same reason — a filing's measurements are the least-verified thing in it. |
| **⚠⚠ THE LIVE HALF: `PUT` is a full replace, so an omitted field is a WRITE of null** | `IncidentService.update` calls `setLessonsLearned(req.lessonsLearned())` — and the same for `lessonsLearnedAr`, `resolutionDate`, `timelineJson` — **unconditionally**. `IncidentDto` declared 9 of the 15 fields `IncidentResponse` sends and `incToReq` (which builds every PUT payload) carried none of those four. So opening any incident, changing one word and saving **destroyed its post-incident record**. Proven live against a row the probe planted for the purpose ([[F2-206]]'s rule): pre-fix payload → all four NULL; fixed payload → all four preserved and the edit still applied. Measured, dev = prod, 44 live incidents: `lessons_learned`/`_ar` on **3**, `resolution_date` on **6**, `timeline_json` on **3**. |
| **🔑 Invisible from BOTH ends, which is what made it survive** | The read type did not declare the fields either, so nothing rendered them — a user could not see the loss before, during or after. [[F2-198]]'s shape (the wire carries it, the client never declares it) as the **cause** of a destructive write rather than merely an unused column. |
| **⚠⚠ The register was inverted: it hid every real lesson and invented one for everything else** | `derivedLessons` filtered `i.status === 'CLOSED' \|\| i.status === 'RECOVERED'`. `RECOVERED` appears in **zero** rows — a token the vocabulary does not contain — and `RESOLVED` (**10 of 44**) was missing, while all three incidents carrying a real lesson are `INVESTIGATING`/`OPEN`/`OPEN`. **0 of 3 admitted, in both databases.** [[F2-196]]'s rule: an inclusion list over an open vocabulary silently drops whatever nobody remembered. The text it showed instead came from the **severity band** ([[F2-209]]'s shape), the CAPA citation was minted `CAPA-<1000+id>` against real references like `CAPA-2026-19E164FC4A7-00`, and operator-authored lessons went to `localStorage` ([[F2-208]]'s shape) beside a server that already stored, returned **and accepted writes for** all four fields. |
| **🔑 A type gate and a call-site gate answer different questions** | `WireContractTest` checks that the types stay in step; it cannot see the mechanism that caused the loss, because **`incToReq` can omit a field the type happily permits**. Only an FE leg over the payload builder would have caught the defect as it existed. Both now exist, and the split is the lesson: *what may be sent* and *what is sent* are separate claims. |
| **The fix** | `IncidentDto`/`IncidentRequest` re-declared against `IncidentResponse`; `incToReq` carries all four; the lessons register reads `lessonsLearnedAr \|\| lessonsLearned` per language with **no status predicate at all** — a lesson exists because someone wrote one; `onAddLesson` writes through `PUT /incidents/{id}` and replaces the row from the server's response. The localStorage store, the minted CAPA reference, the derived text and the `userAdded` badge are deleted. Three dead `CyberVulnDto` fields deleted, `capaId` kept with the reason recorded. **0 backend changes, 0 migrations.** |
| **⚠⚠ FOUND IN THE BROWSER AFTER EVERY GATE WAS GREEN — fifth consecutive slice — and one of the two was MINE** | **(a)** The lessons badge read `{n} closed` / `{n} مغلقة`. While the register filtered CLOSED\|\|RECOVERED that word described the predicate; **removing the filter is what made the label false**, and it was then wrong for 3 of 3 rows. [[F2-208]]'s label-versus-predicate rule arriving from the inside: 🔑 **when you remove a filter, read every label that was describing it.** **(b)** Six lines below the register this slice had just made honest sat *"CAPA Themes (90d)"* — five **inline** hard-coded themes with counts summing to **18**, against a live register of 16 rows in dev and 13 in prod. `capa.tasks` has 26 columns and **no theme, root-cause or incident-link column**, so a theme was not reconstructible at all ([[F2-209]]'s third state); the "(90d)" was a second claim with nothing behind it. That is [[F2-211]]'s own headline — *the component next to the one you fixed* — one card across. |
| **🔑 Three de-mocking gates were blind to that panel at once, each for a reason already on the record** | `kpiProvenance` keys on the `<Kpi>` tag ([[F2-195]]); `pageDataProvenance` asks whether the **page** calls a server, and this one does ([[F2-198]]); [[F2-194]]'s census looks for an exported `const` array, and this literal is **inline in JSX**. Sixth instance of *the invariant is real, its POPULATION is narrower than it looks*. Replaced with the real relation the platform does record — the CAPAs whose `origin_type` is an incident, read through the register hook [[F2-208]] rewired: **exactly 1 in both databases**, rendered with its real server-minted reference. |
| **⚠ And the replacement panel had a defect of its own, caught by asking who can actually read it** | The new card calls the CAPA register, so a persona holding `INCIDENT:READ` without `CAPA:READ` would have got a raw 403 rendered as an error box. Measured, identical in dev and prod: **11 of the 29 roles holding INCIDENT:READ do not hold CAPA:READ** — and they include `IR_LEAD`, `FORENSICS_LEAD` and `REGULATOR_VIEWER`, the people most likely to be on this page. The hook now lives in a subcomponent mounted only when entitled, so no pointless request is made, and the no-access state says so **in words that cannot be read as a clean bill**: *"this is not a statement that none exist."* 🔑 **"You cannot see this register" and "no corrective action has been raised" are different facts, and an empty panel says both at once** — the same confusion this programme keeps finding in fabricated surfaces, arriving here through a permission boundary instead. |
| **⚠ My own gate then failed on my own refactor, for the right reason in the wrong way** | The leg asserted the identifier `incidentCapas`, and extracting the card into a component renamed the local to `items`. [[F2-197]]'s rule — *a rule keyed on a name cannot see the alias* — on a gate written after quoting it. Rescoped to the **shape** of the claim (`originType?.trim().toLowerCase() === 'incident'`), with a self-test that the bare literal comparison fails, so it survives renaming and still catches dropping the [[F2-179]] normalisation. |
| **Gates** | `WireContractTest` (backend, hermetic) renamed from `PrivacyWireContractTest` and extended to **8** tests over 6 registers, resolving every client field against its handler's return type by reflection, with `everyServerAcceptedIncidentFieldSurvivesAClientRoundTrip` and `vulnerabilityFieldsAreTheOnesTheSchemaKeeps`. `incidentPostIncidentRecord.test.ts` (**8**, FE) asserts the payload builder carries each at-risk field via `new RegExp(f + '\\s*:\\s*i\\.')` — the **assignment**, not the word — bans the derived lesson, the minted CAPA and the localStorage store, refuses any status inclusion list, and pins both browser findings: the badge label is checked **per language** (Arabic is primary, house rule 7, and [[F2-208]] found exactly this drift in the Arabic only) and the CAPA card must **call** `useCapas(` rather than merely import it. Every leg carries a self-test against the exact pre-fix shape. |
| **⚠ Two harness faults that are not gate holes, and the distinction matters** | Run 1 reported 2 SURVIVED that were **ANCHOR-MISS**: both anchors spanned lines and the tree is CRLF (4,646 CRLF, 0 bare LF), so a `\n` could never match. Re-run with the working copy normalised, both were **KILLED**. 🔑 **An anchor miss is the harness declining to run, and if you only count failures it reads exactly like a mutation the gate caught** — so it is now a distinct outcome that exits non-zero. |
| **Verification** | Backend **3850/0/0** · FE **749/749** across 68 files · typecheck clean · `WireContractTest` 8/8. Pre-fix control **32/32 detectors fire, 0 silent** (against `git show master:`). Mutation **14/14 killed** across three runs, SHA-256 restore CLEAN. Live probe **20/20** as `compliance` (never `admin` — PLATFORM_ADMIN bypasses in code), planting and removing its own row; register 44 before and after. Browser-confirmed in Arabic: badge *"3 بدرس مسجَّل"*, the three real lessons, and the one real incident-origin CAPA. **No migration.** |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-15** — `cbdf362a` (fix) + this entry. |
| **Filed by this slice** | **(a)** `privacy.data_breaches` carries the synonym pair `UNAUTHORISED_ACCESS` / `UNAUTHORIZED_ACCESS` under **no CHECK** — [[F2-196]]'s shape, and collapsing synonyms rewrites live rows, so it is an owner decision. **(b)** The breach `status` vocabulary is open: 7 stored values, no CHECK, no declared machine, read by two *exclusion* lists ([[F2-196]]'s rule unapplied). **(c)** Three incident-ish registers at three endpoints — `/api/v1/incidents` **44**, `/api/v1/cyber/incidents` **24**, `/api/v1/scm/incidents` **11** — [[F2-196]]'s disjoint-register shape for one concept. **(d)** `capa.tasks` records no theme and no incident link, so "CAPA themes" is not computable by any surface; the incidents page now shows the origin relation instead. |
| **Lesson** | 🔑 **A wire-contract gate proves the types agree; it cannot prove the payload builder sends what the type permits — and where the verb is a full-replace PUT, the gap between those two claims is silent data destruction.** The corollary for choosing what to measure: adjudicate against **the type the handler actually returns**, because a register whose endpoint returns a response record rather than an entity will otherwise be measured against the wrong artefact and every finding on it will be noise. 🔑 And the one that came from my own fix: **removing a filter can turn a label that accurately described it into a false claim** — the predicate and the words above it are two artefacts, and only one of them is in the diff you are reading. |

## F2-211 · The breach register's PDPL Article 20 countdown has never rendered, and the demo corpus is why nobody noticed

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-211 *(measured 2026-08-15. Lineage: [[F2-198]] → [[F2-199]] → [[F2-203]] → [[F2-205]] → [[F2-208]] → [[F2-209]] → [[F2-210]] → this. Chosen from [[F2-210]]'s own filed item (a), re-measured before being built on — which corrected it.)* |
| **Severity** | **P1.** A statutory countdown on a PDPL breach register had never once displayed against real data, for any tenant; and the register's severity filter removed every row when used, which reads as *"no breaches of that severity"* rather than as a broken control. |
| **⚠⚠ The four fields** | `PrivacyBreachDto` declared `severity`, `occurredAt`, `reportedAt` and `affectedRecords`. `GET /api/v1/privacy/breaches` returns the `DataBreach` **entity**, and `privacy.data_breaches` — read from `sys.columns`, **25 columns, 17 live rows, identical in dev and prod** — has a column for **none of them**. They could never arrive. |
| **⚠⚠ The sharpest consequence** | The column headed with the **PDPL Article 20 72-hour notification clock** opened `if (!r.occurredAt) return '—'`. `occurredAt` is never present, so **the countdown returned early on every row, always**. Beside it: the Severity badge rendered a neutral em-dash on all 17 rows; the Records count rendered `—` while `data_subjects_affected_count` is non-null on all 17; and the *"Occurred"* date was empty while `discovered_at` is **NOT NULL**. On `PrivacyBreachDetailPage` the same four killed the hero countdown badge, the affected-records panel and both classification rail fields. |
| **⚠⚠ The filter is worse than inert** | `advFilters.severity && b.severity !== advFilters.severity` compares against `undefined` on every row, so **choosing any band filtered the entire register away**. 🔑 **An inert control is a nuisance; a control that empties a statutory register produces a false all-clear** — an empty table reads as "there are none of those", not as "this control is broken". |
| **🔑 Why nobody noticed: the demo corpus is a SECOND wire contract, and nothing was checking it** | `mockPrivacy.ts`'s `BREACHES` — the `useApiList` fallback — set **all four** fields on every row, with `occurredAt` minted from `Date.now()` at module load. So those four columns and the countdown rendered **only there**, and rendered plausibly: [[F2-194]]'s rule, that a clock-anchored fabrication has no tell. [[F2-158]]'s lesson was *"when a page has a client-side fallback, hit its endpoint directly before believing the page"* — **this is the mechanism underneath it.** |
| **⚠⚠ The type annotation that enforces nothing** | `export const BREACHES: PrivacyBreachDto[] = demoRows([…])` looks like a contract. `demoRows<T>(rows: T[]): T[]` is **generic**, so TypeScript infers `T` from the literal and then checks `T[]` for **assignability** — where extra properties are legal. The excess-property check that fires on a direct annotation never runs. Proof it is not theoretical: [[F2-210]] renamed `retentionPeriod` → `retentionPeriodMonths` one slice earlier and the ROPA corpus **kept setting the retired key through a full clean typecheck**. 🔑 **F2-184's shape on a corpus: an artefact that answers the question a reader was about to ask.** |
| **⚠⚠ The measurement error this slice made, and the rule that comes out of it** | "Absent from the wire" was measured first, and it named **ten** dead fields across the four privacy DTOs. The entity says **four**. Under `default-property-inclusion: non_null`, *"the DTO declares a field the server has no column for"* and *"the column exists and every row is null"* are **byte-identical on the wire** — and they demand **opposite** fixes. `sdaiaSubmissionRef` / `sdaiaSubmittedAt` (real columns, no SDAIA submission recorded yet) and **all six** suspect `DpiaDto` fields (`processing_activity_id`, `dpo_id`, `assessor_id`, `approved_at`, `rejected_at`, `rejection_reason` — all real, all null on 6 rows) are correct declarations. 🔑 **6 of 6 refuted on the DPIA half** — worse than the ~2-in-10 rate [[F2-188]], [[F2-192]] and [[F2-204]] each measured, and the cause was choosing an instrument that cannot see the distinction. **Only `sys.columns` adjudicates; the wire only nominates.** |
| **🔑 [[F2-209]]'s own headline, one component up, missed by the slice that wrote it** | `PrivacyPage` renders `PdplBreachConsole` — which [[F2-209]] had just corrected to derive severity from the subject count, resolve awareness from `discoveredAt` and discharge the clock from `sdaia_notification_status` — **and the register table immediately below it did none of those things**. [[F2-196]]'s question (*how many things read this, and do they agree?*) with both readers on one route. F2-209 recorded that its own correct reader "was 200 lines below in the same file"; this is the same sentence one component out. |
| **The fix** | Four fields deleted from `PrivacyBreachDto`; `pdpcNotificationRequired` added (on the wire 17/17). Three shared predicates in `lib/pdplBreach.ts` — `breachAwarenessAt`, `breachSeverityInputs` and the existing `isSdaiaSubmitted` — consulted by **all three** surfaces, so a statutory question cannot be answered two ways on one page. Records → `dataSubjectsAffectedCount`; *Occurred* → **Discovered** (a different fact, so the header says which, `colDiscovered` in both languages); severity derived with [[F2-209]]'s provisional disclosure; the filter compares the same derived band the column shows. The clock now states *"Not notifiable"* where `pdpcNotificationRequired` is false rather than showing a bare dash that reads as missing data ([[F2-197]]'s rule). |
| **⚠ The dead `??` chain that was right by accident** | Both console call sites opened `b.reportedAt ?? b.occurredAt ?? b.discoveredAt`. The first two operands can never be defined, so the chain always resolved to the third — **a correct outcome via two dead operands**, reading as though the platform prefers a "reported" stamp and merely falls back. It has no such column. One accessor now. |
| **Gates** | `PrivacyWireContractTest` (6, backend, hermetic) resolves every field of **all four** privacy client types against its entity by reflection, with an empty exemption map enforced in both directions — it **generalises and replaces** `RopaWireContractTest` rather than sitting beside it, because two instruments answering one question is this programme's own recurring defect. `demoCorpusWireContract.test.ts` (5) derives its population from the tree (**50 typed corpora, 49 resolved**) and holds a **hard zero** with no exemptions. `sdaiaNotificationProvenance.test.ts` grew 6 legs for the register surfaces. |
| **🔑 Neither gate is sufficient, and saying so is the point** | The corpus gate compares corpus ⊆ DTO, so it catches a corpus that has **drifted** from its type — it would **not** have caught this defect, because the DTO declared all four too. The backend gate compares DTO ⊆ entity. Composed, they are the contract that matters: **corpus ⊆ DTO ⊆ entity.** |
| **⚠ Scope a leg to the two holes the type system leaves, not to the field names** | The first draft banned `\.severity` on the breach surfaces and fired instantly on `advFilters.severity` — the **filter-state key**, a legitimate use. Writing it properly showed the useful thing: now that the DTO does not declare these fields, **`tsc` already refuses `r.severity`**. Exactly two shapes escape it, and both produced this defect — a **widening cast** (`item as PrivacyBreachDto & { reportedToAuthority?: boolean }`, which is how a badge read a key the wire has never carried) and a **corpus key**. Those two are what the gate asserts. |
| **⚠⚠ The heredoc landmine fired twice in one slice, and a self-test is the only reason it was caught** | CLAUDE.md records that `\b` written into a bash heredoc becomes a literal **backspace (0x08)**. It happened once in a Python census (a `SyntaxError`, loud) and once in a TypeScript gate leg written with `cat >>` — where `\\b` collapsed to `\b`, which inside a **template literal** is a backspace, so the regex could never match. **That leg reported "no surface reads a dead field" over a tree full of them.** The SELF-TEST leg was the only thing that disagreed. 🔑 **A detector that cannot match reads exactly like a clean tree, and it under-reports — the dangerous direction.** |
| **⚠ A rule this repo carries, sharpened — and a surviving mutant that was not a hole** | CLAUDE.md says to strip comments *"in ONE left-to-right alternation — **the order is load-bearing**"*. Measured in node: **within one alternation the BRANCH order is a no-op.** `//` and `/*` can never match at the same position, so leftmost-match consumes the line comment first whichever branch is written first, and both orderings return the identical answer on the exact `App.tsx` shape. The defect [[F2-198]] measured is **two sequential passes**, which the doc's own example correctly describes — only the words *"the order is load-bearing"* over-generalised. Consequence for instrument design: a self-test whose "broken" variant is the reordered alternation passes on a correct tree **and** on a rotted one, so the negative control must be the **two-pass** form. 🔑 **A surviving mutant is a hole only if the mutated code is actually WRONG** — [[F2-206]]'s rule, second instance, and the reason mutation #17 was reclassified rather than "fixed". |
| **⚠ And a real hole the harness DID find, in a leg written after quoting the lesson** | *"the register asks the statutory questions through the shared predicates"* was a **presence check**, and `PrivacyPage` calls `breachAwarenessAt` **twice**. Inlining one site left the assertion true, so the mutation **survived**. That is [[F2-203]]'s count-with-a-floor and [[F2-209]]'s `>= 2` for the third time in this lineage. The fix is not a bigger number — it is a **shape ban**: only `lib/pdplBreach.ts` may read `.discoveredAt`, which no site count can defeat. Both sites are now mutated independently and both are killed. |
| **Verification** | Backend 3848/0/0. FE 741/741 + typecheck clean. Pre-fix control **22/22 detectors fire, 0 silent**. Mutation **17/17**, SHA-256 restore clean. Live probe **22/22** as `compliance` (never `admin` — PLATFORM_ADMIN bypasses in code). Browser-confirmed. **No migration.** |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-15** — `3c460197` (fix) + `pending` (records). |
| **Lesson** | 🔑 **A demo fallback corpus is a second wire contract, and the `: Dto[]` annotation that appears to bind it enforces nothing.** It is the mechanism behind [[F2-158]]'s "hit the endpoint before believing the page": the fallback can populate fields the real endpoint cannot send, so a column renders in demo and dies in production, invisible from either side. 🔑 And the measurement rule that made this slice honest: **the wire nominates, `sys.columns` adjudicates** — a field absent from a `non_null` response is equally consistent with "no column" and "no data", and those two want opposite fixes. |

## F2-210 · The PDPL Article 31 ROPA wizard has never been able to create a record, and the register reported a complete statutory field as missing

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-210 *(measured 2026-08-14/15. Lineage: [[F2-198]] → [[F2-199]] → [[F2-203]] → [[F2-205]] → [[F2-208]] → [[F2-209]] → this. Chosen by generalising [[F2-209]]'s filed item (c) — a client-declared field the wire never carries — into a question asked of every register: **diff the client's field names against the wire in BOTH directions.**)* |
| **Severity** | **P1.** The creation path of a statutory register (PDPL Article 31, the record SDAIA asks for in an inspection) has never once worked, failing with a message that names no field; and the register's own completeness panel reported a mandatory field missing on every row that has it. |
| **⚠⚠ The write half: every submission 400s, and the message names nothing** | `POST /api/v1/privacy/ropa` takes `@RequestBody ProcessingActivity` — the **entity** — and Spring Boot disables `FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES`, so unknown keys are discarded in silence. `PrivacyRopaRequest` declared `processNameEn` / `processNameAr` / `dataCategories` / `retentionPeriod`; the entity declares `activityNameEn` / `activityNameAr` / `purposeEn` / `legalBasis` / `retentionPeriodMonths` / `dataCategoriesJson` / `status`. Probed live with the **exact** payload `RopaWizard` sends: **HTTP 400 — *"A required field was not supplied. Check the request body against the endpoint's schema."*** because `activity_name_en` is NOT NULL and arrived null. The same probe with the entity's names returns **201**. 🔑 **Only `status` bound, which is why the failure looked partial rather than total** — and the diagnostic names no field, on a form where nothing is in fact missing, so an operator has no way to act on it. All 11 rows in dev and prod are seeded; no ROPA has ever been created through the platform. |
| **⚠ Two more fields silently lost on the same call** | The wizard **collects a purpose of processing** (step 1) and never sent it — a mandatory Article 31 field. And it composed the retention period into prose (`"60 months — <rule>"`) for a string key the endpoint does not bind, so both the number and the rule went nowhere; `retention_period_months` is an INT column. |
| **⚠⚠ The read half, and the reason this is worse than an empty column** | The wire carries `retentionPeriodMonths` — **non-null on 11 of 11 rows** (24 / 36 / 60 / 84 / 120) — and the client read `retentionPeriod`, non-null on **0 of 11**. Three surfaces were wrong: `PrivacyPage`'s ROPA **Retention column**, `RopaDetailPage`'s **Data retention → Period** rail, and `RopaDetailPage`'s **"Completeness check (SDAIA examiner expectations)"** panel, whose `<Check yes={!!item.retentionPeriod}>Retention period set</Check>` therefore rendered UNCHECKED for every activity. **The platform was telling a DPO that its statutory register was incomplete on a point where it is complete.** |
| **🔑 The DIRECTION of the error is the new part** | [[F2-193]]'s cadences, [[F2-195]]'s KPI tiles and [[F2-205]]'s fabrications **all erred flatteringly**, and the register recorded "do not assume that again". This one errs **pessimistically**: it creates no false assurance, but it sends someone to remediate data that is already correct — and it is **far less likely to be reported**, because *"no data yet"* is a plausible reading of an empty column, whereas a suspiciously good number invites a question. |
| **⚠⚠ [[F2-198]] and [[F2-207]] both CITED this wizard as evidence the real surface was complete** | Both retired a fabricated ROPA surface on the reasoning that *"`RopaWizard` creates through `privacyApi.createRopa`"*. Neither probed the create. 🔑 **A capability claim is the least-verified thing in a filing** ([[F2-188]], [[F2-192]], [[F2-204]] each measured this in someone else's reasons; here it is in mine, twice) — **"there is a wizard" is not "the wizard works".** The retirements were still right; the evidence offered for them was not checked. |
| **⚠ Status words aligned to the register's own stored vocabulary, not the wizard's** | The wizard wrote `PUBLISHED` / `REVIEWED` / `DRAFT`; `processing_activities.status` has **no CHECK**, so those would have stored verbatim — while the register's tone map and the completeness panel read `DRAFT` / `UNDER_REVIEW` / `APPROVED` / `ACTIVE`. Measured stored values: **ACTIVE 10, UNDER_REVIEW 1**. Enabling the create while keeping the wizard's words would have introduced [[F2-196]]'s disjoint-vocabulary defect on a statutory register; it costs nothing to align because no stored row carries the old words. |
| **⚠⚠ The instrument I did NOT ship, and why** | The obvious general gate — diff every FE `*Dto` against its backend type by name — was built first and **rejected**: it resolved **73 of 163** interfaces, and its 96 "orphans" were dominated by `BaseEntity` fields (`id`, `createdAt`, `organisationId`) that a per-file scan cannot see. [[F2-206]]'s rule exactly: **"unresolved" reads identically to "missing"**, so shipping it would have manufactured findings at scale. Ground truth is the **wire**. |
| **⚠⚠ And measuring from the wire still produced 4 false positives out of 5, because I paired the endpoints BY HAND** | The paired diff flagged 5 "likely renames". Verified against **the endpoint each client actually calls**: `KriDefinitionDto`'s three (`greenMax`/`amberMax`/`categoryId`) are **refuted** — the column that renders them is `FrameworkKriRowDto` from a different endpoint, `KriAdminPage` reads the server's names directly, and `RiskRegisterPage` explicitly maps `greenMax: d.greenThreshold`; `BcmBiaDto.overallImpact` is **refuted** — I compared it with `/bcm/bia-assessments` while the client calls `/bcm/bia`, where it is non-null on 10 of 10. 🔑 **A scan locates; the pairing is the measurement, and a guessed pairing manufactures phantom findings.** 1 of 5 survived — a worse rate than the ~2-in-10 [[F2-188]]/[[F2-192]]/[[F2-204]] each measured, and the cause was entirely mine. |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-15** — `dae5dee1`. `PrivacyRopaRequest` and `PrivacyRopaDto` re-declared against the entity the endpoint binds; `RopaWizard` sends the activity name, the purpose, the integer retention and the blob; one shared `formatRetentionMonths` in `lib/format.ts` read by the list and the detail view so the label rule cannot drift. Gate: `RopaWireContractTest` (**4**), resolving every field of both types against `ProcessingActivity` by reflection, with a self-test that feeds the parser the pre-fix names and requires four to be rejected. **Backend 3846/0/0 · FE 729/729 + typecheck clean · live probe 9/9** as `compliance` (pre-fix payload still 400, fixed payload 201, name + purpose + retention + status all persisted, read-back carries `retentionPeriodMonths` on 12/12), planting its own row and cleaning up — **11 live activities before and after**. **No migration.** |
| **Filed by this slice** | **(a)** `PrivacyBreachDto` declares `severity` / `occurredAt` / `reportedAt` / `affectedRecords` and the wire carries a non-null value for **none** — so the breach register's Severity column renders an em-dash on every row and its severity filter can never match ([[F2-209]] filed this; still open, and it is the same shape as the ROPA read half). **(b)** `CyberVulnDto` declares four fields the wire never carries (`status`, `capaId`, `discoveryDate`, `targetResolutionDate`); `CyberPage` is **defended** by `r.workflowStatus ?? r.status`, so these are dead declarations that invite the next reader to make the ROPA mistake. **(c)** `IncidentDto` never declares `lessonsLearned`, `lessonsLearnedAr`, `resolutionDate` or `timelineJson`, all of which the wire carries — [[F2-198]]'s shape, real data unused. **(d)** The wizard has no Arabic activity-name field, so a record created through it cannot satisfy house rule 7; `activity_name_ar` is nullable, so this is a form gap rather than a failure. **(e)** `processing_activities.status` has no CHECK and no declared machine — [[F2-183]]'s rule (a CHECK and its writer land together) is now cheap to apply because the only writer is the one this slice fixed. |
| **Lesson** | 🔑 **Diff the client's field names against the wire in BOTH directions, and remember that the two directions fail differently.** A field the wire carries and the client never declares makes a page invent its own number ([[F2-198]]); a field the client declares and the wire never carries makes a column render an em-dash forever and a filter match nothing — and on a *completeness checklist* it inverts into an assertion that a complete record is incomplete. Both are invisible to every provenance gate in this tree, because the page genuinely calls a server and the data genuinely arrives. And the corollary that cost the most here: **when an endpoint binds an entity rather than a DTO, an unknown key is not an error — it is a silent deletion**, so the write path can be broken from the day it was written without a single log line.

## F2-209 · A fabricated PDPL Article 25 submission to SDAIA, and a statutory gate reading the wrong column

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-209 *(measured 2026-08-13/14. Lineage: [[F2-194]] → [[F2-198]] → [[F2-199]] → [[F2-201]] → [[F2-203]] → [[F2-205]] → [[F2-207]] → [[F2-208]] → this. Chosen by re-measuring [[F2-208]]'s filed item (e), the browser-side reference minters: the real population is **49 sites in 24 files, 41 with browser entropy**, not the filed 14 — and ranking them by *what kind of thing is being minted* separated internal references from **authority-owned** ones (`NCA-ACK-`, `SAMA-CTI-`, `NCEMA-`, `PDPL-N-`), which pointed here.)* |
| **Severity** | **P1.** The platform generated, displayed and offered for download a complete Saudi PDPL Article 25 personal-data-breach notification to SDAIA whose substantive content was invented — including two paragraphs of **statements of fact about the organisation's incident-response conduct** — and the console that exists to surface an undischarged 72-hour statutory clock filtered out the four breaches most obviously in breach of it. |
| **⚠⚠ The harm differs in KIND from [[F2-199]], one step further along the same axis** | [[F2-199]] established the ladder: a fabricated dashboard misleads whoever is looking at it and looking again corrects it; a fabricated **export** leaves the platform, where nothing downstream can tell the figures were invented. This adds the next rung: a fabricated **statement of conduct**. `containmentMeasures` read *"Affected systems isolated from the network within the first hour of detection. Privileged access tokens revoked. Forensic image of impacted hosts captured for SDAIA inspection."* — identical for every breach in every tenant — and the platform's own runbook (`docs/operations/sdaia-breach-notification-workflow.md`, and the entity javadoc) says the DPO transcribes this into the SDAIA portal **by hand**, because SDAIA has no machine-readable API. So the text was authored to be copied out. 🔑 **A fabricated metric misstates your posture; a fabricated statement of conduct invites the regulator to ask for a forensic image that may not exist.** |
| **What `generateSdaiaNotification` invented, measured against `sys.columns`** | `privacy.data_breaches` has **25 columns**, **17 live rows**, **0 CHECK constraints**, identical in dev and prod. There is **no column** for: the categories of personal data affected, the likely consequences for data subjects, the containment measures taken, the remediation measures proposed, the reporting controller's identity, the DPO's contact details, or a `severity`. All seven were literals in the shipped bundle. `categoriesAffected` was derived from the **severity band**, so *"Financial / transactional data"* was asserted to the regulator because a row count crossed a threshold; `likelyConsequences` was one of three canned paragraphs. |
| **⚠⚠ The controller was the software vendor, with one CR number, for every tenant** | `DEFAULT_CONTROLLER` = `'TSS Saudi Holding'` / `'القابضة السعودية للتقنية'` / **CR `1010299292`** / DPO `'Mona Al-Bishi'` / `dpo@tss.sa` / `+966 11 200 0000`. **The same hard-coded CR number [[F2-199]] found on the fabricated NCA ECC return**, so the rule it recorded holds a second time and in a second regulator's filing: *a tenant-specific fact appearing as a literal in a shipped bundle cannot be right for more than one tenant and is most likely right for none.* `Mona Al-Bishi` is the **eleventh** invented officer in this programme and a member of [[F2-207]]'s measured 65-name cast — she appears in eight other product files, which is why this slice's identity gate is scoped to the two files it owns rather than app-wide. |
| **⚠⚠ Why [[F2-199]]'s and [[F2-203]]'s gates were GREEN over it — the hybrid document** | `exportProvenance` asks *does the page emitting a document have server data in scope?* — yes: the console is handed real `PrivacyBreachDto` rows and fetches `/breaches/{id}/sdaia-submission`. [[F2-203]] sharpened that to *which of this file's data reaches the thing it emits?* — and here the **same** data reaches it: `downloadPacket` wrote `JSON.stringify({ packet, breach })`, the invention and the genuine server row **in one file**, named from a client-minted `PDPL-N-<id>-<year>`. 🔑 **Both instruments are FILE-level, and this document was a hybrid: the real fields are what made the invented ones credible.** [[F2-203]]'s CMA packet contradicted itself on the same page (eight invented engagements beside twenty real findings) and that is part of how it was found; this one is seamless. The eleventh instrument therefore asks the question **per FIELD**. |
| **⚠⚠ THE LIVE HALF: the statutory gate read the breach lifecycle status, not the SDAIA column** | The console answered *"has SDAIA been notified?"* with `breach.status === 'NOTIFIED'`. The platform owns a dedicated column for exactly that question — `sdaia_notification_status`, with a four-state machine (`NOT_REPORTED → IN_PREPARATION \| SUBMITTED → ACKNOWLEDGED`, terminal, guarded) declared in `PrivacyService`. Probed live: **4 of 17 live breaches in BOTH databases are `status = NOTIFIED` with `sdaia_notification_status = NOT_REPORTED`** (ids 8, 9, 13, 16), all four flagged `pdpc_notification_required`, and **113 / 128 / 173 / 193 days past** a 72-hour window. `needsSdaia` excluded exactly those four, so **the one screen built to surface an undischarged Article 25 clock was the screen that hid them.** Tenant-wide: **10 rows require notification, have never been reported, and are past 72h**; **0 of 17 carry `sdaia_submitted_at`**, so the statutory discharge has never once been stamped. |
| **🔑 The correct reader was 200 lines below, in the same file, under a comment saying so** | `SdaiaSubmissionPanel` fetches the authoritative status, uses `sdaiaNotificationStatus`, renders the **server-computed** `pdplArticle31DeadlineAt`, and records the outcome — beneath a comment reading *"SDAIA submission tracking (authoritative, server-backed)"*. [[F2-196]]'s question (*how many things read this status, and do they agree?*) with [[F2-205]]'s follow-up (*and which of them is the server?*), except sharper: **both readers were in one component, and the wrong one decided what the operator saw.** |
| **⚠⚠ `onDispatch` REMOVED, not repointed — and the prop's own contract stated the rule it broke** | It was documented as the *"Real SDAIA dispatch action"*, warning *"we never want this regulatory action to 'succeed' without actually transitioning state."* The single call site passed `notifyDataOfficeAction` → `POST /breaches/{id}/notify-data-office`, whose whole body is `setPdpcNotificationRequired(true)` + `setPdpcNotifiedAt(now)`. It does **not** write `sdaia_notification_status`, does **not** write `sdaia_submitted_at` (the field the server's own javadoc calls the discharge of the Article 31 clock), and emits **neither** the F7 audit row **nor** the F8 `BREACH_REPORTED_TO_SDAIA` event that `recordSdaiaSubmission` — in the same service — emits. And because the button's own disabled/label gate read a column that action never sets, it never even relabelled itself: a second click re-stamped `pdpc_notified_at`. **Latent, not live: 0 rows in either database carry `pdpc_notified_at`, so it had never been clicked.** 🔑 [[F2-184]]'s shape — *a comment that answers the question a reader was about to ask* — on a prop contract. |
| **⚠ And it could not be fixed by pointing it somewhere better** | Nothing in this platform can dispatch to SDAIA: there is no machine-readable API, the submission is a human filling in a portal, and the entity javadoc says so. A button reading *"Dispatch to SDAIA"* is therefore a claim no endpoint could ever make true. The honest control already existed below — *record the outcome of the manual submission* — so it is now the only one, promoted to primary. 🔑 **When a control's label describes something the platform cannot do at all, the fix is deletion, not rewiring.** |
| **⚠⚠ Not rewireable, and that is [[F2-207]]'s question with a THIRD answer** | [[F2-207]] asks: diff the client's tokens against the target column before choosing rewire over retire. There the tokens were **refused** by a CHECK → retire. [[F2-208]] added: the server's machine is merely **coarser** → rewire and delete the granularity. Here: **there is no column at all**, so reconstructing the fields would be [[F2-196]]'s defect — the same reason [[F2-198]] *deleted* `lastReviewedAt`/`nextReviewAt` rather than inventing them. |
| **⚠⚠ Deleting the section would have ASSERTED READINESS, so it was replaced, not removed** | An empty space where a submission draft used to be reads as *"nothing further is required"* — [[F2-197]]'s rule on a statutory filing. `ARTICLE_25_FIELDS` declares the same twelve fields, each naming the `PrivacyBreachDto` property it reads or `null`. The console renders **three** distinct states, and the distinction between the last two is the point: a **value**; *"not yet recorded"* (a column exists and is empty — somebody can fill it in here); and *"—" + "DPO supplies"* with a bilingual hint on both `title` and `aria-label` (no column exists — no amount of data entry here will produce it). **6 held / 6 not held.** |
| **⚠ The severity band was PROVISIONAL and presented as an assessment** | The call site passed `financial: breach.breachType === 'CONFIDENTIALITY' && records > 5_000` — an inference no column supports, asserting that a large confidentiality breach involved financial data. That promotes the band to HIGH and with it the **Article 26 determination that affected individuals must be notified directly**. There is no special-category flag, no data-category list and no `severity` column, so the affected-record count is the only real input; the badge now carries `· provisional` with a bilingual explanation, and `severityIsProvisional` is a function rather than a constant so adding those columns turns the caveat off in one place. |
| **⚠⚠ MY FIRST FIX CONTAINED THE SAME DEFECT ONE NOTCH MILDER, and only asking why an export was unused found it** | I wrote `isSdaiaReported` for the urgency pool and the countdown KPI, leaving `isSdaiaSubmitted` with no caller. `IN_PREPARATION` **discharges nothing** — so the pool would have dropped a notification begun six months ago and never sent, and the 72-hour KPI would have rendered in **success green** for it ([[F2-197]] again). 🔑 **An exported predicate with no caller is a question about the predicates that DO have callers.** Pool and KPI now ask `isSdaiaSubmitted`; the panel's Record-vs-Update label correctly asks `isSdaiaReported`. |
| **⚠⚠ MY OWN GATE COMMITTED [[F2-203]]'S DEFECT, in a leg written after quoting it** | The shared-predicate leg counted `isSdaiaReported(` and required **`>= 2`**. There are three call sites, so the mutation reverting the submission panel to its own inline comparison left two behind and **SURVIVED**. [[F2-203]] recorded this in these words — *a count with a floor cannot see one member vanish* — and I wrote a floor anyway. Replaced with a ban on the **shape**: no inline comparison against any of the four SDAIA state tokens anywhere in the console, so reverting any single site fails regardless of how many others remain. 🔑 **Scope an assertion to the shape of its claim, not to a population count.** |
| **⚠ Two more of my own instrument errors, both caught by running things** | (a) The stripper self-test used a surviving-**character** ratio (`> 40% of raw`) and failed on a correct tree, because this file is legitimately **62% comment** — the header explaining a retirement is longer than the code replacing it. [[F2-199]] had already recorded the right instrument and I reached for a ratio anyway: count declarations **anchored to line starts**, which a comment can never satisfy. (b) Adding `format: 'datetime'` to two inventory entries made **both** parsers (TS and Java) return **10 of 12**, dropping exactly the two entries that had changed — a gate keyed to a literal entry shape reports a SMALLER population the moment a field gains a property. It failed loudly **only because the leg asserts a minimum size**; without that anti-vacuity floor it would have silently stopped checking the two most recently edited entries. |
| **⚠⚠ A key-usage detector must match every call shape, and `t\(` matches the `t(` inside `set(`** | The dead-key scan reported **32** dead `pdpl*` keys; **17 were false positives** built by concatenation (`t('pdplSev' + severity…)`, `t('pdplExtCbtStatus_' + status)`) — the tell being that the concatenation **stem** shows up in the referenced-but-undeclared list, which is self-diagnosing once you look for it. It also reported `pdplReportable` and `sdaiaDraftEn` as undeclared translation keys; both are **object property names** passed to `set('pdplReportable', v)`, and `t\(` matched the `t(` inside `set(`. 🔑 Nth instance here of a pattern satisfied by something other than its claim; it **over**-reports, the safe direction for a delete, but it sends the reader to investigate two non-issues. Honest answer: **15 dead keys removed** — exactly the ones the retirement orphaned — **19 added**, 0 undeclared. |
| **⚠⚠ FOUND IN THE BROWSER, AFTER EVERY GATE WAS GREEN — and the text leg fired before that** | The new leg over the module's own keys immediately caught `pdplConsoleEmpty`: *"No open personal-data breaches.
