The database's own answer to `SELECT CASE WHEN N'critical' = N'CRITICAL'` is **equal**, which is what makes the CHECK useless as a guard here. |
| **Why a connector is the realistic caller** | The controller javadoc says drift observations are "typically recorded by **automated monitoring jobs**", and the channel the drift path uses is `API_INGESTION`. Machine-to-machine integrations are exactly where casing conventions differ and nobody eyeballs the payload — and the failure mode is silence, so the first symptom is a model that drifted critically and stayed in production. |
| **The fix, and the one decision in it** | Normalising `severity` (and `observationType`, which has the same shape via `CK_ml_drift_type`) to upper case on write makes the CHECK, the Java trigger and the frontend's `MlDriftSeverity` label map all agree — and is decision-free, because the CHECK already restricts the value set and the collation already considers the cases equal. The alternative, `equalsIgnoreCase` at the trigger, is one character shorter and **wrong**: it leaves `'critical'` in the column, where `SEVERITY_LABELS[s]` misses and the register renders a drift row with no severity label. ⚙ The genuine decision, and the reason this is filed rather than bundled into F2-175: **whether `MAJOR` should escalate too.** That is a governance call about AI post-market monitoring (EU AI Act Art. 72 / SDAIA), not a casing bug, and answering it while fixing the casing would smuggle a policy change in under a typo fix. |
| **⚠ Do not fix it by tightening only the DTO** | An `@Pattern` on the request would refuse lower case at the door and leave the same trap for every other writer of this column — including any future scheduler. The value is already constrained by the database; what is missing is that **the code reading it back does not use the database's notion of equality.** Look for the same pair elsewhere: `ExerciseObserverService` holds the identical five-token list as a Java `Set.of(...)` against a CI column. |
| **⚠⚠ That last sentence was wrong, and checking it took two minutes** | `ExerciseObserverService` is **already closed**: `normaliseRole`/`normaliseType`/`normaliseSeverity` each `trim().toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT)` *before* testing the `Set`, and every write path goes through them. It is the model to copy, not a second defect. Third instance in this program of a finding asserting something about existing code without opening it, after [[F2-175]]'s two false architectural claims and [[F2-178]]'s recommendation for a report that had already shipped. 🔑 **Read the code before believing a register row's claim about it — including a row you wrote yourself.** |
| **The scoped sweep that replaced the guess, in four numbers** | Since the guess was wrong, the population was measured instead: **347** closed upper-case CHECK vocabularies (of 389 single-column CHECKs), all on case-insensitive collations → **207** reachable through an entity field → **79 with an open writer** (a caller's casing reaches the column) → **25** of those also read back by a case-sensitive Java comparison. **0** non-canonical values are stored in dev today, so this was latent rather than realised — the trap is reachable only through the API, which is exactly where machine-to-machine callers live. ⚠ The scoping rule is `module(entity) == module(file) AND accessor-name == column-name`, deliberately narrow after F2-180's unscoped-cross-check lesson; its residual imprecision is that two entities in one module sharing a column name can cross-pair, which produced exactly one false pairing (`bcm.exercise_observation.severity`'s writer against `BcmGap.severity`'s readers) and it is **not** reported as a finding. |
| **⚠ My own scan reported 0 of 389 on its first run** | `\b(IN\|=)\b` can never match `=`, because `=` is not a word character and the boundaries fail. The anti-vacuity print is the only reason that was visible immediately rather than becoming a "there is no population" conclusion. Same family as F2-180's `PEND` phantom and F2-175's `.replace("N","")`: **a regex over someone else's language needs a leg that fails when it stops matching.** |
| **⚠⚠ The severe instance was found by the sweep, not by this finding** | The 25 included `ethics.whistleblower_case`, and its three helpers were worse than the drift one on every axis. `submitCase` is the platform's **public, unauthenticated** portal. `isAnonymousReporterType` asked `"ANONYMOUS".equals(<the RAW request value>)`, so a reporter declaring anonymity as `reporterType: "anonymous"` — with the `isAnonymous` flag absent — was recorded `is_anonymous = FALSE`, and the next branch **persisted their name, email, phone and employee id.** Keeping the reporter's identity out of the record is the one thing the module exists to do. Separately, `safeSeverity`'s case-sensitive `switch` missed `'critical'` and returned **`MEDIUM`**, silently downgrading the triage band of a fraud or corruption allegation and discarding the reporter's own assessment. `safeChannel` and `safeReporterType` returned their argument unchanged — the `safeRole(String role) { return role; }` decoy shape F2-175 deleted, second instance, **in a different module: the name is the tell, not the module.** |
| **⚠ Why the existing suite was green over the identity bug, which is the reusable part** | `WhistleblowerCaseServiceTest.submit_anonymousRequest_persistsTokenAndStripsContactFields` has asserted exactly the right thing since it was written — `isAnonymous` true, all four contact fields null — and it passes. Its fixture sets **both** `reporterType = "ANONYMOUS"` **and** `isAnonymous = true`: the belt and the braces. The defect lived in the braces alone. 🔑 **A fixture that satisfies a condition twice cannot tell you which half is load-bearing**, so the new legs supply one at a time. |
| **What shipped** | `common/validation/ClosedVocabulary` — declare/`require`/`orDefault`/`coerce`/`is`, refusing at construction a set with no constraint name, lower-case tokens, or an empty vocabulary, and refusing at use a fallback outside its own vocabulary. ⚙ **It is not new code so much as code that was in the wrong package**: `module/cyber`'s `CyberInputValidation#checkEnum` has done exactly this since CY-H — trim, upper-case, validate, 400 naming the set — used **6 times, all inside `module/cyber`**, which ADR-012/018 forbid a peer from importing. So every other module hand-rolled something weaker or nothing. · `MlModelDriftService`: two vocabularies, normalise-on-write, the trigger reads the normalised value, `ESCALATING_SEVERITY` named so the `MAJOR` question has one place to be answered. · `WhistleblowerCaseService`: four vocabularies, the anonymity decision reading one normalised value, and the three helpers deleted. |
| **The one decision, still the owner's** | **Whether `MAJOR` should escalate too** is untouched — a governance call about AI post-market monitoring (EU AI Act Art. 72 / SDAIA), not a casing bug. `ESCALATING_SEVERITY` is a single named constant so answering it is a one-line change with a test that says so. |
| **⚠ And a second per-field decision that had to be made, not assumed** | `require` vs `coerce` differs only in what happens to a value **outside** the vocabulary, and the right answer is not uniform. Drift severity: `require`, because a 400 beats a silently-defaulted governance signal. Whistleblower severity: **`coerce`**, because `safeSeverity` already accepted an unrecognised token as `MEDIUM` and *the report arrived* — converting that to a 400 would make submissions that succeed today start failing, and on a whistleblowing channel a lost report is worse than a mis-graded one. `CyberInputValidation`'s own javadoc draws that line ("no request that succeeds today can start failing"); `coerce` exists to honour it while still fixing the casing. |
| **Gates** | `ClosedVocabularyTest` (9) — the three admission modes, the message carrying nothing but the caller's value (this reaches anonymous callers), immutability, and `is()` refusing a token the column cannot hold. · **`ClosedVocabularyPinTest` (3) — the durable instrument**: every `ClosedVocabulary` anywhere in main sources is checked against the CHECK constraint it *names*, so a new vocabulary is covered from the commit that adds it, with no hand-maintained registry. Truth read by **reflection**, never a source regex (CLAUDE.md records why: `FrontendEndpointContractTest`'s regex half matched a javadoc sentence and reported 1,763 phantom failures); a source scan only narrows the candidate list, and `MUST_BE_FOUND` is a floor so a narrowing that breaks fails loudly. · `WhistleblowerVocabularyTest` (10) — belt-alone, braces-alone, both, and the negative control that an identified reporter is still identified. · `MlModelDriftServiceTest` +4. · `MigrationVocabulariesTest` (5) — see below. |
| **⚙ The migration parser was extracted, and that is where the mutation harness earned its keep** | Three test classes had each grown a copy of the "read the CHECK vocabularies out of the SQL" walk; F2-179 needed a fourth, so it became `support/MigrationVocabularies` (F2-178's predicate-sharing lesson). The harness then found that **two of its safety rules mask each other**: remove the literal-stripping and `ratification_state <> N'PENDING'` yields the phantom column `PEND`, but that makes the column count **two**, so the multi-column rule drops the whole constraint instead of admitting the phantom — and every downstream assertion stayed green. 🔑 **Two guards that each hide the other's failure are, between them, one guard that nothing tests.** `MigrationVocabulariesTest` now asserts both directly. |
| **⚠⚠ And it corrected F2-180's own record** | That row credits the **literal-stripping** with killing the `PEND` phantom. Measured here: the load-bearing half is the **word boundary** — `N'PENDING'` cannot yield `PEND` while `\bIN\b` is required, because the `IN` inside `PENDING` has word characters on both sides. F2-180 shipped two changes together and attributed the fix to the wrong one. Both remaining parser mutations survive for this reason: the code is **over-defended, not under-tested**, and killing them would need a synthetic migration whose literal contains a space-delimited ` IS `. Reported as 21/23 with both survivors explained rather than as 23/23 with a contrived test. 🔑 **When two changes ship together, only a mutation tells you which one was doing the work.** |
| **Mutation** | **21/23 caught.** Every original defect restored verbatim (raw-severity trigger, both un-normalised writes, the audit line echoing the caller, the raw anonymity comparison, the case-sensitive severity switch, raw channel/category/triage); three plausible **weaker** fixes (`equalsIgnoreCase` at the trigger with the caller's casing left in the column — caught only by the stored-value assertion; `coerce` where `require` belongs; a whistleblower category coerced to `OTHER` instead of refused); six of the primitive's own guards; three of the parser's. ⚠ One mutation had to be rewritten because it **would not compile** — a mutation that fails to compile reddens the suite for the wrong reason and counts itself as caught, which is a false kill and worse than a survivor because it is invisible. |
| **Live probe (31/31)** | Backend run from the freshly built jar on :8084 (prod :8090 untouched throughout). **A (11 legs):** a `severity: "critical"` drift → 201, `triggeredIssueId = 103` (**NULL before**), the column holding `CRITICAL` **byte-exact under `Latin1_General_100_BIN2`** rather than merely CI-equal, `observation_type` canonical, and the model flipped `IN_PRODUCTION → REVISION`; an out-of-vocabulary severity and observationType each **400 naming the field and the offending value**, where the CHECK previously answered 409. **B (18 legs, no `Authorization` header at all):** `reporterType: "anonymous"` → `is_anonymous` TRUE and all four identity columns NULL; `'critical'` stored `CRITICAL` not `MEDIUM`; `'SEV1'` **still accepted** and coerced to `MEDIUM` (the fail-soft path deliberately unchanged); lower-case channel/category/severity all canonical; an unknown category 400 naming the vocabulary and **leaking no schema to an anonymous caller**; and the negative control — an identified reporter still identified, `reporter_type` normalised to `EMPLOYEE`. **C:** before/after snapshot of all four tables equal, cleanup by id captured at creation plus a `CHARINDEX` belt, and an **anti-vacuity leg that failed on the first run** because no whistleblower rows had been created — which is precisely what makes "back to baseline" mean something. ⚙ Two probe bugs cost one run each and both were named by the platform's own diagnostics: `@Valid` firing before `@PreAuthorize` on two required owner ids, and the public portal's `?org=` short code (F2-83's 404 *"must carry a valid 'org' short code"* — the counter-example to F2-180's foreign-key message). |
| **Effort** | M (1 new kernel class, 2 services, 1 test-support extraction, 4 new test classes + 2 repointed, ~70 assertions, 23 mutations, 31 live probe legs, **0 migrations, 0 frontend change**) |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-11.** Backend suite **3,633/0/0**, FE **487/487** in 50 files + `tsc` clean, mutation **21/23** (both survivors explained), live probe **31/31**, `mvn -o clean package` hermetic, census `--check` clean. Filed on the way out: **[[F2-182]]** (the residual 10 measured sites across 8 modules) and **[[F2-183]]** (`consumer.complaint`, where the vocabulary has **no CHECK at all** and the Java switch substitutes silently). |
| **Lesson** | ⚙ **Read the code before believing a register row's claim about it — including your own**: this finding's own "look here next" pointer named a class that was already correct, and the real instance was three times more serious and in a module nobody had mentioned. ⚙ **A fixture that satisfies a condition twice cannot tell you which half is load-bearing.** ⚙ **`require` vs `coerce` is a product decision per field, not a house style** — a lost whistleblower report is worse than a mis-graded one, and the opposite holds for a governance escalation. ⚙ **Two guards that each mask the other's failure are one guard that nothing tests**, and **when two changes ship together only a mutation tells you which one was doing the work.** ⚙ And the one that keeps recurring: **an anti-vacuity leg is what separates "there is no population" from "my regex stopped matching."** |

## F2-175 · A second writer to `intake.intake_records` bypassed `IntakeService` entirely — and one of its five divergences made the record unpromotable

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-175 *(opened 2026-08-09 by a tree-wide grep for `IntakeRecordRepository` while investigating vanished rows, NOT by reading `module/intake`; worked 2026-08-10)* |
| **Module** | `module/ai/governance` (`MlModelDriftService#openCriticalDriftIssue`) writing `module/intake`'s table · `module/intake` (`spi`, `service`) |
| **Category** | Two writers, one invariant — the shape [[F2-168]] and `AttachmentAccessPolicy` both document: **a rule enforced at one writer is not enforced** |
| **Severity** | **P3 Medium by realised harm** (0 rows written, ever) — but see the row on what "benign" was doing in the filing |
| **What was wrong, in five measured ways** | A CRITICAL model-drift observation opened a `RISK_ISSUE` intake by constructing an `IntakeRecord` by hand and calling `intakeRepo.save()`, so it consulted **none** of what F2-172 installed. ① **The assignee**: the catalogue routes `RISK_ISSUE` to `RISK_OFFICER`; this hard-coded `RISK_MANAGER`, a *role name* lifted from `MlModelDriftController`'s own `hasAnyRole` guard. ② **The reference code**: `ISS-{epoch36}-{4hex}` against the catalogue's `RI-XXXX-YYYY` — three prefix letters where every other code has two, under a pair no catalogue entry uses. ③ **The payload**: hand-concatenated JSON with its own `esc()`. ④ **No history**: `submit()` writes the `SUBMITTED` and `TRIAGING` events that are an intake record's entire audit trail; this wrote neither, so the record arrived with an empty timeline. ⑤ **The SLA**: `plusDays(14)` against the catalogue's `24 * 14` hours. |
| **⚠ ③ is the one that was not cosmetic — it broke the escalation the mechanism exists to perform** | `esc()` covered backslash, quote, `\n` and `\r`. JSON requires **every** C0 control character escaped, and `IntakeService#contextFor` parses the payload with Jackson before promotion, reporting failure as *"has an unreadable payload and cannot be promoted"*. So a CRITICAL drift on a model whose title carried a **tab** — the character a title acquires by being pasted out of a spreadsheet — filed an issue that could **never be escalated into the risk register**, and the error named `intake` while the fault sat in `ai/governance`. Verified against Jackson directly before writing any fix (`Illegal unquoted character ((CTRL-CHAR, code 9))`), then live end-to-end: a real model title with a real tab, promoted through the real endpoint. |
| **⚠⚠ "Currently benign" was the wrong claim, and the difference matters** | The filing said the bypass was benign because the submitter binding is correctly absent for a system actor. Measured 2026-08-10: dev holds **26 drift observations, 2 of them CRITICAL, and `triggered_issue_id` is NULL on all 26**, with `IDENT_CURRENT` at 27 over 26 rows — they were seeded by `seed_gov_ai.py`. `intake.intake_records` was at **0**. So **this code path had never once run**, in dev or anywhere the register can see. 🔑 **Benign and unexercised are different claims, and only the second was supportable.** A path that has never executed cannot be observed to be harmless; it can only be observed to be untested — and one of its five divergences was a functional break waiting for the first real CRITICAL drift. |
| **⚠⚠ The existing test asserted the defect as correct** | `MlModelDriftServiceTest.recordCriticalDrift_autoOpensIssueAndFlipsModel` asserted `getReferenceCode()).startsWith("ISS-")` and `getStatus()).isEqualTo("SUBMITTED")` — both true of the code, both wrong about the platform. Its payload assertion was `contains("MODEL-2026-001")`, which a hand-built string satisfies whether or not it is valid JSON. Nothing here was careless: the assertions were written by **reading the implementation**, and a test written that way can only ever agree with it. Second instance in this program after [[F2-159]], whose test asserted that a `targetId` overload correctly discarded its `targetId`. 🔑 **The question a test has to answer is not "does the code do this" but "should it" — and only the second one can be got wrong in a way worth catching.** |
| **🔑 The fix is one construction site, not one call site** | The filing prescribed exposing `submitSystemIntake(…)` on `IntakeService` and repointing the caller. That is necessary and **not sufficient**: a second `new IntakeRecord()` inside `IntakeService` is the same defect one file further in. So `fileDraft(Draft)` is now the only place in the platform an `IntakeRecord` is constructed; `submit()` and `fileSystemSubmission()` each decide only what is genuinely theirs (who filed it; whether an anonymity claim is honoured) and hand the rest over. The seam is an **interface** — `intake.spi.SystemIntakePort`, the inbound counterpart to `RegisterPromotionPort` — so a peer can file a submission while importing nothing of intake's internals. |
| **⚠ The architectural half of the filing was wrong, in both directions** | It said the edge "crosses the ADR-012 boundary" and that `ModuleGraphRatchetTest` should see it. Neither holds. ADR-018 homes `intake` in **Base** and `ai/governance` is a sold SKU, so `ai → intake` is **SKU → Base, the legal direction**. And that test's `KERNEL_ISH` set is `{platform, integrations, dashboard}`, so this edge is neither a kernel inversion nor half of a business cycle — it could not have fired, and raising nothing to admit it was never required. What was actually violated is **encapsulation**, which nothing in this tree measured until `IntakeSingleWriterInvariantTest`. ⚙ Reading the guard before believing the finding's claim about it cost five minutes and removed a whole imagined slice. |
| **⚠⚠ And "fixing" the assignee made it resolve to nobody — stated rather than dressed up** | Measured in `iam.roles` (70 rows): **`RISK_MANAGER` exists and `rmanager` holds it. `RISK_OFFICER` does not exist.** So the hard-coded value was, by accident, a resolvable role name and the catalogued one is not. This is still the right change, for a reason that has to be given rather than assumed: `assigned_to` is a **stakeholder-code** column, not a role column — **10 of the catalogue's 14 codes are not role names** (`CAB`, `CSIRT`, `ETHICS_CTE`, `TPRM_LEAD`, `BCM_LEAD`, `AUDIT_LEAD`, `POLICY_OFFICER`, `COMPLIANCE_LEAD`, `CISO_OFFICE`, `RISK_OFFICER`), and **nothing in `module/intake` resolves the column at all** — it flows into `IntakeRecordDto` and renders as a label. Nobody was notified before and nobody is notified now. What changed is that the value agrees with the one catalogue [[F2-174]] can fix in a single place, and `IntakeCatalogueParityTest` pins that catalogue field-by-field, so keeping `RISK_MANAGER` would have meant diverging from the pinned source of truth. **Do not read this row as "the assignee now works."** ✅ **Closed by [[F2-174]] 2026-08-11** — the catalogue now says `RISK_MANAGER`, so the derivation and the resolvability are both right. 🔑 **The hard-code this slice deleted was right about the name and wrong about the mechanism**, which is why the fix was to correct the single source rather than keep the copy. |
| **Two defects fixed that the filing did not mention** | **(a)** The payload serialised `notesEn` and **dropped `notesAr` on the floor** — on a platform whose bilingual rule makes Arabic mandatory on user-visible records, in the one field where a drift analyst's own words are carried. **(b)** The audit line named the observation and **never the issue**, so a CRITICAL drift left no audit trace of the escalation it raised. The `Receipt` returned by the port exists so it can: the line now reads `… · issue RI-K7MP-3QXZ → RISK_OFFICER`. |
| **What shipped** | `intake/spi/SystemIntakePort.java` — the inbound port, with `SystemSubmission` (org, kind, channel, severity, systemActor, `Map` payload) and `Receipt` (id, referenceCode, assignedTo, slaDueAt). `IntakeService implements SystemIntakePort`: one private `Draft` record, one `fileDraft()` construction site, `writePayload()` via the injected `ObjectMapper`, and fail-closed validation on the organisation and the actor label. `MlModelDriftService` states the drift facts as a `Map` and calls the port; `esc()`, `safeRole()` and `generateIntakeRef()` are **deleted rather than moved**, following F2-172's stance on the client's own minters — only one place may issue a tracking code or a deadline. |
| **⚠ `safeRole(String role) { return role; }`** | Deleted with the rest. A private static method named as if it validates, which returns its argument unchanged — the [[F2-159]] decoy shape in miniature, and the only thing it ever did was make a hard-coded role name look like it had been checked. |
| **Gates** | `IntakeSystemSubmissionTest` (13) — one test per property the second writer lacked, plus the payload round-trip, the two fail-closed refusals, and *a machine is not a whistleblower* (`submitter_user_id` NULL **and** `submitterIsAnonymous` FALSE; `SystemSubmission` has no anonymity field, so a caller cannot ask). Built with a **real** `ObjectMapper`, because the payload assertion is about actual serialisation. · `IntakeSingleWriterInvariantTest` (4) — `new IntakeRecord(` appears **exactly once** in 1,869 main sources; `IntakeRecordRepository` has **exactly one** main-source user; **no peer module imports anything of `module/intake` but its `spi`** (hard zero, no allow-list beyond the seam); plus an anti-vacuity leg asserting the walk found the tree, that **both** seam directions are genuinely imported from outside (13 outbound adapters, ≥1 inbound caller), and that the comment stripper actually strips — `MlModelDriftService`'s javadoc names both retired tokens on purpose, so a raw-text scan would read its own explanation as a violation. · `MlModelDriftServiceTest` rewritten to assert only what the drift monitor is entitled to decide. |
| **⚠ These are invariants, not ratchets, and the distinction is the finding's own** | A ceiling tolerates the population it measures. The population here is **one**, and the whole defect is that a second member went unnoticed from the day it was written — so a count to raise would make a tolerated writer indistinguishable from a reviewed one. Same reasoning CLAUDE.md records for F2-61(c)'s `BARE_EXPORT_CEILING` after the sweep landed. |
| **⚙ Writing the mutation for one test exposed that the test could not fail** | `RISK_ISSUE`'s catalogued SLA is `24 * 14` hours, which `plusDays(14)` equals **exactly** — so the mutation restoring the retired arithmetic survived, and the assertion was measuring a coincidence. Fixed by adding a second case on `WORKPLACE_INJURY` (the **24-hour** GOSI notification, where 14 days late is the entire cost), for which the two answers differ. 🔑 **Asserting a derivation on an input where the derivation and the bug agree asserts nothing** — and the coincidence is also precisely why five years of this code never diverged visibly. |
| **Mutation** | **17/17 caught.** Each of the five divergences restored one at a time (local minter, hard-coded assignee, `plusDays(14)`, `SUBMITTED`, dropped history, hand-built payload); both fail-closed checks disabled; `require` downgraded to `get`; a system record filed as anonymous; the locale hard-coded back to `"en"`; `notesAr` dropped; the receipt id replaced with a literal; the audit line silenced; a second construction site added inside `IntakeService`; a peer re-importing the entity; and the invariant scan's own comment stripper neutered. |
| **Live probe (42/42)** | On an isolated backend (:8085) after a forced clean rebuild — F2-172's recorded trap is a mutation harness leaving a mutant compiled into `target/classes` for the probe to measure. `ranalyst` is refused model creation (403). `rmanager` creates a model whose `title_en` contains a **real tab**, then files a CRITICAL drift over HTTP: 201, and the record intake wrote carries `RI-????-????` (not `ISS-`), `TRIAGING`, `RISK_OFFICER`, `API_INGESTION`, `HIGH`, `locale` NULL, `submitter_user_id` NULL, `submitter_is_anonymous` 0, and `DATEDIFF(HOUR, acknowledged_at, sla_due_at) = 336`. The payload parses, the tab round-trips byte-exact, `notesAr` is present. Two `intake_events` rows, one naming the monitor and one naming the route. The model flipped to `REVISION`, the drift row points at the intake id, and the audit line contains the reference code. Then `compliance` **promotes it**: 200, `promoted_to_entity_type = RISK`, and the `risk.risks` row the server named exists with a genuinely Arabic title. **Negative control:** an intake row carrying exactly the payload the old `esc()` would have emitted, promoted through the same endpoint, is **refused** naming the unreadable payload — and is **not** marked promoted. Cleanup is **by id captured at creation** (the reference code is server-minted and cannot carry a tag — the trap F2-178's probe fell into), with a `CHARINDEX` sweep on the columns the probe owns, and a before/after snapshot of all five tables as a **failing leg**. |
| **⚠⚠ The live probe found a regression the whole green suite could not: a ROWVERSION stale-update 500** | The first probe run answered **500 — `ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException` / `StaleObjectStateException` on `MlModelDriftObservation#28`.** The old code did `save → open the issue → mutate → save AGAIN`, and that survived for as long as it existed **only because nothing between the two saves forced a flush**: the issue was inserted in the very same persistence context, so Hibernate batched the observation's INSERT and UPDATE together. Routing the insert through the `@Transactional` port put a real boundary there, the intermediate flush happened, and the second save's `UPDATE … WHERE row_version = <what this session last saw>` matched **zero rows**. Fixed by filing the issue **before** the single `save()` — nothing in the payload ever needed the observation's id, so the second save was never necessary. Pinned with `verify(driftRepo, times(1)).save(...)` plus an `InOrder` check that the port is called first. 🔑 **A latent double-save is not a style problem; it is a defect waiting for somebody to add a transactional call between the two writes** — and CLAUDE.md's rule ("native first, mutate + save once") had been sitting there for months naming only the loudest trigger. ⚠ **No unit test could have caught it: a mocked repository has no `row_version`.** 25/25 green, 3,577/0/0 green, and the real database said no. This is house rule 4 — *live-probe every slice* — earning its place in one measurement. |
| **⚠⚠ And then the probe found a SECOND defect the suite could not: promoting a `RISK_ISSUE` had never once worked** | With the ROWVERSION fix in, the chain got one step further and stopped at `PUT /api/v1/intake/{id}/triage` → **409**. The backend log: *"The INSERT statement conflicted with the CHECK constraint `CK_risks_status`… column 'status'"*. `RiskPromotionAdapter` passed **`"IDENTIFIED"`**; the constraint allows `OPEN\|UNDER_REVIEW\|MITIGATING\|ACCEPTED\|CLOSED\|ARCHIVED\|TRANSFERRED`. Its javadoc even *argued* for `IDENTIFIED` — *"a promoted risk has been raised, not assessed"* — which is exactly right about the intent and was never a value this column accepts. Fixed to `OPEN`, the member of the constrained vocabulary carrying that meaning. ⚙ **Two independent reasons nobody had seen it**, and that is the reusable part: [[F2-172]] live-probed promotion into `privacy.dpia` and reasoned about the other twelve adapters from their source; and the only kind routed to `RISK` is `RISK_ISSUE`, whose sole producer was the drift monitor — a path *this* finding measured as **never having run**. 🔑 **A defect sitting behind two blind spots is not found by probing either end. It took a probe of the whole chain, which is what this slice happened to be.** Pinned by `RiskPromotionStatusTest`, which reads the vocabulary **out of the migration SQL** rather than the database, so `mvn -o clean package` stays hermetic — and asserts the vocabulary is non-empty first, because a regex that stops matching turns the pin into decoration. |
| **⚙ Probe friction worth recording, because it cost a run** | Creating the fixture model answered **409 with `conflictKind: REFERENCE`** and *"either something it refers to does not exist, or the record is still referenced elsewhere"* — while the actual cause was a **CHECK-constraint** violation (`model_type` must be `CLASSIFICATION`, not `CLASSIFIER`; `business_domain` `CREDIT_DECISION`, not `CREDIT`). `ml_model` has **no foreign keys at all**, so the message describes a mechanism the table does not have and sends the reader hunting a missing reference. Not filed as its own finding — noted here so the next person reading that 409 checks `sys.check_constraints` first. |
| **Filed** | **[[F2-179]]** — the escalation trigger is `"CRITICAL".equals(severity)`, a case-**sensitive** Java comparison behind a case-**insensitive** CHECK constraint, so `"critical"` records a CRITICAL drift that never escalates. Found by asking what validates the trigger while repointing the method, reproduced live in probe leg 9, and **filed rather than bundled** because the honest fix carries a governance question (should `MAJOR` escalate too?) that a casing fix must not smuggle in. ⚙ The reason it surfaced at all: repointing a caller means reading what it *says*, and `severity` was the one field passed straight through. |
| **Effort** | M (1 port, 1 service refactor, 1 caller, 3 test classes, ~40 assertions, 17 mutations, 42 live probe legs, 0 migrations, 0 frontend change) |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-10.** Backend suite **3,579/0/0**, FE **487/487** in 50 files + `tsc` clean, mutation **17/17**, live probe **42/42**, `mvn -o clean package` hermetic, census `--check` clean. |
| **Lesson** | ⚙ **A rule enforced at one writer is not enforced** — and the fix is one construction site, not one call site, because moving the bypass inside the class it bypassed is the same defect one file further in. ⚙ **"Benign" and "unexercised" are different claims**: the register asserted the first about a path that had never executed, and one of its divergences was a functional break waiting for the first real input. ⚙ **Read the guard before believing a finding's claim about it** — two of this filing's three architectural assertions were false, and checking cost five minutes. ⚙ And the sharpest one, because it is the second instance: **a test written by reading the implementation can only agree with it.** Both of this defect's cosmetic halves and one of its real ones were pinned as correct by a green test for as long as the code existed. |

## F2-172 · The platform's front door filed every submission into the submitter's own browser — the server rejected 10 of 26 forms, admitted 3 of 69 roles, and promotion created no register record on either side

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-172 *(filed 2026-08-09 as [[F2-171]]'s capability half; worked the same day, in two slices that met in a merge — see the last row)* |
| **Module** | `module/intake` (controller / service / entity / DTOs / `spi`) + 13 adapters in the modules that own the target registers · `lib/intake`, `lib/api`, `lib/promotedRecords`, `lib/promotedAdapters` → 11 register pages + 5 screens; V374 |
| **Category** | A built capability nothing called — plus RC-E (server truth taken from the caller) and a governance action that records an outcome it did not perform |
| **Severity** | **P2 High** — every intake submission the platform ever received was invisible to the triager it was routed to; two of the ten rejected kinds carry a statutory clock; and every promotion was a fiction on both sides |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-09.** Backend suite **3,509/0/0**, FE **477/477** in 49 files, `tsc` + `vite build` clean, mutation **16/16 + 12/12 + 13/13**, live probes **27/27 + 16/16**, browser-verified across 5 screens, census +0 on every gated figure |
| **How it was found** | F2-171 closed by making the browser-local promoted row *safe*; its follow-up row said the fix was to "call `POST /api/v1/intake` on submit and `PUT …/triage` on triage". Measuring what that rewire would actually hit — **before** writing it — is what produced this finding. Three of the four defects below would have shipped as regressions if the client had simply been repointed. |
| **① The client offered 26 intake kinds; the server accepted 16** | `IntakeService` held `SLA_HOURS`, `DEFAULT_ASSIGNEE` and `CODE_PREFIX` as three parallel maps with 16 entries each, and `submit()` gates on the first: `if (!SLA_HOURS.containsKey(kind)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown intake kind")`. The frontend `INTAKE_CATALOG` holds **26** — the five DD-88 HRSD workflows and the five DD-94 MOC workflows were added later. Among the ten the server would have refused: the **24-hour GOSI workplace-injury notification** (failure to notify shifts medical-claim cost to the employer) and the **monthly WPS payroll confirmation** (non-compliance suspends new hires and visa renewals). The service's own javadoc said the metadata "is mirrored from frontend INTAKE_CATALOG so the two stay in sync" — it was mirrored **once**, at DD-82, and nothing ever asked again. ⚙ Two copies of a routing table where only one side is exercised do not drift slowly — they drift completely and silently. |
| **⚠ The three-map shape was a second, quieter defect** | Only `SLA_HOURS` was the gate. A kind present there and missing from the other two did **not** fail: `CODE_PREFIX.getOrDefault(kind, "II")` minted a reference code under a prefix that means nothing, and `DEFAULT_ASSIGNEE.get(kind)` routed the submission to `null`. Three literals that must agree, with one of them as the validity check, is a shape where two of the three can be wrong invisibly. Replaced by one `IntakeKindRouting.Routing` record per kind — a kind is now either fully described or absent. |
| **② `INTAKE:WRITE` was held by 3 of 69 roles, all administrators** | Measured in `iam.role_permissions`: `COMPLIANCE_OFFICER`, `GRC_ADMINISTRATOR`, `ORG_ADMIN`. Of the seven documented dev personas only `compliance` held it. The intake substrate is where **new work originates** — reporting a security event (NCA ECC 6.1, ISO 27001 §6.8), a privacy breach (PDPL Art. 27), a workplace injury (GOSI), raising a risk, submitting a BIA, blowing the whistle (Nazaha, ISO 37001 §8.3), disclosing a conflict of interest. Under that guard an ordinary employee could do none of it. **Repointing the client without noticing would have converted a universally-available front door into an administrators-only one, and the failure would have arrived as a 403 on "Report a security event".** |
| **🔑 And it subsumes an endpoint already sanctioned for exactly this reason** | `ETHICS_DISCLOSURE` is one of the 26 kinds, and `CoiController#submitDeclaration` was admitted to ADR-010 §Sanctioned exceptions at F2-144(b) *because* declaring a conflict is a duty every employee is under. Gating the same duty two different ways depending on which screen the employee reached was indefensible on its face — so the argument for this one did not have to be constructed, only noticed. |
| **⚠ The unbound submitter, and why the order of the fix is the fix** | `intake.intake_records` had **no column naming a platform user**. `submitterName`, `submitterEmail`, `submitterPhone`, `submitterRole` and `submitterIsAnonymous` were all read from the body and stored verbatim — RC-E in the platform's front door, latent only because the guard admitted three administrators. This is F2-144's trap exactly: **opening the guard first would have traded a lockout for an impersonation path.** V374 adds `submitter_user_id`; `IntakeService` fills it from `CurrentActor` and ignores the body's identity claims (following `CoiService#declarantFor` — a rejection would leak whether another identity exists). |
| **⚠⚠ The anonymity flag had no COI counterpart, and it is the sharper half** | `submitterIsAnonymous` also arrived from the body. A server that simply obeyed it would let **any caller make any submission unattributable on request** — the open guard would then be the impersonation path the binding exists to close, entered through the field that exists to protect whistleblowers. The claim is now honoured only for the three kinds whose catalogue entry sets `allowsAnonymous` (SPEAKUP, BREACH_REPORT, VRP_DISCLOSURE) and refused everywhere else; where it *is* honoured **nothing identifying is stored** — not the user id, and not the name/email/phone the body still carried. Probed live: the SPEAKUP event trail reads `['anonymous', 'system']`. |
| **③ Promotion was implemented on NEITHER side** | `triage()` took `promotedToEntityType` **and** `promotedToRecordId` from the request body and created nothing, under a DTO comment saying they were *"echoed back so the frontend can deeplink to the new register row"* — a sentence that assumes a row. F2-171 had found the client minting `Date.now() % 1_000_000`, a positive integer in exactly the range real IDENTITY values occupy. So the platform had **two** implementations of promotion and neither created the record: the client fabricated an id in `localStorage`, and the server would have stored whatever id it was handed — strictly worse, because it is durable and visible to every user in the tenant, under a permanent audit note reading *"Promoted to DPIA #482913"*. |
| **🔑 The design decision for ③, and why it is not "call the module's REST endpoint"** | Promotion fans out into **14 registers**, and ADR-018 homes `intake` in **Base** — mandatory, shipped to every customer. Twelve of those registers are *sold* SKUs (privacy → PDPL, tprm → TPRM, bcm → BCM, ethics → ETHICS…). Importing them from intake would make the mandatory kernel depend on commercial modules, which `change_adapters`' own package-info already names as the worse of the two boundary mistakes. So the arrows point **inward**: `intake.spi.RegisterPromotionPort` is declared in Base, and each of the 13 adapters lives in the module that **owns the record**, where the entity, the service and the SKU homing already are. A SKU depending on a Base interface is the correct direction. |
| **The four properties the mechanism buys** | **(1)** the **target comes from the kind's catalogue entry**, so a client cannot promote a DSR into the risk register; **(2)** `promoted_to_record_id` is stamped **from the row that was written**, and the request DTO no longer has a field for it; **(3)** promotion requires the **target module's own write permission** on top of `INTAKE:TRIAGE`; **(4)** a target with no adapter is a **409 that names it**, never a promotion that flips the status and writes nothing. The create and the stamp share one transaction, so the intake row cannot outlive its own claim. |
| **Why (3) rather than trusting `INTAKE:TRIAGE`** | Otherwise one permission becomes a create-anything door into fourteen modules, reachable without holding a single one of their guards — the [[F2-04]] shape, two routes to one write with only one guarded. **Measured before choosing it, not after:** exactly one non-admin user in dev holds `INTAKE:TRIAGE` (`compliance`, via `COMPLIANCE_OFFICER` + `GRC_ADMINISTRATOR`) and that user already holds all 8 distinct permissions the 13 adapters name. The rule costs nothing today and closes the door before the grant widens. |
| **⚠ Guessing the permission from the target name is the trap** | `EthicsCaseController` guards with **`COMPLIANCE:WRITE`**, not `ETHICS:WRITE` — and `ETHICS` *does* exist in the catalogue, so the obvious guess compiles, reads correctly, and produces a 403 nobody can explain. Same for the whole `policy` module. Each adapter's declared pair is checked against the set of `hasPermission(…)` pairs any `@PreAuthorize` in the platform actually uses, **read from annotation values by reflection** — never from source text, because a source regex over guards is what invented 21 ghost roles in [[F2-170]]. |
| **The Arabic title is load-bearing, not decoration** | The bilingual rule makes `*_ar` backend-mandatory on user-visible records, and on `change_request.title_ar` it is a `NOT NULL` **column** — so a blank is a constraint violation surfacing as a 500 from inside a promotion. Intake payloads carry almost no Arabic (one form asks: `vendorNameAr`). Copying the English text into the Arabic column would satisfy the constraint and lie to the reader, so the title is **composed** from the catalogue's own Arabic kind-name plus the reference code — genuinely Arabic and genuinely descriptive. `IntakeCatalogueParityTest` pins both titles and asserts `titleAr` actually contains Arabic script, because an English string copied across is invisible to a reviewer who does not read Arabic. |
| **Statutory clocks start at receipt** | PDPL Article 10 gives 30 days **from receipt**, and `PrivacyService` only defaults `due_date` later, on the first status change. For a promoted DSR that would hand the organisation however many days the triage queue took — silently, on a statutory deadline, in the direction that looks *more* compliant on the dashboard. Both `received_at` and `due_date` are stamped from the intake's `acknowledged_at`. Same reasoning for the breach 72-hour clock and the incident `discovery_date`. |
| **⚠ One adapter can legitimately refuse, and that is the honest outcome** | `bcm.bia_record` has **no `organisation_id` of its own** — tenancy comes from the parent `CriticalProcess`, and `createBia` throws without one. The BIA form collects `businessUnit` / `processName` as **free text**. So the adapter resolves the name against the tenant's own processes and, on a miss, throws naming what it could have matched. Inventing a process would put an assessment against the wrong service. The same shape applies to a policy exception, which must hang off the policy it excepts. |
| **What shipped** | **Server** — `IntakeKindRouting` (26 kinds × 7 fields, replacing 3×16 maps); submitter binding + the anonymity rule; `POST` opened to `isAuthenticated()` under ADR-010; `GET /api/v1/intake/{id}` implemented at last (advertised in the controller javadoc since DD-82, never written) returning a DTO because `history` is a LAZY `@OneToMany`; `triage()` derives the target from the kind, calls the port, and stamps the id from the row it wrote. **Client** — `useIntake()` is server-backed (`items`/`error`/`submit`/`triage`/`refreshOne`), `SEED_INTAKE`'s 5 fabricated records deleted, the `grc.intake` localStorage overlay deleted, the hardcoded `'demo.triager@tss.sa'` actor deleted, `generateReferenceCode()` and `slaDeadline()` **deleted** rather than moved, and the promoted-records overlay retired outright. |
| **Gates** | `IntakeCatalogueParityTest` (6) reads the TypeScript and fails on any divergence in **either** direction on **any** of the seven fields, with an anti-vacuity test that fails if the parse resolves less than 26 · `IntakeSubmitGuardTest` (4) pins `isAuthenticated()` on submit **and** that read/triage stay permissioned — the asymmetry is the design · `IntakeSubmitterBindingTest` (12) pins both identity properties and all three promotion-target properties · `IntakePromotionContractTest` (11) — the DTO cannot name the record; every catalogued target has a port or a *reasoned* gap; no duplicate targets; every declared permission is one the platform uses; the registry refuses an unknown target **and** a port that returns nothing; and `module/intake` imports no peer module, so Base stays Base · `IntakePromotionServiceTest` (9) — the stamped id is the register's, the port sees the submission's own facts, double-promote is refused, a missing target permission is a 403 naming it · `ControllerAuthorizationRatchetTest` `SELF_SCOPED` floor 22 → 23 · `FrontendEndpointContractTest` clientless 421 → **417**, guarded writes 208 → **206** · `intakePromotionPersists.test.ts` (16) · `publicPortalBackedByServer.test.ts`'s premise **inverted**. Anti-vacuity floors on every scan. |
| **⚙ The gate that decided the slice boundary** | The server half was scoped server-only, planning the client rewire as a follow-up. `FrontendEndpointContractTest` **refused the commit**: adding `GET /{id}` with no caller pushed the clientless ceiling from 421 to 422, and its message says *"either wire the new endpoint from a screen, or raise this baseline deliberately and say why"*. Raising it would have been F2-171's own defect class — capability the buyer cannot reach. **The repo made a scoping decision better than mine, and it made it in the direction a ceiling normally cannot fire in.** |
| **⚠ The mutation harness left the running backend executing a mutant** | 15/15 mutations were caught, then the live probe failed one leg: the promotion note still read `"Promoted to INCIDENT #482913"`. The source was clean. The **build** was not — `shutil.copy2` restores the original mtime, so Maven saw the file as unchanged and skipped the recompile, leaving mutation #14 compiled into `target/classes` and hot-restarted into the dev backend. So 26 of the 27 probe legs had been measured against code that differed from the tree. Same trap as F2-80's SHA-verified byte-for-byte restore leaving a stale build. 🔑 **A mutation harness that restores sources must force a rebuild before anything is probed** — and the probe caught it only because one mutation happened to be observable end to end. |
| **⚠ The browser found what the unit test and the live probe both could not** | `IntakeRecordDto` declared `submitterUserId` and `from()` **never copied it**, so every HTTP response reported the submitter as `null` — identified or not. Both existing checks were green over it: `IntakeSubmitterBindingTest` asserts on the entity captured at `repo.save`, and the live probe read the column with `pyodbc`. Neither goes through the mapper. A field that always answers "nobody" is [[F2-159]]'s decoy shape. One browser call caught it. 🔑 **Assert on the artefact the consumer receives** — the entity and the column are intermediate representations, and a mapper sits between them and every caller. |
| **⚠⚠ A SECOND defect the browser found, by clicking: the public DSR form's Submit button was dead** | The shared `Button` defaults to `type="button"` **deliberately** (its own comment: a Button inside a form must not auto-submit, so pages needing it "pass type=submit explicitly"). `DsrPortalPage` did not, and its `onClick` was an empty function annotated *"form onSubmit handles it"* — so **clicking Submit on the public PDPL Art. 4 rights form did nothing at all**, and only pressing Enter in a field ever worked. Measured: 19 files render a `<form onSubmit>`, 16 pass `type="submit"`, and of the three that do not the other two call their handler from `onClick` — **this was the only dead one.** ⚙ Why nothing caught it: every guard on this page asked what the submit path *does*; none asked whether it can be *entered*. |
| **⚠⚠⚠ And the guard written for that shipped VACUOUS, twice, in two different ways** | **(1)** The first version asked whether the FILE contained `type="submit"` — and passed with the dead button re-inserted, because the javadoc explaining why this button needs `type="submit"` says so three times. `stripComments` did **not** help, because it does not strip a JSX `{/*…*/}` block. The remedy that worked is neither a better regex nor a stripper but **a matcher scoped to the element it judges**, where surrounding prose cannot reach. **(2)** The element-local version then read every button as alive, because `<Button(\s[^>]*?)>` cannot capture JSX attributes: the `>` in `=>` truncates them, so an inline arrow handler was invisible. Both were caught by mutation and neither by reading. |
| **⚠ A third thing only the browser showed: the row-summary formatter was fixture-shaped** | The inbox headline handled 5 of 26 kinds and dumped raw JSON for the rest — and those 5 are **exactly** the kinds the deleted `SEED_INTAKE` fixture contained. It had been written to make the fabricated rows read well, and nothing else could reach the list, so the fallback was unreachable in practice. The first real submission filed in the browser — a GOSI workplace-injury notification — rendered as `{"summary":"…","category":"PHISHING","obser`. ⚙ **A fixture-shaped code path is invisible while the fixture is the only input.** |
| **⚠ The contract test measured its own fixture** | Its port scan is a classpath scan for `RegisterPromotionPort`, and the file's own `FakePort` sits in that very package — so the first run instantiated the fixture with nulls and reported `target()=null` as a shipped adapter. Filtered to `@Component`. Another instance of *the matcher was looking at the wrong span* ([[F2-137]], [[F2-165]], [[F2-171]]), in a newer disguise: the wrong **classpath**, not the wrong text. |
| **➕ An existing guard caught a real design question** | `ChangeModuleBoundaryTest` refused the change adapter: ADR-012 forbids `module/change_mgmt` importing any peer, so a `change_mgmt/intake` adapter is illegal — and `module/intake` cannot hold it either, because Base must not depend on a SKU. `module/change_adapters` is the only place both halves are legal. Its peer list went 5 → 6 **with the reason recorded**, including that this entry is the one that points the *other* way: the five existing adapters implement change's outbound ports, this one implements intake's. |
| **The retirement, and why it is a deletion** | With promotion persisting there is nothing left for the placeholder machinery to guard, so `promotedRecords.ts`, `promotedAdapters.ts`, the merges on **10 register pages** and the **15 inert row-action sites** are gone rather than disabled — a module still exporting `addPromoted` invites the next feature to call it, and the whole defect was one call site away from correct. **Proven before removing, not after:** a promoted DPIA comes back from `GET /api/v1/privacy/dpias` (live-probed, id in the list). The provenance badge survives, re-pointed at the intake row's own `promoted_to_record_id` — it now states a fact instead of reading a cache, and degrades to *no badge* rather than a wrong one when the caller lacks `INTAKE:READ`. |
| **⚠ `assertNotPlaceholder` is KEPT, and that is a deliberate divergence from the filing** | F2-172 was filed asking for it to be removed *"once promotion persists"*, and its population is indeed now empty. It stays because it is an **invariant, not a ceiling**: every id this platform issues is a SQL Server IDENTITY or a UUID, so "a negative integer path segment" is unreachable by construction and free to assert. A ceiling tolerating a population has to go with the population; a total assertion at the one choke point every call passes through costs a regex and turns the next accidental placeholder scheme into a named error rather than an unexplained 404 — which is exactly how F2-171's harms presented. Its javadoc and user-facing message were rewritten, because the old ones cited a mechanism that no longer exists. |
| **⚠ A guard had gone VACUOUS rather than red, which is the quieter half of this defect family** | `publicPortalBackedByServer`'s premise test asserted *"lib/intake really does make zero network calls"* — by grepping for `fetch(`, `api.get` and `axios`. The new calls go through the `intakeApi` client, so **it kept passing while being false**. A premise test that cannot notice its own premise changing is the same defect as the code it guards. Inverted to assert the property that now holds: `lib/intake` must reach the server and must hold no submission store of its own. |
| **⚠ Two assertions failed against source they should have matched** | They were written against a Python probe that matched and failed in vitest against the same source. Cause: `core.autocrlf` gives this checkout `\r\n`, `readFileSync(f,'utf8')` hands them through verbatim, and Python's `read_text()` translates them — so any multi-line anchor agrees in one language and not the other. It surfaced loudly here (*"this moved"* when nothing moved); the quiet version of the same bug is an assertion that silently never matches, which is [[F2-169]]'s vacuous `.not.toMatch`. |
| **Live probe (27/27 + 16/16)** | `ranalyst` — a persona holding **zero** INTAKE permissions — POSTs a SECURITY_INCIDENT and gets **201**, with `submitter_user_id = 5` and `assigned_to = CSIRT`; claiming anonymity on that kind is **refused** and the caller still bound; a SPEAKUP claim is honoured with `uid/name/email/phone` all NULL; all **10** formerly-rejected kinds accepted, WORKPLACE_INJURY minting `WI-…` rather than the `II` fallback; `ranalyst` gets **403** on the inbox and on `GET /{id}`; the unauthenticated tracker answers 200 with exactly `[acknowledgedAt, kind, referenceCode, slaDueAt, status]` and 404 for an unknown code. Then, on the promotion half: promote → 200 and **the DPIA the server named exists in `privacy.dpia`** with the submitted activity name, an Arabic title that is Arabic rather than a copy of the English, `DRAFT`, and the caller's org; the history note names the created record; second promotion → 409; `CONTROL_TEST` → 409 naming the gap **and the refused submission is not marked promoted**; DSR `due_date = received_at + 30 days` with `received_at` equal to the intake acknowledgement to the second. Probe rows tagged `[REVIEW-TEST]`, deleted with `CHARINDEX`, table returned to 0 rows. |
| **Browser, signed in as `compliance`** | The inbox showed **2 real submissions and none of the 5 seeds**; Promote issued `PUT /api/v1/intake/41/triage → 200`; the DPIA rendered on `/privacy?tab=dpia` with a live `/dpias/12` link, and `POST /dpias/12/submit-for-review → 200` moved it to **IN REVIEW** — the governance chain F2-171 said could not proceed. **Negative control:** all six pre-existing DPIAs unchanged. |
| **⚠ Not proven live** | **(a) Cross-tenant isolation.** Dev has 3 organisations but **all 7 users sit in org 1**, so there is no second-tenant login to probe with. The service filters `findById` on `TenantContext` for `findOne` and `triage`, and `list` is org-scoped in the repository — read from the code, not measured. **(b) The target-permission gate**, for the same measurement that justified the rule: no dev persona holds `INTAKE:TRIAGE` without also holding all eight target permissions, so producing a live 403 would mean revoking a grant from the shared dev database. Both stated rather than faked. |
| **⚠ Not attributed: three committed rows vanished between two measurements** | Rows 27–29, created through the API and confirmed by `GET /{id}`, were gone minutes later with `IDENT_CURRENT` at 38 — nine identity values consumed and unaccounted for. No `IntakeRecord` row in `platform.audit_log`, no scheduled sweep anywhere in `module/intake`, and the probe's `CHARINDEX` cleanup keys on a tag those payloads did not carry. Most likely [[F2-74]]'s recorded hazard — a sibling process on the shared dev `TSS_GRC`. **Stated rather than explained**; it did not affect any verified property. |
| **⚠⚠ The two halves were built independently and met in a merge — and that is the last lesson** | The front-door half landed on `master`; the promotion half was still on its branch, both filed under F2-172 on the same day. Git found **10 conflicting files**; the ones that mattered were not textual. Two generated catalogues (`IntakeKindRouting` and `IntakeCatalog`) that git would have kept **both** of, since they are different files — reconciled to one, extended with the titles the adapters need. Two tests whose *premise* the other half falsified: `thePromotionNoteSaysTheTargetDoesNotExistYet` asserted the honest thing to say while nothing created the row, and became false the moment something did. And an entry in `KNOWN_DARK` for `intakeApi.track`, correct when written and wrong once the other half wired the case tracker — caught because that ratchet fails on a **decrease** too. ⚙ **When two slices close the same finding from different ends, the merge conflicts are the least of it: what needs re-deciding is every claim each side made about what was still missing.** |
| **Effort** | XL (1 SPI package, 13 adapters across 11 modules, 1 catalogue, V374, 7 test classes, ~70 assertions, 41 mutations, 43 live probes, 2 browser verifications, 10 register pages retired, 1 two-way merge) |
| **Filed** | **F2-173** (prefix `CR` is shared by `CHANGE_REQUEST` and `CR_ANNUAL_CONFIRMATION`, so a submitter cannot tell the two tracking codes apart — ceilinged at exactly one collision) · **F2-174** (`assigned_to` holds stakeholder codes like `TPRM_LEAD` and `CSIRT` that resolve to no role and nothing routes on, the F2-94 recipient-key class one table over) · **F2-175** (`MlModelDriftService#openCriticalDriftIssue` is a second writer to `intake.intake_records` bypassing `IntakeService`) · **F2-176** (six `CONTROL_TEST` kinds have no register to be promoted into, and now fail with a 409 naming the gap — a functional regression against the fabricated behaviour they had, taken deliberately). |
| **Residue** | `/portal/dsr` remains blocked by [[F2-138]] — no anonymous intake endpoint exists, so a data subject is refused. What changed is that the page now **shows** the refusal (bilingual, naming the PDPL right and directing them to the DPO) instead of writing to `localStorage` and issuing a reference code; it posts to the real endpoint with `anonymous: true` so it starts working by itself when F2-138 lands. |
| **Lesson** | ⚙ **"Implemented on neither side" is a state two half-built implementations produce and neither reveals.** The client minted an id and the server accepted one; each looked like the other end's job was done, and the only artefact was a history note quoting a number. ⚙ **Measure what a rewire will hit before writing it** — three of the four defects here would have shipped as regressions from a mechanical repointing, and two carry statutory clocks. ⚙ And the corollary this slice added to the fabrication family: **when the cause is removed, check the guards that were written for it — a premise that silently stops holding is worse than a guard that fails.** |

## F2-171 · Intake promotion writes the register row to `localStorage`, with a positive id, and eleven registers render live governance buttons on it

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-171 *(opened 2026-08-09 out of [[F2-170]]'s triage residue — "16 entities no screen can create" — by reading the service instead of the client)* |
| **Module** | Platform-wide: `lib/intake`, `lib/promotedRecords`, `lib/promotedAdapters` → 11 register pages (privacy, risk, incidents, TPRM, ethics, change, BCM, compliance ×2, CAPA) |
| **Category** | Fabricated data substituting for a server write — undisclosed, **and acted upon** |
| **Severity** | **P2 High** — certain harms on every promotion; the wrong-record harm is rare but grows with tenant size |
| **Status** | ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-09** — `promotedIntakeSafety.test.ts`, 14 tests, mutation **11/12** (the 12th is a stated limit), live-probed + browser-verified. FE suite 473/473 in 49 files |
| **How it was found** | F2-170's residue listed `dpiaApi.create` as a dark method and I filed "16 entities cannot be created" as capability backlog. The **root cause is not a missing button.** `PrivacyPage.tsx:323` reads *"DD-76: route DSR / breach / DPIA creation through Services Center"* — creation is **deliberately** routed to intake, and `dpiaApi.create` is dark **because that other path exists**. Following it is what produced this finding: the other path does not write to the server |
| **What promotion actually does** | `intake.ts`'s `triage(…, 'PROMOTE', …)` calls `addPromoted()`, which writes to `localStorage['grc.promotedRecords']` **and nothing else**. No `privacy.dpia` / `risk.risks` / `incident.incidents` row is created. The row is invisible to every other user and machine, and clearing site data destroys it. The intake record's permanent history note reads *"Promoted to DPIA #482913"* — naming a record that does not exist |
| **⚠ The server side was already built** | `module/intake` has `IntakeController` + `IntakeService` (DD-82) with submit / list / triage / public-tracker, and `intake.intake_records.promoted_to_record_id`. **No product code calls `/api/v1/intake`** — one mention exists, in a test's comment. Live-probed: `GET /api/v1/intake` → **200, totalElements 0**; the table exists and holds **0 rows**; `PUT /api/v1/intake/999999/triage` → a correct 404 ProblemDetail. So the capability is implemented, reachable, and has never been used. `IntakeService`'s own javadoc says it *"Implements the same … lifecycle the React useIntake() hook drives"* — nothing drives it |
| **🔑 Three files, three accounts of one value** | `promotedAdapters.ts` opened with *"Promoted records use **negative** synthesized ids … so they never collide with backend-assigned ids"*. `PromotedRecord.id` was documented *"highest existing + 1"*. `intake.ts` actually minted **`Date.now() % 1_000_000`** — a **positive** integer in exactly the range SQL Server IDENTITY values occupy. Every one of the twelve numeric adapters then passed it through with `typeof p.id === 'number' ? p.id : Number(p.id)`. **The file that documented the hazard was the file that let it through** — [[F2-168]]'s shape precisely, where `entityAnchors.ts` opened with the mock-id range and the bug lived at the call site. Exactly **one of thirteen** adapters honoured the contract: `toCapaFromObservation`, which mints a string |
| **The harms, ordered by certainty** | **(1) Certain, every promotion:** nothing is persisted; the promotion is a fiction with an audit note. **(2) Certain:** the row renders the same live actions as a server row — Approve/Submit/Reject/Expire a DPIA, advance an incident phase, close a risk, delete a vendor — each addressing an id the server never issued, so the governance chain cannot proceed. **(3) Certain:** the title was a `<Link to={/dpias/:id}>` to a nonexistent record. **(4) Rare but scaling:** measured in dev, **0.056% of promotions** would name *some* real record across the eleven registers (Σ max(id) ÷ 1,000,000 = 560/1e6), and that share grows linearly with every row a tenant adds — on such a promotion `dpiaApi.approve(d.id)` approved a **real, unrelated** DPIA while the screen showed the promoted row's title |
| **⚠ Why five existing guards were all green** | [[F2-137]] asks whether a route backed by `lib/intake` is **public** — its scope is the `/portal/` and `/public/` prefixes, and this path is entirely authenticated (a signed-in DPO presses New → DPIA and a triager promotes it). Its premise test, *"lib/intake really does make zero network calls"*, is what proves the substrate is still client-only — it measured the fact and its scope excluded the consequence. [[F2-167]] disabled actions on fabricated rows but resolves on the **demo** flag (`isDemo`/`demoMode`/`showingDemo`); a promoted row is not demo, so `disabled` was false for it. `demoFallbackContract` matches `/mock/i` in the import path, and this store is named after the domain it fakes. [[F2-168]]/[[F2-169]] swept the mock corpus, which this is not part of. **A fourth source of fabricated rows that no fabrication guard measured** |
| **Fix — two layers, and only one of them is the control** | **(a) Structural:** `assertNotPlaceholder()` at all **three** network entry points in `lib/api.ts` (`request`, `downloadFile`, `uploadFile`) refuses a negative-id path segment before `fetch`, throwing an `ApiError(0, …)` that names the cause. Total and un-forgettable: whatever a page misses, the request cannot leave. **(b) UX:** `mintPromotedId()` is negative by construction (a negative id cannot name a SQL Server IDENTITY row **ever** — the property bought is not "collision unlikely"); `promotedId()` **coerces on read** with `-Math.abs(n)`, because overlays minted before this fix sit in users' browsers and localStorage has no migration step; `isUnsyncedId()` is a total predicate, so the 15 row-action sites need no page flag; the DPIA tab drops its `<Link>` and shows a **"Not saved"** badge instead of a fabricated `#id` |
| **Verified live** | Seeded one promoted DPIA through the real overlay in the browser, signed in as `admin`: the row rendered `disabled: true` on both PDPL workflow buttons with the Arabic reason on each, `links: []`, and the **"غير محفوظ"** badge — while all **six real DPIAs on the same screen** kept `/dpias/1…6` and live buttons. A guard that disabled everything would have looked identical without that negative control. Server-side: `POST /dpias/-1754000000000/approve` → **404 "Resource Not Found: DPIA"**, which is the bare, unexplained failure a user used to get |
| **⚠ Two of my own assertions shipped vacuous before mutation caught them** | The query-string test used `?delta=-5&sort=-id` — no value is preceded by a slash, so it passed whether or not the query was stripped, asserting its named property only by coincidence. The second attempt, `?filter=/-5&sort=-id`, **also** passed: the segment matcher needs `/` or end-of-string after the digits and `&` is neither. Only `?sort=-id&filter=/-5` distinguishes the implementations. Separately the source scan tested `/isUnsyncedId/.test(src)`, which the *import line* satisfies — so the regression a reviewer would actually make (editing the condition, keeping the import) passed clean; it is now anchored inside `disabled={…}`. Third occurrence of "the matcher was looking at the wrong span of text" ([[F2-137]], [[F2-165]]) |
| **⚠ And my own harness misreported 11 of 12 mutations** | The runner's `Tests N failed` line is ANSI-coloured, so `/Tests\s+\d+ failed/` never matched and every mutation printed **MISSED** over a visible `FAIL`. A harness that misreports is worse than none — it would have sent a genuinely unguarded assertion to the register as proven. Same class as the `nohup` wrapper exiting 0 over a dead application |
| **Stated limit, measured not assumed** | The source scan resolves **per file**, so a page with several action sites passes on the strength of any one. Mutation confirms it: replacing `PrivacyPage`'s `const unsynced = isUnsyncedId(d.id)` with `false` leaves it green, because that file's DSR and breach tables still carry inline guards. Accepted rather than fixed, because layer (a) is the enforced property; recorded in the test itself so nobody reads the pass as coverage |
| **Effort** | M (4 lib files, 8 pages, 1 test file of 14 assertions, 12 mutations, 1 live probe, 1 browser verification) |
| **Follow-up filed** | **[[F2-172]] — ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-09.** The intake record itself now persists server-side (submit / list / triage / one-record read), and the rewire found two defects that would have shipped as regressions had the client simply been repointed: the server accepted **16 of the 26** intake kinds, and `POST /api/v1/intake` was held by **3 of 69 roles, all administrators**. ⚠ The *second* half is still open and unchanged: nothing creates the downstream register row on either side, so `promoted_to_record_id` is NULL by design and the placeholder machinery this finding shipped stays in place until an adapter per target module exists. [[F2-138]]'s anonymous-DSR endpoint stays owner-blocked and gates the public half |
| **Lesson** | ⚙ **"Nothing can create X" is a statement about the code you have not read yet.** F2-170 filed this as capability backlog on the strength of reading one service, and the classification was right — but the *reason* was wrong, and the real reason was a P2. The client told me the create method was uncalled; only the page comment said creation had been deliberately re-routed, and only following that route showed where it went. ⚙ Corollary for the fabrication family: **five guards can be green because each measured a different property of the same defect class.** When a new source of fabricated rows appears, ask which existing guard's *scope* excludes it — not whether one exists |

## F2-162 — The register contradicted itself: one finding filed twice with opposite states, one closed as collateral still reading OPEN

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-162 *(found 2026-08-08 while answering "what remains in the plan" — the answer was meant to be a report, and measuring it found the instrument wrong)* |
| **Category** | Programme integrity — the register is the flat per-finding record, outlives the plan, and is what an external auditor is handed |
| **Severity** | **P3** — no code defect. The harm is that the two documents this programme plans against disagreed, in the direction that **overstates what remains**: a reader would have re-done V361's work and re-opened `sharia`'s guards |
| **Current State** | ✔ **CLOSED 2026-08-08.** Four cells corrected and `FindingsRegisterConsistencyTest` added (5 checks, **8/8 mutation**, 2 of the 8 asserting the gate does *not* fire) |
| **The measurement** | 146 rows parsed by heading, each row's state read from its own block. **1 duplicated id** (`F2-45`, two rows, `⬜ OPEN` vs `✅ CLOSED`) · **1 row with no state field at all** (`F2-131`, withdrawn, disposition in the heading only) · **2 cells contradicted by evidence elsewhere in the repo** (`F2-120`, `F2-146`) |
| **🔑 Why `F2-127` was updated and `F2-120` was not — the transferable half** | Both were closed by the same slice, F2-145(e). `F2-127` is `openbanking`'s row and that slice was *named* after the module, so its row was visited. `F2-120` is `sharia`'s, closed as **collateral** — F2-145's own cell records *"`sharia` FULLY CLOSED … and with it [[F2-120]]"* — and nothing visited it. ⚙ **A finding closed as a side effect is the one nobody updates**, and the claim that it closed is sitting in another row where a mechanical check can read it |
| **⚠ The witness that was measured and REJECTED** | The obvious third rule — *a packaged migration whose header names `F2-nnn` closes it* — would have caught `F2-146` (V361's header names it). It is **not** a rule, because `V359`'s header names `F2-130` while fixing `F2-81`: it cites F2-130's *shape* ("a permission nobody holds") as the reason for its own design, and F2-130 is genuinely open. **Naming a finding is not a claim to close it.** A rule that invents defects gets switched off and takes the true findings with it |
| **⚠ So state what the gate cannot see** | It could not have caught `F2-146` — remedy shipped, both the register and the plan kept reading `OPEN`, and **neither document contradicted the other because both were stale**. Nor is "the plan and the register must agree" available: the plan tracks findings in more than one shape (78 of 140 ids in row shape), so a plan-side state extractor would report disagreements that are not there |
| **⚠ A mutant survived the first version of the rule, and the reason generalises** | The natural definition — *open if the cell carries an open marker and no closed marker* — left the gate **green** when `F2-120` was reverted to `🔴 OPEN`, because the rest of that cell narrates its own closure and contains the word *shipped*. A state cell here is mostly prose, so any-marker matching reads "mentions a closure" as "is closed". Fixed by **position**: the first disposition marker in the cell is the state. ➕ That is also the more honest reading — it moves 7 rows from closed to open (`F2-30`, `F2-33`, `F2-112`, `F2-115`, `F2-133`, `F2-141`, `F2-148`), every one a `🟡`/`🔶` row whose leading marker says *partly* |
| **⚠ Two row schemas, pinned rather than unified** | **62** rows carry `**Status**` as the state (the older schema, where `Current State` describes the *defect*); **83** carry `**Current State**` as the state; **60** carry both. A script reading `Current State` as the status silently reads a problem description for 62 rows — which is what this slice's own first pass did, reporting **101 of 146** findings as not-closed. Rewriting 62 rows is a bigger and riskier edit than the defect warrants, so the canonical reading (`Status` wins) is pinned in the test where every future scan can read it |
| **Fix** | `F2-120` → closed by F2-145(e)/V367 · `F2-146` → closed by V361, re-verified live (27/27 columns in dev, 13/13 of the `AuditFinding` set) · `F2-131` → state cell added · `F2-45` → consolidated into one row, keeping the three things the filed row said that the worked row did not · plan-side: `RC-A`, `F2-77` and `F2-146` status cells corrected |
| **➕ It also corrected the answer this slice was asked for** | The report that started it said *"17 findings open-but-tripwired"* — the tripwired subset. Under one uniform reading the register holds **36 open or partly-open rows** against 145. Neither figure was wrong about its own population; the first was quoted for a question about the whole |
| **References** | `tss-grc-backend/src/test/java/com/tss/grc/config/FindingsRegisterConsistencyTest.java` · sibling of `FindingsRegisterCoverageTest` (plan→register coverage; deliberately not merged — a ratchet answering two questions reports one number and hides whichever half is failing) · [[F2-45]] · [[F2-120]] · [[F2-130]] · [[F2-131]] · [[F2-146]] |
| **Lesson** | **This programme has an instrument for baselines going stale and had none for the register that records the findings.** `MeasuredBaselineFreshnessTest` gates the measured numbers, `GovernanceDocumentIntegrityTest` gates the HISTORIC stamps, `ModuleRegistryContractTest` gates the module count — and the document an auditor is actually handed could contradict itself for a day with a green build. ⚙ **The gap is always the artefact nobody thinks of as code** |

## F2-161 · The exercise runtime was platform-administrator-only, and the person facilitating the exercise could only watch

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-161 *(measured 2026-08-08, the second consumer of [[F2-159]]'s ownership mechanism)* |
| **Category** | Authorisation / **a ghost role name plus an unpopulated real one**, on the path a business-continuity tool is used from during a live exercise |
| **Severity** | **P2 High.** `ExerciseRuntimeController`'s write guards were `hasAnyRole('FACILITATOR','BCM_MANAGER','PLATFORM_ADMIN')`. `FACILITATOR` matches no row in `iam.roles` and **`BCM_MANAGER` has 0 users**, so dispatching an inject, adding an on-the-fly inject, transitioning the run and assigning or removing an observer were reachable by the **platform administrator and nobody else**. ⚠ This is worse than [[F2-159]]'s model case in one specific way: the model register is read at leisure, and this is the screen someone is on **while the exercise clock runs** |
| **Provenance** | Not sought — it is the item [[F2-159]] named as next, on the strength of `bcm.exercise_run.facilitator_user_id` being populated **4/4**. The 0-user `BCM_MANAGER` half was not predicted and only appears when you ask who actually holds the surviving names |
| **Current State** | ✔ **FIXED 2026-08-08.** `ExerciseRunOwnershipResolver` (one new class — the registry made the second consumer cheap) plus **15** guard conversions: 6 on `ExerciseRuntimeController` (`#id`) and 9 on `ExerciseObserverController` (`#runId`, where every route names a run). Ghost role names **4 → 3**; pure role sites **425 → 410**. All four dev runs are facilitated by `rmanager`, who could read them (RISK_MANAGER is on the read guards) and not drive them; live-proven **201 on `POST /observers`** and a **409 from the service** on `custom-inject` — the guard admits, the business rule refuses a run that has not started |
| **🔑 The converse is proved per record, not per user** | There is no run `rmanager` does *not* facilitate, so the converse could not come from a second row. It was proved by pointing the **same endpoint, same token** at a run whose `facilitator_user_id` was temporarily somebody else: **403**, then restored. That is the property a `FACILITATOR` role could never have had — with a role, the facilitator of run 1 could drive run 4, which during a live exercise is precisely what must not happen |
| **⚠ Three routes cannot be bound, and getting this wrong is a 500 rather than a 403** | `POST /` starts a run that does not exist yet; `GET /` is a collection; `by-exercise/{exerciseId}` is scoped by **exercise** — one exercise has many runs, possibly with different facilitators, so the exercise id cannot answer *"do you facilitate this run"*. The identical wide guard text sat on both bindable and unbindable routes, so the conversion had to be done **per line, not per guard string**: a textual replace would have put `#id` into the expression of a method with no such parameter, and SpEL then throws — **a 500 on the run list**. `ExerciseRunOwnershipGuardTest` pins both directions, including the copied-`#runId`-as-`#id` mistake |
| **Why the observation endpoints are bound too** | Recording, flagging and promoting an observation are findings *about* the exercise its facilitator ran, normally V367's self-review shape. Two measured reasons they are safe: `flagObservationForAar` already enforces authorship **in the service** — *"Only the observation author can change the AAR flag"* — so the guard is a coarse outer gate over a real inner control; and `promoteObservationToGap` creates a tracked `BcmGap`, which is self-incriminating rather than self-serving. `removeObserver` soft-deletes the assignment only and audit-logs it, so it cannot erase a finding |
