Four distinct name-sets onto **six** actions. Pure role sites **456 → 430**; names recited **44 → 43** (`ETHICS_OFFICER` was named nowhere else). **Live 42 matrix cells + 10 assertions**, 7 personas × 6 tiers, and the two personas that make the slice observable had to be **seated by the probe** because the roles carrying the distinction have no users. **9/9 mutants killed** — including the tidy simplification that edits the controller *and* the test's own constant together. Suite **3,420/0/0**, FE **325/325** |
| 🔑 ⚠ **THE SAME TRAP AS SLICE 5, ONE MODULE LATER — AND THIS TIME IT HIDES AN INDEPENDENCE CONTROL THAT V367 HAD JUST BEEN SHIPPED TO BUILD** | Measured as **users** in dev, three of the four name-sets are the same two people (`admin`, `compliance`): the COI register, the hotline triage tier and the retaliation tier. As **roles** they are three different authorities, separated entirely by `ETHICS_OFFICER` and `BOARD_SECRETARY` — **0 active users each**. Mapping triage and retaliation onto `ETHICS:WRITE`, which the catalogue's own description invited, would have measured population-preserving and let **the ethics officer who triaged and investigated a whistleblower case rule on the retaliation complaint brought about that investigation**. That is the identical self-review defect [[F2-145]](b) removed from `sharia` three slices earlier with **V367** — re-introduced in a different module, inside the same programme, with a green measurement. In the other direction, `ETHICS:READ`'s holders include `BOARD_SECRETARY`, whose guard covers the COI register and not the hotline: one shared read action would have put a board secretary inside case files that may name, or be about, the board. 🔑 **Slice 5's lesson is not a fact about `aml`; it is a property of the instrument.** An absence — who is deliberately NOT on a list — is what a population diff is worst at noticing, and unstaffed roles make every absence invisible |
| 🔑 **A catalogue that has never been consulted is not evidence of anything — which INVERTS the discipline the five previous slices used** | `ETHICS:READ`, `ETHICS:WRITE` and `ETHICS:APPROVE` had carried grants for months while `hasPermission('ETHICS'` occurred **zero** times in the whole of `src/main`. Their descriptions named COI declarations, whistleblower cases and recusals, so they were catalogued **for** these three controllers and never wired to them. For `aml`/`cpty`/`sharia`/`openbanking` the grant table was the population to preserve; here it conferred nothing, so the **guard** was the only ground truth and V371 could both add and revoke without changing one person's real access. That is what licensed the single revocation — `INTERNAL_AUDITOR`'s `ETHICS:READ`, which no guard ever honoured (the COI register's role list never named internal audit, and the hotline read it *is* named on became `READ_CASES`). ⚙ Generalises: **a catalogue entry's grants are evidence of intent only once something reads them**, and the register's own “prepared control” idea has this as its converse |
| ➕ **What the guards' shapes said that the counts could not: two data domains, not one module** | The COI **register** (declaration campaigns, declarations, recusals) is curated by ethics, the board secretary and compliance — `READ` / `WRITE` / `APPROVE`, one population, three actions, so a tenant can let a board secretary read the register without running campaigns. The whistleblower **case file** is confidential to ethics, compliance and internal audit — `READ_CASES`, deliberately excluding the board secretary — and directing a case (`TRIAGE`) drops internal audit, which reads a case without steering it. Retaliation disposition is `PROTECT`, one role. Live, all three distinctions are observable for the first time: seated `ETHICS_OFFICER` **triage 200 / retaliation 403**; seated `BOARD_SECRETARY` **register 200/201/200 / hotline 403/403/403**; `auditor` **hotline read 200 / register 403 / triage 403 / retaliation 403**; `compliance` all six; `admin` all six holding **no ETHICS grant at all** (the evaluator's in-code bypass); `ranalyst` and `so_officer` refused all six |
| ➕ **V371 asserts two ABSENCES by name, because an absence is exactly what the previous checks could not express** | Alongside the usual containment (nobody directs a case they cannot read) and strictness (3 › 2 › 1) checks that V370 established, V371 THROWs if **any role other than `COMPLIANCE_OFFICER` holds `ETHICS:PROTECT`** and if **`BOARD_SECRETARY` holds any hotline action**. Both are properties no count can carry: a grant total of 1 is satisfied by the wrong role, and a nested-set check is satisfied by a set that nests for the wrong reason. Two further checks pin the COI tier to exactly its three roles from both sides (9 rows present, 0 rows outside the set), so the deliberate revocation cannot be quietly reversed and no fourth role can drift in |
| ➕ **A conversion is not finished until every route agrees — and this slice found the fifth and sixth members of that list** | `CoiService#declarantFor` recited the same three role names to decide who may file a declaration on an employee's behalf (F2-144a's mechanism); leaving it behind would have split one authority in two, so a tenant granting `ETHICS:WRITE` to a fourth role would get campaign management and silently not filing-on-behalf. And `AttachmentAccessPolicy`'s `COI_CAMPAIGN` / `WHISTLEBLOWER_CASE` entries carry the parents' read lists — that class's own `FRAUD_CASE` comment already states the rule (“it has to move WITH the parent, not later”). ⚠ The second needed a **new expression**: the registry could say `MODULE_READ`/`MODULE_WRITE` or a role name, and ethics is the first module whose read tier is a *named* action, so `perm("ETHICS")` would have been wrong in both directions at once — admitting a board secretary the parent excludes, and refusing a role holding only `ETHICS_READ_CASES`. Added `ParentGuard.authorities(…)` |
| ⚠ **Three stale comments that told a future reader the opposite of the truth** | `CoiController` and `CoiService` both stated that `ETHICS_OFFICER` “exists in no row of `iam.roles`” — true when F2-144 wrote it, false since **V362** seated the role (id 10076, now holding all six ETHICS actions). A comment saying a guard leg is permanently dead, on a leg that has since come alive, is worse than no comment: the class javadoc explicitly reasoned that dropping the name would “silently ratify compliance-officer ownership of ethics oversight”, and a reader acting on the stale half could have dropped a live grantee. Corrected to past tense with the seating named. ⚙ Third: `WhistleblowerRetaliationController` promised an “HR Director” independent protector — no `HR_DIRECTOR` row exists (`HR_LEAD` does) and the guard never named either, so the protector has always in practice been the compliance officer. `ETHICS:PROTECT` is granted faithfully to that one role and the gap is **filed**: after the conversion, widening it is a grant a tenant can make rather than a jar somebody must ship, which is the entire argument for F2-05 |
| ➕ **The FE invariant caught a phantom action created by my own documentation** | F2-63's `permissionMatrixActions.test.tsx` derives the backend's action vocabulary by regex over Java source **including comments**, so an illustrative `hasPermission('MODULE','NAMED_ACTION')` written in an `AttachmentAccessPolicy` javadoc became a real action it then demanded a matrix column for (FE 325 → 324). Rewritten in prose, with a warning at the site. ⚙ Small but generalisable: **a measurement that reads source text cannot distinguish an example from a fact**, and the failure mode is a demand for a column that should not exist rather than a missing one |
| **What shipped, and the mechanism matters** | **V362** seats the **9** domain roles that were job families nothing recorded, catalogues **17** permissions across the six modules and writes **57** grants derived from the guards' own HTTP verbs. 🔑 **No code change was needed**: `hasAnyRole` compares role NAMES, so the guards that had always recited `SHARIA_OFFICER` began matching the moment the row existed — **live-proven 403 → 200** on `/api/v1/sharia/scholars` with `ShariaController` untouched, plus **201** on its write guard, and still **403** on a licensed-but-ungranted module so the seating is scoped |
| **🔑 Two of the eleven ghosts already had their answer in the database** | `MODEL_OWNER` is **not** seated: `ai_governance.ml_model.model_owner_user_id` is populated on **25 of 25** rows and resolves to real users, so a role would be **looser than the column** — the owner of model A could act on model B. `SHARIA_BOARD_CHAIR` is **not** seated: `sharia.sharia_scholar` already holds the board — 5 rows, `ssb_role` ∈ {CHAIRMAN, MEMBER×3, SECRETARY}, terms, credentials, COI declarations — and a chair is a term-limited **seat** held by someone who may be external. Both stay declared gaps rather than fabricated roles. *Answering this row's (a)-or-(b) uniformly would have created a role for a fact the schema already records* |
| **⚠ Corrections to this spec, from re-measuring rather than re-reading** | **`ai` does not belong in the seven** — it is the only one with a catalogued permission module and its surviving population (RISK_MANAGER 23, CISO 20, DPO 19, AUDITOR 14) is a defensible AI-governance population; by this spec's own criterion (*“usually COMPLIANCE_OFFICER”*, here 5 of 26 sites) it is excluded. **Six modules.** `ETHICS_OFFICER` is **22** sites, not 23 — D-13 removed one. And `consumer` is the severe case, not `sharia`: **PLATFORM_ADMIN and COMPLIANCE_OFFICER and nobody else on all 9 guards** |
| **⚠ The grant derivation caught itself being wrong** | Classifying the action by METHOD NAME made `WhistleblowerCaseController#updates` — a `@GetMapping` whose name is the plural noun *updates* — a write, and would have granted `ETHICS:WRITE` to `INTERNAL_AUDITOR` on the strength of a regex. Reclassified by **HTTP verb**, then `review` was restored to the APPROVE shapes because `CoiController#reviewDeclaration` is a POST deciding somebody else's declaration and its omission left `ethics` with no APPROVE at all. The two matrices were **diffed**: exactly 3 cells moved, all three that endpoint's grantees |
| **⚠ Why this is not closed, stated with the number that proves it** | Inside `SHARIA`, **`COMPLIANCE_OFFICER`, `SHARIA_OFFICER` and `SHARIA_AUDITOR` all hold READ+WRITE+APPROVE** — three roles, one privilege set, which is **not** a separation of duties; the same in `AML` and `CONSUMER`. So the *access* claim is answered and the *independence* claim — the one this spec calls the control — is not. Narrowing compliance out of Sharia approval removes access somebody may be using today, which ADR-010's Consequences gate behind a per-tenant impact query. **Left visible rather than smuggled into a migration**, and the identical-grant check is computed by the generator, not asserted by me |
| **➕ It also amended another ADR** | ADR-010's *“conversion is behaviour-preserving”* rule is **unsafe for exactly this set**: granting `CONSUMER:*` to the roles that could ever match would encode compliance's monopoly in the grant table — turning a dead guard leg, which is at least evidence of unmet intent, into a decision an auditor reads. The rule now requires resolving the ghost **first** |
| **The measurement** | Every guard on `ShariaController` reads `PLATFORM_ADMIN │ COMPLIANCE_OFFICER │ … │ SHARIA_OFFICER │ SHARIA_AUDITOR`, plus `SHARIA_BOARD_CHAIR` on the scholar path. **All three exist in no row of `iam.roles`** — and neither does `CRO`, which the read guards also recite. So the effective population for the whole module is `PLATFORM_ADMIN`, `COMPLIANCE_OFFICER`, `RISK_MANAGER`, `INTERNAL_AUDITOR` |
| **🔑 Why that is a governance defect and not a typo** | **A Sharia scholar, auditor or board chair cannot reach the Sharia module at all, and a compliance officer can do everything in it.** A Sharia board exists to be independent of the compliance function; here the guard *says* that and the database does not deliver it. The endpoints work, the register fills, and the separation is absent |
| **⚠ Why the ghost legs must NOT be dropped** | The reflex from the rest of this sweep is wrong here. For `CISO_GOVERNANCE` — one dead leg among eleven real roles — dropping it loses nothing and was done. For Sharia the ghosts are **the only surviving record of intended access**: delete them and the guard reads as a deliberate decision to hand Sharia oversight to compliance, which nobody made. *Removing evidence of unmet intent is not the same as meeting it* |
| **How it was found** | Reading `target/role-guard-sites.txt`, the reflection dump `RoleGuardConversionRatchetTest` writes. ⚠ A `grep` over `hasAnyRole(...)` for the same names returned **one** guard, because these span source lines — the trap that test's own javadoc records (F2-13a: **3 by grep, 73 by reflection**) and which I reached for first anyway |
| **Recommendation** | **(a)** catalogue and seat the three Sharia bodies as roles, making the guards work as written; or **(b)** convert the module to `SHARIA:READ/WRITE/APPROVE` per F2-05's standing direction and grant to whichever real roles a tenant's Sharia governance uses. **(b)** is the platform's stated direction and survives a tenant whose scholars are external — and [[F2-26]] already models governance **seats** separately from roles, which may be where a board chair belongs |
| **Effort** | **M** — and it is a decision first |
| **References** | [[F2-52]] · [[F2-05]] · [[F2-26]] · [[F2-120]] · [[F2-115]] · `ShariaController` · `ShariaControllerGuardTest` · `ShariaLifecycleTest.theGuardConstantsAreConvertedToPermissions` · `V362` · `V367` · `MeasuredBaselineFreshnessTest` · `target/role-guard-sites.txt` |
| **⚠ Sharia is not special — it is the clearest case of a pattern** | Grouping all ghost names by module (24 at the time of measurement, **23 after F2-144(b) retired `USER`** — the seven modules below are unaffected, because `USER` was nobody's domain role) shows the same shape in **seven modules**, every one of them a Saudi or financial-sector module whose domain role exists only in guard text: `sharia` — `SHARIA_OFFICER` 21 sites, `SHARIA_AUDITOR` 17, `SHARIA_BOARD_CHAIR` 4 · `ethics` — `ETHICS_OFFICER` 23 · `openbanking` — `OPEN_BANKING_OFFICER` 15 · `ai` — `MODEL_OWNER` 14 · `aml` — `AML_OFFICER` 14, `KYC_OFFICER` 6, `ONBOARDING_AGENT` 5 · `cpty` — `CREDIT_OFFICER` 12 · `consumer` — `CONSUMER_PROTECTION_OFFICER` 9. **In each, the module's only domain-specific role is a ghost, so the module belongs to whoever else the guard lists — usually `COMPLIANCE_OFFICER`.** F2-144 already recorded the ethics case from the other direction: an ethics officer cannot manage the COI register they own |
| **What the pattern is not** | ⚠ Three modules look similar and are **fine**: `privacy` (`PRIVACY_OFFICER` is a ghost but `PRIVACY_MANAGER` **and** `DPO` are real), `bcm` (`FACILITATOR`, `INCIDENT_COMMANDER`, `CRISIS_COMMANDER` are ghosts but `BCM_MANAGER`, `CRISIS_MANAGER`, `EMERGENCY_RESPONDER` are real), and `cyber` (F2-52 cleared `SOC_LEAD` because `CISO` sits in the same guards). There the ghost is a synonym for a role that exists, and dropping it is the right move — which is what makes the seven above different and worth a decision rather than a sweep |
| **Separately — a different mechanism, and ⚠ I first overstated it** | The `dashboard` module contributes **seven** names that are not roles: `CYBER_READ`, `INCIDENT_READ`, `COMPLIANCE_READ`, `RISK_READ`, `SCM_READ`, `BCM_READ`, `PRIVACY_READ`, in two `hasAnyAuthority(...)` guards on `DashboardController`. **Correction (same day):** I recorded these as sites with "no real non-admin role beside them", candidates for being reachable by nobody. **That is wrong.** `ModulePermissionEvaluator` documents granted authorities as `MODULE_ACTION` and matches that exact string at line 42, so `RISK_READ` *is* a real granted authority and these guards work for every user holding the permission — the normal population. What they lose is the `ROLE_PLATFORM_ADMIN` bypass the evaluator applies first, so the failure is **too tight for admins only**, exactly the direction F2-53 predicted. They are worth rewriting as `hasPermission(...)` for consistency and to regain the bypass; they are **not** broken authorisation, and my ghost-name gate counting them as absent roles is a labelling artefact, not seven defects |
| **Lesson** | **A guard that names a role nobody created is a design document, not a control.** It reads as separation of duties, passes review, and delegates the module to whoever else is on the list. The ghost-name gate found it in a week; the guard had been asserting that separation for months. 🔑 And the generalisation is the real finding: **the platform's Saudi and financial-sector modules were built with their domain roles written into guards and never into `iam.roles`** — so exactly the modules a regulator would ask about are the ones where the named specialist has no access |

## F2-146 — A fresh install cannot read compliance findings: 13 mapped columns no migration creates

|  |  |
|---|---|
| **ID** | F2-146 *(found 2026-08-06 by F2-09's schema-convergence diff, first run)* |
| **Category** | Deployment correctness — the dev schema and a migration-built schema are not the same database |
| **Severity** | **P1** — not a cosmetic gap: on a fresh install, ordinary reads of the compliance findings register fail at the SQL layer |
| **Current State** | ✔ **CLOSED 2026-08-07 — V361 `fresh_install_missing_columns`.** All **27** columns shipped as one idempotent, self-checking migration whose definitions are copied from dev's own `sys.columns` rather than invented: 13 on `compliance.findings` (this row's P1 half), 11 on `evidence.evidence_items`, `cyber.cyber_sub_controls.description_ar`, `evidence.sub_controls`, and V99's `bcm.crisis_events.cycle_id`. Re-verified live 2026-08-08: **27/27** present in dev and **13/13** of the `AuditFinding` set. The 3 tables are deliberately **not** created — [[F2-140]] / ADR-017 **D-15** decided *no DDL*, and dropping them from dev stays owner-authorised. ⚠ **This cell read `⬜ OPEN` for a day after its own remedy shipped**, and no mechanical witness could have caught it: V361's header names this finding, but *a migration naming a finding is not a claim to close it* — measured on V359, which cites [[F2-130]]'s shape while fixing [[F2-81]]. See the rejected-rule note in `FindingsRegisterConsistencyTest` |
| **The measurement** | `schema_convergence.py --stop 330` diffs a Flyway-built database against the Python-bootstrapped dev schema and partitions every difference by which migration would create it. Of 134 raw differences: **77 tables + 27 columns** come from migrations above the chain's stopping point (unrun, **not defects**), **0** are guard-skipped, and the real residue is **3 tables + 26 columns that no migration anywhere creates** |
| **🔑 Why it is P1 and not bookkeeping** | Thirteen of those 26 columns are on `compliance.findings`, and `AuditFinding` **maps them with `@Column`** — `capa_stage` at [AuditFinding.java:50](tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/compliance/entity/AuditFinding.java:50), `owner_test_result` at [:56](tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/compliance/entity/AuditFinding.java:56), plus `audit_signoff_at/by_id/notes`, `clause_ref`, `independent_test_at/by_id/notes/result`, `owner_test_at/evidence_id/notes`. With `ddl-auto=none` Hibernate creates nothing, so **on a migration-built install every SELECT through this entity names columns that do not exist** and fails with an invalid-column error. The whole audit-signoff / owner-test / independent-test workflow is dev-only |
| **The rest of the residue** | 3 tables — `compliance.compliance_assessments`, `compliance.compliance_findings`, `compliance.evidence_items` — which are **exactly** [[F2-140]]'s three, confirming that finding was precise rather than a sample. Remaining columns: `cyber.cyber_sub_controls.description_ar` (a bilingual column, so also [[F2-141]]'s shape) and four on `evidence.evidence_items` (`collected_at`, `collection_method`, `collector_id`, `collector_name`) |
| **One separate case** | `bcm.crisis_events.cycle_id` is named by **V99**, at or below the stop, and is absent from the built database — so either an idempotency guard skipped the `ALTER`, or V99's `CREATE TABLE` and the bootstrap disagree about the column set. Only one such case exists in 330 migrations, which is a good result for the guards and a reason to look at this one closely |
| **⚠ What this finding is not** | It is **not** "the migration set is 134 objects behind". I said that before partitioning and it was wrong — see the correction in `163fd21c`. The migrations are nearly complete; they simply cannot *run* past V331. **The gap that survives partitioning is 3 tables and 27 columns, and only that residue is a defect** |
| **Recommendation** | Write the missing DDL as a migration: 13 columns on `compliance.findings`, `description_ar` on `cyber.cyber_sub_controls`, the four `evidence.evidence_items` columns, and V99's `cycle_id`; the 3 tables wait on [[F2-140]]'s drop-or-keep decision. ➕ Then make this permanent — F2-09's purpose was always a **CI gate**, and the residue count is exactly the ratchet: 3 tables / 27 columns today, and it may only fall |
| **Effort** | **M** — the DDL is mechanical; the value is the gate that stops it recurring |
| **References** | `Appendix/scripts/schema_convergence.py` · `AuditFinding.java` · [[F2-140]] · [[F2-141]] · [[F2-143]] · [[F2-09]] |
| **Lesson** | **Every finding in this programme was verified against a database no customer will ever have.** Dev is Python-bootstrapped, a customer's is Flyway-built, and until this diff existed nothing compared them — so "verified in dev" carried an unexamined assumption for the whole engagement. F2-143 found the same thing in the grant tables; this found it in the schema. The instrument mattered more than any single defect it found |

## Sequencing — what to do, in what order

Dependency-ordered, not severity-ordered. Severity says what matters; this says what is *possible*.

| Wave | Items | Why this order |
|---|---|---|
| **First (this week, ahead of everything)** | **F2-21 vote provenance** · F2-22 audit script + `@JsonIgnore` mitigation | F2-21 invalidates the platform's central control claim and takes ~2 days. Nothing else in this register earns more per hour. F2-22 rides alongside because it is the same question — *who is allowed to set this field?* |
| **Now (days)** | F2-10 restart · F2-02 three files · F2-07 reconciliation matrix · F2-08a export-toolkit promotion · F2-08b boundary ratchet · F2-19 CI-generated baseline · F2-20 delete | Highest value per hour. Each is small, independent, and needs no decision. |
| **Wave 1 (weeks)** | F2-01 module registry → then F2-03 test floors, F2-05 permission conversion, F2-06 enforcement test | The registry is the spine: floors, permissions, schemas and navigation all attach to it. Nothing durable is buildable before it. |
| **Wave 2** | F2-04 entitlement **rollout** (**gated on the per-module SKU decision**) · F2-09 schema convergence · F2-13 grant tightness · F2-14 control-health SPI | Wave 2 is where the modular business model becomes real — and where the platform's assurance story becomes saleable. F2-04 is a rollout of an existing subsystem, so it is days rather than weeks. |
| **Wave 3** | F2-07 workspace IA · F2-11 i18n convergence · F2-12 `ndi` · F2-16 monoliths · F2-15 remaining mocks · F2-17 performance · F2-18 integration tests | Larger, benefits from Waves 1–2 being in place (IA needs entitlement; `ndi` needs test floors). |

**The one decision that must be made before Wave 2:** is the commercial model **per-module SKUs** or a
single suite? F2-04, F2-05 and F2-06 are P0/P1 under the first reading and P2 hygiene under the second.
This is Baseline §9 question 2, and it is a business decision — it is not ours to assume.

## F2-276 · A gate's population had three narrowings, not one — and the sibling gate is immune because it reflects

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | 🟢 CLOSED 2026-08-22 (`8219c056`) |
| **Severity** | **P3** — a latent-hazard closure, not a defect discovery, and saying which is the point (F2-274). 29 bilingual pairs were outside the write-symmetry gate's population; **0** of them turned out to be asymmetric. The one live thing found was a capacity asymmetry on `cyber.cyber_frameworks`, where an English framework name the register could not hold had an Arabic translation it could |
| **Found by** | executing [[F2-275]]'s own filing and **disbelieving it** |
| **Fix** | the bare-stem pair branch + FQN keying + import-resolved writers in `BilingualWriteSymmetryTest` · a new declared-capacity leg in `BilingualInvariantRatchetTest` · `V390` widens two English columns to mirror their Arabic siblings · the census published to `target/bilingual-write-symmetry.txt` |
| **Verified** | gate **597 pairs / 0 asymmetric** (585 suffix + 12 bare-stem) · V390 applied twice, both pairs mirrored, Arabic untouched, 6 rows unchanged · live probe **9/9** as `so_officer` · harness **6 killed / 0 survived / 0 anchor-miss** · backend **4407/0/0** |

### F2-275's filing was wrong, and the refutation is the finding

That filing named nine EN_ONLY members in `evidence` and described one of them as *"an `evidence_guidance_ar`
with **no English sibling** — the mirror case."* Measured across both databases, Arabic columns with no
English half of **any** spelling number **0**. The English half is `evidence_guidance` — a **bare stem** with
no `_en` suffix — populated on **654 of 654** rows against the Arabic half's **610**.

So the pair is complete, the data is fine, and the defect was in the instrument. `BilingualWriteSymmetryTest`
pairs `xEn` with `xAr`; so does `BilingualInvariantRatchetTest`, whose two buckets (ASYMMETRIC, EN_ONLY) are
both keyed on the English half carrying the suffix. **A pair spelled `evidenceGuidance` / `evidenceGuidanceAr`
is in neither bucket and outside both gates** — not tolerated, not exempted, never asked about.

🔑 F2-198's shape after a filename, a three-entry allow-list, a module name, an `extends` clause, a field-name
list inside a fix and a claim shape in a gate. Here the narrowing is **a naming convention**. Measured: **12**
such pairs on entities, **13** columns in the database.

### The second narrowing, and why the sibling gate never had it

An annotation sweep over the 12 printed `!! 2 entity files named Vendor.java`, which is how the next one
surfaced. `BilingualWriteSymmetryTest` keyed its field map on the entity's **simple name** in a
`LinkedHashMap`, so for the 15 simple names this platform declares in two packages the second file visited
**overwrote** the first — not a union, a replacement — and every bilingual pair on the losing twin left the
population. Measured cost: **568 pairs where 585 exist.**

🔑🔑 **`BilingualInvariantRatchetTest` cannot have this defect, because it enumerates entities by REFLECTION and
gets distinct `Class` objects.** My gate reads source. CLAUDE.md records the rule — *"measure this from
BYTECODE, never a source regex"*, with four pattern mistakes and three phantom counts behind it — and I wrote
a source-reading gate one slice ago knowing it. [[F2-222]] filed the duplicate-name hazard as latent on the
ground that *"no key collapses two registers today"*; **a census keyed on the same name is exactly where it
stops being latent**, and it fails in the quiet direction, because fewer pairs reads as a cleaner tree.

The writer resolution moved to the **import** at the same time, and the direction is what matters:
over-approximating the ARABIC half **hides** an asymmetry, which is the whole defect this gate exists to catch.

### The third narrowing was honest, and it is a filing

The database shows 13 bare-stem columns and the gate reports 12. `privacy.privacy_assessments.title /
title_ar` belongs to a `V1` table with **no `@Entity`, no repository and no controller** — [[F2-204]]'s
`NO_SERVER_SURFACE` shape, 6 live rows — so no entity-side gate can pair it. Its module's
`package-info.java` still advertises `PrivacyAssessment` as a module type ([[F2-184]]'s shape). Filed rather
than mapped: `privacy.dpia` is the real assessment register, so adding a second is [[F2-196]]'s defect.

### The live half: the two halves of a pair had different CAPACITIES

V387, V388 and V389 each assert that a **new** Arabic column mirrors its English sibling's width. That had
never been applied to the pairs already there. Measured over both databases, **643 pairs, exactly 2
mismatches**, both on `cyber.cyber_frameworks` and both with the **English** half narrower:

| column | was | sibling |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | NVARCHAR(100) | `name_ar` NVARCHAR(255) |
| `description_en` | NVARCHAR(500) | `description_ar` NVARCHAR(MAX) |

⚠⚠ **The entity is the tell, and the bean-level symmetry is what concealed it.** `descriptionEn` and
`descriptionAr` carry the **identical** annotation — `@Column(columnDefinition = "NVARCHAR(MAX)")` — against
columns of 500 and MAX. `columnDefinition` is a **claim**, not a constraint: Hibernate only emits it when it
generates DDL, and `ddl-auto=none` means this platform never does. And `name` carried
`@Column(nullable = false)` with **no length at all**, so the bean assumed JPA's 255 default against a
100-character column — a 101-character English framework name passes every validator and is refused by SQL
Server as **error 2628**, a 500 rather than a 400 naming the field, and 2628 does not report the limit
([[F2-185b]]'s family).

V390 **widens the English halves and never narrows the Arabic**: widening cannot refuse a row that exists
today, the Arabic widths are the ones V37 chose deliberately, and it makes the entity's own declared intent
true for the first time. Six self-checks THROW, including one asserting the Arabic halves were **not** touched,
because the mirror can be satisfied from either side and narrowing Arabic is the wrong repair. Longest stored
values are 9 and 175 characters, so this closes a latent asymmetry rather than repairing damage.

⚠ **The new capacity leg would NOT have caught it, and it says so.** Both halves declared the same capacity;
the asymmetry was between the declaration and the column, which no hermetic gate can see under
`ddl-auto=none`. What the leg closes is the **inverse** hazard — declaring different capacities, where the
declaration is all a reader has. The schema half is enforced by V387–V390's own THROWing self-checks.

### All three mutation survivors were equivalent on this corpus, and each was a missing floor

With `asymmetric = 0` and every declared capacity matching, reverting the writer narrowing, dropping the
bare-stem spelling from the capacity leg, or ignoring `columnDefinition` entirely all changed **nothing
observable**. Per [[F2-206]] a survivor is a hole only if the mutated code is wrong — all three were wrong,
and undetectable. Closed by assertion rather than recorded as equivalent ([[F2-263]]'s precedent):

- **the pair floor sits at 590**, between the largest wrong answer (~580, the broken keying plus the
  bare-stem branch) and the truth (597). A floor of 500 — or of 570 — cannot tell the fix from its absence
  ([[F2-215]]).
- **the capacity leg counts its own bare-stem and `columnDefinition` comparisons** and requires both to be
  non-trivial, so a leg that stops reading either reports it.
- **the import narrowing is asserted by measurement**: at least one field on a duplicate-named entity must
  give a different writer answer for its two twins, or the per-owner narrowing is doing nothing.

6 killed / 0 survived / 0 anchor-miss after. One anchor-miss was mine, from restructuring the code the anchor

## F2-277 · A derived label inherits its parent's bilingualism only if the derivation copies both halves

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | 🟢 CLOSED 2026-08-22 (`d86b3fcc`) |
| **Severity** | **P2** — one live 500 on `POST /api/v1/cyber/controls`, opened by V390 one slice earlier and reachable by any tenant with a framework name over 100 characters; plus four registers rendering a governance label English-only on an Arabic-primary UI (house rule 7), the largest being all **154** cyber controls |
| **Found by** | executing [[F2-276]]'s filed EN_ONLY work list and reading its members against the OTHER families on this register |
| **Fix** | `V391` (widen the copy to its source + four Arabic halves, backfilled BY DERIVATION) · both halves derived at all five writers · `labelsFor`/`labelArFor` on the three directories · two new legs in `ParentIdentityCopyContractTest` · four wire types and four render sites |
| **Verified** | probe **7/7 pre-fix, 11/11 post-fix** as `so_officer` · V391 applied twice, guarded branch exercised by a planted divergence · harness **13 killed / 0 survived / 0 anchor-miss** · backend **4419/0/0** · frontend 75 files / 814 tests, `tsc` clean |

### The filing was right and its GROUPING was wrong

[[F2-276]] filed nine `evidence` EN_ONLY members as the next work, and [[F2-275]] had already recorded
the better rule: **group an EN_ONLY work list by CONCEPT, not by module.** Applying that to the full
35-member census found three members that are not house-rule-7 gaps at all — they are
[[F2-245]]'s **parent-identity copies**, where a child stores a parent's id beside a copy of that
parent's label. [[F2-272]] had already noticed one (`CrossBorderTransfer.ropaTitleEn`) and filed it
as a one-off, with the correct reasoning: *adding `ropa_title_ar` would create a **third** place one
ROPA's name is spelled; the fix is to derive it from the parent, which yields both languages free.*

Measured, that is a population and not an incident.

### The two censuses overlap and neither gate can see the other

`BilingualInvariantRatchetTest` buckets a `*En` field with no `*Ar` sibling as EN_ONLY.
`BilingualWriteSymmetryTest` pairs the same two spellings. **A monolingual identity copy spelled
BARE — `framework_name`, `subject_name`, `signer_name`, `asset_name` — is in NEITHER bucket and
outside BOTH gates**: it is not `xEn`, so it is not EN_ONLY, and there is no `xAr`, so it is not a
pair.

🔑 [[F2-198]]'s shape after a filename, a three-entry allow-list, a module name, an `extends` clause,
a field-name list inside a fix, a claim shape in a gate and a naming convention. Here the narrowing
is **the absence of a suffix**. And note it is the *complement* of [[F2-276]]'s finding: there a
bare-stem pair was complete and invisible, here a bare-stem column is *incomplete* and invisible.

### Which half is wrong is decided by the PARENT, and by measurement

For a copy of a parent's identity the language question is settled by the parent: if the parent
stores `name_en` and `name_ar`, a single bare column on the child can only hold one of them, so it
is monolingual **by construction**.

Resolved by **value agreement** against every bilingual label pair in the database — never by name,
because [[F2-252]] established the mechanism: a scan locates and **the pairing is the measurement**,
and when two registers share an id space a guessed pairing *dereferences cleanly and lies*. Measured
over both databases:

| | |
|---|---|
| monolingual name-like identity copies | **32** (dev), 30 in prod |
| of which spelled BARE, invisible to both gates | **30** |
| **full value agreement with a BILINGUAL parent** | **4** |
| partial agreement | 9 — all the `scm`/`tprm` vendor registers, whose parent `scm.vendors` is itself monolingual ([[F2-246]]/[[F2-247]]'s two-vendor-register question) |
| no bilingual parent agrees | 19 — person *attributions* now holding usernames ([[F2-236]]/[[F2-249]]), offices rather than names, and the asset registers [[F2-249]] filed as unresolvable |

The four:

| child | parent | derivable |
|---|---|---|
| `admin.committee_meetings.committee_name_en` | `admin.committees.name_ar` | 34/34 |
| `cyber.cyber_controls.framework_name` | `cyber.cyber_frameworks.name_ar` | 153/154 |
| `ethics.aml_alerts.subject_name` | `ethics.kyc_subjects.full_name_ar` | 2/2 |
| `platform.signatures.signer_name` | `iam.users.full_name_ar` | 1/4 |

🔑🔑 **Every one of the four was CLOSED by an earlier slice of this programme, and every one of those
slices derived the English half alone** — [[F2-252]] built `CyberFrameworkReferenceResolver.labelFor`,
[[F2-250]] `KycSubjectDirectory`, [[F2-249]] `TenantUserDirectory` (and named `platform.signatures`
the family's *exemplar*). [[F2-215]]'s two-of-N: a reader who finds a resolver deriving the label
does not then ask **which language** it derived. [[F2-252]]'s own filing said
*"`cyber.cyber_controls.framework_name` has no `*_ar` while `cyber_frameworks` carries `name_ar`"* —
filed as one member; measured, it is four.

⚠ `TenantUserDirectory.labelFor`'s javadoc is the sharpest instance. It discusses the blank
fallback, the difference between a reference and an attribution, and cites `platform.signatures` as
the correct member of this family — and never mentions that it reads one of the two names its parent
holds. **A careful comment about a column is not a comment about its language.**

⚠ `CommitteeCalendarService` is the sharpest in code: it reaches for `committee.getNameAr()` **three
lines below** copying `getNameEn()` into the name column, for the meeting *title*. The writer knew
the parent was bilingual; the derivation read one of the two columns in front of it.

### The live half: V390 made a derived copy narrower than the column it copies

`cyber.cyber_controls.framework_name` was `NVARCHAR(100)` and holds a copy of
`cyber.cyber_frameworks.name`, which **V390 (F2-276, one slice earlier) widened to 255** so it would
mirror `name_ar`. So a framework name of 101–255 characters became legal in the parent and refused
by the copy.

**The two databases disagree, and that disagreement is the evidence:**

```
dev  (V390 applied)   framework_name 100  <-  name 255    COPY NARROWER
prod (V390 pending)   framework_name 100  <-  name 100    consistent
```

Probed live as `so_officer` (never `admin`): `POST /frameworks` with a 150-character name → **200**,
then `POST /controls` linked to it → **500**, while the identical call against a short-named
framework → **200**. Post-fix the same call answers **200** with a 150-character derived label.

🔑 **A width invariant scoped to the two halves of a bilingual pair WITHIN one entity cannot see a
derived copy in another table — and widening the source is what makes the copy overflow.** F2-276's
own capacity leg is exactly that shape. Latent rather than live (0 stored names exceed 100 today),
and saying which is the point ([[F2-274]]).

⚠ The entity is the second tell: `CyberControl.frameworkName` carried `@Column(name =
"framework_name")` with **no length**, so the bean assumed JPA's 255 default against a 100-character
column — the same declaration-versus-column gap F2-276 found on the parent, one table down.

### The backfill is DERIVED, not authored — which is why this family may be backfilled at all

[[F2-271]]'s rule is that an Arabic governance value must never be manufactured: an empty column is
an honest *not recorded*, a machine translation is a fabricated record. That rule is about
**inventing** text. Here the text already exists in the parent row this column is a copy of, and the
UPDATE performs exactly the operation the writer performs. **190 of 194 linked rows** were filled
without anything being authored.

⚠⚠ **Guarded on agreement**, because three of the four are point-in-time snapshots (a signature's
signer name is documented as surviving later user renames). Copying today's Arabic onto a row whose
English half no longer matches the parent would record a name the row never had. Measured 0
disagreements in both databases — so the guard is a no-op everywhere it can be measured, and the
branch is exercised by a deliberately diverged `[REVIEW-TEST]` row rather than assumed ([[F2-183]]).
It correctly left that row NULL.

⚠ V391 carries **no** check comparing an English copy against its parent. It was written and
removed: on a customer database a committee renamed after its meetings were created legitimately
leaves the older snapshot, so the check would THROW and block the whole chain. **A migration may
assert its own writes and never tenant data** ([[F2-260]]) — and that is also why check 4 *is* safe,
since the four columns are created by this file, so every non-null value it sees is one it just
wrote. The structural claim (this migration writes no English column) is asserted hermetically
instead.

### The gate, and the hole the harness found in it

Both legs live in `ParentIdentityCopyContractTest`, because that is where the identity-copy
**enumerator** already is and [[F2-276]] filed *two test-support entity enumerators for one question*
as [[F2-190]]'s shape. A third would be worse.

⚠⚠ **The structural leg's first draft asserted the Arabic setter was PRESENT in the method, and the
harness showed it green over a deleted derivation.** Every one of these methods writes the Arabic
half in **two** branches — derive when the parent resolves, clear when the caller unlinks — so
dropping the derive branch leaves the clear branch and `contains("setXAr(")` is satisfied by it.
[[F2-194]]'s substring-satisfied-by-something-else, in a leg written after quoting it. Replaced by
**equal counts**: the two halves must be written the same number of times, which is what *"the
Arabic half rides with the English one at every site"* actually means, and which survives a local
being renamed ([[F2-197]]).

⚠ Two more real holes, both closed rather than recorded as tolerated (all four survivors were
**wrong** code, so none is an equivalent mutant — [[F2-206]]): nothing asserted that a contradicting
**Arabic** label is refused, and nothing asserted the backfill's agreement guard exists.

⚠ And one survivor was the harness's own fault: M2 was classified against
`ParentIdentityCopyContractTest` while the assertion that catches it lives in
`CyberControlFrameworkReferenceTest`. **Classify a mutation by its assertion, not by the file it
edits** ([[F2-208]]).

### `FullReplaceUpdateContractTest` failed, correctly about the contract and not about its own stated harm

It reported that `PUT /api/v1/cyber/controls/{id}` writes `frameworkNameAr`, which its client
cannot send. Its stated harm — *"the field arrives null on every call and is written null"* — does
not apply: the value is derived from the resolved framework. It fires because its taint analysis
cannot tell a resolver's RESULT from its ARGUMENTS, and **[[F2-233]] made exactly that narrowing in
the sibling gate `ServerStampedFieldContractTest`** (*"the id is the caller's; the row it names is
the server's"*) **while this gate never got it.** Filed as an instrument observation rather than
fixed here: changing a shared gate's taint rule inside a slice that is not about it risks weakening
it, and an honest alternative was available.

The alternative taken: declare the Arabic half on `CyberControlRequest` **and consult it**, exactly
as the English half is consulted. Merely declaring it would be an inert field telling a caller their
value matters ([[F2-184]]). Both halves now accept an ECHO and refuse a CONTRADICTION
([[F2-231]]/[[F2-234]]), so a form that round-trips the whole row keeps working in either language.

⚠ Extracting the shared refusal flattened two remedies into one, and an existing test caught it: an
id sent with a wrong label means *"send the id alone, or send the real name"*, while a label
differing with no id sent means *"send frameworkId to change the link"* — the caller is trying to
relink BY NAME, the one operation this pair's hazard forbids. **A shared refusal must carry the
remedy, not just the reason.**

### Two of my own errors, the second after correcting the first

My unit test asserted that omitting `frameworkId` on update *unlinks* and clears both halves.
[[F2-252]] deliberately made an omitted id mean **leave the link alone** — copying the pair in
`applyEditable` is what nulled `framework_id` on 75 of 75 live rows — so there is no unlink path on
update and the leg was testing something the service is written not to do. Replaced by the claim
that does exist: an edit **re-derives both halves together**, so one can never be fresh while the
other is stale.

🔑 **I then left the identical wrong expectation in the live probe and it failed there too.**
[[F2-215]]'s two-of-N inside one slice, on my own correction. And a guessed method name
(`materialise` for `CommitteeCalendarService#generateAnnualCalendar`) was caught by the new gate's
own (class, method) pair — which is exactly why that pair is self-verifying.

### Filed

- **The 9 `evidence` EN_ONLY members still stand**, unchanged by this slice and still a migration
  plus nine writers rather than a batch. `EN_ONLY` fell 35 → 34 and `BASELINE_ARABIC_NOT_GUARANTEED`
  194 → 193, from `committee_name_en` gaining its sibling.
- **`FullReplaceUpdateContractTest` lacks [[F2-233]]'s store-read taint narrowing** that its sibling

## F2-278 · A coverage leg ran over twelve hand-listed sites beside a leg measuring 83, and deriving it found a regression the previous slice had introduced

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | 🟢 CLOSED 2026-08-22 (`b277c5ed`) |
| **Severity** | **P2** — an unconditional write of a field the wire cannot carry on the PDPL Article 31 ROPA register, **created by [[F2-272]] one slice earlier**; a mandatory categories-of-personal-data field discarded on every edit of that same register; and two Arabic labels frozen on **8 of 11 live rows in both databases** on a screen an operator edits (house rule 7) |
| **Found by** | re-deriving [[F2-277]]'s own top filing — and **refuting it by measurement** before writing any code |
| **Fix** | `FullReplaceUpdateContractTest`: population DERIVED (30) instead of hand-listed (12) · service resolved by IMPORT · helper following made TRANSITIVE · the coverage claim split into **RESET** (hard zero) and **FROZEN** (named map, both directions) · `purposeAr` declared on `PrivacyRopaRequest` · `dataCategoriesJson` added to `updateRopa`'s whitelist · `nameAr`/`descriptionAr` declared, collected and rendered for report schedules |
| **Verified** | probe **16/16** as `compliance` against planted rows · pre-fix control: **3 of 3** tree-dependent legs fire, naming exactly `purposeAr` and `nameAr`/`descriptionAr` · harness **5 killed / 0 survived / 0 anchor-miss** (a 6th withdrawn as invalid) · backend **4425/0/0** · frontend 75 files / 814 tests, `tsc` clean |

### The filed item was refuted, and the refutation is the result

[[F2-277]] filed this as its sharpest unread item: *"`FullReplaceUpdateContractTest` lacks
[[F2-233]]'s store-read taint narrowing that its sibling `ServerStampedFieldContractTest` has."*
Measured first ([[F2-221]]), it is **false in both halves**.

The narrowing that exists is `loadsARow`, whose vocabulary is `get|mustGet|find*|load*|fetch*` —
so it cannot see `frameworks.require(...)` or `labelsFor(...)`, the shapes [[F2-277]] actually hit.
🔑 **[[F2-217]]'s headline about the filing that quoted it: a census keyed on a list of names
measures the list.** And porting it — in either the sibling's exact form or a resolver-aware
widening — changes **nothing**: 0 fields lost at any of the 12 sites. The reason is one line
`CyberControlService:116`, `target.setFrameworkName(sentName)` — the **bare-label branch
[[F2-246]] requires to stay legal**, which writes the caller's own value verbatim, so the field is
genuinely written from the request whatever the resolver does.

So the narrowing would have been a pure weakening of a security gate with no measured benefit.
🔑 **The right answer to a filed change to a gate is sometimes "measure it and do not make it" —
and the measurement is what separates that from not doing the work.**

### The population was a hand-written list of twelve, beside a leg measuring 83

Asking the general question instead — *what IS this leg's population?* — found the real finding.
`SITES` is **twelve hand-listed** sites. `theEntityBoundPutPopulationIsMeasured`, a leg **in the
same class**, measures **83 entity-bound PUT handlers** decrease-only. `SITES`'s own comment read
*"Adding a row is how a new full-replace update gets covered"* — an instruction with no
enforcement, which is [[F2-52]]'s `AttachmentAccessPolicy` shape and [[F2-265]]'s (an instruction
not to copy a figure is not an enforcement).

🔑 **A reader who finds a hard-zero coverage leg beside a measured 83 reads the zero as covering
the 83.** Derived, the joinable population is **30** — an entity-bound PUT whose path also has an
`api.put` with a named payload type. The other 52 have no typed frontend client at all, so the
coverage question has nothing to compare and they are *counted* rather than claimed.

### Why it was a list: the leg's claim was narrower than its detector

The coverage leg's harm sentence is *"the field arrives null on every call and is written null"* —
and that is **FALSE when the write is null-guarded**, because an omitted field then keeps its
stored value. One question was doing the work of two, and switching to a derived population
without splitting it fails on `PolicyManagementService#update`: **eleven undeclarable fields,
every one guarded**, i.e. a gate failing on correct code, the one failure a gate must never have
([[F2-214]]).

🔑🔑 **That is why the population was hand-written: the leg's claim was narrower than its
detector, and nobody wrote that down, so the list read as laziness rather than as a necessary
narrowing.** The discriminator already existed in the same file —
`unguardedWritesFromRequest`, leg 4's detector — and the two legs had never met ([[F2-190]]).

- **RESET** — unconditional write of a field the only client cannot declare. **Hard zero, no
  exemption map**: the fix is always available (declare it, stop writing it, or guard it).
- **FROZEN** — the same write GUARDED. A named map keyed `endpoint :: field`, enforced both ways.
  The reasons repeat where the finding is genuinely per-site: `CyberPolicyRequest` is a narrow
  ten-field form against a service that writes about twenty columns *and is reached by a second
  route with no typed client at all*, so eleven near-identical per-field reasons would be eleven
  fluent unverified claims ([[F2-188]]) where the fact is one.

### Three narrowings, and the third was hiding a field

**(a) One helper hop where the chain is two.** `CyberControlService`'s chain is
`updateControl → applyEditable → applyFrameworkReference`. Resolving the population from the
controllers (which name `updateControl`) therefore lost `frameworkId`, `frameworkName` and
`frameworkNameAr` — and lost them **into the REVERSE leg**, where three real writes read as
*three fields the client sends and the server ignores*, i.e. as three inert form inputs.
🔑 **A hand-written population can encode a detector's limit as a naming convention — `SITES`
names helper methods, and that is WHY — and then the limit is invisible, because the list looks
like a choice.**

**(b) The service resolved by FILENAME.** There are two `AuditEngagementService.java`
(`module/audit_eng` and `module/compliance`) and the `audit_eng` twin has no `update` method, so
`findFirst()` on the file name picked the wrong one and the site read as **"parsed nothing"** — the
quiet direction, indistinguishable from a clean site. [[F2-276]] found exactly this with a
`LinkedHashMap` keyed on an entity's simple name silently overwriting one of a pair; [[F2-222]]
measured **15** such duplicate simple names and filed it as latent because *"no key collapses two
registers today"*. 🔑 **A derived population is where that stops being latent.** Resolving by
import surfaced a genuine frozen field the filename bug had hidden —
`audit-engagements :: findingsCount`, a caller-supplied aggregate whose *sibling register derives
the same field from its linked finding ids* ([[F2-197]]'s "a computed count is not a measured one",
across two registers for one concept).

**(c) The 52 backend-only sites**, honestly counted rather than claimed.

### The defect I introduced one slice earlier

`PrivacyService#updateRopa` writes `existing.setPurposeAr(req.getPurposeAr())`
**unconditionally**, and `PrivacyRopaRequest` did not declare `purposeAr` — so a `PUT` sending
exactly the shape the type declares nulls the Arabic purpose of a PDPL Article 31 processing
activity. **That is the defect [[F2-214]] fixed for `crossBorderTransfer` in the same method,
whose explanatory comment sits eight lines above.**

[[F2-272]] created it: that slice added `setPurposeAr` to the whitelist so V388's new column would
stop being permanently uneditable, and left the wire unable to carry it. 🔑🔑 **Its own comment
reads *"F2-214's shape, not F2-213's reset"* — true of the code it replaced and false of the code
it wrote. Fixing "this field can never be changed" by making the write unconditional converts an
ignored field into a destroyed one, for exactly the callers that cannot send it.**

⚠ Latent, and worth saying rather than implying otherwise: `purpose_ar` is populated on **0 of 11**
live rows in dev, the **column is ABSENT in prod** (V388 is one of the 47 pending migrations), and
`updateRopa` has **no caller** — `apiClientMethodReachability` records it as
*"HOLE: a RoPA record can be created and never corrected"*. 🔑 **That entry adjudicates the CLIENT
and says nothing about the ENDPOINT, so it reads as an invitation to build the edit screen that
would fire the erasure** — [[F2-214]]'s own words, about this very endpoint.

### Two more, found by the reverse direction over the derived population

**`updateRopa` never wrote `dataCategoriesJson`**, which `PrivacyRopaRequest` has *always*
declared. So the register's categories-of-personal-data field — collected by `RopaWizard`, stored
on create — was **discarded on every edit** with HTTP 200 ([[F2-214]]'s shape). Populated on 2 of
11 live rows in both databases. Nothing recorded it as a decision, which is why the leg that found
it is the reverse one, *the direction nobody writes first* ([[F2-199]]).

**`ReportScheduleService#update` writes `nameAr` and `descriptionAr` from the request** (guarded,
so nothing was destroyed) and `ReportScheduleDto` declared neither — so the Arabic name and
description of a scheduled regulatory report were **frozen**: settable only by a seed or a direct
API call, never editable from `ReportSchedulesPage`, which **is** the screen that edits this
register and calls `update` from its edit form. Populated on **8 of 11 live rows in BOTH
databases**. [[F2-275]]'s shape — *an Arabic column that EXISTS is not one that can be WRITTEN* —
with [[F2-198]]'s for the read half, since the handler returns the entity so the wire always
carried them.

### The instrument landmine: a control script that restores a backup with its original timestamp

The probe reported **14/16** with the two failures being exactly the server-behaviour legs, which
is the stale-listener signature — and it reproduced identically after a **full backend restart**.
It was not a stale listener. `shutil.copy2` preserves mtime, so the pre-fix control's
revert → compile → `shutil.move` restore left `target/classes` **newer** than the restored source,
Maven's incremental compiler treated the stale class as up to date, and **the fix sat correct on
disk, uncompiled, indefinitely**. `javap` on the compiled method was what settled it (0 occurrences
of the new call).

🔑 **A fix that is correct on disk and never compiled is indistinguishable from a wrong fix, and it
survives a restart — which is what rules out the diagnosis a probe failure normally suggests.**
Same mechanism as the recorded *"46 `NoSuchMethodError` while `test-compile` said nothing to
compile"*, in the other direction. The control script now restores content and stamps a fresh
mtime; `touch` + `mvn -o compile` + `javap` is the three-step check.

⚠ And the harness's own bookkeeping: one mutation was **killed by `javac`**, not by an assertion —
it weakened `.hasSize(30)` to `.isLessThanOrEqualTo(30)`, which does not compile on a `ListAssert`.
🔑 **A mutation killed by a compile error is not a kill.** It was **withdrawn as invalid** rather
than repaired, because you can always relax an assertion, so mutating the CHECK proves nothing
([[F2-206]]/[[F2-235]]).

### Filed

- **`/api/v1/bcm/bia/{} :: linkedRiskId`** — `BcmBiaRequest` declares it and
  `BcmService#updateBia`'s seven-field whitelist omits it, so a BIA's linked risk is settable on
  create (the endpoint binds `BiaRecord`) and frozen thereafter. Populated on **0 of 10** live rows
  in both databases, so latent. [[F2-275]]'s shape; filed rather than fixed inside a slice about the
  instrument.
- **`audit-engagements :: findingsCount`** — the aggregate whose sibling register derives it.
  Deriving it here changes what an IIA engagement reports: an **owner decision**.
- **The eleven frozen policy fields**, including `summaryAr` (house rule 7). Widening
  `CyberPolicyRequest` is a product decision about the policy register, and the second route
  (`/api/policy/documents/{}`) has no typed client at all, so the honest first step is deciding
  whether that route should have one.
- **The 52 backend-only entity-bound PUTs** — no typed frontend client, so the coverage question
  cannot be asked of them at all. That is [[F2-213]]'s structural root restated: **83 entity-bound
  PUT handlers**, where a purpose-built request record per endpoint would make resets, refusals and
  mass assignment alike unrepresentable.
- **`FullReplaceUpdateContractTest` still lacks [[F2-233]]'s store-read narrowing** — correctly, and
  now with a measurement behind it rather than a filing. Do not port it: it changes nothing today
  and weakens the taint analysis. Recorded so the next reader does not re-open it.
