## F2-279 · An entity that maps a subset of its table is outside the platform's tenant machinery by construction

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | 🟢 CLOSED 2026-08-22 (`6d750f5c`) |
| **Severity** | **P2** — on `bcm.bia_records`: the **database column DEFAULT decided every row's tenant** rather than `TenantContext`; a row whose own `organisation_id` named another tenant was **served to an org-1 caller**; and `DELETE` answered **204 with the record still in the register**. All three probed live, dev = prod |
| **Found by** | re-deriving [[F2-278]]'s own filing — and **refuting its premise** before writing any code |
| **Fix** | `BiaRecord` maps `organisation_id` and `is_deleted` and carries `@Where(is_deleted = 0)` · `createBia` stamps the tenant unconditionally · `requireOwnedBia`/`listBia`/`getStats` scope on the row's own tenant column · `deleteBia` sets the soft-delete flag instead of writing a status token · `updateBia` writes `linkedRiskId` (the filed freeze) · new `TenantColumnMappingContractTest` |
| **Verified** | probe **10/10 pre-fix and 10/10 post-fix** as `compliance` against planted rows · pre-fix control: **3 of 3** tree-dependent legs fire · harness **10 mutations** · backend **4437/0/0** |

### The filed premise was false, and the refutation is the finding

[[F2-278]] filed this as its readiest unread item: *"`/api/v1/bcm/bia/{} :: linkedRiskId` is
declared by `BcmBiaRequest`, omitted from `BcmService#updateBia`'s seven-field whitelist, so
settable on create and frozen after."* The freeze is real. Its stated premise is not.

`BcmService#createBia` carried this comment:

> *"BiaRecord carries no organisationId column; tenant scoping is inherited via the parent
> CriticalProcess link, so the target process must be validated to belong to the current
> tenant before persisting."*

Measured from `sys.columns`, identical in dev and prod: **`bcm.bia_records` has 29 columns**, and
`organisation_id BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT ((1))` is one of them. The entity mapped **eleven**.

🔑 **The column order in the migration is the fingerprint.** `V1__core_schemas.sql` — the *first*
migration — creates the table with all 29, and its first eleven columns are **exactly** the
entity's eleven, in the entity's order, with everything the entity omits following after. The
table was extended and the entity never followed. By mapped-field gap this is the widest in the
platform: **18 columns**, against `cyber.incidents` at 8.

### The narrowing is a property the entity declines to declare

`TenantWriteGuardInterceptor` is the platform-wide tenant write backstop —
`application-prod.yml` calls it the guarantee that *"a single missed per-service guard cannot
silently write across tenants"*. It resolves the tenant by property name:

```java
int orgIdx = indexOf(propertyNames, ORG_PROP);
if (orgIdx < 0) {
    // Entity doesn't have an organisationId — out of scope for …
```

So an entity that does not map the column is outside the backstop **by construction**, and the
guard says so in a comment nobody had cause to read.

🔑🔑 **[[F2-216]] found and closed one narrowing in this exact class** — it exempts a row whose
`organisationId` is **null**, which on eight tables means *every tenant*. The narrowing one level
up, *the entity has no such property at all*, was never counted. F2-198's shape after a filename,
a three-entry allow-list, a module name, an `extends` clause, a field-name list inside a fix, a
claim shape in a gate, a naming convention and the absence of a suffix.

**Measured:** of **432** shipped entities, **35** declare no `organisationId`, and **exactly one**
of those 35 maps a table that has the column. Identical in both databases.

### Three live consequences, all probed

Probed as `compliance` (holds `BCM:READ`/`WRITE`/`DELETE`), against processes and rows the probe
planted itself ([[F2-206]]) — **10/10 pre-fix**:

| | pre-fix | post-fix |
|---|---|---|
| a body claiming `organisationId: 2` | silently discarded — the property did not exist | overridden by the stamp |
| a row whose own `organisation_id` = 2, parent process org 1 | **served to the org-1 caller** | withheld |
| a row with `is_deleted = 1` | **served** | filtered |
| `DELETE` then `GET` | **204, and still in the list** (`status = 'DELETED'`, `is_deleted = false`) | 204, gone; `status` still `DRAFT` |
| `PUT linkedRiskId 5 → 6` | 200, stored **5** | 200, stored 6 |
| `PUT linkedRiskId → null` | 200, stored **5** | 200, cleared |

The tenant half is **latent on data** and the reason is worth stating: every active user is in
organisation 1, *and* `bcm.critical_processes` holds org-1 rows only, so no second tenant can
reach the create at all. What was demonstrable — and was demonstrated — is that neither the write
path nor the read path consulted the column.

⚠ **An index on an unmapped column is the tell.** `V228__backfill_org_indexes.sql` built
`ix_bia_records_org (organisation_id, is_deleted)` over **both** omitted columns, and nothing has
ever used it. 🔑 **A migration that indexes a column no entity maps is a statement that somebody
expected a query that does not exist.**

### The false premise was written twice, and the test asserted the defect

The claim appeared in `BcmService#createBia` **and** as the section comment over the BIA tests in
`BcmServiceTest` (*"BiaRecord has no organisationId column; tenant ownership is enforced via the
parent CriticalProcess"*). 🔑 **Two independent artefacts agreeing, with nobody maintaining the
agreement** ([[F2-177]]) — correct both, or the next reader finds the survivor.

And `deleteBia_of_own_tenant_soft_deletes_via_save` asserted:

```java
assertThat(b.getStatus()).isEqualTo("DELETED");
```

— the status token, under a name that says *soft_deletes*. Nth instance after [[F2-159]],
[[F2-175]], [[F2-227]], [[F2-234]], [[F2-236]], [[F2-243]] and [[F2-244]]. 🔑 **Hardest to spot
when it describes the code accurately, and its NAME is what stops you reading the assertion.**
Repurposed rather than deleted: the half that protects the record — never a hard delete, exactly
one save — is kept.

⚠ A sibling leg was **vacuous**: `verify(biaRepo, never()).findByProcessId(...)` pointed at a
finder the new `listBia` never calls, so it would have passed trivially forever. **When you change
a repository, re-point every `never()` at the finder the code now reaches.**

### Only one of the two mapped fields needed scrubbing

`isDeleted` is one of `ServerOwnedFieldsModule`'s nine server-owned fields, and that introspector
reports them `READ_ONLY` on **any** `@Entity` — not only `BaseEntity` subclasses. So mapping it
closes the wire automatically, pre-empting [[F2-215]]'s born-deleted defect (`"isDeleted": true`
on a create storing a row `@Where` hides from every query *including* the service's own duplicate
check).

That same javadoc states it *"does not touch `organisationId`, which is
`MassAssignmentRatchetTest`'s own"* — so the tenant stamp has to be explicit and
**unconditional**, which is [[F2-216]]'s recorded pattern. 🔑 **Check which mechanism already covers a field before
writing a guard for it, and check which does not.**

### The gate verifies rather than asserts, and that was a measurement

The obvious instrument is a named map of reasons — *"this table has no tenant column
because…"* — and [[F2-188]] measured what that produces: five claims, five false, with fluency
doing the work. It is unnecessary here, because the question is answerable from the **migration
corpus**, the same hermetic source `MigrationVocabularies` reads for CHECK constraints.

Measured: **all 35 resolve to a `CREATE TABLE`, 0 unresolved.** So
`TenantColumnMappingContractTest` ships as a **hard zero with no exemption map at all** — mapping
the column is always available, so it cannot fail on correct code ([[F2-214]]) — and an
unresolved table **fails** rather than dropping out of the population, because *unresolved reads
identically to clean* ([[F2-206]]).

⚠ **Only 2 of its 8 legs discriminate on this tree, and it says so** ([[F2-225]]). The pre-fix
control fires `noEntityOmitsATenantColumnItsTableDeclares` and
`biaRecordMapsItsTenantAndItsSoftDeleteFlag`; the rest are synthetic self-tests, anti-vacuity
floors, or **pins whose tripwire is in the future** — including the
`is_deleted`-without-`@Where` census, which passes on master precisely because `BiaRecord` does
not map the flag there. **A green pin is not a discriminating pass.**

⚠ **A ceiling I predicted was wrong.** I wrote `BASELINE_MAPS_DELETED_WITHOUT_WHERE = 14` from
*"fifteen minus the one I just fixed"*. Measured, it is **9**. 🔑 **A baseline lifted from a
prediction is worse than no baseline, because it looks measured** ([[F2-195]]) — caught before
commit by asserting zero once and reading the failure message.

### The filed freeze was the least of it, and fixing it does not fix the reference

`linkedRiskId` is writable now. It is **still unverified**: `module/bcm` has **0 imports of
`module/risk`**, so validating the reference needs a new module edge and `ModuleGraphRatchetTest`
is decrease-only and may never be raised. Nothing in the platform dereferences the column today,
so no reader can be misled by a bad id — **a fact about today, not a property of the control**
([[F2-182]]).

⚠ **And the picker was measured and not built.** The form collects `linkedRiskId` as a raw
**number input** — [[F2-245]]/[[F2-246]]'s collect-a-label-instead-of-a-link shape, with
`processId` on the *same form* already a select. A risk picker needs `RISK:READ`, and **5 of the
10 roles holding `BCM:WRITE` do not hold it** (`PLATFORM_ADMIN` among them, though it bypasses in
code). 🔑 **A picker would be worse than the number box: it implies the reference is guaranteed
while the server still cannot check it** — [[F2-184]]'s shape at an affordance. Measure the
picker's guard before offering one ([[F2-250]]).

### Filed

- **The 17 still-unmapped columns**, which hold real data no wire can carry:
  `financial_impact` / `operational_impact` / `regulatory_impact` / `reputational_impact` — **the
  four ISO 22301 §8.2.2 impact dimensions a BIA exists to record, on 7 of 10 live rows** — plus
  `owner_name` and `business_unit` on 10 of 10, `notes` on 7, `approved_by`/`approved_at` on 1.
  [[F2-198]]'s shape at eight fields at once; mapping them is a product change.
- **`criticality` is `NOT NULL DEFAULT ('MEDIUM')` and unmapped**, so a created BIA silently
  disagrees with its own mapped `overall_impact` from birth, and the table stores `TIER_2`/`TIER_3`
  beside `CRITICAL`/`HIGH`/`MEDIUM` under **zero CHECK constraints** ([[F2-196]]'s shape inside one
  column). Collapsing two notations on live rows is an **owner decision**.
- **The 9-member `is_deleted`-without-`@Where` census** — `compliance.assessments`,
  `evidence.evidence_links`, `risk.risk_categories` and six `platform.*` integration logs. Mostly
  append-only, where the flag is vestigial; clearing it means reading each one.
- **The cross-module reference validation** and **the risk picker**, both above.
- **Three services outside `BcmService` still read BIAs by the parent-process link**
  (`DependencyCascadeService`, `BcmBoardPackService`, `MtpdInheritanceService`), each passing a
  process-id list it resolved from its own tenant's processes — tenant-correct by that route, so
  re-scoping them is defence in depth rather than a defect.

## F2-280 · "Privileged" was answered twice in one module, and the stored answer had no writer

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | 🟢 CLOSED 2026-08-22 (`ed2697fe`) |
| **Severity** | **P2** — the break-glass dashboard's *"Privileged holders"* KPI read `iam.roles.is_privileged`; the auto-scheduled quarterly NCA ECC 2-2 / SAMA CSF 3.3.5 privileged access review derived the same question from APPROVE/DELETE grants. **12 roles disagreed in dev and 7 in prod**, `CISO` among them — held, granting `IAM:BREAK_GLASS`, and inside the review while absent from the KPI. The stored half had **no write path of any kind**: probed live, a role created through the Access Governance console granting `ADMIN:APPROVE` is `is_privileged = 0` forever and the KPI does not move when it is granted |
| **Found by** | asking F2-279's question one level up — *which entities map a STRICT SUBSET of their table, and do the omitted columns hold real data?* — then ranking the 26 answers by what the omission can make **wrong** rather than by size |
| **Fix** | `RoleRepository.PRIVILEGED_ROLE`: one spliced SQL clause, the **union** of the stored flag and the derived grant test, consumed by both readers · `Role` maps `is_privileged` · `RoleSummary`/`GovRoleDto` report the effective classification and `AccessGovernancePage` renders it · new `PrivilegedRolePredicateSharingTest` |
| **Verified** | probe **11/11 pre-fix and 13/13 post-fix** as `compliance` against a planted `[REVIEW-TEST]` role · pre-fix control reverts six sources, recompiles and confirms the two discriminating legs fire, `javap` checked both ways · harness **11 killed / 0 survived / 0 anchor-miss** · backend **4448/0/0** · frontend 75 files / 814 tests, `tsc` clean |

### The route in, because it generalises F2-279 rather than repeating it

[[F2-279]] measured **one column name**. Its gate asks whether an entity maps the
`organisation_id` its table declares — 35 entities declare no `organisationId`, exactly one of
those mapped a table that has it — and its own filing then named **seventeen** unmapped columns
on that one table. So the general question was never asked: *which entities map a strict subset
of their table, and what do the omissions cost?*

Measured by reflection over `target/classes` against `sys.columns` in both databases:
**26 of 432 shipped entities map a strict subset**, 4 more resolve to no table at all. Ranked by
consequence rather than by gap size, three kinds:

| kind | members | what it costs |
|---|---|---|
| **NOT NULL + DEFAULT, unmapped** | **8** | Hibernate never names the column in its INSERT, so **the database default decides the value** — F2-279's mechanism, generalised |
| **populated, unmapped** | 37 | real data no wire can carry (F2-198's shape) — invisible, not wrong |
| **empty, nullable** | 47 | latent |

`bcm.bia_records` is still the widest gap (16 after F2-279's two), `cyber.incidents` next at 8.
🔑 **But the sharpest member is not the widest — it is a single column on `iam.roles`,**
`is_privileged`, because it is a **security classification** whose default is the *flattering*
value and because something reads it.

### Two definitions, one module, and they disagree

Two native queries, both feeding the access-governance surface:

* `BreakGlassEventRepository#countPrivilegedHolders` — *"Distinct users holding at least one
  privileged role"* — read the **stored** flag, `r.is_privileged = 1`. It is the
  *"Privileged holders"* / *"حاملو صلاحيات مميزة"* KPI rendered on `AccessAssuranceTabs`.
* `AccessReviewItemRepository#generateItems` with scope `PRIVILEGED` — **derived** it from the
  grants, `p.action IN ('APPROVE','DELETE')` — and said so in its class javadoc. It populates
  the campaign `RecertificationService#autoScheduleForOrg` opens every quarter as
  *"Q{n}-{year} privileged access review"*.

Measured, both databases:

| | dev | prod |
|---|---|---|
| STORED `is_privileged = 1` | **14** roles | **14** roles (byte-identical set) |
| DERIVED grants APPROVE or DELETE | **24** roles | **19** roles |
| disagreeing | **12** | **7** |

The disagreeing set is not obscure: `CISO`, `CFO`, `CRO`, `BOARD_SECRETARY`, `CHANGE_MANAGER`,
`AML_OFFICER`, `ETHICS_OFFICER`, `SHARIA_OFFICER`, `LEGAL_COUNSEL`, `SERVICE_OWNER`,
`CONSUMER_PROTECTION_OFFICER`. And **2 of the 3 roles holding `IAM:BREAK_GLASS` are not flagged
privileged** — `CISO` and `IR_LEAD` — on a KPI that sits on the break-glass dashboard.

The reverse case matters as much: **`EMERGENCY_RESPONDER` is flagged privileged and grants no
APPROVE or DELETE**, so it is in the KPI and *outside* the quarterly review's scope.

### Why the stored half could never be right

`Role` did not map the column, and `RoleUpsertRequest` declares
`roleName`/`displayNameEn`/`displayNameAr`/`isActive` and nothing else. So there was **no writer
of any kind** — not a screen, not an endpoint, not a service. `is_privileged` is
`NOT NULL DEFAULT 0`, and Hibernate never names an unmapped column in an INSERT, so every role
the platform has ever created took the database's default. That the flagged set is
**byte-identical in dev and prod** is the evidence: it is exactly what V272 seeded, and nothing
has moved it since.

Probed live as `compliance` (GRC_ADMINISTRATOR, the only holder of `IAM:WRITE` — `admin` proves
nothing about authorization), against a `[REVIEW-TEST]` role the probe plants itself:

```
POST /api/v1/iam/governance/roles            201  (a role the console can create)
PUT  /api/v1/iam/governance/roles/{}/matrix  200  ADMIN:READ + ADMIN:APPROVE
   stored flag    = 0        <- the database default decided it
   derived        = 1        <- the quarterly review covers its holders
   GET /roles     : no `privileged` key at all — the console cannot even report it
   GET /analytics : privilegedHolders 5 -> 5 after granting the role  <- the KPI does not move
   review scope   : 6                                                <- 1 holder reviewed and uncounted
```

### Why the answer is their UNION, and not a choice between them

Neither half is a copy of the other, so [[F2-251]]/[[F2-257]]'s rule applies —
*ask whether the label is a copy before reaching for the derive-from-the-parent fix.*

* The **flag** carries a judgement the grants cannot express: break-glass is privileged although
  it grants no APPROVE or DELETE. Collapsing to the derived half discards that.
* The **derived** half covers a role a tenant creates, which the flag never could. Collapsing to
  the stored half leaves every future role unclassified.

A union is also the safe direction for a privileged-access review: over-scoping costs a
reviewer's time, under-scoping is the finding an examiner writes up ([[F2-196]] — an unrecognised
member should be chased, not excused).

`RoleRepository.PRIVILEGED_ROLE` is that clause, spliced into both readers — the
`CommitteeMemberTermRepository.CURRENT_SEAT_WINDOW` precedent, and it inherits both of that
constant's recorded traps: it **leads with a newline** (Java strips *trailing* whitespace in a
text block, so `"… WHERE" + PRIVILEGED_ROLE` would otherwise emit `WHERE(r.is_privileged` and
kill the app at context startup), and its inner aliases are `rp_priv`/`p_priv` so splicing it
into a host that already joins `rp`/`p` cannot collide.

### 🔑 The file already held the correct rule, about a different predicate

`RoleRepository`'s own javadoc, on the F2-94 holder count:

> *"The holder predicate is **deliberately identical** to
> `UserRepository#findActiveByOrganisationIdAndRoleName` … F2-62's defect was a report and an
> enforcement point computing access separately and drifting apart, each half defensible
> alone."*

That is this finding's shape, written on this very interface, one predicate over. [[F2-195]]
again — **the codebase can hold the correct rule, in prose, beside the place it was not
applied.** And `Role` carries a careful multi-paragraph essay about `is_active` having been a
dead control directly above a second governance flag it declined to declare: [[F2-215]]'s
two-of-N, inside one entity. **A reader who finds one governance flag explained at length does
not then ask which others are missing.**

### What was deliberately NOT done

* **No write path for the flag.** Flagging a role is scrutiny-increasing and safe; *un*-flagging
  one narrows a privileged-access review, which is a governance decision about a customer's
  organisation and not a side effect of a mapping fix. With the union in place a role granting
  APPROVE or DELETE is privileged automatically, so the residual capability is only *flag a role
  that grants neither* — filed.
* **No migration.** The column has existed since V272 and nothing needed backfilling; the union
  changes what is *computed*, not what is stored.
* **No third reader.** `SodViolationRepository`'s `p.action IN ('WRITE','APPROVE','DELETE')` is a
  different question — *a read-only persona that can write* — and the gate's pattern is
  deliberately the **two-element** list so it cannot fire on it. A gate that fails on correct
  code trains the next reader to edit the assertion ([[F2-214]]).

### Instrument notes

`PrivilegedRolePredicateSharingTest` is a **hard zero with no exemption map**: sharing the
constant is always available, so there is no correct code for it to fail on. Eight legs — the
clause written once (comparison-shaped, because `@Column(name = "is_privileged")` is a *mapping*
and a bare-token pattern fires on it and fails on correct code, which is what the first draft
did), both readers consuming it, the leading newline, paren balance and alias hygiene, the union
being a union, the entity mapping, both halves of the wire, and a stripper self-test whose
negative control is the **two-pass** form rather than a reordered alternation ([[F2-211]]).

⚠ **The stripper is load-bearing here because of this slice's own javadoc**: `RoleRepository`'s
comment quotes `p.action IN ('APPROVE','DELETE')` and `BreakGlassEventRepository`'s quotes
`r.is_privileged = 1`, both explaining what they replaced. Reading raw source counts the epitaph
as the corpse ([[F2-193]]) — mutation M11 confirms it.

⚠⚠ **Two of my own gate legs fell to the harness, and both are shapes this register already
names.** *(a)* The frontend leg was `contains("privileged")` over raw `api.ts`, and the JSDoc
above the field says *"privileged-access classification"* — so **deleting the field left the leg
green**. [[F2-194]]'s substring-satisfied-by-something-else, in a leg written after quoting it;
now comment-stripped and asserted as `privileged\s*:\s*boolean`. *(b)* The unit test drove
`listRoles`, which calls the two-argument summary directly, so making the **single-role** summary
read `r.getIsPrivileged()` survived the whole build — [[F2-205]]'s rule that a leg exercising one
path says nothing about the path beside it. `createRole`/`updateRole` now have their own leg.
**11 killed / 0 survived / 0 anchor-miss** after.

### Filed

* **The 26-entity subset-mapping census**, with the three kinds above and the eight
  NOT-NULL-with-a-DEFAULT members named. It is a filing rather than a gate because a *hermetic*
  instrument would have to enumerate every column of a table from the 379-file migration corpus
  (`CREATE TABLE` plus every `ALTER … ADD`), where this measurement used `sys.columns`; a
  half-parsed census reports a smaller population, which reads exactly like a clean tree
  ([[F2-206]]). **No verdicts** ([[F2-188]]).
* The sharpest unread members: **`cyber.incidents`' eight unmapped PDPL columns**
  (`affects_personal_data`, `pii_classified_at/by`, `linked_data_breach_id/code`,
  `data_categories_affected`, `data_subjects_affected_est`, `personal_data_pii_assessment`) and
  the **mirror five on `privacy.data_breaches`** (`source_cyber_incident_id/number`,
  `auto_generated`, `auto_generated_at`, `auto_generation_rule`) — both ends of the cyber→PDPL
  bridge, written by `CyberPdplBridgeService`'s **deliberate native SQL** and readable by nothing
  else. The bridge log has its own entity and controller, so an operator can see *that* it fired;
  whether an incident affects personal data is not on the incident's own wire.
* **`iam.roles.description_en` is populated on 60 of 70 roles in dev and 49 of 59 in prod and is
  mapped by nothing** — F2-198's shape on the role catalogue. Not mapped here, because a column
  mapped with no surface is an inert mapping ([[F2-184]]); it needs a surface decision.
* **`iam.users.password_changed_at`** (5 of 7 rows) and **`mfa_secret`** are likewise unmapped, so
  no password-age policy can read or display the former.
* **`bcm.critical_processes`' `mtpd_hours`/`rto_hours`/`rpo_hours`** — the ISO 22301 recovery
  objectives, unmapped and empty on all 10 rows, beside a live `MtpdInheritanceService`.
* **Whether a tenant admin may declare a role privileged** (and un-declare one) — an owner
  decision, and the only part of the stored half this slice deliberately left closed.
* `SubprocessorController`'s javadoc cites `is_privileged` as evidence that `PRIVACY_MANAGER` is
  a real privacy job family. It is true today and it is a **third artefact reasoning about the
  flag**, in prose, in another module — outside any scan of readers ([[F2-193]]).

## F2-281 · The PDPL Article 20 notification omitted the two facts Article 20 turns on, and the same row stored both

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | 🟢 CLOSED 2026-08-22 (`9d3d50d3`) |
| **Severity** | **P2** — `GET /api/v1/incidents/{id}/regulatory-templates` renders the PDPL Article 20 personal-data-breach notification an operator files with the **Saudi Data Office**, and that body carried neither the number of affected data subjects nor the categories of personal data affected. Probed live: incident 1 stores **1,450** data subjects and `EMAIL,NATIONAL_ID,PHONE_NUMBER` and the generated notification contained neither. The **HRSD** body went further and printed `EMPLOYEES AFFECTED: <count>` and `DATA CATEGORIES AFFECTED: <e.g. salary, ID, contract>` — literal placeholders asking a human to re-source values the row already held |
| **Found by** | executing [[F2-280]]'s top filing and reading the emitting service rather than the columns: *what does an emitted document assert, and what does it ask a human to supply that the platform already knows?* |
| **Fix** | `Incident` maps the eight cyber → PDPL bridge columns **read-only** (`insertable = false, updatable = false` + `@Setter(AccessLevel.NONE)`) · one predicate `Incident#isPiiConfirmed()` · `renderDataOfficeBody` and `renderHrsdBody` carry the stored values, with `notAssessed(...)` so an unassessed count renders as absent and never as `0` · every template carries `piiClassification` · `phaseSnapshot` carries the classification beside the notification stamp · `IncidentResponse` + `IncidentDto` declare it, `IncidentRequest` deliberately does not · new `PdplClassificationWireContractTest` |
| **Verified** | read-only probe **16/16 pre-fix**, **22/22 post-fix** as `so_officer` (the last three plant their own victim and prove the column, not just the response, is untouched) · pre-fix control reverts four production sources + one fixture, recompiles, and **14 discriminating legs fire**, `javap` checked both ways, 32/32 after restore · harness **13 killed / 0 survived / 0 anchor-miss** · backend **4464/0/0** · frontend `tsc` clean, 76 files / 818 tests · browser confirms incident 1 renders `DATA SUBJECTS AFFECTED (EST.): 1450` with a `badge-danger` badge, and an unclassified incident a **neutral** one |

### The route in, and why it is a different question from F2-280's

[[F2-280]] closed one member of its 26-entity subset-mapping census and filed the rest. Its
sharpest unread entry was *"`cyber.incidents`' eight unmapped PDPL columns and the mirror five on
`privacy.data_breaches` — both ends of the cyber → PDPL bridge, written by
`CyberPdplBridgeService`'s deliberate native SQL and readable by nothing else."*

Re-derived first ([[F2-221]]), the filing's list is exactly right and its **category** was
understated. Measured against `sys.columns` in both databases:

| | dev | prod |
|---|---|---|
| `cyber.incidents` columns / mapped by `Incident` | 39 / 30 | 39 / 30 |
| rows | 44 | 48 |
| classified as affecting personal data | 2 | 2 |
| `privacy.data_breaches` columns | 27 | 25 (V387 pending) |

`affects_personal_data` is **`smallint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0`**, so it is F2-280's **kind 1** — the
category where the database default decides the value — not the kind-2 *"populated and unmapped,
invisible rather than wrong"* the filing implied. Here the default happens to be **correct** (a new
incident affects no personal data until somebody classifies it), which is why the mapping is
`insertable = false`: leaving the column out of Hibernate's INSERT is what lets the default apply.

🔑 **The cost was not that the classification was invisible. The cost was in a document that
leaves the platform.**

### The emitted notification

`IncidentService#regulatoryTemplates` builds five Saudi regulator notifications, each with its own
deadline, submission channel and a `prefilledBody` the operator copies out. `IncidentsPage` renders
all five with a per-template *"mark notified"* button, so this is a routed, reachable, rendered
surface — not dark code.

Before the fix, `renderDataOfficeBody` was:

```
BREACH NOTIFICATION — PDPL Article 20
INCIDENT TITLE / DISCOVERED AT / NATURE OF BREACH / SEVERITY
LIKELY CONSEQUENCES: <to be completed by DPO>
MITIGATION ACTIONS: <to be completed>
DPO CONTACT: <to be completed>
DESCRIPTION: …
```

Nothing about how many people were affected, and nothing about what kind of personal data — while
`data_subjects_affected_est` and `data_categories_affected` sat on the row being rendered.

🔑 **This is a new rung under [[F2-199]]'s harm ladder rather than a repeat of it.** F2-199 and
[[F2-209]] were about a document asserting things the platform had *invented*. This one asserts
nothing false; it **omits what the platform knows** and asks a human to supply it by hand — and a
hand-typed count can disagree with the record it was supposed to come from, on the notification
that starts a 72-hour statutory clock.

The HRSD body is the same defect one degree sharper, because it names the gap out loud:

```
DATA CATEGORIES AFFECTED: <e.g. salary, ID, contract>
EMPLOYEES AFFECTED: <count>
```

Three placeholders were **kept**, and the difference is the point ([[F2-209]]'s third state):
likely consequences, mitigation actions and the DPO contact have **no column anywhere**, so there
is nothing to fill them from. A placeholder over a column that exists is a defect; a placeholder
over a column that does not exist is a disclosure.

### The applicability question the platform could answer and asked anyway

`applicabilityHint` is prose for a human to judge — *"For SAMA-licensed financial institutions"*,
*"For telecom and cloud-provider customers"*, *"If the breach affects employee personal or payroll
data"*. That is **right** for SAMA, CITC and HRSD: the platform cannot know whether its tenant is a
bank. It is wrong for PDPL Article 20, which is exactly the question `affects_personal_data`
answers, on the row, stored, since V-whatever created the column.

Probed live: a non-PII incident is offered the Article 20 notification and flagged **overdue**.

⚠⚠ **The template is still offered and `overdue` is unchanged, and that withdrawal is asserted in
both directions.** Suppressing the notification for an unclassified incident would convert *"nobody
has assessed this yet"* into a clean bill on a statutory clock — and under-scoping a statutory
obligation is the finding an examiner writes up ([[F2-196]]), while [[F2-197]] is the rule that an
invented all-clear closes a question an invented figure would merely raise. What ships is the
classification **carried** (`piiClassification: CONFIRMED | NOT_CLASSIFIED`) and disclosed on the
Article 20 card as a neutral *"not yet assessed"* badge rather than a green one. A one-directional
gate would let a later reader add the suppression as an apparent improvement, so
`theClassificationIsCarriedAndDoesNotSuppressATemplate` asserts that no template is conditional and
that all five are still built.

### Read-only, and why that is stronger than a guard

The eight columns are mapped `insertable = false, updatable = false`. The classification is a
privacy-module decision, so putting a writable mapping on the incident entity would create a way to
forge a PDPL classification from an incident-module route — [[F2-213]]'s family, latent rather than
absent.

Each also carries **`@Setter(AccessLevel.NONE)`**, which is the **first use of that idiom in this
codebase** (0 of 432 entities used it). The reason is worth the eight lines: a Lombok setter over a
non-updatable column compiles, runs and **silently does nothing** — the decoy shape [[F2-184]]
named, because it answers the question a reader was about to ask. Suppressing it makes the write a
**compile error**, which is stronger than any gate and cannot rot.

⚙ The cost is visible in the test fixture: `classified(...)` has to use
`ReflectionTestUtils.setField`, because **no production API can build that state**. That is the
honest shape rather than a workaround — only `CyberPdplBridgeService`'s native SQL may write these,
and a fixture that reaches past the API is documenting exactly that.

### One predicate, because F2-280 measured what a second copy costs

Four surfaces ask *"is this incident classified as affecting personal data?"* — the Article 20 body,
the HRSD body, the template applicability and the response DTO. `Incident#isPiiConfirmed()` is the
only comparison, and `theClassificationIsComparedInExactlyOnePlace` holds it at exactly one in the
entity and zero in the service. One slice earlier, F2-280 measured what the alternative costs: two
readers of one governance fact, disagreeing on 12 roles in dev and 7 in prod.

⚠ Its first draft was `affectsPersonalData\s*(?:!=|==|>|<)` and **failed on the correct code**,
because `isPiiConfirmed()` is `affectsPersonalData != null && affectsPersonalData != 0` — two
matches, one of them a null check. A gate that fails on correct code trains the next reader to edit
the assertion rather than the code ([[F2-214]]), so the pattern is now scoped to a comparison
against a **numeric literal**: the shape of its claim, not the field's name.

### What the census could not see, and what it did

The eight columns were written by **one** writer and read by **none** — grep over the whole backend
and the whole frontend returned zero readers outside `CyberPdplBridgeService` itself. So no
reachability, provenance or wire-contract instrument in the tree could have surfaced this:

- `apiClientMethodReachability` resolves API-client methods — the bridge's client exists and is called.
- `pageDataProvenance` asks whether a page calls a server — `IncidentsPage` does.
- `exportProvenance` asks whether an emitting file has server data in scope — it does, and
  [[F2-203]]/[[F2-205]] sharpened that to *which* data reaches the emission, which is also satisfied:
  the body genuinely is built from the loaded row. **The row simply did not carry the fields.**
- `PrivacyWireContractTest` adjudicates the privacy DTOs against their entity ([[F2-211]]'s *the wire
  nominates, `sys.columns` adjudicates*). This is the **mirror** case: the column exists, is
  populated, and no wire nominates it — so there was nothing for that instrument to adjudicate.

🔑 **That last one is the reusable shape. [[F2-211]] built an instrument for "the DTO declares a
field the table does not have." The inverse — "the table has a populated column no DTO declares" —
is F2-198's shape, and it is only findable by starting from the TABLE.** F2-280's census is that
starting point, which is why this finding came out of it rather than out of any gate.

### Found in the browser after every gate was green, and it was mine

The badge and both bodies rendered correctly, and the Article 20 line read:

```
PERSONAL DATA AFFECTED: CONFIRMED (classified 2026-05-07T14:29:52.134)
```

`LocalDateTime.toString()`, two lines under `DISCOVERED AT: 2026-04-05`, on a document going to a
regulator — a raw ISO stamp with milliseconds beside a plain date, on an Arabic-primary platform.
[[F2-209]] recorded this exact blemish on the SDAIA console (*"the awareness timestamp printing raw
`2026-08-14T12:21:45` beside localised dates everywhere else"*), and I introduced it in the line I
added. 🔑 **Nth consecutive slice where the browser finds something no code-scoped gate can see —
and the first where the thing it found was written by the slice itself.** Fixed to
`.toLocalDate()`, pinned by an assertion that the body contains no `T`-separated stamp at all
rather than by asserting the corrected string alone.

### A second gate fired, and it was right to

Mapping the columns made `pii_classified_by` visible to [[F2-256]]'s
`UnwritableActorColumnContractTest` — an actor column no Java writer sets — and the full build
failed on it. That is two instruments in series, the second becoming *able* to see the column
because the first mapped it, which is [[F2-236]]'s recorded rule (*after converting an
attribution, run the other gate*).

The verdict is BY DESIGN and it names something worth keeping: the column **is** written, by the
bridge's native `UPDATE`, in the **same statement** as `pii_classified_at`. So unlike every other
member of that map the clock and the actor have one owner and neither is blank. It reads as
unwritable because the derivation resolves **setters** — F2-256 recorded Jackson as the one write
mechanism bytecode cannot see, and **native SQL is the second**. And the absence of a setter here
is the *fix*, not the defect.

### Measured in passing, and filed

- **CORRECTED after the residue sweep — one anomaly, not three.** The first draft of this item read
  *"The bridge log and the register disagree, in both databases … 8 rows claiming three bridge
  firings and one link; the incident register shows two classifications … Byte-identical across two
  independently-used databases, so seed-origin."* Arithmetically right and **wrongly attributed**,
  and the residue sweep is what showed it. Re-measured row by row against both databases including
  soft-deleted rows:
  - Log rows **1–5** are correct and fully consistent: incidents 1 and 4 classified, breaches 6 and
    7 created and back-referenced, one legitimate `BRIDGE_SKIPPED` re-evaluation.
  - Log rows **7–8** name incident 24, which in prod is `[REVIEW-TEST] CY-B consolidation test` —
    **soft-deleted probe residue from 2026-07-04**, whose breach 20 is also soft-deleted and does
    back-reference it. In dev the same two rows were **hard-deleted**, so the log points at nothing.
    That is not a bridge defect: an audit log **should** outlive the records it describes, and
    `cyber_breach_bridge_log` carries no FK precisely so it can. 🔑 **The dangling reference is a
    difference in how two cleanups were done, and calling it seed-origin because the two databases
    agree was the error — they agree because the LOG was never cleaned in either.**
  - Row **6** is the one real anomaly and it stands: event code **`BREACH_LINKED`, written by no
    code path in the platform** (the service writes only `BRIDGE_FIRED`, `BREACH_CREATED`,
    `BRIDGE_SKIPPED`), naming incident 2 ↔ breach 1 where **neither side carries a link**
    (`linked_data_breach_id` NULL, `source_cyber_incident_id` NULL, `auto_generated = 0`).
    Byte-identical in both databases at 2026-05-09 13:23, so seed-origin. **Owner decision.**
  🔑 **The reusable part: "the two databases agree, so it is seed data" (F2-280's evidence rule) is
  sound for a WRITTEN value and unsound for a DANGLING one — a reference both databases fail to
  resolve may simply be one nobody cleaned up in either.**
- **Pre-existing `[REVIEW-TEST]` residue in the PRODUCTION database, from earlier slices.** Measured
  while sweeping this one: **11 columns across 9 prod tables** carry the tag, including
  ⚠ **Corrected by [[F2-285]]'s sweep, 2026-08-22: that figure counted the tables this entry
  goes on to NAME. The full sweep of every text column says 19 columns across 12 tables,
  21 rows in 10 registers** — the omissions are `cyber.incidents.description`,
  `cyber.incidents.personal_data_pii_assessment`, `evidence.evidence_request_comments.body`,
  `socops.security_event.rule_name`, `.source_system`, and the two append-only trail tables
  (`platform.audit_log` 145 messages, `platform.notifications` 11). The newest tagged register
  row is `risk.risks` at **2026-07-06** and the newest tagged prod audit message is
  **2026-07-09**, so the dating holds and nothing since has added to it. 🔑 **A count produced
  by naming what you can see measures your own enumeration** — print the sweep's total beside
  it. ⚙ The DEV half of the same sweep is the control worth keeping: **11 columns and ZERO
  register rows**, every hit append-only trail, which cannot be cleaned without deleting audit
  history — so a non-zero dev column count is not by itself residue.
  `cyber.incidents.title` ×4 (all soft-deleted, all created 2026-07-04 by `admin` — the CY-B / CY-C
  / SOC-C probes), `cyber.cyber_action_plans.description_en` ×4, `cyber.cyber_incidents.title_en` ×2,
  `socops.security_event.external_id` ×2, and one row each in `capa.tasks` (already filed by
  [[F2-275]]), `cyber.vulnerabilities`, `cyber.vuln_exceptions`, `privacy.data_breaches` and
  `risk.risks`. None is from this slice — every script here targeted `TSS_GRC` and `:8084`. Removing
  a row from a customer database needs the user's explicit OK (house rule 6), so this is **reported,

- **A dangling parent-identity copy.** Incident 13 carries `linked_data_breach_code =

  data exfiltration — DLP triggered"*, in `CONTAINMENT`. The code is lower-case where the bridge's
  two are upper-case, so it was not written by the bridge, and it resolves to no breach in either
  database. [[F2-245]]'s shape with the id absent — and it means one row simultaneously says *"no
  personal data"* and *"here is the PDPL breach record"*. **Owner decision.**
- **No non-admin persona can operate the bridge.** `POST /api/privacy/cyber-bridge/trigger` demands
  `PRIVACY:WRITE` **and** `CYBER:WRITE`. `so_officer` is the CISO, holds `CYBER:WRITE` and
  `INCIDENT:WRITE`, and is **403 even on the bridge log** ([[F2-209]] measured that CISO holds no
  PRIVACY grant at all). So the classification that feeds the Article 20 notification is reachable
  only by the platform administrator — [[F2-253]]'s shape, at the intersection of two permissions.
- **The trigger form asks an operator to type a raw numeric incident id** (`kind: 'number', required:
  true`), with no picker — [[F2-246]]'s collect-a-label-instead-of-a-link shape, and

- **All five notification bodies are English-only**, on an Arabic-primary platform whose SDAIA
  portal is Arabic (house rule 7). Pre-existing across the whole family, not introduced here.
- `privacy.data_breaches` still has `title_ar`/`description_ar` in dev only (V387 is one of the 47

## F2-282 · Three readers of one BIA register, two orderings and three null behaviours — and a `default` method would have hidden the fix from every test that mocks the repository

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | 🟢 CLOSED 2026-08-22 (`bb59b2bf`) |
| **Severity** | **P3 (latent, and it gates an ISO 22301 control)** — a process can carry several BIA records and two of the ten live ones do. All three readers of `BiaRecordRepository#findByProcessIdIn` chose one per process with a hand-rolled loop, and the three loops disagreed on the ordering *and* on what to do with a null MTPD. RTO ≤ MTPD by definition, so the reader a control consults decides whether a continuity plan is compliant — and the vendor-inheritance control asks exactly that of a supplier's attested recovery time. They coincide on every live row today, which is what made it invisible |
| **Found by** | asking F2-196's question of `bcm.bia_records` — *how many things read this, and do they agree?* — after F2-280 filed `bcm.critical_processes`' unmapped MTPD/RTO/RPO. Measured **nine** MTPD columns across `bcm`/`bcm_lc`, then read the three services that share one |
| **Fix** | `module/bcm/service/BiaObjectives.authoritativeByProcess(...)` — one pure function, lowest stated MTPD, a row stating one always beating a row that does not · all three callers ask it · `ImpactRow`/`CascadeImpactRow` gain `mtpdSourceStatus` so an unapproved objective is visible · new `BiaObjectiveSelectionSharingTest` |
| **Verified** | live read-only probe **14/14** as `compliance` + `rmanager` (13 impact rows across 3 cascades, every objective and status matching the lowest-MTPD BIA) · pre-fix control reverts the three callers and **2 of 8 legs fire**, `javap` checked, 8/8 after restore · backend **4473/0/0** · frontend `tsc` clean · `MtpdInheritanceServiceTest` passes **unchanged**, which is the tell that the second design was right |

### Route in, and two redirections that are part of the finding

[[F2-281]] filed two items. Re-deriving the first ([[F2-221]]) **weakened my own filing**: it said
*"no non-admin persona can operate the bridge at all"* — true — while omitting that `ORG_ADMIN`
holds **both** `PRIVACY:WRITE` and `CYBER:WRITE` and merely has no live holder. That is
[[F2-253]]'s distinction, which the filing failed to apply: a role nobody holds has an
administrator remedy, and a permission nobody can hold does not. Measured, every alternative grant
is too wide — `DPO`/`PRIVACY_MANAGER`/`GRC_ADMINISTRATOR` would gain the **18-role** cyber write
surface, `CISO`/`SECURITY_ANALYST` the whole privacy write surface including the DSR queue. So it
is a narrower finding than filed, with a remedy, and the filing is corrected rather than executed.

Then I asked F2-281's *question* of the whole emitting population — *what does a document ask a
human to supply that the platform already knows?* Census: **36 placeholder literals in 19 files**.
Refined to placeholders that instruct a human rather than HTML tags or `nullSafe` fallbacks, the
population is essentially `IncidentService` **alone**, and F2-281 already closed the only two with
a column behind them; the remaining seven are [[F2-209]]'s third state. 🔑 **A generalisation that
returns nothing new is a result, not a dead end** ([[F2-216]]) — and saying so is what stops the
next reader re-running it.

### Nine columns for three objectives

Measured against `sys.columns` in both databases, MTPD alone lives in nine places:

| column | rows | values |
|---|---|---|
| `bcm.bia_records.mtpd_hours` | 10/10 | **72, 168, 336, 1** |
| `bcm.bia_assessments.mtpd_hours` | 8/8 | 8, 12, 24, 48, 72, 216 |
| `bcm_lc.bia_records.mtpd_hours` | 8/8 | 8, 24, 12 |
| `bcm.bcp_plans.mtpd_hours` | 10/10 | 8, 12, 24 |
| `bcm.dr_plans.mtpd_hours` | 16/17 | 8, 24, 48 |
| `bcm.mtpd_inheritance_finding.process_mtpd_hours` | 8/8 | 4, 4, 8, 8 |
| `bcm.plan_templates.default_mtpd_hours` | 8/8 | 24, 8, 48, 120 |
| `bcm.bia_quantitative.mtpd_breach_at` | 1/1 | **`'72h'` — an `nvarchar`** |
| **`bcm.critical_processes.mtpd_hours`** | **0/10** | the canonical register, unmapped ([[F2-280]]'s filed item, confirmed) |

⚠ Two hypotheses were **refuted** before the real one landed, and both refutations matter.
`BcmBiaAssessmentService` *does* enforce ISO 22301 — `validateRtoMtpd` blocks the `APPROVED`
transition when RTO > MTPD — and it reads both from **one entity**, so it is internally sound.
And the two selection rules that do differ **agree on all 8 processes today**, because in both
multi-BIA cases the latest record also happens to be the lowest. The divergence is latent.

### Three copies of one decision

| reader | ordering | a null MTPD |
|---|---|---|
| `DependencyCascadeService` | lowest | may seed the map, then replaced by any non-null row |
| `BcmBoardPackService` | lowest | **`continue`d past** — a process whose only BIA left MTPD blank was *absent from the board pack* rather than present with no objective |
| `MtpdInheritanceService` | **latest by `assessmentDate`** | filtered only **after** selecting — so a blank MTPD on the most recent record cost the process its objective entirely, and the vendor gap became unmeasurable |

🔑 **What made it harmless was three independent implementations happening to coincide, and nobody
was maintaining that** ([[F2-177]]). The rule chosen is **lowest stated MTPD**, by measurement
rather than taste: two of the three already did it, it is the conservative direction, and adopting
it changes nothing on either live database.

⚠ The cascade's own javadoc said step 3 uses *"first-found ordering"*. **False** — it has always
preferred the lowest. The comment understated the code, which is the safe direction to be wrong in,
and it is corrected rather than deleted because the ordering is the whole reason a process with two
BIAs gets a defensible answer ([[F2-184]]'s shape, benign variant).

🔑 **And the comment that named these three callers was mine.** [[F2-279]]'s
`BiaRecordRepository` javadoc enumerates all three and asks only the **tenant** question of them.
[[F2-215]]'s two-of-N inside a comment: a reader who finds the callers listed and one question
answered does not then ask what the other question is.

### The design correction, which is the reusable part

⚠⚠ The first draft put the predicate on `BiaRecordRepository` as a **`default` method**. It
compiled, it passed all eight of its own legs — and it **broke two existing
`MtpdInheritanceServiceTest` cases**, because **a Mockito mock does not execute default methods**.
The mocked repository answered nothing, the stubbed `findByProcessIdIn` went unused (surfacing as
`UnnecessaryStubbing`) and the resolved MTPD silently became empty.

🔑🔑 **A decision placed on a mockable interface is a decision every test that mocks that interface
silently loses.** [[F2-237]]'s family — *a mocked collaborator answers, and then the test is
asserting the mock* — at a new site, and the failure mode is the dangerous direction: had those two
tests not existed, the predicate would have shipped returning nothing under every mock in the tree.

A static function over a supplied list has no such hole: the callers keep their existing query, so
**the two tests then passed unchanged**, which is the tell that the second design was right rather
than merely different. `theRepositoryDeclaresNoDecision` keeps it off the interface.

### What is deliberately not fixed

⚠⚠ Neither the old loops nor the new predicate consults `status`, and **4 of 8 processes resolve to
an unapproved BIA**. For `Core Banking Operations` (CRITICAL) the winner is an `IN_PROGRESS` record
stating MTPD **1h** over an `APPROVED` one stating **72h** — a 72× difference on the process a
Saudi bank's continuity plan is built around. `bcm.bia_records` has **zero CHECK constraints** and
holds `APPROVED` 6 / `IN_PROGRESS` 2 / `UNDER_REVIEW` 1 / `DRAFT` 1.

Preferring the approved row would make these controls report **less** disruption on a customer's
data, and nothing here can tell whether 1h or 72h is that organisation's real tolerance — 72 hours
for core banking is implausible, which is itself a reason to think the *draft* is the better number
and the approved figure is stale seed data. So the status is put **on the wire**
(`mtpdSourceStatus`, disclosed on every cascade impact row) and the choice is filed.
🔑 [[F2-197]]: disclose, never manufacture an all-clear — and a control reporting less risk is
exactly the change that must not be a side effect of a de-duplication.

### My own errors, both caught by running things

⚠ The gate's detector had **two loose alternatives**, one of them
`(?:<|>)\s*\w+\.getMtpdHours\(\)` — and **a Java lambda arrow contains a `>`**, so
`.filter(b -> b.getMtpdHours() != null)` matched and the gate failed on the correct code this slice
had just written. A gate that fails on correct code trains the next reader to edit the assertion
rather than the code ([[F2-214]]). Requiring the getter on **both** sides is the pattern's actual
claim, and the two lambda shapes are now must-not-match cases.

⚠ The pre-fix control initially reverted the repository too, so the test referenced a method that
did not exist and the control **failed to compile** — and a control that cannot run reads exactly
like a gate that passed ([[F2-278]]/[[F2-212]]). Rescoped to the three callers it fires **2 of 8**;
the other six are the predicate's own unit tests, the detector self-test with its positive and
negative controls, and the written-once pin on the file the control deliberately keeps ([[F2-225]] —
name which legs discriminate rather than counting green).

⚠ And the probe guessed a route again: `/api/v1/bcm/mtpd-inheritance/dependencies` is
`/api/v1/bcm/process-vendor-dependencies`, and `/assessments` is guarded
`hasAnyRole('BCM_MANAGER','RISK_MANAGER','CISO','AUDITOR','PLATFORM_ADMIN')` — so `compliance`
getting **403 was correct behaviour**, not a defect. Resolve routes and guards from the controller
(the recurring landmine since [[F2-198]]); the corrected probe asserts that 403 as a leg.

### Measured in passing, and filed

- **`bcm.critical_processes.{mtpd,rto,rpo}_hours` — NULL on all 10 rows, unmapped.** The canonical
  process register states none of the three ISO 22301 objectives; every reader goes to a BIA
  instead. F2-280's filed item, confirmed and still open: mapping columns that are empty everywhere
  would be an inert mapping ([[F2-184]]), so this needs a product decision about whether the
  process or the BIA owns the objective.
- **Two live BIAs per process for the two most critical processes**, differing 72× and 168×
  (`Core Banking Operations` 72h/1h, `Customer Onboarding` 168h/1h), identical in dev and prod.
  Whether both should exist is an owner decision; the platform has no uniqueness constraint and no
  supersede path on that register.
- **`bcm.bia_assessments.process_id` is NULL on all 8 rows**, so the register the ISO 22301
  RTO ≤ MTPD gate guards is linked to **no process at all** and no process appears in both BIA
  registers. F2-196's disjoint-register shape, and the reason the gate's own soundness does not help
  the three readers.
- **`bcm.mtpd_inheritance_finding.process_mtpd_hours` holds 4/4/8/8** — matching neither the lowest
  nor the latest BIA for those processes, so the stored SAMA-outsourcing findings are stale seed
  values and a recompute moves them. For process 1 it would go 4h → 1h, widening the gap against
  vendor 8 from 4h to 7h and turning vendor 3's `INFO` into a finding.
- **`DependencyCascadeService` has no test of any kind** ([[F2-248]]), which is why the detector plus
  its controls carries the weight for that caller.
- `MtpdInheritanceController` guards five routes with `hasAnyRole(...)` naming **`BCM_MANAGER`**, the
  zero-holder role [[F2-253]]/[[F2-254]] measured — another F2-05 conversion site, not this slice.
- **F2-281's bridge filing, corrected**: `ORG_ADMIN` holds both required permissions and has no live
  holder, so there is an administrator remedy; every alternative grant is too wide.

## F2-283 · Six hypotheses refuted, one untested service — the value of the slice was the refutations, and the work was the test nobody had written

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | 🟢 CLOSED 2026-08-22 (`f7d7e5e8`) |
| **Severity** | **P4 (two latent defects closed, one untested read aggregator covered)** — `DependencyCascadeService` had **no test of any kind**, and [[F2-282]] had just changed how it selects a process's recovery objectives, leaving a source-scanning detector as the only thing watching it. Writing the test found two latent defects: a **soft-deleted process could conduct the cascade** to the live consumers behind it, and **`SOVEREIGN` ranked below `LOW`** in the criticality tiebreak |
| **Found by** | executing [[F2-282]]'s filings and disbelieving each in turn ([[F2-221]]). Every substantive hypothesis fell; the one unambiguous gap left was the missing test, and writing it is what surfaced the two latent defects |
| **Fix** | `DependencyCascadeService`: the BFS no longer enqueues a consumer absent from the tenant's process register, and `criticalityRank` knows `SOVEREIGN` (5) with the unknown-token case documented as a decision · new `DependencyCascadeServiceTest`, 15 tests |
| **Verified** | per-fix control reverts each change **separately** and each one's leg fires (two-at-once cannot tell which leg catches which defect) · 15/15 after restore · backend **4488/0/0** · live probe **14/14 unchanged** — the two changes are provably inert on this data (0 affected rows), so the probe is a no-regression check and says so |

### The refutations, which are the substance

Six hypotheses, measured in both databases and all **refuted**. Recording them is the
point: each one is a thing the next reader should not re-derive.

| hypothesis | measured | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `bia_assessments.approval_status = 'ACTIVE'` on 2 rows is unmovable ([[F2-203]]'s shape) | the machine declares `DRAFT → UNDER_REVIEW → APPROVED → ACTIVE → ARCHIVED`, and `ACTIVE` has two outgoing edges | **refuted** — all four stored values are declared |
| `overall_criticality = 'SOVEREIGN'` is a *tier* value in a criticality column | the javadoc declares it (*"if `national_sovereign ≥ 4`, criticality → SOVEREIGN"*) and there is a `BIA_CRITICALITY_SOVEREIGN` event | **refuted** — it is the top of that vocabulary |
| `recomputeCriticality` erases a classification when the matrix is empty (it *does* set null, under a comment reading *"leave criticality null"*) | **0 of 8** rows carry a criticality without a matrix behind it | **refuted as live** — latent only |
| the duplicate `bia_code` `BIA-2026-000007` means no uniqueness | `UX_bia_assessments_org_code` is unique on `(organisation_id, bia_code)` **filtered `WHERE is_deleted = 0`**, and one of the pair is soft-deleted | **refuted** — and it is [[F2-266]]'s filtered-index rule applied correctly |
| dev has uniqueness/CHECK invariants prod can never get ([[F2-255]]'s bootstrap-only shape, at the schema) | **12 dev-only unique indexes and 39 dev-only CHECKs, and every single one is created by a migration** — zero orphans | **refuted** — the 47-migration deployment gap explains all of it |
| a soft-deleted process conducts the cascade *today* | **0** dependency edges name a deleted or nonexistent process, in either database | **refuted as live** — latent, and fixed anyway |

🔑 **The fifth is the one worth keeping.** `UX_bia_assessments_org_code` is created by
`V366__deployed_schema_missing_uniqueness_and_rto_check.sql` — a migration whose *name* says a
prior slice already found prod was missing it. The gap is pending deployment, not a hole.
⚙ And the diff produced **2 "prod-only" unique indexes** that are not differences at all:
`UQ__framewor__357D4CF9…` and `UQ__nafath_t__85C600AE…` are **auto-named** constraints whose
system-generated suffix differs per database. 🔑 **A schema diff keyed on constraint NAME reports
every auto-named constraint as a difference** — key on (table, columns, filter) or accept the noise
knowingly.

### The work: a read aggregator with no test

`DependencyCascadeService` answers *"if core banking fails at 09:00, what breaches by 13:00?"* —
BFS over `bcm.process_dependencies`, a depth-weighted reach hour, a breach verdict against each
process's MTPD (or RTO when MTPD is absent), cumulative 1h/4h/8h/24h bands and a confidence ladder.
None of it was asserted anywhere. [[F2-248]]'s rule: **a path with no test is not a path somebody
decided was safe** — and [[F2-282]] had just changed its BIA selection, with only a
source-scanning detector watching this caller.

### Two latent defects the test surfaced

**A soft-deleted process could conduct the cascade.** The BFS enqueued each consumer *before*
checking it was in `processById`, which comes from the tenant's process register and so excludes
soft-deleted rows. The row was correctly dropped from the **output** (`if (p == null) continue`) —
it had already been enqueued, so it propagated reach to whatever sat behind it, and *its* depth set
*their* depth. A decommissioned business process still conducting a dependency cascade. Latent: 0
edges name a deleted process. Closed anyway, because what made it harmless was the data
([[F2-182]]).

**`SOVEREIGN` ranked below `LOW`.** `criticalityRank` knew CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW and defaulted
everything else to 0, so the platform's own top tier sorted *last* in its tie group.
`bcm.critical_processes.criticality` has **no CHECK**, so nothing stops the value being stored
there. ⚠ The unknown case still ranks 0 and that is now a **documented decision** rather than an
oversight: this is a tiebreak within one breach-and-depth group, so "unclassified sorts after
classified" is honest, and inventing a rank for a word the platform does not define would be worse.
It matters because unrecognised criticality words do exist in this schema —
`bcm.bia_records.criticality` stores `TIER_2`/`TIER_3` beside `CRITICAL`/`HIGH`/`MEDIUM`
([[F2-279]] measured it) and neither column is constrained.

### What the test pins that nothing did

BFS records the **shallowest** depth (a shortcut edge wins over a long chain); a cycle back to the
source terminates; the walk stops at `MAX_DEPTH = 6`; the depth→hour ladder is 1/4/8/24 with
everything past depth 3 at 24; confidence is 1.0/0.75/0.5/0.25; breach is `reachHour >= threshold`
so a 2h tolerance survives a 1h reach; **RTO substitutes for a missing MTPD**, which is the
conservative direction since RTO ≤ MTPD by definition; a process with no BIA is reported and
**never breached**, because claiming a breach would invent a tolerance nobody recorded; the hour
bands are cumulative and the widest equals the total; the sort is breach-then-depth-then-criticality;
and — [[F2-282]]'s disclosure, end to end — **the objective and `mtpdSourceStatus` describe the same
BIA row**, which is what makes the disclosure worth having rather than worse than none.

⚠ Each fix's control was run **separately**. Reverting both at once cannot tell which leg catches
which defect, and a leg that fires for the wrong reason is a leg you do not have.

### Filed

- **`bcm.bia_assessments` has six declared link columns nothing populates** — `process_id`,
  `bia_owner_id`, `service_owner_id`, `process_owner_id`, `evidence_id`, `reviewer_id`, all **0/8**
  in both databases. [[F2-280]]'s kind 3 (empty, nullable), so latent; and `process_id` being empty
  is why the register carrying the ISO 22301 `CK_bia_rto_le_mtpd` constraint is joined to no
  process at all, while the register three services *do* read has no such constraint.
- **`bcm.bia_assessments.service_id = -1`** on one live DRAFT row, and **`bcm` has no service table
  of any kind**, so the column references a register that does not exist. The same row duplicates a
  soft-deleted `bia_code` and has `department = '-'`, so it reads as seed residue — but nothing
  validates the reference, and a negative id is not a plausible key.
- **`bcm.critical_processes` has zero CHECK constraints**, so `criticality` is narrowed only by the
  Java ladders that read it — and two of those ladders (this one and `bia_records.criticality`'s)
  use different vocabularies.
- The **auto-named-constraint blind spot** in any schema diff keyed on name.

## F2-284 · F2-230's gate keys on SQL, so every hand-rolled Java rank ladder was outside it — and my own census manufactured a ladder that does not exist

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | 🟢 CLOSED 2026-08-22 (`394376fb`) |
| **Severity** | **P4 (instrument gap, no product defect found)** — [[F2-230]] built `OrderedVocabulary` for the question *is this ordered vocabulary being sorted lexically?* and its gate keys on **SQL**: derived `OrderBy…` query names and `CASE … END DESC` inside `@Query`. A **Java** `switch (token) { case "CRITICAL" -> 4; … }` is invisible to it by construction. [[F2-283]] is what that cost — `criticalityRank` ranked `SOVEREIGN` below `LOW`, and it took writing that service's first unit test to find it |
| **Found by** | executing [[F2-283]]'s filing (*two Java ladders read a criticality column with different vocabularies*) and asking the general question: how many such ladders exist, and do they agree? |
| **Fix** | new `JavaRankLadderCensusTest` — derives every Java token→int ladder from source and holds **7** of them as exact maps, with the duration/multiplier subtraction pinned in both directions. **No production change**: nothing it found was a defect |
| **Verified** | control deletes F2-283's `SOVEREIGN` arm and the census fails naming the exact diff — *"expected {SOVEREIGN=5, CRITICAL=4, …} but is {CRITICAL=4, …}"* — so this gate would have caught that defect the day the ladder was written · 4/4 after restore · backend **4492/0/0** |

### The seven refutations that preceded it

This slice began by re-deriving F2-283's filing and every product-level hypothesis fell. Recorded so
the next reader does not re-derive them:

- **`MtpdInheritanceService#severityRank` is correct.** It is documented *"lower rank = more
  urgent"* and used with `comparingInt` **ascending**, so `CRITICAL = 0` sorts first. Inverted
  relative to the cascade's ladder and **not** a defect — the direction is part of the ladder.
- **Its repository query `…OrderBySeverityAsc` is lexical and harmless**, because the service
  re-sorts the stream with `severityRank()` before returning. It is the exemplar of the safe form.
- **The four lexical graded sorts with no Java re-sort are all `AutomationRule.priority`, which is
  `int`** — and for a numeric column a lexical sort *is* a correct numeric sort ([[F2-230]] recorded
  that 4 of its 10 candidates were numeric for the same reason).
- **`ThreatIntelCorrelationService#severityRank` correctly has no `SOVEREIGN`** — that is a BCM
  national-criticality tier, not a threat-intel severity band. The absence is right.

🔑 **And the four "inverted pairs" that looked sharpest were my detector, not the code.**
`TenableInboundService.slaDays` is `CRITICAL=0, HIGH=0, MEDIUM=1, LOW=3`;
`CyberAssessmentService.dueDaysForRisk` is `LOW=60, HIGH=14, CRITICAL=7`. Both read as inverted
ranks and both are **days**. `RiskExposureService.effectivenessFactor` is a multiplier. Counting
those as ranks produced **11 "inverted pairs", almost all noise**. [[F2-268]] recorded the same rule
one noun over — *a COUNT of days is not a deadline* — and here it is **a duration is not a rank**.
That subtraction is now a gate leg with its own reverse direction, so an entry excluded as a
duration must still *be* a ladder in the tree and must not have rank-shaped numbers.

### Why an exact map and not a rule

There is no rule to assert. The ladders legitimately differ in **direction** and in **vocabulary**,
so a shared-convention assertion would fail on correct code — the one failure a gate must never have
([[F2-214]]). Each ladder therefore declares its exact token→rank map: adding a token, dropping one
or renumbering fails, and a new ladder fails until it is declared and therefore read. Nothing in it
is prose that can rot.

### My own census manufactured a ladder, and that is the finding

⚠⚠ The first draft resolved the enclosing method with a pattern matching only an **int-returning**
signature. A ladder inside a method returning anything else resolved to `"?"`, and every unnamed
ladder in one file then collapsed into **one bucket** — fusing `WorkflowRequestService`'s two
unrelated switches, `hopVia`'s candidate order (`SUBMITTED=0, RESUBMITTED=1`) and the WF-9 quorum
**threshold** (`ANY=1, MAJORITY=(total/2)+1`), into a phantom vocabulary
`{ANY, RESUBMITTED, SUBMITTED}` that exists nowhere in the codebase.

🔑🔑 **It did not merely mislabel a ladder — it manufactured one.** With methods resolving, `hopVia`
has **two** tokens and the quorum switch has **one** integer-literal arm (`MAJORITY` and `QUORUM`
map to expressions, not literals), so both sit below the three-token threshold and **neither is a
ladder at all**. Fused, they summed *past* it. **A phantom merge is worse than a miss, because a
population that grew looks measured.**

⚠ And `theDerivationFindsAllThreeSyntaxesAndSplitsByMethod` **claims** to guard exactly this — its
fixture simply had three nameable methods, so it could not see the unnameable case. 🔑 **A
self-test that only exercises the resolvable case cannot see the unresolvable one collapsing.**

⚠ The second draft then over-corrected: a signature pattern widened to any return type matches
`return switch (s) {` as type=`return`, name=`switch`, so **every** ladder keyed as `#switch` and all
twelve collapsed into a single bucket. 🔑 **Widening a pattern and excluding what the widening newly
admits are one change, not two.** Keywords are excluded now, and an unresolved ladder is keyed by its
own offset so two can never merge.

⚠ Two of my declared keys were also **guessed method names** — `#ndrProgress` for what is an inline
switch in `dashboard()`, and `#hopVia` for a ladder below the threshold. Both were corrected from the
gate's own output rather than from reading, which is the right direction: **the census is the
authority for what the census contains.**

### The seven ladders

| ladder | vocabulary | direction |
|---|---|---|
| `DependencyCascadeService#criticalityRank` | SOVEREIGN 5 → LOW 1 | higher = worse |
| `MtpdInheritanceService#severityRank` | CRITICAL 0 → LOW 3 | **lower = worse**, used ascending |
| `ThreatIntelCorrelationService#severityRank` | CRITICAL 4 → LOW 1 | higher = worse |
| `CptyService#bandRank` | BREACH 3, RED 2, AMBER 1 | SAMA large-exposure RAG |
| `DataclassService#classOrder` | TOP_SECRET 4 → PUBLIC 1 | NCA/SDAIA classification |
| `ControlMapService#coverageRank` | EXPIRED 2, PARTIAL 1, GAP 0 | staleness |
| `DataOfficerQueryService#dashboard` | ACCEPTED 3, SUBMITTED 2, READY 1 | NDR cycle progress |

⚙ Note what this slice did **not** do: it changed no production code. Every product hypothesis was
refuted, and inventing a change to justify the measurement would have been the error. What ships is
the instrument that makes F2-283's defect class unrepresentable — plus the record of why the
obvious-looking convergence of these seven ladders is not something to enforce.

## F2-285 · The breach end of the cyber→PDPL bridge, and the half a read-only mapping does not cover: unwritable to the database is not absent from the response

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | 🟢 CLOSED 2026-08-22 (`611657d7`) |
| **Severity** | **P3** — five columns on `privacy.data_breaches` written by one native-SQL writer and read by **nothing**: zero references in either tree outside `CyberPdplBridgeService`. On the PDPL Article 20 register an operator could not tell which breaches the bridge raised from a security incident, or which incident — while the bridge's own audit line has always claimed the link is **bidirectional**. And the endpoints **bind the entity**, so mapping them the naive way would have let a caller forge that provenance |
| **Found by** | executing [[F2-281]]'s filing — the mirror columns it left open — after F2-284's filings turned out to be refutations and owner decisions |
| **Fix** | `DataBreach` maps the five **read-only** (`insertable = false, updatable = false` + `@Setter(AccessLevel.NONE)`) · one predicate `isBridgeRaised()` · a `@PrePersist` clears them so the *response* cannot echo a forgery either · `PrivacyBreachDto` declares them and no request type does · `PrivacyBreachDetailPage` discloses provenance bilingually with the incident reference · new `BreachProvenanceWireContractTest` |
| **Verified** | live probe **9/9** as `compliance` against a planted `[REVIEW-TEST]` breach · pre-fix control reverts the entity and the wire and **4 of 8 legs fire**, `javap` checked, 8/8 after restore · backend **4500/0/0** · frontend 818 tests, `tsc` clean |

### The asymmetry F2-281 made visible

The bridge writes both ends and says so — its audit line reads *"DataBreach … created and
**bidirectionally** linked to incident INC-00001"*. Only one end was ever readable. [[F2-281]] put
`linkedDataBreachCode` on the incident's wire, which is what turned a symmetric-looking write into
a visible one-way link: **an incident could name its breach and a breach could name nothing.**

Nor could the bridge log answer it. All three of `CyberBreachBridgeLogRepository`'s finders key on
`cyberIncidentId` and **none on `dataBreachId`** — though the entity has that column and the bridge
writes it. [[F2-178]]'s rule: a report keyed by X cannot answer a question asked from Y. Measured:
**zero** readers of any of the five columns anywhere in the backend or the frontend.

⚙ No new endpoint was added, deliberately. Putting `sourceCyberIncidentId` on the breach's own wire
makes the **existing** `/log/by-incident/{id}` route reachable from a breach, so the asymmetry is
resolved by data rather than by a route that would ship with no client ([[F2-201]] — an unused
client method should not ship).

### Why read-only was required rather than preferred

⚠⚠ `PrivacyController` returns **and binds** the entity: `createBreach(@RequestBody DataBreach req)`.
A writable mapping would let any caller assert *"this breach was auto-generated from cyber incident
N"* — a provenance claim on a PDPL Article 20 statutory record.
`ServerOwnedFieldsModule` covers `BaseEntity`'s nine fields and cannot help.

🔑 **And `createBreach` already hand-scrubs four fields for exactly this reason, with a javadoc
quoting F2-215's headline** — *"fixing the field you noticed leaves the remainder looking covered,
because the mechanism that covers them is visibly present."* **These five ARE that remainder.** They
were invisible only because they were unmapped, so the naive mapping would have created the defect
that comment warns about.

### The half a read-only mapping does not cover

⚠⚠ The probe found it, and it refuted **this slice's own gate leg**. `theCreateStillScrubs…` was
first written to assert that the create must **not** scrub the five, reasoning that they are
unwritable so a scrub would be decoration ([[F2-184]]). Live:

```
POST /api/v1/privacy/breaches  { autoGenerated: 1, sourceCyberIncidentNumber: "INC-FORGED", … }
→ 201  { autoGenerated: 1, sourceCyberIncidentNumber: "INC-FORGED", … }
   row: (0, null, null, null, null)
```

Hibernate refused to **store** it and `createBreach` returns `breachRepo.save(req)` — the caller's
own deserialised instance — so the **response echoed** a provenance the row does not carry. A client
trusting the response body would render the breach as bridge-raised; only a re-fetch shows the
truth.

🔑🔑 **Unwritable to the database is not absent from the response.** That is the reusable sentence,
and the direction matters: the read-only mapping is doing its job perfectly at the column and says
nothing about the object handed back.

⚙ Fixed with a **`@PrePersist` on the entity**, not a scrub in the service, for three reasons that
each make it the smaller change: the five have `@Setter(AccessLevel.NONE)` so no service *can* clear
them; it fires on the same instance the service returns, so the echo is fixed too; and it makes the
invariant the entity's own, so a future create path cannot forget it — F2-215's remainder problem
pre-empted rather than repeated.

⚠ It cannot affect the bridge, and the gate asserts why: `CyberPdplBridgeService` writes both ends
in **native SQL** and never persists an entity, so the only rows the `@PrePersist` touches are
Hibernate-created ones — exactly the ones that must carry no provenance. A leg holds the bridge to
native SQL, because the day it starts persisting a `DataBreach` the `@PrePersist` would silently
erase the fields it is trying to set.

### Filed

- **`CyberBreachBridgeLogRepository` has no by-breach finder.** Now unnecessary for the UI, since
  the breach's own wire carries the incident id — but a caller holding only a breach id still cannot
  page that log directly. Cheap, and it needs a client to justify the route.
- **`auto_generated` is `smallint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0`** and the `@PrePersist` sets it to `null`,
  which the database then defaults to 0 on insert. Correct, and worth knowing: the response for a
  freshly created breach reports `autoGenerated: null` rather than `0`, so a client must treat
  absent-or-zero as "not bridge-raised" — which is what `isBridgeRaised()` does and why it is one
  predicate rather than three inline comparisons.
- The **English-only notification bodies** and the breach `status` vocabulary having no CHECK remain
  as [[F2-209]]/[[F2-281]] filed them; nothing here touched either.
