## F2-387 — an inverted change window (`scheduledStart > scheduledEnd`) bypassed the CH-17 freeze and hid schedule conflicts

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-27 |
| **Severity** | P2 — a missing range validation on a caller-bound date window defeats an ITIL/CH-17 change-freeze control. `ChangeManagementController` binds the `ChangeRequest` **entity** on `POST /api/v1/changes` and `PUT /{id}` (both `CHANGE:WRITE`); `ChangeManagementService.apply()` copied `scheduledStart`/`scheduledEnd` (both `LocalDateTime`, nullable) null-safely with no `start <= end` check. An inverted window makes the change's effective interval empty, so `enforceFreeze`'s overlap test `!start.isAfter(w.getEndsAt()) && !end.isBefore(w.getStartsAt())` reads false → a change is SCHEDULED **inside an active freeze/blackout** (the emergency-only window a governance freeze exists to enforce); `findScheduleConflicts` (`c.scheduledStart <= :windowEnd AND COALESCE(c.scheduledEnd, c.scheduledStart) >= :windowStart`) returns no collisions; and `findScheduledBetween` / `findForwardScheduled` (the change calendar and FSC) drop the change. Reachable by any `CHANGE:WRITE` holder or a machine caller posting a mistyped window ([[F2-179]] — reachability is a fact about today). |
| **Registers** | none — `ChangeManagementService.apply()` (one guard on the merged pair); `ChangeManagementServiceTest` +4 (existing class). No schema, no migration. |
| **Standards** | [[F2-215]] (two-of-N — the sibling `createFreezeWindow` in the SAME service guards exactly this ordering, `endsAt.isBefore(startsAt) -> throw`, for freeze windows and not for the change's own window; the module knew to check it); [[F2-292]] (validate the RESULTING row, not the request — a partial PUT that sets only one end inverts the STORED window, which a request-only check misses); [[F2-190]] (add the legs to the existing test class, not a new artefact); [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]] (hermetic — Mockito, no DB); [[F2-179]] (reachable via a machine caller even if the UI date-picker would prevent it); [[F2-221]] (re-derived — confirmed the controller binds the entity, `apply` copies the pair unguarded, `enforceFreeze` reads the change's own stored window set via `apply`, and the sibling guards the same ordering). |
| **Found by** | An Explore sweep for a `@RequestBody` (record or entity) carrying a start/end date pair the storing service does not validate for `start <= end`, where a JOINT consumer reads both columns (an interval-overlap test, a `BETWEEN` over both, or a duration) so an inverted range silently returns nothing or bypasses a control. Of ~20 paired-date candidates this was the one match on the exact shape: caller-bound, unguarded, jointly consumed by conflict/freeze/FSC/calendar overlap logic, with the same module guarding its sibling pair. Re-derived against the code ([[F2-221]]). |
| **Verification** | hermetic (Mockito, no DB — [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]]). `ChangeManagementServiceTest` +4: (1) an inverted `create` is rejected with `IllegalArgumentException("scheduledEnd must be on or after scheduledStart")` and nothing saved (`verify(never()).save`); (2) forward and zero-length (`start == end`) windows are allowed through `create`; (3) a missing window (both fields null) is allowed — the guard must not fire on a null; (4) the sharp leg — a partial PUT setting only `scheduledStart` past the stored `scheduledEnd` is refused, proving the guard validates the MERGED row rather than the request (which carries no end to compare). 39 run / 0 failed. Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]] / [[F2-287]], fix committed first — [[F2-297]]): surgically remove only the guard block — the test references no new symbol, so it still compiles — → exactly legs (1) and (4) RED, the three allow-legs green. Full backend build 4895/0/0. |

### Fix

`ChangeManagementService.apply()` — after copying `scheduledStart`/`scheduledEnd` from the request — validates the resulting `target` pair: if both are non-null and `target.getScheduledStart().isAfter(target.getScheduledEnd())`, it throws `IllegalArgumentException("scheduledEnd must be on or after scheduledStart")` (mapped to 400). Validating `target` (not the request) means a partial PUT that sets only one end and inverts the STORED window is caught too ([[F2-292]]); `isAfter` allows `start == end` (a zero-length window), mirroring the sibling `createFreezeWindow`, which uses `isBefore` and permits an equal pair. `apply` runs on both `create` and `update`, so both paths are covered by one guard; the fix prevents an inverted window from ever being stored, closing every downstream consumer (`enforceFreeze`, `findScheduleConflicts`, `ChangeScheduleService.overlaps`, `findScheduledBetween`, `findForwardScheduled`) at their common source.

🔑 **When a request carries a paired date/time window, an inversion is consequential only when three things hold: the pair is caller-supplied, there is no `start <= end` guard, and a JOINT consumer reads BOTH columns (an interval-overlap test, a `BETWEEN` over both, or a `Duration.between`). A consumer that reads only the end column is a different, degenerate-bound question — a `start > end` inversion there changes nothing. And the guard belongs on the merged row, not the request: a partial update that sets only one end inverts the stored window, and a request-only check never sees it.**

### Filed ([[F2-188]])

The sweep's other caller-supplied, unguarded pairs are all weaker because their consumers read only one column: `EvidenceItem.validFrom/validTo` and `DataException.validFrom/validUntil` feed an expiry sweep and a lapsed-waiver dashboard that key on the end column alone, so a `start > end` inversion is inconsequential — the real exposure there is a **degenerate or unbounded end** (no `@Future`, no bound) letting stale evidence read as covered forever or hiding a lapsed control waiver, which is a distinct "missing temporal bound" vein, not this joint-interval one. The single-column/no-consumer tail — `scm ContractDtos` (endDate-only stats), `bcm BcmAssessmentCycle` (endDate-only closeout sweep), `privacy` notices and cross-border transfers (no active-as-of query), `ethics/coi` campaigns (status-driven gate, no date consumer), `board_pack` period and `compliance/obligation` attestation period (echoed to the response, no consumer) — is recorded here so the next reader does not re-investigate. Already guarded and NOT to be re-opened: `iam/governance CreateAccessRequest.validFrom/validTo` (`AccessRequestService`) and `CreateCampaignRequest.windowStart/windowEnd` (`RecertificationService`), plus `ChangeFreezeWindow.startsAt/endsAt` (`createFreezeWindow`) — the sibling that proved the intent.

## F2-386 — DLP critical-event ingest let a forged `reviewed=true` silence the AR-136 SOC critical-unreviewed escalation

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-27 |
| **Severity** | P2 — a mass-assignment on a machine-ingest path defeats an NCA ECC DLP-monitoring SOC escalation. `DlpEventController.ingest` is `POST /api/v1/socops/dlp/ingest`, bound as `@RequestBody DlpEvent body` (the whole entity), guarded `hasAnyRole('DLP_INGEST','PLATFORM_ADMIN','CISO')` — `DLP_INGEST` is precisely a DLP connector service account. `DlpEventService.ingest`'s create branch scrubbed only `id` (SEC-CYB-002) and took `reviewed`/`reviewOutcome`/`reviewNotes` straight from the request. The AR-136 escalation fires only when `"CRITICAL".equalsIgnoreCase(saved.getSeverity()) && !Boolean.TRUE.equals(saved.getReviewed())`, so a caller (or a compromised connector) POSTing `{severity:CRITICAL, reviewed:true}` had the event born "reviewed" → `DLP_CRITICAL_UNREVIEWED` never published, no SOC page, `reviewOutcome` empty. `reviewed` is the analyst's act, written only by the dedicated `review()` route. |
| **Registers** | none — `DlpEventService.ingest` (create branch scrubs the three review fields); a new `DlpEventServiceTest`. No schema, no migration. |
| **Standards** | [[F2-206]] / [[F2-215]] (server-owned field — a field the server owns must not be caller-settable; `reviewed` is DlpEvent-specific, so `ServerOwnedFieldsModule`, which reports READ_ONLY for only `BaseEntity`'s nine, does NOT cover it — which is why no gate caught it); [[F2-217]] (`MassAssignmentRatchetTest`'s `AUTHORITY_SHAPE` vocabulary lists `reviewedAt`/`reviewer`/… but NOT the bare boolean `reviewed`, so the ratchet is blind to this field — a gate keyed on a name list measures the list); [[F2-248]] (the service had no test); [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]] (hermetic — Mockito, no DB). |
| **Found by** | A multi-agent semantic audit (control-checks-the-wrong-thing shape): a "reviewed/approved/attested" flag written by an ingest/update path that should only be set by the dedicated route. Of the four agents' leads, the un-filed non-owner-decision ones were this and the data_officer DPIA double-count; the BCM close-evidence FK-presence (F2-362) and cyber action-plan terminal-status-on-update (F2-328) were already filed as owner-decisions. Re-derived against the code ([[F2-221]]): confirmed the controller binds the entity, the create branch scrubs only `id`, `review()` is the sole intended writer, and the re-ingest (dedup) branch returns the stored row untouched (so only the create branch needs the scrub). |
| **Verification** | hermetic (Mockito, no DB — [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]]). New `DlpEventServiceTest` (3): the load-bearing leg ingests a CRITICAL event with a forged `reviewed:true` and asserts the stored entity is `reviewed=false` with null outcome/notes AND that `DLP_CRITICAL_UNREVIEWED` is published (ArgumentCaptor on the publisher); a regression leg (an honestly-unreviewed CRITICAL still escalates); a re-ingest leg (dedup returns the existing row untouched, no save, no escalation). Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]] / [[F2-287]], fix committed first — [[F2-297]]): surgically remove only the three `in.setReviewed(false)`/`setReviewOutcome(null)`/`setReviewNotes(null)` lines (the method still compiles) → exactly the forged-reviewed leg RED (`saved.getReviewed()` stays true, escalation not published), the honest-path and re-ingest legs green. Full backend build 4891/0/0. |

### Fix

The create branch of `DlpEventService.ingest` scrubs `reviewed=false`, `reviewOutcome=null`, `reviewNotes=null` before `repo.save(in)` — the same server-owned-field discipline as the adjacent SEC-CYB-002 `in.setId(null)` scrub. A freshly-ingested event has not been reviewed; `review()` (`POST /{id}/review`, guarded for analyst roles) is the sole writer of the review fields. The re-ingest (dedup) branch already returns the stored row without copying the request, so it needed no change.

🔑 **`ingest` binds the whole entity, so every column is caller-controlled; the only fields the create branch defended were the ones a prior finding had noticed (`id`). A server-owned field that is not one of `BaseEntity`'s nine is invisible to `ServerOwnedFieldsModule`, and a boolean completion flag (`reviewed`) is invisible to `MassAssignmentRatchetTest`'s name-keyed `AUTHORITY_SHAPE` — so when an escalation gates on `!reviewed`, a machine-ingest path binding the entity can silence it, and no existing gate sees it. When a control keys on a boolean flag, check every write path that can set that flag.**

### Filed ([[F2-188]])

`ServerStampedFieldContractTest` (F2-218) is designed to catch "a create accepts a field a guarded route stamps," which is exactly this shape (`review()` stamps `reviewed`, `ingest` accepted it) — yet it did not flag `DlpEvent`, a blind spot worth its own slice (likely because `ingest` binds a whole entity rather than a request DTO, and `review()` sets `reviewed` from a literal rather than a server value). Also: the data_officer DPIA `APPROVED_WITH_CONDITIONS`-counted-as-both-open-and-approved double-count (agent 2's drift lead), the cyber_lc vulnerability SLA anchored to triage `now()` rather than detection (agent 4's lead, carrying a bug-vs-documented-design question), and reginspect/outsourcing overdue sweeps that are defined but have no scheduler caller — each a distinct future slice.

## F2-385 — obligation-attestation campaign rollups drifted on every attestation, reporting 0% completion until close

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-26 |
| **Severity** | P2 — a governance completion KPI read wrong for the whole life of a campaign. `ObligationAttestationCampaign` carries denormalized status rollups (`total_in_progress`, `total_attested`, `total_attested_with_excs`, `total_overdue`, `total_na`), and `stats()` derives `completionPct = round(attested * 100 / invited)` from the STORED columns. `recomputeRollups` was called from ONE path — `closeCampaign` — while the request-reachable attestation paths (`recordAttestation` → `POST /api/v1/compliance/obligation-attestations/record`, `reviewAttestation` → `POST /{id}/review`) change a child's `attestation_status` and never touched the campaign. So between open and close the counts stayed frozen at their post-open values (0), and `stats()` / `CampaignResponse` reported **0% completion no matter how many owners attested** — on a SAMA/NCA obligation-attestation-completion figure read by `AUDITOR`/`RISK_MANAGER` before the campaign closes. `total_overdue` under-counted too. |
| **Registers** | none — a new `ObligationCampaignRollups` `@Component` (the single recompute), `ObligationCampaignService` (delegates + drops its own copy), `ObligationAttestationService` (record/review recompute); tests for all three. No schema, no migration. |
| **Standards** | [[F2-215]] (two-of-N — the tprm sibling `VendorBcpAttestationService` recomputes after every submit/accept/reject/mark-out-of-scope, so the correct pattern was in the tree; the compliance module was missing exactly those calls); [[F2-282]] (two readers of one figure — the stored rollup vs the live child count — disagreed, and `stats()` read the stale one); [[F2-190]] (one shared recompute, not a hand-rolled copy per path); [[F2-237]] (the campaign-service test uses a REAL rollups over mocked repos so its recompute assertions stay meaningful); [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]] (hermetic — Mockito, no DB). |
| **Found by** | A denormalized-counter-drift sweep — a stored `*_count`/`total_*` aggregate maintained by an explicit recompute that some child-mutation path skips. Of ~12 aggregates examined this was the one genuine drift; the others (tprm `VendorBcpCampaign`, consumer `ComplaintAggregateReport`, ethics `CoiDeclarationCampaign`, the committee tallies, `VendorAssessment`) route every mutation through one recompute or are computed on-read / point-in-time. Re-derived against the code ([[F2-221]]): confirmed `stats()` reads the stored columns (so the drift is user-facing, not a latent stored-column-only issue) and that the naive tprm-mirror fix is blocked by a circular dependency. |
| **Verification** | hermetic (Mockito, no DB — [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]]). New `ObligationCampaignRollupsTest` (4): the recount sets all five totals from the live counts; the id-overload loads org-scoped and no-ops on a null (ad-hoc) or absent campaign. `ObligationAttestationServiceTest` (+2): `recordAttestation` and `reviewAttestation` each call `recompute(org, campaignId)`. `ObligationCampaignServiceTest` uses a REAL rollups so `closeCampaign`'s recompute assertions still exercise the real recount ([[F2-237]]). Batch 41/0/0. Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]] / [[F2-287]], fix committed first — [[F2-297]]): surgically remove only the two `rollups.recompute(...)` calls (keep the field + constructor so the test compiles) → the 2 attestation legs RED ("Wanted but not invoked"), the component + campaign legs green. Full backend build 4888 tests, 0/0. |

### Fix

`recomputeRollups` is extracted into a shared `ObligationCampaignRollups` `@Component` depending only on the two repositories, with `recompute(campaign)` (the moved body) and `recompute(orgId, campaignId)` (loads org-scoped, no-op on null/absent). Both services depend on it one-directionally: `ObligationCampaignService#closeCampaign` calls `recompute(c)`; `ObligationAttestationService#recordAttestation` / `#reviewAttestation` call `recompute(org, campaignId)` after saving the child.

🔑 **The naive fix — mirror the tprm sibling by injecting the campaign service into the attestation service — would be a circular constructor dependency, because `ObligationCampaignService` already injects `ObligationAttestationService` (for its escalation step). A shared component depending only on the repositories breaks the cycle ([[F2-190]]) and is the general answer when two services both need one piece of shared logic — reach for it rather than `@Lazy`.** The recompute is synchronous and same-transaction: the child is saved first, so the count queries auto-flush and see it; the campaign is a different entity, loaded-mutated-saved once, so there is no double-flush of a `@Version` entity.

### Filed ([[F2-188]])

`escalateOverdue` sets `total_overdue` inline to only the rows it flipped in that call, and the org-wide overdue sweep (`sweepOverdueForOrg` / `flipToOverdue`) flips rows to `OVERDUE` across campaigns without recomputing any campaign — so `total_overdue` can drift between attestations. Both are scheduler/escalation paths with their own transaction shape (routing `escalateOverdue` through the full recompute would double-save the `@Version` campaign it already saves), so the `total_overdue` residual is filed rather than folded into this request-path fix. The core completion KPI (frozen at 0 from the normal attest flow) is fully closed.

## F2-384 — the SoD governance-admin gate treated a soft-deleted (retired) role's grant as still conferring admin

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-26 |
| **Severity** | P3 (latent). `SodViolationRepository#countUserRole` — the native query behind `SodService#isGovernanceAdmin`, which gates SoD overrides (`AccessRequestService`) and recertification closures (`RecertificationService`) — joined `iam.user_roles` to `iam.roles` by name and omitted `AND r.is_deleted = 0`. The platform's authz SOURCE OF TRUTH, `RoleRepository#findRoleNamesByUserId` (the native query `CustomUserDetailsService` uses to build a user's JWT authorities), filters retired roles, as do `privilegedRoleIds` and `countActiveHoldersByRole` — so a soft-deleted role confers no authority anywhere, and `countUserRole` was the lone outlier: a retired admin role's surviving grant still conferred governance-admin authority in the SoD engine while conferring nothing in the JWT authz path. Latent because `GRC_ADMINISTRATOR`/`PLATFORM_ADMIN` are system roles that `AccessGovernanceService#deleteRole` refuses to retire (so no such row is reachable via the API), but the drift is real and the alignment is provably non-breaking — the filter can only exclude a role the JWT path already excludes ([[F2-182]]: reachability is a fact about today). |
| **Registers** | none — one native `@Query` (`countUserRole`) gains `AND r.is_deleted = 0`; a new `GovernanceAdminRoleGateFiltersRetiredRoleTest`. No schema, no migration. |
| **Standards** | [[F2-282]] (one concept — "does this user hold role X?" — read two ways that disagreed on a soft-deleted role); [[F2-205]] (the authoritative reader filters; the SoD gate was the drifted outlier); [[F2-182]] (reachability is a fact about today, not a property of the control — the fix aligns a security gate with the source of truth regardless of whether a role is retireable today); [[F2-188]] / [[F2-278]] (the detective-scan roles-joins are a distinct, semantically-ambiguous question — a gate and a report ask different questions — so filed, not force-changed); [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]] (hermetic — reflection over the `@Query` SQL, since a native query cannot run under a mocked repo and there is no DB). |
| **Found by** | A native-query soft-delete-filter sweep (the "native SQL must filter `is_deleted` — `@Where` doesn't apply to native queries" landmine). No native SELECT/COUNT surfaced soft-deleted rows in any user-facing list/count/export — a clean sweep of the vein ([[F2-216]]) — but the one borderline case, `countUserRole` omitting `is_deleted` on a soft-deleting `iam.roles` join, was re-derived against the authz source of truth ([[F2-221]]) and confirmed a genuine drift on a security authz gate rather than the ambiguous owner-decision it first looked like. `countUserRole` has exactly one caller (`isGovernanceAdmin`), so the scope is isolated. |
| **Verification** | hermetic (reflection over the `@Query` annotation value — `@Retention(RUNTIME)`; a native query can't run under a mock and there's no DB — [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]]). `GovernanceAdminRoleGateFiltersRetiredRoleTest` (2): `countUserRole`'s SQL filters `r.is_deleted = 0` on its `iam.roles` join; the anchor leg asserts `findRoleNamesByUserId` (the JWT-authorities lookup) still filters too, so the gate is proven to AGREE with the source of truth (and if the source of truth ever stops filtering, the premise changed and the gate re-derives — anti-vacuity). Batch with the sibling SoD/privilege tests 13/0/0. Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]] / [[F2-287]], fix committed first — [[F2-297]]): revert `SodViolationRepository` to master → the gate leg RED (`r.is_deleted = 0` absent), the source-of-truth anchor green. Full backend build 4882 tests, 0/0. |

### Fix

`countUserRole`'s native query gains `AND r.is_deleted = 0`, matching `RoleRepository#findRoleNamesByUserId`. Only the authz GATE is changed. The detective-scan queries in the same repository (`pairConflictUsers`, `readonlyPersonaWriters`, `serviceMultiModuleUsers`, and the `NOT EXISTS PLATFORM_ADMIN` exclusions) deliberately keep their unfiltered `iam.roles` joins — those are a DETECTION/report concern, and whether a dangling grant to a retired role is a live SoD signal ("the live grant landscape", per the repository's own class comment) is a governance-policy call, filed for the IAM owner rather than changed here. A gate must reflect effective authority now; a report may legitimately want to flag dangling grants ([[F2-278]]: a gate and a report ask different questions).

🔑 **The reusable rule: an authz GATE that asks "does this user hold role X?" must agree with the platform's authz source of truth (the query that builds JWT authorities) on soft-deleted roles. When several native queries read `iam.roles`, check they all filter `is_deleted = 0` — the one that doesn't grants authority the login path would deny ([[F2-205]]: find the authoritative reader; [[F2-282]]: the drifted one is the tell).**

### Filed ([[F2-188]])

The SoD detective-scan native queries omit `is_deleted = 0` on their `iam.roles` joins, so a dangling grant to a retired (custom, retireable) role can contribute to a reported SoD violation. Whether that is a false positive (the retired role confers no effective access) or a legitimate cleanup/reinstatement-risk signal ("the live grant landscape") is a governance-policy decision for the IAM owner, with harm in both directions (a retired `PLATFORM_ADMIN` grant also wrongly suppresses a scan via the `NOT EXISTS` exclusion).

## F2-383 — the anonymous submitter's bearer token leaked into staff-facing response DTOs across all three public-intake modules

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-26 |
| **Severity** | P1 (whistleblower) / P2 (vendor BCP) / P3 (complaint). Each of the three public-intake modules mints a per-row `UUID submissionToken` that is the anonymous submitter's ONLY credential — it authenticates the module's `permitAll` public endpoints. Each correctly withholds the token from its public/tracking shape, but the STAFF-facing response DTO carried it verbatim. **Whistleblower `CaseResponse`** (returned to `ETHICS:READ_CASES`/`TRIAGE`): the token authenticates `permitAll POST /public/reply/{token}` (`WhistleblowerCaseService#reportByToken`), so any case reader could post follow-ups AS the anonymous reporter and track them — a deanonymisation + integrity breach on the hotline (P1). **Vendor BCP `AttestationResponse`** (broad `TPRM:READ`): the token authenticates `permitAll POST /by-token/{token}/submit`, so a reader could harvest tokens and submit/forge a vendor's BCP attestation (P2). **Complaint `ComplaintResponse`** (`CONSUMER:READ`): lower — the complaint token's only public path is the read-only, PII-stripped `/public/track/{token}` — but a bearer credential must not sit in a wider-audience response ([[F2-182]], P3). |
| **Registers** | none — three response DTOs (`WhistleblowerDtos.CaseResponse`, `ComplaintDtos.ComplaintResponse`, `VendorBcpAttestationDtos.AttestationResponse`) drop the `submissionToken` component, the vendor service mapper drops the arg, and the three FE staff interfaces match; a new `SubmissionTokenNotOnStaffDtoTest`. No schema, no migration. |
| **Standards** | [[F2-215]] (two-of-N — each module's public/submit shape already withheld the token, so the correct pattern was in the tree; the staff shape was the drifted reader); [[F2-282]] (two readers of one concept — public vs staff response — and the credential-bearing one is the leak); [[F2-182]] (the complaint token has no current write path, but reachability is a fact about today, not a property of the control); [[F2-159]] (checked — no existing test asserted the leaked field: the four existing token assertions are all on the by-design submit responses); [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]] (hermetic — reflection over the record shapes + plain-Jackson serialisation, no Spring context). |
| **Found by** | An Explore-agent sweep for credential/secret/token fields reachable on a response body — a genuinely untouched category (the platform's gates cover the WRITE side via `ServerOwnedFieldsModule` and lazy-entity serialisation, not "does a read path expose a secret") — re-derived against the code ([[F2-221]]). The token is `nullable = false` + `= UUID.randomUUID()` on all three entities (always present → `@JsonInclude(NON_NULL)` cannot suppress it), and the breaking-change check came back clean: no staff frontend component reads `submissionToken` off a staff DTO (the only FE readers are the two public submission pages reading the one-time submit response, by design), so removal is not a breaking change. Negative-reachability confirmed by the sweep — `User.passwordHash` never returned (only `UserResponse` DTO is), integration-config secrets `mask()`ed, MFA/TOTP unwired, no secret logged — so this is the one genuine exposure, not a population. Reached after clean sweeps of the arithmetic/overflow/scheduler/status-label/count-minter/soft-delete/`capa` veins ([[F2-216]]). |
| **Verification** | hermetic (reflection + plain-Jackson serialisation; no Spring context — [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]]). `SubmissionTokenNotOnStaffDtoTest` (6): the three staff records have no `submissionToken` component (a record only serialises its declared components, so this is a complete proof the key cannot reach the wire), and `CaseResponse.from`/`ComplaintResponse.from` do not serialise the token value; a positive control pins that the two one-time submit responses keep it by design. Backend batch of the 5 touched suites + the new test 69/0/0; FE `tsc --noEmit` clean + `npx vitest run` 841/841 (proving no staff component consumed the removed fields). Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]] / [[F2-287]], fix committed first — [[F2-297]]): revert the four backend files + the two positional controller-test stubs to master → the 3 reflection legs and 2 serialisation legs RED (`["submissionToken"]`; `"submissionToken":"<uuid>"` in the JSON dump), the positive control green. Full backend build 4880 tests, 0/0. |

### Fix

Each staff-facing response DTO drops the `submissionToken` record component (and the vendor service's `toResponse` drops the arg); the token stays on the one-time submit responses (`CaseSubmissionResponse`, `SubmitComplaintResponse`), which are returned once to the submitter so they can capture it — the by-design delivery. The three FE staff interfaces (`CaseResponse`, `ComplaintResponse`, `VendorBcpAttestation`) drop the field to match the server contract; the submit-response interfaces keep it. No backend consumer read the token off a response DTO (grep for the `.submissionToken()` accessor: none) and no staff frontend consumed it, so the field simply leaves the wire with no behaviour change.

🔑 **The reusable rule: a bearer credential minted for one party (an anonymous reporter, a vendor) must not appear in a response served to a wider audience (staff). When you find a token field, trace it to a response body and check the AUDIENCE of every handler that returns the carrying type — a module that correctly strips it from its public shape can still leak it through the staff shape ([[F2-215]] two-of-N), and "the write path that weaponises it doesn't exist yet" is not a defence ([[F2-182]]).**

### Filed ([[F2-188]])

The vendor-portal auth is "the token IS the credential" with a documented follow-up for a hardened realm (rate-limit, MFA bind, audit); that hardening is a separate design track, unchanged by this slice, which only stops the token being broadcast to staff.

## F2-382 — NDI improvement-plan rollup averaged CAPA progress_pct with integer division, truncating a governance completion figure

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-26 |
| **Severity** | P2 — a precision defect on a governance completion figure, not a catastrophic one. `NdiImprovementPlanService` averaged CAPA `progress_pct` (an `Integer` 0–100) with plain `int / int` division at two sites: `rollup()` (the `PlanRollup.progressPct` field returned to callers) and `recomputeRollup()` (the stored `ndi_improvement_plan.progress_pct` column). Integer division truncates toward zero, so a mean of 50.5 stored **50** — a consistent downward bias of up to ~1 percentage point on the NDI (NDMO) improvement-plan completion percentage. `progress_pct` is display-only: the plan's auto-complete gate keys on `completed == total`, not on progress, and no reader applies a `>= N` threshold to it, so the truncation biased a shown figure without flipping a gate. |
| **Registers** | none — one service (`.../ndi/plan/service/NdiImprovementPlanService.java`: the two mean-progress expressions round half-up) + a new `NdiImprovementPlanRollupRoundingTest` (3 legs). No schema, no migration. |
| **Standards** | [[F2-215]] (two-of-N — the sibling `NdiGapService#aggregate` computes the same "mean of CAPA `progress_pct`" correctly, so the correct idiom was in the module the whole time); [[F2-282]] (one concept, several readers — the plan rollup and the gap aggregate; the drifted rounding is the tell); [[F2-188]] (the differing denominators — plan-item count here vs CAPA count in the gap aggregate — are deliberate modeling choices, left alone; only the rounding was fixed); [[F2-369]] (a comparable small-arithmetic wrongness on a governance figure with the correct idiom nearby); [[F2-248]] (the service had no test at all); [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]] (hermetic — pure service arithmetic, so assert the average directly). |
| **Found by** | An Explore-agent sweep for integer-division truncation in percentage/rate/score computations (the "KPI reads wrong" shape), then re-derived against the code ([[F2-221]]). The catastrophic `a / b * 100 → 0` form does NOT exist in the backend — every percentage promotes to `double`/`float`/`BigDecimal` before dividing (confirmed near-misses: `CompliancePostureService`, `BcmReadinessScoreService`, `CyberDashboardService`, `SocOpsDashboardService`, `GreenFinanceMath`, `FinancedEmissionsService`, `CptyService.computeUtilisationPct`, and the `* 100.0` percentage methods across the audit-committee / sust / dashboard packages). This mean-of-integers form in `NdiImprovementPlanService` was the only genuine instance the sweep surfaced. Reached after seven consecutive clean sweeps ([[F2-216]]). |
| **Verification** | hermetic (Mockito, no DB — [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]]). `NdiImprovementPlanRollupRoundingTest` (the service's first test, [[F2-248]]): a mean of 50.5 rounds to 51 at the DTO (`rollup()`) and at the stored column (`recomputeAllForOrg()` → `recomputeRollup()` → captured `plans.save`), where pre-fix truncation gave 50; and a round-DOWN guard (mean 10.33 → 10) proving the fix is round-half-up, not a blanket increment (it passes on both trees, round == truncate there). Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]] / [[F2-287]], fix committed first — [[F2-297]]): revert only the two `(int) Math.round((double) …)` expressions to `sum / total` (the test uses only public API — `rollup()`, `recomputeAllForOrg()`, `PlanRollup.progressPct()` — so it still compiles) → the 2 mean legs RED (`expected 51 but was 50`), the round-down guard green. Full backend build 4874 tests, 0/0. |

### Fix

Both mean-progress computations round half-up, matching the module's established idiom in `NdiGapService#aggregate` (`(int) Math.round((double) progSum / all.size())`):

- `rollup()`: `int avg = total == 0 ? 0 : (int) Math.round((double) sumProgress / total);`
- `recomputeRollup()`: `p.setProgressPct(total == 0 ? 0 : (int) Math.round((double) sum / total));`

The denominator is unchanged. The plan rollup divides by the plan's **item count** (`rows.size()`, treating an item whose CAPA is missing as 0% — a deliberate "unactioned item is 0% done" choice) while the gap aggregate divides by the **CAPA count**; those are different populations by design, so aligning the rounding without touching the denominator is the bounded fix ([[F2-188]]). No schema, no migration — the column is already `Integer` and the value stays in 0–100.

🔑 **The reusable rule: when a metric is computed as `int / int` and its result is meant to be a fraction, percentage, rate or score, check the sibling that computes the same quantity — a rounding-convention drift between two readers of one concept (here truncate vs `Math.round`) is the tell, and the correct idiom is usually already in the tree ([[F2-215]]).**

## F2-381 — SIEM/scanner push-ingest stored oversized descriptive fields raw into bounded columns and lost the ingestion

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-26 |
| **Severity** | P2 — a machine SIEM/SOAR feed (or a vulnerability-scanner adapter) sending a descriptive field longer than its target column was silently lost. `SocOpsIngestService.ingestSiemEvent` and `ingestScannerRun` copied external fields straight into bounded `SecurityEvent`/`ScannerRun` columns (`rule_name` 300, `source_host`/`destination_host`/`username` 255, `source_ip`/`destination_ip` 45, `category` 60, `scanner` 40, `scan_name` 300). The `@Valid @RequestBody` request declared only `@NotBlank` (presence), no `@Size` (length), so an oversized field reached the column → SQL Server 8152 → opaque 500 (SEC-CFG-001 strips the class in prod). Both methods are `@Transactional`, so the overflow rolled back the whole ingestion: the security event was neither recorded (`security_events`) nor escalated. |
| **Registers** | none — one service (`.../socops/service/SocOpsIngestService.java`: a private `truncate` helper + capped descriptive setters) + a new `SocOpsIngestTruncationTest` (4 legs). No schema, no migration. |
| **Standards** | [[F2-349]] / [[F2-338]] / [[F2-380]] (the bounded-column overflow family; here a RAW-field store rather than a composed string, in a different service); [[F2-215]] (two-of-N — the sibling `CrowdStrikeInboundService` truncates the identical `SecurityEvent` columns and SocOps did not); [[F2-179]] (don't lose a security report — truncate-and-record beats reject, for the descriptive fields); [[F2-196]] (a vocabulary field must not be truncated — `severity`/`status` left raw); [[F2-197]] (a ratchet keyed on a shape flags your refactor — but here it was RIGHT, see below); [[F2-283]] (latent in data, live in code — reachable with an oversized field through ordinary ingestion; not re-measured against a backend, none up); [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]] (hermetic — a mocked repo has no column, so assert the cap the service applies before save, with column widths by reflection). |
| **Found by** | Applying [[F2-380]]'s composed-overflow lens to the external ingestion services. `CrowdStrikeInboundService` (`truncate(d.detectionId(), 64)`, `truncate(d.hostname(), 255)`, `buildRuleName` → `truncate(join, 300)`) and `TenableInboundService` (`truncate(title, 500)`, description NVARCHAR(MAX)) are both cap-aware; `SocOpsIngestService.ingestSiemEvent` stored the same `SecurityEvent` columns raw, and `SiemEventIngestRequest`/`ScannerRunIngestRequest` carry no `@Size`. Reading the two entities' `@Column(length)` values against the raw setters confirmed the descriptive columns fed unbounded. Reached after clean sweeps of `@Cacheable`, `findAll`, `BigDecimal.equals`/`divide`, boxed `==`, `toMap`, `Pattern.compile`, `@Query` SQLi/cross-tenant, `Enum.valueOf`, `Comparator.comparing` nullable, `@Async` ThreadLocal, `getTotalElements` ratio ([[F2-216]]). |
| **Verification** | hermetic (Mockito, no DB — [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]]). `SocOpsIngestTruncationTest` (4): an oversized SIEM event → each captured `SecurityEvent` descriptive field ≤ its `@Column(length)` by reflection (cap and column cannot drift); the upstream identity fields (`externalId`/`sourceSystem`) are left RAW even when oversized and the dedup lookup uses the RAW key; short values pass through untruncated (a working request is unaffected); the scanner path caps `scanner`/`scan_name`. Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]] / [[F2-287]], fix committed first — [[F2-297]]): strip the `truncate(req.X(), N)` wrappers (keeping the helper so the test compiles) → the 2 cap legs RED, the identity-raw pin and short-values legs green. Full backend build 4871 tests, 0/0. |

### Fix

Each **descriptive** external field is capped to its `SecurityEvent`/`ScannerRun` column width via a private `truncate(s, max)` — the same plain `substring(0, max)` helper `CrowdStrikeInboundService` uses for the identical columns (no ellipsis: a truncated host/IP/rule-name must stay a valid literal, unlike F2-380's composed-title ellipsis; a private copy per ADR-012/018, no cross-module import of a peer's internals). The full untruncated alert is preserved on `raw_payload`, so truncation loses nothing recoverable. No schema, no migration.

`externalId` (64) and `sourceSystem` (60) — the upstream system's own identity AND the dedup key — are left **raw**, not truncated: silently mangling an upstream id would collide the dedup key `(organisation_id, sourceSystem, externalId)` and break correlation with the upstream system. A malformed `>64` id is a far-fetched edge left to fail at the DB (or be `@Size`-rejected later — filed), never rewritten. `severity` (SIEM) and `status` (scanner) are vocabulary fields left raw too: truncating `severity` would corrupt `computeSlaDue` (a garbage-truncated severity falls to the default 72h window instead of CRITICAL's 1h) and the `"CRITICAL".equalsIgnoreCase` fast-lane (F2-196).

🔑 **The first draft truncated the dedup key too, and `ClientSuppliedReferenceRatchetTest.everyUpstreamOwnedReferenceIsStillOneAndIsNamed` (F2-287's `UPSTREAM_OWNED` reverse leg) failed on it** — the gate's `UPSTREAM_OWNED` set names `SocOpsIngestService#ingestSiemEvent`'s `setExternalId(req.externalId())` as a legitimate upstream-owned reference, and my `setExternalId(extId)` refactor stopped the detector recognising it. The right response was **not** to update the gate to accept the mangling but to stop mangling: an upstream-owned identity must be stored intact or rejected, never silently truncated into a colliding key. A ratchet that flags your fix may be telling you the fix is wrong, not that the ratchet is stale ([[F2-197]] inverted).

The reusable rule: **when one ingestion path into an entity truncates its bounded columns and a sibling path into the same entity stores raw, the raw path loses the whole record on any oversized field — grep every writer of a bounded column, not only the one you are reading. But an upstream-owned identity / dedup key is truncated by NO path: it is preserved or rejected, never rewritten.**

### Filed (F2-188)

A `@Size(max = N)` on the request DTO fields (turning a `>N` field's opaque 8152 into a clean 400 naming the field, via the `@Valid` the controller already binds) would protect the fields truncation must NOT touch — `externalId`/`sourceSystem` (a malformed upstream id → clean 400 rather than an 8152) and `severity`/`status` (a malformed vocabulary → clean 400). It rejects rather than preserves, which is right for an identity/vocabulary and wrong for a descriptive field, so it is a distinct boundary-hardening choice from this "don't lose the alert" fix, with its own reachability question. F2-380 filed the same `@Valid`/`@Size` boundary theme on `SiemInboundPayload.title`.

## F2-380 — a long SIEM alert title crashed auto-escalation and rolled back the whole ingestion

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-26 |
| **Severity** | P2 — a severity≥3 SIEM/SOAR alert (exactly the escalation-worthy band) with a title of 479–500 characters was silently lost on ingestion. `BcmAuditCompletionService.ingestSiemEvent` composes a `CrisisEvent` title as `"SIEM auto-escalation: " + row.getTitle()`. Both `SiemInboundEvent.title` and `CrisisEvent.title_en` are `@Column(nullable = false, length = 500)`, so a 479–500 char SIEM title (which stores fine in the SIEM row) plus the 22-char prefix reached up to **522 chars** and overflowed `crisis_events.title_en` → SQL Server 8152 → opaque 500 (SEC-CFG-001 strips the class in prod). `ingestSiemEvent` is `@Transactional`, so the overflow on the crisis insert **rolled back the whole ingestion**: the alert was neither recorded (`siem_inbound_events`) nor escalated. |
| **Registers** | none — one service (`.../bcm/cycle/service/BcmAuditCompletionService.java`: cap the composed title + a private `cap` helper + `CRISIS_TITLE_MAX`) + a new `BcmAuditCompletionServiceTest` (3 legs). No schema, no migration. |
| **Standards** | [[F2-338]] (the exact shape — a server-composed string into a narrower column; capped to the column length via the same private `cap` helper `CrisisAarService` uses one file over); [[F2-185b]] (a length budget must account for everything the code prepends, here the 22-char prefix, not just the caller's field); [[F2-283]] (latent in data, live in code — reachable with a 479–500 char sev≥3 SIEM title through ordinary ingestion; not re-measured against a backend, none up); [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]] (hermetic — a mocked repo has no column, so a unit test cannot reproduce the 8152; assert the cap the service applies before save). |
| **Found by** | Sweeping `set(Title\|Name\|Code\|...)` setters fed by string concatenation into a bounded column ([[F2-338]]/[[F2-346]]/[[F2-347]]'s family) — most were already `cap()`-protected or built from bounded values (Long ids, 4-digit years, short codes). `BcmAuditCompletionService:148` composed a crisis title from the SIEM alert's own title (variable-length) with no cap; reading the two `@Column(length)` values (both 500) and the 22-char prefix confirmed the composition can reach 522. Reached after clean sweeps of `Enum.valueOf`, `Comparator.comparing` nullable-NPE, `@Async` ThreadLocal reads, and `getTotalElements` ratio mismatch this window ([[F2-216]]). |
| **Verification** | hermetic (Mockito, no DB — [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]]). `BcmAuditCompletionServiceTest` (3): ingest a sev=4 alert with a 500-char title → the captured `CrisisEvent`'s `titleEn` ≤ 500 (`CRISIS_TITLE_MAX`); a short title composes untruncated (`"SIEM auto-escalation: Ransomware on core banking"`); `CRISIS_TITLE_MAX` equals `CrisisEvent.title_en`'s `@Column(length)` by reflection (cap and column cannot drift). Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]] / [[F2-287]], fix committed first — [[F2-297]]): un-cap the composed title (keeping `cap`/`CRISIS_TITLE_MAX` so the class compiles) → only the long-title leg RED (522 > 500), the short-title and mirror legs green. Full backend build 4867 tests, 0/0. |

### Fix

The composed crisis title is capped to `CrisisEvent.title_en`'s column length via a private `cap(s, max)` (the same truncate-with-ellipsis helper `CrisisAarService` uses for the AAR title — F2-338). `CRISIS_TITLE_MAX` mirrors the `@Column(length)` and a test asserts the equality by reflection. The full alert title is preserved on `siem_inbound_events.title`, so truncation loses nothing recoverable. No schema, no migration.

The reusable rule: **when a server composes a string into a bounded column, the length budget must account for the prefix AND the source field's own column width — a source that is itself `@Column(length = 500)` can fill a 500-wide target on its own, so any prefix overflows it.**

### Filed (F2-188)

`BcmAuditCompletionController.ingestSiem` binds `@RequestBody` **without `@Valid`**, so a `@Size(max = 500)` on `SiemInboundPayload.title` would be inert ([[F2-184]]) — adding `@Valid` to enable it (turning a >500-char title's opaque 8152 at the SIEM-row save into a clean 400 naming the field) is a separate boundary-hardening concern with its own reachability question; filed rather than folded into this composed-overflow fix.

## F2-379 — four evidence statuses rendered a raw English token + grey badge on an Arabic-primary UI

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-26 |
| **Severity** | P3 — a house-rule-7 (Arabic-primary) rendering defect on the compliance assurance core, in a status-label/tone map. `EvidencePage` renders both the evidence-items table and the evidence-requests table via the shared `statusLabel` / `STATUS_TONE` (`lib/labels.ts`). The two declared machines produce `PENDING_REVIEW` / `REJECTED` / `NEEDS_REVISION` (`EvidenceItemService.ITEM_STATUSES`) and `SUBMITTED` / `REJECTED` (the request machine's allowed set) — **none of the four was in `STATUS_KEY`**, so `statusLabel` fell back to the raw token and `STATUS_TONE[status] ?? 'neutral'` fell back to grey. An evidence item in the review queue (PENDING_REVIEW), a rejected item/request, a revision-requested item and a submitted request each printed a raw English token + a grey badge, beside correctly-localised neighbours — which is what makes it read as a data/logic defect rather than a missing translation. `REJECTED` was absent from the shared map entirely. |
| **Registers** | none — `lib/labels.ts` (four `STATUS_KEY` + four `STATUS_TONE` entries), `translations/en.ts` + `translations/ar.ts` (four bilingual keys each), and a pin leg in `breachStatusToneCompleteness.test.ts`. No backend change, no schema, no migration. |
| **Standards** | [[F2-357]] / [[F2-359]] (the exact precedent — "fixed the label, left the lookup", and the in-neither-map blind spot: a status absent from `STATUS_KEY` is outside the completeness gate's population, so the gate cannot catch it; F2-359 fixed incident RESOLVED, this fixes the evidence register); [[F2-211]] (the shared-map raw-token fallback on a bilingual UI); [[F2-340]] (`translationKeysDeclared` — the four new keys are declared in both dictionaries, en/ar sets stay identical); house rule 7 (Arabic primary); [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]] (hermetic — vitest + tsc, no backend); [[F2-188]] (the systematic cross-codebase gate to catch the whole blind-spot class is filed, not forced — it is a substantial instrument). |
| **Found by** | Cross-referencing the 14 frontend pages that import the shared `statusLabel` / `STATUS_TONE` against the backend registers' declared status machines. `EvidencePage` uses the shared map for both its item and request tables; `EvidenceItemService.ITEM_STATUSES` (read this window for F2-378) and `EvidenceRequestService`'s allowed set are declared, transition-enforcing Sets, so their vocabularies are authoritative (measured from the machines, not guessed — [[F2-359]]'s rule, applicable here because both machines enforce transitions, unlike the CHECK-less breach column). Four of the produced statuses were in neither shared map. Reached after clean reads of the automation/evidence/signature/attachment cores and the openbanking / KbArticle services this window ([[F2-216]]). |
| **Verification** | hermetic (vitest + `tsc --noEmit`, no backend — [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]]). `breachStatusToneCompleteness.test.ts` (+1 leg): the four evidence statuses carry their label key and non-neutral tone (`PENDING_REVIEW`→info, `REJECTED`→danger, `NEEDS_REVISION`→warning, `SUBMITTED`→info); the F2-357 completeness leg (`STATUS_KEY ⊆ STATUS_TONE`) stays green; `translationKeysDeclared` green (en/ar identical, keys used). `npx tsc --noEmit` clean; full frontend suite 841 passed. Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]] / [[F2-287]], fix committed first — [[F2-297]]): revert only `lib/labels.ts` to pre-fix (keeping the pin) → the F2-379 pin leg RED (the four statuses undefined in both maps), the completeness + F2-357/359 pins green. |

### Fix

Added `PENDING_REVIEW`, `REJECTED`, `NEEDS_REVISION`, `SUBMITTED` to `STATUS_KEY` (label keys `statusPendingReview` / `statusRejected` / `statusNeedsRevision` / `statusSubmitted`) and `STATUS_TONE` (info / danger / warning / info, following the platform convention — info = in the review pipeline, warning = awaiting author action, danger = bad outcome), plus the four bilingual keys in `en.ts` + `ar.ts`. Pinned in the completeness gate so a revert to grey/raw fails there.

The reusable rule: **a page rendering a register's status via the SHARED `statusLabel`/`STATUS_TONE` inherits that map's coverage gaps — cross-reference every such page against its backend register's declared status machine, because a status in neither shared map renders raw + grey and the `STATUS_KEY ⊆ STATUS_TONE` completeness gate cannot see it (F2-359's blind spot).**

### Filed (F2-188)

The durable fix for this recurring blind spot is a **cross-codebase gate** (a backend test reading `lib/labels.ts` and every register machine that a shared-map page renders, asserting each produced status is covered) — but it must first enumerate which of the 14 pages use the shared map for which register, and read each register's machine, so it is a substantial instrument (its own slice, [[F2-266]]). The per-register fix here matches the F2-357/359 cadence.

## F2-378 — replacing an APPROVED evidence item's file left un-reviewed content APPROVED (four-eyes bypass)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-26 |
| **Severity** | P2 — a four-eyes / segregation-of-duties bypass on the compliance assurance core (every framework control resolves to one or more APPROVED evidence items). `EvidenceItemService.attachFile` — the real multipart upload, `POST /evidence/items/{id}/file`, wired from the FE as `evidenceApi.uploadFile` — overwrote `evidenceHash` (the chain-of-custody hash a reviewer signed off), `fileName`, `fileSize`, `mimeType` and `collectedAt` **in place** and saved with **no status reset**, on an item of any status, guarded only by `EVIDENCE:WRITE`. So an APPROVED item's bytes could be swapped **post-approval** and stay APPROVED — un-reviewed content presented as four-eyes-reviewed evidence. Live-reachable through the UI: `EvidencePage` shows the attach button on every row with no status condition. |
| **Registers** | none — one service method (`.../evidence/service/EvidenceItemService.java`, `attachFile()` gains a reviewed-state reset) + four `EvidenceItemServiceTest` legs. No schema change, no migration. |
| **Standards** | [[F2-215]] (two-of-N — the four-eyes mechanism is visibly present at `approve()` and on create/update, so the upload path read as covered; an invariant asserting "this content passed review" must be re-checked at every writer of the content it certifies); SEC-EVD-002 (the file's own comment states the invariant this violates — approved evidence has passed four-eyes review and status changes flow exclusively through the state machine); [[F2-283]] (live in code, reachable through ordinary use via the UI; not re-measured against a backend, none up); [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]] (hermetic — Mockito, no Spring/DB); [[F2-188]] (the two-path versioning coordination is filed as an owner decision, not forced). |
| **Found by** | Reading the evidence subsystem's core item lifecycle (`EvidenceItemService`, un-read this window — the chain verifier `EvidenceChainService` was read separately and is clean) and asking the non-four-eyes integrity question: does re-uploading a file to an APPROVED item reset it for re-review, or silently keep it APPROVED? `attachFile` sets a new `evidenceHash` and never touches `status`; the SEC-EVD-002 comment 100 lines below states the invariant it breaks; `approve()` enforces creator≠approver, so the platform demonstrably cares about four-eyes on evidence. Confirmed live-reachable by reading `EvidencePage` (attach button on every row) rather than assuming the UI gates it ([[F2-222]]). Reached after two clean-search firings and reads of the automation engine/executor, the hash-chain verifier and MlModelService — the mature core is well-remediated ([[F2-216]]). |
| **Verification** | hermetic (Mockito, no Spring/DB — [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]]). `EvidenceItemServiceTest` (+4): attach to an APPROVED item resets it to PENDING_REVIEW (`resp.status()` and the entity both), and emits `EVIDENCE_SUBMITTED` with `previousStatus=APPROVED` / `status=PENDING_REVIEW` (re-enters the reviewer queue); attach to a DRAFT item stays DRAFT and emits only `EVIDENCE_FILE_ATTACHED` (working states unaffected, no spurious re-review). The class already locked SEC-EVD-002 on create and update — `attachFile` was the uncovered writer. Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]] / [[F2-287]], fix committed first — [[F2-297]]): set `resetForReview = false` (keeping the block so the class compiles) → both APPROVED legs RED (`resets_to_PENDING_REVIEW` FAILURE — status stays APPROVED; `emits_re_review_trigger` ERROR — no `EVIDENCE_SUBMITTED`), the DRAFT regression leg green. 23/23 after; the whole class was 19 before the +4. |

### Fix

`attachFile` captures the item's status before replacing the file, and if it was `APPROVED` resets it to `PENDING_REVIEW` — a declared `ITEM_TRANSITIONS` edge (`APPROVED → PENDING_REVIEW`, already legal) — then emits `EVIDENCE_SUBMITTED` so downstream re-review workflows pick it up again. `approve()` re-applies the creator≠approver SoD gate on the replaced content. Working states (DRAFT / NEEDS_REVISION / REJECTED) and an in-flight PENDING_REVIEW are content-editable and keep their status, so the normal DRAFT-build-then-submit flow is unchanged. The `EVIDENCE_FILE_ATTACHED` emit's `previousStatus` argument was corrected from `item.getStatus()` (which, since attach had not changed status, was the current status) to the real prior status. No schema change, no migration.

The reusable rule: **a four-eyes / SoD control certifies a piece of CONTENT (a hash, a document, a value), not just a status. Grep every path that WRITES that content — not just the paths that write the status — because the certificate is only as strong as the content's weakest writer.**

### Filed (owner decision — [[F2-188]])

The evidence subsystem has **two uncoordinated file paths**: `attachFile` (the real multipart upload — replaces bytes in place, no version row, no WORM hash-chain extension) and `EvidenceMatrixService.snapshotVersion` (creates an `EvidenceVersion` row and extends the `previousHash`/`currentVersionNo` chain, but takes the new hash from a `body` map rather than a real uploaded file). Neither is a real versioned file-REPLACE path, so an in-place `attachFile` replacement loses the prior `evidenceHash` from the WORM chain — while the `EvidenceVersion` entity comment says *"replacing an evidence file produces a new EvidenceVersion row; the previous is kept."* How the two paths should coordinate (whether `attachFile` should snapshot a version on replacement, which path is canonical) is a product/design decision entangled with the FE and the WORM model, not a bounded hermetic fix — filed rather than forced.

## F2-377 — four-eyes SoD bypassed by delegating an approval request back to its raiser

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-26 |
| **Severity** | P2 — a segregation-of-duties bypass on the universal approval workflow engine. `ApprovalRequestService.create` enforces the four-eyes control (`assignedTo != requestedBy`, F2-226 leg 2), but `transition(DELEGATED)` reassigned `assignedTo` with **no equivalent check**. Since `assignedTo` **is** the authorisation input `transition()` checks (SEC-IAM-002, `callerUsername.equals(assignedTo)`), a request could be delegated back to its RAISER, who then re-pends it (`DELEGATED → PENDING`) and approves their own request — `requestedBy == decidedBy` on the final record, the exact self-approval the create check exists to prevent. |
| **Registers** | none — one service method (`.../approvals/service/ApprovalRequestService.java`, `transition()` DELEGATED branch gains an SoD guard) + two `ApprovalRequestServiceTest` legs. No schema change, no migration. |
| **Standards** | [[F2-215]] (two-of-N — the four-eyes mechanism is visibly present at create, so the delegate path read as covered; an invariant that must hold at all times must be re-checked wherever the field it constrains is written); [[F2-222]] / [[F2-226]] (the create-time four-eyes control this extends across delegation; a server-enforced SoD control must not rely on the assignee's discretion — the audit trail told the truth about who acted while nothing stopped them); [[F2-179]] (case-insensitive comparison — `requested_by` collates CI, so a capitalisation must not walk through the gate); [[F2-283]] (latent in code, reachable through ordinary use; not re-measured against a backend, none up); [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]] (hermetic — Mockito). |
| **Found by** | Reading the heavily-remediated `ApprovalRequestService` (F2-206/226/172d/48/275, SEC-IAM-002) and asking whether the four-eyes SoD invariant (raiser ≠ decider), enforced at create, survives delegation. The `create` check's own comment names why `assignedTo` matters ("it IS the authorisation input transition() checks"), and the DELEGATED branch writes that exact field with no guard. Reached after four clean SOC-ops reads (prior firing) and the sanctions/knowledge/rrp/board_pack/controlmap reads — the mature core is well-remediated ([[F2-216]]). |
| **Verification** | hermetic (Mockito, no Spring/DB — [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]]). `ApprovalRequestServiceTest` (+2): delegating to the raiser (`admin`, and a differently-cased/padded `  ADMIN `) throws the SoD `IllegalStateException` ("Segregation of duties") and `verify(never()).save`; the existing "delegate to a different reviewer" test still succeeds (no regression). Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]] / [[F2-287]], fix committed first — [[F2-297]]): surgically remove only the delegate SoD `if` block (keeping the `newAssignee` local + setter so the class compiles) → both delegate-to-raiser legs RED ("Expecting actual throwable" — no throw), the other 17 green. |

### Fix

The `transition(DELEGATED)` branch now refuses `newAssignedTo == requestedBy` — the same segregation-of-duties invariant `create` enforces, extended across delegation. It uses the SAME 409 (`IllegalStateException` → CONFLICT, the platform's four-eyes convention — matching `NdiEvidenceItemService`'s SEC-NDI-003 gate and the create check, not the outlier `BusinessRuleException` 403) and the SAME case-insensitive comparison (`requested_by` collates CI, [[F2-179]]). No legitimate flow is broken: delegating to anyone except the raiser is a normal reassignment; delegating to the raiser is exactly what four-eyes forbids. No schema change, no migration.

The reusable rule: **when a four-eyes / SoD check appears on a create, grep every OTHER path that writes the constrained field (delegate, reassign, transition) — the invariant is only as strong as its weakest writer.**

## F2-375 — a sanctions check-code minter collides under concurrency, losing a screening — and F2-356's gate missed it

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-26 |
| **Severity** | P2 — a concurrency-collision on the sanctions screening register (a regulatory AML control). `SanctionsScreeningService.nextCheckCode` minted `SCR-{year}-{count(...IsDeletedFalse)+1}` with no skip-loop: two screens running concurrently for one tenant both read the same count, both mint the same code, and the second INSERT violates the filtered unique index `UX_screening_check_org_code` → an opaque 500 (SEC-CFG-001 strips the class in prod) and a **LOST sanctions screening** (a compliance gap on a regulatory register). Reachable via batch screening, the scheduler + a manual screen, or two operators. |
| **Registers** | none — one service method (`.../aml/sanctions/service/SanctionsScreeningService.java` `nextCheckCode` gains a skip-loop) + two `SanctionsScreeningServiceTest` legs. The `existsByOrganisationIdAndCheckCodeAndIsDeletedFalse` finder already existed (unwired). No repository change, no schema change, no migration. |
| **Standards** | [[F2-337]] / [[F2-354]] / [[F2-355]] (a count-seed reference minter re-mints a used ordinal under concurrency; the fix is a skip-loop over the unique index, or a MAX-seed — here a skip-loop mirroring the platform's own `WhistleblowerCaseService#generateCode`); [[F2-356]] (the count-minter gate — whose scanner MISSED this minter, see *Found by*); [[F2-283]] (latent in code, concurrency-reachable — no soft-delete path for a screening check, so only a simultaneous double-screen collides; not re-measured against a backend, none up); [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]] (hermetic — a mocked repo has no unique index, so assert the SOURCING: the mint consults `existsBy` and skips a taken ordinal). |
| **Found by** | Confirming F2-356's `CountBasedReferenceMinterRatchetTest` covers this minter — it does NOT. Its `COUNT_SEED` requires `count(...)` immediately followed by `+ 1`, but `nextCheckCode` stores the count in a local (`long total = count(...); ... total + 1`); and its `METHOD_HEADER` requires an access modifier, while `nextCheckCode` is **package-private**. Two scanner blind spots, hiding a **population of 4** count-minters (`nextCheckCode`, `FraudService#nextExternalRef`, `SustainabilityReportService#generateReport`, `WhistleblowerCaseService#generateCode`) — F2-356 declared "every genuine unmitigated count-minter is now closed." F2-356's own recurring lesson (a detector that under-reports reads exactly like a clean vein) landing on the gate F2-356 built. Reached after a thorough clean search this firing: four shape-sweeps (caller-moment deadlines, `BigDecimal.divide`, cross-tenant `@Query`, `Collectors.toMap`) and eight module reads (controlmap, knowledge, rrp, board_pack, sanctions-matcher, digital-signature, zt-maturity, fair-calculator) — all clean/well-remediated ([[F2-216]]). |
| **Verification** | hermetic (Mockito, no Spring/DB — [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]]). `SanctionsScreeningServiceTest` (+2): a count+1 ordinal already taken (a concurrent screen that committed first) is skipped for the next free one — `SCR-2026-000043` not `...000042` (the discriminating leg); the no-collision case still mints the count+1 seed (regression guard). Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]] / [[F2-287]], fix committed first — [[F2-297]]): revert only `nextCheckCode`'s body to the bare `count+1` seed (keeping the UUID import so the class compiles) → the skip leg RED (`expected SCR-2026-000043 but was SCR-2026-000042`), the mint leg green. |

### Fix

`nextCheckCode` gains a collision skip-loop backstopped by the filtered unique index — the platform's own established pattern, identical to `WhistleblowerCaseService#generateCode`: seed from `count(...)+1`, and while the candidate `SCR-{year}-{seq}` already exists (`existsBy...CheckCodeAndIsDeletedFalse`, which agrees with the `WHERE is_deleted = 0` index), advance to the next ordinal; a random-suffix fallback after 1000 attempts guarantees termination. The loser of a concurrent race retries the next free ordinal instead of 500-ing. The finder already existed and was simply not wired in; no repository, schema or migration change.

The valuable meta-finding — F2-356's scanner has two blind spots (a count stored in a local then `local + 1`, and package-private methods) that hid a population of 4 count-minters — is **filed** for a dedicated gate-hardening slice: extending `COUNT_SEED` with a precise variable-bound local-indirection alternative and dropping the `METHOD_HEADER` access-modifier requirement (both measured to add no false positives on the current tree), then fixing/enumerating each surfaced member (`FraudService#nextExternalRef` is another unmitigated minter; `SustainabilityReportService#generateReport` and `WhistleblowerCaseService#generateCode` are already skip-loop-mitigated). That is its own slice because closing the scanner honestly forces the gate to FAIL on each unmitigated member ([[F2-266]] / [[F2-356]]: the gate is its own slice, it must fix each instance it flags).

## F2-374 — a KB slug freed only by a soft delete 500s on recreate instead of a clean 400

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-25 |
| **Severity** | P3 — latent opaque-500 on the Knowledge Base create path. `kb.articles` carries `@Where(is_deleted = 0)` on the `KbArticle` entity, so `KbArticleService.create`'s uniqueness guard (`findByOrganisationIdAndSlug`) cannot see a soft-deleted row — but `uk_kb_slug` (V21) is a **PLAIN** `UNIQUE (organisation_id, slug)` constraint that counts every physical row. So an admin `DELETE /api/kb/articles/{slug}` (soft-delete, `is_deleted=1`, row stays) followed by an author `POST` of the same slug passes the finder guard (the row is invisible to the app) and violates the constraint at INSERT: an opaque 500 (SEC-CFG-001 strips the class in prod) where the guard's own `IllegalArgumentException("… already exists")` promised a clean 400. [[F2-309]] / [[F2-337]] guard-blind-to-a-`@Where`-hidden-row family, on a plain CREATE guard rather than a minter. |
| **Registers** | none — two production files (`.../knowledge/service/KbArticleService.java` create-guard; `.../knowledge/repository/KbArticleRepository.java` gains a native `countBySlugIncludingDeleted`) + a new `KbArticleServiceTest`. No data change, no migration, no schema change. |
| **Standards** | [[F2-309]] / [[F2-337]] (a `@Where`-filtered finder over an UNFILTERED unique index disagrees with it about what a duplicate is — a soft-deleted row is invisible to the app and visible to the constraint); [[F2-283]] (latent in data — admin-plus-author reachable through ordinary use; not re-measured against a backend, none up); [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]] (hermetic — a mocked repo has no unique index, so a unit test cannot reproduce the 500; assert the SOURCING — the create consults the deleted-inclusive count and refuses on it); [[F2-190]] / [[F2-248]] (new `KbArticleServiceTest` — `create` had no behavioral test). |
| **Found by** | Reading the genuinely un-read `knowledge` (Knowledge Base) module end-to-end after four clean shape-sweeps this firing (caller-moment deadlines, `BigDecimal.divide`, cross-tenant `@Query`, `Collectors.toMap` — all well-defended, [[F2-216]]). The tell: `create`'s guard uses the `@Where`-filtered finder while the entity soft-deletes and V21 declares a PLAIN (not filtered) unique on slug — so the finder and the index cannot agree after a soft delete. |
| **Verification** | hermetic (Mockito, no Spring/DB — [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]]). `KbArticleServiceTest` (new, 3 legs): a slug held only by a soft-deleted article → clean `IllegalArgumentException` naming "reserved" + `verify(never()).save` (the discriminating leg); a live duplicate keeps the pre-existing "already exists" message; a fresh slug creates AND consults `countBySlugIncludingDeleted`. Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]] / [[F2-287]], fix committed first — [[F2-297]]): surgically remove only the deleted-inclusive `if` block from the service (keep the repository method so the test compiles) → the discriminator RED ("Expecting actual throwable" — no throw) + the wiring leg RED ("Wanted but not invoked") while the live-duplicate leg stays green. |

### Fix

`create`'s uniqueness guard now checks both: the existing `@Where`-filtered `findByOrganisationIdAndSlug` (a LIVE duplicate keeps the accurate "already exists" message) AND a new native `countBySlugIncludingDeleted` (native SQL bypasses Hibernate's `@Where`, which applies only to entity queries), so a slug held only by a since-deleted article returns the clean 400 the code already intends rather than an opaque unique-index 500. No schema change and no semantics change: the plain `uk_kb_slug` index already forbids reuse (a slug is an addressable URL, so a since-deleted one stays reserved — repurposing a URL would silently point every bookmark / cross-link at different content); the code now reports that cleanly instead of crashing. The [[F2-309]]-convention alternative — a filtered unique index (`DROP CONSTRAINT uk_kb_slug` + `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX … WHERE is_deleted = 0`) making slugs reusable — is filed as an owner/schema decision: strictly-more-permissive and provably safe without a both-DB measurement (it can only reject fewer rows than the plain constraint), but a pure migration is un-appliable/un-verifiable this window (no backend), and for a URL slug permanence is the defensible choice. `uk_kb_external` is the same plain-unfiltered shape but `external_id` is server-minted random ([[F2-48]]), so a post-delete collision there is astronomically unlikely (not reachable).

## F2-373 — a future breach detected-at pushed the PDPL Art.20 72-hour SDAIA clock into the future

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-25 |
| **Severity** | P2 — latent statutory-clock defect on the PDPL Art. 20 personal-data-breach path (Data Officer toolkit). `PrivacyAssuranceService.createBreach` sets `sdaiaDeadline = req.detectedAt().plusHours(72)` — the 72-hour SDAIA notification clock — from the caller-supplied detection moment, but does **not** bound it. So a breach recorded with a **future** `detectedAt` (an API/machine caller, or a mistyped form year — e.g. 2027 for 2026) silently pushes the statutory deadline into the future, so the breach never surfaces as overdue for SDAIA notification. The DSR path **next door** (`DataSubjectRightsService.createDsr`) already refuses a future `receivedAt` ([[F2-123]], the mirror defect — a future receipt extending the 30-day clock); the breach sibling was left unbounded ([[F2-215]] two-of-N). |
| **Registers** | none — one method (`.../data_officer/service/PrivacyAssuranceService.java`, `createBreach` gains a fail-fast future-date guard) + a new `DataOfficerLifecycleTest` leg. No data change, no migration, no schema. |
| **Standards** | [[F2-121]] / [[F2-123]] (bound a caller-supplied real-world moment that feeds a statutory deadline — refuse a future value, allow a past one; do NOT stamp `now()`, which would corrupt the deadline the disclosure is judged against); [[F2-215]] (two-of-N — the DSR fix was applied and the breach sibling in the same service was left, the classic "the mechanism that fixed the first is visibly present so the sibling reads as covered"); [[F2-283]] (latent in data — a normal operator enters a past/present detection time; API/machine-caller reachable; not re-measured against a backend); [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]] (hermetic — Mockito, no Spring/DB). |
| **Found by** | Sampling the un-read `data_officer` module (PDPL/NDMO Data Officer toolkit — DPIA/breach/ethics-review; [[F2-363]] filed only an attribution gap). The DSR path's own F2-123 comment was the tell: it says "the breach path next door already did this correctly — `sdaiaDeadline` is `req.detectedAt().plusHours(72)`," which is true about *using* `detectedAt` rather than `now()`, but the breach path lacks the future-date *bound* the DSR path adds (its line 100). Same regulation family, same caller-supplied real-world moment, one guarded and one not. |
| **Verification** | hermetic (Mockito, no Spring/DB — [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]]). `DataOfficerLifecycleTest.aFutureDetectionMomentIsRefused` (new): `createBreach` with `detectedAt = now().plusDays(1)` throws `IllegalStateException` naming "future" (the discriminating leg), and `detectedAt = now().minusDays(2)` (a legitimate past detection) is accepted. The existing `theSdaiaDeadlineRunsFromDetection` source-scan pins the `req.detectedAt().plusHours(72)` clock itself. Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]] / [[F2-287]], fix committed first — [[F2-297]]): `git checkout fb0cad4d -- PrivacyAssuranceService.java` (public API unchanged, so the test compiles) makes ONLY the new leg RED ("Expecting code to raise a throwable" — a future `detectedAt` did not throw) while the other 11 stay green. |

### Fix

`createBreach` gains a fail-fast guard right after the reference-exists check: `if (req.detectedAt().isAfter(LocalDateTime.now())) throw new IllegalStateException("Detected-at … is in the future — a breach cannot be detected before it occurs, and the PDPL Art.20 72-hour SDAIA notification clock runs from detection.")`. `detectedAt` is `@NotNull` (so no NPE — a null is a 400 before the service). A past value is deliberately allowed: a breach found last week and entered today has a clock — possibly already breached — that correctly runs from then. Inline, mirroring the DSR path's own inline future-refusal (line 100); a shared `DataOfficerSupport.requireNotFuture(moment, message)` could consolidate the two but is deferred as beyond the fix ([[F2-190]] / [[F2-188]]).

## F2-372 — the NDMO asset classification was stored verbatim, so a lowercase token bypassed the high-classification automation gate

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-25 |
| **Severity** | P2 — latent security-control bypass on an NDMO/SDAIA data-classification register. `DataclassService.classifyAsset` stored `req.classification()` verbatim (the request field is `@NotBlank` only; `dataclass.data_asset.classification` has **no CHECK** and is case-insensitively collated), while every reader is **case-SENSITIVE**: `classOrder()` (the `DATA_ASSET_RECLASSIFIED_UP` upgrade ladder), the V210 automation rule `{"classification":{"in":["CONFIDENTIAL","TOP_SECRET"]}}` (matched against the emitted event's payload with `Objects.equals` in `AutomationRuleEngine`), and the frontend label map (keyed uppercase). So an API/machine caller sending `"confidential"` (lowercase) would store it verbatim, **bypass the high-classification NDMO automation gate**, mis-rank the upgrade ladder (`classOrder("confidential") = 0`, so a real `PUBLIC → confidential` upgrade ranks `0 > 1 = false` and the `RECLASSIFIED_UP` security event never fires), and render unlabelled. |
| **Registers** | none — one method (`.../dataclass/service/DataclassService.java`, `classifyAsset` + a `normaliseClassification` helper) + a new `DataclassLifecycleTest` leg. No data change, no migration, no schema. |
| **Standards** | [[F2-179]] / [[F2-366]] (a caller value stored verbatim on a case-insensitive CHECK-less column, then compared case-sensitively to fire a control — fix is normalise-on-write, not `equalsIgnoreCase`, because a second reader is why); [[F2-182]] (coerce, not require — no upstream coercion and no CHECK, so a 400 would break a request that succeeds today; the FE sends valid uppercase so nothing breaks); [[F2-283]] (latent in data — the FE always sends uppercase, so the bypass is API/machine-caller reachable; not re-measured against a backend); [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]] (hermetic — Mockito capture, no Spring/DB). |
| **Found by** | Sampling the genuinely un-read `dataclass` module (NDMO/SDAIA data classification; [[F2-335]] touched only a quality-run band) after two firings of exhaustive clean searches across the backend (services, repositories, `@Query` tenant-filters) and frontend (status-predicates, arithmetic, mock-corpus gates), all exemplary. The `classOrder` grading was the entry point — it handles exactly the 4-level NDMO scheme (`PUBLIC/INTERNAL/CONFIDENTIAL/TOP_SECRET`, confirmed against the entity comment, the FE type, and package-info, so it is complete, **not** [[F2-283]] mis-ranked) — but reading it surfaced that its input, and the automation-gate event payload, come from an unvalidated caller-supplied `classification`. |
| **Verification** | hermetic (Mockito, no Spring/DB — [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]]). `DataclassLifecycleTest.classificationIsNormalisedToTheCanonicalNdmoToken` (new): reclassifying a `PUBLIC` asset with `" confidential "` (lowercase, whitespace-padded) asserts (1) the saved `DataAsset.classification` is the canonical `"CONFIDENTIAL"` (the value pin — the stored value everything reads), (2) the `DATA_ASSET_CLASSIFIED` event payload's classification is `"CONFIDENTIAL"` (so the V210 automation gate matches), and (3) the `DATA_ASSET_RECLASSIFIED_UP` event fires (the ladder ranks `PUBLIC(1) → CONFIDENTIAL(3)`; pre-fix the case-mismatched token ranked 0 so the upgrade went undetected). Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]] / [[F2-287]], fix committed first — [[F2-297]]): `git checkout 5f082c37 -- DataclassService.java` (its public API is unchanged, so the test still compiles) makes ONLY the new leg RED (`expected "CONFIDENTIAL" but was " confidential "`) while the other 11 stay green. |

### Fix

`classifyAsset` normalises the caller-supplied classification once — `normaliseClassification(req.classification())` = `trim().toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT)`, null-safe — and uses the canonical token everywhere it previously read `req.classification()` raw: the setter, the timeline note, the `classOrder` ladder comparison (both the new value and `prev`, so a legacy lowercase stored value also ranks correctly), and both event payloads. Coerce, not require ([[F2-182]]): the column has no CHECK and nothing coerces upstream, so refusing an out-of-vocabulary token with a 400 would break a request that succeeds today; the FE sends valid uppercase, so nothing that works breaks.

### Note

Latent in data ([[F2-283]]): the frontend's `CLASSIFICATIONS` set and `Classification` type are uppercase, so a normal operator always sends a canonical token — the bypass is reachable only through the API / a machine integration, which is exactly where a case variant would arrive. No CHECK was added: `dataclass.data_asset.classification` is CHECK-less and adding one is a separate migration + both-database measurement (an out-of-vocabulary or non-canonical live row would fail Flyway on deploy — [[F2-183]]), and normalise-on-write is the correct primary treatment regardless because the collation is case-insensitive (a CHECK cannot see case — [[F2-179]]).
