### Fix

Mirror the established MAX-seed idiom (`ComplaintService#generateNextComplaintNo`; the native MAX-seed precedents `TreatmentPlanRepository` / `VendorEsgSurveyRepository`). Two new `RegInspectionRepository` finders: a native `findMaxOsiOrdinal(org, pat)` = `SELECT ISNULL(MAX(TRY_CAST(RIGHT(external_reference, CHARINDEX('-', REVERSE(external_reference)) - 1) AS INT)), 0) FROM reginspect.reginspect_inspection WHERE organisation_id = :org AND external_reference LIKE :pat` — the MAX of the last `-NNN` segment across ALL rows including soft-deleted ones, so a used ordinal is never re-issued (`TRY_CAST` ignores a non-numeric tail such as a random-suffix backstop; `ISNULL(…, 0)` seeds an empty quarter at 1) — and a derived `existsByOrganisationIdAndExternalReference` (live-only, `@Where`-scoped) for the skip-loop. `generateReference` seeds `next = MAX + 1` over `pat = %-OSI-<year>-Q<q>-%` (every regulator's inspection that quarter — the ordinal is a shared per-quarter sequence, and the reference stays unique because the full string carries the regulator prefix), steps over any live collision, backstopped by the unique index and, after 1000 attempts, a random suffix. This also removes the latent 200-row capped-window undercount. Format-preserving, so no owner decision ([[F2-310]]).

**Filed / not done.** The remaining count-minter candidates are recorded rather than fixed here ([[F2-188]] — do not force a mitigated / milder change): `CrisisAarService.nextReportCode` and `MtpdInheritanceService.generateAssessmentCode` are count-seeded but already carry bounded skip-loops (a soft-delete gap larger than the loop bound would still 500, but low-risk); `RegInspectService:189`'s document-request reference has no unique index (a count collision is a silent duplicate, not a 500); `RrpService.nextOrdinal` is one-per-fiscal-year (a > 200 window is implausible). The durable resolution is a gate correlating a `count…() + 1` reference seed with a filtered unique index on that column ([[F2-266]]) — deferred as its own slice (it must also fix each instance it finds).

| **Found by** | Asking [[F2-345]]'s / [[F2-197]]'s capped-list-then-aggregate question of BACKEND aggregates — sweeping `PageRequest.of(0, N)` / `findRecent` / `.limit(N)` sources feeding a sum / group / count. Most hits were correct: `PageRequest.of(0, 1).getTotalElements()` minters read the FULL total, and `recentCounterparties` / `topUtilisedLimits` are legitimate capped previews ([[F2-197]]). `CptyService.dashboard()`'s `totalExposureSarM` / `bySector` / `byInternalGrade` were the aggregate over a capped page. |
| **Verification** | hermetic ([[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]]) — the defect is which set the aggregate reads, so `CptyServiceTest` (new — the service had NO test, [[F2-248]]) pins the SOURCING: `totalExposureSarM` sums all rows (null exposure ignored), `bySector` / `byInternalGrade` cover all rows (null grade skipped), and `verify(never())` the capped `Pageable` overload. ### Fix

Replace the capped `findByOrganisationIdOrderByReferenceAsc(org(), PageRequest.of(0, 50))` with a new uncapped overload `List<Counterparty> findByOrganisationIdOrderByReferenceAsc(Long organisationId)` and iterate ALL counterparties. The grouping arithmetic (sum `totalExposureSarM`, `merge` into `bySector` / `byInternalGrade`, skip null grade / null exposure) is byte-identical; only the source is uncapped. The `recentCounterparties` preview keeps its `.limit(10)` (a capped list is fine to render — [[F2-197]]), now taken from the same uncapped list. Not a SQL `SUM` / `GROUP BY`: that would move the null-grade skip and grouping into SQL, unverifiable hermetically ([[F2-345]]'s rule). The new finder respects the entity's `@Where(is_deleted = 0)`, so it agrees with the existing capped finder's soft-delete scoping.

**Filed / not done.** The DTO field `recentCounterparties` is populated from a finder ordered `OrderByReferenceAsc` (alphabetical), not by date — an [[F2-197]] mislabel, left because changing the ordering to by-date is a product decision on what the preview shows; behaviour is unchanged by this slice.

## F2-351 — a run-code minter seeded from a COUNT re-mints a live ordinal, 500ing on the unique index

Mirror `ComplaintService#generateNextComplaintNo` (the platform's established sequential-minter idiom): seed from the MAX ordinal via a new `findTopByOrganisationIdAndExerciseIdOrderByRunCodeDesc` (regex-guarded so a caller override that sorts higher — [[F2-350]] — leaves `next = 1`), then a skip-loop against a new `existsByOrganisationIdAndRunCode`, with a UUID-suffixed backstop. A MAX never drops on a mid-sequence delete, so a used ordinal is not re-issued; the skip-loop absorbs the residual concurrency race ([[F2-267]]); and because the unique index is FILTERED (`WHERE is_deleted = 0`), a soft-deleted code is free to be re-used and the `@Where`-scoped finders agree with it.

## F2-350 — a long run-code override returned an opaque 500 instead of a 400

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-25 |
| **Severity** | P3 — a client-input boundary error surfacing as an opaque 500, on the BCM exercise-runtime create path. `ExerciseRuntimeService#startRun` (line 176) stores a caller-supplied `runCode` (`req.runCode().trim()`) directly into `ExerciseRun.run_code` `@Column(length = 64)` when non-blank (else auto-generates), and `StartRunRequest.runCode` carried no `@Size` — so a > 64-char override on `POST /api/v1/bcm/exercise-runs` (`BCM:WRITE`, routed, FE client) hits `NVARCHAR(64)` → SQL Server error 8152 → opaque 500 (in prod SEC-CFG-001 strips the class, so it reads as an outage rather than "your run code is too long"). A 400 naming the field is due. |
| **Registers** | none — a request-validation defect on `bcm.exercise_run`. No data change. |
| **Standards** | RFC 7807 ProblemDetail; the F2-185(b) request-`@Size`-mirror family, sibling of the [[F2-338]] / [[F2-346]] / [[F2-347]] server-composed-overflow family. |
| **Found by** | Executing [[F2-347]]'s own filing (*"`StartRunRequest.runCode` has no `@Size`, so a > 64-char code 8152s on the `ExerciseRun` insert itself — a milder [[F2-185b]] boundary question, a 500 where a 400 naming the field is due"*), after a diligent-negative sweep of `BigDecimal.divide` (all guarded by `scale, RoundingMode` / a bounded `MathContext` and `signum()==0` / ternary checks; only a pathological −100 % discount rate in `StrategyRoiService` is theoretically unguarded — not fixed, F2-188). |
| **Verification** | hermetic ([[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]]) — a unit test cannot trigger a real 8152, so `RequestSizeCapMirrorTest` registers the mirror `StartRunRequest#runCode` → `ExerciseRun.run_code` and asserts `@Size(max)` equals `@Column(length)` (64) by reflection, exactly as [[F2-346]] / [[F2-347]] proved their caps. Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]] / [[F2-287]]): removing ONLY the `@Size` annotation (fix committed first — [[F2-297]]) turns `everyEnabledSizeCapEqualsTheColumnItGuards` RED (*"StartRunRequest#runCode declares no @Size — the mapping is stale"*). `RequestSizeCapMirrorTest` + `InertValidationConstraintTest` + `NestedRequestCascadeTest` green; full backend suite green. Latent until a > 64-char override; no dev backend to live-probe. No migration. |

### Fix

`@Size(max = 64)` on `StartRunRequest.runCode`, mirroring `ExerciseRun.run_code`'s `@Column(length = 64)`. This is F2-184's "cap == column → enable" case: the database already refuses a longer value, so the only change is a 400 that names `runCode` instead of a truncation 500 — no request that works today can start failing. The service additionally stores a `trim()` of the raw value, so `@Size(max = 64)` on the raw never accepts an overflow (stored ≤ raw ≤ 64); it may reject a value padded past 64 with whitespace that would have trimmed-to-fit, which is the safe direction and consistent with every sibling `@Size` in the file.

**F2-215 sweep.** The other uncapped text fields on `StartRunRequest` are safe: `channel` is a closed vocabulary that `normaliseChannel` refuses (→ 400) or coerces to `IN_PERSON`, its members ≤ 12 chars; `facilitatorNotesEn`/`facilitatorNotesAr` are `NVARCHAR(MAX)`, correctly uncapped (F2-184). So `runCode` is the sole overflow field.

## F2-349 — an oversized file upload returned an opaque 500 instead of a 413

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-25 |
| **Severity** | P3 — a client-input error surfacing as an opaque 500, on the evidence/attachment upload path. The platform configures `spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size` (50 MB, both `application.yml` and `application-prod.yml`) and has multipart upload endpoints (`AttachmentController`, `EvidenceItemController`, `FileUploadController`), so a file over the limit throws `MaxUploadSizeExceededException` during multipart parsing. It is a `MultipartException` / `RuntimeException` matched by no handler in `GlobalExceptionHandler`, so it fell through to `@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)` → `handleGeneral` → opaque 500. A user uploading a large evidence document got *"An unexpected error occurred"* + a correlation id (in prod SEC-CFG-001 strips the class), indistinguishable from an outage, rather than "your file is too large." |
| **Registers** | none — an exception-routing defect in `GlobalExceptionHandler`. No data. |
| **Standards** | RFC 7807 ProblemDetail; RFC 9110 §15.5.14 (413 Content Too Large); the F2-227 / [[F2-339]] / [[F2-348]] opaque-500 family. |
| **Found by** | Continuing the opaque-500 sweep ([[F2-348]]): which JDK / framework exceptions on a caller-input path fall to `handleGeneral`? Confirmed all three conditions — a configured `max-file-size`, multipart upload endpoints, and no `MaxUploadSizeExceededException` / `MultipartException` handler anywhere in the tree. |
| **Verification** | hermetic ([[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]]) — the defect is one of ROUTING, so the load-bearing leg asserts Spring's own resolution: `new ExceptionHandlerMethodResolver(GlobalExceptionHandler.class).resolveMethod(<MaxUploadSizeExceededException>)` resolves to `handleUploadTooLarge`, not `handleGeneral`. Plus a direct-call leg (413, the 50 MB limit named in the detail, no class/root leak) and a verbose leg. Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]] / [[F2-287]]): disabling ONLY the `@ExceptionHandler(MaxUploadSizeExceededException.class)` annotation (keeping the method so the direct-call legs still compile — [[F2-339]]'s control) turns the routing leg RED (`expected "handleUploadTooLarge" but was "handleGeneral"`); fix committed first ([[F2-297]]). 24/24 `GlobalExceptionHandlerTest`; full backend suite green. Latent until an oversized upload occurs; no dev backend to live-probe, so the resolver leg is the proof ([[F2-348]]'s precedent). No migration. |

### Fix

One `@ExceptionHandler(MaxUploadSizeExceededException.class)` → **413 Payload Too Large**, mirroring F2-348's `DateTimeParseException` → 400. The limit is derived from the exception itself (`getMaxUploadSize()`, bytes ÷ 1 MiB → "50 MB") so the message names it without duplicating the `max-file-size` config value; the class name and root message stay dev-only (SEC-CFG-001), the same gate as the catch-all. The three conditions (a configured limit so the exception can fire, an upload endpoint so it is reachable, no dedicated handler) were each confirmed before fixing rather than assumed.

| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-25 |
| **Severity** | P3 — a client-input error surfacing as an opaque 500. Several controllers and intake adapters parse a caller-supplied date field with a manual `LocalDate.parse(...)` / `LocalDateTime.parse(...)` (`AuditEngagementController:88`, `EsgMetricController:80`, `NdiOperationalExcellenceKpiController:90`, `OutsourcingController:252`, `BreachPromotionAdapter`, `PolicyExceptionPromotionAdapter`, `ChangePromotionAdapter`, …), rather than a typed `@RequestParam LocalDate` (which `MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException` already maps to 400). `DateTimeParseException` is a `java.time` `RuntimeException`, not an `IllegalArgumentException`, so `handleIllegal` never caught it and it matched only `@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)` → `handleGeneral` → opaque 500. A user submitting a form with a mistyped date got *"An unexpected error occurred"* + a correlation id (in prod SEC-CFG-001 strips the class), indistinguishable from an outage. |
| **Registers** | none — an exception-routing defect in `GlobalExceptionHandler`. No data. |
| **Standards** | RFC 7807 ProblemDetail; the F2-227 / [[F2-339]] opaque-500 family (a real, classifiable exception dressed as an internal error). |
| **Found by** | Sweeping `LocalDate.parse` / `LocalDateTime.parse` / `Instant.parse` on caller-derived strings, then checking `GlobalExceptionHandler` for a `DateTimeParseException` / `DateTimeException` handler — there is none, and `DateTimeParseException` is not an `IllegalArgumentException`, so it falls to the catch-all. [[F2-339]]'s own note pointed here: *"asking F2-227's question of the OTHER opaque-500 family."* |
| **Verification** | hermetic ([[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]]) — the defect is one of ROUTING, so the load-bearing leg asserts Spring's own resolution: `new ExceptionHandlerMethodResolver(GlobalExceptionHandler.class).resolveMethod(<DateTimeParseException>)` resolves to `handleBadDate`, not `handleGeneral`. Plus a direct-call leg (400, no class/root leak) and a verbose leg (class surfaced under `verboseErrors`). Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]] / [[F2-287]]): disabling ONLY the `@ExceptionHandler(DateTimeParseException.class)` annotation (keeping the method so the direct-call legs still compile — [[F2-339]]'s exact control) turns the routing leg RED (`expected "handleBadDate" but was "handleGeneral"`); fix committed first ([[F2-297]]). 21/21 `GlobalExceptionHandlerTest`; full backend suite green. No migration. |

### Fix

One `@ExceptionHandler(DateTimeParseException.class)` → 400, mirroring F2-339's `NoResultException` → 404: it closes every manual-date-parse site platform-wide in one place. 400 is unambiguous — a parse failure means the string did not match the expected date format, which only a caller (or a malformed stored value) can produce; the server never mints a date string it then fails to parse. The class name and root message stay dev-only (SEC-CFG-001), the same gate as the catch-all.

### Scope

`MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException` (already handled → 400) covers Spring's own conversion of a typed `@RequestParam LocalDate`; this handler covers the MANUAL `.parse(string)` sites, a disjoint population. `DateTimeException` (invalid date components, zone-rules errors) is deliberately NOT handled — a parse failure is unambiguously caller input, while a general `DateTimeException` could be a server bug that a 400 would hide. The per-site alternative (a try/catch at each of the ~8 sites) was rejected: one handler is the smaller, F2-339-consistent change.

## F2-347 — an exercise-observation gap title overflowed the 255-char title_en column when the run code was long

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-25 |
| **Severity** | P2 — the [[F2-215]] sibling of [[F2-346]], flagged in that slice and left. `ExerciseObserverService.promoteObservationToGap` composes the gap title as `"Exercise finding (" + run.getRunCode() + "): " + truncate(observation, 180)` into `BcmGap.title_en` `@Column(length = 255)`. `run_code` is CALLER-SUPPLIED (`StartRunRequest.runCode`, no `@Size`) up to its `@Column(length = 64)`, so 18 (prefix) + 64 + 3 + 180 = 265 can exceed 255 → SQL Server 8152 → 500 on promoting an observation to a gap, for a run with a long descriptive code. The free text was truncated to 180 for readability but the caller-supplied run code was never budgeted. Latent in data, live in code — reachable with a 55+ char run code and a 180+ char observation. |
| **Registers** | `bcm.gaps.title_en` (the gap raised from an exercise observation), composed from a caller-supplied `exercise_runs.run_code`. No data change. |
| **Standards** | ISO 22301 / NCEMA exercise programme (observation → gap → remediation); the [[F2-338]] / [[F2-346]] / [[F2-185b]] server-composed-string-overflow family. |
| **Found by** | Directly — [[F2-346]] flagged this exact site (*"capped at 180 but check the gap title column"*) and deferred it. Confirmed: `run_code` is caller-supplied with no `@Size`, column 64, so `18 + 64 + 3 + 180 = 265 > 255`. Its sibling composition (`:445`, the Arabic title) has the same shape and was fixed too. |
| **Verification** | hermetic ([[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]]) — `ExerciseObserverServiceTest` drives `promoteObservationToGap` with a 60-char run code + a 300-char observation and asserts both the EN and AR gap titles are ≤ 255 and the run reference survives; a reflection leg mirrors `GAP_TITLE_MAX` against `BcmGap.title_en`'s `@Column(length)`. Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]] / [[F2-287]]): un-capping the EN title turns the leg RED (261 > 255); fix committed first ([[F2-297]]). The test also adds the `BcmRemediationService` / `BcmGapRepository` mocks the promote path needs — the existing suite never exercised it ([[F2-248]]). 25/25; full backend suite green. No migration. |

### Fix

Cap the whole composed title (EN and AR) to `GAP_TITLE_MAX = 255`, reusing the existing `truncate()` helper (identical to F2-338's `cap`). `GAP_TITLE_MAX` mirrors `BcmGap.title_en`'s `@Column(length)` by reflection so the cap and the column cannot drift. The inner `truncate(text, 180)` readability cap is kept; the outer cap only bites when the run code is long, and the run reference (prefix + code, ≤ 85 chars) always survives.

### Filed

`StartRunRequest.runCode` has no `@Size`, so a caller-supplied run code > 64 chars 8152s on the `ExerciseRun` insert itself — a milder [[F2-185b]] instance (a 500 where a 400 naming the field is due). Not fixed here (a distinct boundary-validation question); the gap-title cap makes the overflow that reaches the gap harmless regardless of run-code length.

## F2-346 — an auto-raised CAPA's title overflowed the 255-char title_en column when the violation description was long

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P2 — a latent-in-data, live-in-code 500 on a regulator-facing write. `EsgHorizonService.recordViolation` (the NCEC environmental-permit violation register, plan §5.6 / V293) raises a CAPA per violation and composed its title as `"NCEC violation on permit " + permitNumber + ": " + descriptionEn`, stored into `CorrectiveAction.title_en` `@Column(length = 255)`. `descriptionEn` is `@Size(max = 500)` at the controller and `EnvPermitViolation.description_en` is `NVARCHAR(500)`, so a long-but-legal violation description (> ~228 chars) composed a title exceeding 255 → SQL Server error 8152 (string-or-binary truncation) → 500 on `POST /esg/permits/{id}/violations`. The violation and its auto-CAPA share one `@Transactional`, so the whole recording rolls back — an NCEC violation with a verbose description cannot be recorded at all. |
| **Registers** | `sust.corrective_action.title_en` (the auto-raised CAPA), composed from `sust.env_permit_violations.description_en`. No data change. |
| **Standards** | NCEC (National Center for Environmental Compliance) permit-violation register; the [[F2-338]] / [[F2-185b]] server-composed-string-overflow family (a length budget must account for everything the code prepends, not just the caller's field). |
| **Found by** | Sweeping title/name/subject/code setters fed by string concatenation (F2-338's shape) for a composed string wider than its target column. `recordViolation` composes the whole 500-char-capable `descriptionEn` into a 255-char title. Its sibling compositions (`target_code` 40-wide at :160/161, `permit_number` 60-wide at :267/:305/:306) compose ≤ 94 chars and are safe — no [[F2-215]] sibling. |
| **Verification** | hermetic ([[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]]) — a unit test cannot hit a real 8152 (the mocked repository has no column), so it asserts the cap the service now applies before saving (F2-338's pattern). New `EsgHorizonServiceTest`: the composed title is ≤ 255 and ends with an ellipsis on a 500-char description; whole (no ellipsis) on a short one; `recordViolation` does not throw on a maximal description; and `CA_TITLE_MAX` mirrors `CorrectiveAction.title_en`'s `@Column(length)` by reflection so the cap and the column cannot drift. Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]] / [[F2-287]]): un-capping the composition turns the cap leg RED (title ~543 chars > 255); fix committed first, recoverable by `git checkout` ([[F2-297]]). 4/4 `EsgHorizonServiceTest`; full backend suite green. No migration. |

### Why cap and not widen the column

The full violation text is preserved on `EnvPermitViolation.description_en` (`NVARCHAR(500)`) and the CAPA links back via `source_ref = "ENV_PERMIT_VIOLATION:<id>"`, so truncating the title loses nothing recoverable ([[F2-338]]). Widening `title_en` would mean widening it on every CAPA writer platform-wide, and 255 is the platform's standard title width. The fix mirrors F2-338's `CrisisAarService.cap`.

### Not a ROWVERSION double-save

`recordViolation` saves the violation, saves the CAPA, then saves the violation again (to stamp `linked_capa_id`) — the [[F2-175]] / [[F2-227]] double-flush shape. Checked and refuted: neither `EnvPermitViolation` nor `CorrectiveAction` extends `BaseEntity` or carries `@Version`, so the second save is an ordinary by-id UPDATE with no optimistic-lock check.

### Filed

There are now four private `cap` / `truncate` copies (`CrisisAarService`, `ExerciseRunProjections`, `ExerciseObserverService`, `EsgHorizonService`) — an [[F2-190]] `common/` extraction candidate, deliberately deferred: F2-338 chose a private copy (no `common/` primitive exists), and an extraction touches four files plus their tests and is its own slice.

## F2-345 — the incident MTTR KPI averaged over the 200 newest-created incidents, not all resolved

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P3 — a latent-at-scale correctness defect in a dashboard KPI (no wrong figure at current data volumes). `IncidentService.getStats().avgDays` — the NIST SP 800-61r2 mean-time-to-resolve figure — was averaged over `findRecent(orgId, PageRequest.of(0, 200))`, the 200 most-recently-**created** incidents (`ORDER BY createdAt DESC`), then filtered to those with both a discovery and a resolution date. Its six sibling figures in the same `IncidentStats` (`total`, `open`, `investigating`, `resolved`, `critical`, `high`) are exact all-time `countBy…`, so the average was the only windowed figure in the strip. Two defects: (1) once a tenant exceeds 200 incidents, long-resolved older incidents fall out of the window; (2) ordering by `createdAt` over-weights freshly-created incidents — which resolve fast or are still open — biasing MTTR downward (the flattering direction). Latent today (`module/incident` → `cyber.incidents`, ~48 rows < 200, so the window contains everything and the figure is currently correct), wrong at scale. |
| **Registers** | `cyber.incidents` (via `module/incident`) — the canonical incident register the dashboard KPI reads. No data change. |
| **Standards** | NIST SP 800-61r2 (incident response; MTTR); [[F2-197]]'s "a capped list is fine to render and wrong to count" family; [[F2-215]]'s two-of-N. |
| **Found by** | Sweeping backend `findTopN` / `PageRequest.of(0, N)` results feeding a count / sum / aggregate for [[F2-197]]'s capped-then-counted shape. `IncidentService.getStats` computed a mean over a capped `findRecent(200)` while its sibling counts were uncapped `countBy…` — the inconsistency within one stats object is the tell. [[F2-195]] wired this real `avgDays` over a fabricated hardcoded `"4.2h"` and inherited the 200-cap unscrutinised ([[F2-215]]). |
| **Verification** | hermetic ([[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]]) — pure read-path logic, no live probe (no dev backend up). New `IncidentRepository.findResolvedWithDates(orgId)` (org-scoped, uncapped, `WHERE` both dates present — mirroring the old Java filter exactly, fetching only the rows the mean needs); `getStats` averages over it, arithmetic unchanged. `IncidentServiceTest` gains a leg pinning the sourcing (`verify(findResolvedWithDates)` + `verify(never).findRecent`) and the average incl. the `d >= 0` negative-diff drop; the capped `findRecent` is stubbed to a different mean (15.0 vs 3.0) so the leg discriminates on the value too. Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]] / [[F2-287]]): reverting only the service's source line to `findRecent(200)` turns the leg RED (`expected 3.0 but was 15.0`); fix committed first, recoverable by `git checkout` ([[F2-297]]). 24/24 `IncidentServiceTest`. api.ts doc corrected (it had documented the 200-cap — [[F2-184]]). No migration. |

### Why the fix is the uncapped set and not a SQL AVG

The existing computation does the day-diff in Java (`ChronoUnit.DAYS.between`) with a `d >= 0` guard that drops data-error rows where resolution precedes discovery. A pure SQL `AVG(DATEDIFF(...))` would not load rows but would change the arithmetic (DB-specific date math, and the negative-drop would move into a WHERE) — unverifiable hermetically with no DB. The uncapped `findResolvedWithDates` query provably preserves the exact arithmetic (same `ChronoUnit.DAYS.between`, same `d >= 0`, same `.average().orElse(0.0)`), removing only the cap and the `createdAt`-DESC bias, and it fetches a *smaller* set than `findRecent(200)` — only resolved-with-dates rows.

### Scope

`findRecent` is kept — `getRecent()` (the "5 most recent incidents" panel) legitimately uses it. Only `getStats`'s MTTR source changed. `discoveryDate` / `resolutionDate` are `LocalDate` (date-only), so `ChronoUnit.DAYS.between` is exact calendar days.

## F2-344 — the 72-hour PDPL breach notification was mis-cited as Article 23 (the DSR article) across the crisis module and UI

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P3 — a wrong statutory citation on regulator-facing content (no wrong figure or broken deadline; the 72-hour window itself is correct, only the cited PDPL article was wrong). The 72-hour SDAIA personal-data-breach notification is PDPL **Article 20** — the canonical `lib/moduleAnchors.ts` records it (`Article 20 → "Data-breach 72-hour notification window"`), and the `privacy` / `data_officer` modules cite it. **Article 23 is the data-subject-request 30-day article.** The crisis (`module/bcm/cycle`) module and several UI surfaces mis-cited the 72-hour breach as Article 23, so an operator / DPO reading the regulator countdown, the After-Action Report or the breach wizard saw the wrong legal basis. |
| **Registers** | citation text (not data): `module/bcm/cycle` (RegulatorCountdownService legal basis, CrisisAarService AAR line, BcmAuditCompletionService drafter message + audit line, CrisisEvent/Controller comments), `module/ai` (AiSuggestionService consequence), `module/platform/completion` (PrivacyGapService), and FE `bcmRegulatorCountdown.ts`, `workflowCatalog.ts` (EN + Arabic), `CyberIncidentWizard`, `BuyerGapPage`, `BreachNotificationWizard`. |
| **Standards** | PDPL Article 20 (72-hour breach notification) vs Article 23 (data-subject rights, 30-day); the [[F2-207]] / [[F2-214]] / [[F2-281]] citation-correctness family; canonical source is `lib/moduleAnchors.ts` (the regulator-citation catalogue W2-1a-i deliberately keeps). |
| **Found by** | [[F2-215]]'s two-of-N: [[F2-214]] fixed one wizard's two Article-23 citations and its own note (`BreachNotificationWizard.tsx`) said it fixed *"two places"* — leaving the family, which the wrong comments then propagated through the crisis module. Grepping every `Article 23` / `Art. 23` / `المادة ٢٣` and classifying breach-context vs DSR found 24 breach-context mis-citations across 13 files. |
| **Verification** | hermetic — a wrong citation is text, and only a live probe could see it rendered, so it is pinned structurally ([[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]]). `PdplBreachArticleCitationTest` (cross-codebase, reads both trees) has three legs: no source line ties an Article-23 citation to a 72-hour / breach context (line-scoped, with a DSR disambiguator so *"Article 23 is the 30-day data-subject article"* is not a violation, and stripping is unnecessary because the correct header carries no 72/breach on the Article-23 line); `moduleAnchors.ts` keeps the canonical Article 20 ↔ breach / Article 23 ↔ DSR mapping; and a self-test that the detector fires on a synthetic mis-citation and spares the DSR article. Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]] / [[F2-287]]): reverting one canonical citation turns the scan leg RED naming exactly that line while the anchor + self-test stay green; the fix was committed first so the control is recoverable by `git checkout` ([[F2-297]]). Backend build + `tsc` + FE suite (827/827) green. |

### Why it spread — and why the comments were fixed too

F2-214 corrected the two rendered citations it noticed in `BreachNotificationWizard` and left the rest, including the crisis entity's own comment (`CrisisEvent` — *"PDPL Article 23 72-hour deadline"*) which the drafter, controller, AAR and countdown all copied. A wrong comment is the input to the next reader's citation ([[F2-184]] / [[F2-205]]), so this slice fixed the comments as well as the rendered strings — otherwise the gate (which scans source, comments included) could not be a clean hard zero, and the error would re-propagate.

### Scope — what was left untouched

The correct DSR / 30-day **Article 23** citations (`DsrRequestLifecycle`, `dsrLifecycle.ts`, `moduleAnchors.ts:49`, `entityAnchors.ts`, `PrivacyService`, the DSR lifecycle tests) and the generic placeholder examples (`"e.g. PDPL Art. 23"` in wizard input hints and `submitWizard`/`WorkflowSubmission` docs) are correct and unchanged. The separate question of whether the DSR 30-day clock is Article 23 or Article 4 (both are cited in the tree) is a distinct citation-consistency matter, deliberately out of scope.

## F2-343 — the fraud dashboard's "Open Cases" headline counted a stale inclusion list, dropping the non-terminal outcome states

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P3 — a governance headline KPI wrong in the flattering direction, latent in data. `FraudService.dashboard()` reads `FraudCaseRepository.countOpenByOrg`, which counted `status IN ('DETECTED','TRIAGE','INVESTIGATING')`. That inclusion list had two faults: `'TRIAGE'` is a DEAD token (never persisted — `triage()` sets INVESTIGATING/FALSE_POSITIVE, and its own comment models triage as *"an intermediate state that closes immediately"*), proving the list was not derived from the machine; and it dropped the non-terminal outcome states CONFIRMED/CLEARED/FALSE_POSITIVE, each of which still transitions to CLOSED. So a CONFIRMED fraud case awaiting recovery / SAR filing — an emphatically open matter — read as NOT open, under-counting the SAMA fraud dashboard's "Open Cases" / "قضايا مفتوحة" headline. |
| **Registers** | `fraud.fraud_case.status` — read by `FraudCaseRepository.countOpenByOrg`, rendered by `FraudDashboardPage`'s "Open Cases" KPI. |
| **Standards** | SAMA fraud-management dashboard; the [[F2-196]] "open = complement of a declared terminal set, never a second inclusion list" family; [[F2-290]] (the same fix on the `ethics.cases` case register — a substantiated-but-not-closed case is open) and [[F2-341]] (the CAPA one). |
| **Found by** | asking [[F2-196]]'s question of a financial-sector module not previously swept: is "open" the complement of the machine's terminal set, or an inclusion list that drops states? `countOpenByOrg`'s `{DETECTED, TRIAGE, INVESTIGATING}` was the sharpest — a list with a dead token, dropping three non-terminal states, on a dashboard headline. |
| **Verification** | hermetic — `FraudOpenCountContractTest` reflects the machine constant and reads the repository source; no DB (the `@Query`'s row selection is SQL, only a live probe could count rows — [[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]]). Three legs: (A) the machine's terminal set, DERIVED from `ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS` (a status with no outgoing edge), is exactly `{CLOSED}`; (B) `countOpenByOrg`'s `@Query` excludes exactly that terminal set (`status <> 'CLOSED'`), never a bare inclusion list, and carries no dead token; plus a self-test that the query-extraction is non-vacuous. Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]] / [[F2-287]]): reverting the query to the old inclusion list turns the two query-dependent legs RED while the machine-only leg stays green; the fix was committed first so the control is recoverable by `git checkout` ([[F2-297]]). |

### Why the complement, and why "Investigating" being a separate tile settles it

The fraud machine (`ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS`) has one terminal state: `CLOSED → {}`. Every other status — DETECTED, INVESTIGATING, CONFIRMED, CLEARED, FALSE_POSITIVE — has an outgoing edge, so all are non-terminal and, by the platform's ratified convention, open until CLOSED. The dashboard already shows a separate **"Investigating"** tile (`investigatingCount`), so "Open Cases" is meant to be the broader umbrella — but the old `{DETECTED, INVESTIGATING}` list made it barely broader than the Investigating tile, dropping every case that had reached an outcome (fraud confirmed, cleared, or ruled a false positive) but not yet been administratively closed. The complement (`status <> 'CLOSED'`) is what the label means and what the ethics register already does ([[F2-290]]).

### Derive the terminal set; pin the @Query against it

`TERMINAL_STATUSES` is derived from `ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS` (the states with an empty outgoing set), never a second typed list ([[F2-196]]). The `@Query` is a necessary second copy of the vocabulary (JPQL cannot reference the Java constant at runtime), so `FraudOpenCountContractTest` parses the query's excluded token and asserts it equals the derived terminal set — adding a terminal state to the machine fails the build until the query is updated ([[F2-299]]). The adjacent `confirmedLossYtd` query legitimately uses `status IN ('CONFIRMED','CLOSED')` — a distinct "confirmed loss" scope, not an "open" count ([[F2-290]]'s narrower-question exception), and the gate is scoped to `countOpenByOrg` so it is untouched.

## F2-342 — the access-governance evidence package dropped the DECIDER from its SoD and recertification sheets

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P3 — an evidence-completeness defect on a regulator-facing EXPORT ([[F2-199]] harm ladder): no crash and no wrong value, but an omission of the load-bearing attribution. `AccessEvidencePackageService` builds the one-click access-evidence ZIP a SAMA/NCA inspector reads (NCA ECC 2-2 / SAMA CSF 3.3.5). Its `SoD_Violations.xlsx` sheet emitted the disposition note and accepted-until but **neither `dispositionBy` (WHO accepted the segregation-of-duties risk) nor `dispositionAt` (WHEN)**; its `Recertification_Evidence.xlsx` sheet emitted the decision and `decidedAt` (WHEN) but **not `decidedBy` (WHO recertified)** — a decision timestamp with no decider. For a four-eyes / maker-checker access review the decider identity IS the evidence, and the file left the platform stating *"a decision was made at T"* without saying by whom. |
| **Registers** | `iam.governance` — `SodViolation.dispositionBy`/`dispositionAt` and `AccessReviewItem.decidedBy`, emitted by `AccessEvidencePackageService`'s SoD_Violations and Recertification_Evidence sheets. |
| **Standards** | NCA ECC 2-2 (access management) / SAMA CSF 3.3.5 (access review); the [[F2-325]] / [[F2-326]] "the file that leaves the platform drops the actor" family; [[F2-249]] (`TenantUserDirectory`, the one person-reference resolver); [[F2-236]] / [[F2-256]] (the decider is the attribution an auditor reads). |
| **Found by** | [[F2-215]]'s two-of-N applied to the multi-sheet regulator bundles — F2-325/F2-326 made the audit-trail sheet of `BcmEvidencePackageService` / `RegulatorPackageService` whole; the OTHER package services' OTHER sheets were unexamined. `AccessEvidencePackageService`'s two governance sheets emitted a decision WHEN with no WHO. |
| **Verification** | hermetic — the two row-builders + header arrays extracted as package-private units and unit-tested over a stub resolver; no DB / PDF / ZIP / brand ([[F2-320]] / [[F2-325]] calibration). The decider is a real column, not a blank: `SodService` co-stamps `dispositionBy` + `dispositionAt` + `acceptedUntil` and `RecertificationService` co-stamps `decidedBy` + `decidedAt`, so the WHO is present on exactly the rows carrying the WHEN the sheets already showed ([[F2-198]] satisfied via the writer, not a DB query — the [[F2-325]] "co-populated, 0 divergent" precedent taken at the writer). Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]] / [[F2-287]]): reverting the decider columns turns all 5 legs RED (header absent + row/header size mismatch); the fix was committed first so the control is recoverable by `git checkout` ([[F2-297]]). 5/5 legs; no migration. |

### Blank-safe, never fabricated

The decider ids resolve through `TenantUserDirectory` (F2-249) via `resolve(id).map(labelFor).orElse("")` — an undisposed/undecided row (null id) or an id resolving to nobody (a deleted user, a foreign-tenant id) renders `""`, never a throw and never an invented name ([[F2-213]] / [[F2-209]]: an honest blank beats a fabricated actor, and an evidence export must not 500 on one stale id). Memoised per id, since a campaign is dispositioned by a handful of reviewers.

### Why the audit-trail-sheet fix did not cover this

F2-325 added the actor to `BcmEvidencePackageService`'s `audit_log.csv`; F2-326 swept the *same entity* (`AuditLogEntry`) across `RegulatorPackageService`'s audit-trail sheet. Neither touched the access-governance package, whose decider lives on different entities (`SodViolation`, `AccessReviewItem`) in different sheets. [[F2-215]]'s two-of-N: the mechanism that made the audit-trail sheets whole was visibly present, so the sibling package's sibling sheets read as covered.

### Filed

The other multi-sheet package services were NOT swept this slice ([[F2-326]]'s rule — check every other bundle before calling the family done): `NdiSubmissionPackageService` (NDI/NDMO submission), `CommitteeFormExportService`, `AiRegistryExportService`. Each should be read for a sheet that emits a decision/status without its actor.

## F2-341 — the annual IFRS S2 / TCFD climate report counted outstanding CAPAs with a two-token list, dropping COMPLETED + VERIFIED

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P3 — a completeness defect on a regulator-facing EXPORT, in the flattering direction, but latent in data and dropping the near-complete states rather than the urgent ones. The `sust.corrective_action` machine declares `TERMINAL_STATUSES = {CLOSED, CANCELLED}`, so "outstanding" is the four-state complement `{OPEN, IN_PROGRESS, COMPLETED, VERIFIED}`. `TcfdReportService.generateAnnualReportData` (section 9, `gapsCapa`) typed an inline `List.of("OPEN", "IN_PROGRESS")`, dropping COMPLETED and VERIFIED — so the "Open CAPA" KPI on the exported IFRS S2 / TCFD report PDF cover (plus the "Gaps & Corrective Actions" section and the XLSX sheet) under-counted outstanding remediation. The report is persisted whole into a DRAFT `ClimateReport.content_json` and rendered by `ClimateReportExportService`, so the under-count leaves the platform ([[F2-199]] harm ladder). The CAPA tab's own authoritative `aggregate()` counts all four non-terminal states and documents VERIFIED as *"awaiting closure"*, i.e. still outstanding — so the report had drifted from the module's own definition. Latent in data — needs a COMPLETED or VERIFIED (not-yet-CLOSED) CAPA to exist. |
| **Registers** | `sust.corrective_action.status` — read by `TcfdReportService` for the annual climate report and by `CorrectiveActionService.aggregate()` for the CAPA-tab KPI strip. |
| **Standards** | IFRS S2 / TCFD annual climate disclosure; CMA sustainability disclosure; the [[F2-196]] "open = complement of a declared terminal set, never a second list" family; [[F2-336]] (the same shape on the BCM CAPA readers); [[F2-282]] / [[F2-205]] "one concept, one definition, and which reader is authoritative." |
| **Found by** | asking [[F2-196]]'s / [[F2-336]]'s question of the non-BCM inclusion-list status counts — is "outstanding" the COMPLEMENT of a declared terminal set, or a typed subset that drops states? `TcfdReportService`'s `List.of("OPEN","IN_PROGRESS")` on a CAPA register was the sharpest: a two-token list on a machine with four non-terminal states, feeding an exported disclosure. |
| **Verification** | hermetic — pure read-path assembly logic, no DB / tenant / collation dimension ([[F2-320]]/[[F2-325]] calibration). New `TcfdReportServiceTest` (9 mocked collaborators) asserts COMPLETED + VERIFIED survive into `gapsCapa` and that no reader queries the old `StatusIn`; `CorrectiveActionServiceTest` gains a consolidation leg (`aggregate()` queries the `NotIn(TERMINAL_STATUSES)` complement, old `StatusIn` gone) and an arithmetic pin (`STATUSES \ TERMINAL_STATUSES == {OPEN, IN_PROGRESS, COMPLETED, VERIFIED}`). Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]]/[[F2-287]]): surgically reverting only the two query call sites turns 4 query-dependent legs RED via assertion failures (Mockito's default empty list, not an NPE) while the query-independent arithmetic pin stays green; the fix was committed first so the control is recoverable by `git checkout` ([[F2-297]]). 25/25 backend legs; full build green. |

### Why the two dropped states are outstanding, not resolved

The `sust.corrective_action` lifecycle is `OPEN → IN_PROGRESS → COMPLETED → VERIFIED → CLOSED`, with `CANCELLED` terminal. COMPLETED = remediation done, awaiting independent verification; VERIFIED = verified effective, awaiting formal closure. Neither is CLOSED, so both are still outstanding governance items — and the platform's own `CorrectiveActionService.aggregate()` says so twice: it counts both in `activeTotal`, and its overdue loop carries the comment *"VERIFIED items are no longer 'overdue' — they're awaiting closure."* Awaiting closure is outstanding. The annual report dropping them under-reported exactly the CAPAs an IFRS S2 assurer expects to see as open-but-nearly-done.

### One declared terminal set, two readers

`TERMINAL_STATUSES` is now `public` on `CorrectiveActionService` — the single source of truth. Both readers derive "outstanding" as its complement via a new `CorrectiveActionRepository.findByOrganisationIdAndStatusNotIn`, so a new non-terminal state added to the machine is counted automatically rather than silently dropped by a stale inclusion list ([[F2-336]] / [[F2-196]]). `aggregate()`'s query was already correct (a four-token `StatusIn` == the complement today) and was consolidated onto the same terminal-set derivation — behaviour-identical today, drift-proof tomorrow ([[F2-282]]: a third reader, never a third copy). Its display-bucket seed (an ordered `{OPEN, IN_PROGRESS, COMPLETED, VERIFIED}` for the KPI strip) is left as an explicit ordered list — a display concern, not an open-set copy.

### Scope and Filed

Only the outstanding-CAPA count was the defect. No migration, no CHECK, no vocabulary change — the fix is which statuses each reader queries. The `gapsCapa` field/comment still calls it "gaps + corrective actions" although the code queries only the CAPA register (the sust climate report has no separate gaps query) — a pre-existing naming looseness, not touched. The other non-BCM inclusion-list counts the sweep surfaced (`reginspect`, `regreporting`, `sharia`, `aml` screening) each ask a genuinely narrower question against their own machines and were read and left ([[F2-290]]'s "narrower question" exception): none typed a subset of a declared terminal complement the way this one did.

## F2-340 — a t('key') whose key is never declared rendered the raw key string to the user

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P3 (localization / UX quality; visible in both languages) — `i18n.tsx`'s translator is `t = (key, fallback?) => dict[key] ?? fallback ?? key`, so a single-literal `t('key')` for a key absent from BOTH dictionaries returned the key STRING itself and rendered it on screen. Three keys were referenced at 24 sites and declared nowhere: `loading` (20×), `loadingEllipsis` (3×), `toastValidationFailed` (1×). The last is the sharpest — `toast.danger(t('toastValidationFailed') ?? 'Required fields missing')` on `IncidentsPage` showed the literal string *"toastValidationFailed"* as a red validation toast, and the author's intended English text was stranded in a `??` JS fallback that `t()` — always returning the truthy key — never reaches. Live and reachable through ordinary use; no backend needed to observe. |
| **Registers** | frontend i18n: `tss-grc-ui-v2/src/translations/en.ts` + `ar.ts` (the two flat dictionaries) and `tss-grc-ui-v2/src/lib/i18n.tsx` (the `t()` fallback). Call sites span ~15 governance registers — evidence chain, risk scenarios, fourth-party, DR plans, processor / supplier / third-party assessments, contract clauses, data sharing, emerging risk, framework controls, committees, TPRM overview, RCA, signatures, incidents. |
| **Standards** | house rule 7 (bilingual parity, here the two dictionaries); the [[F2-201]] lineage of translation-key detection — F2-201 found DEAD keys (declared-but-unused); this is the INVERSE (used-but-undeclared, the one that renders a raw key to the user); [[F2-192]] (a key extractor must be string-aware — a line-first regex under-reads a multi-key line). |
| **Found by** | asking the inverse of [[F2-201]]'s dead-key question: sweeping every single-literal `t('key')` across `.ts`/`.tsx` against the declared key set. 3 undeclared keys / 24 sites, 0 false positives — `\bt\(`'s word boundary never matches `set(`, and no non-i18n `t` was hit on the tree. |
| **Verification** | hermetic — no DB / tenant / backend dimension ([[F2-320]]/[[F2-325]] calibration). `npx tsc --noEmit` clean; a string-aware tokenizer re-run shows raw-key sites 24 → 0 and the dictionaries balanced (5732 == 5732, 0 missing either direction, 0 dups); full frontend suite **827/827**. New gate `translationKeysDeclared.test.ts` — 4 legs: (A) used single-literal keys ⊆ declared (hard zero), (B) en/ar identical key sets, (C) no duplicate keys, plus a self-test driving both detectors over synthetic input. Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]]/[[F2-287]]): reverting only the two dictionaries fails leg (A) naming exactly `loading` (20), `toastValidationFailed` (1), `loadingEllipsis` (3) while B/C/self-test stay green; the fix was committed first so the control is recoverable by `git checkout` ([[F2-297]]). |

### Why the raw key rendered

`i18n.tsx`'s `t` returns `typeof dict[key] === 'string' ? dict[key] : (fallback ?? key)`, and the interface doc says so — *"the fallback / key itself if missing."* With the three keys absent from both dictionaries and no fallback argument passed, `t('loading')` returned `'loading'`, `t('loadingEllipsis')` returned `'loadingEllipsis'`, and `t('toastValidationFailed')` returned `'toastValidationFailed'`, each rendered verbatim in whichever language was active. 🔑 The `?? 'Required fields missing'` after the incidents-page call is therefore DEAD code — `t()` never returns a falsy value, so a JS `??` after it can never fire; the fallback has to be `t()`'s own second argument.

### Two invariants nothing guarded

(A) **every single-literal `t('key')` used in a component is declared** — violated at 24 sites. (B) **`en.ts` and `ar.ts` declare identical key sets** — held today (5732 each), but by hand: `BilingualInvariantRatchetTest` ([[F2-271]]) checks entity `*_en`/`*_ar` fields on the BACKEND, and the frontend dictionaries were unguarded. Both are now hard zeros with an empty exemption map, because there is always a correct alternative — declare the key, or pass a 2-arg default `t('key', 'Default')` which renders the default rather than the key ([[F2-214]]). The three keys are declared in both files matching `riskLoading`'s `'Loading risks…'` ellipsis style; `loading` and `loadingEllipsis` are synonyms kept for the two call-site idioms (table-cell placeholder vs `InlineEmpty`).

### The extractor must be string-aware — F2-192 against my own detector

A first-cut `^\s+(\w+):` regex reported `critHigh`/`critMedium`/`critLow` as undeclared. They ARE declared — en.ts packs four keys on line 1012 (`critCritical: 'Critical', critHigh: 'High', ...`) and a line-first regex captures only the first key on the line. So the extractor is a char-scan that skips string and comment spans and captures `<ident>:` at object depth 1, robust to multiple pairs per line and to commas inside string values. It also made an initial en/ar "5726 == 5726, clean" reading a coincidental under-count in both files; re-run string-aware, the true pre-fix count is 5729 and still balanced. This is the eighth-or-so instance in this programme of a source regex measuring its own shape rather than the code, and the first caught mid-slice against a detector I had just written.

### Scope and Filed

Single-literal `t('id')` only. A two-arg `t('id', 'default')` call has a fallback and cannot render a raw key — it is a separate, milder house-rule-7 question (the Arabic user sees the English default) and is **filed, not fixed here**: a cluster on `AuditCommitteeDashboardPage`, `AuditCommitteeSnapshotPage` and `RiskControlFindingPivotPage` uses ad-hoc capitalised keys like `t('Cancel', 'Cancel')`, `t('Annual', …)`, plus one odd `t('en', …)` — ~25 undeclared 2-arg keys. Whether each should become a real bilingual key or is intentional English chrome is a per-site reading job ([[F2-188]]: no manufactured verdicts). Dynamic / concatenated keys are not statically resolvable and are not flagged ([[F2-201]]).

## F2-339 — a jakarta.persistence.NoResultException escaped every DB handler and surfaced as an opaque 500 instead of a 404

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P3 (diagnostic quality; live in code) — `GlobalExceptionHandler` had no `@ExceptionHandler(NoResultException.class)`. `jakarta.persistence.NoResultException` (thrown by `em.getSingleResult()` when a query returns zero rows) is a `jakarta.persistence.PersistenceException`, **not** a Spring `DataAccessException`, so it did not match `handleMissingDbObject(DataAccessException)` or any other DB handler, and Spring's `PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor` — which would have translated it into a Spring exception — fires only for `@Repository`-annotated beans, not a `@Service` calling the `EntityManager` directly. The raw jakarta type therefore matched only `@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)` → `handleGeneral` → **HTTP 500** with the bare *"An unexpected database error occurred."* body, for what is really a "record not found" condition. Live in code and reachable through ordinary use; not measured against a running backend this slice. |
| **Registers** | platform-wide error mapping (`common/exception/GlobalExceptionHandler`); reachable throwers today: `EvidenceChainService.verifyChain` / `getChainStatus` (`GET /evidence-chain/{id}`, `POST /evidence-chain/{id}/verify`), and `CyberPdplBridgeService.triggerForIncident` ([[F2-281]]'s filed instance). |
| **Standards** | RFC 7807 problem responses; the [[F2-227]] lineage — an opaque 500 that cannot be diagnosed from the response gets rediscovered instead of fixed (F2-180: a wrong-but-specific diagnostic at least sends the reader somewhere; a generic diagnostic from a specific handler sends them nowhere). |
| **Found by** | asking [[F2-227]]'s question of the other opaque-500 families: a sweep for `getSingleResult()` (which throws `NoResultException` on empty) found `EvidenceChainService` selecting an evidence row by id, and the handler carried no mapping for the jakarta type — so it fell to the catch-all. [[F2-281]] had already observed the same behaviour on `CyberPdplBridgeService` and filed it. |
| **Verification** | hermetic — the fix is pure handler logic with no DB / tenant / row_version / collation dimension ([[F2-320]]/[[F2-325]] calibration), so no live probe. Extends the existing `GlobalExceptionHandlerTest` ([[F2-190]], not a new class) with three legs: (1) `handleNoResult` returns 404 with title *"Resource Not Found"* and no leaked exception class or root message under `verboseErrors=false` (SEC-CFG-001); (2) under `verboseErrors=true` the class name and JPA root message are surfaced while the status stays 404; (3) — the load-bearing one — `new ExceptionHandlerMethodResolver(GlobalExceptionHandler.class).resolveMethod(new NoResultException(...)).getName()` is `handleNoResult`, i.e. Spring's own resolution now routes the exception to the dedicated handler rather than to `handleGeneral`. Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]]/[[F2-287]]): disabling only the `@ExceptionHandler(NoResultException.class)` annotation (leaving the method so the two direct-call legs still compile and stay green — they test the method body) fails the resolver leg alone, `expected: "handleNoResult" but was: "handleGeneral"`; the fix was committed first so the control is recoverable by `git checkout` ([[F2-297]]). Full hermetic build **4771/0/0**. |

### The defect is one of routing, and why the routing was wrong

`@ExceptionHandler` methods on a `@RestControllerAdvice` are resolved by Spring's `ExceptionHandlerMethodResolver`, which picks the handler whose declared exception type is the *nearest supertype* of the thrown exception. Before this slice the only ancestor of `NoResultException` with a handler was `Exception` (via `handleGeneral`), because:

1. `NoResultException` extends `jakarta.persistence.PersistenceException` extends `RuntimeException` — none of which had a handler.
2. It is **not** a `org.springframework.dao.DataAccessException`, so `handleMissingDbObject(DataAccessException)` (which F2-227 established was the handler that swallowed DB exceptions into a generic 500) never matched it either.
3. Spring only translates a raw `PersistenceException` into a `DataAccessException` for beans it wraps with `PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor` — i.e. `@Repository` beans. The throwers here are `@Service` classes calling `EntityManager.getSingleResult()` directly, so no translation happened and the raw jakarta type propagated all the way to the advice.

So the exception surfaced as `handleGeneral`'s catch-all 500. The fix adds `@ExceptionHandler(NoResultException.class)` returning a 404, which the resolver now prefers (exact match beats the `Exception` supertype).

### Why 404 is unambiguously correct here (no policy choice)

A blanket "map exception X to a friendlier status" is usually a product decision, because X may arise from several conditions. Not here: `getSingleResult()` is the **only** thing that throws `NoResultException`, and it throws it in exactly one situation — a query that expected a single row got zero. Every reachable thrower in the tree is a lookup of a governance record by its id (with a tenant filter), so zero rows means the id is unknown, belongs to another tenant, or is soft-deleted — i.e. *not found*. There is no thrower for which the old 500 was the right answer, so there is nothing to weigh: 404 is honest for every case, and no working request is broken (nobody depends on a 500).

### Reachability

`EvidenceChainController` exposes `GET /evidence-chain/{evidenceId}` (`EVIDENCE:READ`) → `getChainStatus` and `POST /evidence-chain/{evidenceId}/verify` (`EVIDENCE:WRITE`) → `verifyChain`, both taking `evidenceId` straight from the path, and the underlying `SELECT … FROM evidence.evidence_items WHERE id = :id AND organisation_id = :org AND is_deleted = 0` `.getSingleResult()` throws `NoResultException` on any id that is unknown, foreign-tenant or soft-deleted. So the opaque 500 is reachable through ordinary use — e.g. opening the chain view for a record that was just deleted. State which you have ([[F2-283]]): the code defect is live; it was not re-measured against a running backend this slice (none up), and the fix does not change the isolation behaviour (a foreign id still returns nothing, now as a 404 rather than a 500).

### Filed

- The per-site `getSingleResult()` calls (`EvidenceChainService`, `CyberPdplBridgeService`) are left as-is: the handler fix covers them platform-wide, and rewriting each to `getResultStream().findFirst().orElseThrow(...)` would be churn for no additional behaviour. `CyberPdplBridgeService`'s instance was [[F2-281]]'s filed item and is now closed by this handler.
- `NonUniqueResultException` (the sibling `getSingleResult()` throws when a by-id query returns more than one row) is deliberately **not** remapped: that is a genuine data-integrity bug where a named 500 is the honest answer, not a 404, and no reachable thrower produces it today.
- `org.springframework.dao.EmptyResultDataAccessException` (the `JdbcTemplate.queryForObject` equivalent) is a `DataAccessException` and so is already caught by `handleMissingDbObject`; it is a different family and nothing in the tree throws it on a by-id lookup, so it is out of scope here.

## F2-338 — After-Action Report title composed from a 500-char source into a 300-char column, with no cap: a long-but-legal crisis title 500s AAR generation

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P2 (latent in data, live in code) — `CrisisAarService.generate` composed the NCEMA / ISO 22301 After-Action Report title as `"After-Action Report — " + crisisEvent.getTitleEn()` (a 22-char fixed prefix plus the crisis title) and stored it in `bcm.crisis_aar.title_en`/`title_ar` (`NVARCHAR(300)`, `@Column(length = 300)`), with no cap on the composition. `bcm.crisis_events.title_en` is `NVARCHAR(500)` (V102 drops the V1 300-char table and re-creates it at 500; the entity is `@Column(length = 500)`), so a crisis with a legal title of 279–500 characters overflows the 300-char AAR column with a raw SQL 8152 → **500 on generating the After-Action Report**. Because the AAR title is server-composed there is no `@Valid`/`@Size` request boundary between the source and the store, so the overflow is a 500 rather than a 400 that names the field. F2-185b's length-budget family, one step out. Latent in data (no stored crisis title measured at that length this slice; no dev backend up) but live in code and reachable through ordinary use, so a latent-hazard closure that is live-reproducible given a long-but-legal crisis title ([[F2-283]]). |
| **Registers** | `bcm.crisis_aar.title_en` / `title_ar` (NCEMA After-Action Report), composed from `bcm.crisis_events.title_en` / `title_ar` |
| **Standards** | NCEMA after-action reporting; ISO 22301 §9.1 post-incident review; the [[F2-185b]] length-budget family (a cap must account for everything the code adds, not just the caller's field). |
| **Found by** | applying [[F2-185b]]'s arithmetic to SERVER-composed strings rather than request `@Size` caps: where does a service store a value it composes (prefix + another entity's field) into a column narrower than the source it composes from? A sweep of `setX("literal" + …)` sites found `CrisisAarService` composing a 22-char prefix onto a 500-char-capable crisis title and storing it in a 300-char AAR column. |
| **Verification** | hermetic Mockito `CrisisAarTitleLengthTest` (2 legs) drives `generate` with mocked repositories: (1) a crisis whose `title_en`/`title_ar` are at the source ceiling (500 chars, legal there) produces an AAR title that fits the target column — asserted `<= CrisisAar`'s own `@Column(length)` read by reflection, and `TITLE_MAX` asserted equal to that length so the service cap and the column cannot drift ([[F2-185b]] mirror); the fixed prefix survives the cap; (2) an ordinary short title is left intact with no ellipsis. Pure composition logic, fully visible to a mock — no DB / tenant / row_version / collation dimension — so verified hermetically ([[F2-320]]/[[F2-325]] calibration), no live probe. Pre-fix control ([[F2-274]]/[[F2-287]]): a surgical revert of only the two `cap(...)` wraps (keeping the helper so the test compiles, since it references `CrisisAarService.TITLE_MAX`) fails the long-title leg (`522 > 300`) while the short-title leg still passes; a wholesale revert would not compile, which would read as a gate that passed. Full hermetic build **4768/0/0**. |

### The fix

The AAR title is a governance record's title, composed and stored by the server — there is no request DTO, so [[F2-185b]]'s `RequestSizeCapMirrorTest` (which pins request `@Size` caps against `@Column(length)`) has nothing to see. The cap belongs on the composition:

1. **Cap the composed string to the column length** — `cap("After-Action Report — " + safe(ce.getTitleEn()), TITLE_MAX)` and the same for `title_ar`, where `cap(s, max)` returns `s` when it fits and `s.substring(0, max - 1) + "…"` when it does not (the platform's established truncation semantics; the ellipsis is one BMP code unit, so the result is exactly `max` units — `NVARCHAR` and Java `String.length()` agree for BMP characters, and titles are text, not emoji).
2. **`TITLE_MAX = 300` mirrors `@Column(length = 300)`** on `CrisisAar.titleEn`/`titleAr`, and the test asserts `TITLE_MAX == columnLen("titleEn") == columnLen("titleAr")` by reflection, so widening or narrowing the column without moving the constant fails the build and points at the constant.

No canonical `common/` string-cap utility exists (checked), and the only other copy of this truncation is `ExerciseRunProjections.truncate`, a projection helper in the sibling `bcm.cycle.runtime` sub-package whose semantics are unrelated to AAR titles — so a small private helper here is the right shape, not [[F2-190]] duplication of a shared primitive.

### Why the cap and not a wider column

Widening `crisis_aar.title_en` to 522 would move the boundary rather than remove it — the prefix is fixed but the source column could itself be widened later, and a title is a title, not a body: an AAR whose title is a 500-character sentence is worse UX than a capped one with an ellipsis. Capping to the column is the same call [[F2-185b]] made (fix the arithmetic at the point the code adds length, do not chase the column). The `executive_summary_*`, `timeline_md_*` and the other narrative bodies are already `NVARCHAR(MAX)`, so only the two `title_*` columns are bounded and only they needed the cap.

### Reachability

`POST /api/v1/bcm/aars/generate/{crisisEventId}` → `CrisisAarService.generate` (guarded `hasPermission('BCM','WRITE')`), with a `lib/aar.ts` FE client (`api.post(.../generate/${crisisEventId})`) rendered from the crisis workspace — so the compose path is exercised end-to-end, not dark. The overflow fires on any crisis whose title runs 279 characters or more, which is legal in the source column and realistic for a descriptive crisis title (a multi-region outage sentence, say). State which you have ([[F2-283]]): the code defect is live and reproducible given such a title; whether any crisis title stored in dev or prod reaches that length today was not measured this slice (no dev backend up), so the closure is latent-in-data.

### Filed

- No migration and no CHECK: the fix is pure composition logic and the column widths are unchanged. A broader sweep of the F2-185b server-composition family (a service storing `prefix + anotherEntity.maxLengthField` into a narrower column) is possible — e.g. `ExerciseObserverService` composes a gap title from a caller-supplyable `run_code` (`NVARCHAR(64)`, no `@Size`) plus a truncated observation into a 255-char gap title, whose worst case (`21 + 64 + 180 = 265`) exceeds 255 but requires a pathological 55+ char run code — but those remaining members are narrower/latent and read per site rather than swept, since each needs its own source/target arithmetic (F2-188: do not manufacture a population).

## F2-337 — open-banking incident reference minted from a COUNT, not a MAX: a collision the filtered unique index turns into a 500

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P2 (latent) — `ObService.generateIncidentReference` built the SAMA open-banking incident reference `OBI-<year>-NNN` from `count(this-year incidents among the 500 most recent, live) + 1`. A count re-mints an ordinal already in use whenever a reference is absent from the counted set: **deterministically** once a tenant passes 500 incidents in a year (the `PageRequest.of(0, 500)` window then always returns 500 rows, so the count sticks and every subsequent create re-mints the same ordinal), and after any soft-delete or under a concurrent create. `ob_incident.reference` carries a FILTERED unique index `ux_ob_incident_reference` on `(organisation_id, reference) WHERE is_deleted = 0`, which then rejects the duplicate INSERT with a **500 on raising a SAMA-reportable incident**. F2-48's collision minter. Latent (no soft-delete path today; deterministic only past 500/year; a race at any volume), so a latent-hazard closure rather than a live-reproducible defect ([[F2-283]]). |
| **Registers** | `openbanking.ob_incident.reference` (SAMA Open Banking incident register) |
| **Standards** | SAMA Open Banking Framework — incident register / reporting; the F2-48 collision-minter family; [[F2-266]]/[[F2-267]]'s reference-mint idiom. |
| **Found by** | asking [[F2-197]]'s capped-list question of BACKEND minters and metrics (not just frontend KPI tiles): which count/aggregate is computed over a limited (`findTop…` / `PageRequest.of(0, N)`) result, where the cap can be exceeded? The incident-reference minter counted the top-500 to derive the "next" ordinal. |
| **Verification** | hermetic Mockito `ObIncidentReferenceMintTest` (4 legs) drives `raiseIncident` with a mocked repo and an `ArgumentCaptor` on `save`, `tppId` null so no consent/TPP path is touched: (1) a MAX of `OBI-<year>-003` with a gap below it mints `-004` (a COUNT would have re-used a lower, in-use ordinal); (2) the skip-loop steps over an existing `-004` to mint `-005`, backstopped by the unique index; (3) the first incident of the year starts at `-001`; (4) the reference matches the canonical `OBI-\d{4}-\d{3}` format. Pure synchronous minting logic, fully visible to a mock — no DB / tenant / row_version / collation dimension — so verified hermetically ([[F2-320]]/[[F2-325]] calibration), no live probe. Pre-fix control: reverting `ObService` to the count-based minter makes all 4 legs FAIL (the reverted body calls the un-stubbed top-500 finder and the STRICT stubs go unused — the test is coupled to the max-based contract and cannot pass on the pre-fix tree). Full hermetic build **4766/0/0**. |

### The fix

Mirror `ComplaintService#generateNextComplaintNo`, the platform's own sequential-minter idiom:

1. **Seed from the MAX, never a COUNT** — `findTopByOrganisationIdAndReferenceStartingWithOrderByReferenceDesc(org, "OBI-<year>-")` returns the highest live reference for the org+year (ordinals are zero-padded, so a lexicographic DESC is a numeric DESC within the format's domain), parse the tail, `+ 1`. A MAX survives a gap: deleting the middle of a sequence does not lower it, so a used ordinal is never re-issued.
2. **A collision-skip loop** — try `OBI-<year>-NNN`, `NNN+1`, … skipping any candidate `existsByOrganisationIdAndReference` already holds, backstopped by the filtered unique index for the residual concurrency race (the loser of a true race gets the 500 and the caller retries — the same accepted residual `ComplaintService` and `SubprocessorService` carry, [[F2-267]]).

Both new repository finders are scoped by the entity's `@Where(is_deleted = 0)`, so they see exactly the set the filtered unique index enforces — a soft-deleted reference is free to be re-used, and the loop agrees with the index on that.

### Why format-preserving MAX, and not entropy

[[F2-266]]/[[F2-267]] established `ReferenceCodeMint` (entropy) as the collision-proof primitive "because a per-tenant sequence needs a read-then-write so two concurrent creates race." Entropy would change `OBI-2026-001` to `OBI-2026-<entropy>` — a visible format change to a regulator-facing reference, which is a product decision with no defect behind it ([[F2-267]] made exactly this call for `subprocessorCode`). The MAX-seed + skip-loop is a **strict improvement that preserves the format**: it removes the deterministic collisions (window, gap) entirely and reduces the residual to the pure concurrency race, which the pre-existing unique index already backstops. So no owner decision is forced — the reference is still `OBI-<year>-NNN`, the server still mints it, and the only thing that changed is that a used ordinal is no longer re-issued.

### Reachability

`POST /api/v1/openbanking/incidents` → `raiseIncident` (`@Valid @RequestBody`), with a `lib/openbanking.ts` client (`raiseIncident`), so the minter is exercised end-to-end — not dark. The collision itself is latent: there is no soft-delete path for `ob_incident` in `ObService` today (so the gap-collision is not reachable via the API), and the window-cap collision needs > 500 incidents in one year for one tenant. State which you have ([[F2-283]]): this is a latent-hazard closure, and the deterministic window bug plus the concurrency race are what make it worth closing rather than filing.

### Filed

- No migration and no CHECK: the fix is pure minting logic, and the unique index already exists. `ob_incident` has no other count-based reference minter (the module's only one). The `OBI-<year>-NNN` format caps display niceness at 999/year (`%03d`); beyond that the skip-loop still produces valid uniques, and the format itself is the limiting factor, not the minter.

## F2-336 — "open" corrective actions / gaps counted by a single status token, under-reporting the NCA/ISO 22301 readiness KPI

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P2 — the BCM CAPA machine has 8 states, terminal `= {CLOSED}`, so 7 are open: OPEN (the initial state), ASSIGNED, IN_PROGRESS, EVIDENCE_SUBMITTED, UNDER_REVIEW, **OVERDUE**, REOPENED. `BcmReportService#bcmReadiness` (NCA ECC §3-5 / ISO 22301 `BCM_READINESS`), `#cmaAnnualDisclosure` (CMA annual disclosure) and `BcmRemediationService#stats` (dashboard) each defined "open corrective actions" with a DIFFERENT single token — `{IN_PROGRESS}`, `{IN_PROGRESS}`, `{OPEN}` — dropping 6 of the 7 open states, flatteringly. "Open gaps" was consistently `{OPEN}`, dropping the 4 actively-worked states (ASSIGNED, IN_PROGRESS, UNDER_REVIEW, REOPENED). So an OVERDUE corrective action past its deadline, and a freshly-created OPEN one, were invisible on a readiness KPI — the single most important row for such a report. Live on any tenant with a CAPA in a state other than the one counted token. |
| **Registers** | `bcm.corrective_actions.status`, `bcm.gaps.status` (BCM remediation) |
| **Standards** | NCA ECC §3-5 / ISO 22301 BCM readiness; CMA annual BCM disclosure; the [[F2-196]] "open = complement of a declared terminal set, never a second list" family, and [[F2-282]] "one concept, one definition." |
| **Found by** | asking [[F2-196]]'s question of every inclusion-list status count in services — is "open" the COMPLEMENT of a declared terminal set, or a single token that drops states? — then [[F2-282]]'s follow-up: how many readers of this concept exist, and do they agree? |
| **Verification** | hermetic Mockito `BcmOpenRemediationCountTest` (4 legs): each of the three defective readers now returns the complement count (distinct sentinels stubbed on `countByOrganisationIdAndStatusNotIn`), with `verify(never())` on the old single-token `countByOrganisationIdAndStatus(_, "OPEN"|"IN_PROGRESS")`; a constant-grounding leg pins `CAPA_RESOLVED={CLOSED}` / `GAP_RESOLVED={CLOSED,ACCEPTED_RISK}`, asserts the dropped states are open, and (by reflection) that each resolved token is a member of the register's declared vocabulary so a rename cannot leave it dangling. Pre-fix control: the 3 behavioural legs fail on the reverted readers (`expected 42L but was 0L`). Repurposed `BcmReportServiceTest`'s single-token stub-and-assert ([[F2-159]] shape). Full hermetic build **4762/0/0**. No migration, no DB write, no live probe (pure read-path logic — [[F2-320]]/[[F2-325]] calibration). |

### The fix

Declare the resolved sets ONCE on `BcmRemediationService` (the owner of `CAPA_STATUSES`/`GAP_STATUSES` and both transition machines) and have every reader count the complement via a new `countByOrganisationIdAndStatusNotIn`. This is [[F2-196]]'s rule (open = complement of a declared terminal set, so a state nobody remembered is CHASED rather than excused) with [[F2-282]]'s follow-up (a concept read by several places must be read the same way, from one definition). All readers are in `module/bcm/cycle/service/`, the same package as `BcmRemediationService`, so a reader references `BcmRemediationService.CAPA_RESOLVED` directly — a third reader of the definition, never a third copy of it.

### The authoritative reader was already right, and three others drifted from it

`BcmBoardPackService#capaSnapshot` computes `activeOpen = open + assigned + inProgress + evidence + review + overdue + reopened` — the full complement of `{CLOSED}` — and its overdue sweep uses `done = List.of("CLOSED")`. So the platform already had the correct definition; the readiness report, the CMA disclosure and the dashboard each picked a different single token and disagreed with it. [[F2-205]]'s question (how many things read this, and which is authoritative?) with the answer that the board pack was authoritative and three readers had drifted — and [[F2-290]]'s corollary that consistency among the drifted readers (the gaps were uniformly `{OPEN}`) is not correctness.

### Why ACCEPTED_RISK is resolved, and not a manufactured verdict

For gaps the one judgement is whether `ACCEPTED_RISK` (risk formally accepted, remediation deliberately not pursued) is "open." It is treated as resolved everywhere else in the platform: `AttackSurfaceFindingService.CLOSING_STATUSES` includes it; the NDI gap sibling computes "critical open" as `not (RESOLVED|CLOSED|ACCEPTED_RISK)` (`NdiGapService`, `NdiDashboardService`, `NdiSubmissionPackageService`); and `MassAssignmentRatchetTest` pairs "CLOSED/ACCEPTED_RISK" as the operator dispositions. So `GAP_RESOLVED = {CLOSED, ACCEPTED_RISK}` follows the platform's own consistent treatment ([[F2-205]]) rather than inventing one ([[F2-188]]). CAPAs have no such disposition state — every non-CLOSED CAPA status is an active workflow step, including OVERDUE — so `CAPA_RESOLVED = {CLOSED}`, matching the board pack.

### Filed

- `BcmReportService#ncaCyberContinuity`'s `openGapsTaggedCyber` was also converted to the complement in this slice (it is a gap reader), so the five report readers + the two `stats` readers all converge; the board pack was left as-is (already correct, and its per-state breakdown is legitimate detail).
- No migration and no CHECK: this is pure read-path counting. `bcm.gaps.status` / `bcm.corrective_actions.status` vocabularies are enforced by the transition machines, not a CHECK — that is [[F2-221]]'s separate question and its writers were not touched here ([[F2-183]]).

## F2-335 — a case-sensitive control branch skips the NDMO data-quality RED escalation for a lowercase band

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P3 (latent) — `DataGovernanceService.recordQualityRun` stored a caller-supplied RAG `band` verbatim and fired the `QUALITY_RUN_RED` escalation on a case-sensitive `"RED".equals(req.band())`, so a machine caller sending `band: "red"` skips the escalation the dashboard + automation engine react to. A SECOND reader — `DataOfficerQueryService#qRed30`, the "RED runs (30d)" dashboard KPI — filters `"RED".equals(r.getBand())`, so the same lowercase band also vanishes from the RED count. Reachable only through the API (no `@Pattern`, no CHECK), so latent ([[F2-182]]: reachability is a fact about today). |
| **Registers** | `data_officer.quality_run.band` (NDMO data-governance quality runs) |
| **Standards** | NDMO Data Governance (data-quality monitoring); the [[F2-179]] case-insensitive-collation family |
| **Found by** | asking [[F2-179]]'s question of request-derived control branches (a value stored verbatim then compared case-sensitively to fire a control), narrowed from 389 raw candidates to the request-derived, upstream-ungated ones. |
| **Verification** | hermetic Mockito unit test (`DataGovernanceServiceTest`, 4 legs) capturing the saved `QualityRun.band` and `verify(support).emit(...)` — the defect is pure Java logic (a case comparison + emit), fully visible to a mocked collaborator, with no DB / tenant / collation dimension, so no live probe ([[F2-320]]/[[F2-325]] calibration). Pre-fix control: 3 of 4 legs fail on the reverted service (the canonicalisation legs), including the load-bearing `lowercaseRed…andEscalates`. Full hermetic build **4758/0/0**. |

### The fix

Normalise the band on write — `String band = req.band() == null ? null : req.band().trim().toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT)` — and use it for both `run.setBand(band)` and `if ("RED".equals(band))`. This is [[F2-302]]'s rule: normalise on write so the stored value is canonical and BOTH readers (the escalation emit and the `qRed30` filter) agree, rather than `equalsIgnoreCase` at the emit site, which would leave the odd casing in the column and miss the dashboard filter. It is `coerce`, not `require` ([[F2-182]]): nothing upstream refuses a non-vocabulary band today (no coercion, no CHECK), so a 400 would break a working request; canonicalising refuses nothing and only RED escalates, correctly.

### Why 389 raw candidates are not 389 defects

A single-line grep for `"UPPER".equals(getX())` in services returns ~389 hits; a regex cannot tell a request-derived value from an entity-derived one ([[F2-182]]: reachability is a dataflow question). The defect bites only when the value comes from the REQUEST, is stored/acted-on with no upstream vocabulary gate, and the wrong branch skips a control. Two high-harm-looking candidates were read and REFUTED: `FraudService.setOutcome` runs `guardTransition(c.getStatus(), req.getOutcome())` FIRST — a machine check that refuses a non-vocabulary token ([[F2-179]]'s safe shape) — and `DrPlanService.recordTest` guards `if (!TEST_OUTCOMES.contains(req.outcome())) throw` on the line above the FAILED/GAP → CAPA escalation. Both are correct; both would read as defects to the naive grep because the guard is on a separate line from the `.equals`.

### Filed

- whether `band` should be server-DERIVED from `passPct` (a quality-rule threshold) rather than caller-supplied — an owner/product decision ([[F2-221]]: do not invent a machine), not this family's defect.
- any existing non-canonical stored `band` rows — a one-time UPDATE needing a DB measurement in both databases + house rule 6 authorisation, not measurable this slice (no dev backend running); the normalise-on-write fix makes all NEW rows canonical.

## F2-334 — census reconciliation: eleven mass-assignment NEEDS-VERDICT rows adjudicated (19 → 8)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P3 (instrument hygiene) — a CEILING does not force the census update its own contract asks for ([[F2-330]]), so closed / inert / by-design mass-assignment rows accumulate printing `NEEDS-VERDICT`. That is worse than a missing row ([[F2-250]]): it sends the next reviewer to re-read a guarded path, or to "re-fix" it. Continuing [[F2-333]]'s audit, eleven more such rows were read and adjudicated; **no new live forge was found** (the readable set is exhausted — [[F2-333]]'s ThreatIntel actioned-ledger forge was the last clean one). |
| **Registers** | instrument only — `MassAssignmentRatchetTest.ADJUDICATED` / `BASELINE_UNADJUDICATED_NEW_CRIT` |
