| **Standards** | — (mass-assignment / F2-22b family: [[F2-172]](d)-adjacent hygiene) |
| **Found by** | continuing [[F2-330]]/[[F2-333]]'s per-member audit of `target/mass-assignment-risk.txt`. |
| **Verification** | each of the eleven read against its service this slice (F2-188 — a scrub/guard present, a whitelist confirmed, or an undesigned lifecycle with no route to bypass), never trusted from prose. `MassAssignmentRatchetTest` 8/8 with the surfaced-unadjudicated count re-derived `still unadjudicated = 8` (F2-207 — off the regenerated census, not guessed). Full hermetic build **4754/0/0** (unchanged — no production code touched, no new test). |

### The eleven verdicts

- `CyberController#saveAssessment` / `#updateAssessment(ControlAssessment)` — **BY DESIGN**: `approveAssessment` (POST /{id}/approve) only sets `status=APPROVED` with no attribution, SoD or audit, so it is a redundant shortcut rather than a control save/update bypass; `status`/`reviewerName` are undesigned caller-set fields; org is stamped on create and never copied on update.
- `KycController#recordHit(ScreeningHit)` — **CLOSED [[F2-288]]**: `recordHit` scrubs `decidedAt` (and `decidedByName`/`dispositionNotes`); the decision belongs to `POST /hits/{id}/disposition`. `disposition` itself is caller-set by design (the screening feed classifies).
- `CmaDisclosureController#update` / `TcfdItemController#update` — **CLOSED / INERT [[F2-297]]**: create scrubs `approvalStatus`/`lastReviewedAt`; update never copies `approvalStatus`, guards `disclosureStatus` via `sameState()` (`markReviewed` fires only on a real change), and `reviewerName` is a partial-update data field.
- `PolicyController#update` / `CyberPolicyController#update(PolicyDocument)` — **CLOSED [[F2-222]]**: both route to `PolicyManagementService.update`, whose whitelist never copies `status`/`publishedAt`; `approverName` is frozen (transition() stamps it from the principal once the C-6 SoD check passes), owner is editable only in DRAFT, and a PUBLISHED plan locks to review-only edits.
- `PolicyController#updateException(PolicyException)` — **INERT [[F2-231]]**: `updateException` is a whitelist (title / justification / compensating-controls / risk / dates / notes); `status`, `reviewerName`, `reviewedAt`, `approverName` and `rejectedAt` belong to `transitionException()`, which stamps the actor from the principal.
- `MaDueDiligenceController#create` / `#update(MaDueDiligence)` — **BY DESIGN [[F2-218]]**: `loiSignedAt` is the caller's (an M&A letter-of-intent signing date the operator records; no dedicated route owns it); org is stamped from `TenantContext` on create and `copyMutable` never copies it on update.
- `CommitteeMemberRegistryController#addSkill(CommitteeMemberSkill)` — **BY DESIGN**: `lastReviewedAt` is a caller-set skill-assessment date (defaulted to today when omitted); no dedicated skill-review route owns it and there is no state machine; org stamped from `TenantContext`, id nulled.

### Why no code changed, and why that is the slice

The forge hunt is the primary value (it is how [[F2-328]]…[[F2-333]] each found a live defect); when it comes up empty, the reconciliation is what remains, and it is not busywork. F2-330 recorded that a ceiling tolerates a mislabelled row indefinitely, so the census drifts unless a reader adjudicates each member and re-derives the ceiling in the same commit. Eleven rows that were closed/inert/by-design were printing `NEEDS-VERDICT` — each an invitation for the next reviewer to re-read a guarded path. Recording the verdicts and lowering the ceiling 19 → 8 closes exactly that gap. Manufacturing a verdict for a row not read, or forcing a "fix" onto an undesigned lifecycle, would be the ([[F2-188]]) / ([[F2-221]]) trap; the eleven were all read this slice.

### The remaining eight

Left `NEEDS-VERDICT` as genuine owner-decisions / filed items (a manufactured verdict is worse than an honest gap):

- `CyberController#updateActionPlan(CyberActionPlan)` — [[F2-329]]: the update-path status jump needs a state machine designed (owner decision).
- `CyberController#updateException(VulnException)` — [[F2-328]]: same, on the vuln-exception register.
- `DataSharingAgreementController#create(DataSharingAgreement)` — the `isActive` question filed since [[F2-331]].
- `ControlLibraryController#createMapping` / `#updateMapping` / `#linkRiskToControl` / `#updateLink` — [[F2-231]]: `setLastReviewedAt(now())` fires on every update, so recording a review requires designing a review trigger (owner decision).
- `IrPlaybookController#save(IrPlaybook)` — [[F2-333]] read it and left it: an undesigned review lifecycle (`status`/`lastReviewedBy` caller-set, `recordInvocation` a legacy shim, no dedicated review/attest route), so a fix is a product decision.

## F2-333 — a save could forge ThreatIntel's SOC-E actioned-ledger summary with no ledger row

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P2 — `ThreatIntelService.copyMutable` (the explicit-update branch of `save`) copied `actioned` / `actionedAt` / `actionedByUserId` / `actionNotes` from the request, and the create path (`orElseGet`) saved the request entity directly. Those four columns are the **denormalised summary** of the append-only `threat_intel_action` ledger, written by exactly one route — `actionIoc()` (POST /{id}/action), which APPENDS an immutable `ThreatIntelAction` row (stamping `actionedByUserId` from `CurrentActor`, `actionedAt` from the clock) BEFORE flipping the parent summary and audits `TI_ACTIONED`; the entity's own comment says *"the full history lives in threat_intel_action."* So a caller could `POST`/`PUT` a `ThreatIntel` marked *actioned by X at T* with **no ledger row and no `TI_ACTIONED` audit** — falsifying the SOC-E record that a Saudi-CERT / NCA / MISP advisory was handled — or flip `actioned` back to `false` to hide that an IOC was handled. It is also a **privilege boundary** ([[F2-330]]): `save` admits `TI_INGEST` (a feed-ingestion role) that `/action` does not, so an ingest caller lacking `SECURITY_ANALYST` could mint a forged actioned-by-analyst record. [[F2-331]]/[[F2-332]]'s ledger-pointer shape, one register over. |
| **Registers** | `socops.threat_intel` · `socops.threat_intel_action` |
| **Standards** | SOC-E IOC action record (NCA / Saudi-CERT threat-intel handling; the append-only `threat_intel_action` ledger + `TI_ACTIONED` audit as the record of that a bulletin was actioned, by whom, and against which asset/vuln/detection). |
| **Found by** | reading the mass-assignment `NEEDS-VERDICT` work list. `ThreatIntelController#save`'s *flagged* fields (`organisationId`/`publishedAt`) were both benign; the forge was in fields the ratchet's authority vocabulary never spells, found by reading the service against `actionIoc()` — exactly as [[F2-331]]/[[F2-332]] were found by reading rather than by the scan flagging the field. |
| **Verification** | two unit tests (`ThreatIntelServiceTest`): an explicit update carrying a forged summary leaves the loaded row's summary untouched and appends **no** ledger row (`verify(actions, never()).save(...)`); a create is born un-actioned, scrubbing a body-supplied summary. Full hermetic build **4752 → 4754/0/0**; `MassAssignmentRatchetTest` re-derived 8/8 with the surfaced-unadjudicated count = **19**. No live probe: a synchronous scrub, the permission boundary read from the two `@PreAuthorize` annotations ([[F2-325]]…[[F2-332]]'s standard); the FE has no threat-intel save/create client (it actions IOCs only via POST /{id}/action), so `save` is API/ingestion-only. |

### The fix

`save` has three paths. The **dedup-update** path (`.map(existing -> ...)`, when an advisory re-arrives on the same `(source, externalId)`) already copied a safe subset that never touched the summary. The **explicit-update** path (`copyMutable`) copied all four summary columns; it now copies none, so an update **preserves** whatever `actionIoc` last set on the loaded row (the [[F2-332]] scrub-on-update shape — stop copying, keep the ledger-derived value). The **create** path (`orElseGet`) saved the request entity directly; it now scrubs the four so a freshly ingested advisory is born un-actioned. The summary's only writer is `actionIoc`, which appends the immutable ledger row first.

### Census reconciliation (F2-330's rule)

A CEILING does not force the census update its own contract asks for, so closed/inert rows accumulate mislabelled `NEEDS-VERDICT` ([[F2-330]]). Hunting this forge read ten more rows, all already closed/inert/undesigned service-side; each was adjudicated against its service this slice ([[F2-188]]) and `BASELINE_UNADJUDICATED_NEW_CRIT` was re-derived **29 → 19** off the regenerated census (F2-207), never guessed:

- `ThreatIntelController#save` — BY DESIGN (flagged fields) + this fix.
- `DpiaController#addReview` — CLOSED F2-22b(vii): stamps `reviewerId`/`reviewerName` from `CurrentActor`, `decidedAt` from the clock; the call IS the review.
- `DpiaController#addMitigation` — BY DESIGN F2-22b(vii): `status` caller-set (no verify endpoint, no state machine); `verifiedAt` a server-value ternary.
- `RegulatorExaminationController#save` / `#update` — BY DESIGN: an undesigned SAMA/NCA examination tracking register (no dedicated transition route, no state machine); `status`/`closedAt` are milestone fields; org stamped from `TenantContext` / never in `copyMutable`.
- `SustainabilityEvidenceController#create` / `#update` / `#supersede` — CLOSED SEC-ESG-003 (create scrubs the approval/attribution set) / INERT (update whitelist omits it) / CLOSED (supersede delegates to create).
- `BcpPlanController#update` — INERT F2-330: `status` via `requireUnchanged`, `lastAttestedAt`/`publishedAt` never in the whitelist.
- `CorrectiveActionController#update` — INERT: whitelist omits `status`/`closedAt` (`transition()`'s), refuses editing a CLOSED/CANCELLED row.

`IrPlaybookController#save` was **left `NEEDS-VERDICT`** rather than over-reaching: it is the same undesigned-lifecycle shape (no dedicated review/attest route, `recordInvocation` a legacy shim) but was read less deeply than the ten, and a manufactured verdict is worse than an honest gap ([[F2-188]]).

### Filed

The threat-intel `save`/`/action` guards and this fix stand; not addressed here (owner-decisions / read-per-member): the remaining **19** `NEEDS-VERDICT` rows (read per member); whether `TI_INGEST` should reach `save` at all (it is an ingestion role, and its legitimate need is to create advisories, not to action them); and `IrPlaybook`'s undesigned review lifecycle (`status`/`lastReviewedBy` caller-set with no dedicated review route — designing one is a product decision).

## F2-332 — a PUT could move a forensics artefact's custody with no chain-of-custody ledger row

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P2 — `ForensicsArtefactService.copyMutable` copied `currentCustodian` AND `currentLocation` straight from the request. Those are the denormalised pointer to the latest row of the SOC-D append-only custody ledger, written by exactly one route — `transferCustody(id, newCustodian, newLocation, notes)`, which APPENDS an immutable `forensics_custody_event` TRANSFER row *before* moving the pointer and audits `FORENSICS_CUSTODY_TRANSFER` so the chain can be reconstructed verbatim in court. `copyMutable` runs **only on the update branch** of `save` (a create uses the request entity directly and seeds a CAPTURE ledger row from these fields), so a `PUT /{id}` moved the custodian/location of court-bound evidence with **no ledger row and no audit** — the chain-of-custody invariant `current_custodian == latest ledger row` broken silently. The `transferCustody`, `create` and `update` routes all carry `hasAnyRole('FORENSICS_LEAD','IR_LEAD','CISO', ...)`, so it is a **same-permission control-defeat** — [[F2-331]]'s forge one field-pair over, on the same register. |
| **Registers** | `socops.forensics_artefact` · `socops.forensics_custody_event` |
| **Standards** | chain-of-custody integrity (ISO/IEC 27037 acquisition/handling; the append-only SOC-D custody ledger + `FORENSICS_CUSTODY_TRANSFER` audit reconstructed verbatim in a courtroom) |
| **Found by** | [[F2-331]]'s own filed *"custody pair"* item — reading `ForensicsArtefactService.copyMutable` against `transferCustody()` and the CAPTURE-seed on the create path. |
| **Verification** | two unit tests (an update leaves the custody pointer unchanged and appends **no** ledger row; a create keeps the request custodian and seeds the CAPTURE row); full hermetic build 4750 → 4752/0/0; `tsc` clean (no FE change — the custodian already rendered). **Latent in data, live in code** ([[F2-283]]): all **4** artefacts in dev **and** prod carry a custodian with **0 ledger rows** — seeded by direct SQL, bypassing `save()`, so no CAPTURE row exists and no pointer has been silently moved — but the `PUT` path is reachable by any of the four privileged roles. No live probe: a synchronous copy removal, the permission boundary read from the controller's `@PreAuthorize` annotations ([[F2-325]]…[[F2-331]]'s standard); the FE has no create/update client (only `forensicsTransferCustody`), so the route is API-only. No initialiser removed (both columns are nullable), so no `Moved` gate entry — a pure `copyMutable` scrub. |

### The sibling forge, one field-pair over

[[F2-331]] closed the integrity attestation pair (`integrityStatus`/`integrityVerifiedAt`) in `copyMutable` and **filed the custody pair beside it**. This is that pair. `transferCustody`'s own comment states the design: *"APPEND an immutable custody-transfer row to the ledger BEFORE moving the artefact's current-holder pointer — the chain is only ever extended, never overwritten. The artefact's current_custodian is a denormalised pointer to the latest ledger row."* `copyMutable` copying `currentCustodian`/`currentLocation` from a `PUT` body wrote the pointer with no ledger extension — the one operation the SOC-D design exists to make impossible. 🔑 **[[F2-215]]'s two-of-N: F2-331 fixed the pair it noticed and the mechanism that fixed it (the `copyMutable` scrub) was visibly present, so the sibling pair looked covered. The reusable lesson is to sweep *every* field-pair a shared create-or-update `save`/`copyMutable` shares with a dedicated route, in the same slice — not just the one that motivated the finding.**

### Create is legitimate; only update is the forge

`save` branches on `isNew`: a create uses the request entity as `target` (so the initial custodian/location come from the request) and then **seeds a CAPTURE ledger row** from `saved.getCurrentCustodian()`/`getCurrentLocation()` (lines 79–84), so the pointer and the ledger agree from acquisition. Only the `else` (update) branch calls `copyMutable`. So the fix is simply to stop copying the two fields in `copyMutable`: an update now leaves the pointer where `transferCustody` last set it, and a create is unchanged. The `update_cannotMoveCustodyWithoutLedger` test asserts both halves that matter — the pointer is untouched **and** `verify(ledger, never()).save(...)` — and `create_keepsRequestCustodian_andSeedsCaptureLedger` pins the create-legitimate half so a future over-zealous scrub cannot break acquisition.

### Filed

The seed gap is real and separate: all 4 seeded artefacts have a `current_custodian` but **0 custody-ledger rows**, because `seed_real_data.py` inserts them by direct SQL rather than through `save()` (which writes the CAPTURE row) — *"Don't 'seed' an empty table before checking it's wired."* Back-filling a CAPTURE row into a customer database is a destructive write on a court-bound register (house rule 6), so it is reported, not done. The remaining forensics filings from [[F2-331]] stand: `DataSharingAgreementController#create`'s `isActive`, the FE/BE integrity-vocabulary mismatch ([[F2-196]]), and the **29** remaining mass-assignment `NEEDS-VERDICT` rows (read per member, [[F2-188]]).

## F2-331 — a forensics artefact could be born VERIFIED, and a PUT could un-corrupt court evidence

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P2 — `ForensicsArtefactController#create` and `#update` both route to `ForensicsArtefactService.save`, whose `copyMutable` copied `integrityStatus` AND `integrityVerifiedAt` straight from the request. Those two are the `verifyIntegrity()` attestation — owned by `POST /{id}/verify-integrity`, which emits `FORENSICS_INTEGRITY_LOST` (paging legal + CISO) and audits the check. All three routes carry `hasAnyRole('FORENSICS_LEAD','IR_LEAD','CISO','PLATFORM_ADMIN')`, so a same-permission caller could `PUT` a `CORRUPTED` artefact — court evidence flagged unusable — back to `VERIFIED` with no event and no integrity audit. A **same-permission control-defeat** ([[F2-328]]/[[F2-329]]'s shape, not [[F2-330]]'s privilege boundary), on *"the table whose history might end up in court"*. And the entity carried the [[F2-238]] landmine in the flattering direction (`integrity_status NOT NULL = "VERIFIED"`), so a created artefact was born asserting a verification that never ran. |
| **Registers** | `socops.forensics_artefact` |
| **Standards** | chain-of-custody integrity (ISO/IEC 27037 acquisition/verification; the `verifyIntegrity` attestation + `FORENSICS_INTEGRITY_LOST` escalation to legal + CISO) |
| **Found by** | auditing the `mass-assignment-risk.txt` work-list ([[F2-218]]) — `ForensicsArtefactController#create(ForensicsArtefact) :: integrityVerifiedAt`, read against `save`/`copyMutable` and `verifyIntegrity()`; the entity initialiser was the second half. |
| **Verification** | three unit tests (a create is born `UNVERIFIED`; a create scrubs a forged `VERIFIED` + timestamp; a `PUT` cannot flip a `CORRUPTED` artefact to `VERIFIED`); full hermetic build 4747 → 4750/0/0; census gate re-derived to 29; `tsc` clean. **Latent in data, live in code** ([[F2-283]]): dev and prod both hold 4 artefacts, all legitimately `VERIFIED` with a real `integrity_verified_at`, so 0 rows are born-VERIFIED-never-checked today — but the create default and the update copy are reachable by any of the four privileged roles via the API (the register has no UI create/update client). No live probe: a synchronous scrub, the permission boundary read from the `@PreAuthorize` annotations ([[F2-325]]…[[F2-330]]'s standard); no CHECK on the column, so no migration ([[F2-183]]). |

### The forge: a dedicated attestation route's fields, copied from the request beside it

`integrity_status`/`integrity_verified_at` are written by exactly one route — `verifyIntegrity(id, verified)`,
which sets `VERIFIED`/`CORRUPTED` + `now()` and, on failure, publishes `FORENSICS_INTEGRITY_LOST` (AR-140:
page legal counsel + CISO before any further handling) and audits an integrity check. `copyMutable`
copied both columns unconditionally, so an ordinary `PUT /{id}` could rewrite the attestation with no
event and no integrity audit — most sharply, flip a `CORRUPTED` artefact back to `VERIFIED`, erasing the
record that the evidence was compromised. `create` was the same shape from the other side (a caller could
`POST` a `VERIFIED` artefact with a chosen timestamp). Same-permission throughout, so the object-level
`verifyIntegrity` route was the only control and `copyMutable` bypassed it — [[F2-328]]/[[F2-329]]'s shape,
and [[F2-213]]'s create-side blind spot for the create half (the update-shape gate cannot see a create that
binds a new entity). The fix removes both columns from `copyMutable` (they are `verifyIntegrity()`'s alone).

### F2-238 in the flattering direction, on court evidence

`integrity_status` is `NOT NULL` and the entity initialised it `= "VERIFIED"`. `save` persists the request
entity on create, so an omitted `integrityStatus` deserialised to `"VERIFIED"` — every artefact born
asserting a re-verification that never happened, with `integrity_verified_at` null and no
`FORENSICS_INTEGRITY_LOST`/audit. The vocabulary V152 documents (`VERIFIED/CORRUPTED/UNVERIFIED`) has a
distinct `UNVERIFIED` for exactly the "captured, hash recorded, not yet re-verified" state, so
birth-`VERIFIED` was the defect and not a domain intent. The fix removes the initialiser and owns
`UNVERIFIED` on the create path ([[F2-238]]'s remedy), registered in
`NeverFiringNullGuardContractTest.everyRemovedInitialiserHasAWriterOnTheCreatePath` so a create that stops
owning it fails rather than 500s on the NOT NULL column.

### The FE renders a backend value it did not know

`ForensicsPage`'s `INTEGRITY_TONE`/`INTEGRITY_LABEL` handled `VERIFIED/UNKNOWN/COMPROMISED/CORRUPTED` and
**not** `UNVERIFIED`, so the new birth state would have rendered as a raw token with a neutral badge
([[F2-205]]'s browser-after-green, pre-empted by reading rather than a running server). `UNVERIFIED` is
added to both maps (`warning` / *Unverified* / *غير مُحقَّقة*), and the `socops.ts` vocabulary comment is
corrected. The FE and backend vocabularies are otherwise disjoint — `UNKNOWN`/`COMPROMISED` are FE tokens
the backend never writes ([[F2-196]]) — which is an owner decision, filed rather than reconciled.

### The census reconciliation (F2-330's meta-finding, continued)

Auditing the create-side work-list per member ([[F2-188]]) found nine more rows already CLOSED or INERT
while printing NEEDS-VERDICT, because `BASELINE_UNADJUDICATED_NEW_CRIT` is a ceiling that does not force
the census update its own contract asks for ([[F2-330]]). Each verdict was read against its service — a
scrub or guard present, or a whitelist confirmed not to write the field — never trusted from prose:
`PolicyController#create`/`createAttestation` and `DataSharingAgreementController#create` ([[F2-219]]),
`BcmBiaAssessmentController#create` ([[F2-22b]]) and `#update` ([[F2-297]]),
`BcmRemediationController#createCapa` ([[F2-234]]) and `#updateCapa` (INERT whitelist). `reviewerId` on the
two BCM registers is an **assignment** (no `reviewedAt`/`reviewerName` column, no route stamps it —
[[F2-226]]/[[F2-236]]), so legitimately caller-set. Ceiling re-derived 38 → 29 off the regenerated census
([[F2-207]]/[[F2-258]]).

### Filed

`DataSharingAgreementController#create` stays NEEDS-VERDICT: its `isActive` (`Short NOT NULL = 1`) has no
reader/writer in the `dsa` module, so it is likely inert, but it was not verified this slice and a wrong
CLOSED is worse than a NEEDS-VERDICT ([[F2-188]]). The FE/backend integrity vocabulary is disjoint
([[F2-196]]). The sibling custody pair (`currentCustodian`/`currentLocation`, owned by `transferCustody`,
which appends a custody-ledger event) is copied by `copyMutable` on update, bypassing the ledger append — a
completeness gap of a different shape (create-legitimate, update-questionable), filed. And the remaining
**29** NEEDS-VERDICT rows are read per member, not swept.

## F2-330 — a BCP plan could be born with a forged attestation trail, and a ceiling let nine closed rows sit mislabelled

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P3 — `BcpPlanService.create` binds the `BcpPlan` entity and scrubbed status/approvedBy/approvedAt/publishedAt ([[F2-220]]) and currentVersion ([[F2-234]]) but not the attestation trail `lastAttestedAt`/`lastAttestedByName`/`lastAttestedById`, written ONLY by `PlanReviewService.attest()` — whose route is `hasPermission('BCM','APPROVE')`, a HIGHER grant than the `BCM:WRITE` on create. So a `BCM:WRITE` holder could `POST` a continuity plan born *"last reviewed by X on Y"* (the entity comment says the UI renders that string, and `reviewState` filters treat an attested plan as review-current), forging by mass assignment the attestation the APPROVE-gated `/attest` route exists to earn — a **privilege-boundary crossing**, not [[F2-329]]'s same-permission control-defeat. |
| **Registers** | `bcm.bcp_plans` |
| **Standards** | ISO 22301 / NCEMA continuity-plan review sign-off; the plan-review-currency filter (`reviewState`) |
| **Found by** | auditing the `mass-assignment-risk.txt` work-list ([[F2-218]]) — `BcpPlanController#create(BcpPlan) :: lastAttestedAt,publishedAt,status`, read against the service and `PlanReviewService.attest()`. |
| **Verification** | unit test (a create carrying a forged `lastAttestedAt`/`_by_name`/`_by_id` is scrubbed to null); full hermetic build 4746 → 4747/0/0. No live probe: the scrub is synchronous and the privilege boundary is read from the two `@PreAuthorize` annotations, not a mock ([[F2-325]]…[[F2-329]]'s calibrated standard). |

### F2-215's two-of-N, a sixth time on one create

`BcpPlan.lastAttestedAt`/`lastAttestedByName`/`lastAttestedById` are stamped only by
`PlanReviewService.attest()` (which sets `now()` plus the attesting principal's name and id) and carry
**no `@JsonProperty(READ_ONLY)`**, so Jackson binds them from the `@RequestBody BcpPlan`. The create
scrubs five sibling server-owned fields — [[F2-220]] added the status/approvedBy/approvedAt/publishedAt
scrubs and [[F2-234]] added `currentVersion`, each under a comment about *"the field a reader stops
looking for"* — and the attestation trail was the field after that. Only `lastAttestedAt` is
authority-shaped enough for `MassAssignmentRatchetTest` to name (`attested`+`At`); `_by_name`/`_by_id`
end in `Name`/`Id` and are invisible to the pattern ([[F2-236]]'s attribution-beside-the-timestamp),
but they are the same trail and forgeable in the same breath, so all three are scrubbed together.

### The meta-finding: a ceiling does not force the census update its own contract asks for

`BASELINE_UNADJUDICATED_NEW_CRIT` is a **ceiling** and the adjudication column is a hand-maintained map,
so a create closed service-side — a scrub `FullReplaceUpdateContractTest` and this scan cannot see —
drops the defect without lowering the count or annotating the row. Nine counted rows were already
CLOSED or INERT while printing NEEDS-VERDICT: [[F2-220]], [[F2-231]], [[F2-233]] (×2), [[F2-297]],
[[F2-328]], [[F2-329]]. A closed defect printing *"unread"* is worse than a missing row ([[F2-250]]):
it sends the next reviewer to re-read a guarded path. Each of the ten (the nine plus this slice's own
BcpPlan fix) was read against its service — guard present, or whitelist confirmed — rather than trusted
from prose ([[F2-188]]), and the ceiling was re-derived from the regenerated census (48 → 38), not
guessed ([[F2-207]]/[[F2-258]]). The remaining 38 are a work list to read per member, not a sweep.

## F2-329 — a cyber action plan could be created with a forged escalation trail, silently defeating its overdue sweep

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P3 — `CyberController#saveActionPlan` binds the `CyberActionPlan` entity, so a `CYBER:WRITE` holder could `POST` with `escalatedAt` already set. `CyberActionPlanSlaScheduler` selects `…EscalatedAtIsNull…` for its escalation pass and skips reminders when `escalatedAt != null`, so the plan — a cyber remediation — is **never escalated when overdue and never chased**, from a single POST. A caller can also be born COMPLETED with a forged `completedAt`, and forge `reminderCount`/`lastReminderAt`. No escalation (all four routes are `CYBER:WRITE`) — a control-defeat, not a permission bypass. |
| **Registers** | `cyber.cyber_action_plans` |
| **Standards** | NCA ECC remediation SLA (overdue escalation / reminders); the complete action as a dated step |
| **Found by** | the `mass-assignment-risk.txt` NEEDS-VERDICT backlog ([[F2-218]]) — `CyberController#saveActionPlan(CyberActionPlan) :: escalatedAt,workflowStatus`, read against the service and the scheduler. |
| **Verification** | unit tests (a born-COMPLETED create is refused; the scheduler/complete trail is scrubbed on create); full hermetic build 4744 → 4746/0/0. No live probe: a synchronous create-guard with no database / tenant / auth dimension a mock cannot see ([[F2-325]]/[[F2-326]]/[[F2-327]]/[[F2-328]]'s calibrated standard). |

### The create is F2-213's defect on the path its gate cannot see

[[F2-213]] found that a service persisting the bound request entity erases/forges everything the
request should not own, and built `FullReplaceUpdateContractTest` — a structural hard zero that no
method may **load a `T` and persist its own `T` parameter**. That catches the UPDATE shape (load, then
save the request); it is blind to the CREATE shape (a new entity bound from the request, saved without
a load). `saveActionPlan` is exactly that: it set `titleEn`/`organisationId`/`isDeleted` and
`save(ap)`, persisting the caller's `escalatedAt` / `lastReminderAt` / `reminderCount` / `completedAt` /
`workflowStatus`. F2-213 scrubbed these on the UPDATE path (`applyEditable`, whose own comment lists
them as *"written by the scheduler … and the source link at creation"*) and **left the create** —
[[F2-215]]'s two-of-N. [[F2-328]] is the same shape on the vuln-exception register, one slice earlier.

### 🔑 The sharp field is `escalatedAt` — it does not display wrong, it defeats a control

`CyberActionPlanSlaScheduler`'s escalation pass is
`findByWorkflowStatusNotInAndEscalatedAtIsNullAndDueDateBefore(TERMINAL, today)` and its reminder pass
does `if (ap.getEscalatedAt() != null) continue;`. The CY-E comment says `escalatedAt` *"guards the
sweep so an overdue plan is escalated exactly once."* So a plan **created** with `escalatedAt` already
set is read as already-escalated: excluded from the escalation query, suppressed from reminders. A
cyber remediation can be filed overdue-destined and then sit overdue forever — no escalation to
management, no reminder to the owner — from a single POST. Not a cosmetic forgery (F2-328 was a
fabricated approval); a functional defeat of the SLA sweep, which is why it is the sharper instance.

### The fix

`saveActionPlan` scrubs `escalatedAt` / `lastReminderAt` / `reminderCount` / `completedAt` (all
scheduler- or complete-owned) and refuses `workflowStatus == "COMPLETED"` (a 400 naming
`POST /api/v1/cyber/action-plans/{id}/complete`). Null-safe `equalsIgnoreCase`, so an omitted status
keeps the entity's `OPEN` initialiser. The 5-state lifecycle is undesigned (no CHECK, no machine —
[[F2-221]]), so only the terminal COMPLETED is withheld; the review states (OPEN / IN_PROGRESS /
CANCELLED) stay caller-settable — forcing a single initial state would break the informal advance
([[F2-214]]). Two unit tests.

### Filed

The create-side of [[F2-213]] is a **population**, not two incidents: `mass-assignment-risk.txt`'s
CREATE rows are the census, and `FullReplaceUpdateContractTest` is blind to all of them (it is an
UPDATE-shape gate). [[F2-328]] and F2-329 are two members read and fixed; the rest await per-member
reading, not a sweep ([[F2-188]]). And `updateActionPlan`'s `applyEditable` still sets `workflowStatus`
from the request, so an edit can jump to COMPLETED — the same undesigned-machine question filed at
[[F2-328]]/[[F2-221]].

## F2-328 — a vulnerability exception could be created born-APPROVED with a forged approval date

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P3 — `CyberController#saveException` binds the `VulnException` entity, so a `CYBER:WRITE` holder could `POST /api/v1/cyber/exceptions` with `workflowStatus=APPROVED` and a `approvedAt` of their choosing → a formal NCA ECC risk-acceptance **born APPROVED from a single POST, skipping `approveException`** (the sole writer of the real approval date). No privilege escalation — all four exception routes are `CYBER:WRITE`, so the caller could approve legitimately; this is a control-integrity / attribution defect (a fabricated approval), not a permission bypass. |
| **Registers** | `cyber.vuln_exceptions` |
| **Standards** | NCA ECC (vulnerability risk-acceptance); the approve action as a distinct, dated step |
| **Found by** | the `mass-assignment-risk.txt` NEEDS-VERDICT backlog ([[F2-218]] invited continuing it) — `CyberController#saveException(VulnException) :: approverName,workflowStatus`, read against the service. |
| **Verification** | unit tests (a born-APPROVED create is refused; a REQUESTED create scrubs `approvedAt`); full hermetic build 4742 → 4744/0/0. No live probe: a synchronous input-guard (`if APPROVED throw` → 400 via the ubiquitous `IllegalArgumentException` path) with no database / tenant / auth dimension a mock cannot see, proportionate per the calibrated standard of [[F2-325]]/[[F2-326]]/[[F2-327]]. |

### The bypass

`approveException` is the dedicated approval route: it sets `workflowStatus = "APPROVED"` and stamps
`approvedAt = LocalDate.now()`. But `saveException` (the create) set only `titleEn`/`organisationId`/
`isDeleted` and then `exceptionRepo.save(e)` — persisting the caller's bound `workflowStatus` and
`approvedAt` unscrubbed. So a single `POST` could create a risk-acceptance already `APPROVED`, dated
whenever the caller liked, having gone through no approval action. `approveException` is where the
approval date is minted; a create that reaches `APPROVED` mints a fabricated one.

### 🔑 The lifecycle is undesigned, so the clean primitives are too strong

`VulnException.workflowStatus` has **no CHECK constraint, no declared state machine**, and five
informal states in the FE dropdown (`REQUESTED → IMPACT_ASSESSMENT → COMPENSATING_CONTROLS → APPROVED
→ EXPIRED`) — yet the only backend transition is `approveException`'s slam to `APPROVED`. The
intermediate review states are reachable **only** through the edit form's status dropdown, which is
the informal (if undesigned) advancement path. So `ServerOwnedState.requireInitial` (force REQUESTED
only) and `requireUnchanged` (refuse every change) are both too strong — they would refuse a
legitimate create-at-review-state or a review-stage advance, breaking a working screen ([[F2-214]]).
The unambiguous invariant is narrower: **`APPROVED` is reachable only via `approveException`, which
owns `approvedAt`.**

### The fix

`saveException` refuses `workflowStatus == "APPROVED"` on create (a 400 naming
`POST /api/v1/cyber/exceptions/{id}/approve`) and scrubs `approvedAt = null` — so the approval date is
the approve path's alone ([[F2-213]] established that for the update path and left the create). The
intermediate states stay caller-settable (the undesigned lifecycle is not this slice's to redesign).
`equalsIgnoreCase` is null-safe, so an omitted status still defaults to the entity's `REQUESTED`
initialiser. Two unit tests: a born-APPROVED create is refused; a REQUESTED create scrubs `approvedAt`.

### Filed (the entangled rest — [[F2-221]]/[[F2-236]] owner-decisions, not this slice)

- **The update path is the same bypass, one route over.** `applyEditable` sets `workflowStatus` from
  the request, so an edit can jump `REQUESTED → APPROVED` (skipping `approveException`). Closing it
  correctly needs the entity initialiser removed (an omitted status on the entity-bound `PUT` else
  deserialises to `REQUESTED` and reads as a false change — [[F2-237]]/[[F2-250]]) **and** a real
  state machine to tell a legal review-stage advance from the illegal approval jump. That machine
  does not exist; declaring it (states, transitions, a CHECK) is [[F2-221]]'s owner-decision.
- **`approveException` does not stamp the approver.** It sets `workflowStatus`+`approvedAt` but never
  `approverName`, so the approver of a risk-acceptance is always caller-supplied (via create/edit),
  never verified against the approving principal — [[F2-236]]'s attribution gap. Fixing it means
  deciding `approverName` is stamped at approval, a design choice.
- The `mass-assignment-risk.txt` row for `saveException`/`updateException` stays NEEDS-VERDICT because
  its `approverName` half is the attribution gap above; only the `workflowStatus`/`approvedAt` create
  half is closed here.

## F2-327 — a realtime subscription that re-renders a cache instead of re-fetching is inert for cross-user updates

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P3 — two lifecycle pages (`RiskLifecyclePage` ERM treatment plans, `AuditLifecyclePage` internal-audit findings) subscribed to a server broadcast and answered it with a bare `setTick`, so another user's transition re-rendered this browser's STALE hydrate-once cache. The data is correct on manual reload and the user's OWN changes still re-render; the realtime feature was silently inert for the cross-user liveness it exists to deliver. |
| **Registers** | `risk_lc.treatment_plans` / `audit_lc.findings` (frontend realtime handlers) |
| **Standards** | — (realtime liveness; [[F2-205]]'s recorded blind spot) |
| **Found by** | applying [[F2-205]]'s own generalisation — *"when you find a realtime subscription, read what its handler does with the frame"* — to every `useRealtimeOrgEvent` consumer. No instrument in the tree could see it (F2-205 said so), so this slice also builds the gate. |
| **Verification** | the gate (`realtimeSubscriptionRefetches.test.ts`) with a pre-fix control that FAILS when the handlers are reverted to bare `setTick` (non-vacuous — [[F2-208]]); `tsc --noEmit` clean; full FE vitest suite green; the cache/refetch dataflow traced by reading |

### F2-205's blind spot had two more instances

[[F2-205]] found that `VulnerabilitiesV2Page` subscribed to `changed.vulnerability` and answered it by
re-reading a browser-local store — a websocket frame refreshing a constant no server event could
change — and fixed it to `hydrateVulns(true).then(() => setAllVulns(loadVulns()))`, force-refetching
because *"a broadcast means the server's copy has moved, so the cached promise must not be reused —
the only reading under which the subscription means anything."* It recorded the generalisation and
noted **no instrument in this tree can see it**: every component is genuine, only the direction the
data flows is wrong, so a reachability scan (is the symbol called?) and a provenance gate (does the
page call a server?) both answer yes.

Asked of every `useRealtimeOrgEvent` consumer (5 sites), two were the exact shape:
- `RiskLifecyclePage` `changed.treatment_plan` → `() => setTick(t => t + 1)`.
- `AuditLifecyclePage` `changed.audit_finding` → `() => setTick(t => t + 1)`.

Both read a **hydrate-once server cache** — `hydrateTreatmentPlans` / `hydrateAuditLifecycle`, each
`if (_promise && !force) return _promise`, with `loadTreatmentPlans()` / `loadFindings()` returning
the cached array. A bare `setTick` only re-renders; the module cache is refreshed **only** by a forced
hydrate. So this user's own transition re-renders (the local mutation replaced the cache and emitted),
but **another user's transition — the whole reason to subscribe — arrived as a frame that re-rendered
the unchanged cache**. Inert until a manual Refresh or a remount.

### 🔑 The comment described the mechanism and was wrong

Both handlers sat under a comment claiming the tick *"combines local + remote events through the same
`_tick` so the page re-derives memoised data from either source"* / *"re-derives for either local or
remote events."* False for the remote source: re-deriving from `_tick` re-reads the cache, and the
remote change was never fetched into it. [[F2-184]]'s shape — the comment answers the question a reader
was about to ask, incorrectly — so the fix corrects the comment with the code.

### The fix

Both handlers become the F2-205 pattern: `() => { void hydrateX(true).then(() => setTick(t => t + 1)); }`.
`force = true` bypasses the cached promise, refetches, replaces the cache and `emit()`s; the
`.then(setTick)` re-renders over fresh rows. Two one-line changes.

### Gate

`realtimeSubscriptionRefetches.test.ts` closes F2-205's blind spot: it enumerates every
`useRealtimeOrgEvent` handler (paren-matched from comment-stripped source) and holds a named map with a
verdict per site — `REFETCH` (with the exact force-refetch token the handler must contain:
`hydrateVulns(true)`, `loadDsrCases()`, `hydrateTreatmentPlans(true)`, `hydrateAuditLifecycle(true)`) or
`FILED`. The population is asserted **exactly** ([[F2-204]]): a new consumer with no verdict fails the
forward leg, a stale verdict fails the reverse. A self-test proves the classifier flags a bare
`setTick`, and a pre-fix control confirms the gate FAILS when the two handlers are reverted
([[F2-208]]/[[F2-274]] — a green gate shown to fire on the defect).

### Filed

`BcmLifecyclePage` subscribes to `changed.bcm_invocation` and answers with a bare `setTick` — but
`bcmLifecycle.ts`'s `loadInvocations()` reads a **pure browser-local store** (`grc.bcm.invocation.v1`,
`SEED_INVOCATIONS` fallback) with **no server hydrate at all**. So it is not a stale-cache (F2-327) but
an **unwired store receiving a server broadcast it cannot act on** — [[F2-204]]'s Kind-B shape. The fix
is to wire the invocation store to a server endpoint first (a reading job: does one exist?), then the
handler can force-refetch. Held as a `FILED` verdict in the gate so it cannot masquerade as fixed. Not
this slice.

## F2-326 — the flagship regulator evidence package named the actor and dropped the role held

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P3 — `RegulatorPackageService`'s `Audit_Trail.xlsx`, the platform-wide pack an auditor or regulator is handed, carried the actor (`user_username`) but **not** the role that actor held at the time. The actor being present makes this a completeness gap on the segregation-of-duties axis, not the attribution failure [[F2-325]] fixed in the BCM package. |
| **Registers** | `platform.audit_log` |
| **Standards** | Saudi GRC prompt §29 (who/when/what/where); segregation-of-duties / least-privilege review ([[F2-54]]); ISO 22301 / regulator evidence packaging |
| **Found by** | applying [[F2-325]]'s own generalised rule — *when an export and an on-screen view read the same record, diff their columns* — to every OTHER consumer of `AuditLogEntry`. It refuted a cross-tenant-leak hypothesis on this file and surfaced the role gap ([[F2-215]]'s two-of-N: a sweep of one export is not a sweep of the family). |
| **Verification** | the sharp hypothesis refuted by reading (the leak); full `generate()`-path behavioural test reading the XLSX out of the ZIP with POI (the fix); mutation harness **3 killed / 0 survived / 0 anchor-miss**; co-population cited from [[F2-325]]'s both-database measurement; suite **4741 → 4742/0/0** |

### A sweep of one export is not a sweep of the family

[[F2-325]] added the actor and the role to the BCM evidence package's `audit_log.csv` and closed with the
rule *"when an export and an on-screen view read the same record, diff their columns — the one that leaves
the platform is the one nobody re-reads."* Asking that of every OTHER reader of `AuditLogEntry` found a
**second** regulator export of the same data: `RegulatorPackageService` — the platform-wide,
framework-agnostic pack its own javadoc describes as *"a single self-describing archive an auditor or
regulator can be handed"* — whose `Audit_Trail.xlsx` sheet named `Time, Action, Module, Entity, Code,
User, Severity, Message`. It carried the actor (so [[F2-325]]'s attribution failure was **not** repeated
here) and dropped `user_role`. 🔑 [[F2-215]]'s two-of-N at the level of an export family: fixing the actor
in one export left the same data leaving through a second with the SoD field dropped, and the mechanism
that made the first export whole (the actor column) was visibly present, so nothing invited a re-read.

### 🔑 The refuted hypothesis was the sharper one

The gather block scopes controls and evidence with `controlRepo.findByOrganisationId(org, …)` /
`evidenceRepo.findByOrganisationId(org, …)` — explicit tenant arguments — and the audit trail with
`auditLogService.list(null, null, null, 0, MAX_AUDIT)`, **no org argument**. A regulator package that
embedded another tenant's audit rows would be a cross-tenant leak in a document handed to an external
party — far sharper than a dropped column, and the tell (two org-scoped lines then one that is not) sat in
plain sight. **Refuted:** `AuditLogService.list` scopes to `TenantContext.getCurrentTenant()` internally,
and `generate()` resolves the same tenant through `TenantContext.requireOrganisationId()` on-request (via
`ExportController`), so the trail is tenant-scoped to the same org as the rest of the pack. Recording the
refutation is the result ([[F2-221]]/[[F2-283]]): the audit trail does not leak.

### The two readers, and the one-field diff

The platform's unified viewer (`AuditLogPage.tsx`) renders the actor **and the role held** —
`{r.userUsername ?? '—'}` followed by `· {r.userRole}`. Diffing the viewer against this export column for
column, the export is otherwise **richer** than the viewer (it adds `Module` and `Code`); the only field
the viewer carried that the export dropped was `user_role`. So the finding is precisely one field, on the
axis an auditor reads to ask *"who did this, and were they authorised to?"* — the role held **at the time**,
which is not the same as the actor's role now.

### The fix

`Role` is added to the header immediately after `User`, and `nz(a.getUserRole())` to the row after the
username (when→who→what order, matching [[F2-325]] and the viewer). 🔑 `user_role` is co-populated
**exactly** with `user_username` ([[F2-325]]'s both-database measurement: 0 rows carry one without the
other), so it adds no blank beyond where the actor itself is absent. Where a row has no principal — an
off-request sweep, an automation firing — the role cell is **blank, never fabricated**, the honest state
the viewer shows as `—` ([[F2-213]]/[[F2-209]]). `user_id` is not added, being 0% populated in both
databases ([[F2-198]]'s blank-column trap), consistent with [[F2-325]].

### Gate

`RegulatorPackageServiceTest.auditTrailSheetCarriesTheActorAndTheRoleHeldAndBlanksItHonestlyWhenAbsent` —
a full `generate()`-path behavioural test (a first for this service, which had none — [[F2-248]]): it plants
one row with a principal and one without, generates the real ZIP, extracts `Audit_Trail.xlsx`, opens it with
POI, and asserts the header names `Role` **immediately after** `User` in the full expected order, the
principal row carries the role, and the no-principal row blanks both actor and role. Mutation harness:
dropping `Role` from the header (**KILLED** by the ordered header assertion), dropping it from the row
(**KILLED** by the role-value assertion), and reordering `Role` to the end of the header (**KILLED** by the
order assertion).

### Filed

`RegulatorPackageService` caps the audit trail at `MAX_AUDIT = 1000` "recent" entries and prints
`audit.size()` as the count in the README KPI (*"Audit / N / Trail entries"*) and the manifest. dev org 1
holds 3,809+ audit rows ([[F2-321]]), so the cap bites and the printed count is the size of the *sheet*, not
of the platform's trail — the count is honest about the file's contents, but the KPI label does not say
"recent, up to 1000", so a reader could take N for the total ([[F2-197]]/[[F2-324]]'s truncated-count shape).
A wording judgment on a deliberately-capped view, not this fix.

## F2-325 — the regulator audit trail exported when/what/where and dropped who

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P2 — the BCM evidence package's `audit_log.csv`, handed to an external auditor for SIEM import, omitted the actor of every governance action — present on 89 of the 90 on-request rows it exports and shown by the platform's own audit viewer. |
| **Registers** | `platform.audit_log` |
| **Standards** | Saudi GRC prompt §29 (who/when/what/where/before/after/correlation); ISO 22301 / NCEMA evidence packaging; the audit ledger (F7) |
| **Found by** | [[F2-215]]'s two-of-N question of [[F2-324]]'s own file — *what else does this export assert that another reader shows and this one drops?* — one column over from `source_module`. |
| **Verification** | live column-population measured in **both** databases (the defect); full `generate()`-path behavioural test (the fix); mutation harness **3 killed / 0 survived / 0 did-not-run**; suite **4740 → 4741/0/0** |

### The export named when/what/where and dropped who

`BcmEvidencePackageService`'s `audit_log.csv` — the artefact a regulator or external auditor imports
into their own SIEM (its own comment says so) — wrote
`id, created_at, action_type, entity_type, entity_id, entity_code, severity, source_module,
correlation_id, message`. The `AuditLogEntry` entity's own javadoc cites the requirement as Saudi GRC
prompt §29 — **who / when / what / where / before / after / correlation** — and the CSV had *when*
(`created_at`), *what* (`action_type`/`entity_*`), *where* ([[F2-324]] had just added `source_module`)
and *correlation*, and **no who**. An audit trail handed to an auditor that says *a BCP plan was
approved at 14:32* without saying **who approved it** is an event log, not an audit trail.

### 🔑 It is an oversight, not a format choice — the two readers disagree

The column has a second reader: `GET /api/v1/audit-log` returns the whole `AuditLogEntry`, and the
platform's own unified audit viewer (`AuditLogPage.tsx`) **renders a "User / المستخدم" column**
(`r.userUsername ?? '—'`) for every row. So the same data is shown complete on screen and exported
incomplete to a regulator — [[F2-215]]'s two-of-N (one column over from F2-324's `source_module`, same
writer) and [[F2-205]]'s *which reader is authoritative* inverted: here the on-screen view is complete
and the file that **leaves** the platform is the poorer one. No comment claimed the omission was
deliberate; the CSV writer was added in the original Audit-Fix #7 and never revisited for the actor,
under a javadoc reading *"No row counts are excluded — auditors need the full register."*

### The actor is populated where it matters

Measured in both databases: `user_username` is overall 41.7% / 31.7% populated, but that figure is
dragged down by machine-actor rows (`REFRESH_TOKEN_ISSUED` 4068, `RULE_FIRED` 506) that legitimately
have no principal. On the **governance** action types it is near-universal — `TRANSITION` 955/984,
`CREATE` 895/930, `EXPORT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE`/`MEMBER_APPOINT`/`RESOLUTION_VOTE` 100% — and on the
**exact rows the package exports** it is present on **89 of 90 (dev) / 12 of 13 (prod)** of the
on-request `source_module='bcm'` subset (61.6% / 32% of the widened selector, the remainder being the
off-request automation/ingest/sweep rows that legitimately have no actor). So the column is
meaningfully populated, not a blank ([[F2-198]]).

### The fix, and the honest blank

`user_username` and `user_role` are added after `created_at` (canonical when→who→what order).
🔑 `user_role` — the role the actor held at the time, [[F2-54]]'s first-class audit field, relevant to
an auditor checking segregation of duties — is co-populated **exactly** with `user_username`
(username-without-role = 0 and role-without-username = 0 in both databases), so it adds no blank beyond
where the actor itself is absent. `user_id` is **not** exported: it is 0% populated in both databases
(the service records the username, never the id — [[F2-198]]'s blank-column trap). ⚠ Where a row has no
principal — an off-request sweep, an automation rule firing, a SIEM ingest — the actor cell is
**blank, never fabricated**: the honest state the viewer already shows as `—` ([[F2-213]]/[[F2-209]]),
and exposing it is more truthful for a regulator than hiding that a third-to-two-thirds of the trail
has no recorded actor ([[F2-197]]).

### Gate

`BcmEvidencePackageServiceTest.auditCsv_carriesTheActorAndRoleAndBlanksItHonestlyWhenAbsent` — a full
`generate()`-path behavioural test: it plants one row with a principal and one without, generates the
real ZIP, extracts `audit_log.csv`, and asserts the header names the actor columns **in order**, the
principal row carries the username and the (comma-bearing, so quoted) role, and the no-principal row
blanks the actor rather than inventing one. Mutation harness: dropping the columns from the header
(**KILLED**), dropping them from the row writes (**KILLED**), fabricating `"system"` for a null actor
(**KILLED**).

### Filed

The same CSV still omits *before/after* (`workflow_status_before`/`_after`), but those are genuinely
sparse — 0.2% / 0.5% populated, and even on `TRANSITION` rows the states live in the `message` — so
adding them would export a near-blank column ([[F2-198]]); the transition narrative is already in
`message`. Not this fix.

## F2-324 — the audit ledger's source_module had two readers and almost no writers

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P2 — a regulator-facing evidence export carried 15% of its own audit trail, and a platform-wide governance filter saw ~13% of the ledger. |
| **Registers** | `platform.audit_log` |
| **Standards** | ISO 22301 / NCEMA evidence packaging; the platform audit ledger (F7) |
| **Found by** | Asking [[F2-196]]'s question of F2-321's filed remainder — *how many things read this column, and what do they see?* |
| **Verification** | live probe **10/10** as `auditor`/`compliance`; mutation harness **9 killed / 0 survived**; suite **4728 → 4740/0/0** |

### The column had two readers and 686 of 722 writers could not set it

`source_module` is the `sourceModule` filter on `GET /api/v1/audit-log` — a **free-text control** on a
sidebar-linked page whose own subtitle promises *"Every state-changing action across modules —
filterable and traceable"* — and it is how `BcmEvidencePackageService` selects the BCM evidence
package's `audit_log.csv`. Measured over both live databases it was **NULL on 87.1% of dev rows and
93.6% of prod rows**, because `AuditLogService.log(...)` constructs its own builder internally and
never set it: **686 of the 722 audit-writing sites** could not attribute themselves however carefully
they were written. Only the 19 builder chains and 5 interceptor/whistleblower sites could.

### 🔑 The consequence was in the emitted artefact, not the filter

`BcmEvidencePackageService.generate` selected the package's audit CSV on `source_module = 'bcm'` alone,
under a comment saying the regulator wants *"the whole tenant picture."* Measured: the CSV carried
**15.0% of the BCM trail in dev and 6.8% in prod**, omitting **136 and 119 `BcmAssessmentCycle`
rows** — the audit trail of the very cycle the package documents — while `README.pdf` printed the
truncated count as the total. Probed live: the widened selection returns **442 of 442 BCM rows** where
the module-only predicate returned 85.

### The fix: derive, correct by construction

`recordEvent` now derives `source_module` from the caller's package when the builder is silent. 🔑 The
vocabulary is **not a list**: a top-level package under `com.tss.grc.module` *is* a module, enumerated
once by `module-registry.yaml` and gated by `ModuleRegistryContractTest` ([[F2-217]]: a check keyed on
a list measures the list). An explicit `sourceModule(…)` always wins; a caller outside the module root
(`config`, `security`, `common`) derives null rather than a fifth invented token.

### ⚠⚠ The frame walk must survive the CGLIB proxy, and F2-321's did not

`callerOf()` (built by F2-321 for the F2-320 warning) and the new derivation share one walk. F2-321
filtered `!c.equals(AuditLogService.class.getName())` — an **exact-equality** test. `recordEvent` is
`@Transactional`, so the bean is CGLIB-proxied and the generated subclass is named
`…AuditLogService$$SpringCGLIB$$0`, which is **not equal to** that name. 🔑 **Probed live with F2-321's
filter restored: the export's own audit row landed `source_module=None`** — i.e. the walk returned a
frame outside `com.tss.grc` entirely, so F2-321's warning has been naming Spring's proxy machinery, not
the caller, all along. The walk now narrows on the platform *root* with `startsWith`, robust to the
proxy by construction.

### ⚠ The historical rows stay NULL — the ledger is append-only

The column is filled for every row written from now on; it may **not** be back-filled, because the
ledger is append-only and F2-31 hash-chains it, so a back-fill would rewrite history **and** invalidate
every seal. So the evidence package recovers pre-F2-324 rows through the column that *is* populated —
`entity_type` — with the BCM entity vocabulary **derived from the JPA metamodel** ([[F2-217]] again).

### The three stored non-modules

Of the 14 values the column held, **11 were registry modules and 3 were not**: `automation` and
`licensing` are `platform` **sub-packages** and `ethics.whistleblower` is a dotted
`module.subpackage` token — three vocabularies in one column, with a fourth in
`ExportAuditInterceptor.moduleFromPath`'s `"EXPORT"` default arm, which named an **action**. All
narrowed to the module (`platform`, `platform`, `ethics`); the automation/licensing sites lose their
explicit value and take the derived `platform`, because the `RULE_FIRED`/`LICENSE_*` action type
already carries the finer detail.

### Gates

* `AuditSourceModuleContractTest` (hermetic) — every audit `sourceModule` literal names a registry
  module (hard zero, no exemptions); `moduleFromPath`'s arms all name modules; the frame walk is
  narrowed by root not by name; a caller outside the module root derives nothing; both readers still
  exist; and a positive control for the registry parser (three of 59 entries span lines, so a same-line
  parser reports 56 — a smaller vocabulary, which reads exactly like a clean tree).
* `AuditModuleDerivationTest` — the positive twin, and **it lives in `module/bcm` on purpose**: a walk
  that failed and returned `AuditLogService`'s own frame derives `platform`, which is exactly what a
  correct walk derives for a caller in the ledger's own package, so the failure is invisible from
  there. Asserting `bcm` from `module/bcm` can only be produced by a walk that actually skipped every
  `AuditLogService` frame.
* `BcmEvidencePackageServiceTest` — the metamodel filter narrows to this module's package, and with a
  metamodel present `generate` uses the widened finder.

### ⚠⚠ Two gate holes the mutation harness found

* **M6 survived the first draft**: the `moduleFromPath` leg extracted arms with `->\s*"…"`, and the
  `default` arm returns through a ternary (`seg.isEmpty() ? "EXPORT" : …`), so the literal it returns is
  **not adjacent to the arrow**. 🔑 A regex keyed on the shape it had already seen missed the one shape
  the mutation used. Rewritten to scan every uppercase-only literal in the switch (case labels are
  lowercase URL segments, so uppercase-only is the return value).
* **M5 was an ANCHOR-MISS, not a survival** — the harness patch itself failed on a Python escape error,
  and *did-not-run* is kept distinct from *survived* ([[F2-212]]).

### Filed

* `ExportAuditInterceptor.moduleFromPath`'s `default -> seg.toUpperCase()` arm is **deliberately not
  closed** and the gate says so: it has only ever produced registry modules (the URL segment happens to
  be the package name — `PRIVACY`, `TPRM`), and narrowing it to a known set would drop those real
  attributions. The path→module mapping is a mapping job, not a scan.
* The AuditLogPage `sourceModule` filter is a **free-text box**; now that the column holds a gated
  vocabulary it could be a `<select>` over the registry modules (a product change, not this fix).

## F2-323 — the census asked of the boundary instead of the catch, and the catch was dead code

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P3 — latent. Cross-schedule atomicity on a 60-second scheduler, plus one transaction held open across N report generations. |
| **Registers** | `reporting.report_schedules`, `reporting.report_runs` |
| **Standards** | — |
| **Found by** | Running the census [[F2-322]] filed |
| **Verification** | **2 killed / 2 equivalent / 1 invalid**; suite **4727 → 4728/0/0** |

### The census

[[F2-317]] measured *"0 of 33 looping sweeps lack a per-item catch"* — true, and it counted the
**catch**. Asked of the **boundary** instead — *does the loop body open its own transaction, or does a
batch-wide `@Transactional` make the catch meaningless?* — the answer is **1 of 21**:
`ReportSchedulerService#tick`.

### ⚠⚠ Reading it changed the finding

`runOnce` has its **own** try/catch that persists `FAILED` and returns normally, so `tick`'s
per-schedule catch was **unreachable dead code** — which is exactly why it read as a decoy. The hazard
was never the catch:

* all due schedules shared **one** transaction, so a database-level failure persisting the fifth
  schedule's run row would discard the first four's rows and their `next_run_at` advances
* and that transaction stayed open across up to **eleven report generations** — each rendering a PDF or
  workbook — on a 60-second scheduler

🔑 **And the catch becomes reachable *and* useful now**: a commit failure in one schedule's own
transaction throws into the loop and is handled without touching the others. It was written for a world
where each schedule had its own boundary; it simply did not have one.

### The rationale was already written in the tree

`EmergencyRatificationSlaScheduler`'s javadoc: *"one unwritable change cannot roll back the escalations
already recorded for the others. A batch control that is all-or-nothing fails closed on the whole
tenant the first time one row misbehaves."* Its optional **non-final** `txManager` field is copied here
so `@RequiredArgsConstructor` is unchanged and `ReportCadenceContractTest`'s two direct constructions
keep compiling.

### The census became an invariant

Hard zero, **empty exemption map**: dropping `@Transactional` or wrapping the body is always available,
so there is no correct code for it to fail on ([[F2-214]]). ⚠ It asks whether a boundary is **opened**,
not whether the isolation works — the latter is not unit-observable, because the wrappers run inline
when no transaction manager is present, and the leg says so.

### Mutation results, stated honestly

| | |
|---|---|
| **KILLED** | the true pre-fix state (annotation **and** boundary), and the wrapper's null-tolerance |
| **SURVIVED — equivalent** | `@Transactional` alone (`REQUIRES_NEW` suspends the outer transaction, so it is still correct); removing the boundary alone (harmless with no batch transaction) |
| **WITHDRAWN — invalid** | disabling my own assertion, which always survives ([[F2-206]]) |

🔑 My first pre-fix mutation restored **only** the annotation and survived — correctly. **The regression
is both changes together**, and treating that survival as a hole would have produced a gate assertion
that fails on correct code. ⚙ The null-tolerance survival *was* a real gap: no test calls the reporting
tick, so nothing exercised that path. Closed by asserting it structurally for **both** wrappers this
family added.

### Filed

* `RiskReviewService.flag` per-row isolation, unchanged from [[F2-322]]'s filing.

## F2-322 — the per-org catch was a decoy, and fixing it is structural rather than a wrapper

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P3 — a resilience control that read as working and discarded every tenant's work on any tenant's failure. Ungated and hourly. |
| **Registers** | `iam.user_roles` (time-bound revocation), `platform.audit_log` |
| **Standards** | NCA ECC 2-2 / SAMA CSF 3.3.5 (access governance) |
| **Found by** | Executing [[F2-317]]'s filing — it recorded this and declined to fix it, correctly |
| **Verification** | mutations **3/3 killed**; suite **4726 → 4727/0/0** |

### Why F2-317 filed it instead of fixing it

`audit.log` is `@Transactional` and **joins** the caller's transaction. With `scheduledExpirySweep`
itself `@Transactional`, a failure on one organisation marked the batch-wide transaction
rollback-only, so **every** organisation's work was discarded at commit — while the per-org
`catch (RuntimeException)` made the method read as resilient. 🔑 **The catch created the appearance of
resilience while changing nothing**, and removing that appearance needs a transaction boundary, not a
wrapper.

⚙ This sweep is `@Scheduled(PT1H)` and **ungated**, so it runs hourly in every environment — which is
why it is the member worth fixing.

### The idiom was already in the tree, including in a scheduler

Five files use `TransactionTemplate` with `PROPAGATION_REQUIRES_NEW`, one of them
`EmergencyRatificationSlaScheduler`. The sweep is no longer `@Transactional` and each organisation's
work runs inside `inNewTransaction(...)`.

### ⚠⚠ The isolation is not unit-observable, and the leg says so

`inNewTransaction` runs **inline** when `txManager` is null — the case for a directly-constructed
service — so in a unit test the boundary does not exist and a failure propagates exactly as before.
That precedent's own javadoc records the same trap in the same words: *"the inline path is why the six
unit tests could not catch the missing transaction."*

🔑 **A leg that cannot see the thing it is named for is worse than one that says so.** The two halves
are testable to different depths:

| | observable inline? |
|---|---|
| control flow — one org's failure does not stop the loop | **yes** (the catch runs either way) |
| isolation — the other orgs' committed work survives | **no** — structural only |

### RiskReviewService is re-filed rather than swept in

Its scheduler is **off by default**, and its `flag` has **two callers whose atomicity requirements
differ**: the controller path wants one atomic result, the sweep wants per-row isolation. Splitting it
is a design decision, and threading a flag through a shared helper is the shape [[F2-306]] warned
against.

### Filed

* `RiskReviewService.flag` per-row isolation, with the two-caller tension stated.
* The other looping sweeps were measured at **0 of 33** missing a per-item catch ([[F2-317]]) — but
  that measurement counted the *catch*, not whether the catch means anything. 🔑 **The same question
  asked of the transaction boundary rather than the catch is a different census, and it has not been
  run.**

## F2-321 — my own warning would have named nothing, for 92% of its callers

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P4 — a diagnostic that looks informative and is not. Corrects [[F2-320]], shipped one slice earlier. |
| **Registers** | `platform.audit_log` |
| **Standards** | — |
| **Found by** | Reading the **rows** rather than the code, after the chain was closed |
| **Verification** | mutations **2/2 killed**; suite **4726/0/0** |

### The measurement

Of **3,809** off-request audit entries in dev, `source_module` is NULL on **3,524** — because the
`log(...)` convenience method never sets it, and that is what almost every writer uses. So [[F2-320]]'s
warning, which printed the action type and the source module, would have read *"module null"* for the
majority of the population it exists to surface.

🔑 **An artefact that looks informative and is not** — the shape this whole chain has been about, in my
own fix. A warning naming nothing locatable is worse than none, because it looks like an answer and
the reader stops.

⚙ It names the **calling class** now, walked with `StackWalker` rather than a materialised
`Throwable` trace, since this runs on every unanchored write. The leg asserts both that the class
appears **and** that the message contains no `"null"`.

### The blast radius, quantified from data

| | dev | prod |
|---|---|---|
| off-request audit rows (`NO_PRINCIPAL`) | 3,809 | 762 |
| of those, filed under organisation 1 | **3,786** | **762 — every one** |
| written by the automation engine ([[F2-319]]) | 285 | 44 |

### 🔑 And the sharpest justification for F2-320's shape was in the same method

The actor half already **declared** its absence explicitly — `user_role_source = NO_PRINCIPAL`, 3,809
rows — while the tenant half silently defaulted. **One method, two absent values, one declared and one
defaulted.** [[F2-195]]'s shape at the tightest range in this chain, and it is why "make the fallback
opt-in" was the right fix rather than an invention.

### Refuted on the way

Three dev rows name **organisation 5, which does not exist**. Checked: user 24 is deleted, **no** user
names a nonexistent org, and prod has **none**. They are residue from a deleted probe tenant that the
append-only trail correctly outlives ([[F2-281]]'s rule) — not a defect, recorded so nobody re-files it.

### Filed

* Nothing. Whether `log(...)` should set `sourceModule` is a separate question: 3,524 rows would gain
  a module, which is a **data** improvement rather than a correctness one, and the warning no longer
  depends on it.

## F2-320 — the fallback was right for one caller and silent for four, so it is opt-in now

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P3 — the structural close of [[F2-317]]/[[F2-318]]/[[F2-319]]. No behaviour change on any working path. |
| **Registers** | `platform.audit_log` |
| **Standards** | audit integrity; multi-tenancy |
| **Found by** | Completing the population: `afterCommit` callbacks were the one off-request kind still unmeasured, and they were **refuted** — which left the root |
| **Verification** | mutations **4/4** + F2-318's **5/5** re-run; suite **4724 → 4726/0/0** |

### The population is now complete

| entry point | audit writers | unanchored |
|---|---|---|
| `@Scheduled` ([[F2-318]]) | 8 of 33 | 4 |
| `@Async` / `@EventListener` ([[F2-319]]) | 3 of 4 | 1 |
| programmatic `afterCommit` | 1 file, 2 sites | **0** — both on-request and same-thread, so the tenant is intact |

Four were defects. **One** — `DbSizeMonitorJob`, auditing the size of the database itself — is
genuinely org-less, and the fallback is its intended behaviour.

### 🔑 The fallback is not the defect; being silent is

Without a way to say *"this belongs to no tenant"*, that case and *"I lost the tenant"* are **the same
call** — which is precisely why all four stayed invisible. So `recordEvent` warns, naming the action
type, unless the caller declared `systemEvent()`; and `logSystem(...)` mirrors the `log(...)` the one
qualifying caller already used.

⚠ **A WARN rather than a throw, deliberately.** Off-request audit paths cannot be enumerated
statically (listener registration, reflection, SpEL), so refusing would risk breaking a path nobody
has seen — the one failure a fix must not have ([[F2-214]]). The default is unchanged; only its
visibility is.

### ⚠⚠ The fix turned an exemption into a property

`DbSizeMonitorJob` had a named entry in the gate's exclusion map, exempted as *"genuinely org-less"* —
which asserts that somebody read the file once. It now satisfies the invariant on its own merits
(**anchor a tenant OR declare the event org-less**), so the entry is **deleted**. 🔑 **An exemption is a
weaker artefact than a property; when a fix lets one become the other, delete the exemption rather
than keeping both** ([[F2-205]]). The two pollers keep theirs, because they **refuse** rather than
declare — a third correct answer the invariant cannot express structurally.

⚙ The reverse leg is what caught this: after the change `DbSizeMonitorJob` no longer matched the audit
pattern, so its exclusion said nothing, and the leg failed. That is the direction nobody writes first
([[F2-199]]) earning its place.

### Three of my own errors, all caught by running things

* ⚠⚠ **My first behavioural leg was theatre.** It attached a Logback appender it never read and
  asserted through a helper that **reimplemented the condition** — proving the helper agreed with
  itself, the defect this register keeps recording, inside the leg meant to observe a warning.
  Replaced with one that constructs the real service over mocks, invokes `recordEvent` and reads the
  appender.
* **The builder's fields are package-private**, so my first repoint of the three existing
  `DbSizeMonitorJobTest` legs could not compile from `module.platform.health`. 🔑 That is what made
  `logSystem(...)` the right shape rather than widening the builder's API for a test ([[F2-192]]'s
  seam concern) — and it kept those legs asserting the **action type** instead of merely that some
  audit call happened.
* Two mutations reported **ANCHOR-MISS** because they pointed at text this slice changed. Re-aimed
  rather than counted: **a mutation that does not run is neither a kill nor a hole.**

### Filed

* Nothing new. Per-row `REQUIRES_NEW` stands as [[F2-317]] filed it.

## F2-319 — the automation engine runs on a pool thread, so no publisher could set its tenant

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | **P2** — latent, and unconditional: not "when a caller forgets" but *always*. |
| **Registers** | `platform.automation_rule_runs`, `platform.audit_log` |
| **Standards** | multi-tenancy; audit integrity |
| **Found by** | Asking [[F2-318]]'s question of the **other** off-request entry points — `@Async`, `@EventListener`, `@TransactionalEventListener` |
| **Verification** | 3 new legs (13/13); mutations **3/3 killed**; suite **4721 → 4724/0/0** |

### The population, and the one member

**4 such entry points, 3 write audit rows, 1 anchored no tenant**:
`AutomationRuleEngine#onDomainEvent`, which carries `@Async` **and** `@EventListener` on one method.
`@EnableAsync` is present on `GrcApplication`, so it runs on a **pool thread** — and `TenantContext`
is a `ThreadLocal`.

So `AuditLogService`'s `org != null ? org : 1L` applied to **every** audit row the engine and
`AutomationActionExecutor` write — **nine sites** — **unconditionally**.

### 🔑 Why this is structurally different from F2-317 and F2-318

There the tenant was absent because nobody set it, and a caller *could in principle* have. **Here the
ThreadLocal does not cross the async boundary, so no publisher could ever have helped.** That is what
makes one anchor at the **thread boundary** the right fix rather than nine at the writers — and it is
the answer to "the caller should have set it", which is not available.

### The tell, three lines from the defect

`recordRun` does `r.setOrganisationId(rule.getOrganisationId())` **explicitly**; the
`audit.recordEvent` beside it took the fallback. The run row org-correct, the audit row not — fifth
instance of that asymmetry in this family.

### Latent, and the seeded rows nearly said otherwise

All **673** automation runs in dev and **217** in prod are organisation 1. There *are* 10
organisation-2 `RULE_FIRED` audit rows, which looked at first like the defect having fired — but four
share **one timestamp to the second** (the bulk-write fingerprint, [[F2-256]]'s rule) and there are
**zero** organisation-2 runs, so they are seeded. The 13 rules each in organisations 2 and 3 have
never fired. 🔑 **The observable when one does is that the two tables disagree**: the run row in its
own tenant, the audit row in tenant 1.

### ⚠ The restore matters more on a pool thread

A scheduler owns its thread for the run; a **pool thread is reused**, so a tenant left set leaks into
the next event — a rule for one organisation audited under whichever organisation the previous task
belonged to. That mutation is killed, and so is one replacing the anchor with a literal `1L`.

⚙ The `event.organisationId() == null` refusal stays **before** the anchor, deliberately:
`setCurrentTenant(null)` would put the thread back into exactly the state the fallback exists for.

### Filed

* Nothing new. Per-row `REQUIRES_NEW` stands as [[F2-317]] filed it.

## F2-318 — the other three off-request audit writers, and three of the four wrote the org into the prose

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | **P2** — latent, but one member is ungated and hourly, so ordinary use fires it. |
| **Registers** | `iam.user_roles` (time-bound revocation), `iam.sod_violations`, `cyber.vulnerability_sla_finding`, `platform.audit_log` |
| **Standards** | NCA ECC 2-2 / SAMA CSF 3.3.5 (access governance, SoD); multi-tenancy |
| **Found by** | Generalising [[F2-317]]: `AuditLogService` falls back to tenant 1 for **every** off-request writer, so how many are there? |
| **Verification** | mutations **5/5 killed** (after the harness found a hole in my own gate); suite **4717 → 4721/0/0** |

### The population

Measured over all **33** `@Scheduled` methods, following one hop of delegation because F2-317's defect
was exactly one hop down: **8 reach `audit.log`, 4 anchored no tenant.** F2-317 closed one; these are
the other three.

| | |
|---|---|
| `AccessRequestService#scheduledExpirySweep` | ⚠ `@Scheduled(PT1H)` and **ungated** — runs hourly in every environment |
| `SodService#nightlyScan` | 02:30 UTC across all tenants |
| `VulnerabilitySlaComputeService#runEscalationCheck` | `orgId` arrives as a **parameter** |

### 🔑 Three of the four put the organisation in the audit MESSAGE

`"(org " + org + ")"`, `"for org " + org`. **That is the signature: an author who needs the
organisation in the row and cannot get it there writes it into the prose.** And in every case the
notification or `DomainEvent` beside the audit row was already org-explicit while the audit row was
not — the same asymmetry F2-317 found, now four times.

⚠ Two of the four javadocs said *"off-request-safe"* — true about not crashing, silent about
attribution ([[F2-184]]'s shape on the exact concern).

### Latent, but not equally

Every row in both databases is organisation 1, so no mismatch has occurred: what made all four
harmless is the **data**, not the code ([[F2-182]]). But the IAM sweep is **ungated and hourly**, so an
expiring time-bound assignment in any other tenant fires it through ordinary use — unlike F2-317,
which needs a configuration change.

### RESTORE, not clear — at all three sites

Restoring is correct whether or not an ambient tenant exists; clearing is only correct when one does
not, so it has to be re-justified every time a caller is added. Two of the three have an on-request
sibling that a plain `finally { clear(); }` would have broken.

### The gate's first run surfaced four more, and three are legitimate

Each for a **different** reason, which is why they are a named map rather than a blanket rule:

* `CrowdStrikeInboundService`, `TenableInboundService` — they **read** the tenant and refuse when it
  is absent, so off-request they do nothing rather than mis-attribute. 🔑 **A `setCurrentTenant` scan
  cannot tell consulting the tenant from ignoring it**, so both needed reading.
* `DbSizeMonitorJob` — **genuinely org-less**: it audits the database itself, `entityType Database`
  with a null entity id, so the tenant-1 fallback is intended and anchoring one would invent it.

### ⚠⚠ And the harness found a hole in my own gate

**All three pre-fix mutations SURVIVED.** The anchor pattern matched any
`TenantContext.setCurrentTenant(...)` — and every fix in this family adds **two**: the real anchor
plus a `finally { setCurrentTenant(ambient) }` restore. Deleting the anchor left the restore, which
still matched.

🔑 **A substring check satisfied by something other than its claim — and the thing satisfying it
existed only because of the fix, so the gate got weaker the moment it was applied.** Narrowed to
exclude the ambient argument; **5/5** after, with the deliberate `clear()`-instead-of-restore mutation
correctly **surviving**.

⚙ The tenant-1 fallback itself is asserted. If `AuditLogService` ever starts refusing an unset tenant,
this family becomes a loud failure rather than a silent mis-attribution, and these legs should be
re-read rather than left asserting a mechanism that is gone.

### Filed

* Nothing new. Per-row `REQUIRES_NEW` stands as [[F2-317]] filed it.

⚙ Two recorded landmines walked into: the first scan's method regex used a lazy type class and
**backtracked catastrophically**, hanging a whole-tree walk past the timeout (anchored to line starts
after); and an inline `py -c` mangled its escapes again.

## F2-317 — a cross-tenant sweep whose audit rows all landed in tenant 1

| | |
|---|---|
