| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | **P2** — latent. A cross-tenant audit mis-attribution: one tenant's log gains entries about other tenants' risks, and those tenants get none. |
| **Registers** | `risk.risks`, `platform.audit_log` |
| **Standards** | multi-tenancy; audit integrity |
| **Found by** | Asking F2-191's question — *which scheduled sweeps abort on one bad row?* — which was **refuted at 0 of 33**, and reading the four that delegate one hop |
| **Verification** | 5 unit legs; mutations **3/3 killed**; suite **4712 → 4717/0/0** |

### Two callers, one of them with no tenant

```
runOverdueSweepForTenant()   tenant-scoped query, called from RiskReviewController
runOverdueSweepAllTenants()  cross-tenant query,  called from RiskReviewScheduler
```

Both delegate to one private `flag(List<Risk>)`. `AuditLogService.recordEvent` does
`org != null ? org : 1L` — *"fall back to tenant 1 (system events)"* — so on the scheduler path every
`RISK_REVIEW_OVERDUE` row was stamped **organisation 1** whatever tenant's risk it described.

🔑 **The `DomainEvent` two lines below already passed `r.getOrganisationId()` explicitly. Within one
loop body the event was org-explicit and the audit row beside it was not** — that asymmetry is the
whole tell.

### Latent, and the configuration is what made it so

`grc.risk.review-scheduler-enabled` defaults **false** and is set in no profile, so the sweep has
never run; all 7 existing rows came from the per-tenant path (org 1, no mismatch). Measured
identically in both databases: **24 risks are past their review date and unflagged — 4 in org 1, 10
in org 2, 10 in org 3.** So enabling one flag would have mis-stamped twenty audit rows. What made it
harmless was the configuration, not the code ([[F2-182]]).

### RESTORE, not clear — and the naive fix is a mutation that gets killed

`runOverdueSweepForTenant` is called from a **controller**, so the request continues after this
returns; a plain `finally { clear(); }` would strip its tenant mid-request. `EvidenceItemService
.expireStaleEvidence` clears and is **right** to — its only caller is a scheduler with no ambient
tenant to lose. 🔑 **Restore-versus-clear is a property of the callers, not a house style.**

### The per-item catch this slice set out to add is deliberately absent

`audit.log` is `@Transactional` and joins this transaction, so catching its failure still leaves the
transaction rollback-only and the whole batch fails at commit. 🔑 **The catch would create the
appearance of resilience while changing nothing** — the decoy shape this register keeps finding. Doing
it properly needs a per-row `REQUIRES_NEW` boundary (the recorded engine-wiring rule) and is filed.

### The population is exactly two, and the other one was already right

Two cross-tenant finders exist in the platform. `expireStaleEvidence` anchors the tenant on the row
and carries an [[F2-242]] comment explaining why. **The correct idiom was in the tree beside the one
place it was not applied** — [[F2-195]]'s shape, third slice running.

⚠ A gate leg holds the shape because the population will grow. **My first draft failed on this very
fix**: it looked forward a fixed number of characters from the call site, and the per-row setter lives
in `flag`, which the long javadoc above it pushed past the window. A gate that fails on correct code
trains the next reader to edit the assertion ([[F2-214]]), so it is class-scoped now with that
limitation **stated** — it catches a cross-tenant sweep in a class that never anchors a tenant and
would miss one anchoring in a different method.

### No live probe, deliberately

The only reachable path is the per-tenant sweep, which would flag **four real overdue risks** and
write four **irreversible** audit rows on a customer-shaped database (house rule 6, [[F2-206]]). The
unit leg captures `TenantContext` at the moment of each audit call — 🔑 **a mock that records only its
arguments cannot see this defect, because the organisation is never an argument.**

### Filed

* Per-row `REQUIRES_NEW` for this and the sibling sweep, so one bad row genuinely does not abort the
  batch rather than appearing not to.
* The **24 unflagged overdue risks** and whether `grc.risk.review-scheduler-enabled` should be on —
  an owner decision, now safe to make.

## F2-316 — the platform already had the right idiom, and the reporting module was the one place that broke it

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P4 — makes [[F2-315]]'s defect unrepresentable rather than validated. No behaviour change on any working path. |
| **Registers** | `reporting.report_schedules` |
| **Standards** | — |
| **Found by** | Asking [[F2-315]]'s question one level up: across **all 23 download handlers**, is the declared MIME type decided by the same thing as the filename extension? |
| **Verification** | probe **9/9**; mutations **4/4 killed** (one after closing a real residual); suite **4711 → 4712/0/0** |

### The generalisation answered itself

| | |
|---|---|
| `NdiReportController#streamBytes` | **one switch**, each arm assigning `body` + `ct` + `ext` together, `default -> throw` |
| `MlModelController#export` | one `boolean pdf` feeding the bytes, the MIME and the extension |
| the other **20** handlers | the format is in the **route** (`/export.pdf`, `/export.xlsx`), so the question cannot arise |

🔑 **The report scheduler was the only export surface that put the format in a COLUMN and then read
it from three separate switches** — [[F2-195]]'s shape, the codebase holding the correct rule beside
the one place it was not applied. `ClimateReportController` is the clearest contrast: two endpoints,
each appending the extension as a literal matching its own hard-coded type.

### Why do this having just validated it

[[F2-315]] refuses an unrenderable pair at the **write boundary**. A row can reach the scheduler
without passing one: `seed_real_data.py` is exactly how [[F2-293]]'s unhandled `SEMIANNUAL` cadence
got in, and it produced **13 consecutive daily failures** in both databases. So the boundary check is
necessary and not sufficient — `renderBody`/`filenameFor`/`mimeFor` become one `render` returning a
`Rendered` record, built only by three factories that each pair **one** extension with **one** MIME
type.

⚙ The two label switches are **deleted**. Their shared `default -> pdf` is the entire mechanism: a
format with no case of its own was labelled a PDF whatever bytes it held.

### The gate leg is replaced, not weakened

F2-315's leg asserted that every declared non-PDF format had an explicit `case` in `filenameFor`
**and** `mimeFor`. Those methods no longer exist, so its **subject** is gone — and the leg replacing
it fails if either switch comes back, and requires that only the three factories may construct a
`Rendered`.

### ⚠⚠ The mutation harness found a real residual

Three factories make a mismatched label **pair** unrepresentable. They do **not** stop an arm handing
XLSX bytes to `pdf(...)` — the original defect, moved upstream of the factories. That mutation
**survived**, and the mutated code is genuinely wrong, so it was a hole rather than an equivalent
mutant ([[F2-206]]).

🔑 **Collapsing switches removes the disagreement between labels and leaves the disagreement between
bytes and label** — ask which one a collapse actually closes. Now every factory call inside `render`
must be handed bytes from a generator naming the same format, in its method-name suffix
(`riskRegisterXlsx`, `generatePptx`) or as a literal argument (`export("XLSX")`).

⚠ That is a **naming** rule, which [[F2-217]] warns measures the list its author knew. Stated as a
limitation rather than hidden: a generator naming no format is reported **unresolvable** rather than
passed, so the answer cannot quietly shrink.

### The honest observable

With SMTP unconfigured in dev the filename and MIME **never leave the process**, so the probe cannot
see them. What it can see is *which generator ran*: all six renderable pairs render, and each type's
two formats produce different byte counts (`RISK_REGISTER` 31 400 / 9 758, `BOARD_PACK` 40 407 /
34 906, `AI_MODEL_REGISTRY` 27 042 / 6 767). My first probe asserted the filename from the response
and read 5/10 — **an assertion about something the observable does not carry**, corrected rather than
explained away.

### Filed

* Nothing new. The seven un-rendered report types stand as [[F2-293]] filed them.

⚙ One slip: the patch script used a `\` line continuation inside a **non-raw** Python triple-quoted
string, so Python ate the Java text-block joiners and three assertion messages shipped with runs of
embedded spaces. Repaired; scripts are raw strings now.

## F2-315 — three switches decide the report format and none of them compares the others

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P3 — latent. A scheduled report emailed to its recipients as bytes of one format under another format's name and MIME type. |
| **Registers** | `reporting.report_schedules` (11 live rows, dev = prod) |
| **Standards** | — |
| **Found by** | Executing [[F2-293]]'s filing, and re-deriving it ([[F2-221]]) — which showed the filing was **narrower than the defect** |
| **Verification** | probe **13/13**; mutations **8/8 killed**; suite **4703 → 4711/0/0** |

### One pair, three switches

```
renderBody   branches on the REPORT TYPE   PDF ? …Pdf : …Xlsx      (BOARD_PACK: PPTX ? pptx : pdf)
filenameFor  branches on the FORMAT        PPTX -> pptx, XLSX -> xlsx, default -> pdf
mimeFor      branches on the FORMAT        PPTX, XLSX,               default -> application/pdf
```

So `DOCX` + `RISK_REGISTER` produced **XLSX bytes** named `.pdf` with an `application/pdf` MIME type,
and `XLSX` + `BOARD_PACK` produced **PDF bytes** named `.xlsx` with an Excel MIME type — an
attachment that will not open, from a schedule the console reports as SUCCESS.

🔑 **[[F2-293]] filed the first and missed the second, because it looked for `DOCX`.** The defect is
not a format: it is **two switches over one pair with nobody comparing them** ([[F2-177]]). And
`DOCX` was offered by the form while **no report type can emit it at all** — [[F2-193]]'s rule, a
catalogue must not claim a capability that does not exist.

### Fixed the way F2-293 fixed the sibling column

One declaration (`ReportSchedulerService.SUPPORTED_FORMATS`), two readers, a boundary refusal that
names the field. Three design points that are not stylistic:

* ⚠⚠ **The pair is validated on the RESULTING row, never the request.** `apply` copies `reportType`
  and `format` independently, so a partial update may change only the format while the type comes
  from storage — **checking the request alone passes exactly the update that produces a mislabelled
  file.** That mutation is killed.
* ⚠ **A report type this platform cannot render at all is left alone.** Seven of the eleven live
  schedules hold such a type ([[F2-293]]), one of them with format `XLSX`; refusing here would turn a
  rendering gap into a **data-entry lockout** ([[F2-183]]).
* ⚠ **The label carries the restriction, because the select is flat.** It cannot narrow by report
  type, so *"Excel (not for the board pack)"* is the only thing an operator can read before the
  server refuses. A gate holds the labels against the matrix **in both directions** — an unqualified
  partial format invites a 400 nobody could predict, and a qualifier left on a format that became
  universal states a restriction that is gone ([[F2-212]]).

### The load-bearing gate leg

Every declared **non-PDF** format must have an explicit `case` in `filenameFor` **and** `mimeFor`.
Both end `default -> pdf`, so a format with no case of its own is labelled a PDF whatever bytes it
holds — that is the entire mechanism, and `DOCX` had no case in either. `PDF` legitimately *is* the
default, so it is excluded and `pdfIsRenderableForEveryDeclaredType…` asserts the basis on which
`requireRenderableFormat` tolerates a null format.

⚙ The keys of `SUPPORTED_FORMATS` must equal `renderBody`'s `case` labels, both ways, so **a new
report type cannot ship without declaring its formats**.

### Latent, and said so

Every live schedule in both databases is `PDF` — which every declared type handles — or a type with
no generator. So this is a **latent-hazard closure, not a defect discovery** ([[F2-283]]), and there
is no pre-fix live behaviour on real data to contrast against: that the checks are load-bearing is
established by the **mutation harness**, not claimed. `require` rather than `coerce` ([[F2-182]]):
nothing that succeeds today starts failing.

### One of my own assertions was wrong about the code

I expected a null format to stay null on create. [[F2-293]] removed the entity initialisers and moved
the default into `create()`, which runs `apply()` first and `DEFAULT_FORMAT` after — so the null
branch is genuinely reachable and the stored value becomes `PDF`. Corrected against the code rather
than the reverse ([[F2-206]] applied to an assertion).

⚠ And the route was **guessed** — `/api/v1/report-schedules` where the controller says
`/api/v1/reporting/schedules` — costing one probe run that read 0/9 with every leg 404. The grep that
resolves it had printed the answer one line earlier.

### Filed

* The **seven report types with no generator** stand exactly as [[F2-293]] filed them: a build plus a
  decision about which framework each pack must satisfy.
* `FORMAT_OPTIONS`' three labels are **literals rather than translation keys**, so the qualifier an
  operator reads is English-only (house rule 7). Pre-existing; the gate checks the English.

## F2-314 — the persona guide probes are designed from denied a grant the persona holds

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P3 — a document whose stated purpose is authorization-probe design, wrong in the direction that makes a correct server look broken. No production change. |
| **Registers** | — (`iam.role_permissions`, read per persona) |
| **Standards** | — |
| **Found by** | Measuring the mirror of [[F2-313]] — *which roles can ACT on a module without being able to READ it?* — which was **refuted**, and the refutation needed the persona grants, which is where the stale claim was |
| **Verification** | probe **7/7**; matrix published and derived per database |

### The refuted question first, because it is the more useful half

[[F2-313]] measured pairs nobody can satisfy. The mirror is [[F2-259]]'s hand-found case — *"the
attest tier was WIDER than the tier producing the artefact it attests to"* — and V380's self-check
asserts containment (*"nobody seals a ledger they cannot read"*) for exactly one pair. Nobody had
measured it.

**Two metric corrections, both from reading rather than counting:**

* **Module-scoped containment is the wrong unit.** *"Acting without that module's READ"* reported
  **27** rows; `BOARD:EXPORT` ANDs **`ADMIN:READ`** — a *different* module's read. 🔑 **The guard
  names which READ matters; the module boundary does not.**
* **Per-guard, the direction matters.** Composed-guard halves reported **60** rows, and holding
  `CHANGE:READ` without `CHANGE:EXPORT` is *least privilege working*. Only the **acting half without
  the gating half** is interesting.

Corrected, the answer is **two rows** — `BCM:EXPORT` held by `CISO` and `CFO` without `BCM:READ`.

### And both are documented, in a comment above the guard

`BcpBinderController#download` says:

> *"V320 grants BCM:EXPORT to CISO and CFO, which this list allows but the catalogue did not —
> without that grant the AND would have denied two roles the endpoint has always permitted."*

So the grant exists **solely** to satisfy one composed guard's AND, and was never a general BCM
export capability. It is load-bearing where it was created for and insufficient on three siblings it
was never meant to reach. 🔑 **Neither granting `BCM:READ` nor revoking `BCM:EXPORT` is a pure
improvement** — the first widens access to a customer's continuity plans, the second breaks the
binder download — so there is nothing to fix. Probed **7/7**: `so_officer` is **403** on
`/bcm/plans/14/export.pdf` and **200** on `/bcm/plans/14/binders`, same role, same module, same
permission.

### The actual finding was in the guide the probe was designed from

CLAUDE.md's persona-grant paragraph exists so a slice can pick the right persona. It named **5 of
`so_officer`'s 60** grants and asserted *"**no** COMPLIANCE/BCM"*. COMPLIANCE is right; **BCM is
false**. 🔑 **Several slices in this programme have chosen probe personas from that line, and a probe
expecting 403 where the persona holds the permission reads as a defect in the code.**

Two more claims read the wrong way round:

| Claim | Measured |
|---|---|
| `auditor` = "EVIDENCE_WRITE + COMPLIANCE_WRITE + BCM_READ" | **62 grants over 31 of 37 modules** — against `rmanager` 22, `ranalyst` 13. The wrong persona to reach for as low-privilege. |
| `viewer` reads as read-only | holds **`EXPORT` in every module where it holds `READ`**, statutory registers included |

⚙ `ranalyst`'s four denials (`BCM`, `CYBER`, `PRIVACY`, `TPRM`) are **all still correct**, which is why
it is the right persona for an expected-403 leg — and the paragraph's closing claim about covering
three shapes still holds.

### Deleted rather than corrected

An enumeration is a copy of a measurement ([[F2-273]]) and this one had gone stale twice — its own
text records one earlier repair (*"this line said READ only until 2026-08-06 and the omission cost a
probe iteration"*). So the matrix is **published** as §G of `ROLE_GUARD_CENSUS.md`, derived per
database, and only the **denials** stay in prose, because a denial is what a 403 expectation rests on.

⚠⚠ **§G then refuted a comparative claim I had just written into CLAUDE.md** — *"auditor is the widest
read surface"* — when `compliance` is, at **35 of 37**. Corrected in place. And the last hard-coded
figure in the new section (*"5 of 60"*) was **derived**, because on the deployed server the total is
55: 🔑 **a copy-of-a-measurement defect reappearing inside the section written to remove them.**

⚙ `admin` holds **47 grants over 14 modules — fewer than `auditor` or `compliance`** — because
`PLATFORM_ADMIN` bypasses in code and V272 records it as needing no grants. A concrete illustration
of *admin proves nothing about authorization*, and §G says so on the row.

### Filed

* Nothing. The containment question is answered and its two rows are documented; the guide now points
  at a derived matrix.

## F2-313 — the census tracking the conversion backlog was blind to the half it converts into

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | 🟡 MEASURED + INSTRUMENTED 2026-08-24 — the remedy is tenant data, not a jar |
| **Severity** | **P2** — a whole module's surface reachable only through the `PLATFORM_ADMIN` code bypass, including two sidebar-linked consoles |
| **Registers** | `platform.issues` (13 live rows), `platform.calendar_events`, `platform.departments`, file upload, branding, tenant onboarding |
| **Standards** | — (the Issue register is where NCA ECC / SAMA CSF control-test escalations land) |
| **Found by** | Asking [[F2-253]]'s question of the *destination*: `ROLE_GUARD_CENSUS.md` measures **role** guards, and `hasPermission` is [[F2-05]]'s ratified target |
| **Verification** | probe **13/13** as six real personas; census run against **both** databases |

### The instrument was scoped to the thing being retired

`ROLE_GUARD_CENSUS.md`'s §B2b asks *"which pure **role** guards admit nobody, by holder
attrition?"* — [[F2-253]]'s question, and the reason §B2b exists. Every section of that report is
about role guards, because that is what it was built to track.

🔑 **`hasPermission` is the ratified destination of the whole F2-05 conversion programme, and the
same question had never been put to it.** So the census measuring the backlog could not see a defect
in the half it converts *into* — [[F2-198]]'s shape, where the narrowing is the artefact's own
subject.

### What it found

Joining the pairs guards cite — the artefact `PermissionCatalogueUsageTest` already publishes — against
active holders:

| | dev | prod |
|---|---|---|
| unsatisfiable pairs | **7** of 131 | **5** of 131 |
| routes they close | **36** | **34** |

`PLATFORM:READ` / `WRITE` / `EXPORT` are granted to **`ORG_ADMIN` alone, which has no active user**,
so `module/platform`'s entire surface — **29 routes** — is reachable by a platform administrator and
nobody else:

* `/issues`, **sidebar-linked**: the cross-module Issue console
* `/calendar`, **sidebar-linked**: the platform calendar and its `.ics` export
* departments, file upload, branding writes, tenant onboarding

Probed **13/13**: `compliance`, `so_officer`, `auditor`, `rmanager`, `ranalyst` and `viewer` all
**403 on every Issue route including READ**, on `/api/v1/calendar/events`, on the `.ics` export and on
departments; `admin` 200 throughout. (`brand-theme` READ is correctly `isAuthenticated()` — only its
write is behind `PLATFORM`.)

🔑 **Two automated ladders escalate into that register** — `CcmService` on the third consecutive
CRITICAL control-test failure ([[F2-228]]) and `KriBreachService` on a KRI breach — across 7 source
modules. **So the platform writes escalations into a console no non-administrator can open**, and
because READ is included, nobody can even see that they exist.

### The others, and why counting them is the point

`CHANGE:DELETE` (4 routes), `REPORTING:DELETE`, `CPTY:APPROVE`, `AML:REFRESH_LISTS`. [[F2-260]] filed
`CPTY:APPROVE`; [[F2-293]] filed `REPORTING:DELETE`; `CHANGE:DELETE` had never been mentioned.
🔑 [[F2-266]]'s headline: **filings one at a time is what a population looks like when nothing counts
it.**

### The remedy is tenant data, and that is a precedent rather than a preference

All seven are granted to a role that **exists and is seated in nobody**, so an administrator can
assign it without a new jar — a **remedy, not a defence** ([[F2-253]]). [[F2-282]] settled the fix for
this kind on exactly this role: **seat `ORG_ADMIN`, do not widen the grant.** Granting `PLATFORM` to
`GRC_ADMINISTRATOR` would hand the GRC content administrator the **branding, tenant-onboarding and
department** registers, which is a different job family and wider than the shipped guard's own
audience ([[F2-260]]: for a grant, the shipped audience is the evidence and convention is the thing to
argue against).

⚙ **None** is granted to no role at all, so nothing here needs a migration — and the report says that
explicitly, so [[F2-260]]'s `RRP` case reads as genuinely absent rather than merely unlisted.

### Two refinements found by running it

* **The rows are not of equal weight** — `PLATFORM:WRITE` guards 16 routes, `REPORTING:DELETE` one —
  so the guarded-route count is **derived from the source**, not written into the prose ([[F2-273]]).
* ⚠⚠ **Running against prod put `PLATFORM_ADMIN:READ/WRITE` into the table and the 42-route total**,
  because there V369+ is pending so those rows really are ungranted — while the note beneath said they
  are by design. **A caveat in prose contradicting the number above it** ([[F2-197]]), in the section I
  had just written. The bypass module is excluded from the population now and the exclusion is
  **printed**, so it is a measurement rather than a silent filter. 🔑 Only the second database showed
  it ([[F2-259]]).

### Filed

* **Seat `ORG_ADMIN`** in each tenant — the whole of `module/platform` depends on it. Tenant data, so
  an owner action.
* Whether a cross-module Issue should be visible to holders of its **source module's** READ rather
  than to `PLATFORM:READ` is a product question ([[F2-259]]: converting a READ tier can widen a

## F2-312 — a leg named for three exercised four and missed the fifth

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P4 — a coverage gap in an instrument, plus one refuted hypothesis worth recording. No production change. |
| **Registers** | — (`common/validation/ServerOwnedState`, the platform's refusal primitives) |
| **Standards** | — |
| **Found by** | Asking a question of this session's **own output**: I had extended `ServerOwnedState` twice ([[F2-302]], [[F2-306]]) and it now holds several near-identical refusal primitives — do any two answer the same question differently? |
| **Verification** | suite **4701 → 4703/0/0**; mutations **4/4 killed** |

### The leg's name was a population claim, and it was wrong

`ServerOwnedStateContractTest.allThreeEntryPointsAgreeOnCase` is this class's
one-question-one-answer leg — the one that exists to prove the primitives do not disagree. It
exercised `sameState`, `requireInitial`, `requireCreatable` **and** `requireUnchanged`: **four**,
against a name that says three. And it did not touch `requireImmutableReference` at all, which
[[F2-306]] added four slices earlier.

🔑 **A leg named for a count goes stale the moment the class grows, and the miss is invisible because
the name reads like a complete population** — in the class whose entire subject is one question, one
answer.

### So the population is derived

`everyComparingEntryPointIsExercisedHere` reflects over `ServerOwnedState`'s public static methods:
one taking two `String`s (a candidate and what it is measured against) or a `Set` of legal values is
a comparing primitive, and must be exercised by this class or the build fails. [[F2-299]]'s rule —
derive the vocabulary, do not hold a list — applied to the list a test's own *name* implies.

### REFUTED: the divergence was already pinned, in two classes

My hypothesis was that the one branch where the two update-side primitives differ was unasserted.
It is not:

| | |
|---|---|
| `requireUnchanged` **refuses** when the stored value is absent | `ServerOwnedStateContractTest.requireUnchangedRefusesAValueForAnAbsentField` |
| `requireImmutableReference` **permits** it — settable while absent | `ReferenceRenameContractTest.aReferenceIsSettableWhileAbsent` |

**Neither test names the other**, so the contrast holds by two artefacts happening to agree with
nobody maintaining the agreement ([[F2-177]]).

🔑 **What that costs is legibility at the moment it matters.** A reader who merges the two primitives
makes ONE of those tests fail, in a class they are not editing, with a message about an ethics
outcome — which reads as *"that test is now wrong"* rather than *"you have just broken the other
primitive."* The new leg asserts both behaviours **side by side**, deliberately as a third assertion
of already-covered facts, because the thing being protected is that they **differ**.

### And the divergence is sharper than I had described it

`requireUnchanged` has **no absent branch at all** — it refuses any change and merely words the
message differently (*"has no X yet"* versus *"is at Y and cannot be moved to Z"*). The reference
primitive has an explicit early return. That is the whole difference, and the file already carries a
comment warning that a de-duplication must not reword the 400 it emits — prose that is now a build
failure.

### Mutations 4/4

| Mutation | |
|---|---|
| the reference primitive inherits `requireUnchanged`'s refusal | KILLED |
| `requireUnchanged` stops refusing an absent stored value | KILLED |
| a **new** comparing primitive is added and nobody exercises it — the F2-312 defect | KILLED |
| the reflective derivation resolves nothing | KILLED |

⚠ Two harness bugs of mine first: `-Dtest=A+B` is not a selector (surefire wants a **comma**), and my
first M3 did not compile — **a mutation that does not compile is neither a kill nor a hole**, and my
harness reported it as `DID-NOT-RUN` beside real results. That first M3 also tested something the leg
does not claim: the derived leg asks *"is this primitive exercised anywhere in this class"*, not *"in
that particular leg"*.

### Filed

* Nothing. The primitives are now covered by a derived population, and the divergence fails the build
  in both directions.

## F2-311 — the map called IGNORED held two fields that are CONSULTED, and it said so itself

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P4 — an instrument's verdict vocabulary understating what two routes do. No production change. |
| **Registers** | `bcm.bcm_plans`, `compliance.audit_engagements` (the two mislabelled), `policy.documents`, `privacy.data_subject_requests` |
| **Standards** | — |
| **Found by** | Executing [[F2-296]]'s filing, which is written **inside one of the map's own entries** |
| **Verification** | suite **4700 → 4701/0/0**; controls kill a mis-declared verdict in **both** directions |

### The finding was already written down, in the artefact it is about

`FullReplaceUpdateContractTest.DERIVED_IGNORED_FIELDS` carried this, in the entry F2-296 added:

> ⚠ Note this map's own vocabulary has no bucket for it — the field is neither a form input that does
> nothing nor an immutable the server ignores: it is CONSULTED and never written, which is a third
> kind, and calling it 'ignored' understates what the route does.

🔑 **[[F2-224]]'s shape: a verdict vocabulary limited to the verdicts an earlier slice happened to
reach.** Measured, the split is **2 CONSULTED / 2 IGNORED** — `BcmService` compares the status with
`sameState`, `AuditEngagementService` with `requireUnchanged`, while the other two only ever read the
**stored** row and never the request's value.

### `unwritten` is the accurate name, and the verdict says why

Both kinds share one property — neither is written **from the request** — so the map is
`DERIVED_UNWRITTEN_FIELDS` now, and each entry declares:

* **CONSULTED** — the server compares the caller's value and refuses a change while tolerating an
  echo. A caller can observe it: a different value is a 400.
* **IGNORED** — the field arrives and is silently dropped.

### The verdict is derived, not trusted

The distinction is mechanical — a consulted field is compared by one of this platform's refusal
primitives (`requireUnchanged`, `sameState`, `requireImmutableReference`) — so the leg reads the
services and checks the declared token against them ([[F2-299]]'s rule: derive the vocabulary rather
than hold a list). ⚠ **Enforced in both directions**, and the second is the dangerous one: a field
declared CONSULTED whose service does not consult it **tells a reader a guard exists** where the
value is silently dropped. Controls kill a flip either way.

### The leg found a fourth entry on its first real run

Three of the four reasons opened *"BY DESIGN."* and my edit replaced those; the fourth opened *"When
the request arrived."*, so it had no verdict at all. 🔑 **An edit keyed on a prefix reaches only the
entries that share it** — and the leg caught what the edit missed, which is the argument for deriving
the check rather than trusting the pass.

### Two smaller notes

* The same reason text appears in **two** maps (`FROZEN_FIELDS` at line 586 and this one), so the
  patch had to be applied by line rather than by content. They describe the field from two different
  angles, so it is not a duplication defect — but it is why a content-keyed edit matched twice.
* An inline `py -c` mangled an anchor containing a newline, again. The rule stands: use the Write
  tool for any payload carrying escapes.

## F2-310 — the filed question was refuted, and the rule that settles it

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P4 — a **decision**, not a change. Four consecutive slices filed the same follow-up; measuring it showed the premise does not hold, and the reasoning is now recorded with a gate so nobody re-opens it. |
| **Registers** | the nine whose reference [[F2-306]]–[[F2-309]] froze |
| **Standards** | — |
| **Found by** | Executing [[F2-309]]'s filing (*"nothing mints any of the twelve, so all remain caller-named at birth — [[F2-172]](d)'s question"*) |
| **Verification** | suite **4699 → 4700/0/0**; a control adding a mint to one frozen service fires and names it |

### The premise did not hold

Of the nine code fields, **seven have a create FORM FIELD** in the frontend (`EthicsPage`,
`CompliancePage`, `ChangesPage`, `NdiPage`, `ChangeModelCatalogue`), one is declarable only
(`gapCode`) and one is sent by code. 🔑 **So this platform's design is that the ORGANISATION names
its own records, and minting them would be a product change rather than a fix** ([[F2-214]]).

### The rule that separates the two cases

```
quoted to an OUTSIDE party       ->  the server must mint it   (F2-172(d))
the organisation naming its own  ->  the operator names it     (this population)
```

[[F2-172]](d)'s actual subject is a **tracking code quoted to the public** — the intake reference the
whistleblowing and breach-report portals hand a reporter, which `CaseTrackerPage` renders as
`rec.referenceCode`. That one **is** server-minted through `ReferenceCodeMint`, and
`ClientSuppliedReferenceRatchetTest` holds it at zero. **Checked: none of the frozen twelve reaches
an external party.** An operator-chosen control code like `AC-2` or `POL-INFO-001` is a naming
convention its organisation owns, and a mint would overwrite it.

### What makes the decision safe is F2-309, not this finding

A caller-named code was a real hazard **while a duplicate was storable**. With tenant-scoped
uniqueness in place a collision is refused at the index, so *"the operator names it"* costs nothing
that uniqueness does not already cover. 🔑 **The two filings looked like one question and were two:
uniqueness was the defect, and authorship is a product decision.**

### The gate records a decision, and states the boundary in both directions

None of the nine services may call `ReferenceCodeMint` — a control adding one fires and names it —
**and** the intake service must still call it. ⚙ Without that second half the leg would read as
*"never mint anything"*, which is the opposite of the rule.

### Filed

* Nothing further on authorship. If a register's code genuinely becomes externally quoted, mint it
  **and say so in the gate** rather than doing it silently.

## F2-309 — immutable + not unique means a duplicate is PERMANENT

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P3 — the other half of [[F2-306]]–[[F2-308]], and a consequence those slices created. Nine tenant-scoped unique indexes; latent everywhere (0 duplicates today) but unrepairable once it happened. |
| **Registers** | `ethics.cases`, `ethics.disclosures`, `ndi.gap`, `ndi.corrective_action`, `compliance.audit_engagements`, `change_mgmt.change_requests`, `ndi.improvement_plan`, `ndi.report_definition`, `compliance.controls` |
| **Standards** | The references a NAZAHA investigation, an NDMO gap review, an IIA engagement and a CAB record each cite |
| **Found by** | Asking [[F2-267]]'s unique-index question of what F2-306–F2-308 had just built |
| **Verification** | V396 applied **twice** to dev, idempotent; nine indexes unique, enabled, correctly filtered; a duplicate refused live by name; suite **4698 → 4699/0/0** |

### The question gave the opposite answer to the one that established it

[[F2-267]] asked *"is a duplicate storable?"* of ten caller-named references and found **9 of 10**
already carried a unique index — so caller-naming was a naming question rather than a defect. Asked
of the nine registers F2-306–F2-308 made immutable, **8 of 9 have none at all**; only
`compliance.policies` did.

🔑 **And the combination is worse than either half:**

```
immutable + not unique  =  a duplicate is PERMANENT
```

**Before F2-306 a collision could be renamed away. After it, the guard protecting the reference is
exactly what prevents the repair.** So this is the other half of my own three previous slices — the
kind of consequence that only surfaces if you ask a question of the **result** rather than of the
code you were about to change.

### Three deliberate properties of V396

* **Tenant-scoped**, keyed `(organisation_id, code)`. A global unique index would let one tenant's
  reference block another from using the same string — a multi-tenancy defect dressed up as
  strictness (V385's rule).
* **Filtered** on the eight nullable columns. SQL Server treats NULLs as **equal** for uniqueness,
  so a plain index would permit at most **one** code-less row per tenant, refusing a state the
  column's own nullability allows. `compliance.controls.code` is NOT NULL, so its filter is omitted
  **deliberately rather than by oversight**.
* **A pre-flight that names the offending rows.** A bare *"duplicate key"* sends the reader nowhere,
  and this file blocks every later migration until resolved ([[F2-299]]).

Measured in **both** databases before writing ([[F2-183]]): 0 duplicate groups, 0 NULL codes. So no
`WITH NOCHECK` and nothing to reconcile — and F2-183's sequence holds in the right order for once,
because the **writers were closed first**, across three slices.

### The gate asserts the pairing, not a count

Every register whose reference is frozen must have a tenant-scoped unique index declared in the
migration corpus. ⚙ The two views cannot be derived from each other — a Java field name does not give
you a column name — so they are linked by **arithmetic**, and adding a guarded site without an index
makes the counts diverge.

### Two smaller lessons

* **`RAISERROR` arguments must be constants or variables, never function calls**, so `NCHAR(10)`
  cannot be passed as a substitution. Build the message into a variable first.
* `core.autocrlf=true` here stores **LF** in the object database and checks out **CRLF**, so
  LF-in-blob with CRLF-in-worktree is normal rather than drift. That sharpens [[F2-301]]'s note:
  `SchemaContractRatchetTest` was notable precisely because it had *escaped* that normalisation.

### Filed

* The **eleventh and twelfth** frozen references (`ethics.cases`, `ethics.disclosures`) are covered
  here; nothing mints any of the twelve, so all remain **caller-named at birth** — [[F2-172]](d)'s
  question, still a separate slice.
* V396 joins the **52** migrations pending the deployed server's next jar.

## F2-308 — the last five kind-1 renames, and a reset claim of mine that was false

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P3 — five more references renameable after the fact, closed; census **38 → 33**. One of the two "reset" claims I wrote was **false**, and the other is on a **dark** method. |
| **Registers** | `ndi.improvement_plan`, `ndi.report`, the BCM crisis-comms templates, `compliance.controls`, `compliance.policies` |
| **Standards** | NDMO / NDI improvement plans; NCEMA crisis communications; NCA ECC control library; policy governance |
| **Found by** | Executing [[F2-307]]'s filed remainder |
| **Verification** | suite **4698/0/0**; probe **5/5** as `compliance`; census confirms **33**, matching the prediction |

### The mint question again, and it settled all five the same way

Each has exactly **one** write of the code — the caller's — so nothing mints any of them and
`requireImmutableReference` is the fit ([[F2-307]]'s rule).

### The claim I got wrong, and what showed it

Two of the five wrote the code **unconditionally**, and my first note said a body omitting it
therefore **cleared** it. 🔑 **That is false for `ComplianceService`, and only reading the request
type showed it:** `ControlRequest.code` is `@NotBlank` and the route binds `@Valid @RequestBody`, so
an omitted code is refused by bean validation **before the service is entered** — probed, HTTP 400.
**[[F2-182]]'s recorded blind spot: a guard living in a DTO annotation, which no setter-site scan can
see.** The unconditional write was never a reset; it was only a rename vector.

For `PolicyService` the reset really *was* expressible — `update` binds the **entity**, and
`@Column(nullable = false)` is not a bean-validation annotation, so an omitted code would have
reached a NOT NULL column. But it is a **latent-hazard closure and saying which is the point**
([[F2-283]]): `PolicyService#update` has **no controller**. [[F2-187]]'s `DarkServiceMethodTest` holds
that whole legacy write lifecycle as dark, retired in favour of `PolicyManagementService#transition`,
which `RegChangePolicyController` names.

⚙ Both comments are corrected **in place** rather than quietly softened, because a stale claim about
what a guard prevents is the input to somebody's next estimate.

### One more measurement error

I queried `policy.documents` for the `code` column and it does not exist — `Policy` maps
`compliance.policies`. The guessed-identifier error, this time in the **query** rather than the code.

### Filed

* **28 sites remain**, now essentially all kinds 2 and 3 — a pointer to another record (legitimately
  editable) and an authority-issued reference (correctly caller-supplied). The kind-1 sweep is
  **complete** as far as the census can see it.
* **Nothing mints any of the eleven codes closed across [[F2-306]]–F2-308**, so all remain
  **caller-named at birth** — [[F2-172]](d)'s question and a separate slice from the rename.

## F2-307 — measure whether the server mints it before choosing the guard

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P3 — four more governance references renameable after the fact, closed; census **42 → 38**. |
| **Registers** | `ndi.gap` (`gap_code`), `ndi.corrective_action` (`action_code`), `compliance.audit_engagements` (`engagement_code`), `change_mgmt.change_requests` (`change_code`) |
| **Standards** | NDMO / NDI gap remediation; IIA Standard 2010 (the engagement code); ADR-017 §D-3 (the change code a CAB record cites) |
| **Found by** | Executing [[F2-306]]'s filed kind-1 members |
| **Verification** | suite **4697 → 4698/0/0**; the census confirms **38**, matching the prediction; a control removing one guard fires and names the file |

### The measurement that decides the guard

🔑 **Whether the server MINTS a code determines which rule is right, and getting it backwards would
bless the defect.** If something mints it, the create must not accept a caller value at all
([[F2-172]](d)) and immutability would ratify a caller-named reference. Measured per candidate:
**nothing mints any of these four**, so `requireImmutableReference` is the fit — settable at birth,
fixed thereafter.

### Three measurement corrections before any code was touched

* **Three of my candidate paths did not exist** — guessed from the module name. `CrisisCommsService`
  is in `bcm/`, not `bcm/comms/`; `NdiReportService` in `ndi/reports/`, not `ndi/report/`;
  `PolicyService` in `compliance/`, not `policy/`. The recurring guessed-identifier error.
* **`AuditEngagementService` resolves to TWO files** — `audit_eng/` and `compliance/` — the duplicate
  simple name [[F2-278]] and [[F2-286]] both lost a hypothesis to. Only the `compliance` one holds
  the site, and only that one's `apply` is shared with its create. 🔑 **A census keyed on a simple
  name cannot tell you which twin it measured.**
* **`setActionCode` is in `NdiGapService#updateCapa`**, not `AuditLifecycleService` — so that one
  file holds **two** of the four, which is why the structural leg counts its guards rather than
  merely checking the file mentions the primitive.

### The wiring is asserted structurally, and that is proportionate rather than lazy

The primitive's behaviour is unit-tested. What no cheap behaviour test can see is whether each
**site** still routes through it: the four sites live in three services with three different mock
sets. Every one of them began as a one-line `if (src.getX() != null) target.setX(src.getX())`, so
restoring that shape is a single-line change no behaviour test in the owning service would notice.
⚠ Asserted per **(file, field)** rather than by counting call sites, because a count cannot see one
site being replaced while another is added, and three of these files hold other reference setters
that are kinds 2 and 3 ([[F2-306]]'s per-field lesson). A control removing one guard fires and names
the file.

### Filed

* **34 sites remain** on the census, now dominated by kinds 2 and 3 — a pointer to another record
  (legitimately editable) and an authority-issued reference (correctly caller-supplied). The
  remaining kind-1 candidates are `setPlanCode`, `setReportCode` and two `setCode` sites, each
  needing the mint question asked of it first.
* **Nothing mints any of the six codes closed so far**, so all remain **caller-named at birth** —
  [[F2-172]](d)'s question, and a separate slice from the rename.

## F2-306 — a reference the caller can RENAME, and a census scoped to creates could not see it

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P3 — two governance references renameable after the fact, and a **42-site population nobody had measured** because the existing census is scoped to create paths. |
| **Registers** | `ethics.cases` (`case_code`), `ethics.disclosures` (`disclosure_code`) |
| **Standards** | NAZAHA / Saudi Whistleblower Protection Law (the case code an investigation cites); SAMA conflict-of-interest disclosure |
| **Found by** | [[F2-302]]'s filing that `gapCode` is caller-writable on create **and** update, generalised |
| **Verification** | suite **4690 → 4697/0/0**; the Java gate and the throwaway measurement agree at 42 |

### The population was outside the instrument by construction

`ClientSuppliedReferenceRatchetTest`'s business-reference leg is scoped to `CREATE_ISH`, a verb list
where **`update` is deliberately absent** because that leg's claim is *"a reference is chosen when a
record is born"*. 🔑 **So the rename question was never in its population — and renaming is arguably
the sharper harm: the record already exists, an auditor may already cite the code, and the citation
breaks silently.**

### Measured: 42 update-path sites across 34 services, in three kinds

Only **one** kind is a defect, which is why the census ships with no per-site verdicts ([[F2-188]]):

1. **The record's own identifier** — `setEngagementCode`, `setChangeCode`, `setCaseCode`,
   `setDisclosureCode`, `setGapCode`, `setPlanCode`, `setReportCode`. Renaming one breaks every
   citation of it.
2. **A pointer to another record** — `setEvidenceRef` (nine sites), `setClauseRef`, `setSourceRef`,
   `setContractRef`. Correcting which clause a finding maps to is **legitimate**, and refusing it
   would fail on working usage ([[F2-214]]). Whether the pointer *resolves* is a different question
   ([[F2-242]], [[F2-252]]).
3. **An outside authority's reference** — `setSamaLicenceRef`, `setSamaNonObjectionRef`,
   `setBoardResolutionReference`, `setFilingArtifactReference`. Caller-supplied is **correct**: a
   reference only an authority can issue is received and recorded, or absent ([[F2-209]],
   [[F2-269]]), and the server may not mint it either.

### The two closed, and why they were closeable together

Both are in `ethics` and both are reached through an `apply(target, src)` helper **shared by create
and update**, with **nothing minting either code** — so a caller named it at birth and could rename
it afterwards. [[F2-292]] had already filed the disclosure one.

### The primitive gained an expression rather than the callers routing around it

`requireUnchanged` is the right mechanism and the wrong sentence. Its wording is lifecycle-flavoured
— *"is at X and cannot be moved to Y by an update. That move goes through ⟨route⟩"* — and is
deliberately frozen, because its own comment records that two tests assert it and a caller's
integration may match on it. For a reference every clause is wrong: a code is not *"moved to"*
another code, and there is **no route**, because the reference is fixed once assigned. 🔑 **Naming a
route that does not exist is [[F2-302]]'s defect, in this same primitive** — so
`requireImmutableReference` was added rather than hand-rolled at two call sites ([[F2-190]]).

Settable while absent, immutable once set: that shape covers the create and the update in one place
with no flag threaded through the shared helper, and is **stronger** than an update-only guard
because it also stops a second write on any other path. An echo is accepted case-insensitively,
because the ethics edit form round-trips the whole record and refusing that would break the screen
that works today ([[F2-296]], [[F2-231]]).

### DisclosureService had no test class at all

A path with no test is not a path somebody decided was safe ([[F2-248]]).
`ReferenceRenameContractTest` covers the rule in both directions, including that the refusal must
**not** name a route.

### One measurement error of mine

Subtracting guarded sites **per method** reported **39** where the answer is **42**. Both `apply`
helpers also write `setClauseRef` and `setRegulatorReference` — kinds 2 and 3, which must stay
counted — so the subtraction has to be **per field**. 🔑 **An over-subtraction reads exactly like
progress.**

### Filed

* The **40 remaining sites**, with the three-kind framework but no per-site verdicts. `setGapCode`
  ([[F2-302]]'s filing) and `setEngagementCode` are the readiest kind-1 members — the latter matters
  more than it looks, because [[F2-203]] measured **five disjoint engagement code spaces** already.
* Nothing mints `case_code` or `disclosure_code` at all, so both are still **caller-named at
  birth** — [[F2-172]](d)'s question, and a separate slice from the rename.

## F2-305 — three lifecycle diagrams documented the happy path while the machines allowed more

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P4 — a documentation defect in the artefact a developer reads before writing a client, and it is [[F2-303]]'s defect one layer out: there the refusal could not name the legal moves, here the prose did not. No production behaviour changes. |
| **Registers** | `bcm.bia_assessments`, `bcm.bcp_plans`, `bcm.crisis_events` (the diagrams; the machines were already correct) |
| **Standards** | — |
| **Found by** | Executing [[F2-303]]'s own filing that the javadoc edge lists had become a second copy beside each declared map |
| **Verification** | suite **4689 → 4690/0/0**; controls **3 killed / 1 withdrawn as invalid** |

### Measured against the maps F2-303/F2-304 declared

| file | edges documented |
|---|---|
| `BcmBiaAssessmentService` | **6 of 11** |
| `CrisisEventService` | **7 of 11** |
| `BcpPlanService` | **8 of 9** |

An ASCII-art diagram is a summary, and an incomplete one gives a reader consulting it to learn what
is legal a **narrower** answer than the machine. 🔑 **The four `CrisisEventService` omissions are the
ones a reader most needs**: `DETECTED → ACTIVATED` (a crisis obvious on sight, skipping assessment),
`ASSESSING → CANCELLED`, `ACTIVATED → RECOVERED`, and `CONTAINED → ACTIVATED` — the machine's only
backwards edge, a **re-escalation** of a crisis that worsened after containment.

Rewritten as complete `FROM -> A | B` tables, the form `CrisisCommsTemplateService` already used,
which is also the one form a gate can parse — so the prose is the specification rather than a second
copy nobody maintains ([[F2-177]], [[F2-191]]'s precedent).

### The obvious gate was built and rejected, and that is the reusable judgement

Parsing every `A → B` in every comment reported **6 disagreements across 8 machines** and almost all
were the detector's fault. This codebase documents lifecycles as ASCII-art happy paths
(`DRAFT → UNDER_REVIEW ─┬─> APPROVED`), as narrative chains inside
`@Operation(summary = "Move a case through INTAKE → TRIAGE → …")`, as single-edge remarks in code
comments, and in one case as an **HTTP transcript**. 🔑 **An arrow in prose is not a claim about a
complete outgoing set, and a gate that treats it as one fails on correct code** ([[F2-214]]).

So the population is the four files whose `<pre>` block is a real table, and a block qualifies only
if it is **all** edge lines — an ASCII diagram yields one or two accidental matches and must not
count as one. ⚙ The other four machines have no such table and are **deliberately not gated**:
inventing one so the leg could cover them would be documentation written to satisfy a test.

### The floor cannot be made load-bearing here, and saying so is the point

The controls killed the three mutations that matter — a table dropping an edge, a map gaining an
undocumented one, and a table reverted to ASCII art. The fourth, weakening the anti-vacuity floor,
**survived and is withdrawn as invalid**: you can always weaken an assertion ([[F2-206]]), and on a
clean corpus a lower floor changes nothing. 🔑 **The per-file *"no table could be parsed"* problem
already catches an empty parse, so the floor only covers a *coordinated* narrowing of both parsers —
defence in depth rather than the thing doing the work.** Recording that is better than presenting
three kills as four.

### Two corrections of mine

`TreeSet` was unimported (the compiler caught it), and the parser first accepted only ASCII `->`
while `CrisisCommsTemplateService`'s table uses the unicode arrow. Forcing one spelling across the
codebase would be churn rather than a contract, so the parser accepts both.

## F2-304 — the six filed refusals split four ways, and one was never a transition refusal at all

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-24 |
| **Severity** | P3 — the tail of [[F2-303]]: five refusals converted from a 400 that named nothing to a 409 that names the available moves, and one **reclassified** as a required-field refusal where 400 is correct. |
| **Registers** | `ethics.aml_alerts`, `ethics.disclosures`, `ethics.cases`, `platform.issues`, `workflow.instances` |
| **Standards** | — (the platform's own refusal contract) |
| **Found by** | Executing [[F2-303]]'s census of six unread sites |
| **Verification** | suite **4688 → 4689/0/0**; probe **6/6**, showing `409` with `allowed: []` on both converted registers |

### Reading them was the whole value, because they split four ways

A count could not have ranked these, which is exactly why the census shipped with the honest reason
*"not yet read"* rather than six manufactured ones ([[F2-188]]).

* **Three had `allowed` already in a local and threw it away** — `AmlAlertService`,
  `DisclosureService`, `EthicsCaseService`. One-line fixes, and the same shape as
  `ChangeManagementService.guard`: the set the refusal needed was on the line above. ⚙
  `EthicsCaseService` gets it from a declared `EthicsCaseLifecycle` **class**, which is why my
  "declared machine" detector reported False for it — a detector artefact, not a fact about the code.
* **One was an inline switch with no declared map** (`IssueService`), and its refusal explains the
  under-count that made F2-303 file this at all: 🔑 **the message sat on a CONTINUATION LINE**, so a
  pattern anchored on `IllegalArgumentException("Illegal` could never match it. **Wording was only
  half the reason a single-line grep found five of eleven; a line break is the other half.**
* **One was a different shape, in the platform's workflow engine** — adopted by 14 modules.
  `executeTransition` refuses an action code with no row for the instance's current state: a conflict
  rather than malformed input, and the available action codes were **already queryable** via
  `findByDefinitionIdAndFromStateIdOrderBySortOrder`. It names them now. ⚠ The repurposing is stated
  rather than quiet: this machine is **data-driven**, so its next states are reached *by action
  code*, and `to`/`allowed` carry actions where `IllegalTransitionException`'s javadoc describes
  states. Both lookups sit inside `orElseThrow`, so they run only on the refusal path.
* **One is not a transition refusal at all.** *"supersededById is required when transitioning to
  SUPERSEDED"* is a **required-field** refusal, and 400 is the right answer for a missing field. The
  gate's pattern over-matches it — 🔑 **a fact about the pattern rather than about the code.**

### Why that one is a named exemption rather than a narrowed pattern

Narrowing on the word *"required"* would silently exempt every future message containing it. So the
exemption is named, and a new leg keeps it honest **in both directions**: the message must still
match the pattern (a rewording or deletion forces the entry out — [[F2-199]]'s rule that an exemption
for something not in the population reads exactly like one for something that is), and the file's
*real* lifecycle refusal must still be the typed 409. The point of the exemption is that this file
has **both kinds**, and only one of them is a 400.

### Six test assertions pinned the old contract, and one was pinned by its NAME

`executeTransition_unknown_action_throws_IllegalArgument` — 🔑 **the strongest form of a test locking
in the thing being changed, because a reader trusts the name before the body.** All six now assert
the new **capability** rather than the new type: that the refusal names the moves available,
including `allowed: []` from a terminal state and `TRIAGE` where the way through is not empty.

### Two probe corrections, and one is a permission fact worth recording

The ethics body key is **`target`**, resolved from `EthicsCaseController` rather than guessed. And
`compliance` is **403** on `/api/v1/issues` — `PLATFORM:WRITE` is held by one role with **zero active
users**, which [[F2-238]] already recorded, so that register is reachable in dev only by `admin`.
That leg therefore runs as `admin` **with the reason stated**, because it tests data semantics and
not authorization, and `admin` proves nothing about the latter. A separate leg asserts the 403 so the
lockout is measured rather than worked around silently.

### Filed

* **`platform.issues` is administrator-only in dev** — `PLATFORM:WRITE` has one holder role with no
  active users. F2-238 filed it; this slice re-confirmed it live and it is unchanged.
* One error of mine: I guessed `WorkflowState::getStateCode` and the field is `code`. The compiler
  caught it — resolve an accessor from the entity, never from the shape of the name.

## F2-303 — a refusal that cannot name what it would accept, and a grep that found five of eleven

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-23 |
| **Severity** | P3 — **a diagnostic and status-code defect on six lifecycle registers, and a measurement error that halved the population.** A refused transition answered **HTTP 400** (malformed input) for a request that was well formed and merely arrived from the wrong state, and its message could name only the move that was *rejected*, never the moves that would have been accepted. |
| **Registers** | `bcm.bia_assessments`, `bcm.bcp_plans`, `bcm.crisis_events`, `platform.authority_documents`, `tprm.questionnaire_templates`, `change_mgmt.change_requests`, `bcm.crisis_comms_templates` |
| **Standards** | — (the platform's own refusal contract; `IllegalTransitionException` → 409 + structured ProblemDetail) |
| **Found by** | [[F2-297]]'s designated filing (*"the four machines declare themselves as an inline switch … must not be smuggled into a slice about something else"*), re-derived first ([[F2-221]]) |
| **Verification** | suite **4684 → 4688/0/0**; probe **5/5** as `compliance`, confirming 409 + a structured `allowed` array on the wire and the vocabulary refusal still 400 |

### The two halves had one cause

**139 sites** throw `IllegalTransitionException`, which carries `from`, `to` and `allowed` and which
`GlobalExceptionHandler` maps to **409** with a structured ProblemDetail. Five threw a bare
`IllegalArgumentException("Illegal transition: FROM → TO")`.

Each of the five declared its edges as an inline `switch` of `Set.of(...).contains(...)`, so
🔑 **the legal-target list was not derivable at runtime — the refusal could not name it because
nothing could be asked.** And `CrisisCommsTemplateService`, the one member whose refusal *did* name
its targets, paid for that with a **second copy of the whole machine** in an `allowedFrom` helper:
three copies counting its javadoc, agreeing, with nobody maintaining that ([[F2-177]]). The two
switches were written in different **forms** — `"IN_REVIEW".equals(to)` against
`Set.of("IN_REVIEW")` — which is what makes a drift between them invisible in a diff.

Six machines now declare their edges once as `Map<String, Set<String>>`, with terminal states present
as an **empty set** so the terminal set is derivable rather than typed a second time ([[F2-196]]).

### The sixth was the sharpest and a grep could not see it

`ChangeManagementService.guard` **already** computed `allowed` from a declared map on the line above
and then **discarded it**, throwing a bare 400 — the set it needed was one step away. Its message
says *"Cannot transition from"*, so a grep keyed on `IllegalArgumentException("Illegal` missed it
entirely.

### And the real population is eleven, not five

Scoped to the **shape** — any transition-mentioning message — rather than to a spelling, the gate
finds **11**. 🔑 **A detector keyed on the wording you have already seen returns a smaller
population, and a smaller population reads exactly like a cleaner tree.** One of them is a **second**
refusal inside `AuthorityDocumentService`, a file this slice had already converted.

Six remain **unread** and ship as an exactly-asserted census with the honest reason *"not yet read"*
rather than six manufactured ones ([[F2-188]] measured what happens otherwise: five claims written
fluently, all five false). A new bare refusal fails the gate, and a converted one must be deleted
from the set in the same commit.

### The vocabulary check in front of each guard deliberately stays a 400

An unknown token **is** bad input; a known token from the wrong state is a conflict with the record's
state. Conflating them is exactly what the bare refusal did, and it is the same family as
[[F2-230]]'s 547 naming no field and [[F2-210]]'s diagnostic that sends the reader nowhere. Probed
both ways: `{"to": "PUBLISHED"}` from DRAFT is **409** with
`allowed: ['CANCELLED', 'UNDER_REVIEW']`, and `{"to": "TOTALLY_MADE_UP"}` is still **400**.

### Six test assertions pinned the old contract

Each asserted `isInstanceOf(IllegalArgumentException.class)` on a refused transition — the 400 being
replaced. A test written against a contract you are about to change is not evidence, it is the old
contract ([[F2-300]]). Each was rewritten to assert the new **capability** rather than merely the new
type: that the refusal names the moves the machine would accept, including `allowed: []` from a
terminal state.

### Three errors of mine, all caught by running something

* **A field inserted between `@Transactional` and its method produced six "cannot find symbol:
  variable `log`" errors in an untouched file.** One Lombok-processed file failing aborts annotation
  processing build-wide, so every `@Slf4j` logger vanishes. 🔑 **One root cause, six errors pointing
  at files you never touched** — anchor on the whole declaration including its annotations, never on
  the signature line.
* **The duplicate-detection leg first banned any `case "STATE" ->` arm** and fired on
  `case "DETECTED" -> "بحاجة للتقييم"`, an Arabic **label** map, which legitimately switches on the
  same states. A gate that fails on correct code trains the next reader to edit the assertion
  ([[F2-214]]), so it is scoped to arms that **yield a machine**.
* **A blanket prefix-replace on the gate's path keys hit both of its maps**, so a declared machine
  resolved to `.../com/tss/grc/com/tss/grc/module/...`. It failed loudly on `Files.exists`, the safe
  direction; both maps and the scan now share one key space so a mismatch cannot make a leg vacuous.

### And two probe errors, one of which passed for the wrong reason

The body key is **`to`**, not `status` — resolved from `BcpPlanController`'s `TransitionBody` record
rather than guessed. With the wrong key `toStatus` arrived null, so three legs failed for a reason
unrelated to their claim — and 🔑 **the leg asserting "an unknown token is still 400" PASSED, because
the vocabulary check produced the same 400 from a different cause.** A leg can pass for the wrong
reason whenever an earlier error yields the status it expects.

### Filed

* **The six unread bare refusals**: `AmlAlertService`, `DisclosureService`, `EthicsCaseService`,
  `AuthorityDocumentService` (a second site), `IssueService`, `WorkflowEngineService`. Each needs its
  own machine read — whether it has a declared map to name, and whether the refusal is even a
  lifecycle refusal. The destination is zero; nothing correct stands in the way, only reading.
* **The javadoc `<pre>` edge lists** are now a second copy beside each declared map. [[F2-191]]'s
  precedent is to **parse the javadoc and compare it edge-for-edge**, so the prose becomes the
  specification rather than a stale copy — worth doing, and not smuggled into this slice.

## F2-302 — a @PrePersist default is not a guard, and the status and the close date had two writers

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-23 |
| **Severity** | P3 — **one live screen-reachable inconsistency, one API-reachable state jump, and a big refutation of my own hypothesis.** The NDI Gap Register's status column is an inline `<select>` sending `{status}` alone, so one click produced **RESOLVED with no close date** — a state the CAPA rollup can never reach — rendered beside the progress bar showing `0% · 0/1`. And the create could name RESOLVED outright. Harm is confined to the stored record: `actual_close_date` is read by **nothing**. |
| **Registers** | `ndi.gap` — **18 rows, OPEN ×9 / IN_PROGRESS ×9, 0 RESOLVED, 0 CLOSED, 0 non-canonical casings**, identical in dev and prod; **1 row (gap 1) is IN_PROGRESS carrying a 2026-05-17 close date**, seed-origin |
| **Standards** | NDMO / NDI data-governance gap remediation (the CAPA rollup the status is derived from) |
| **Found by** | [[F2-296]]'s last unread census member, which [[F2-297]] kept by lowering that ceiling 7 → 1, re-derived first ([[F2-221]]) |
| **Verification** | suite **4674 → 4684/0/0**; probe **4/6 pre-fix, 8/8 post-fix** as `compliance`; harness **6 killed / 0 survived** after closing a hole in my own test |

### The big refutation is mine, and it is the most useful thing here

I read `createGap`, found it never sets `status`, found **no field initialiser** on `NdiGap#status`,
saw `@Column(nullable = false)`, and concluded the register's create path had never worked — F2-210's
ROPA-wizard shape, where *"all 11 rows in dev and prod are seeded"*. The live probe returned
**HTTP 200**.

`NdiGap` has a `@PrePersist` that defaults eight fields including `status = "OPEN"`.
🔑🔑 **[[F2-215]] records that a column can be filled four ways — an annotation, a lifecycle
callback, a field initialiser, or `insertable = false` — and I checked one and concluded "no
writer".** A `@PrePersist` is invisible to both a scan of the service and a check for an initialiser,
and it is *stronger* evidence of server ownership than an initialiser, because it fires at flush time
after every setter.

### What survived: a default is not a guard, at a lifecycle callback

That callback **defaults** and does not **refuse**, so `POST /api/ndi/gaps` with `status: "RESOLVED"`
returned 200 and stored it — the state the CAPA rollup derives, on a row the same callback had just
given `capaCount = 0`. [[F2-218]]'s headline (*"`if (x == null) x = INITIAL` is a default, not a
guard"*) at a `@PrePersist` rather than in a service, which is the reason it reads as covered.

### And the pair had two writers

`recomputeRollup` has always owned `(RESOLVED, actual_close_date)` — when every corrective action is
complete it sets the status **and** stamps the date in one breath, and it refuses to move a gap that
is already CLOSED or ACCEPTED_RISK. `updateGap` wrote the two fields independently. One private
writer owns the pair now, shared by the update path and the rollup: entering RESOLVED stamps a date
if none is set, and returning to a not-closed state clears it, because a gap that is open was not
closed.

⚠ **CLOSED and ACCEPTED_RISK are left alone in both directions, and that boundary is a test.** The
rollup refuses to move either and nothing in this platform declares whether they carry a close date,
so a rule for them would be **invented** rather than enforced ([[F2-183]]). If a later slice decides
closure must be dated, that test is the thing to change deliberately.

### The shared refusal was asserting something false

`ServerOwnedState.requireInitial`'s message hard-codes *"which checks the state machine and records
who made the change"*. This register has **no state machine** (no transition route, no declared
edges — [[F2-297]] established that) and its PUT records **no actor**, so the 400 sent an operator to
a mechanism that does not exist — [[F2-210]]'s defect inverted. 🔑 **[[F2-296]]'s finding one phrase
over**: that slice widened this same primitive to take a `field`, because three callers were emitting
a 400 naming a field their request never carried. A six-argument overload takes the clause and the
five-argument form passes the old sentence verbatim, so **none of the 28 existing call sites
changes**. A primitive that cannot express what a caller needs is one callers route around
([[F2-190]]), and the divergence is then invisible.

### F2-179's defect inside this slice's own fix

Asking why the census member's comparison was *still* there found it. `NdiGap.RESOLVED.equals(next)`
and `NOT_CLOSED.contains(next)` both compare **exactly**, and `ck_ndi_gap_status` accepts
`'resolved'` and stores it verbatim — so a lower-case status would have matched **neither** branch,
skipping the stamp and the clear alike. 🔑 **That is worse than the split it replaced, because it
looks like the rule ran.** Closed with `ClosedVocabulary` naming the constraint, so
`ClosedVocabularyPinTest` mirrors the five tokens against the migration by reflection; `require` not
`coerce` by [[F2-182]]'s mechanical test. The audit branch now compares the **saved canonical** value
against the previous one — without that, a case-variant echo reads as a CHANGE and publishes a
TRANSITION row for a move that never happened, which is exactly what [[F2-297]] found on
`CmaDisclosureService` and `TcfdItemService`.

### Two probe-design errors of mine, both caught by running it

* The leg asserting a reopened gap keeps its stale date **could not test its claim**, because the
  *previous* leg's defect left the date null, so the precondition never existed. 🔑 **A leg whose
  precondition the defect it follows prevents is untested, not refuted** — the pre-fix behaviour is
  established by reading (nothing else touched the date) and by that one seeded row, and is stated
  that way rather than claimed as probed.
* An anchor to move the close-date write matched **0**, because the write is already immediately
  before the status. The accumulator had written nothing, which is why a patch script must build then
  write rather than write per edit.

### The harness found a hole in my own boundary test

Widening `NOT_CLOSED` to include `CLOSED` — which would wipe a date the rollup had stamped —
**SURVIVED the whole build**. The assertion meant to forbid it starts from a gap whose
`actual_close_date` is already null, so *"CLOSED does not clear it"* holds whatever the code does.
🔑 **[[F2-293]]'s shape inside the boundary test written to pin the boundary: a test that picks the
case where the principle holds trivially.** 6/6 killed once the fixture carried a date.

### Filed

* **`gapCode` is caller-writable on create and update** — probed, a PUT renamed it to
  `NDI-GAP-RENAMED` and stored it, so a caller can name *and rename* the reference an NDMO reviewer
  cites. [[F2-172]](d)'s family, and outside `ClientSuppliedReferenceRatchetTest`'s setter key.
* **Whether CLOSED should carry a close date** — an owner decision, not a side effect of this fix.
* **Gap 1 is IN_PROGRESS with a 2026-05-17 close date** in both databases. Seed-origin, and any PUT
  on it now clears the date — repairing the row directly rewrites live data, so it is reported.
* **The status `<select>` lets an operator jump straight to CLOSED or ACCEPTED_RISK**, after which
  the rollup will never move the gap again. Plausibly by design (an operator decision), and
  deliberately not refused.

## F2-301 — a missing table errors; a confusably named one succeeds with the wrong rows

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | ✅ CLOSED 2026-08-23 |
| **Severity** | P3 — a **latent-hazard closure with a measured cost already paid.** No production code changes and no data defect: this slice adds the instrument that would have stopped [[F2-300]] drawing four wrong conclusions from `bcm.bcm_exercises`. Five tables have a name that shadows a table the platform maps, and **every one returns a different count from its twin**, so a lookup by name yields a plausible number rather than an error. |
| **Registers** | The five shadows and their live twins, dev rows, identical in production: `bcm.bcm_exercises` **14** → `bcm.exercises` **13** · `compliance.compliance_assessments` **10** → `compliance.assessments` **4** · `compliance.compliance_findings` **18** → `compliance.findings` **41** · `workflow.workflow_definitions` **20** → `workflow.definitions` **6** · `workflow.workflow_instances` **14** → `workflow.instances` **12** |
| **Standards** | — (an instrument over the schema contract) |
| **Found by** | [[F2-300]]'s own measurement error, generalised: it filed the orphan as an open question, and the orphan's *disposition* was already recorded. Asking what was genuinely unmeasured gave the **hazard** rather than the status. |
| **Verification** | suite **4672 → 4674/0/0**; mutation harness **6 killed / 0 survived / 0 anchor-miss**, two of them after correcting holes the first run found |

### The disposition was recorded; the hazard was not

`TABLE_DISPOSITION.md` has carried `bcm.bcm_exercises` since [[F2-141]] — *"no JPA mapping and no
Java reference; the only writer is a seed script"* — and `SchemaContractRatchetTest`'s
`BASELINE_NO_CODE_TABLES = 36` counts it. So F2-300's filing of it as *"dead schema to drop or a
register somebody meant to keep"* was **redundant**, and that is corrected in this slice's docs
rather than left to be re-derived.

🔑 **What no artefact recorded is that the name is confusable.** A table that does not exist makes a
query fail; a table with a name one segment away from the live one makes it **succeed with the wrong
rows**. `compliance.compliance_findings` is the one to fear next: **18 rows against the live
`compliance.findings`' 41**, so measuring the shadow under-reports an audit-findings register by more
than half — wrong in the flattering direction, which is the half less likely to be questioned
([[F2-210]]).

### The shape alone is not the defect, which is why this is a named set and not a rule

**54 mapped tables use the `<schema>_<thing>` shape with no bare twin at all** — `bcm.bcm_plans`,
`cyber.cyber_controls`, `evidence.evidence_items` — so it is house style. What makes a pair dangerous
is the shape *plus* exactly one side being unmapped. Of the six such pairs in the register:

* **five** are these, prefixed side unmapped;
* **none** runs the other way round with the prefixed side live;
* **one has BOTH sides mapped** — `cyber.cyber_incidents` (26 rows, `module/cyber`) beside
  `cyber.incidents` (48 rows, `module/incident`) — two entities in two modules over one concept.
  That is [[F2-196]]'s shape and it is **filed, not fixed**: choosing which register is authoritative
  changes what the platform reports about security incidents.

Asserted **exactly** rather than as a ceiling, because a ceiling would let a new shadow in behind a
dropped one and make a tolerated pair indistinguishable from a reviewed one (house rule 3).

### Three instrument errors of mine, each caught by running something

**(a) A source grep for `@Table` reported SEVEN pairs**, because it cannot see a `@JoinTable`:
`iam.role_permissions` and `iam.user_roles` are mapped by `Role` and `User` and are not shadows at
all. That is precisely the over-reporting `mappedTables()`'s own javadoc warns about, so the gate
takes its population from **reflection**.

**(b) Reading "unmapped" off the register as `jpa_files` being non-empty made all 471 rows read as
mapped and the population ZERO** — `jpa_files` is a **count**, so `"0"` is a non-empty string.
🔑 **A population of zero reads exactly like a clean tree**, and the only reason it was caught is
that a control count printed beside it stayed non-zero.

**(c) Line endings are a PER-FILE fact in this tree, not a repo-wide one.**
`SchemaContractRatchetTest` is pure LF (1,259 bare LF, 0 CRLF) while both files [[F2-299]] and
[[F2-300]] created are pure CRLF, so a patch script must **detect** rather than assume — an anchor
written with the wrong separator matches nothing, and matching nothing reads exactly like the edit
being unnecessary. Eighth instance of the line-ending trap in this lineage, and the first where the
lesson is that the *tree* is mixed. ⚠ The attempt to teach the script that was an inline `py -c`,
which mangled its own escape sequences, missed every replacement and **still printed `patched`** —
the recorded heredoc landmine's dangerous mode, in which a script certifies a write it did not make.

### The harness refuted a claim I had written into the gate

**M3 and M6 both SURVIVED the first run, and both were my error rather than a gate hole**
([[F2-206]]: a surviving mutant is a hole only if the mutated code is actually wrong).

* **M3** widened `shadowOf` to strip the **first** segment rather than the schema name. The javadoc
  claimed a looser rule *"reported all 34"* legitimate parent/child pairs. It does not — those 34
  are mapped on **both** sides, and this gate's left side is always unmapped, so measured over
  today's register a generic prefix/suffix rule and the narrow one return **the same five pairs**.
  🔑 **My own earlier measurement had already printed that (LOOSE 5, TIGHT 5) and I wrote the
  stronger claim anyway.** The narrowing is **prospective**; the javadoc says so now, and the only
  thing carrying it is the synthetic corpus — to which a case was added that a leading-segment
  widening actually fails, because `ml_model_audit` minus its first segment is `model_audit`, which
  nothing maps, so the existing case kills a *trailing* widening and lets a *leading* one through.
* **M6** dropped the no-bare-twin condition from the anti-vacuity floor, moving the count 54 → 55
  against a floor of 40. 🔑 **[[F2-215]]'s rule from the other side: a floor is only worth having if
  it sits above the largest WRONG answer, and here the wrong answer is HIGHER than the right one, so
  no floor can separate them.** An upper bound was the obvious fix and would fail the day a
  legitimate prefixed table is added; the **condition** is asserted instead —
  `cyber.cyber_incidents` has a mapped bare twin, so it must never appear in the house-style set.

### Filed

* **`cyber.cyber_incidents` (26 rows) beside `cyber.incidents` (48 rows)** — both mapped, both live,
  **same schema**, two entities in two modules for one concept, plus `cyber_lc.cyber_incidents` (10
  rows, no server surface) which [[F2-204]] already filed. Three incident registers.
  [[F2-196]]'s shape, and an **owner decision**: picking a winner changes what the platform reports
  about security incidents, and [[F2-212]] and [[F2-281]] have both already done work on
  `cyber.incidents` specifically.
* **The five shadows themselves** remain — dropping a table in a customer database is not a side
  effect of an instrument slice (house rule 6), and they are already counted in
  `BASELINE_NO_CODE_TABLES`. What is new is that the *name* is now held, so a sixth cannot ship
  quietly.
